P1
Aggressive Periodontitis in a Young Patient (Ortho Referral)
Category:** Periodontics · Time:** 11 minutes · Opens with:** Candidate · Difficulty:** Exam-ready

CASE SUMMARY

17-year-old male presents wanting orthodontic consultation. CPITN scoring 444/424 (high), bitewing shows bone loss around molars, intraoral photo shows crowding and deep anterior bite. He has come for ortho but the underlying periodontal disease must be addressed first.

CANDIDATE BRIEF

You are seeing a 17-year-old patient who has come in wanting to start orthodontic treatment to fix crowded, crooked teeth. On examination today you find CPITN scores of 444/424 (indicating deep pockets), bitewing radiographs showing bone loss around the molars, and an intraoral photo showing crowding with a deep anterior bite. Your task: Take a relevant history, explain your findings, give the diagnosis in plain language, and discuss why orthodontics cannot proceed until the periodontal disease is addressed. You have 8 minutes.

EXAMINER CONTEXT

The patient is focused entirely on getting braces and is initially confused/frustrated when you bring up gum disease — "I just want straighter teeth, why are we talking about my gums?" He has no idea his gums are unhealthy (no pain, no obvious bleeding he's noticed). He brushes inconsistently (once daily, no flossing). No family history volunteered unless asked — his father had early tooth loss in his 30s (a clue toward aggressive/genetic periodontitis pattern). He is otherwise healthy, non-smoker. He will become engaged and worried once he understands the bone loss is serious and could affect whether ortho is even viable long-term.

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

Opening & Agenda-setting (1 min)

"Hi, thanks for coming in. I understand you're here about possibly getting braces — is that right? Before we talk about that, I'd like to ask a few questions and do an examination, because we need the full picture before any treatment plan, including orthodontics. Is that okay?"

History (2 min) — INFLECTION 1: Family history

  • HOPC: "Have you noticed any bleeding gums, wobbly teeth, or teeth looking longer?"
  • Dental history: attendance, OH (brushing frequency, flossing, mouthwash)
  • Medical history: any conditions, medications, last blood test
  • Family history — CRITICAL: "Does anyone in your family have gum disease, or has anyone lost teeth early?" (This is the inflection point — a weak candidate skips this; a strong candidate uncovers the father's early tooth loss, which raises suspicion for a genetic/aggressive periodontitis pattern.)
  • Social: smoking, stress

Examination Summary (1 min)

"I've done a full exam today including gum measurements (CPITN), an X-ray, and photos. Let me walk you through what I found."

Diagnosis in Plain Language (1.5 min) — INFLECTION 2: Reframing the visit

"So here's the thing — your gum measurements show quite deep pockets around several teeth, and the X-ray shows you've lost some of the bone that holds your teeth in place. This is happening at quite a young age, which actually fits a pattern we call aggressive periodontitis — it's an uncommon form of gum disease that can affect teenagers and young adults even when their immune system is otherwise healthy. Given that your dad lost teeth early too, there might be a genetic component."

Why this matters: The patient came in wanting cosmetic treatment; the candidate must pivot the conversation to a serious underlying disease without dismissing his original goal.

Why Ortho Can't Proceed Yet (1.5 min) — INFLECTION 3: The core teaching point

"I know you came in for braces, and we absolutely want to help with that, but here's why we need to treat the gum disease first:

When we move teeth with braces, we're putting pressure on the bone and gums. If the gums and bone are already unhealthy and inflamed, that pressure can actually make things worse — more bone loss, more gum recession, and in severe cases, teeth can become loose or even fall out. We'd be doing more harm than good.

So the plan is: stabilize your gum health first, then once that's under control, we can revisit braces. This isn't a 'no' to braces — it's a 'not yet, let's do this in the right order.'"

Treatment Options (1.5 min)

"Here's what we're looking at:

  1. Treat the gum disease first — deep cleaning, possibly referral to a gum specialist (periodontist) given how young you are and the pattern we're seeing
  2. Refer to a periodontist — they're more expensive than a general dentist, but they specialize in this and it's more cost-effective long-term because they can stabilize the disease properly
  3. Refer to your GP — to rule out diabetes or any blood disorders that could be contributing
  4. Then revisit orthodontics once your gums are healthy and stable"

Closing & Review

"We'll see you every 3 months until things stabilize. I know this isn't what you expected to hear today, but the good news is we caught this — let's get your gum health sorted, then get you those straight teeth properly and safely."

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Takes thorough history including family history (critical for aggressive periodontitis pattern recognition)
  2. ✅ Performs/references full periodontal examination (CPITN, X-ray, photos)
  3. ✅ Diagnoses aggressive periodontitis using plain language
  4. ✅ Explains pathogenesis (localized vs. generalized, risk factors)
  5. ✅ Clearly explains WHY ortho cannot proceed before perio stabilization
  6. ✅ Discusses ortho-perio interaction (forces on unhealthy bone cause more damage)
  7. ✅ Refers appropriately (periodontist + GP for blood work)
  8. ✅ Plans 3-monthly review

TG4 ALERTS

No antibiotics for aggressive periodontitis as first-line — TG4 emphasizes mechanical debridement and risk factor control first; antibiotics only adjunctive in specific cases under specialist guidance.
Genetic/family history pattern — Aggressive periodontitis in young patients with family history should prompt specialist referral, not general practice management alone.

INFLECTION POINTS

PointWeakStrong
Family historySkipped entirelyAsks specifically; uncovers father's early tooth loss, raises clinical suspicion
Reframing the visitDismisses patient's ortho goal entirely"This isn't a no to braces, it's a not-yet — let's do this in the right order"
Explaining ortho-perio link"You can't have braces because of your gums"Explains the mechanism: forces on already-compromised bone cause more damage
Specialist referral rationale"You need to see a specialist""They're more expensive but more cost-effective long-term because they can properly stabilize this"

COMMON PITFALLS

  • ❌ Not asking about family history (the key diagnostic clue)
  • ❌ Dismissing the patient's original goal without explaining the "why" and "not yet, but later"
  • ❌ Not explaining the biological mechanism of why ortho force on diseased bone is harmful
  • ❌ Jumping to extraction/scaling without explaining pathogenesis first

NEXT DRILL

Linking systemic/family risk factors to periodontal diagnosis — practice recognizing patterns that suggest genetic or systemic periodontitis (young age + family history + severity disproportionate to plaque levels).

KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • "The bone loss pattern here — primarily around first molars and incisors — is the hallmark distribution of aggressive periodontitis. This is not inadequate brushing; this is a distinct, often genetically influenced disease."
  • "A CPITN of 444 is a screening score — it tells us pockets are deep but not which teeth, not how much bone, not the prognosis. Full periodontal charting gives us the map before we can plan anything."
  • "Family history of early tooth loss is clinically relevant. It raises the probability of a host-susceptibility component to this presentation. I need to ask and document that."
  • "Until the periodontal disease is stable and the bone loss arrested, moving teeth with orthodontics increases the risk of further bone loss — we would be applying forces to a compromised periodontium."
Patient Reframes
  • "Your gums don't hurt because gum disease is mostly silent — that's actually what makes it dangerous. By the time people feel it, they've often already lost significant bone."
  • "Think of your jawbone like the soil holding a tree in place. The tree looks fine until there's not enough soil left to hold it upright. We're trying to stop that process now, before it gets to that point."
  • "Orthodontics without treating the gums first is like straightening a fence post in sandy soil — looks better on the surface, but it won't hold. We need to stabilise the foundations first."
Curveball Deflectors
  • Patient: "But my gums don't bleed when I brush." → "That can actually mean the tissue has become fibrous over time — it doesn't bleed easily, but the X-ray clearly shows bone loss. Absence of bleeding doesn't equal health."
  • Patient: "Can't you just do a really thorough clean today?" → "A scale and clean works above the gum line. What you need is root surface debridement — instrumentation under the gum to remove the bacterial biofilm driving this process. That's a specific treatment, not a clean."
  • Patient: "When can I have braces then?" → "Once we've done active treatment and I can show the disease is stable at your 3-month review — then we can refer. Orthodontics isn't off the table; it's on hold until conditions are safe."
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ▶
STAGE: Opening & Agenda-Setting

"Hi, come on in — I'm Dr. [Name]. Thanks for coming in today. Take a seat and make yourself comfortable." Smiles warmly, maintains open body language.

"So, I understand you've come in today because you're interested in getting braces to straighten your teeth — is that right? That's great that you're thinking about it. Before we get into that, though, I'd like to take a few minutes to ask you some questions and go through the examination findings with you, because we always need the full picture before we can put together the right treatment plan — and that includes orthodontics. Does that sound okay with you?"

Pauses, allows patient to respond.

"Perfect. I promise we'll get to the braces conversation — I just want to make sure we're doing things in the right order for you."

---

History

"So let's start from the beginning. Have you noticed anything going on with your gums lately — things like bleeding when you brush or floss, any teeth that feel loose or wobbly, or maybe your teeth looking a little longer than they used to?"

Pauses to listen.

"How often are you brushing at the moment — once a day, twice a day? And do you floss at all, or use any mouthwash?"

Pauses.

"When did you last see a dentist before today? Have you had any gum treatment in the past — things like a deep clean, or anything where the dentist spent extra time on your gums?"

Pauses.

"Now, I want to ask about your general health. Are you on any medications at the moment, or do you have any medical conditions I should know about? Have you had any recent blood tests?"

Pauses.

"Good. Now, this next question is really important, so I want to make sure I ask it properly — does anyone in your immediate family have gum disease, or has anyone in your family lost teeth quite early — like in their thirties or forties? Your mum, your dad, any siblings?"

Pauses, leans forward with genuine interest.

"Your dad lost teeth in his thirties — okay, that's actually very helpful to know, and I'll explain why that matters in just a moment. One more thing — do you smoke at all, or vape? And are you under a lot of stress at the moment, with school or anything else going on?"

---

Examination Findings & Diagnosis

"Thank you — that all gives me a really useful picture. So let me walk you through what I found on examination today, because I do want to be upfront with you about something we've picked up.

I took some X-rays, I did a measurement of your gums using a small probe — that's what we call a CPITN score — and I've also taken some photos inside your mouth. Here's what those show.

The gum measurements came back quite high — we scored what's called a four in most areas of your mouth, which tells us there are deep pockets between your teeth and gums. In a healthy mouth, those pockets should be two to three millimetres. Yours are deeper than that in almost every area we checked.

More importantly, the X-rays show that you've actually lost some of the bone that holds your teeth in place — particularly around the back teeth, the molars. Now, here's the thing that I want to explain carefully: this amount of bone loss, happening in a seventeen-year-old, is not what we'd expect with ordinary gum disease. In most people, this kind of damage takes decades to develop. In you, it's happening now, and quite rapidly.

That pattern — young person, significant bone loss, disproportionate to the amount of plaque we can see — fits a condition called aggressive periodontitis. It's an uncommon but serious form of gum disease that can affect teenagers and young adults, even people who are otherwise perfectly healthy. And given that your dad lost his teeth early in life, there is very likely a genetic component here — it can run in families. This is not your fault, but it is something we need to take seriously and act on."

---

Why Orthodontics Cannot Proceed Yet

"Now, I know this isn't what you came in to hear today, and I want to acknowledge that — you came in about your teeth, about getting them straightened, and that's completely reasonable. So let me explain exactly why we can't start orthodontic treatment right now, because I think once you understand the reason, it'll make sense.

When braces move teeth, they apply force to the teeth and the bone around them. That's how the movement works — controlled, sustained pressure. But here's the problem: that process only works safely when the bone and gum tissue are healthy and stable. If the supporting structures are already inflamed and already losing bone, applying orthodontic force on top of that is like trying to renovate a house with a crumbling foundation — you're not improving it, you're accelerating the damage.

In practical terms, what that means is: if we put braces on now, the forces from those braces on already-compromised bone could cause more bone loss, more recession, and in a worst-case scenario, teeth could become loose and we could lose them altogether. We'd be doing more harm than good.

So this is absolutely not a 'no' to braces. It's a 'not yet — let's do this in the right order.' Once we get your gum disease stabilised and the bone loss has stopped, we can absolutely revisit orthodontic treatment, and at that point it can be done safely and properly."

---

Management Plan & Referrals

"So here's the plan I'd like to propose. First priority is treating the gum disease. That means a thorough professional clean — what we call debridement or deep cleaning — to remove the bacterial deposits from below the gumline. That is the cornerstone of treatment, and it's where we start. I want to be clear that we do not jump straight to antibiotics — the evidence and our guidelines are very clear that mechanical cleaning comes first, and any decision about adjunctive antibiotics would only be made by a specialist in specific circumstances.

Given how young you are and the pattern we're seeing, I also want to refer you to a periodontist — that's a gum specialist. They have advanced training specifically in this type of disease, and for aggressive periodontitis in a young patient with a family history, that specialist-level management is going to give you the best long-term outcome. It's a more involved process, but it's the most effective way to properly stabilise what's happening.

I'd also like to refer you back to your GP for some blood tests — just to rule out any underlying systemic conditions, like a blood disorder or immune issue, that could be contributing to this. In most cases it comes back clear, but it's an important step.

And then, once the periodontist has given us the all-clear — once those pockets have reduced, the bone loss has stabilised, and your gum health is in a good place — we revisit the orthodontic plan together."

---

Safety Net & Closing

"In the meantime, the most important thing you can do at home is improve your oral hygiene routine. I'd like you brushing twice a day with a soft-bristled brush, spending two full minutes each time, and starting to floss daily — I'll show you the right technique before you leave today.

We'll see you every three months for review appointments — that's closer than a standard recall, but it's what we need to monitor your response to treatment and make sure things are heading in the right direction.

I know this is a lot to take in, and I know it's not what you were expecting when you walked in this morning. But honestly — the good news here is that we found this now. You're seventeen. We have every opportunity to stop this in its tracks, protect the teeth you have, and then give you the straight smile you're after, done properly and safely.

Do you have any questions at all about what I've explained? Is there anything you'd like me to go over again?" Pauses, maintains eye contact, gives patient full space to respond.

"We'll get you a referral letter for the periodontist today, and I'll have my receptionist help you book your next appointment on the way out. You're in good hands — let's get this sorted."

P2
Generalized Periodontitis with Replacement Options (Coeliac + Hypothyroid)
Category:** Periodontics · Time:** 11 minutes · Opens with:** Candidate · Difficulty:** Exam-ready

CASE SUMMARY

55-year-old patient with pain, bleeding gums, mobility of upper lateral incisor (22). OPG shows generalized bone loss, lateral incisor has 90% bone loss. Perio chart shows 7-8mm pockets. Medical history: hypothyroidism (thyroxine), coeliac disease, taking calcium/vitamin D. Patient wants replacement options and prevention advice.

CANDIDATE BRIEF

You are seeing a 55-year-old patient complaining of pain, bleeding gums, and a wobbly upper front tooth (22). Perio charting shows pocket depths of 7-8mm in several sites, and the OPG shows generalized bone loss with the lateral incisor having lost approximately 90% of its supporting bone. Medical history includes hypothyroidism (on thyroxine), coeliac disease, and calcium/vitamin D supplementation. The patient wants to know about replacement options and how to prevent this long-term. You have 8 minutes.

EXAMINER CONTEXT

Patient understands they have "bad gums" but doesn't connect their medical conditions to their dental health. They are frustrated that despite "always being careful," their teeth are getting worse. They will reveal coeliac disease and hypothyroidism details only if asked directly about medical history and how well-controlled each condition is. They are anxious specifically about losing the front tooth (aesthetic concern) and want to know replacement options NOW, before fully processing that the tooth may need to come out due to disease, not just be "fixed."

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

Opening & History (2.5 min) — INFLECTION 1: Medical-dental link

Standard perio history (HOPC, dental history, OH) PLUS:

  • "Tell me about your thyroid condition — how long, what dose, is it well controlled? When was your last blood test?"
  • "And the coeliac disease — are you managing a gluten-free diet? How's that going?"
  • "What about calcium and vitamin D — how long have you been taking those, and why?"

Why this matters: Both conditions directly impact healing and bone metabolism — the candidate needs this info to explain pathogenesis properly.

Diagnosis (1 min)

"Based on your X-ray and gum measurements, you have generalized periodontitis — quite advanced, Stage 3, affecting most of your teeth, with the front tooth (22) having lost about 90% of its supporting bone. That's why it's become so wobbly and painful."

Linking Medical History to Pathogenesis (2.5 min) — INFLECTION 2: The teaching moment

"I want to explain why this might be harder for your body to fight off than for most people, given your other conditions:

Hypothyroidism: Your thyroid hormone plays an important role in tissue healing and repair. When thyroid function is underactive, the healing capacity of your gum tissue is reduced — so even small infections or damage can't repair as well, which lets gum disease progress more easily.

Coeliac disease: This is an immune condition that causes inflammation throughout your body, including around your bones, and it affects how well you absorb calcium and vitamin D from food — which are essential for bone strength. This can contribute to bone loss, including in your jaw.

So even though you've been 'careful,' these two conditions are working against you in terms of healing and bone strength."

Why this matters: This reframes the patient's frustration ("I've been careful, why is this happening?") into understanding — it's not about blame, it's about physiology.

Management — Tooth 22 Replacement Discussion (2 min) — INFLECTION 3: Don't rush to replacement before resolving disease

"Before we talk about replacing this tooth, we need to deal with the disease itself, otherwise any replacement option will fail too. Here's the order of operations:

  1. Treat the active disease first — deep cleaning, possibly referral to a periodontist for surgical management given the severity
  2. Stabilize tooth 22 — given it's lost 90% of its bone support, it has a poor long-term prognosis. We may need to extract it, but let's see how it responds to initial treatment first
  3. THEN discuss replacement options if extraction becomes necessary:
  • Immediate denture (temporary, while healing)
  • Resin-bonded bridge (conservative, but won't suit a site with ongoing bone loss)
  • Implant (only viable once bone is stable, and with osteoporosis/coeliac-related bone issues, success isn't guaranteed)
  • Permanent denture or bridge (long-term option once everything is stable)"

Prevention & Referral (1 min)

"We'll refer you to a periodontist for the advanced treatment, and to your GP to check on your thyroid levels and make sure your coeliac disease is well controlled — both of these will help your gums heal better. In the meantime, oral hygiene instruction and a 3-monthly review."

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Takes thorough history linking medical conditions to perio disease
  2. ✅ Explains how hypothyroidism affects healing capacity
  3. ✅ Explains how coeliac disease affects calcium/vitamin D absorption and bone health
  4. ✅ Diagnoses generalized periodontitis with appropriate staging
  5. ✅ Sequences treatment correctly: stabilize disease BEFORE discussing replacement
  6. ✅ Discusses realistic replacement options (temporary → permanent)
  7. ✅ Refers to periodontist and GP appropriately
  8. ✅ Validates patient's frustration without dismissing their effort

TG4 ALERTS

Implant success in compromised bone metabolism: TG4-aligned caution — implants require stable bone; coeliac-related malabsorption and any associated osteopenia/osteoporosis affect osseointegration success rates.
Thyroxine and bone turnover: Over-replacement of thyroid hormone can itself accelerate bone turnover — coordinate with GP regarding dose adequacy, not just presence of treatment.

INFLECTION POINTS

PointWeakStrong
Medical history depth"Do you have any medical conditions?" (generic)Specifically probes thyroid control and coeliac management
Pathogenesis explanation"Your gums are infected"Links hypothyroidism to healing capacity, coeliac to calcium/vitamin D absorption and bone strength
Replacement timingJumps straight to "let's talk implants""We need to stabilize the disease first, otherwise any replacement will fail too"
Patient validationIgnores patient's frustration"I understand you've been careful — but these conditions make it harder for your body to fight this, it's not about effort"

COMMON PITFALLS

  • ❌ Not connecting thyroid/coeliac history to periodontal pathogenesis
  • ❌ Discussing implant as a simple "yes" option without considering bone quality issues
  • ❌ Jumping to replacement options before addressing the active disease
  • ❌ Failing to validate the patient's frustration ("I've been careful")

STAGE: Opening & History

"Good morning, come in and take a seat. My name is Dr. [Name] — lovely to meet you. I understand you've been having some pain and bleeding from your gums, and you've noticed one of your front teeth has become a bit wobbly. Is that right? I'd also like to hear your thoughts about replacing that tooth and preventing things from getting worse — we'll definitely cover all of that today. But first, would it be alright if I asked you a few questions?"

"How long have you been noticing the bleeding and pain? Has it been gradual, or did things suddenly get worse recently? Have any other teeth felt loose, or is it mainly that upper front tooth?"

"How often are you brushing and flossing? Are you using any special products — an electric toothbrush, interdental brushes, a mouthwash?"

"When did you last see a dentist, and have you had any gum treatment before — deep cleaning or anything like that?"

"Now, I'd like to ask about your medical history, because this is really important for understanding what's happening with your gums. You mentioned you have an underactive thyroid — hypothyroidism. How long have you had that, and are you taking thyroxine? Do you know your dose? And how well controlled is it — when was your last thyroid blood test?"

"And you also have coeliac disease. Are you managing a strict gluten-free diet? How's that going day to day — do you feel it's well controlled?"

"I see you're also taking calcium and vitamin D supplements. How long have you been on those, and did your doctor specifically prescribe them because of the coeliac disease?"

"Any other medications, or any known allergies? Have you ever had any issues with healing after a cut or dental procedure?"

Examination Findings & Diagnosis

"Thank you — that's really helpful. Let me now walk you through what we found today on your examination and on the X-ray."

"Your gum measurements — what we call pocket depths — are showing readings of seven to eight millimetres in multiple sites around your mouth. Healthy gums measure about one to three millimetres, so these are quite deep. Deep pockets trap bacteria and are very difficult to clean at home."

"On your X-ray, we can see bone loss around most of your teeth — this confirms that the infection has been destroying the supporting bone for some time. The upper front tooth, the lateral incisor, has lost approximately ninety percent of its supporting bone. That's why it feels so wobbly and is causing you pain."

"Putting all of this together, you have what we call generalized periodontitis — quite advanced, Stage Three at minimum, affecting most of your teeth. The front tooth in particular is in a very precarious position."

Linking Medical History to Disease Progression

"I want to take a moment to explain something important, because I think it will answer the question you're probably asking yourself — 'I've been careful, so why is this happening?' And I want to be very clear: this is not about blame. These two medical conditions you have are directly working against your body's ability to fight gum disease and maintain bone."

"Starting with your hypothyroidism — thyroid hormone plays a critical role in tissue repair and healing throughout your whole body, including your gums. When thyroid function is underactive, even if it's being treated, the healing capacity of your gum tissue can be reduced. So even minor bacterial damage that a healthy person might repair quietly becomes harder to resolve, and the disease is allowed to progress further."

"And there's another important point here — if your thyroxine dose has ever been slightly too high at any stage, that can actually accelerate bone turnover, which can contribute to bone loss as well. This is something we'll want your GP to review."

"Now, coeliac disease adds another layer. It's an immune-mediated condition that causes inflammation throughout the body. It also significantly impairs your gut's ability to absorb calcium and vitamin D from food — even if you're eating well and following a gluten-free diet, absorption is often incomplete. Calcium and vitamin D are the two most essential nutrients for bone density everywhere in your body, including your jaw. That's why your doctor prescribed the supplements, but even with supplementation, absorption can remain below ideal. So there may well be an element of reduced jaw bone density underlying all of this."

"So those two conditions together — reduced healing response from the hypothyroidism, and impaired bone metabolism from the coeliac disease — are making this harder for your body to fight off than it would be for most people your age."

Management Plan — Sequencing Treatment Before Replacement

"Now, I know you came in today wanting to discuss replacing that front tooth, and we will get to that — but I need to be honest with you about the sequence, because if we skip steps, any replacement option will fail."

"The first priority is to treat the active gum disease across your whole mouth. We'll start with a thorough deep clean — scaling and root planing — to remove the bacteria and calculus from below the gumline. Given how advanced this is, I will be referring you to a periodontist, a specialist in gum disease. They may recommend surgical treatment in some areas to access the deeper pockets properly."

"Regarding tooth twenty-two — the wobbly front tooth — at ninety percent bone loss, I have to be honest with you: its long-term prognosis is very poor. We'll see whether it responds to initial treatment, but it is quite likely that we will need to extract it. I don't want to make that decision today without giving treatment a chance, but I also don't want you to be caught off guard."

"Once the tooth does need to come out, then we discuss replacement. Here are your realistic options. In the short term, an immediate denture can be made before extraction so you're never without a tooth — this is a temporary option while everything heals. Once the site has healed and the disease is fully stabilized, we can look at more permanent options. A resin-bonded bridge is a conservative choice that involves minimal preparation of the adjacent teeth, though it works best in a stable, low-force site. A conventional bridge is another option. An implant would give the best long-term aesthetic and functional result, but I have to be transparent — given the coeliac-related bone metabolism concerns and possible reduced bone density, implant osseointegration success is not guaranteed without thorough assessment. We would need to ensure your bone quality and density are sufficient, and that your coeliac disease is optimally managed, before committing to that pathway."

Prevention, Referrals & Safety Net

"For prevention going forward, we'll provide thorough oral hygiene instruction — including the correct technique for interdental brushes and flossing in deeper pocketed areas. We'll place you on a three-monthly maintenance and review cycle rather than six-monthly, given the severity and your medical background."

"I'll also write to your GP to request a review of your thyroid levels — specifically to confirm your thyroxine dose is appropriate, not over-replaced — and to discuss whether your calcium and vitamin D absorption is being adequately monitored given the coeliac disease. Better systemic control will directly support better healing in your mouth."

"If you notice the front tooth becomes significantly more painful, more mobile, or if you develop any swelling or difficulty eating before your next appointment, please contact us immediately."

"I know today has been a lot to take in. You came looking for answers about a replacement, and I've given you a broader picture — but everything we're doing is to make sure that replacement, when the time comes, actually lasts. Do you have any questions for me?"

P3
Chronic Generalised Periodontitis with Smoking (Specialist Referral)
Category:** Periodontics · Time:** 11 minutes · Opens with:** Candidate · Difficulty:** Exam-ready

CASE SUMMARY

55-year-old patient, hasn't seen a GP in 10 years, attends for routine cleaning. OPG shows generalized bone loss. Diagnosis: generalized periodontitis Stage 4, Grade C. Patient is an ex-smoker. Candidate must explain the reason for specialist referral and address concerns.

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

Opening (1 min)

"Thanks for coming in today. I understand you wanted a clean — before we do that, I'd like to share some findings from your examination and X-ray, if that's okay?"

History (2 min) — INFLECTION 1: The "haven't seen a GP in 10 years" detail

Standard perio history, plus:

  • "When was the last time you saw your GP or had any blood tests done?" (He'll reveal 10 years — this is a red flag for undiagnosed diabetes or other systemic conditions that could be driving the severity of his perio disease)
  • Smoking history (quit when, how much before)
  • Family history of gum disease/diabetes

Diagnosis (1 min)

"Your gum measurements and X-ray show you have generalized periodontitis — Stage 4, which means quite advanced bone loss, affecting most of your teeth."

Explaining Smoking's Role (Even as Ex-Smoker) (1.5 min) — INFLECTION 2

"Even though you've quit, smoking has a lasting effect. While you were smoking, it would have:

  • Reduced blood flow to your gums, masking bleeding (so you may not have noticed early warning signs)
  • Weakened your immune response to the bacteria causing this
  • Promoted growth of more harmful bacteria types

The good news is, now that you've quit, your healing capacity is improving, and your treatment will work better than if you were still smoking. That's a real win."

The 10-Year GP Gap — Diabetes Screening (1.5 min) — INFLECTION 3

"I also want to mention — you said it's been about 10 years since you've seen your GP. Given how advanced your gum disease is, I'd really recommend getting a check-up, including a blood test for diabetes. Diabetes and gum disease are closely linked — each can make the other worse, and sometimes gum disease is actually the first sign that blood sugar might be a problem. It would be really valuable to rule that out."

Management & Referral (2 min)

"Here's the plan:

  1. I can do a superficial scaling today to remove the visible deposits and reduce some of the bleeding
  2. Given the severity (Stage 4), I'm going to refer you to a periodontist for deeper, more advanced treatment — possibly flap surgery, bone grafting, or guided tissue regeneration depending on what they find
  3. I'd also like you to see your GP for a general check-up and blood test
  4. We'll splint the wobbly teeth for now and reassess with the specialist
  5. Review every 3 months once you've finished specialist treatment"

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Identifies the 10-year GP gap as a red flag and recommends screening
  2. ✅ Explains smoking's lasting impact even after quitting (masked bleeding, immune suppression)
  3. ✅ Diagnoses and stages periodontitis correctly (Stage 4, Grade C)
  4. ✅ Explains rationale for periodontist referral (severity beyond general practice scope)
  5. ✅ Performs appropriate immediate management (superficial scaling)
  6. ✅ Links potential undiagnosed diabetes to periodontal severity

TG4 ALERTS

Bidirectional diabetes-periodontitis relationship — TG4 emphasizes screening for undiagnosed diabetes in patients with severe, disproportionate periodontal disease, especially with long gaps in medical care.
Ex-smokers still at elevated risk — vascular and immune changes from smoking can persist; full risk reduction takes years after cessation.

INFLECTION POINTS

PointWeakStrong
10-year GP gapNot explored or treated as irrelevantFlagged as red flag; diabetes screening recommended
Ex-smoker status"Good thing you quit" (dismissive)Explains lasting vascular/immune effects, while reinforcing that healing will now improve
Severity justification for referral"You need to see a specialist" (vague)"Stage 4 is quite advanced — this needs surgical-level intervention that's beyond what I can offer here"

STAGE: Opening & Agenda-Setting

"Good morning — come on in and take a seat. My name is Dr. Chen, lovely to meet you. I understand you've come in today for a routine clean — is that right? Before we get to that, I've had a chance to look at your X-ray and examine your teeth and gums, and I'd really like to share some important findings with you first, if that's okay. I want to make sure you have the full picture before we do anything. Does that sound alright?"

Pauses to allow patient to respond and settle. Maintains open, unhurried posture.

"Great. So I'll ask you a few questions, explain what I've found, and then we'll work out a plan together. You're very much part of this conversation."

---

History

"To start with — how have your teeth and gums been feeling lately? Any bleeding when you brush, any teeth that feel wobbly, or any discomfort in your gums at all?"

Listens attentively, nods, reflects.

"And can I ask — how long has it been since your last dental visit? And when you brush, are you using any particular technique — how often, and do you floss at all?"

"Now, I also want to ask about your general health. Are you on any medications at the moment, or do you have any medical conditions you're being treated for?"

Pauses. Patient mentions no regular GP visits.

"And when was the last time you saw your GP, or had any blood tests done?"

Listens. Patient reveals it has been approximately ten years.

"Okay, thank you for telling me that — I'll come back to that in a moment because it's actually quite relevant to what I've found. Now, I understand you used to smoke — is that right? When did you stop, and roughly how much were you smoking before you quit, and for how long?"

Listens and notes pack-year history.

"And does anyone in your close family — parents, siblings — have gum disease, or has anyone lost teeth earlier than expected?"

Records responses carefully, acknowledges patient's answers warmly.

---

Diagnosis and Explanation of Findings

"Thank you for sharing all of that. Let me now walk you through what I've found, and I'll try to explain it in plain language.

Your gum measurements and your X-ray together show that you have a condition called generalised periodontitis — gum disease — and I have to be honest with you, it is quite advanced. We classify it as Stage Four, which means there is significant bone loss around most of your teeth. The bone I'm referring to is the bone inside your jaw that actually holds your teeth in place. In some areas, quite a large amount of that bone has been lost, and that's why some of your teeth may feel a little loose. We also classify this as Grade C, which means it has been progressing at a faster rate than we would normally expect, even accounting for the amount of deposits present. That tells me there are likely other factors that have been driving this along, and I want to go through those with you."

---

Explaining Smoking's Role and the GP Gap

"One important factor is your smoking history. Even though you've quit — and that is genuinely great news, and I mean that — smoking has a lasting effect on the gums that doesn't simply disappear overnight. While you were smoking, a few things were happening. Firstly, smoking reduces blood flow to the gum tissue, which actually masks one of the main warning signs of gum disease — bleeding. So you may not have noticed any bleeding even though disease was progressing. Secondly, smoking suppresses your immune response, meaning your body was less able to fight the bacteria causing this damage. And thirdly, smoking actually promotes the growth of more harmful bacterial species in the mouth. The really encouraging news is that now that you've quit, your healing capacity is genuinely improving — and any treatment we do will work significantly better than it would if you were still smoking. That is a real advantage going forward.

Now — and I want to raise this gently — you mentioned it's been about ten years since you last saw your GP or had a blood test. Given how advanced this gum disease is, and how quickly it appears to have progressed, I want to mention something important: there is a very well-established two-way relationship between gum disease and diabetes. Diabetes makes gum disease significantly worse, and severe gum disease can actually push blood sugar levels higher in return. Sometimes, advanced gum disease like yours is actually the first visible sign that blood sugar may have been elevated for some time without anyone knowing. Given the severity of what I'm seeing, and given you haven't had any bloods done in a decade, I would really strongly recommend seeing your GP as a priority for a general health check, including a fasting blood glucose or HbA1c test. I'm not trying to alarm you — I just want to make sure we're not missing something that could be making this harder to treat."

---

Management Plan and Referral

"So here is the plan I'd like to put to you, and I'm happy to answer any questions as we go.

Today, I can do a superficial scale — a thorough clean of all the visible deposits above the gum line. This will help reduce the bacterial load and the inflammation straight away, and it will also give your gums some immediate relief. However, I have to be honest with you: given that this is Stage Four periodontitis, the level of treatment required goes beyond what I can safely and effectively provide here in general practice. You need specialist care, and I'd like to refer you to a periodontist — that is a gum specialist. They will assess you thoroughly and will likely recommend more advanced treatment, which could include a deeper, root-level clean under local anaesthetic, and depending on what they find, possibly surgical options such as flap surgery, guided tissue regeneration, or bone grafting to try to rebuild some of the support that has been lost.

Regarding the teeth that are feeling loose — we can look at temporarily stabilising those while you await the specialist appointment, and the periodontist will advise on the longer-term prognosis for each tooth.

So in summary: I'd like to do the superficial scale today, refer you to a periodontist for specialist management, and refer you to your GP for a health check and blood tests. Once you've completed your specialist treatment, we'll bring you back here every three months for maintenance — that's a critical part of keeping things stable long-term.

I know this is a lot to take in when you came in expecting a clean. Do you have any questions about anything I've said? I'm happy to go over any part of this again."

Provides written referral letters for both the periodontist and GP. Gives patient an appointment card for the scale today and the three-month recall.

"You've done the right thing coming in. We've caught this, and with the right team around you, there's a lot we can do."

P4
Acute Periodontal Abscess (Smoker, Extruded Tooth)
Category:** Periodontics · Time:** 11 minutes · Opens with:** Patient · Difficulty:** Exam-ready

CASE SUMMARY

Female patient, sore upper central incisor (11), mobility grade II. PA shows horizontal bone loss around 14, 15, 16, severe bone loss around 11. Patient smokes 25/day. Differential diagnosis and treatment options required.

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

Opening & Empathy (1 min)

"I can see you're in pain — let's get this sorted. Before I examine you further, can I ask a few questions?"

History (2 min) — INFLECTION 1: Smoking quantity

  • Pain history (onset, character, triggers, severity)
  • Perio history: when did gap/elongation start, bleeding, wobbly teeth
  • "How many cigarettes a day do you smoke, and for how long?" (25/day is heavy — this changes risk stratification and prognosis discussion)
  • Medical history, family history of early tooth loss/diabetes

Diagnosis & Differential (1.5 min)

"Based on my exam and the X-ray, you have an acute periodontal abscess on your front tooth — that's a build-up of infection in the pocket between your gum and tooth. I can also see you have more widespread bone loss around your back teeth, suggesting a longer-standing gum condition — generalized periodontitis."

Explaining the Smoking Link Directly (1.5 min) — INFLECTION 2

"Smoking 25 a day is a significant factor here. It works against you in several ways:

  • It reduces blood flow to your gums, so your body can't fight the infection as effectively
  • It actually changes the type of bacteria that live in your mouth, favoring more harmful species
  • It masks the warning signs — smokers often have less visible bleeding even with active disease, which is part of why this may have progressed without you noticing

I really want to support you in cutting down or quitting, because it will make a big difference to how well treatment works."

Management (2.5 min) — INFLECTION 3: Treating abscess vs. underlying disease

"Today, the priority is draining the abscess and getting you out of pain. We have options:

  1. Draining via the pocket — I can clean out the pocket and remove the source of infection under local anaesthetic
  2. Extraction — if the tooth is too compromised to save, but let's see if we can save it first
  3. Antibiotics — only if you have facial swelling or fever, or if you can't get treatment within 24 hours; otherwise we don't need them, as draining the abscess directly is more effective

For the bigger picture — your back teeth also show bone loss, so once this acute issue settles, we'll need to do a full periodontal assessment and likely refer you for more comprehensive treatment, alongside smoking cessation support."

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Manages acute pain/infection appropriately (drain, don't just prescribe antibiotics)
  2. ✅ Identifies smoking quantity and explains its direct mechanistic role
  3. ✅ Distinguishes acute abscess management from underlying chronic disease management
  4. ✅ Offers smoking cessation support without being preachy
  5. ✅ Uses antibiotics judiciously (only with systemic signs) — TG4 aligned
  6. ✅ Plans follow-up for the broader periodontal disease

TG4 ALERTS

Antibiotics only with systemic involvement — TG4: facial swelling, fever, or inability to access treatment within 24h. Local drainage is the primary treatment for periodontal abscess, NOT antibiotics alone.
Heavy smoking (25/day) — significantly elevates risk; 4-5x more likely to develop periodontal disease vs. light smokers per TG4-aligned evidence.

  • "After acute management, I need to see her back to discuss full-mouth periodontal assessment and treatment planning. Extraction of 11 is likely in the medium term — but that conversation belongs after the acute episode settles."

Drainage today gives you immediate relief and removes the source. I can give antibiotics as well, but they're not the treatment — they're the backup."

Candidate enters, introduces themselves warmly, and establishes eye contact.

"Hello, I'm Dr. Chen — lovely to meet you. Please come in and take a seat. I can see you're in some discomfort today, so let's get to the bottom of this and get you feeling better. Before I look further at your tooth, I'd like to ask you a few questions first — is that alright with you?"

Pauses, allows patient to settle.

"Now, you're having some pain with your upper front tooth — can you tell me a bit about what's been happening? When did it start, and what does the pain feel like?"

Listens attentively without interrupting. Nods and acknowledges: "Right, so it's been building for a little while. That's really helpful, thank you."

---

History Taking

"On a scale of zero to ten, how would you rate the pain right now? And is it constant, or does it come and go? Does anything make it worse — touching it, biting down, temperature?"

"Have you noticed the tooth looks longer than it used to, or that there's a gap between the tooth and the gum? Has it been feeling loose at all?"

"Now I do need to ask you about smoking. Do you smoke at all?" — waits for response — "Twenty-five cigarettes a day — thank you for being honest with me. And how long have you been smoking at that level?"

"From a health perspective, can I ask — any medical conditions I should know about, like diabetes or heart conditions? Any medications? And is there any history of gum disease or early tooth loss in your family — parents, siblings?"

"How are you going with your oral hygiene at home — brushing twice a day, any flossing or interdental brushes?"

---

Diagnosis and Explanation of Findings

Refers to the periapical radiograph on the desk.

"Thank you — that's all very helpful. Let me now walk you through what I've found on your examination and X-ray today, and I'll explain things in plain language as I go."

"What you have on this front tooth is an acute periodontal abscess. That means there's a collection of infection that has built up inside the pocket — the space between your gum and the root of the tooth. The infection is causing that pain and tenderness, and it's also why the tooth has been pushed slightly out of position and feels loose. That movement we call extrusion — the pressure from the pus literally pushes the tooth upward."

"Now, on your X-ray I can also see something important in the bigger picture. Around your back upper teeth — the premolars and molar on the right — there's a noticeable amount of horizontal bone loss. And around your front tooth, the bone loss is unfortunately quite severe. This tells me that the abscess we're dealing with today is not an isolated event — it's sitting on top of a longer-standing gum condition called generalized periodontitis, where the bone and attachment supporting your teeth has been gradually breaking down, likely over a number of years."

"Does that make sense so far? Do you have any questions before I go on?"

---

Explaining the Smoking Link

"I want to be really honest with you about smoking, because it's directly relevant to what's happening here — and I want you to understand the 'why,' not just hear me say it's bad."

"Smoking twenty-five cigarettes a day puts you in the category of heavy smoking, and the evidence is very clear — heavy smokers are around four to five times more likely to develop and progress gum disease compared to non-smokers. Here's what's actually happening biologically:"

"Firstly, nicotine causes the small blood vessels in your gums to constrict, which reduces blood flow. Less blood flow means your immune system can't deliver the white blood cells it needs to fight infection effectively — so infections like this abscess take hold more easily and spread more readily."

"Secondly, smoking changes the bacterial environment in the pocket — it actually favors the more harmful, destructive species of bacteria that drive bone loss."

"And thirdly — and this one really matters — smoking suppresses the bleeding response in your gums. Most people notice gum disease first because of bleeding when they brush. Smokers often don't get that warning sign, which is part of why this can silently progress for a long time without being noticed."

"I want to support you in reducing or quitting, because the evidence is equally clear that stopping smoking significantly improves how well gum treatment works. There are some excellent resources and support services I can refer you to — completely without judgment. Would you be open to that?"

---

Management Plan

"So let's talk about what we do from here, starting with today."

"The immediate priority is draining this abscess and relieving your pain. The most effective way to do that is to clean out the infected pocket directly — I'll give you some local anaesthetic, then use instruments to remove the bacteria and debris from inside the pocket. This releases the pressure, eliminates the source of infection, and will give you significant relief quite quickly. This is the primary treatment — draining the infection is far more effective than antibiotics alone."

"Regarding antibiotics — I won't prescribe them today unless you develop facial swelling, a fever, or feel generally unwell, because in a straightforward periodontal abscess without those systemic signs, drainage is the treatment, and antibiotics won't substitute for it. If you do develop swelling or fever over the next twenty-four hours, I want you to call us straight away."

"For pain relief at home in the meantime, paracetamol one gram every four to six hours is your first line — take it regularly rather than waiting for the pain to peak. If you need something stronger and you have no stomach issues or blood pressure concerns, ibuprofen four hundred milligrams every six to eight hours with food can be added alongside it."

"Now — regarding the front tooth itself. Given the severity of the bone loss I can see on the X-ray, its long-term prognosis is guarded. I want to drain the abscess today and see how it responds before making any final decision. If it settles and we can get some stability, we'll try to save it. If the bone loss is too far advanced, extraction may ultimately be in your best interest — and we would then discuss replacement options."

"For the bigger picture — once this acute episode has settled, I'd like to do a full periodontal assessment of all your teeth, including complete charting and updated radiographs, and then refer you to a periodontist for comprehensive management of the generalized periodontitis. That will involve a course of thorough debridement and a structured maintenance program. Alongside that, I'll provide a referral for smoking cessation support."

"We'll review you in one week to see how the tooth is responding and to plan next steps. Does that all make sense? Do you have any questions?"

P5
Peri-Implantitis (Smoker, Bleeding Gums)
Category:** Periodontics / Implants · Time:** 11 minutes · Opens with:** Candidate · Difficulty:** Exam-ready

CASE SUMMARY

Patient with implant-supported bridge (32-42), pocket depths 6-7mm, redness and bleeding gums, smoker. Main concern: bleeding gums.

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

History — FDOSS framework (2 min)

Family, Diabetes, Oral hygiene, Smoking, Stress — standard perio risk factor screen, plus implant-specific:

  • "When did you get the implants, and why did you need them originally?"
  • "When did the bleeding start?"
  • "Do you feel the implant might be a bit loose?"

Diagnosis (1.5 min) — INFLECTION 1: Distinguishing from natural tooth perio

"You have a condition called peri-implantitis — it's similar to gum disease around natural teeth, but specifically affecting the tissue and bone around your implants. The pocket depths around your implants are 6-7mm, which is deeper than ideal, and there's bone loss happening underneath."

Explaining Pathogenesis & Risk Factors (1.5 min)

"Bacteria build up around the base of the implant, below the gumline, where it's hard to clean. This causes inflammation, and the gum tissue pulls away, creating these pockets. A few things make you more at risk:

  • Smoking — reduces blood supply, weakens your body's ability to fight the infection
  • Previous gum disease history
  • How well you've been able to clean around the implants (flossing/brushing technique with implants is different from natural teeth)"

Management — INFLECTION 2: Scope of practice

"Here's the thing — treating implants is a bit beyond what I can do in general practice. I can do superficial cleaning around your other teeth today, but for the implants specifically, I need to refer you to a specialist. They'll do a deeper clean using special instruments designed not to damage the implant surface, and possibly some bone grafting if needed.

In the meantime, I'll show you how to use interdental brushes and superfloss specifically designed for implants, and we really need to talk about smoking cessation, because that's going to significantly affect how well any treatment works."

Prognosis & Review

"If we don't get this under control, you risk losing the implant altogether. But if we act now with specialist treatment plus better home care plus addressing smoking, we have a good chance of saving it."

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Distinguishes peri-implantitis from natural tooth periodontitis
  2. ✅ Identifies risk factors (smoking, OH technique, prior perio history)
  3. ✅ Recognizes scope of practice limitation — refers to specialist for implant-specific deep cleaning
  4. ✅ Provides implant-specific OHI (interdental brushes, superfloss)
  5. ✅ Discusses smoking cessation as integral to treatment success
  6. ✅ Explains consequence of inaction (implant loss)

TG4 ALERTS

Implant-specific cleaning instruments required — Standard scaling instruments can damage implant surfaces; titanium-safe instruments needed (specialist scope).
Smoking and osseointegration/peri-implant health — Smoking significantly elevates peri-implantitis risk and treatment failure rates.
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • "Peri-implantitis is not the same as periodontitis — implants lack a periodontal ligament, so infection spreads in a circumferential pattern around the threads rather than the more contained pattern around natural teeth. A 6mm pocket on an implant carries a different prognosis than a 6mm pocket on a tooth."
  • "The evidence base for peri-implantitis treatment is less mature than for periodontitis. For pockets >5mm with radiographic bone loss, surgical access with surface decontamination is generally the recommended pathway — non-surgical treatment alone has limited evidence at this severity."
  • "Smoking is a significant risk factor for peri-implantitis — it impairs osseointegration maintenance. I would address that directly as part of the management plan."
  • "The implant-supported bridge complicates home hygiene considerably. I need to specifically assess whether she's accessing the sub-pontic area and abutment margins — floss threaders, interdental brushes, or a water flosser are all options depending on embrasure space."
Patient Reframes
  • "Think of the implant like a post set in concrete. If the concrete starts to break down around it, the post loosens. That's what peri-implantitis does to the bone — and the implant-supported bridge means that process affects the whole structure, not just one point."
  • "Implants are designed to last decades — but they need different maintenance to natural teeth. Once we address the infection and get the home care right, we can stabilise this."
  • "The bleeding and discomfort you're noticing are your body's warning signs — catching this now, before significant bone loss, gives us much better options."
Curveball Deflectors
  • "I thought implants couldn't get gum disease." → "That's a common misconception — implants can't get cavities, but the gum and bone around them absolutely can become infected. Peri-implantitis is essentially gum disease around an implant, and it needs the same serious attention."
  • "Can't you just clean around it?" → "Professional cleaning around implants — which requires specific instruments to avoid damaging the surface — is part of the treatment. But with pockets this deep and bone loss present, we also need surgical access to decontaminate the implant surface. A clean alone won't be enough at this stage."
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ▶
STAGE: Opening & Presenting Concern

"Good morning, I'm Dr. [Name]. Please come in and take a seat. How are you today? What brings you in to see me?"

Listens as patient describes bleeding gums around the front implant area.

"Thank you for telling me that. I can see you're worried about the bleeding, and I want to reassure you that you've done the right thing coming in. I'll ask you a few questions first, then we'll have a good look and I'll explain exactly what's going on and what we can do about it. Is that okay?"

---

History — Risk Factor Screen

"How long have you noticed the bleeding? Is it happening when you brush, or does it bleed on its own?"

"Do you have any pain or discomfort around the front teeth area? Does the implant bridge feel at all loose or different to how it felt before?"

"When did you first have the implant bridge placed, and can you tell me why you needed it — was it from gum disease, an accident, or something else?"

"Have you had gum disease or gum treatment around your natural teeth in the past?"

"How are you cleaning around the bridge at the moment? Are you using a toothbrush, floss, or anything else between the teeth?"

"Now, I do want to ask — are you currently smoking? If so, roughly how many cigarettes per day, and for how long?"

"Do you have any medical conditions — in particular, have you ever been told you have diabetes or high blood sugar? Are you taking any regular medications?"

"Any significant stress lately? Sometimes that can affect how our bodies respond to infection."

"Is there any family history of gum disease or tooth loss?"

---

Diagnosis & Explanation

"Thank you — that's really helpful. Based on what you've told me and what I can see today, I want to explain what's happening. You have a condition called peri-implantitis. It's similar to gum disease around natural teeth, but it specifically affects the gum tissue and the bone supporting your implants. The pocket depths I'm measuring around your implants are between six and seven millimetres, which is significantly deeper than we'd want to see. Ideally, pockets around implants should be no more than three to four millimetres. That depth tells me there's active inflammation and that some bone underneath has already been lost."

"The reason this is different from gum disease around a natural tooth is important. Implants don't have a periodontal ligament — that cushioning layer of fibres that natural teeth have — so once bone loss starts around an implant, it can progress quite quickly and the tissue doesn't protect itself in the same way."

"I want to be honest with you — this is something we need to take seriously, but the good news is we've caught it and there are things we can do."

---

Pathogenesis & Risk Factors

"Let me explain why this has happened. Bacteria build up around the base of the implant posts, below the gumline, in an area that's very difficult to clean properly at home. This causes the gum to become inflamed, and over time, the gum pulls away, forming these deeper pockets. Bacteria then go even deeper, and the bone starts to break down around the implant."

"A few things are making this worse in your case. Smoking is the biggest one. Smoking reduces blood flow to the gum tissue, which means your body's immune response is weakened and healing is significantly impaired. Research consistently shows that smokers have much higher rates of peri-implantitis and much lower success rates with treatment. Ideally, I'd love to help you work towards quitting — even cutting down substantially makes a real difference. I can refer you to Quitline, or we can discuss nicotine replacement options today."

"Your previous gum disease history is also relevant — it means your immune system has a pattern of responding this way. And cleaning around an implant bridge is genuinely different from cleaning natural teeth. Standard floss doesn't work well here — we need to use superfloss and small interdental brushes to clean underneath the bridge and around each implant."

---

Management Plan

"Now, here's what I'd like to do. I can provide some cleaning around your natural teeth today — addressing any calculus and plaque there. However, the implant-specific treatment is beyond what I can safely provide in general practice, and I want to be upfront with you about that. The instruments used to clean around implants have to be specially designed — titanium-safe curettes and plastic-tipped instruments — because standard metal scalers can scratch the implant surface, which actually makes it easier for bacteria to stick. That kind of deep implant debridement, and an assessment of whether bone grafting might be needed, is best handled by a specialist periodontist."

"I'll write you a referral today with all your clinical notes and measurements. At the specialist, they'll do a thorough assessment, a deeper clean using the correct instruments, and discuss further options depending on how much bone has been lost."

"In the meantime, let me show you how to use superfloss and interdental brushes specifically for your bridge — I'll demonstrate on a model so you can see the technique clearly. This needs to happen twice a day."

---

Prognosis, Smoking Cessation & Safety Net

"I want to be honest about what happens if we don't address this. Without treatment, the bone loss will continue, and there's a real risk of losing the implant bridge altogether — which would be a significant setback given what you've already been through. But if we act now — specialist treatment, improved cleaning technique at home, and seriously working on the smoking — there is a genuinely good chance of stabilising this and keeping the implants."

"Regarding smoking, I'd strongly encourage you to call Quitline on 13 7848 — they're free, very effective, and can support you with a personalised plan. This really is one of the most important things you can do for the health of your implants."

"In terms of next steps: I'll refer you to a periodontist, I'll clean around your natural teeth today, and I'd like to see you back in four to six weeks to check on how your home care is going and whether you've had any contact from the specialist. If you notice the area becoming painful, the implant feeling loose, or the bleeding getting significantly worse before then, please call us straight away. Do you have any questions about anything we've discussed?"

P6
Smoking Cessation & Risk Factor Counseling (Standalone Communication Station)
Category:** Periodontics / Preventive · Time:** 11 minutes · Opens with:** Candidate · Difficulty:** Exam-ready

CASE SUMMARY

A focused communication station: patient with moderate periodontitis who has been told before to quit smoking but hasn't. Candidate must use behavior-change techniques, not just repeat advice.

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

Opening — Permission-based approach (1 min)

"I know we've talked about smoking before. Would it be okay if we revisit that today, in the context of your gum health?"

Assess Readiness to Change (2 min) — INFLECTION 1: Motivational interviewing, not lecturing

"On a scale of 1 to 10, how ready do you feel to think about cutting down or quitting?"

[Listen to response]

"What would need to happen for that number to go up?"

"What's stopped you in the past when you've tried to cut down?"

Why this matters: A weak candidate launches straight into "smoking is bad for your gums" — a strong candidate explores the patient's own motivation and barriers FIRST.

Personalized Risk Communication (1.5 min)

"Specifically for your gums — smoking is one of the biggest things working against the treatment we're doing. It reduces blood flow, which means less oxygen and nutrients getting to the area that needs to heal, and it actually changes which bacteria thrive in your mouth toward more harmful types."

Offering Support Without Pressure (2 min) — INFLECTION 2

"There's no pressure today, but if you ever do want support, there are some really effective options:

  • Quitline — free phone support, well-proven approach
  • Nicotine replacement (patches, gum) — your GP can discuss prescription options like varenicline too
  • Apps that track progress and savings

Would it be helpful if I sent you some information, even if you're not ready to act on it yet?"

If patient says no to quitting now:

"That's completely okay — it's your choice, and I respect that. For now, let's focus on what we CAN do — keeping your appointments regular, doing the deep cleaning, and at minimum, if you could avoid smoking for 72 hours around any dental procedures, that would help healing."

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Asks permission before raising smoking again
  2. ✅ Assesses readiness to change using a scaling question (motivational interviewing technique)
  3. ✅ Explores barriers and previous quit attempts
  4. ✅ Provides personalized (not generic) risk information tied to current treatment
  5. ✅ Offers specific support resources (Quitline, NRT, medications)
  6. ✅ Respects patient autonomy if they decline — doesn't lecture or guilt
  7. ✅ Provides a realistic fallback (72-hour avoidance around procedures) if full cessation isn't accepted

TG4 ALERTS

Pharmacotherapy options — Varenicline and NRT are evidence-based; refer to GP for prescription options as appropriate.
Motivational interviewing > lecturing — Repeated unsolicited advice without exploring readiness reduces patient engagement and is less effective per behavior-change evidence.

INFLECTION POINTS

PointWeakStrong
Opening approachLaunches into "you really need to quit smoking"Asks permission first: "Would it be okay if we talk about this again?"
Readiness assessmentSkippedUses scaling question (1-10) to gauge motivation and explore barriers
Risk communicationGeneric ("smoking is bad for you")Specific and personalized ("it reduces blood flow to the exact area we're treating")
If patient declinesPushes harder or gives up entirelyRespects autonomy, offers smaller realistic win (72-hour avoidance around procedures)
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • "Brief advice at every dental visit — even 30 seconds — increases quit attempts by 50–70% compared to no advice. The dental setting is an evidence-based intervention point."
  • "Combination NRT — patch for background plus short-acting (gum, lozenge, inhaler) for cravings — has significantly higher quit rates than patch alone. This is the first-line recommendation."
  • "Varenicline (Champix) has the highest single-agent efficacy in randomised controlled trials — approximately 2–3× better than placebo. It's PBS-subsidised in Australia. The key contraindication to screen for is history of serious psychiatric illness."
  • "The 5 A's framework: Ask, Advise, Assess, Assist, Arrange. In a dental context, 'Arrange' means a follow-up call or referral to Quitline (13 7848) — not just verbal advice and goodbye."
Patient Reframes
  • "You've tried before — and that's actually encouraging. The research tells us most people who successfully quit have made multiple attempts first. Every attempt isn't a failure; it's a rehearsal."
  • "Smoking doesn't just stain teeth — it actively destroys the bone holding them in place, and it does it silently by suppressing the bleeding that would otherwise alert you. Quitting is the single most powerful intervention for your gum health — more than any treatment I can do."
  • "I'm not here to lecture you or make you feel guilty. I just want to make sure you have access to the support that actually works — because 'just try harder' is not a treatment plan."
Curveball Deflectors
  • "I've tried everything and nothing works." → "Tell me what you've tried — I want to understand what's happened before. Because the combination approaches and the prescription options are very different in efficacy, and most people haven't tried everything. There's almost always something we haven't optimised."
  • "I'll quit when I'm ready." → "That's completely your choice and I respect that. Can I just ask — what would 'ready' look like for you? Because sometimes knowing exactly what support is available changes when 'ready' feels like it could be."
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ▶
STAGE: Opening — Permission-Based Approach

"Hello again, it's good to see you. Before we get started today, I just wanted to check in with you about something we've touched on before. I know we've spoken about smoking in previous appointments, and I completely understand if it feels like a topic that keeps coming up. Would it be okay with you if we revisited it today — specifically in the context of how your gum treatment is going? I want to make sure we're giving your gums the best possible chance, and I think it's worth having an honest conversation about it together."

Pauses and waits for the patient's response, maintaining open, non-judgmental body language.

"Thank you — I really appreciate you being open to that. I promise this isn't going to be a lecture. I'm much more interested in hearing where you're at."

---

Assessing Readiness to Change

"So, if you think about it honestly — on a scale of one to ten, where one means 'I have absolutely no interest in cutting down or quitting right now,' and ten means 'I'm ready to make a change today' — where would you put yourself?"

Listens attentively to the patient's response without interrupting.

"That's really helpful, thank you. So you're at around a [patient's number]. Can I ask — what would need to happen for that number to go up, even just by one or two points? What would make quitting feel more possible or more worthwhile for you personally?"

Listens again, reflecting the patient's words back.

"And thinking back — have you ever tried to cut down or quit in the past? What happened then? What got in the way?"

Allows patient to respond fully before moving on.

"I hear you. It sounds like [barrier identified — e.g., stress, habit, previous withdrawal] has been a real challenge. That's actually one of the most common reasons people find it difficult, and it makes complete sense given everything you're managing."

---

Personalised Risk Communication

"I want to share something with you that's specific to your situation — not just general information about smoking, but how it's directly affecting the treatment we're doing together right now. With moderate periodontitis like yours, the gum tissue and the bone supporting your teeth are already under stress. Smoking works against us in a few important ways. It reduces blood flow to the gum tissue, which means less oxygen and fewer nutrients reaching exactly the areas that need to heal after our deep cleaning appointments. It also actually shifts the balance of bacteria in your mouth toward the more harmful types — the ones that drive bone loss. And unfortunately, because smoking suppresses the early signs of inflammation, like bleeding, it can mask how serious things are until the damage is more advanced. So in a very real sense, every cigarette is working against the treatment we're investing time and money into together."

---

Offering Support Without Pressure

"Now — and I want to be really clear about this — there is absolutely no pressure today. This is your decision, and I respect that completely. But I do want you to know that if you ever feel ready, even just curious, there is genuinely effective support available.

The Quitline — 13 7848 — is a free phone counselling service, and it has really strong evidence behind it. Nicotine replacement therapy, things like patches or gum, can help take the edge off cravings significantly. And there are prescription medications your GP can discuss with you — varenicline in particular has very good evidence for improving quit rates. There are also apps that can track your progress and show you how much money you're saving, which some people find really motivating.

Would it be helpful if I wrote down a couple of those resources for you today — even just to have them? You don't need to do anything with them straight away."

Waits for response.

---

Respecting Autonomy and Safety Net

If the patient declines to commit to quitting: "That is absolutely okay. I genuinely mean that — it's your choice, and I'm not going to push you. What I'd love for us to focus on together is everything we can control right now: keeping your review appointments regular, completing the root surface debridement, and making sure your home care is as strong as possible.

One thing that would genuinely help your healing, even if full cessation isn't something you're ready for — if you could avoid smoking for at least seventy-two hours around any of our treatment appointments, that window makes a real difference to how the tissue responds and recovers. Even that small step would support what we're doing.

I'll keep this door open. Whenever you want to revisit it — next month, next year — I'm here, and we'll work through it together without any judgment."

"Is there anything else on your mind today that you'd like to talk about?"

E1
RCT-Treated Tooth, Patient Wants Extraction (Differential Diagnosis of Post-Treatment Pain)
Category:** Endodontics · Time:** 11 minutes · Opens with:** Candidate · Difficulty:** Exam-ready

CASE SUMMARY

Patient with severe pain on upper left side, several teeth root-treated months ago (per OPG). Patient angry, wants extraction. Candidate must work through differential diagnosis (odontogenic vs. non-odontogenic) before agreeing to or refusing extraction.

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

Opening & De-escalation (1 min)

"I can see you're in a lot of pain and frustrated — that's completely understandable. Let's work through this together so we can figure out exactly what's going on before we decide on treatment. Can I ask you some questions first?"

SOCRATES History (2 min)

Full pain history: Site, Onset, Character, Radiation, Associations (dry mouth, discharge, blocked nose), Timing, Exacerbating/relieving, Severity

Dental & Medical History (1 min) — INFLECTION 1: The sinusitis clue

  • "When was the RCT done? Does this pain feel similar to before the treatment, or different?"
  • "Any recent colds, sinus issues, or hayfever?" (This is the critical question — if there's a recent respiratory infection, maxillary sinusitis becomes a strong differential, especially with upper posterior teeth)

Explaining the Differential Diagnosis (2.5 min) — INFLECTION 2: The core teaching point

"I want to explain why I'm not jumping straight to extraction. Pain after root canal treatment can come from a few different sources, and it's really important we identify the right one, because pulling teeth that AREN'T the problem won't fix your pain — and you'd lose a tooth unnecessarily.

Possible dental causes:

  • A crack in the tooth (these RCT teeth have big fillings without crowns protecting them — cracks can develop)
  • The root canal treatment may not have fully cleared the infection (sometimes there are tiny extra canals that are hard to find)

Possible non-dental causes:

  • Your sinuses — the roots of your upper back teeth sit very close to your sinus cavity. If you've had a cold or sinus infection, that can cause pain that feels exactly like tooth pain, even mimicking the pain you had before your root canal
  • Jaw muscle tension (myofascial pain)
  • Nerve-related pain (less common, but possible)

This is actually really important, because if it's a sinus problem, taking the teeth out won't fix it — you'd still have the pain, plus you'd have lost healthy teeth."

Investigations & Plan (1.5 min)

"To figure out which it is, I want to:

  1. Examine all the teeth in that area for cracks
  2. Do a bite test and cold test on the RCT teeth and neighbors
  3. Take a new X-ray, possibly a 3D scan (CBCT) if a specialist needs to look closer at your sinuses
  4. If sinus infection seems likely given your symptoms, I may also suggest seeing your GP about that

I know you came in wanting these teeth out, and I hear that — but let's make sure we're solving the right problem first. Pulling the wrong tooth means you're still in pain. Does that make sense?"

Closing
