"Once we know what we're dealing with, we'll talk about the right treatment — whether that's extraction, re-treatment of the root canal, or treating a sinus infection."

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Performs full SOCRATES pain history
  2. ✅ Specifically asks about recent respiratory/sinus symptoms
  3. ✅ Generates broad differential (crack, failed RCT, sinusitis, myofascial pain)
  4. ✅ Explains WHY extraction shouldn't happen until cause is confirmed (validates patient's frustration while redirecting)
  5. ✅ Plans appropriate investigations (cold test, bite test, imaging)
  6. ✅ De-escalates anger without dismissing patient's request
  7. ✅ Avoids unnecessary antibiotics (TG4 — antibiotics don't reach inside the tooth/treat sinusitis caused by dental source effectively without addressing source)

TG4 ALERTS

Antibiotics ineffective for MSEO (Maxillary Sinusitis of Endodontic Origin) without treating the source — TG4: antibiotics may temporarily resolve symptoms but won't address the underlying dental infection if present; symptoms recur.
Avoid extraction without diagnostic clarity — Removing teeth based on patient request alone, without confirming odontogenic source, risks unnecessary tooth loss and unresolved pain (potential complaint/litigation risk).

INFLECTION POINTS

PointWeakStrong
Sinus historyNot askedSpecifically asks about colds, sinus issues — uncovers key differential clue
Handling angry patient wanting extractionEither extracts to appease, or refuses without explanationValidates frustration, explains WHY identifying cause first matters, redirects collaboratively
Differential breadthOnly considers "the tooth is the problem"Considers crack, failed RCT, sinusitis, myofascial pain, referred pain
Antibiotic decisionPrescribes "just in case"Explains why antibiotics won't fix sinusitis of dental origin without treating the source
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • "Before I can agree to an extraction — or refuse one — I need to localise the source of pain. With multiple root-treated teeth visible on this OPG, I cannot assume it's the most recently treated one. It could be a different tooth, a crack, a missed canal, or a non-odontogenic source entirely."
  • "Post-RCT pain persisting beyond 2 weeks warrants CBCT. I need to assess for missed canals, a vertical root fracture, an apical cyst that hasn't resolved, or signs of failure. A periapical radiograph alone isn't sufficient to make that call."
  • "Vertical root fracture is in my differential — it's the one diagnosis where extraction is genuinely the only option, and the clinical signs (halo or J-shaped radiolucency, isolated deep probing defect) guide that. If I identify a VRF, I will tell you directly."
  • "Non-odontogenic pain — particularly atypical facial pain, myofascial pain, or a sinus-related source — can mimic dental pain precisely. SOCRATES history is essential before any irreversible procedure."
Patient Reframes
  • "I completely understand the frustration — you had treatment done, you expected relief, and instead things feel worse. That's not acceptable, and we're going to find out exactly why today."
  • "I'm not refusing to extract — I'm asking for 15 minutes to investigate properly first, so that if we do extract, we're certain that's the right tooth and the right decision. If we remove it and the pain continues, we've lost the tooth for nothing."
  • "Think of the root canal like fixing a pipe — occasionally a hairline crack develops that's nothing to do with the repair itself. We need to find out what we're actually dealing with before choosing the tool."
Curveball Deflectors
  • "I've decided — I want it out, just do it." → "I hear you, and it's your right to make that decision. But I have a duty to make sure you've got all the information first — including the possibility that extraction may not resolve your pain if the source is elsewhere. Give me 10 minutes to examine properly. If the tooth needs to come out, I'll tell you honestly and we'll do it."
  • "The last dentist said the RCT was fine." → "That may well be the case — and I'm not here to contradict them without evidence. But 'fine' at completion doesn't always mean the situation can't evolve. Let me take a fresh look and we'll go from there."
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ▶
STAGE: Opening & De-escalation

"Hello, come in and take a seat. I'm Dr. [Name]. I can see from your expression that you're in a lot of pain and I can hear that you're really frustrated — that's completely understandable. You've already been through root canal treatment and you're still hurting, and that's not what anyone expects. I want to help you get out of pain as quickly as possible, and I absolutely hear that you want these teeth out. What I'd like to do is ask you some questions and do a thorough examination first, because I want to make sure we find the right answer — not just a quick answer. Is that okay with you? I promise I'm not stalling; I just want to make sure we fix the actual problem rather than take out teeth that might not be causing this. Can I start by asking about the pain itself?"

---

SOCRATES Pain History

"I want to understand exactly what you're feeling. Can you point to where the pain is worst right now?" Candidate notes patient points to the upper left posterior region. "Is it one specific tooth, or does it feel more spread across the whole area — or even up into your cheek or under your eye?"

"When did this pain start — was it there straight after the root canal treatment, or did it settle for a while and then come back? Or has it been there the whole time since treatment finished?"

"Can you describe what the pain actually feels like — is it a throbbing, a constant ache, a sharp shooting pain, or more of a pressure or heaviness?"

"Does the pain travel anywhere — up toward your forehead, behind your eye, down into your lower jaw, or into your ear?"

"Have you noticed anything else going on at the same time — any swelling in your face, any discharge or bad taste, any blocked nose or feeling of fullness in your cheek, any difficulty opening your mouth?"

"Is the pain there all the time, or does it come and go? Is it worse at any particular time of day — like first thing in the morning, or when you bend forward to pick something up?"

"What makes it worse — biting, hot or cold, touching the tooth? And what helps — painkillers, lying down, anything else?"

"On a scale of zero to ten, where zero is no pain at all and ten is the worst pain you can imagine, where would you put this right now?"

---

Dental & Medical History — The Sinusitis Inflection Point

"Thank you — that's really helpful. Now let me ask a few things about your dental background. When were the root canal treatments done on these upper left teeth, and do you know if they were completed fully or if there were any complications mentioned at the time?"

"After the treatments finished, did you have any period where the pain completely went away — even briefly? Or has it been pretty much continuous?"

"Were any crowns placed on these teeth after the root canal? The reason I ask is that root-treated teeth without crowns are quite vulnerable to tiny cracks, which can cause exactly this kind of pain."

"Now — and this is actually a really important question — have you had any colds, blocked nose, or sinus trouble recently? Any hayfever, any facial congestion, any feeling of pressure under your cheekbone on that same side?" Candidate listens carefully to response. "The reason I ask is that the roots of your upper back teeth sit extremely close to your sinus cavity — sometimes the tip of the root actually touches the sinus lining — and sinus inflammation can produce pain that feels almost identical to toothache, including pain that can mimic exactly what you felt before the root canal treatment."

"Any medical conditions I should know about — heart conditions, diabetes, blood thinners, any medications? Any known allergies?"

---

Explaining the Differential Diagnosis

"Thank you for being so thorough with me — it really does help. Now I want to explain something important, because I think it'll make sense of why I'm asking you to hold off on extraction for now — and I genuinely understand that's not what you want to hear.

Pain after root canal treatment can come from a few different sources, and some of them have nothing to do with the teeth themselves. Let me walk you through the possibilities.

From a dental point of view: one possibility is a crack in one of the treated teeth. Root-treated teeth become more brittle over time, and without a crown protecting them — especially with large fillings in place — they can develop fine cracks that are almost invisible on X-ray but cause significant pain, particularly on biting. Another dental cause is that the root canal treatment itself may not have fully cleared the infection — sometimes there are very small extra canals inside the root that are genuinely difficult to find, and bacteria can survive there.

But here is the critical point: one of the most important non-dental causes is your sinuses. The roots of your upper back teeth sit right next to your maxillary sinus — that's the air-filled cavity inside your cheekbone. If you have a sinus infection or inflammation, whether from a cold, hayfever, or a sinus problem in its own right, it creates pressure and pain in exactly the area where your root-treated teeth are. That pain can feel completely indistinguishable from toothache. It can feel like the same pain you had before your root canal. It can even refer to individual teeth. And here is why this matters so much for your decision today: if the cause of your pain is actually your sinuses, removing those teeth will not fix your pain. You will still have the sinus inflammation, you will still have the pain — and you will also have lost teeth that were not causing the problem. That is something I cannot let happen to you without at least ruling it out first.

Other less likely but possible causes include jaw muscle tension from clenching or guarding around a sore area, or in rarer cases, nerve-related pain."

---

Investigations & Proposed Plan

"So here is what I'd like to do today, and I want to explain the reason for each step.

I'm going to examine all the teeth in that area carefully — I'll check for cracks using a special dye and a bite test, where I ask you to bite down on a small stick on individual cusps to locate any crack. I'll do a cold test on the root-treated teeth and the neighbouring teeth to check how each one responds. I'll also gently feel along your cheekbone and the area below your eye to check for sinus tenderness, which would be a strong clue pointing toward a sinus cause.

I'll take a new X-ray today and examine the root tips carefully. If things are not clear on a standard X-ray, I may refer you for a CBCT — that's a three-dimensional scan — which gives us a much clearer picture of both the root tips and the sinus floor.

If, after all of this, the picture points toward a sinus infection rather than a dental problem, I'll recommend you see your GP as well, because treating the sinus with appropriate management would resolve your pain without removing a single tooth.

I want to be honest with you: if we find clear evidence that one of these teeth is cracked beyond repair, or that the root canal treatment has genuinely failed and cannot be salvaged, then extraction absolutely becomes part of the conversation — and we'll discuss that openly, including your replacement options. But I cannot in good conscience agree to removing teeth before we know what we're dealing with. Removing the wrong teeth means you're still in pain, plus you've lost teeth you didn't need to lose, and that creates a whole new set of problems.

Does that explanation make sense? I do hear you — I know you came in wanting this fixed today. Let's do the examination right now and work through this together."

---

Safety Net & Closing

"Once we've completed the examination and any imaging, I'll sit back down with you and give you a clear answer about what I think is going on and what I recommend. If it turns out to be a failed root canal, we can discuss re-treatment by a specialist endodontist, or extraction with a replacement option such as an implant or bridge. If it's a crack, we'll discuss whether the tooth is salvageable. And if your sinuses are involved, we'll get that pathway started straight away.

One more thing I want to mention: I know antibiotics might seem like an obvious option when you're in this much pain, but I want to be upfront — antibiotics alone won't fix this, regardless of the cause. If there's a dental source, antibiotics cannot reach inside the tooth, and they will not address the root of the problem. They might reduce symptoms temporarily, but the pain will return. We need to treat the source, not just the symptoms.

I'll also make sure you have adequate pain relief while we work this out — paracetamol one gram every four to six hours is your best first-line option, and you can add ibuprofen four hundred milligrams every six

E2
Acute Irreversible Pulpitis, Patient Travelling Interstate
Category:** Endodontics · Time:** 11 minutes · Opens with:** Candidate · Difficulty:** Exam-ready

CASE SUMMARY

Patient with severe tooth pain (lower right molar), needs to travel interstate in 2 days, doesn't want to start RCT, wants painkillers only.

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

Opening & Empathy (1 min)

"I can see this has been troubling you, and I understand you've got travel coming up — let's work out the best plan together. Can I ask a few questions?"

History (1.5 min)

Pain history (character — spontaneous, lingering after hot/cold = key for irreversible pulpitis diagnosis), dental history (previous filling/symptoms on this tooth), medical history, "How long will you be away, and is it possible to reach a dentist there if needed?"

Diagnosis & Explanation (1.5 min) — INFLECTION 1: Why painkillers alone won't work

"Based on what you're describing — pain that lingers after hot or cold, and keeps you awake at night — this is a condition called irreversible pulpitis. It means the nerve inside your tooth is severely inflamed and won't recover. I need to explain something important: painkillers alone won't fix this.

Pain medication can't really reach the inflamed nerve effectively because of how pressure builds up inside the tooth. The only things that actually treat the problem are removing the infected nerve (root canal treatment) or removing the tooth. Painkillers just mask it temporarily — and this pain is likely to get significantly worse, possibly while you're travelling, which would be a much harder situation to manage."

Negotiating the Travel Timeline (2.5 min) — INFLECTION 2: Practical problem-solving

"Given you're travelling in 2 days, here's what I'd suggest:

Option 1 — Start the root canal treatment now: I can do the first stage today — that's removing the infected nerve and placing a temporary filling. This typically gives the most relief and reduces the risk of it flaring up while you're away. When you're back, we complete the final stages.

Option 2 — Emergency pulpotomy: A faster, partial version if you're short on time today — removes the most inflamed part of the nerve to relieve pressure, with a plan to complete proper RCT when you return.

Option 3 — Extraction: If you really don't want to keep the tooth, we could take it out today instead — but I'd want you to know the trade-offs (losing a natural tooth, future replacement cost) before deciding.

Option 4 — Painkillers only: This is an option, but I want to be honest — there's a real risk the pain will worsen significantly while you're away, possibly into a swelling or infection, which would be much harder to manage if you're not near your usual dentist.

Given you have 2 days, I'd really recommend at least starting the first stage of the root canal — it takes the pressure off and gives you the best chance of a comfortable trip."

If patient insists on painkillers only:

"I respect that's your choice. Let's make sure you have a good supply of paracetamol and ibuprofen, and I'll give you my contact details in case you need advice while you're away, plus information on finding a dentist if needed."

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Diagnoses irreversible pulpitis based on classic symptom pattern (lingering pain, nocturnal pain)
  2. ✅ Explains clearly WHY painkillers alone are insufficient (pulpal pressure mechanism)
  3. ✅ Proposes practical, timeline-appropriate solutions (start RCT, pulpotomy, extraction)
  4. ✅ Respects patient autonomy if they choose painkillers-only, while being honest about risk
  5. ✅ Provides contingency planning for if pain worsens while travelling
  6. ✅ Does NOT just prescribe stronger painkillers without addressing the source

TG4 ALERTS

Pulpitis is not effectively managed by analgesics alone — TG4: addresses the biological mechanism (inflammation increases intrapulpal pressure, restricting blood flow, reducing analgesic penetration).
Codeine-containing analgesics — TG4 generally advises against for routine dental pain; paracetamol + NSAID combination preferred first-line where not contraindicated.

INFLECTION POINTS

PointWeakStrong
Explaining why painkillers fail"You need a root canal" (dictates without explaining)Explains the pressure/blood flow mechanism so patient understands WHY
Timeline negotiationEither insists on full RCT today or gives up and just prescribes painkillersOffers tiered options (full RCT start, pulpotomy, extraction) matched to 2-day timeline
Respecting final choiceRefuses to provide painkillers if patient declines RCTProvides safe analgesic plan + contingency advice even if patient declines active treatment
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • "Irreversible pulpitis will not resolve with analgesics — the pulp is in an irreversible inflammatory state, progressing to necrosis. Once necrosis occurs, the risk of acute apical abscess with significant swelling is real, and that is a genuine emergency on a plane or in a remote location."
  • "Pulpectomy today — entering the canal, removing the pulp tissue, dressing with calcium hydroxide, and sealing temporarily — provides immediate and reliable pain relief without committing to the full RCT. The patient returns to complete obturation later. This is a well-established emergency protocol."
  • "Barometric pressure changes during a flight can cause significant pain in a tooth with active pulpitis or a necrotic pulp — cabin pressure at altitude is approximately equivalent to 2400m above sea level. This is a real risk, not a theoretical one."
  • "Ibuprofen 400mg + paracetamol 1g together has additive analgesia — the combination is more effective than either alone. If prescribing for the interim, regular dosing around the clock is more effective than PRN."
Patient Reframes
  • "The nerve inside the tooth is essentially dying right now, and that process causes the intense, spontaneous pain you're describing. Once we remove it — which takes one appointment — the relief is often immediate. You'd travel comfortably."
  • "A plane is the worst place to have a dental abscess — pressure changes can take a nagging ache to a 9/10 emergency with no help available. Having a pulpectomy today is essentially dental travel insurance."
  • "I know you didn't plan for this today, but spending 90 minutes now saves you the risk of a genuine emergency when you're far from help."
Curveball Deflectors
  • "Can I just take antibiotics for the trip?" → "Antibiotics won't work here — the pulp has lost its blood supply, so antibiotics can't reach the source of infection. They're useful if the infection spreads to the surrounding bone, but they won't stop the pulp from dying or relieve the pain. The only reliable treatment is removing the pulp."
  • "What if I just take painkillers and it settles?" → "It won't settle — irreversible pulpitis, by definition, doesn't resolve. The pain may fluctuate, but the underlying process will progress to necrosis and then abscess. I can't guarantee when, but I can tell you that risk is highest at the worst possible moment — mid-flight or interstate without your regular dentist."
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ▶
STAGE: Opening & Empathy

"Hi, come in and take a seat. I'm Dr. [Name]. I can see from your notes that you've been having some real trouble with a tooth, and I understand you've got travel coming up in a couple of days — that's a lot to deal with at once. I want to make sure we come up with a plan that works for you. Before we discuss options, would it be alright if I ask you a few questions to get the full picture?"

Listens attentively, makes eye contact, positions as collaborative rather than prescriptive.

---

History

"Can you tell me in your own words what's been happening with the pain? When did it start, and what does it feel like?"

Listens for spontaneous pain, lingering quality after stimulus.

"Does anything set it off — hot or cold drinks, biting? And when it starts, does it ease off quickly, or does it linger for a while after? Is it keeping you up at night?"

"Has this tooth been worked on before — any fillings or treatment? Have you had any swelling around the jaw or face?"

"Any medical conditions I should know about — heart conditions, blood thinners, diabetes, allergies to any medications?"

"Now, practically speaking — how long will you be away interstate, and is it something you could see a dentist for over there if things got worse, or is that very difficult where you're headed?"

---

Diagnosis and Explanation

"Thank you — that's really helpful. Based on everything you've described — the pain coming on by itself, lingering for a long time after something hot or cold, and the fact it's disturbing your sleep — this is a condition called irreversible pulpitis. What that means is the nerve inside your tooth is severely inflamed, and at this stage, it simply won't recover on its own. The nerve is essentially dying."

"Now, I want to be upfront with you about something important, because I think you were hoping painkillers might get you through the trip. I completely understand why — that's a very reasonable thing to want. But I need to explain why that approach carries a real risk here."

"When the nerve becomes this inflamed, pressure builds up inside the tooth. That pressure actually prevents pain medication from reaching the nerve effectively — the blood supply to the area is so compromised that analgesics can't do their job properly in there. Paracetamol and ibuprofen can take the edge off briefly, but they cannot treat the source. And without treating the source, this pain is very likely to get significantly worse — possibly into a spreading infection or swelling — which would be a far more difficult and potentially dangerous situation to manage if you're interstate and not near your regular dentist."

---

Negotiating the Treatment Plan

"So given that you're travelling in two days, let me walk you through your realistic options so we can decide together what makes the most sense."

"Option one, and my first recommendation, is to start the root canal treatment today. I would do the first stage now — that involves removing the inflamed nerve tissue, cleaning the canal, and placing a medicated temporary filling. This typically gives excellent relief and dramatically reduces the risk of things flaring up while you're away. When you're back, we complete the remaining stages at your convenience. This is the option I think gives you the best chance of a comfortable trip."

"Option two is an emergency pulpotomy — a quicker procedure where I remove just the most inflamed portion of the nerve to release the pressure. It's a partial solution, not a permanent one, but it can provide significant relief if time today is very limited, with the understanding that full root canal treatment follows when you return."

"Option three is extraction. If you genuinely don't want to keep this tooth, I can remove it today. I do want to be honest about the trade-offs — you'd be losing a natural molar, which affects chewing function, and replacement options like an implant or bridge involve additional cost and treatment down the track. But it is a definitive solution."

"Option four is painkillers only. I respect that this is ultimately your decision, and I won't force any treatment on you. However, I have to be honest — there is a genuine risk the pain will escalate significantly while you're travelling, and could develop into a swelling or spread of infection. If that happens interstate, you'd be managing a dental emergency in an unfamiliar place, possibly through a hospital emergency department, which I'd really want to help you avoid."

"If you do choose to go with painkillers only, I'd recommend paracetamol one gram every four to six hours, alternating with ibuprofen four hundred milligrams every six to eight hours — provided there's no reason you can't take anti-inflammatories. I want to be clear that codeine-containing products are not recommended first-line and won't add meaningful benefit here. I'll give you my contact details, and I can help you identify a dental practice near where you're staying in case things worsen."

---

Safety Net and Closing

"My strong recommendation, given the two days you have, is that we start the root canal today. It takes the pressure off the nerve, settles the pain, and gives you the best chance of travelling comfortably. We don't need to finish the whole thing now — just the first stage is enough to get you through."

"Whatever you decide, I want you to go away with a clear plan. If you choose treatment today, we can get started right now. If you'd like a moment to think or ask me anything more before deciding, I'm happy to do that too."

"Are there any questions about anything I've explained? And can I ask — how are you feeling about your options?"

Provides written emergency contact details and, if patient declines treatment, provides written information on accessing urgent dental care interstate including the Dental Emergency Helpline.

E3
Pain After RCT Done By Another Dentist (Complaint Handling + Clinical Reasoning)
Category:** Endodontics / Communication & ethics · Time:** 11 minutes · Opens with:** Candidate · Difficulty:** Exam-ready

CASE SUMMARY

Patient had RCT 3 days ago by a different dentist (temporary band + GIC filling). Pain on biting, not sensitive to hot/cold. X-ray shows slightly inadequate obturation. Patient wants to know why the previous dentist did RCT and if something went wrong, plus pain management.

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

Opening (1 min)

"I understand you're in some pain after your root canal treatment a few days ago, and you have some questions about it. Let's start with how you're feeling and what's going on, then we'll figure out the best plan."

History (2 min)

Pain history (biting pain — suggests high filling, occlusal trauma, or inflammation, not necessarily failure), "How are you taking your painkillers — what and how often?", "Does the filling feel high, or like the metal band is rubbing your gum?"

Investigation (1 min)

Clinical exam for high spots, band fit, vitality/crack testing of neighboring teeth, review of X-ray

Explaining Possible Causes WITHOUT Blaming or Defending the Other Dentist (2 min) — INFLECTION 1: The diplomatic tightrope

"There are several possible reasons for pain after a root canal, and most of them are actually quite normal:

  1. Inflammation around the tooth — even after the nerve is removed, the tissue around the root can stay a bit inflamed for several days; this is common and usually settles within 3-5 days
  2. A high filling — if the temporary filling is sitting slightly proud, it can make biting uncomfortable; this is a simple fix
  3. The metal band rubbing your gum — also an easy adjustment
  4. Occasionally, there can be more complex causes — extra canals that are hard to detect, or the filling material not quite reaching the end of the root

I can see on the X-ray that the filling material looks slightly short of where we'd ideally want it. This doesn't necessarily mean anything went wrong — sometimes canals are curved or narrow and difficult to fully instrument, and the dentist will often plan to monitor and complete treatment in further visits. I'd like to speak with your previous dentist to understand the full picture and why they may have scheduled your follow-up in 2 weeks, as root canal treatment can take multiple visits to complete."

Why this matters: The candidate must not throw the other dentist under the bus, nor cover for them — the goal is honest, careful, non-defensive communication.

Addressing "Was something wrong?" Directly (1 min) — INFLECTION 2

"I understand you're wondering if something went wrong. Right now, what I'm seeing is consistent with normal post-treatment healing, possibly with a high spot contributing. The X-ray finding isn't unusual and doesn't necessarily indicate an error — but I want to be straightforward with you: if you have ongoing concerns, you absolutely have the right to ask your dentist directly, or if you're not satisfied with their answer, you can contact the practice manager or, if needed, AHPRA's health complaints process. That's entirely your right."

Management (1.5 min)

"Today, let's:

  1. Check and adjust the band/filling if it's high
  2. Manage your pain with paracetamol and ibuprofen
  3. Review in 3 days — if the pain has settled, you'll go back to your dentist to complete the treatment as planned. If not, we may need to consider re-treatment or referral to a specialist."

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Takes thorough pain history distinguishing biting pain (mechanical) from thermal sensitivity (pulpal)
  2. ✅ Examines for high spots, band fit before assuming treatment failure
  3. ✅ Explains multiple possible causes of post-RCT pain without alarming the patient unnecessarily
  4. ✅ Handles the "did something go wrong" question honestly without defensively covering for colleague OR inappropriately criticizing them
  5. ✅ Informs patient of their right to complain/seek answers (practice manager, AHPRA) without being prompted
  6. ✅ Provides appropriate short-term pain management
  7. ✅ Plans appropriate follow-up and continuity of care back to original dentist

TG4 ALERTS

Post-RCT pain is common and often self-limiting (3-5 days) — TG4: don't over-medicalize normal post-treatment inflammation.
Professional conduct around colleague's treatment — Avoid both unwarranted criticism and inappropriate defense; stick to clinical facts and patient's right to information/complaint processes.

INFLECTION POINTS

PointWeakStrong
"Did something go wrong?"Either says "no, nothing wrong" defensively, or "yes, that looks bad" criticallyExplains findings factually, notes this isn't unusual, but validates patient's right to ask questions/complain
DiplomacyThrows other dentist under the bus OR refuses to discuss the X-ray findingsDiscusses findings honestly and clinically, without assigning blame
Complaint pathway infoNot mentioned unless patient asksProactively mentions practice manager and AHPRA as patient's right
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • "Post-obturation pain at 3 days, particularly on biting, is within the normal range — periapical tissues are inflamed from instrumentation and sealer. This typically peaks at 24–48 hours and resolves over 1–2 weeks. The absence of hot/cold sensitivity post-obturation is reassuring."
  • "The obturation appears short of the apex radiographically. I note this — short fills can increase risk of failure — but I cannot tell the patient this definitively caused their symptoms. Short obturation doesn't always fail. This is something to monitor at 6 months, not to catastrophise today."
  • "If pain persists or worsens beyond 2 weeks, or if there are signs of swelling or sinus tract, I would reassess with CBCT and consider referral to an endodontist for retreatment review."
  • "I will not comment on whether the previous dentist made an error without evidence. I can describe what I observe, note it in the records, and monitor — that is the appropriate medico-legal and professional position."
Patient Reframes
  • "Root canal treatment accesses a space that has been sealed off, often with infection present. The instruments and materials cause temporary inflammation at the root tip — like bruising from the inside. What you're feeling is that healing process."
  • "Think of it like a deep tissue massage — it treats the underlying problem but leaves you sore for a few days after. That soreness is expected; it doesn't mean something went wrong."
  • "The fact that it's sore on biting but not on hot or cold is actually a good sign — hot/cold sensitivity after a root canal would suggest incomplete treatment. Biting soreness is consistent with normal healing."
Curveball Deflectors
  • "Did the other dentist do something wrong?" → "From what I can see today — the discomfort level, the timing — this is within the normal post-treatment range. The fill does look slightly short, which I've documented, and I'll monitor that. But I can't tell you from today's assessment that there was an error. What I can tell you is that I'll keep a close eye on this."
  • "Should I go back to them or come to you?" → "Either is fine — I'm happy to manage this going forward. If you'd prefer continuity with the original dentist, I can write them a note about my findings. The important thing is that someone is monitoring this at 6 months."
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ▶
STAGE: Opening

Greets the patient warmly and settles them into the chair.

"Hello, I'm Dr. [Name]. I understand you've had a root canal treatment done a few days ago and you're experiencing some pain. That must be quite uncomfortable, and I also hear that you have some questions about the treatment itself — I want to make sure we address all of that today. Let's start by hearing how you're feeling, and then we'll have a thorough look and make a plan together. Does that sound okay?"

---

History

"Can you tell me exactly where the pain is and when did it start? Is it the same tooth that had the root canal, or somewhere else?" Listens carefully.

"On a scale of zero to ten, how would you rate the pain? And what brings it on — does it happen when you bite down, or is it there all the time?" Confirms biting pain. "Does the pain linger for a long time after biting, or does it settle quickly once you stop?"

"Very important question — is the tooth sensitive to anything hot or cold at all?" Confirms no thermal sensitivity. "Good, that's actually a reassuring sign. When a root canal is completed, the nerve tissue is removed, so thermal sensitivity typically disappears. Biting pain tells us something slightly different."

"Does the filling or the metal band feel high — like the tooth is hitting first compared to your other teeth? Any discomfort from the band rubbing against your gum?" Notes response.

"Are you taking any pain relief at the moment? What are you taking and how often?" Confirms current analgesic use. "Have you had any swelling, discharge, or fever since the appointment?" Confirms no systemic signs.

---

Clinical Examination

"I'd like to do a few quick checks now — I'll be very gentle."

Performs careful visual and tactile examination of the tooth and surrounding gingiva. Checks the fit and margins of the metal band. Uses articulating paper to assess the occlusion. Notes any high spots on the temporary restoration. Gently palpates the periapical region and percusses the tooth. Reviews the provided radiograph carefully, noting that the obturation appears slightly short of the radiographic apex.

"Thank you for your patience. I have a clear picture now of what's happening."

---

Explaining Possible Causes — Without Blaming or Defending the Previous Dentist

"Let me explain what I'm finding and what might be causing your discomfort, because there are actually several possibilities — and most of them are quite normal after root canal treatment.

First, even after the nerve is removed from inside the tooth, the tissue around the tip of the root can remain inflamed. Your body is still healing from the procedure, and this kind of biting discomfort is very common in the first three to five days — it typically settles on its own.

Second, when I checked your bite with the articulating paper, I can see the temporary filling is sitting slightly high. That means when you close, this tooth is hitting harder than your others, which can create significant soreness. That's a very straightforward adjustment I can make today.

Third, looking at your X-ray — and I want to be honest and clear with you here — I can see the filling material appears to finish slightly short of where we'd ideally want it to be at the root tip. Now, this doesn't automatically mean something went wrong. Canals can be narrow, curved, or have complex anatomy that makes them genuinely difficult to fully instrument and fill. It's also possible your dentist has planned to complete or review the treatment over the course of several appointments, which is entirely appropriate. I'd like to contact your previous dentist to understand their full treatment plan and findings before drawing any conclusions."

---

Addressing "Did Something Go Wrong?" — Honest, Ethical, Non-Defensive

"I understand that this is your main concern — you want to know whether something went wrong. I want to be completely straight with you. What I'm seeing today is consistent with normal post-treatment discomfort, compounded by a slightly high filling, and an X-ray finding that needs further monitoring. I cannot tell you with certainty, without your dentist's full records and clinical notes, whether the outcome reflects a difficult case or something that needs to be revisited.

What I can tell you is this: you have every right to ask your original dentist directly to explain their findings and their plan going forward. If after that conversation you still have concerns and don't feel they've been adequately addressed, you can speak with the practice manager. And if you remain unsatisfied, you are entitled to make a formal complaint through AHPRA's health complaints process — that is absolutely your right, and I'd encourage you to use it if you need to."

---

Management Plan and Safety Net

"Here is what I'd like to do for you today. I'm going to adjust the band and the temporary filling so it no longer sits high — that alone may give you quite a bit of relief.

For pain relief, please take paracetamol one gram every four to six hours as needed, and you can alternate that with ibuprofen four hundred milligrams every six to eight hours — that combination works very well for this type of inflammation. Please take the ibuprofen with food, and if you have any history of stomach problems, high blood pressure, or you take blood thinners, let me know and we'll adjust accordingly.

I'd like to see you back here in three days. If the pain has settled by then, the plan would be for you to return to your original dentist to complete the treatment as they've scheduled — and I'll send them a brief note about today's findings. If the pain is not improving or is getting worse, we may need to discuss further assessment, retreatment, or a referral to an endodontic specialist.

Do you have any questions about anything I've said today? I want to make sure you feel fully informed and comfortable with the plan."

E4
Periapical Infection After Amalgam Filling (Colleague's Work, Apical Radiolucency)
Category:** Endodontics / Communication & ethics · Time:** 11 minutes · Opens with:** Patient · Difficulty:** Exam-ready

CASE SUMMARY

Regular patient, severe pain on lower molar, amalgam filling placed by colleague 2 weeks ago. X-ray shows caries under the filling and apical radiolucency. Patient upset, hasn't slept for 2 nights.

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

Opening & Empathy (1 min)

"I'm really sorry to hear you've been in so much pain and haven't been sleeping — that sounds awful. I'm here to help you today. Let's go through what's happening and sort out a plan."

History (1.5 min)

Pain character, triggers, "What was the reason for the filling? Did you have symptoms before it was placed?", "Did the previous dentist take an X-ray before filling?"

Explanation — Careful, Non-Defensive (2 min) — INFLECTION 1

"I've taken an X-ray, and I can see there's still some decay underneath the filling, and an infection has developed at the tip of the root. I want to explain a few things:

Sometimes, when there's deep decay close to the nerve, dentists make a judgment call to leave a small amount behind on purpose — removing all of it risks exposing the nerve and requiring root canal treatment immediately. This is actually a recognized technique. However, in your case, it looks like there may have been more decay remaining than ideal, or the tooth's nerve may have already been silently dying before the filling was placed — sometimes that happens without any symptoms beforehand.

I don't have your previous records in front of me, so I can't say for certain what the clinical reasoning was at the time. I'd like to speak with my colleague to understand the situation better, and then come back to you with more information. In the meantime, let's focus on getting you out of pain."

Why this matters: The candidate must NOT speculate or assign blame without facts, but also must not dismiss the patient's legitimate concern.

Management — Treating the Infection NOW (2 min)

"Right now, you have an infected tooth, and we need to deal with that today:

  1. Root canal treatment — I can start by removing the infected nerve and placing medication inside to reduce the infection, then a temporary filling. Once you're pain-free, we complete it with a permanent filling and likely a crown given the extent of decay
  2. Extraction — if you'd prefer not to keep the tooth, alongside discussion of replacement options
  3. Pain relief today — paracetamol and ibuprofen"

Addressing the Complaint Pathway (1 min) — INFLECTION 2

"I understand you might be upset about how this has unfolded, and that's completely valid. You do have options: I'm happy to facilitate a conversation between you and my colleague directly, or if you'd prefer, I can take you to speak with our practice manager about a formal complaint process. If at any point you're not satisfied with how this is resolved, you can also contact AHPRA. It's entirely your choice how you'd like to proceed."

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Manages pain and infection as immediate priority (RCT or extraction)
  2. ✅ Explains findings honestly without speculating on colleague's exact reasoning without records
  3. ✅ Avoids both defensive covering AND inappropriate criticism of colleague
  4. ✅ Commits to following up with colleague before drawing conclusions
  5. ✅ Proactively offers complaint pathway options (direct conversation, practice manager, AHPRA)
  6. ✅ Provides appropriate analgesia
  7. ✅ Plans clear next steps for both clinical treatment and the complaint/communication issue

TG4 ALERTS

Periapical infection radiographic timeline — Radiolucency typically takes 3 weeks to several months to become visible; its presence at 2 weeks suggests pre-existing pathology rather than a 2-week-old problem, which is clinically relevant context (not necessarily evidence of treatment error).
Antimicrobial stewardship — Antibiotics only indicated if systemic signs present (swelling, fever) — direct treatment (RCT/drainage) is the primary intervention.

INFLECTION POINTS

PointWeakStrong
Explaining the apical lesion timelineDoesn't mention that radiolucency takes weeks-months to appearExplains this nuance — suggests issue may predate the recent filling, providing important clinical context
Colleague conversationAvoids the topic entirely OR commits to a verdict without facts"I'd like to speak with my colleague to understand the full picture before drawing conclusions"
Complaint pathwayOnly provides if directly askedProactively offers direct conversation, practice manager, and AHPRA as options
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • "The X-ray shows caries under the restoration and a periapical radiolucency — this is consistent with pulp necrosis and periapical periodontitis secondary to an undetected or rapidly progressing deep lesion. Two weeks is sufficient time for pulp death if the decay was within 1–2mm of the pulp."
  • "Acute management tonight: I need to decide between pulpectomy with drainage through the access, incision and drainage if there is a fluctuant swelling, or both. Antibiotics alone are not adequate — the source of infection must be addressed."
  • "Regarding the colleague's work: I observe caries under the restoration on X-ray. I cannot determine from today's radiograph whether that decay was present at time of placement or has progressed since. I document what I see; I do not speculate about causation."
  • "If the patient requests a formal complaint pathway, I explain: AHPRA handles registration and conduct concerns; the HCCC handles specific complaints about treatment. My role is to treat the current problem and provide documentation if formally requested."
Patient Reframes
  • "You haven't slept in two nights and you're in significant pain — that's a dental emergency and we're treating it exactly like that. Let's get you comfortable first, then we'll go through the plan properly."
  • "I know you have questions about how this happened — and those are completely valid questions. But right now, the most important thing is to drain this infection and get you out of pain. Once you're comfortable, I'll explain everything I found."
  • "This isn't about blame — the question of cause matters, but it doesn't change what your tooth needs tonight. We treat the tooth; questions about what happened can be addressed separately and calmly."
Curveball Deflectors
  • "Was the filling done wrong?" → "What I can see on the X-ray is decay under the filling and infection at the root tip. What I can't tell you — and wouldn't be fair to say — is whether that decay was there when the filling was placed or has developed since. I've documented my findings carefully, and if you want to pursue that question formally, I can explain the process."
  • "Who's going to pay for this?" → "That's a fair question. Today's emergency treatment — I'll discuss the fee with you openly. Regarding responsibility for the RCT cost: if you feel the original treatment contributed to this, that's something to raise directly with the treating dentist first. If that's not resolved, there are formal processes through AHPRA and HCCC. I can point you toward those resources."
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ▶
STAGE: Opening & Empathy

Greets patient warmly, makes eye contact, sits at eye level.

"Hi, I'm Dr. [Name], one of the dentists here. Please come in and take a seat — I'm really glad you came in today. I understand you've been having a really difficult time. I'm so sorry to hear you've been in such severe pain and haven't been able to sleep for two nights — that sounds absolutely exhausting and awful, and I want you to know I'm taking this very seriously. My focus today is to understand exactly what's going on, give you some answers, and most importantly, get you out of pain. Is that okay?"

---

History Taking

"Can you tell me a bit about the pain you've been experiencing? Is it constant, or does it come and go? Does anything make it worse — hot, cold, biting down? And on a scale of zero to ten, how would you rate it right now?"

Listens attentively, nods.

"Before the filling was placed two weeks ago, did you have any pain or sensitivity in that tooth? Or was it completely pain-free and the filling was placed because of something found on a routine check?" Pauses to listen. "Did the dentist mention taking an X-ray before the procedure, or discuss how deep the decay was? Did they say anything about it being close to the nerve?"

Listens carefully.

"And since the filling was placed — did the pain start straightaway, or did it build up over time? Have you noticed any swelling in your face or jaw, or do you have a fever at all?"

---

Clinical Findings & Honest, Balanced Explanation

Conducts brief examination — percussion, palpation, temperature test. Notes tenderness to percussion, no response to cold, mild periapical tenderness. Reviews periapical radiograph.

"Thank you for bearing with me. I've had a look in your mouth and reviewed the X-ray, and I want to be completely honest with you about what I can see.

There is some decay remaining underneath the filling, and there is a dark shadow at the very tip of the root — we call that an apical radiolucency — which tells us there is an infection at the root tip. The nerve of this tooth is no longer vital, meaning it has died.

I want to explain something important about that X-ray finding, because I think it may actually help you understand the situation. A shadow like this typically takes several weeks to months to develop and become visible on an X-ray. For it to be present now, two weeks after the filling, it is very likely that this infection, or the process leading to it, was already underway before the filling was placed — the nerve may have been silently dying without causing you any symptoms beforehand. That is a recognised clinical phenomenon.

Now, I also want to acknowledge that there is decay visible under the filling, and that is something I need to look into further. Sometimes, with very deep decay close to the nerve, a dentist makes a deliberate, clinically recognised decision to leave a tiny amount of softened dentine to avoid exposing the nerve — it is called stepwise excavation, and it can be a valid approach. I cannot tell you with certainty what the clinical reasoning was in your case, because I don't have the notes from that appointment in front of me. What I can tell you is that I am not going to dismiss your concerns — they are completely valid — and I will be speaking with my colleague to understand exactly what was found and what decisions were made at the time. I will come back to you with that information. For now, though, I want to focus on getting you better."

---

Immediate Management Plan

"Right now, you have an infected tooth, and that needs to be treated today. I want to go through your options with you.

The first option, and the one I would recommend to save the tooth, is root canal treatment. I can begin that today — I would remove the infected nerve tissue, thoroughly clean and disinfect the canals, and place a medicated dressing inside to settle the infection. I would then seal the tooth with a temporary filling, and we would complete the root canal over one or two more appointments. Given the extent of decay, you would likely need a crown on this tooth long-term to protect it — but that's something we plan together further down the track.

The second option is extraction — removing the tooth entirely. That would resolve the infection and the pain, though we would then want to discuss replacing the tooth, for example with an implant or a bridge, to preserve your bite and jaw bone. That is entirely your choice.

In terms of pain relief — please take paracetamol one gram every four to six hours, and you can alternate that with ibuprofen four hundred milligrams every six to eight hours. Taking them together is safe and very effective. Please take ibuprofen with food. I am not going to prescribe antibiotics at this stage because there are no signs of spreading infection — no swelling in your face, no fever — and the most effective treatment for this infection is actually opening the tooth and removing the source, which is what the root canal achieves. Antibiotics alone would not fix this.

Do you have any questions about those options? Which direction would you like to go?"

---

Addressing the Complaint Pathway & Closing

"Before we get started, I also want to address something, because I think it matters. I understand you may be feeling upset, confused, or let down by what has happened, and that is completely valid. You deserve answers, and you have every right to seek them.

If you are comfortable, I am happy to facilitate a direct conversation between you and my colleague — sometimes there is an explanation we are not yet aware of, and having that conversation can be helpful. Alternatively, if you would prefer a more formal process, I can introduce you to our practice manager today, who can walk you through how to raise a formal complaint within our practice. And if at any point you feel that those options haven't resolved your concerns, you are absolutely entitled to contact AHPRA — the Australian Health Practitioner Regulation Agency — directly. It is entirely your choice how you would like to proceed, and I will support you through any of those options.

I want to be clear: my commitment to you is to be transparent, to follow up with my colleague, and to keep you fully informed. You are a valued patient here, and what you are going through matters.

Do you have any questions before we begin? Let's get you out of pain today."

E5
Dental Abscess with Draining Sinus in a Child (5-Year-Old)
Category:** Endodontics / Pediatric · Time:** 11 minutes · Opens with:** Candidate · Difficulty:** Exam-ready

CASE SUMMARY

5-year-old girl, mild discomfort on primary molars (64/65) previously filled by school dentist. Mother noticed a "sinus"/pimple above the tooth recently. Mother confused why fillings were needed despite controlling sugar intake. No treatment plan required — gather information and answer parent's concerns.

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

Opening & Empathy (1 min)

"Thanks for bringing [child] in today. I understand you've noticed something unusual near one of her teeth — let's talk through what's going on, and I'll do an examination to understand it better."

History (2 min)

HOPC (pain, swelling, when pimple noticed), dental history (previous fillings, OH routine — Brushing, Fluoride, Snacking, Tank water), medical history (allergies especially to milk), social history (diet, water source)

Addressing the Parent's Confusion — INFLECTION 1: "We don't give her sugar, why does she have cavities?"

"I hear that you've been really careful about her sugar intake, and that's great — but cavities can actually develop from a few different sources beyond just obvious sweets. Things like:

  • Natural sugars in fruit, fruit juice, or even crackers and starchy snacks can feed the same bacteria
  • If she's not getting fluoridated water (you mentioned tank water) — fluoride is really protective and without it, teeth are more vulnerable
  • Sometimes, despite a great diet, bacteria can still cause decay, especially in the deep grooves of back teeth where food gets trapped easily

So this isn't about you doing something wrong — there are multiple factors at play, and we can work out what's contributing in her case."

Examination Findings & Diagnosis (1.5 min)

"What I'm seeing is called a dental abscess with a draining sinus — essentially, there's an infection inside one of her back teeth that has tunneled through the bone and gum to the surface, which is what's created that 'pimple' you noticed. The good news is that because it's draining, the pressure is relieved, so she's not in a lot of pain. But the infection itself still needs treatment."

Explaining the Pathway (1.5 min)

"What likely happened: the original filling was quite deep, close to the nerve. Sometimes, despite our best efforts, bacteria can still get into the nerve and cause an infection — this can happen silently, without much pain, which is why you might not have noticed anything was wrong until you saw the sinus tract."

Management Options (1.5 min)

"Because this is a baby tooth and we're getting close to when it would naturally fall out, our main options are:

  1. Temporize the tooth — place a soothing medicated dressing to manage the infection until it naturally exfoliates or until we can plan definitive treatment
  2. Extraction — if the roots have already started resorbing (which is normal as baby teeth prepare to fall out) or if there's significant decay near where the roots meet, extraction with a space maintainer might be the better option, especially since premature loss can cause space problems for the adult tooth coming in

I'll take an X-ray to see how close she is to losing this tooth naturally, and that will help guide which option makes more sense."

Prevention (1 min)

"Going forward — fluoride is going to be really important given the tank water situation, so we'll do fluoride varnish applications, and I'd recommend a fluoride toothpaste appropriate for her age. We'll also look at her diet chart together to spot any hidden sugar sources."

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Validates parent's confusion without dismissing it ("you're not doing something wrong")
  2. ✅ Explains multiple potential causes of decay beyond obvious sugar (juice, snacks, fluoride access)
  3. ✅ Diagnoses dental abscess with draining sinus/fistula correctly
  4. ✅ Explains pathogenesis (deep filling → silent infection → sinus tract formation)
  5. ✅ Discusses age-appropriate management (temporize vs. extract based on tooth's natural exfoliation timeline)
  6. ✅ Identifies fluoride access as a modifiable risk factor (tank water)
  7. ✅ Plans preventive measures (fluoride varnish, dietary review)

TG4 ALERTS

Fluoride access for children on tank/non-fluoridated water — TG4 recommends fluoride varnish and appropriate toothpaste use for children without fluoridated water access.
No antibiotics needed when actively draining — TG4: a draining sinus relieves pressure; antibiotics are not routinely needed unless systemic signs are present.

INFLECTION POINTS

PointWeakStrong
Parent's "we don't give her sugar" confusionImplicitly blames parent or doesn't address the confusionValidates concern, explains multiple non-obvious sugar/risk sources
Tooth management decisionDefaults to "let's just take it out"Considers natural exfoliation timeline via X-ray before deciding temporize vs. extract
Fluoride discussionNot mentionedIdentifies tank water as a risk factor and recommends varnish + appropriate toothpaste
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • "A draining sinus on a primary tooth means chronic periapical infection — the body has found an outlet for the pus. The tooth often doesn't hurt because the pressure is being relieved. That doesn't mean the infection is minor."
  • "Treatment options here are pulpectomy (to retain the tooth and space), or extraction with a space maintainer. The decision hinges on restorability, stage of root resorption, and the proximity of the permanent successor on X-ray."
  • "Primary teeth are not optional — early loss of a primary molar causes space loss that can compromise the eruption pathway of the permanent successor. A space maintainer is not overkill for a 5-year-old; it's standard of care."
  • "Antibiotics alone will not close the sinus — they reduce systemic spread but don't address the source. Pulp treatment or extraction is required to resolve it."
Patient Reframes
  • "The sinus — that little pimple on the gum — is actually your child's body coping with the infection. It's draining it safely rather than letting it spread. But we need to treat the source, or it will keep coming back."
  • "I know it seems dramatic to treat a baby tooth so aggressively — but this tooth is holding space for the adult tooth underneath it. Losing it too early can push other teeth into the gap, which creates a much bigger problem later."
  • "This doesn't mean your child has done anything wrong — or that you have. This type of decay can happen quickly in young children, especially with certain tooth shapes and saliva chemistry."
Curveball Deflectors
  • Parent: "Just pull it out — it's only a baby tooth." → "I completely understand that instinct — but that tooth is acting as a space holder for the adult tooth coming in. If we extract without a space maintainer, neighbouring teeth drift and the adult tooth may not have room to erupt correctly. If we go ahead with extraction, we place a space maintainer at the same appointment."
  • Parent: "Can't you just give antibiotics?" → "Antibiotics will reduce the infection temporarily — but the sinus will return because the source inside the tooth is still there. They're not a definitive treatment here, they're a bridge to the right treatment."
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ▶
STAGE: Opening & Establishing Rapport

Walks to the waiting area, greets mother and child warmly, escorts them into the surgery.

"Hi there, I'm Dr. [name] — it's lovely to meet you both. And what's your name, sweetheart? That's a beautiful name. Come on in and have a seat."

Addresses the mother directly, maintaining a warm and unhurried tone.

"Thanks so much for bringing her in today. I understand you've noticed something a little unusual near one of her back teeth — a sort of pimple on the gum. I can completely understand why that would be worrying, especially when she's only had these fillings done recently. What I'd like to do is have a chat with you first, ask a few questions, and then take a look inside her mouth so I can explain exactly what's going on and what we can do about it. Does that sound okay?"

---

History Taking

"First, has she been bothered by any pain or discomfort around those back teeth? Any sensitivity to hot or cold food, or anything that wakes her up at night?"

Listens carefully to the mother's response, nodding and noting details.

"And when did you first notice that little pimple on the gum? Has it changed in size, or is it the same?"

"Has she had any facial swelling, a temperature, or seemed generally unwell at all?"

"Now, tell me a little about her oral hygiene routine at home — how often are we brushing, and is she using a toothpaste with fluoride in it?"

"And in terms of her diet — I know you mentioned you're careful about sugar, which is wonderful — but does she have fruit juice, dried fruit, crackers, or any other snacks between meals?"

"One important question — what's your water source at home? Are you on town water, or do you use tank water or a filter?"

Notes: mother confirms tank water, low apparent sugar intake, fillings done by school dentist.

"And just to make sure we're thorough — is she on any medications, or does she have any allergies, particularly to penicillin or any antibiotics, or to milk or dairy products?"

---

Addressing the Parent's Concern — "We Don't Give Her Sugar, Why Does She Have Cavities?"

Pauses, makes eye contact with the mother, and speaks with genuine empathy.

"I really want to address something you mentioned, because I think it's been weighing on you — and I want to be very clear: you are not doing anything wrong. You've clearly been thoughtful and careful, and that matters enormously."

"The thing is, tooth decay isn't only about the obvious sweets. Natural sugars in everyday foods — things like fruit, fruit juice, crackers, and starchy snacks — can feed exactly the same bacteria in the mouth that cause cavities. These bacteria don't distinguish between a lolly and a piece of bread; they just need fermentable carbohydrates, and they produce acid regardless."

"The second factor that I think is really significant in your daughter's case is the water supply. Fluoride, which is added to town water here in Australia at around 0.6 to 1.1 parts per million, is incredibly protective for developing teeth. Children on tank water or filtered water miss out on that daily passive protection, and that can make teeth more vulnerable to decay even with a careful diet."

"And finally, the back baby teeth have quite deep grooves where food and bacteria can get trapped very easily — sometimes even with perfect brushing, those pits can harbour decay. So there are multiple factors at play here, and none of them are about neglect on your part."

---

Examination Findings and Diagnosis

Conducts a gentle clinical examination with good light. Notes a parulis — a small, localised swelling on the buccal gingiva above tooth 64/65. Notes the previously placed restorations. No facial swelling, no lymphadenopathy. Child is afebrile and not systemically unwell.

"Thank you for being such a brave girl — you did brilliantly."

Turns to the mother.

"So, what I can see is what we call a dental abscess with a draining sinus tract — sometimes called a fistula. What's happened is there's an infection deep inside the nerve of one of her back teeth, and that infection has slowly worked its way through the surrounding bone and gum tissue to the surface, which is what's formed that little pimple you noticed."

"The actually good news here — and I mean this — is that because it's draining, the pressure inside has been relieved, which is why she hasn't been in significant pain. Her body has effectively found a way to decompress it. But the infection itself hasn't resolved; it's just finding an exit point. So we do need to treat it."

"There are no signs of spreading infection — no facial swelling, no temperature, no swollen neck glands — so she's safe and well today, and we don't need to rush to hospital. Because the sinus is draining, antibiotics are not needed at this stage — they wouldn't address the source of the problem anyway, and we want to be careful about using them only when genuinely necessary."

---

Management Plan

"In terms of what to do next, I'd like to take a small X-ray of that area — it's a very quick, low-dose image — to see exactly how much of the root remains and how close this tooth is to naturally falling out on its own. That will guide us between two sensible options."

"The first option is to temporise the tooth — that means removing the old filling, cleaning out the infected tissue from the nerve space, and placing a soothing medicated dressing. This can settle the infection and allow the tooth to remain in place until it naturally exfoliates, which for a tooth in that position is usually around age ten to eleven."

"The second option, and this may actually be the more straightforward choice depending on what the X-ray shows, is to extract the tooth. If the root has already started to resorb — which is completely normal as baby teeth prepare to fall out — or if the decay is very extensive, extraction is often the simpler and more predictable path. If we do extract it, we would consider placing a space maintainer — a small appliance — to hold the space open for the adult tooth that's coming through, so we don't lose valuable room."

"Once I've seen the X-ray, I'll talk you through exactly what I'm recommending and why, and we'll make that decision together."

---

Prevention and Closing

"Going forward, I'd like to do a fluoride varnish application for her today — it's quick and completely comfortable, and it will give her teeth an immediate boost of protection. For home use, she should be using a toothpaste with at least 1,000 parts per million of fluoride — something like a standard children's toothpaste from the pharmacy. She should be using a pea-sized amount twice a day, and spitting but not rinsing afterwards so the fluoride stays on the teeth longer."

"Because you're on tank water, her dentist should review fluoride supplementation at each visit, and the varnish applications every six months will be really important."

"I'd also love to do a quick diet diary review with you today — sometimes there are hidden sugar sources that surprise families, and it's not about blame at all, just about finding what we can adjust."

"Do you have any questions at all? You've asked really the right questions today, and I hope this has made things a little clearer. She's in good hands and we'll look after her."

S1
Crown Fractured During Extraction — Oroantral Communication
Category:** Oral Surgery | **Time:** 11 min | **Difficulty:** Exam-ready

CASE SUMMARY

Upper left first molar (26) crown fractures at the gingival margin during routine extraction. PA radiograph shows roots divergent, close to maxillary sinus. Candidate must manage the complication, communicate clearly, and assess for oroantral communication (OAC).

CANDIDATE BRIEF

You are extracting tooth 26 (upper left first molar) for a 52-year-old patient. The crown fractures at the gingival margin during luxation. Pre-op PA shows divergent roots with the palatal root estimated 1–2mm from the floor of the maxillary sinus. Manage the complication and communicate with the patient.

EXAMINER CONTEXT

Patient is awake (local anaesthesia only). Initially alarmed when the dentist stops and says something broke. Will ask directly: "Did something go wrong?" and "What happens now?" If tested for OAC (blowing nose, Valsalva), the sinus is communicated — bubbling visible in socket. Patient becomes more anxious when informed of the complication but settles with calm, clear explanation.

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

Immediate management (1 min) — INFLECTION 1

Stop. Do not blindly instrument the socket.

"I need to pause here — the crown has separated from the roots, which can happen with heavily filled teeth. I want to take a moment to assess the situation carefully before we continue."

Assess for OAC (1 min)

"I'm going to ask you to gently blow your nose while I watch the socket — please don't blow hard." Observe for bubbling (positive Valsalva = OAC confirmed).

If OAC confirmed:

  • Do NOT attempt to retrieve palatal root if it is small (<5mm) and asymptomatic
  • Pack socket with haemostatic material
  • Place buccal fat pad flap or refer for Caldwell-Luc if large defect

Communicating the complication honestly (2 min) — INFLECTION 2

"I want to be honest with you about what's happened. The crown broke during the extraction — this can happen with teeth that have large fillings or have been root-canal treated, as they become brittle over time. More importantly, the test I just did showed that a small communication has opened between the tooth socket and your sinus — essentially a tiny hole. This is a known complication given how close your root was to the sinus, and it was mentioned as a risk when we discussed the procedure."

Management plan (2 min)

"Here's what we'll do:

  1. We'll close that opening today with a small procedure — I'll bring some tissue across to seal it
  2. You'll need to avoid blowing your nose, sneezing with your mouth closed, or drinking through straws for 2–3 weeks — pressure differences will reopen the hole before it heals
  3. I'll prescribe a nasal decongestant and chlorhexidine mouthwash
  4. No smoking (impairs healing, worst thing for this)
  5. Review in 1 week, then again at 3 weeks"

If patient asks about the remaining root fragment:

"The small fragment of root near the sinus — if it's small and asymptomatic, leaving it is actually safer than chasing it, which risks pushing it into the sinus. We'll monitor it with X-rays."

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Stops immediately, does not blindly instrument
  2. ✅ Performs Valsalva/nose-blow test to confirm OAC
  3. ✅ Communicates complication honestly, links it to pre-discussed risk
  4. ✅ Manages small root fragment conservatively (leave if <5mm, asymptomatic)
  5. ✅ Post-op instructions specific to OAC (no blowing, straws, sneezing with mouth closed)
  6. ✅ Prescribes nasal decongestant + chlorhexidine, advises against smoking
  7. ✅ Plans review at 1 and 3 weeks
  8. ✅ Knows when to refer (large defect, root displaced into sinus)

TG4 ALERTS

Antibiotics for OAC: TG4 recommends amoxicillin for OAC given sinus communication risk. If penicillin-allergic: metronidazole. Prescribe on the day.
Smoking: TG4 — smoking is the single biggest risk for failed OAC closure. Emphatic advice: no smoking for minimum 2 weeks post-op.

INFLECTION POINTS

PointWeakStrong
Complication managementContinues instrumenting or panicsStops, assesses systematically before acting
OAC testSkippedPerforms Valsalva test and interprets result
Honest disclosureVague ("there was a small issue")Explicit, links to pre-discussed risk, no blame-shifting
Root fragment decisionInsists on removing itMakes evidence-based decision to leave if small + asymptomatic

COMMON PITFALLS

  • ❌ Aggressive instrumentation trying to retrieve root fragment → displaces it into sinus
  • ❌ Not testing for OAC after crown fracture near sinus
  • ❌ Dismissing the complication without proper informed discussion
  • ❌ No post-op OAC-specific instructions (blowing, straws, sneezing)
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • "Oroantral communication diagnosis: I confirm with a Valsalva test — if air moves from the mouth through the socket into the nose, communication is confirmed. An OAC >2mm will not close spontaneously and requires surgical closure."
  • "Immediate management: buccal advancement flap for most OACs, or a figure-8 resorbable suture for very small communications in appropriate patients. The goal is tension-free primary closure over a clot."
  • "Post-operative instructions are specific and non-negotiable: no nose blowing for 2 weeks, no smoking, no straw use, sleep with head elevated. I prescribe nasal decongestant (oxymetazoline) and amoxicillin/clavulanate to prevent sinusitis."
  • "Retained root tip in the sinus: if the root has genuinely entered the sinus, I do not blindly probe or irrigate — that risks pushing it further. CT first, then ENT-assisted Caldwell-Luc or FESS approach if retrieval is needed."
Patient Reframes
  • "The back root of that upper molar sits directly below the floor of your sinus — in some patients, there's almost no bone separating them. When the root came out, it opened a small communication between your mouth and your sinus. That's what we're closing now."
  • "This is a recognised complication of upper molar extractions — it's not a sign of a technical error, it's anatomy. What matters is that we've identified it and we know exactly how to manage it."
  • "The no-nose-blowing rule sounds odd, but it's critical — air pressure from blowing your nose can push bacteria from the mouth into the sinus before the tissue heals. Two weeks of care now saves a chronic sinus infection."
Curveball Deflectors
  • "Did you do something wrong?" → "Oroantral communication is a recognised, documented complication of upper molar extractions — particularly when the roots are close to the sinus floor, which yours were. It's not caused by incorrect technique; it's an anatomical risk. What's important is that I've identified it and I'm managing it correctly right now."
  • "What happens if you don't close it?" → "If left open, you'd develop chronic sinusitis — food and bacteria would enter the sinus with every meal. You'd have persistent sinus pain, discharge, and potentially need ENT surgery later. Closing it now prevents all of that."
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ▶
STAGE: Immediate Management — Stopping and Assessing

Pauses all instrumentation immediately. Places the extracted crown fragment on the bracket tray. Checks the patient is comfortable and suction is clear.

"I just need to stop for a moment — please keep your mouth open for me and try to relax. I can feel that the crown has separated from the roots, which can definitely happen, especially with a tooth that has a large filling like yours. I am not going to continue blindly — I want to take a moment to look carefully at what we have and make the safest decision for you. You're doing really well."

Inspects the socket under good light with a fine suction tip. Assesses root positions clinically. Reviews the pre-operative periapical radiograph — notes divergent buccal and palatal roots, palatal root estimated 1–2 mm from the sinus floor.

"Before we go any further, I need to do a quick, gentle test. I'm going to ask you to pinch your nose closed and blow very, very gently — as if you were trying to pop your ears on a plane. Please do not blow hard, just a soft, gentle puff. Ready? Go ahead."

Observes the socket carefully during the Valsalva manoeuvre. Notes visible bubbling of blood within the socket — positive test confirming oroantral communication.

---

Communicating the Complication Honestly

"Thank you, you can relax now. I want to be completely open with you about what that test has shown, because you deserve to know exactly what's happening."

"The crown broke away from the roots during the extraction. This happens — teeth that have had large fillings placed over many years can become quite brittle, a bit like trying to grip a dry biscuit. The roots are still in the socket, and we'll address those carefully in a moment."

"The test I just did showed that a small opening has formed between the tooth socket and the air space of your sinus — the maxillary sinus — which sits just above that tooth. This is called an oroantral communication. It is a recognised complication of removing upper molar teeth, particularly when the roots are positioned very close to the sinus floor, as yours were on your X-ray. In fact, this was one of the risks we discussed before we started today, and it is something we are well prepared to manage."

"I want to reassure you — this is not a crisis. We have a clear plan to close that opening today, and the vast majority of patients heal very well when we follow the right steps. I'll walk you through everything we're going to do."

---

Managing the Root Fragments and the Communication

Returns attention to the socket. Assesses root fragment size and position carefully against the radiograph.

"Looking at your X-ray and the socket, the palatal root fragment appears small and is very close to the sinus floor. Attempting to chase that fragment carries a real risk of displacing it into the sinus itself, which would create a much more significant problem requiring surgery under general anaesthetic. The safest decision — and the one supported by current guidelines — is to leave that small fragment in place, monitor it with X-rays over time, and intervene only if it causes symptoms. That is genuinely the right call for you, not the easy one."

Irrigates the socket gently with sterile saline. Places a haemostatic dressing to pack the socket. Prepares for primary closure using a buccal advancement flap to seal the oroantral communication.

"I'm going to numb the area a little more and bring a small amount of the soft tissue from the cheek side across to seal that opening. The stitches will hold it in place while it heals. The procedure itself takes around ten to fifteen minutes and you will be comfortable throughout."

Performs the buccal flap advancement under adequate local anaesthesia. Places interrupted resorbable sutures. Confirms tension-free, watertight closure of the communication.

---

Post-Operative Instructions and Prescriptions

"Now, what you do in the next two to three weeks is just as important as what I've done today, so I want to go through this carefully with you."

"You must not blow your nose — not at all — for the next three weeks. If you need to sneeze, let it out through your mouth, not your nose. No drinking through straws. No smoking — and I want to be very direct with you here: smoking is the single greatest thing that can stop this from healing. The suction movement and the chemicals in cigarette smoke dramatically increase the risk of the closure breaking down. I would ask you to stop completely for a minimum of two weeks, and ideally longer."

"I'm going to prescribe two things today.
