First, amoxicillin 500 mg three times daily for five days — because there is now a communication with the sinus, we want to reduce any risk of sinus infection. If you have any allergy to penicillin, please tell me now and I'll prescribe something different. Second, a chlorhexidine 0.2 percent mouthwash — use it gently, twice a day, just letting it sit in your mouth rather than rinsing vigorously. I'll also give you a saline nasal spray to keep the sinus moist and reduce congestion."

---

Safety Net and Review Plan

"I want to see you back here in one week so I can check the closure is holding and remove any sutures that haven't dissolved. We'll take another X-ray at that visit to keep an eye on the root fragment. I'll also see you again at three weeks, and we'll reassess completely at that point."

"If before your review you notice air or fluid coming through that area when you breathe or swallow, if you develop a bad smell or taste, a nosebleed, or any facial swelling or fever — please contact us immediately, do not wait for your appointment. Those signs could suggest the sinus has become infected and we would need to act quickly."

"Do you have any questions about anything I've explained today? I know that's a lot to take in, and I want to make sure you feel clear about everything before you leave."

S2
Consent for Extraction — Warfarin + Denosumab (MRONJ Risk)
Category:** Oral Surgery | **Time:** 11 min | **Difficulty:** Exam-ready

CASE SUMMARY

68-year-old patient on warfarin (INR 2.4 yesterday) and denosumab (for osteoporosis). Needs extraction of tooth 46. Candidate must address both warfarin management and MRONJ risk from denosumab before proceeding.

CANDIDATE BRIEF

You are consenting a 68-year-old patient for extraction of tooth 46 (non-restorable due to caries + periapical abscess). Medical history: atrial fibrillation (on warfarin, INR 2.4 checked yesterday), osteoporosis (on denosumab injection every 6 months, last injection 4 months ago). Your task: obtain consent with appropriate discussion of warfarin management and MRONJ risk.

EXAMINER CONTEXT

Patient is cooperative but anxious after being told by a friend that "you have to stop blood thinners before dental work." Has not heard of MRONJ. Will ask "Is it safe to have the tooth out given all my medications?"

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

Opening (1 min)

"Before we proceed with the extraction today, I want to talk through a couple of things related to your medications — your blood thinner and your bone-strengthening injection — because they both need to be factored into how we do this safely."

Warfarin: Continue, don't stop (2 min) — INFLECTION 1

"I know you may have heard that blood thinners need to be stopped before dental work. For most dental extractions, that's actually NOT the case anymore. Your INR was 2.4 yesterday — that's within the safe range for dental extractions (up to 3.5 is generally acceptable). Stopping warfarin puts you at risk of a clot or stroke, which is a much bigger risk than a bit of extra bleeding in the mouth after an extraction. We manage any extra bleeding locally — with pressure, sutures, and a special foam inside the socket."

MRONJ risk from denosumab (2.5 min) — INFLECTION 2: This is the critical teaching point

"The other medication I want to discuss is your denosumab — the bone-strengthening injection. There is a rare but serious complication called medication-related osteonecrosis of the jaw — MRONJ for short. It means that in a small number of patients on this type of medication, when the jaw bone is disturbed (like with an extraction), the bone doesn't heal properly and a patch of bone can actually die.

The risk is low — probably less than 1 in 100 for someone on your duration and medication. But it's a risk we need to discuss before any extraction. The main way to reduce that risk is:

  • Extracting atraumatically (as gently as possible)
  • Primary wound closure (stitching the gum closed over the socket)
  • Keeping the site very clean afterward
  • Avoiding smoking

There is some evidence that taking a drug holiday (pausing denosumab for a period) may reduce risk, but the evidence is still evolving. I'd recommend we contact your prescribing doctor before proceeding to discuss this, unless the tooth is causing an acute infection that makes it urgent."

Management plan (1 min)

  1. Confirm INR today (or use yesterday's if <24 hrs) — within acceptable range
  2. Contact prescribing GP/specialist regarding denosumab holiday or proceed decision
  3. If proceeding: atraumatic extraction, primary closure, chlorhexidine rinse, no smoking
  4. Review 1 week post-op, then 3 weeks

Safety-netting (1 min)

"After the extraction — watch for: excessive bleeding not controlled by biting on gauze for 30 min, severe pain at day 4–5 (may indicate dry socket), exposed bone in the socket that's white or grey and doesn't heal (this needs prompt review — possible MRONJ). Call us immediately if any of these."

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Warfarin: do NOT stop, explains rationale (clot/stroke risk > local bleeding)
  2. ✅ Confirms INR is within acceptable range for dental extraction
  3. ✅ Explains MRONJ risk from denosumab in plain language
  4. ✅ Quantifies risk appropriately (low but real)
  5. ✅ Discusses risk reduction (atraumatic extraction, primary closure)
  6. ✅ Recommends contacting prescriber re: denosumab holiday decision
  7. ✅ Specific safety-netting for MRONJ (exposed bone, non-healing socket)

TG4 ALERTS

Warfarin: Do NOT stop — TG4: check INR within 24h, proceed if ≤3.5. Local haemostasis (pressure, sutures, haemostatic foam) manages post-op bleeding. Stopping warfarin = stroke/clot risk.
MRONJ: Bone medications — Denosumab and bisphosphonates → MRONJ risk. Atraumatic technique + primary closure + post-op monitoring are the primary risk mitigation strategies.

INFLECTION POINTS

PointWeakStrong
Warfarin advice"Stop the warfarin a few days before" (DANGEROUS)"Continue warfarin — stopping puts you at clot/stroke risk, which is more dangerous"
MRONJ explanationNot mentioned or vagueExplains mechanism, quantifies risk, describes risk mitigation
Denosumab holidayIgnores or dictates decisionRecommends discussing with prescriber; acknowledges evolving evidence
Safety-netting"Call if you have problems"Specific: exposed white/grey bone, non-healing socket = MRONJ red flag
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • "For warfarin: check INR on the day of the procedure. INR <3.5 — proceed with local haemostatic measures (oxidised cellulose, tranexamic acid mouthwash 4.8%, sutures). Do NOT stop warfarin — the risk of thromboembolic event from stopping outweighs the risk of local bleeding we can manage."
  • "For denosumab: this is a RANK-L inhibitor, not a bisphosphonate — different mechanism, but still carries MRONJ risk. Unlike bisphosphonates, the effect is reversible (half-life ~25 days). A drug holiday is not recommended by current evidence, but specialist consultation with the prescribing team is good practice for elective extractions."
  • "Pre-operative: coordinate with the patient's physician. Post-operative: primary closure, oxidised cellulose in socket, tranexamic acid 4.8% mouthwash TID for 5 days, avoid NSAIDs."
  • "MRONJ risk counselling applies regardless of whether the extraction proceeds — the patient should know the signs (exposed bone >8 weeks, non-healing wound) and when to return."
Patient Reframes
  • "We're not stopping your blood thinner before the procedure — the evidence shows that's more dangerous than the bleeding risk we can manage locally. We control any bleeding at the time with packing and a special mouthwash."
  • "The denosumab you're on does affect healing of the jaw bone — it's not a high risk but it's not zero either. I want to explain that so you understand why I'm asking you to watch for any non-healing after the extraction and come back if you're concerned."
Curveball Deflectors
  • "My GP said to stop the warfarin for 3 days before." → "That's a common instruction, but the current dental guideline is actually different from what's recommended for some surgical procedures. For dental extractions, stopping warfarin increases clot risk without significantly reducing bleeding risk — because we can manage the bleeding locally. I'd like to call your GP briefly to align on this, with your permission."
  • "Is it safe to have a tooth out on these medications?" → "Yes — with the right precautions, which we've now planned for. The risk of not extracting an infected tooth is actually higher than the risk of a controlled extraction with proper haemostatic measures."
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ▶
STAGE: Opening and Introduction

"Good morning, come on in and have a seat. My name is Dr. [name], and I'll be looking after you today. Before we go ahead with removing that lower right molar — tooth 46 — I want to sit down with you and talk through a couple of important things related to your medications. You're on a blood thinner called warfarin, and you're also having a bone-strengthening injection called denosumab. Both of these need to be factored into how we do this safely and with your full understanding. Is that alright with you? Do you have any questions before we start?"

Confirms the patient has the INR result from yesterday and has the medical history in front of them.

"So just to confirm — you had your INR checked yesterday, and it came back at 2.4. And your last denosumab injection was about four months ago. Is that right? Good. Let me walk you through what both of those mean for today's procedure."

---

Warfarin Management

"The first thing I want to address is your warfarin. Now, you may have heard in the past that blood thinners need to be stopped before any dental procedure. I want to reassure you that for a straightforward tooth extraction, that is no longer the recommendation — and for very good reason. Your INR of 2.4 is well within the safe range for dental extractions. We consider an INR of up to 3.5 to be acceptable for proceeding. So yours is comfortably within that window.

The reason we do not stop your warfarin is that the risk of stopping it — even for a few days — is actually much greater than the risk of a little extra bleeding in the mouth. You're on warfarin because of your atrial fibrillation, which means your heart is at risk of forming a clot if your blood isn't adequately thinned. Stopping warfarin, even briefly, could put you at risk of a stroke or a serious clot, and that is a far more dangerous outcome than manageable post-operative bleeding.

What we do instead is manage any extra bleeding locally. That means firm pressure with gauze, placing a dissolving haemostatic foam called Surgicel inside the socket, and stitching the gum closed. We'll also give you clear instructions on biting on gauze at home. Most patients on warfarin do very well with this approach. So please do not stop or reduce your warfarin — take it exactly as prescribed."

---

MRONJ Risk from Denosumab

"Now, the second medication I need to discuss carefully with you is your denosumab — the injection you receive every six months for your osteoporosis. This is extremely important, and I want to take a moment to explain it clearly.

There is a rare but serious condition called medication-related osteonecrosis of the jaw — we shorten it to MRONJ. What this means is that in a small number of patients taking bone-modifying medications like denosumab, when the jawbone is disturbed — such as during a tooth extraction — the bone can struggle to heal properly. In some cases, a patch of bone can actually die, becoming exposed in the mouth and failing to recover. This can be quite difficult to treat once it develops, which is why we take it very seriously before proceeding.

I want to emphasise that the risk for someone in your situation — on denosumab for osteoporosis rather than cancer treatment — is low. We estimate it at less than one in a hundred, possibly lower. But it is a real risk and you deserve to know about it and be part of the decision.

The ways we reduce this risk are: performing the extraction as gently and carefully as possible — what we call an atraumatic technique — stitching the gum closed completely over the socket to encourage proper healing, keeping the area very clean with a chlorhexidine mouthrinse afterward, and avoiding smoking entirely during the healing period.

There is also some discussion in the literature about a drug holiday — pausing denosumab for a period around the time of surgery — to allow the bone's normal healing capacity to recover. The evidence on this is still evolving and it's not universally agreed upon, but I would strongly recommend we contact your prescribing doctor or specialist before proceeding, to discuss whether a planned pause is appropriate in your case. If the tooth were causing a severe spreading infection, we might need to act more urgently — but at this stage, taking a short amount of time to coordinate with your doctor is the right approach."

---

Management Plan

"So here is what I'd like to do. I'll write to your general practitioner and the specialist managing your denosumab today, explaining the situation and asking for their input on timing. Once we have their guidance and everyone is in agreement, we'll schedule the extraction. On the day of the procedure, we'll confirm your INR is still within range — ideally checked within 24 hours of the appointment. We'll use a careful, atraumatic technique, place haemostatic foam in the socket, suture the gum closed, and start you on a chlorhexidine mouthrinse twice daily for two weeks. I'll review you at one week post-operatively to check healing, and again at three weeks."

---

Safety-Netting and Closing

"Before we finish today, I want to make sure you know what to watch for after the extraction. Some oozing for the first day or two is completely normal. However, I want you to contact us or present to an emergency department if you experience bleeding that does not stop after biting firmly on gauze for thirty minutes, or if you see bright red active bleeding rather than a gentle ooze.

If you develop severe pain around day four or five, that could indicate a dry socket, which is treatable — please call us promptly. And most importantly, given your denosumab, if you notice any area of exposed bone in the socket — tissue that looks white or grey and is not covered by healing gum — that does not improve over the following weeks, I need you to come back and see me straight away. That is the early sign of MRONJ and the sooner we review it, the better the outcome.

Do you have any questions about anything we've discussed? I know that's a lot of information, so please feel free to ring the practice at any time. I'll make sure all of this is also written up clearly for you to take home today. Thank you for your time — we'll be in touch as soon as we hear from your doctor."

S3
Prednisolone + Bisphosphonate — MRONJ + Adrenal Crisis Risk
Category:** Oral Surgery | **Time:** 11 min | **Difficulty:** Exam-ready

CASE SUMMARY

Patient on prednisolone 15mg/day (3 years, rheumatoid arthritis) and alendronate (bisphosphonate, 5 years). Needs surgical extraction of lower molar. Candidate must identify both MRONJ risk AND adrenal suppression/crisis risk.

CANDIDATE BRIEF

68-year-old patient on prednisolone 15mg daily for 3 years (rheumatoid arthritis) and alendronate weekly for 5 years (osteoporosis). Needs surgical extraction of tooth 36. Your task: assess the risks of both medications and plan the extraction appropriately.

EXAMINER CONTEXT

Patient is cooperative, not anxious about the extraction itself, but has been told by their rheumatologist to "check with the dentist before stopping any medications." Will not volunteer the steroid dose unless specifically asked.

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

History — INFLECTION 1: Get the steroid dose and duration

"Can I ask about your prednisolone — what dose are you on, and how long have you been taking it?"

(15mg daily for 3 years = adrenal suppression is confirmed — this is the critical detail weak candidates miss by not asking specifically)

Explaining the two risks (2 min) — INFLECTION 2

Risk 1 — Adrenal crisis:

"Prednisolone at 15mg daily for 3 years means your body has reduced its own production of cortisol — the stress hormone. Normally, your body produces extra cortisol in response to surgery. Because your adrenal glands have been suppressed by the prednisolone, they may not be able to do that. Without that extra cortisol on the day of surgery, you could experience what's called an adrenal crisis — low blood pressure, dizziness, collapse. It's rare, but we need to manage it.

What this means practically: we need to give you a steroid cover dose on the day of surgery — typically double your usual prednisolone dose on that morning, with your breakfast. I'll coordinate with your rheumatologist to confirm the right cover dose."

Risk 2 — MRONJ from bisphosphonate:

"Alendronate is a bisphosphonate — it strengthens bone but also changes how bone heals after extraction. After 5 years of use, there's a small but real risk of MRONJ — medication-related osteonecrosis of the jaw — where the socket doesn't heal and bone is exposed. The risk for oral bisphosphonates is lower than IV bisphosphonates (used for cancer), but at 5 years, it's not negligible. We manage it with gentle technique, primary wound closure, and careful post-op monitoring."

Plan (2 min)

  1. Contact rheumatologist: confirm steroid cover dose for day of surgery
  2. Proceed with extraction under local anaesthesia
  3. Atraumatic surgical extraction, primary closure
  4. Post-op chlorhexidine, soft diet, no smoking
  5. Review 1 week, 3 weeks (monitor for MRONJ)
  6. Do NOT stop alendronate without rheumatologist input

Safety-netting

"After the extraction — call us if you feel dizzy or faint (could be steroid-related), if you have severe pain at day 4–5 (dry socket), or if you see exposed bone in the socket that's not healing."

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Asks specifically about steroid dose AND duration (15mg × 3 years = suppression)
  2. ✅ Identifies adrenal suppression and explains the physiological mechanism
  3. ✅ Plans steroid cover dose, coordinates with rheumatologist
  4. ✅ Identifies MRONJ risk from 5-year alendronate use
  5. ✅ Plans atraumatic extraction + primary closure
  6. ✅ Does NOT stop either medication without specialist input
  7. ✅ Safety-netting covers both adrenal (dizziness/faint) and MRONJ (exposed bone)

TG4 ALERTS

Prednisolone ≥10mg daily for >3 weeks — TG4: adrenal suppression confirmed. Steroid cover required for surgical stress. Typical protocol: double the morning dose on day of surgery. Coordinate with prescriber.
Bisphosphonate + MRONJ — TG4: risk increases with duration and IV route. Oral bisphosphonates at 5 years carry real risk. Atraumatic extraction + primary closure is the evidence-based mitigation.
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • "Two separate risk conversations required for this patient — do not conflate them: (1) MRONJ from bisphosphonate, (2) adrenal crisis from long-term corticosteroid. Both need to be addressed before proceeding."
  • "Adrenal suppression: patients on prednisolone >7.5mg/day for >3 weeks have likely suppressed the HPA axis. For major dental surgery, supplemental hydrocortisone may be required — this is patient and procedure-specific. Current guidance: minor procedures under LA generally do not require supplementation; major surgery may. Consult with the prescribing physician."
  • "MRONJ — oral bisphosphonate risk: lower than IV bisphosphonates but not zero. Duration and potency matter. For extractions in patients on oral BPs: do not recommend routine drug holiday (no evidence of benefit); ensure primary closure; prescribe CHX mouthwash; 3-monthly review to monitor healing; counsel about risk and signs."
  • "Document the MRONJ consent discussion carefully — specific mention of the risk percentage, the signs, and the patient's understanding."
Patient Reframes
  • "There are two separate things I need to talk you through before we proceed — one about your bone medication, one about your prednisolone. They're not related to each other, but both are important for planning this safely."
  • "The risk of jaw bone problems from your medication is real but small — most patients never experience it. What makes the difference is careful technique, closing the gum over the socket, and monitoring healing closely."
  • "Your prednisolone means your body's stress response is dampened — so we may need to give a small steroid supplement before major procedures to cover that. It's a simple precaution, not a reason to avoid treatment."
Curveball Deflectors
  • "My rheumatologist said it's fine to extract." → "I'm glad they're supportive — and I want to proceed. I just need to be the one who manages the dental-specific risks: the MRONJ risk from the bisphosphonate and the adrenal precautions. Those aren't in your rheumatologist's scope to plan, but they're in mine."
  • "Do I need to stop the prednisone?" → "No — stopping long-term prednisolone suddenly is dangerous. We keep it going exactly as prescribed. What I need to know is whether you might need a small extra dose of steroid on the day of the procedure to help your body cope with the stress of the extraction. That's a conversation with your prescribing doctor."
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ▶
STAGE: Opening and History

"Good morning, come in and take a seat. My name is Dr. Chen — I'm the dentist here today. I understand you're having some trouble with your lower back molar, tooth 36, and we're looking at having it removed. Before we talk about the procedure, I'd like to ask you a few questions about your medical history, because I want to make sure we plan this as safely as possible for you. Is that alright?"

"I can see from your notes you're taking prednisolone — can I ask, what dose are you currently on, and how long have you been taking it?" Listens carefully. Patient confirms 15 mg daily for three years. "And is that for your rheumatoid arthritis? Wonderful, thank you. And who manages that for you — is it a rheumatologist?" Confirms specialist involvement.

"Now, you're also on alendronate — the weekly tablet for your bones. How long have you been on that one?" Patient confirms five years. "And that was prescribed for osteoporosis? Good. Are you taking any other medications, including any over-the-counter supplements?" Confirms no other significant medications.

"Have you had any surgeries or extractions before, and if so, did you have any problems with healing or any complications?" Notes no prior surgical concerns. "Do you smoke, or have you smoked in the past?" Notes non-smoker. "Thank you — that's all very helpful. I need to explain two important things about your medications before we go any further, because they both affect how we'll approach your extraction today."

---

Explaining Adrenal Suppression Risk

"The first thing I want to talk about is your prednisolone. Normally, your body produces a hormone called cortisol — your stress hormone — and when you go through something like surgery, your body automatically makes extra cortisol to help you cope with that physical stress. It's a completely natural response."

"However, because you've been taking prednisolone at 15 milligrams every day for three years, your adrenal glands — the small glands that sit above your kidneys and produce cortisol — have essentially been on a long rest. They've been letting the prednisolone do the work, and over time they've reduced their own output. This is called adrenal suppression, and at your dose and duration, it is confirmed."

"What that means practically is that on the day of surgery, if your adrenal glands can't produce that extra cortisol when they're needed, you could experience what's called an adrenal crisis. That might look like feeling suddenly dizzy, faint, your blood pressure dropping — it's uncommon, but it is serious, and we absolutely need to manage it."

"The way we manage it is straightforward: on the morning of your surgery, you would take double your usual prednisolone dose — so 30 milligrams — with your breakfast, before you come in. However, I won't finalise that plan without speaking to your rheumatologist first, because they know your full picture. I'll contact them before we schedule the procedure to confirm the steroid cover protocol. You should continue your regular prednisolone as normal — please don't stop it."

---

Explaining MRONJ Risk

"The second thing I need to discuss is your alendronate. Alendronate is a bisphosphonate — it works by slowing down the cells that normally break down bone, which makes your bones denser and more resistant to fracture. That's very beneficial for osteoporosis."

"The concern with extractions is that this same mechanism can interfere with how the jaw bone heals after a tooth is removed. In a small but real number of patients on long-term bisphosphonates, the socket doesn't heal properly, the bone loses its blood supply, and you end up with what we call MRONJ — medication-related osteonecrosis of the jaw. That means exposed bone in the socket that simply won't heal over."

"Now, the risk is much lower with your oral alendronate tablet compared to the intravenous bisphosphonates used for cancer treatment. However, at five years of use, your risk is not negligible, and I have to be honest with you about that. We estimate the risk for oral bisphosphonates at approximately 0.1 percent or less, but it is a risk we take seriously."

"Importantly, stopping alendronate before surgery does not reliably reduce that risk — the medication incorporates into your bone and stays there for years. So please do not stop it without discussing it with your prescribing specialist. I will seek their input as part of your pre-operative planning."

---

Management Plan

"So here is exactly how we'll proceed. First, I'll write to your rheumatologist this week to confirm the steroid cover protocol for the day of surgery — most likely double your morning prednisolone dose of 30 milligrams taken with breakfast before you arrive."

"We'll schedule the extraction under local anaesthesia — lignocaine will be appropriate for you. During the procedure I'll use an atraumatic surgical technique: careful, gentle elevation to minimise trauma to the surrounding bone and soft tissue. I'll place sutures to achieve primary closure of the socket — that means stitching the gum closed over the extraction site to encourage proper healing and reduce bone exposure."

"Post-operatively, I'd like you to rinse gently with chlorhexidine 0.2 percent mouthwash twice daily, eat soft foods, avoid alcohol, and avoid any vigorous rinsing for the first 24 hours. I'll see you back at one week to check healing and remove the sutures, and again at three weeks specifically to monitor for any early signs of MRONJ. If I see anything concerning, we'll refer promptly."

---

Safety Net and Closing

"Now, there are a few things I'd like you to call us about straight away after the extraction. If on the day of the procedure you feel dizzy, lightheaded, or faint — even after you leave the surgery — please call us or go to your nearest emergency department, because that could be a sign of adrenal insufficiency and needs to be treated urgently."

"If around day four or five you develop severe, throbbing pain in the socket — worse than the day before — that may indicate a dry socket, which is very treatable. And importantly, if at any point over the following weeks or months you notice exposed bone in the socket — something that looks white or yellow and isn't covered by gum tissue — even if it's painless, please contact us straight away. That needs to be assessed for MRONJ promptly."

"Do you have any questions about anything I've explained today? I want to make sure you feel comfortable and informed before we go ahead. Once I've heard back from your rheumatologist, my receptionist will be in touch to schedule the appointment. Thank you for being so thorough with your medical history — it genuinely helps us look after you properly."

S4
Non-Healing Socket / Dry Socket (Acute Alveolar Osteitis)
Category:** Oral Surgery | **Time:** 11 min | **Difficulty:** Exam-ready

CASE SUMMARY

Patient presents 4 days post-extraction of tooth 36 with severe, throbbing pain radiating to the ear, not responding to paracetamol/ibuprofen. Socket appears empty with exposed bone. Smoker. Diagnosis and management of dry socket (acute alveolar osteitis).

CANDIDATE BRIEF

A 34-year-old patient presents 4 days after extraction of tooth 36 complaining of severe pain radiating to the ear and jaw that started day 2 post-op. They were managing with paracetamol and ibuprofen but the pain is getting worse, not better. They smoke 10/day.

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

Opening & Empathy (1 min)

"I'm sorry to hear you're in so much pain — let's sort this out today. Can you tell me what the pain feels like and when it started?"

History (1.5 min) — INFLECTION 1: Confirm dry socket, rule out infection

  • Pain character: severe, throbbing, radiating to ear (classic dry socket — alveolar osteitis)
  • Timing: onset day 2–3 post-op (fits dry socket timeline)
  • What patient has done since: rinsing, sucking straws, smoking? (all risk factors)
  • Fever, swelling, pus, lymphadenopathy? (absence = dry socket, not infection)

Examination (1 min)

"I'll look at the socket now."

Findings: Empty socket, no clot, exposed bone, food debris, fetid odour. No facial swelling or trismus. Surrounding tissue mildly inflamed.

Diagnosis in plain language (1 min)

"What you have is called dry socket — it's one of the more painful complications that can happen after an extraction. Normally after a tooth is removed, a blood clot forms and protects the bone while healing happens. In your case, that clot either didn't form properly or was dislodged, leaving the bone exposed directly to the air and food — which is extremely painful. This is not an infection — it's bone pain."

Management — INFLECTION 2: Treatment is irrigation + dressing, NOT antibiotics

"The treatment today is:

  1. Gently irrigating the socket with warm saline to remove debris
  2. Placing a medicated dressing — a lint soaked in Alvogyl or a similar obtundent agent — directly into the socket. This protects the exposed bone and significantly reduces the pain, usually within minutes to hours
  3. I'll also pack some of the dressing material around the socket margin

This needs to be repeated every few days until the socket starts to heal from the base up. You'll need to come back in 2–3 days."

Pain management (1 min)

"For pain at home: continue paracetamol 1000mg and ibuprofen 400–600mg, alternating every 3–4 hours (not together — space them out). If you can take ibuprofen on a full stomach, that combination is more effective than either alone."

Smoking (1 min)

"I have to be direct — smoking is the single biggest risk factor for dry socket, because the sucking motion and chemicals both interfere with clot formation and healing. You can see the result here. If you continue smoking, this socket will be very slow to heal. Even cutting down for the next week would make a significant difference."

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Differentiates dry socket from infection (no fever, no swelling, no pus, exposed bone)
  2. ✅ Explains pathogenesis in plain language (clot lost → exposed bone)
  3. ✅ Treatment: irrigation + obtundent dressing (NOT antibiotics)
  4. ✅ Review every 2–3 days until healing from base
  5. ✅ Paracetamol + ibuprofen alternating for home pain control
  6. ✅ Specifically discusses smoking as causal factor (honest, direct)

TG4 ALERTS

Antibiotics NOT indicated for dry socket — TG4: dry socket is NOT an infection. Antibiotics have no role unless there are signs of infection (fever, lymphadenopathy, pus). Obtundent dressing + irrigation is the treatment.
NSAID + paracetamol alternating — TG4 first-line for acute dental pain. More effective than either alone when spaced correctly.

INFLECTION POINTS

PointWeakStrong
Diagnosis"You might have an infection"Correctly identifies dry socket based on timeline, appearance, and absence of infection signs
AntibioticsPrescribes amoxicillin "just in case"Explains antibiotics have no role — this is not an infection
TreatmentPainkillers onlyIrrigation + Alvogyl dressing, repeat in 2–3 days
SmokingMentions it brieflyDirect: "smoking caused this; continued smoking will delay healing significantly"
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • "Dry socket diagnosis: Day 3–5 post-extraction, severe radiating pain not controlled by standard analgesia, visible empty socket with exposed or necrotic bone, halitosis. This is an inflammatory condition, not an infection — antibiotics are not indicated."
  • "Treatment: thorough gentle irrigation with warm saline, placement of an obtundent dressing (alvogyl or zinc oxide eugenol-based) into the socket — not tightly packed, just resting. Analgesia: NSAIDs are first-line (ibuprofen 400mg with paracetamol). Review in 2–3 days and re-dress as needed."
  • "Do not curettage aggressively — this disrupts the healing tissue at the socket periphery without benefit. The dressing provides pain relief; the socket will heal from the periphery inward."
  • "Risk factors to address for patient education: smoking, OCP use (female patients should schedule extractions in the first week of the pill cycle when oestrogen is lowest), traumatic extraction, poor irrigation post-op."
Patient Reframes
  • "Dry socket is painful — genuinely painful — but it's not dangerous. The blood clot that usually forms didn't stay in place, which leaves the nerve endings exposed to air and food. The dressing I'm placing will cover those nerve endings and give you relief within minutes to hours."
  • "This isn't a sign of infection and it's not a sign that anything went wrong — it's a healing complication that occurs in about 3–4% of extractions. Some patients are simply more prone to it."
  • "The dressing doesn't heal the socket — it just makes the healing bearable. The socket will fill in from the edges over the next 2–4 weeks regardless."
Curveball Deflectors
  • "It's infected isn't it? I need antibiotics." → "I understand it feels like an infection because of the pain and the smell — but dry socket is actually an inflammatory condition, not a bacterial infection. Antibiotics won't help here and I wouldn't want to prescribe something that won't work. The dressing is the right treatment."
  • "You must have done something wrong during the extraction." → "I completely understand the frustration — you're in significant pain and looking for an explanation. Dry socket is a known complication that occurs even with textbook extractions. It's related to how your body forms and retains a clot, which varies between individuals and is influenced by factors like smoking and hormones."
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ▶
STAGE: Opening & Empathy

"Hi, I'm Dr. [name], one of the dentists here. Please come in and take a seat. I can see from your notes that you've had a pretty rough few days since your extraction — I'm sorry you're going through this. Let's have a thorough look at what's going on and get you sorted today. Before I examine you, I'd like to ask you a few questions so I understand exactly what's been happening. Is that okay?"

"Can you tell me, in your own words, what the pain has been like?"

History Taking

"When exactly did the pain start? Was it immediately after the extraction, or did it come on a day or two later?"

Candidate listens attentively. Patient describes pain starting around day two, which is worse than the original toothache.

"And where is the pain radiating? Is it going up toward your ear, down into your jaw, or both?"

"On a scale of zero to ten, how would you rate it right now?"

"Have you noticed any swelling on the outside of your face, any pus or discharge from the socket, or any fever — feeling hot and sweaty?"

"Have you had any difficulty opening your mouth, or pain when swallowing?"

"Are you currently taking anything for the pain? How much paracetamol and ibuprofen have you been taking, and is it helping at all?"

"Now I need to ask a couple of important questions about what you've been doing since the extraction. Have you been rinsing vigorously, using a straw, or spitting forcefully at all in the first few days?"

"And I can see from your notes that you smoke — are you still smoking? About how many per day?"

Candidate notes: severe throbbing pain radiating to ear, onset day two post-op, no fever, no facial swelling, no pus, no trismus, pain not responding to analgesia, patient is smoking ten cigarettes per day.

Examination & Diagnosis

"Thank you — that's very helpful. I'd like to examine the socket now. I'm going to have a look with my mirror and a light. I'll be as gentle as possible."

Conducts visual examination. Findings: empty socket with no visible clot, exposed alveolar bone, food debris present, fetid odour, mild surrounding gingival inflammation. No facial swelling, no lymphadenopathy, no trismus, no purulent discharge.

"Okay, I've had a good look. Thank you for bearing with me."

"What you have is called a dry socket — the medical term is acute alveolar osteitis. Let me explain exactly what that means, because I think it will help you understand why you're in so much pain. When a tooth is removed, a blood clot normally forms in the socket and acts like a protective plug over the bone while everything heals underneath. In your case, that clot has either failed to form properly or has been dislodged, and as a result the bone is completely exposed — directly to air, saliva, and food. Bone is exquisitely sensitive, which is why the pain is so severe and why it radiates all the way to your ear along the nerve pathway. I want to reassure you — this is not an infection. There's no pus, no swelling, no fever, and the socket itself looks clean aside from some debris. It's a pain condition caused by exposed bone, and the good news is that we can treat it today."

Treatment — In-Chair Management

"The treatment for dry socket is very specific, and I'll carry it out right now. Antibiotics are not part of the treatment — this is not an infection, and giving antibiotics when they're not needed can cause more harm than good. What we need to do is two things."

"First, I'm going to gently irrigate the socket with warm saline using a syringe. This will flush out the food debris without disturbing anything around the socket. It may feel a little uncomfortable but I'll be as gentle as I can."

Performs gentle saline irrigation of socket. Debris removed. Patient tolerates well.

"Now the second and most important step — I'm going to place a medicated dressing called Alvogyl directly into the socket. This is a lint material soaked in an obtundent agent — it contains ingredients that soothe the exposed nerve endings in the bone. Most patients notice a significant reduction in pain within minutes to a few hours of this dressing being placed. It doesn't make the socket heal faster, but it covers the exposed bone and gives you enormous relief while the healing happens naturally underneath."

Places Alvogyl dressing gently into socket, ensuring adequate coverage of exposed bone.

"How is that feeling already?"

Home Care, Pain Management & Smoking Advice

"For managing pain at home, I'd like you to continue taking paracetamol one gram — that's two five-hundred-milligram tablets — and ibuprofen four hundred milligrams, but I want you to space them out and alternate them rather than taking them together. So for example, take paracetamol at midday, then ibuprofen at three o'clock, then paracetamol again at six. That alternating approach gives you more consistent pain relief throughout the day and is more effective than either medication on its own. Always take ibuprofen with food. If your pain is still severe tonight despite doing this, please call us."

"I need to be very direct with you about smoking, because it's important you understand this. Smoking is the single most significant risk factor for dry socket — more than any other. The sucking action physically dislodges the clot, and the chemicals in cigarette smoke actively interfere with blood clot formation and the healing process. What you're experiencing right now is, at least in part, a direct consequence of smoking. If you continue to smoke at the same level while this socket is healing, it will take significantly longer, the dressing will need replacing more frequently, and your pain will be harder to control. I strongly encourage you to cut down as much as possible — even reducing for the next week to ten days will make a real difference to how quickly you heal."

"I'll need to see you back here in two to three days to check the socket, change the dressing if needed, and make sure you're healing from the base up. We may need two or three dressing changes in total. Each time the dressing is changed, the socket should be a little less painful. If at any point before your next appointment you develop fever, facial swelling, difficulty opening your mouth or swallowing, please come back or go to an emergency department immediately — as those signs would suggest infection requiring urgent assessment. Any questions at all?"

S5
Post-Surgical Swelling + Infection (Penicillin-Allergic Patient)
Category:** Oral Surgery | **Time:** 11 min | **Difficulty:** Exam-ready

CASE SUMMARY

Patient 5 days post-extraction of wisdom tooth (48) with increasing trismus, facial swelling, and pain. Reports penicillin allergy (rash as a child). Candidate must diagnose post-surgical infection, prescribe correctly avoiding penicillin, and decide if referral is needed.

CANDIDATE BRIEF

29-year-old patient, 5 days post-extraction of 48 (lower right wisdom tooth). Now has worsening pain, reduced mouth opening (trismus, opening to ~20mm), and visible swelling over the right cheek/submandibular area. Temperature 37.8°C. Reports a rash to penicillin as a child, never tested further.

EXAMINER CONTEXT

Patient is in pain and worried. Will ask "Is this serious? Do I need to go to hospital?" If asked about the penicillin allergy in detail: rash was hives as a child after a course of amoxicillin, no anaphylaxis, no throat swelling, no breathing difficulty.

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

History & Examination (2 min)

SOCRATES pain, fever, trismus (mouth opening), swelling (fluctuant/indurated), lymphadenopathy, dysphagia/neck pain/breathing difficulty (red flags for deep space infection).

Clinical assessment: Is this serious? — INFLECTION 1

"Based on your exam — you have a post-operative infection with early spread. Your temperature, degree of swelling, and reduced mouth opening tell me this is beyond a simple surface infection. The important question now is whether this is spreading toward deeper spaces in the neck, which can be life-threatening."

Red flags requiring immediate hospital referral:

  • Dysphagia or drooling (can't swallow)
  • Neck stiffness/swelling
  • Trismus progressing rapidly (Ludwig's angina pattern)
  • Systemic toxicity (high fever >38.5, confusion)
  • Airway compromise

If red flags absent: manage in primary care but with close follow-up.

Allergy clarification — INFLECTION 2: The penicillin allergy myth

"Before I prescribe antibiotics, can I ask more about your penicillin allergy? You mentioned a rash as a child — was it just a skin rash, or did you have any throat swelling, difficulty breathing, or collapse?"

(Rash only, no anaphylaxis = low-risk, may be intolerance or co-incidental viral rash)

"About 90% of people who think they're allergic to penicillin actually aren't — the rash in children is very often caused by the viral infection being treated, not the penicillin. However, without testing, I can't rule it out safely. I'll prescribe an alternative."

Prescribing (1.5 min) — TG4 alert

If not safe to use penicillin (even if low risk — candidate right to be cautious without testing):

  • Metronidazole 400mg TDS × 5 days (covers anaerobes, common post-surgical)
  • Plus: clindamycin 300mg QID × 5 days (covers streptococci)

Or:

  • Doxycycline 100mg BD × 5 days as alternative

Note: Do NOT use erythromycin — poor coverage and GI side effects

Management plan (1.5 min)

  1. Prescribe antibiotics (above)
  2. Regular paracetamol + ibuprofen (if no contraindications)
  3. Warm salt water rinse to promote drainage
  4. Review in 24–48 hours
  5. If not improving or worsening → refer to oral and maxillofacial surgery (OMFS) for incision and drainage
  6. Urgent referral NOW if any red flags

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Assesses severity and screens for red flags (dysphagia, neck spread = Ludwig's)
  2. ✅ Knows when to refer urgently vs. manage in primary care
  3. ✅ Clarifies penicillin allergy history (type of reaction, severity)
  4. ✅ Acknowledges 90% of reported penicillin allergy is not true allergy
  5. ✅ Prescribes correctly: metronidazole ± clindamycin (avoids penicillin)
  6. ✅ Review 24–48 hours with escalation plan
  7. ✅ Does NOT dismiss the allergy without formal testing

TG4 ALERTS

Penicillin allergy: ~90% over-reported — TG4: rash in childhood often viral, not penicillin. However, without formal testing, use alternative. Do NOT assume it's safe without allergy history.
Deep space infection = emergency — Dysphagia, neck swelling, or airway compromise = immediate hospital referral. Do not manage Ludwig's angina in primary care.
Erythromycin: Avoid — Poor oral bioavailability, frequent GI side effects, suboptimal coverage. Use clindamycin or metronidazole instead per TG4.
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • "Assess severity first before reaching for the prescription pad: Is this localised (soft fluctuant swelling, contained to one space) or spreading (crossing fascial planes, trismus, dysphagia, dysphonia, raised floor of mouth, systemic signs)? The latter is a hospital emergency."
  • "Penicillin allergy — first-line alternatives for dental infection: clindamycin 300mg TDS is the most common choice (excellent anaerobic cover). If the allergy is mild (rash only), a cephalosporin (cefalexin) may be considered (approximately 1–2% cross-reactivity). If severe IgE-mediated allergy, avoid all beta-lactams — use clindamycin or metronidazole + clarithromycin."
  • "Do not add metronidazole to clindamycin routinely — both have anaerobic cover; the combination increases GI side effects without clear benefit in most dental infections. Metronidazole monotherapy is an option if clindamycin is contraindicated."
  • "Source control: always. The antibiotic treats the spread; the extraction or I&D treats the source. Prescribing antibiotics without a plan for source control is incomplete management."
Patient Reframes
  • "Antibiotics alone won't cure a dental abscess — they slow the spread, but the source of infection is inside the tooth or the socket. We treat both: the source first, the antibiotics to cover the spread."
  • "I know the swelling is alarming — but the fact that it's still localised means we're catching this at the right time. If it were spreading to your airway or deeper neck spaces, you'd need to be in hospital. Right now, we can manage this here with the right antibiotic and source control."
Curveball Deflectors
  • "Just give me the same antibiotic as last time." → "If the same antibiotic didn't resolve it last time — or if you're allergic to penicillin — then repeating that prescription doesn't make sense. I need to prescribe what actually works for this type of infection and is safe for you specifically."
  • "Why is it getting worse if I've already been on antibiotics?" → "Antibiotics work on the spread — but if the source hasn't been treated, the infection keeps producing bacteria faster than the antibiotic can clear them. That's why source control — treating the tooth or the socket — is the most important step."
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ▶
STAGE: Opening & History

"Hi, come on in and take a seat. I'm Dr. [Name]. I understand you're having some trouble after your wisdom tooth was removed last week — I can see you're uncomfortable, so let's get to the bottom of this together. Can you tell me what's been happening since the extraction?"

Allows patient to describe onset of symptoms, then directs with structured questioning.

"When did the pain and swelling start, and has it been getting worse each day or did it improve at first and then come back? On a scale of zero to ten, how would you rate the pain right now?"

"I'd like to ask about a few specific things, if that's okay. Have you noticed any difficulty swallowing — even just saliva? Any pain or stiffness in your neck? Has anyone mentioned your voice sounds different or muffled? Any difficulty breathing, or a sense that your throat feels tight?"

"Have you had a fever? We've measured your temperature at 37.8 degrees today. Have you felt hot or shivery at home over the past couple of days?"

"How wide can you open your mouth? Let me have a look — I can see you're only getting to about 20 millimetres there, which is quite restricted. Any redness, discharge, or bad taste coming from the socket?"

Conducts extraoral examination. Notes firm, indurated swelling over the right cheek extending toward the submandibular region. No fluctuance detected. Palpates cervical lymph nodes — mildly tender submandibular nodes present. No neck swelling. No drooling. Mouth opening confirmed at approximately 20 mm.

---

Clinical Assessment & Inflection 1 — Severity

"Thank you for bearing with me through that. I want to be completely honest with you about what I'm finding, because I think it's important you understand the picture clearly."

"Based on everything — the five days since your extraction, your temperature, the significant swelling over your cheek and under your jaw, and the fact that you can only open about 20 millimetres — I believe you have a post-operative infection that has spread beyond just the surface of the socket. This is more than a simple dry socket or localised wound infection."

"The most important thing I need to check right now is whether this infection is tracking toward the deeper spaces of your neck. When that happens, it can become a very serious — even life-threatening — situation called Ludwig's angina, where swelling can compromise the airway. That's why I asked about swallowing, neck pain, and breathing."

"The reassuring news is that you don't have any of those red flags right now. You can swallow, your neck is not visibly swollen, your breathing is comfortable, and your temperature, while elevated, is not critically high. That means I can manage this with you here today — but I want to be very clear: if at any point you develop difficulty swallowing, your neck starts to swell, your breathing feels restricted, or you develop a high fever above 38.5 degrees, you must go straight to the emergency department. Do not wait. Do you understand that?"

---

Allergy Clarification — Inflection 2

"Before I prescribe antibiotics, I need to ask you carefully about your penicillin allergy, because this affects exactly what I give you. You mentioned you had a rash as a child — can you tell me a bit more? Was it just a skin rash, or did you also have any swelling of the lips or throat, difficulty breathing, or did you collapse or lose consciousness?"

Listens to patient confirm it was a skin rash only, no anaphylaxis, never formally tested.

"That's really helpful, thank you. I want to explain something about penicillin allergy, because it comes up a lot. Research tells us that around 90% of people who believe they're allergic to penicillin actually are not — the rash that children get is very often caused by the viral infection that was being treated at the time, not the penicillin itself. So it may well be that you could tolerate penicillin safely."

"However — and this is important — without formal allergy testing, I cannot confirm that with certainty. It would not be safe for me to prescribe amoxicillin or any penicillin-based antibiotic today without that confirmation. So I will prescribe you appropriate alternatives that will cover this infection well, and I'd encourage you to discuss formal penicillin allergy testing with your GP when this has resolved."

---

Prescribing & Management Plan

"For the infection, I'm going to prescribe you two antibiotics that work together to cover the range of bacteria involved in post-surgical oral infections. The first is metronidazole 400 milligrams, taken three times a day. The second is clindamycin 300 milligrams, taken four times a day. I'd like you to take both for five days. Take them with food to help with any stomach upset, and please avoid alcohol entirely while you're on the metronidazole."

"For pain, I want you taking paracetamol one gram every four to six hours regularly — do not wait until the pain is severe. You can also alternate that with ibuprofen 400 milligrams every six to eight hours with food, as long as you have no stomach problems or blood pressure issues. Taking them together around the clock will keep you much more comfortable."

"I also want you to do warm salt water rinses — about half a teaspoon of salt dissolved in a glass of warm water — gently rinsed around that area three to four times a day, particularly after meals. This helps keep the area clean and encourages any fluid to drain naturally."

"I want to see you back here in 24 to 48 hours so I can reassess the swelling and trismus. If the antibiotics are working, we should start to see some improvement by then. If you are not improving — or if things are getting worse — I will refer you directly to the oral and maxillofacial surgery team at the hospital for assessment, and potentially incision and drainage under their care."

---

Safety Net & Closing

"I want to make sure you're completely clear on when to seek emergency help. If before your review appointment you develop any difficulty swallowing — even with water — any swelling in your neck, any change in your voice to a muffled or 'hot potato' quality, any difficulty breathing, or a high fever above 38.5 degrees, please call triple zero or go straight to the emergency department. Do not wait to call my clinic. This is non-negotiable."

"I'll write all of this down for you, including the antibiotic names, doses, and the warning signs. Do you have any questions about anything I've said today? I know it's a lot to take in when you're already feeling unwell."

"You're doing the right thing by coming in today. We've caught this at a stage where we can manage it, and with the antibiotics on board and a review in 48 hours, I'm expecting you to turn the corner. Take care, and please don't hesitate to call us if you're worried before then."

S6
Antibiotic Prophylaxis — Prosthetic Heart Valve (High Risk)
Category:** Oral Surgery | **Time:** 11 min | **Difficulty:** Exam-ready

CASE SUMMARY

Patient with prosthetic mitral valve requires extraction. Asks "Do I need antibiotics before the extraction?" Candidate must correctly identify this as a HIGH-RISK indication for prophylaxis (unlike joint replacement, which is NOT a routine indication).

CANDIDATE BRIEF

55-year-old patient presents for extraction of tooth 25 (non-restorable). Medical history: prosthetic mitral valve replacement (2018), on warfarin (INR 2.7 checked today). No allergies. Your task: determine if antibiotic prophylaxis is required, and manage accordingly.

EXAMINER CONTEXT

Patient explicitly asks "My heart specialist told me I need to mention my artificial heart valve before any dental work. Do I need special antibiotics?" Patient is cooperative, not anxious about the extraction itself.

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

Confirm the cardiac history (1 min)

"Thank you for mentioning that — it's very important. Can I ask: is it a mechanical valve or a tissue valve? And has your cardiologist given you a letter or a card to carry?"

Answer the prophylaxis question directly — INFLECTION 1

"Yes — a prosthetic heart valve is one of the specific conditions where antibiotic prophylaxis before dental work is recommended. The reason is this: during extraction, bacteria from your mouth can enter the bloodstream. In most people, this is harmless. But with an artificial valve, those bacteria can settle on the valve and cause a serious infection called endocarditis — which can be life-threatening. The risk is low, but because the consequences are so severe, the guideline is to prevent it."

Contrast with joint replacement (INFLECTION 2)

(If patient mentions they also had a hip replacement and asks if that changes anything)

"Interestingly, a joint replacement does NOT require antibiotic prophylaxis for dental procedures — that's a common misconception. Only specific cardiac conditions, including your prosthetic valve, are listed as high-risk."

Prophylaxis regimen (1.5 min)

  • Amoxicillin 2g orally, 30–60 minutes before the procedure
  • If penicillin allergic: clindamycin 600mg, 30–60 min before

Warfarin: Continue (1 min)

"For your warfarin — INR is 2.7 today, which is within the acceptable range. We'll proceed without stopping it. I'll place a haemostatic dressing in the socket after extraction."

Safety-netting

"After the extraction — if you develop fever, chills, night sweats, or feel unwell in the days or weeks following, please contact your cardiologist promptly. These could be early signs of endocarditis."

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Correctly identifies prosthetic heart valve as HIGH-RISK indication for prophylaxis
  2. ✅ Correctly states joint replacement does NOT routinely require prophylaxis
  3. ✅ Explains mechanism (bacteraemia → valve seeding) in plain language
  4. ✅ Prescribes correct regimen (amoxicillin 2g, 30–60 min pre-op; clindamycin if penicillin-allergic)
  5. ✅ Continues warfarin (INR 2.7 = acceptable for extraction)
  6. ✅ Safety-netting for endocarditis signs post-op

TG4 ALERTS

Prosthetic heart valve = HIGH-RISK — TG4: antibiotic prophylaxis required. Amoxicillin 2g orally 30–60 min before procedure.
Joint replacement ≠ prophylaxis indication — TG4: this is a commonly tested misconception. Joint replacement does NOT routinely require prophylaxis for dental procedures.
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • "Antibiotic prophylaxis is indicated for HIGH-RISK cardiac conditions only: prosthetic heart valve, previous infective endocarditis, repaired cyanotic CHD, cardiac transplant with valvulopathy. Not for murmurs, prolapse, stents, or pacemakers."
  • "Regimen (TG4/AHA): amoxicillin 2g orally 30–60 minutes before the procedure. If penicillin-allergic: clindamycin 600mg OR azithromycin 500mg OR clarithromycin 500mg. Single dose only."
  • "Prophylaxis is indicated for procedures that manipulate the gingival tissue, periapex, or perforate the oral mucosa — not for simple examinations, radiographs, or supra-gingival scaling in healthy gingiva."
  • "If the patient has already taken antibiotics recently for an infection, use a different class for prophylaxis — do not repeat the same antibiotic within 10 days as resistant organisms may have emerged."
Patient Reframes
  • "This is a single antibiotic tablet taken one hour before your appointment — not a course, not ongoing. It's a targeted precaution that significantly reduces the risk of bacteria from your mouth reaching your heart valve."
  • "Your heart valve is at higher risk than the average patient because prosthetic materials can act as a surface for bacteria to stick to. That's not a reason to avoid dental treatment — it's a reason to plan it carefully."
  • "Untreated dental disease creates a constant low-level bacteraemia — which is actually more dangerous for your valve than a single managed dental procedure with prophylaxis. Keeping your mouth healthy protects your heart."
Curveball Deflectors
  • "My cardiologist says I don't need prophylaxis anymore." → "Cardiology guidelines have changed in recent years — and if your cardiologist has reviewed your specific case and removed the recommendation, that supersedes my guidance. Can I ask when that was reviewed and whether it was specific to a prosthetic valve? If so, I'll document that clearly and proceed without prophylaxis."
  • "I take antibiotics before every dental visit — even a scale and clean." → "That's a common practice, but current guidelines have narrowed the indications. Antibiotics carry their own risks — allergy, GI side effects, antibiotic resistance — so we give them only when the benefit is clear. I'll confirm exactly which procedures require prophylaxis for you."
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ▶
STAGE: Opening and Cardiac History Confirmation

"Good morning, come on in and take a seat. I'm Dr. [Name], one of the dentists here today. Before we get started, I just want to go through your medical history carefully, because you've mentioned something very important — your prosthetic mitral valve. I'm really glad you brought that up."

"Can I ask a few quick questions about that? When was the valve replaced — was that the 2018 surgery you mentioned? And is it a mechanical valve, or a tissue valve? The reason I ask is that both types are high-risk, but it's helpful for my records. Has your cardiologist given you a card to carry, or a letter outlining your dental precautions?"

Listens attentively to patient's responses. Confirms: mechanical mitral valve replaced 2018, patient carries a wallet card. No drug allergies. Currently on warfarin, INR checked today at 2.7.

"Perfect — thank you. And just to confirm: no allergies to any medications at all, including penicillin or amoxicillin?"

---

Answering the Prophylaxis Question Directly

"So to answer your question directly — yes, you do need antibiotics before this extraction, and I want to explain exactly why, because it's important you understand this."

"When we do an extraction, bacteria that normally live harmlessly in your mouth can enter your bloodstream — we call that a bacteraemia. In most people, the immune system clears those bacteria without any problem. But with an artificial heart valve, those bacteria can travel through the bloodstream, land on the surface of the valve, and establish an infection there. That infection is called infective endocarditis, and it is a very serious — potentially life-threatening — condition that is very difficult to treat once it takes hold."

"Now, the risk of this happening from a single dental procedure is actually quite low — but the consequences if it does happen are so severe that the guidelines are clear: for someone with a prosthetic heart valve, we must give antibiotic prophylaxis before any procedure that might cause that bacteraemia. This is a firm recommendation."

---

Contrasting with Joint Replacement

"I want to mention something while we're on this topic, because it comes up often. If you've ever had a hip or knee replacement — or if anyone ever told you that you'd need antibiotics before dental work for a joint replacement — I want to clarify that for you."

"A joint replacement does not require antibiotic prophylaxis for dental procedures. That used to be recommended, but the current guidelines are very clear: it is not indicated. The only conditions where we routinely give dental prophylaxis are specific cardiac conditions — and your prosthetic mitral valve is right at the top of that list. So your cardiac history is what guides us today."

---

Prescribing the Prophylaxis Regimen

"The antibiotic we use is amoxicillin — two grams taken orally, thirty to sixty minutes before your procedure. That's one dose only; we don't continue it afterwards. I'll write you a prescription for that today, and I'd ask you to take it here before we begin, so we can confirm the timing."

"Now, because you mentioned no allergies, amoxicillin is exactly the right choice for you. Just so you're aware — if you were allergic to penicillin, we would use clindamycin 600 milligrams instead, taken the same way, thirty to sixty minutes beforehand. But that doesn't apply to you today."

---

Managing the Warfarin and Procedural Plan

"Now, your INR today is 2.7 — and I want to reassure you, we are not going to stop your warfarin. The current guidelines are clear that for a straightforward extraction like this, we continue anticoagulation therapy. Stopping warfarin carries a real risk of a serious clotting event, and that risk outweighs any additional bleeding concern here."

"An INR of 2.7 is within the acceptable range for a single extraction. What I will do is use a local haemostatic dressing — a resorbable material placed in the socket after the extraction — to help control bleeding, and I'll ask you to bite on gauze for at least thirty minutes afterwards. We'll make sure bleeding has settled before you leave."

---

Safety-Netting and Closing

"After the extraction, I'd like you to watch for a few specific things over the coming days and weeks. If you develop a fever, chills, night sweats, unusual fatigue, or you just feel generally unwell — even if it seems like a mild flu — please contact your cardiologist promptly and mention that you've had a dental extraction. These can be early signs of endocarditis, and early treatment makes a significant difference to the outcome."

"Do you have any questions about the antibiotics, the warfarin, or what to expect today? I want to make sure you feel completely comfortable before we proceed. Once you've taken the amoxicillin and we've waited the full sixty minutes, we'll get started with the extraction. You're in safe hands."

S7
Hematoma + Trismus After IANB
Category:** Oral Surgery | **Time:** 11 min | **Difficulty:** Exam-ready

CASE SUMMARY

Patient returns 2 days post-inferior alveolar nerve block (IANB) complaining of limited mouth opening (trismus) and a visible bruise/swelling inside the cheek. No extraction was performed. Candidate must diagnose haematoma + trismus, reassure, and manage.

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

History (2 min)

  • What procedure? Was it just the injection or was extraction attempted?
  • Timing of onset (immediate swelling = haematoma; delayed = infection less likely if no extraction done)
  • Pain level, mouth opening degree
  • Any fever, dysphagia, progressive worsening?

Explanation — INFLECTION 1: Clear, reassuring, honest

"What you have is called a haematoma — that's where the injection needle accidentally nicked a blood vessel, and blood has pooled inside the muscle tissue. This causes the bruising and swelling you can see, and because the muscle is swollen with blood, it's harder to open your mouth — this is called trismus. Both of these are known complications of the nerve block injection, not signs of infection or anything more sinister."

Management (2 min)

  • No antibiotics (not an infection)
  • Warm packs (not cold) — 20 min 3–4 times daily from day 3 onwards to help reabsorb the blood
  • Gentle opening exercises (open as far as comfortable, hold, repeat) to prevent muscle fibrosis
  • Paracetamol ± ibuprofen for pain
  • Review in 5–7 days
  • Reassure: most haematomas resolve within 2–3 weeks

INFLECTION 2: When to escalate

"If your mouth opening is getting WORSE not better, or if you develop difficulty swallowing or breathing, a high temperature, or the swelling spreads to your neck — those would be signs we need to see you immediately."

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Diagnoses haematoma + trismus correctly (not infection)
  2. ✅ No antibiotics — not indicated
  3. ✅ Warm packs + gentle exercises from day 3
  4. ✅ Clear safety-netting: worsening trismus, dysphagia, neck spread = escalate
  5. ✅ Reassures patient: most resolve in 2–3 weeks

TG4 ALERTS

No antibiotics for haematoma — TG4: this is NOT an infection. Antibiotics inappropriate and contribute to resistance. Warm packs + exercises + monitoring is the correct management.
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • "Inferior alveolar nerve block haematoma: the needle passes through the pterygomandibular space and may puncture the inferior alveolar artery or pterygoid plexus. Blood tracks into the pterygomandibular and masseteric spaces causing trismus from muscle spasm and oedema."
  • "Management: reassurance (resolves in 10–14 days typically), warm compresses from Day 3 (promotes vasodilation and reabsorption — do NOT use heat in first 24-48 hours as it increases bleeding), analgesia (NSAIDs reduce inflammation), soft diet, physiotherapy exercises when trismus begins to ease."
  • "Monitor for secondary infection: if fever, increasing trismus, dysphagia, or systemic signs develop → urgent review, possible hospital referral."
  • "Trismus differential: haematoma, medial pterygoid needle trauma, temporomandibular dysfunction, infection, tumour. History and timing guide the differential — post-IANB trismus peaking at 24–48 hours is almost always haematoma."
Patient Reframes
  • "The stiffness in your jaw is from blood tracking into the surrounding muscle — think of it like a deep bruise. The muscle has gone into spasm around it. It's uncomfortable but it will resolve on its own over 10 to 14 days."
  • "This happened because the needle passed close to a small blood vessel — it's a recognised complication that occurs in a small proportion of nerve block injections. The anatomy in that area is close and variable between individuals."
  • "Warm compresses after the first 48 hours will really help — they relax the muscle and help the body reabsorb the blood faster. Gently opening the mouth and doing jaw exercises as the soreness allows will also help prevent the muscle stiffening permanently."
Curveball Deflectors
  • "You must have used the wrong technique." → "I used a standard inferior alveolar nerve block — the technique hasn't changed. The complication occurred because of the vascular anatomy in that area, which varies between patients. I can't visualise blood vessels during an injection; this is a recognised risk that I document in my consent process."
  • "It's been a week and it's not better — what's going on?" → "A week is within the expected recovery window — most haematomas take 10–14 days to fully resolve, and trismus can persist a little longer. I'd like to review you now to make sure there's no secondary infection. If it's genuinely stagnant at 3 weeks, I'd refer for imaging."
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ▶
STAGE: Opening & Scene Setting

Candidate enters, greets the patient warmly, and establishes rapport.

"Hello, come on in and take a seat. I'm Dr. [Name] — thanks for coming back to see me today. I can see you're a bit uncomfortable, so I want to make sure we get to the bottom of what's going on as quickly as possible. Is it alright if I ask you a few questions first before I take a look?"

---

History Taking

"So I understand you've come back because of some swelling and difficulty opening your mouth — can you tell me a bit more about what's been happening?"

Listens attentively.

"Just to confirm — when you came in two days ago, we gave you an injection to numb the lower jaw. Was any tooth actually removed, or was it just the injection itself that was given?"

Listens.

"And when did you first notice the swelling and the bruising inside your cheek — was it quite soon after the injection, or did it come on gradually over the next day or two?"

Listens.

"On a scale of zero to ten, how would you rate your pain at the moment? And how wide can you open your mouth — can you get more than two fingers width, or is it less than that?"

Listens.

"Have you noticed any fever, any chills, or feeling generally unwell? Any difficulty swallowing, or any swelling spreading down toward your neck at all?"

Listens. Patient denies fever, dysphagia, neck swelling. Onset of bruising and restricted opening was within hours of the injection. No extraction was performed.

"Thank you — that's really helpful. Would it be alright if I had a quick look inside your mouth now?"

Candidate performs brief extraoral and intraoral examination. Notes visible ecchymosis and firm swelling in the medial pterygoid region, restricted mouth opening of approximately 20 mm, no fluctuance, no pus, no trismus worse than at onset, no lymphadenopathy, afebrile.

---

Diagnosis and Explanation

"Thank you for letting me have a look. I want to explain what I think is happening, and I want to reassure you that this is a recognised complication of the injection itself — it is not a sign of infection and it is not anything dangerous."

"What you have is called a haematoma. What that means is that when the injection needle was placed to deliver the local anaesthetic, it accidentally nicked a small blood vessel in the area. Blood has then pooled inside the surrounding muscle tissue, and that is what is causing the bruising and the firm swelling you can see and feel inside your cheek."

"Now, because that blood is sitting inside the muscle, it causes the muscle to become swollen and irritated, and that makes it very difficult for you to open your mouth fully. This restricted opening is called trismus — it is essentially the muscle going into a kind of protective spasm. Both the haematoma and the trismus are known, documented complications of this type of injection. They are not a sign that anything went wrong in a serious sense, and they are certainly not a sign of infection."

"I know it looks and feels quite alarming, but I want to be very clear — this will get better on its own with some simple measures at home."

---

Management Plan

"Let me walk you through exactly what I'd like you to do over the next few weeks."

"For pain relief, I'd like you to take paracetamol one gram — that is two standard five-hundred milligram tablets — every four to six hours as needed, with a maximum of four grams in any twenty-four hour period. If the pain is not well controlled with paracetamol alone, you can also take ibuprofen four hundred milligrams every six to eight hours with food, as long as you have no history of stomach ulcers, high blood pressure issues, or blood thinning medications. Please do not take both at the same time without checking with me first."

"From today — day two — and going forward, I'd like you to apply a warm pack to the outside of your cheek for around twenty minutes, three to four times a day. The warmth helps the body reabsorb the pooled blood more quickly. Please avoid cold packs from this point on — cold was only appropriate in the very first few hours."

"I also want you to do some very gentle mouth-opening exercises. Open your mouth as far as you comfortably can — do not push through sharp pain — hold that position for about ten seconds, then relax, and repeat that ten times. Do this three or four times a day. This helps prevent the muscle from tightening up permanently, which is something we want to avoid."

"There are no antibiotics needed here, and I want to be clear about that. This is not an infection — antibiotics would not help and would be inappropriate to prescribe."

"Most haematomas like this one resolve fully within two to three weeks. I'd like to review you here in five to seven days to make sure you are improving as expected."

---

Safety Netting and Closing

"Before you go, I need to go through some very important warning signs with you. Most people improve steadily from this point, but I need you to contact us immediately — or go straight to the emergency department — if any of the following occur."

"If your mouth opening is getting progressively worse rather than better, if you develop any difficulty swallowing or any sensation of your airway feeling restricted, if you develop a high temperature above thirty-eight degrees, or if you notice any swelling spreading down toward your neck or under your jaw — those are signs that we need to assess you urgently, as they could indicate a spreading infection that would need immediate treatment."

"Do you have any questions about anything I've explained today? I know it's a lot to take in."

Listens and responds to any questions.

"I'll print out a summary of these instructions for you to take home. Please don't hesitate to call the clinic at any time if you're concerned. I'll see you again in five to seven days — take care of yourself."

S8
Extraction in Immunocompromised Patient (HIV, Torres Strait Islander)
Category:** Oral Surgery | **Time:** 11 min | **Difficulty:** Exam-ready

CASE SUMMARY

37-year-old Torres Strait Islander patient needs extraction of tooth 46. Discloses being HIV-positive, current CD4 count 450, undetectable viral load on antiretroviral therapy (ART). Cultural sensitivity and infection control approach required.

CANDIDATE BRIEF

A 37-year-old Torres Strait Islander man presents for extraction of 46 (non-restorable, symptomatic). He discloses HIV-positive status, CD4 count 450 (moderate), undetectable viral load on ART (tenofovir/emtricitabine/rilpivirine). No known drug allergies. Your task: manage the extraction appropriately with culturally sensitive communication.

EXAMINER CONTEXT

Patient is quiet, reserved, and will not volunteer information unless asked directly. He is worried that the dentist will treat him differently because of his HIV status. He needs to feel respected and not stigmatised. Will open up more if the candidate communicates without judgment. Cultural sensitivity note: direct eye contact may feel aggressive; a softer, side-on approach is culturally comfortable for many Torres Strait Islanders. Ask permission before examining, explain each step.

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

Cultural sensitivity and rapport (2 min) — INFLECTION 1

"Thank you for coming in. And thank you for sharing your medical history with me — I appreciate your trust. Before we get started, is there anything you'd like to know about how we do things here, or anything that would make you more comfortable?"

Ask permission before each step of the exam.

Addressing the HIV status clinically (1.5 min) — INFLECTION 2: No stigma, clinical facts

"Your HIV is well-managed — your viral load being undetectable means the virus isn't actively harming your immune system right now, and your CD4 count of 450 tells me your immune system is still reasonably strong. For dental work, we treat you the same way we treat all patients. The main things I'll factor in are:

  • A bit of extra care around wound healing — your immune system may be slightly less reactive, so we'll keep a close eye on healing afterward
  • Your ART medications — some can interact with pain relievers or antibiotics, so I'll double-check those
  • Standard infection control — which is the same for every patient"

Infection control (1 min)

"Our infection control is the same for every patient regardless of their health status — gloves, masks, sterilized instruments. You don't need to worry about that."

ART interaction check (1 min)

Tenofovir/emtricitabine/rilpivirine — rilpivirine has interactions with some antacids but no significant interaction with lignocaine, NSAIDs, or amoxicillin. If unsure, confirm with pharmacist.

Extraction management

Standard atraumatic extraction technique. Primary closure if possible. Post-op chlorhexidine. Review in 1 week (slightly closer monitoring than typical given immunocompromise).

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Culturally respectful approach (asks permission, explains steps, warm non-judgmental tone)
  2. ✅ Does NOT treat patient differently or refuse treatment based on HIV status
  3. ✅ Explains why well-managed HIV (undetectable VL, CD4 450) = low infection risk
