  4. ✅ Checks ART drug interactions with planned medications
  5. ✅ Applies standard infection control (same as every patient)
  6. ✅ Closer review schedule post-op for immunocompromised patient

TG4 ALERTS

Standard infection control for ALL patients — TG4: do not escalate or change infection control based on HIV disclosure. Standard precautions are universal.
ART interactions — Some antiretrovirals interact with metronidazole (flagyl), antifungals, and some analgesics. Always check before prescribing.
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • "Key parameters for HIV: current CD4+ count and viral load. CD4 >200 cells/µL with undetectable viral load — treat as immunocompetent with standard precautions. CD4 <200 — increased infection risk, consider prophylactic antibiotics (amoxicillin/clavulanate), ensure primary closure, consider hospital setting."
  • "Modern antiretroviral therapy has transformed HIV into a manageable chronic condition. Patients on effective ART with undetectable viral load have near-normal immune function and life expectancy. Do not conflate HIV status with immunocompromise — assess the actual immune parameters."
  • "Cultural context for Torres Strait Islander patients: health literacy in a second language, community-level health trust, potential involvement of family in decision-making, higher burden of dental and systemic disease. Ask about interpreter needs and preferred communication style. Do not assume — ask."
  • "Antiretroviral drug interactions: some ARTs (particularly ritonavir) are potent CYP3A4 inhibitors — check for interactions with local anaesthetics, analgesics, and any sedatives before prescribing."
Patient Reframes
  • "With your viral load being undetectable and your immune cell count where it is, your body's ability to fight infection is actually very similar to someone without HIV. We'll take the same precautions we do for any patient, and we can proceed safely."
  • "I want to make sure I'm communicating clearly — do you have someone with you today, or would you prefer I speak with a family member present? I also want to check whether you'd like me to use an interpreter for any part of this."
Curveball Deflectors
  • "Is it safe to treat me?" → "Absolutely — and I want to be straightforward with you: your HIV status doesn't change whether I can treat you, it changes how I plan the treatment. Based on your current blood results, we can proceed safely with the right precautions."
  • "Do you need to tell anyone about my HIV status?" → "Your medical information is strictly confidential within the clinical team who needs it to treat you safely. I won't share it outside that. Is there anything specific you're concerned about?"
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ▶
STAGE: Opening and Cultural Welcome

Candidate introduces themselves warmly, makes eye contact, and gestures to the chair.

"Good morning, my name is Dr. [Name], and I'll be looking after you today. Please, come in and make yourself comfortable. Can I confirm your name for me? Great, thank you. Before we start, I just want to say — I appreciate you coming in today, and thank you very much for sharing your medical history with me on the intake form. That really does help me give you the best care possible, and I want you to know everything you tell me stays completely confidential here."

Pauses, settles tone.

"Is there anything about the way we do things here that you'd like to know about before we begin? Or anything that would help you feel more comfortable during your appointment today? I'll always explain what I'm doing before I do it, and if you need me to stop at any point, just raise your hand and I will. Your comfort and your say in your treatment matters to me."

---

History and HIV Discussion — Removing Stigma

"So, I can see from your notes that you've been having trouble with that lower right molar — tooth 46. Can you tell me a bit about what's been going on with it? How long have you had the pain? Has there been any swelling or discharge?"

Listens to patient's response attentively.

"Thank you. Now, I also noted that you're HIV-positive and currently on antiretroviral therapy — tenofovir, emtricitabine, and rilpivirine. I want to be straightforward with you: that information helps me look after you properly, and it doesn't change the fact that we're here to help you today. There's absolutely no judgement here."

Tone remains calm and factual.

"Your HIV is actually very well managed. Your viral load being undetectable means the virus isn't actively replicating or causing harm to your immune system right now — that's a genuinely excellent result. Your CD4 count of 450 tells me your immune system is still reasonably strong. For context, we start to have real concerns below 200, so at 450 you're in a moderate, well-maintained range. From a dental perspective, we can proceed safely today. I'll just factor in a couple of things as we go, and I'll explain those now."

---

Clinical Considerations — ART Interactions and Infection Control

"The first thing I want to do is cross-check your medications. Rilpivirine, in particular, can interact with some medications — it has significant interactions with antacids and certain antifungals, but importantly, there are no clinically significant interactions with lignocaine, paracetamol, ibuprofen, or amoxicillin. So the anaesthetic I'll use today, and the pain relief I'll recommend afterward, are all safe with your current regimen. If I ever needed to prescribe something I wasn't completely certain about — like metronidazole, for example — I would check with your pharmacist or physician first. Today we don't need that, so we're straightforward to proceed."

"The second thing — and I want to be clear about this — our infection control procedures are exactly the same for every single patient we see. Gloves, masks, sterilised instruments, full barrier precautions. We don't change or escalate anything based on a patient's health status. Universal precautions protect everyone equally, including our team, and that's always our standard. You don't need to have any concerns on that front."

---

Extraction Procedure

Candidate dons gloves and mask. Asks permission before each clinical step.

"I'm going to have a look inside your mouth now, if that's okay? I'll be gentle. I'll let you know before I touch anything."

Performs clinical examination and confirms 46 is non-restorable.

"Right, so 46 needs to come out — you're right, it's not something we can save. I'll give you a local anaesthetic injection first. You'll feel a pinch and some pressure, but I'll go slowly. I'm using lignocaine with adrenaline, and I'll always aspirate before I inject to make sure I'm in the right place."

Administers inferior alveolar nerve block using standard aspiration technique. Waits for profound anaesthesia.

"I'm going to use a careful, atraumatic technique to remove the tooth — small, controlled movements to preserve as much of the surrounding bone and tissue as possible. This helps with healing."

Performs extraction atraumatically. Achieves haemostasis. Places primary closure with resorbable sutures.

"I've placed a couple of dissolving stitches to help everything close up nicely. Bite down gently on this gauze for about thirty minutes."

---

Post-Operative Instructions, Prescribing, and Safety Net

"For pain relief, I'd recommend starting with paracetamol one gram every four to six hours as needed — that's your first line. If you need a bit more, you can add ibuprofen 400 milligrams every six to eight hours with food, provided you don't have any stomach or blood pressure concerns. I don't think you need antibiotics today — the extraction went cleanly, there were no signs of spreading infection, and your immune system is well supported. Prescribing antibiotics when they aren't needed can actually cause more harm than good."

"I'd also like you to rinse gently with chlorhexidine 0.12% mouthwash twice a day starting tomorrow — not today — to support healing. Avoid smoking, alcohol, and hot foods for the next 24 hours."

"Because your immune system is working a little harder than average, I want to bring you back in one week rather than the usual two — just to check the socket is healing well and there's no sign of infection. That's not a concern, it's just good care."

"Some ooze over the next day or two is completely normal. If you have bright red ongoing bleeding, significant swelling spreading into your neck or face, or a fever, please call us immediately or go to your nearest emergency department. Do you have any questions for me at all? Thank you again for trusting me with your care today — it was a pleasure looking after you."

S9
Uncontrolled Diabetes — Decision to Defer or Proceed with Extraction
Category:** Oral Surgery | **Time:** 11 min | **Difficulty:** Exam-ready

CASE SUMMARY

Patient presents for extraction of lower molar. HbA1c 10.8% (severely uncontrolled), fasting BSL this morning was 14.2 mmol/L. No signs of acute infection. Candidate must decide whether to proceed or defer.

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

History (2 min) — INFLECTION 1: Get the numbers

  • "When was your last HbA1c? Do you know the result?"
  • "Did you eat breakfast this morning? Did you take your diabetes medication today?"
  • "Do you have a blood glucose meter? What was your reading this morning?"

Decision — INFLECTION 2: Defer, with explanation

"I want to be honest about what I'm finding. Your blood sugar this morning was 14.2, and your recent HbA1c of 10.8 tells me your diabetes has not been well controlled lately. This matters a lot for dental surgery:

  • High blood sugar slows healing significantly
  • Your immune system's ability to fight infection is impaired
  • Risk of post-operative infection and dry socket is much higher
  • In extreme cases, high blood sugar combined with surgical stress can trigger a diabetic emergency

Based on TG4 guidelines and best practice, for a non-urgent elective extraction, I'd recommend deferring today and working with your GP to get your blood sugar into a safer range first — ideally HbA1c below 8, ideally below 7.5, and a fasting BSL below 10 mmol/L on the day of the procedure."

Urgent vs. elective distinction

"Now — if you had a spreading infection, facial swelling, or were at risk of airway compromise, we would need to act today regardless of your blood sugar. But this tooth is sore, not an emergency, so we have the opportunity to do this safely."

Plan (1.5 min)

  1. Refer back to GP for diabetes optimisation (medication review, dietary advice)
  2. Schedule extraction in 4–6 weeks
  3. For now: pain relief (paracetamol, ibuprofen)
  4. If infection develops before then → patient should go to hospital emergency
  5. On the day of extraction: morning appointment, patient must have eaten and taken diabetes medication, fasting BSL checked before starting

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Specifically asks for HbA1c and fasting BSL before any decision
  2. ✅ Correctly identifies uncontrolled diabetes (HbA1c 10.8) as a contraindication to elective extraction
  3. ✅ Explains the mechanism (impaired healing, infection risk, surgical stress)
  4. ✅ Distinguishes elective vs. emergency (would proceed if life-threatening infection)
  5. ✅ Refers to GP for optimisation, plans extraction once controlled
  6. ✅ Sets target (HbA1c <8, fasting BSL <10 on day)

TG4 ALERTS

Uncontrolled diabetes — TG4: do NOT extract in primary care. Refer to hospital for urgent cases; defer elective cases until controlled. HbA1c >8% = elevated risk; HbA1c >9% = serious risk.
Diabetic emergency in dental chair — TG4: hypoglycaemia (low BSL) is more dangerous acutely than hyperglycaemia. Ensure patient has eaten and taken medication before morning appointment. Keep glucose tablets available.
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • "The key question is: acute emergency or elective procedure? Acute infection in a diabetic patient should be treated — the infection itself worsens glycaemic control (bidirectional relationship). Deferring treatment of active infection is not appropriate."
  • "For elective procedures: target HbA1c <9% before proceeding. If HbA1c >9% or BSL >15 mmol/L on the day: defer elective treatment, refer to GP/endocrinologist for optimisation."
  • "Day-of-procedure protocol: morning appointment (lowest stress, best glycaemic control), check blood glucose on the day, ensure the patient has eaten and taken their medications as normal, have glucose available in the surgery, keep appointments short."
  • "Post-operative healing: hyperglycaemia impairs neutrophil function, collagen synthesis, and angiogenesis. Healing is impaired in poorly controlled diabetes — infections can escalate rapidly. Closer review intervals post-extraction."
Patient Reframes
  • "Dental infection and diabetes feed each other in a vicious cycle — the infection raises your blood sugar, and high blood sugar makes it harder for your body to fight the infection. Treating the tooth is actually part of managing your diabetes right now."
  • "I'm not able to do elective treatment today because your blood sugar puts your healing at risk — but I want to be clear: once your levels are better controlled, we absolutely can proceed. This is a pause, not a refusal."
  • "A morning appointment works best for you — your blood sugar tends to be most predictable then, and keeping the appointment short means we're not pushing your body's stress response."
Curveball Deflectors
  • "My diabetes is controlled — my doctor said so." → "I'm sure your doctor is managing it well — and I need to see today's blood glucose and your most recent HbA1c to make that assessment for a surgical procedure. Can you tell me your reading this morning? If it's in a safe range, we can proceed."
  • "Can't you just do it today?" → "For the infection — yes, we treat that now because leaving it will genuinely make your diabetes harder to control. For the elective work you also need — that waits until your levels are optimised. It's about managing your risk, not about refusing treatment."
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ▶
STAGE: Opening and Initial Assessment

Candidate greets the patient warmly and makes them comfortable. Reviews the referral note before beginning.

"Hello, come on in and take a seat. I'm Dr. Chen — lovely to meet you. I understand you've come in today because you'd like to have a lower molar taken out. Before we get started, I'd love to ask you a few questions to make sure we plan this as safely as possible for you. Is that alright?"

"Firstly, can you tell me a little about the tooth itself? How long has it been bothering you? Are you having any pain at the moment, and would you describe it as getting worse quickly, or has it been fairly stable over the past week or so?"

Examines the tooth briefly. No facial swelling, no lymphadenopathy, no signs of spreading infection or trismus noted.

"Thank you. Now, I also see from your notes that you have diabetes. I'd really like to talk through that with you in a bit more detail, because it does affect how we approach dental surgery. I hope that's okay."

---

Targeted Diabetes History

"When were you last reviewed by your GP or endocrinologist for your diabetes? And do you happen to know your most recent HbA1c result — that's the blood test that gives us a three-month average of your blood sugar levels?"

Patient confirms HbA1c was 10.8% at their last check approximately six weeks ago.

"Thank you for telling me that. And this morning — did you have any breakfast before coming in? And did you take your diabetes medication as usual today?"

Patient confirms they ate breakfast and took their medication.

"That's really good to hear. Now, do you have a blood glucose meter at home? Were you able to check your blood sugar this morning before you came in?"

Patient confirms fasting BSL this morning was 14.2 mmol/L.

"Right, thank you. Just to complete the picture — have you noticed any recent symptoms like increased thirst, needing to urinate more frequently, or feeling more tired than usual? And have you had any infections recently that were slow to heal — perhaps a cut, a skin infection, anything like that?"

Candidate notes the complete picture: HbA1c 10.8%, fasting BSL 14.2 mmol/L, no acute infection, no emergency features.

---

Decision and Explanation — Deferral

"I want to be completely honest with you about what I'm finding, because I think you deserve a clear explanation of my thinking. Your blood sugar this morning was 14.2 millimoles per litre, and your HbA1c of 10.8% tells me that your diabetes has unfortunately not been well controlled over the past few months. Both of those numbers are significantly above the safe range for dental surgery."

"This matters a great deal for what we're planning today, and here's why. When blood sugar is elevated, the body's ability to heal after surgery is substantially reduced — the tissues simply don't repair themselves as efficiently. At the same time, your immune system's capacity to fight off infection is impaired, which means the risk of a post-operative infection, and something called a dry socket, is much higher than it would be if your diabetes were well controlled. And there's a further concern: the physical stress of a surgical procedure can cause blood sugar to spike unpredictably, and in someone whose levels are already this high, that can in rare cases tip into a diabetic emergency in the chair."

"Based on current best practice and the guidelines I follow, for a non-urgent elective extraction like this one, the recommended approach is to defer the procedure today and work with your GP first to bring your blood sugar into a safer range. We'd be looking ideally for an HbA1c below 8%, and ideally closer to 7.5%, and on the actual day of the procedure, a fasting blood sugar below 10 millimoles per litre."

"I want to be clear — I'm not simply turning you away. I'm asking you to take a few weeks to get your diabetes better optimised so that we can do this procedure for you safely."

---

Urgent vs. Elective Distinction

"Now, I do want to acknowledge something important. If the situation were different — if you had a spreading infection, significant facial swelling, difficulty opening your mouth, or any concern about your airway — we would need to act today regardless of your blood sugar, and I would be referring you directly to the hospital oral surgery team for urgent management. But looking at you today, this tooth is sore and uncomfortable, not an emergency. There is no spreading infection. We have the opportunity to take our time and do this properly."

---

Management Plan and Safety Netting

"So here is what I'd like us to do. First, I'm going to write a letter to your GP today, explaining the situation and asking them to review your diabetes management — whether that means adjusting your medication, discussing your diet, or both. Once your GP is satisfied your levels are more controlled, we'll schedule the extraction here — I'd suggest aiming for around four to six weeks from now."

"In the meantime, for the tooth pain, you can take paracetamol one gram every four to six hours as needed, and if that's not quite enough, you can add ibuprofen 400 milligrams every six to eight hours, provided you have no history of stomach ulcers, kidney problems, or high blood pressure."

"Now, this is important: if at any point before your next appointment you develop facial swelling, swelling spreading toward your neck, difficulty swallowing, or a fever, please do not wait — go straight to your nearest hospital emergency department and let them know you have uncontrolled diabetes and a dental infection. That changes the urgency completely."

"When we do book the extraction, I'll schedule you for a morning appointment. On that day, please make sure you've had a light breakfast and taken your diabetes medication as usual, and we'll check your blood sugar right here before we begin — ideally below 10 millimoles per litre on the day. We'll also have glucose tablets available in the surgery, just as a precaution."

"Do you have any questions at all about what I've explained? I know it's not the answer you were hoping for today, but I genuinely want this to go as smoothly as possible for you."

R1
Caries Risk Assessment + Restorative Planning (Child with Hall Crown)
Category:** Restorative / Pediatric | **Time:** 11 min | **Difficulty:** Exam-ready

CASE SUMMARY

7-year-old with carious lower primary molar (75). Mother asks about filling options. Discussion of Hall technique (stainless steel crown), silver diamine fluoride, and conventional restoration. Caries risk assessment + practical parent communication required.

CANDIDATE BRIEF

You are seeing a 7-year-old for assessment of tooth 75 (lower left primary second molar) with moderate/deep caries visible on clinical exam and bitewing. The child is anxious and uncooperative with drilling. Mother is concerned about "putting a silver cap" on her daughter's tooth. Your task: explain the diagnosis, discuss restoration options appropriate to the child's behaviour and tooth prognosis, and reach a shared decision.

EXAMINER CONTEXT

Mother is intelligent, engaged, and has researched her options online. She's heard about "the Hall technique" but thinks silver teeth look ugly and is concerned. Child will cooperate with exam but objects loudly to the drill (anxious). If the candidate explains the Hall crown benefits clearly and addresses the aesthetic concern honestly, mother gradually accepts it. She will NOT be persuaded if the candidate is dismissive about aesthetics.

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

Opening (1 min)

"Thanks for coming in. I've had a look at the X-ray and the tooth, and I'd like to talk through what's going on and what our options are, because with young patients there are several ways we can approach this."

Caries risk assessment (1.5 min) — INFLECTION 1

  • Dietary history: frequency of sugary snacks, juice, cordial
  • OH: brushing frequency, fluoride toothpaste, supervision
  • Fluoride access: tap water or tank
  • Family history of early caries

Diagnosis & tooth prognosis (1 min)

"Tooth 75 has a moderate to deep cavity. It's a baby tooth that will likely stay until around age 11–12, so it's worth treating — if left, it could become painful, get infected, and we might need to remove it early, which can affect the spacing for the adult teeth."

Restoration options (2.5 min) — INFLECTION 2

Option 1 — Silver Diamine Fluoride (SDF):

"This is a liquid we paint on the cavity — it arrests (stops) the decay from progressing. It stains the decayed area black permanently. It doesn't restore the tooth shape. Best for children who can't cooperate with drilling at all. Good for buying time."

(Honest about the black staining — if you skip this, mother will feel blindsided)

Option 2 — Conventional filling:

"We numb the tooth, remove the decay, fill it with white or tooth-coloured material. Requires a cooperative child and time. Given her anxiety about the drill, this may be stressful."

Option 3 — Hall technique (stainless steel crown):

"This is the one you might have read about. We don't drill at all — we slip a pre-made metal crown over the whole tooth, without removing the decay, and cement it in place. The crown seals the decay and stops it from progressing. It's quick (often under 5 minutes), doesn't usually require local anaesthetic, and has a very high success rate in kids. The downside is it's visually silver, which you mentioned. But for a back tooth that most people won't see, it's often the best balance of effectiveness and minimising trauma for the child."

INFLECTION 3: Addressing the aesthetic concern directly

"I hear you on the aesthetics — and I won't pretend it looks great. But the alternatives for a tooth this size with this amount of decay, in a child who doesn't like the drill, are either a conventional filling (which she'll find more distressing), SDF (which leaves a black stain), or removing the tooth early. The Hall crown is the least traumatic, most effective, and most evidence-based option for this situation."

Reaching a shared decision (1 min)

"Would it be helpful to show you some photos of what it looks like? It is only a back tooth, so it's not usually visible when she smiles. But I want to support whatever you decide — let's talk it through."

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Takes caries risk assessment (diet, OH, fluoride)
  2. ✅ Explains tooth prognosis (primary tooth til ~age 11–12)
  3. ✅ Presents all three options (SDF, conventional filling, Hall crown) with honest pros/cons
  4. ✅ Addresses aesthetic concern directly (doesn't dismiss it)
  5. ✅ Explains Hall technique mechanism (seals decay, no drilling)
  6. ✅ Reaches shared decision — doesn't dictate
  7. ✅ Prevention plan: reduce juice frequency, fluoride toothpaste, supervised brushing

TG4 ALERTS

SDF (Silver Diamine Fluoride): TG4-aligned for caries arrest in non-cooperative children. Always disclose the permanent black staining to parents before use.
Hall technique: High evidence base for primary molar caries management. No drilling = less anxiety, often no LA required. Success rate comparable to conventional restorations at 2 years.
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • "Hall Technique evidence base: multiple RCTs demonstrate equal or superior outcomes compared to conventional restoration (with caries removal) in primary molars. The principle: complete sealing of bacteria from substrate stops caries progression even without caries removal."
  • "Caries risk assessment framework for children: dietary frequency (not just amount — frequency of sugar exposure drives caries, not total sugar), fluoride exposure (toothpaste concentration — 1000ppm for children, 1450ppm if high risk >3 years), saliva flow, plaque levels, socioeconomic factors, past caries experience."
  • "Fluoride varnish application 4x/year for high-risk children is evidence-based (Cochrane review) and PBS-funded. This is part of the management plan, not optional."
  • "Parental motivation is the key variable for caries prevention in young children — the child cannot control their own diet or brushing. The conversation with the parent about technique, timing, and diet is the intervention."
Patient Reframes
  • "I know it sounds counterintuitive to put a crown on a baby tooth with the decay still inside — but the research actually shows this works just as well as removing the decay, and it's much less traumatic for your child. We're sealing the bacteria off from what they need to survive."
  • "Baby teeth matter more than most people realise — they hold space for the adult teeth, help with speech development, and affect eating and nutrition. A badly decayed baby tooth that's lost too early can create problems that last into adulthood."
  • "The pattern of decay I'm seeing isn't about brushing alone — it's usually about how often sugary drinks or snacks are in contact with the teeth during the day. Even healthy foods like fruit juice can cause this if sipped constantly."
Curveball Deflectors
  • Parent: "Why aren't you removing the decay?" → "The Hall Technique is an evidence-based approach where the crown seals the cavity completely, cutting off the bacteria from the nutrients they need. Studies show it works at least as well as drilling — and with much less distress for the child and the parent. The decay stops progressing under the crown."
  • Parent: "It's just a baby tooth — why bother?" → "Because this tooth won't fall out until age 10 or 11 — that's years away. In that time, an untreated abscess can damage the adult tooth developing right underneath it, affect your child's ability to eat comfortably, and make every dental visit a negative experience."
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ▶
STAGE: Opening & Introduction

Candidates enters and greets the mother warmly, crouches briefly to make eye contact with the child at her level.

"Hi there — you must be Emily. I love your shoes. And you must be Mum — lovely to meet you both. I'm Dr [Name]. Thanks so much for coming in today."

Turning to Mum directly: "I've had a good look at Emily's tooth and the X-ray, and I'd love to talk through what I'm seeing and what our options are. With children, there are actually several different ways we can approach treating a tooth like this, so I want to make sure you feel completely comfortable with whatever we decide together. Does that sound okay?"

To Emily: "And Emily, you can just sit and listen — I'm going to talk to Mum first, and you can tell me if you have any questions too, alright?"

---

Caries Risk Assessment

"Before I talk about the tooth itself, I'd like to understand a bit about Emily's diet and routine at home, because it helps me work out why this has happened and how we can stop it happening again. Is that okay?"

"Firstly, what does Emily typically drink throughout the day — water, juice, cordial, soft drink? And how often would she have something sweet or sugary to snack on — are we talking once a day, or more regularly, maybe between meals?"

Listens attentively to Mum's response, nods, and follows up: "And does the family use tap water here, or do you have tank water or a filter at home?" — noting this to assess fluoride exposure from reticulated supply.

"How is the brushing going at home? Is Emily brushing twice a day, and are you still supervising her and helping her at the end? And what toothpaste are you using — do you know if it contains fluoride?"

"Has Emily had any fillings before, or has this kind of problem come up in the family — siblings, or similar issues when you were young yourself?"

Nods thoughtfully: "Thank you — that's really helpful. It sounds like there are a couple of things we can work on together to help protect Emily's teeth going forward, and I'll come back to that."

---

Diagnosis & Tooth Prognosis

"So, let me show you what I'm seeing. This is Emily's lower left back baby tooth — we call it tooth 75. On the X-ray here, you can see this darker shadow, which tells me there's a moderate to deep cavity. The decay is getting close to the nerve, though at this stage I don't see signs that the nerve is already infected."

"Now, I know it's a baby tooth, and I sometimes hear parents say 'it'll fall out anyway' — and that's a completely reasonable thought. But this particular tooth is actually one of the last baby teeth to come out. It will likely stay in Emily's mouth until she's around eleven or twelve years old. That's another four to five years."

"If we leave it untreated, the decay will keep progressing. It could become painful, abscess, or get infected — and then we'd have no choice but to remove it. Losing this tooth early can affect the space available for the adult tooth coming through underneath it, and can sometimes mean Emily needs orthodontic treatment later. So it's genuinely worth treating now, while we have options."

---

Restoration Options — Presenting All Three

"So here's where it gets interesting — because for a child Emily's age, especially one who finds the drill a bit frightening, we actually have three good options, and I'd like to walk you through each one honestly."

"The first option is called Silver Diamine Fluoride — or SDF. It's a liquid we paint directly onto the cavity, and it stops the decay from progressing without any drilling at all. The big advantage is it's completely non-invasive and very quick. The downside — and I want to be upfront about this — is that it permanently stains the decayed area black. The staining doesn't wash off. It won't restore the shape of the tooth either, so it's more of a holding measure. It's a good option when a child absolutely cannot tolerate any treatment, or as a temporary measure, but it's not ideal as a long-term solution for a tooth that needs to last another five years."

"The second option is a conventional filling — we give a local anaesthetic injection to numb the tooth, remove the decay with the drill, and place a tooth-coloured filling. It restores the tooth beautifully. The downside is that it requires Emily to be relaxed and cooperative throughout, and given that she's already a little anxious about drilling, it can be a stressful experience — for her, and for you watching."

"And then there's the third option — which is the one I'd like to explain properly, because I suspect this is what you've read about as the 'silver cap.' It's called the Hall technique, and it uses a stainless steel crown."

"Here's what's actually quite remarkable about it — we don't drill at all. We don't remove the decay. Instead, we select a pre-made metal crown that fits snugly over the whole tooth, and we cement it firmly in place. By sealing the cavity completely, we cut off the bacteria from their food supply and stop the decay in its tracks. The procedure usually takes under five minutes, most children don't need an injection, and the evidence shows success rates that are comparable to — and sometimes better than — conventional fillings in primary teeth over two years. It's probably the most well-researched approach we have for children in exactly this situation."

---

Addressing the Aesthetic Concern & Shared Decision

"Now — I heard you mention you weren't sure about the silver cap, and I want to take that seriously, because aesthetics matter and your concerns are completely valid."

"I won't pretend it looks like a natural tooth. It is silver and metallic. But I want to gently put it in context: this is a back tooth — the second one from the back in the lower jaw. When Emily smiles, talks, or laughs, it's generally not visible. If it were a front tooth, I'd be having a very different conversation with you."

"When I weigh up our options honestly — a conventional filling that Emily will find distressing, SDF that leaves a permanent black stain but doesn't restore the tooth, or a Hall crown that is quick, no drilling, no injection in most cases, highly effective, and keeps that tooth healthy until it falls out naturally — for this tooth, in this child, the Hall crown is the approach I'd recommend most strongly. That said, I want you to feel completely comfortable."

"Would it help if I showed you some photos of what it looks like in a child's mouth? And Emily — would you like to see too? Sometimes it helps to know what to expect."

Pausing to allow response: "Whatever you decide, I'll support you. But if it would help, we could even trial how Emily goes with just a gentle look at the crown before we commit — no pressure at all."

---

Prevention Plan & Closing

"Regardless of which treatment we choose today, I'd like to put a prevention plan in place so we can protect Emily's other teeth and make sure this doesn't keep happening."

"The main things I'd suggest: reducing the frequency of sugary drinks and snacks — it's really the frequency throughout the day, not just the quantity, that matters most for teeth. If Emily is having juice or cordial between meals, swapping those to water would make a big difference. And at home, I'd recommend brushing twice a day with a fluoride toothpaste — a pea-sized amount — and continuing to supervise her brushing until she's around eight, to make sure all the surfaces are being cleaned. If you're on tank water, we might also talk about fluoride supplements or a fluoride varnish here at the clinic."

"I'd love to see Emily every six months so we can keep a close eye on things and catch anything early."

"So, to summarise — tooth 75 has deep decay, it needs to stay until around age eleven or twelve, and based on everything, my recommendation is the Hall crown. But this is your decision and Emily's, and I'm here to support whichever path you choose. Do you have any questions for me right now?"

R2
Amalgam Replacement — Patient Requests Mercury-Free Dentistry
Category:** Restorative | **Time:** 11 min | **Difficulty:** Exam-ready

CASE SUMMARY

Patient (35-year-old, healthy) has multiple large amalgam restorations and requests they all be replaced with composite because she's read that mercury in amalgam is "toxic." Candidate must address her concern, give evidence-based information, and discuss appropriate clinical management.

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

Opening & Validation (1 min)

"I appreciate you sharing that concern — you're definitely not alone in wondering about this. I want to give you accurate, evidence-based information so you can make a truly informed decision."

Evidence-based response on amalgam safety — INFLECTION 1

"Let me explain what we know: dental amalgam does contain mercury, but it's bound in a stable alloy with silver, tin, and copper — this is called elemental mercury, not the organic methyl-mercury that causes poisoning in fish. The amount that's released from fillings as mercury vapour is tiny — well below levels considered harmful by health authorities including the WHO and Australia's TGA. Decades of research have not established a causal link between amalgam fillings and systemic disease in otherwise healthy people."

When amalgam replacement IS appropriate (1.5 min)

"That said, there are situations where replacing amalgam makes clinical sense:

  • The filling has failed (cracks, leaking margins, secondary caries)
  • The tooth needs a crown anyway
  • You're pregnant or breastfeeding (precautionary recommendation)
  • You have known mercury hypersensitivity (rare, usually oral lichen planus pattern)
  • The filling is causing galvanic issues or cracked tooth symptoms"

Risks of replacing functional amalgam — INFLECTION 2

"Here's what I want you to understand: replacing amalgam that's working perfectly well is not risk-free. During removal, mercury vapour exposure is briefly HIGHER than during normal function. There's also:

  • Risk of exposing the pulp if the cavity is very deep
  • Weakening the tooth structure
  • Unnecessary cost and chair time
  • Composite restorations in large cavities wear faster and may not last as long in back teeth"

Clinical examination & plan (2 min)

"Let me assess each filling individually. If any show signs of failure, secondary caries, or cracking — I'd replace those regardless. For the ones that are clinically fine, my recommendation is to monitor them, not replace them."

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Validates concern without being dismissive
  2. ✅ Explains the difference between elemental mercury (in amalgam) and methyl-mercury (toxic form) in plain language
  3. ✅ Cites WHO/TGA position: no causal link to systemic disease
  4. ✅ Lists legitimate clinical indications for amalgam replacement
  5. ✅ Explains the risks of replacing functional amalgam (mercury vapour spike, structural risk)
  6. ✅ Clinical assessment: replace failed fillings, monitor sound ones

TG4 ALERTS

Amalgam in pregnancy: TG4 recommends avoiding amalgam placement or removal during pregnancy as a precautionary measure, not because of proven harm.
Mercury vapour spike during removal: TG4: highest mercury exposure occurs DURING removal. Use rubber dam, high-volume evacuation, and minimize drilling time if replacement is clinically indicated.
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • "The scientific position on amalgam safety is clear: amalgam is safe. The World Health Organization, Australian Dental Association, and the FDA have reviewed the evidence extensively. The elemental mercury in the vapour is very different from the organomercury compounds (methylmercury) that cause neurotoxicity."
  • "The risks of replacing amalgam restorations are real and should be disclosed: further irreversible reduction of tooth structure, risk of pulp exposure in deep restorations, post-operative sensitivity, and composite resin has a lower survival rate in high-load posterior sites compared to amalgam."
  • "Regulatory context: Australia is a signatory to the Minamata Convention — we are phasing DOWN amalgam use (not removing existing restorations, not removing from patients). This is for environmental mercury load reasons, not patient safety reasons."
  • "If the patient still wants replacement after informed consent: replace one quadrant at a time, use rubber dam, take baseline renal/blood mercury levels if they insist, use high-volume suction during removal."
Patient Reframes
  • "I want to be completely transparent with you: the concern about amalgam fillings causing systemic illness is not supported by the current scientific evidence. I'm not saying that to dismiss your concern — I'm saying it because giving you accurate information is my job."
  • "If you still want them replaced after understanding the evidence, I can do that — but I want you to know it involves drilling away more tooth structure, which can't be undone. I'd rather you make that decision with the full picture."
  • "The mercury in amalgam is chemically bound — it's not the same as breathing mercury vapour or eating mercury-contaminated fish. The comparison you may have read online isn't scientifically accurate."
Curveball Deflectors
  • "I read online that amalgam causes [condition X]." → "I understand — there's a lot of information online, and it's hard to know what to trust. The studies that have been done in large populations haven't found a link between amalgam and systemic illness. I can point you toward the WHO summary if you'd like to read the evidence."
  • "Other dentists said they'd replace them." → "Different dentists make different recommendations — and if they offered replacement, they may not have gone through the risks with you. I'm not saying they're wrong to offer it; I'm making sure you've heard the full picture before deciding."
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ▶
STAGE: Opening & Validation

"Good morning! I'm Dr. [Name]. Please come in and take a seat. So, I understand you've come in today because you'd like to talk about your amalgam fillings and the possibility of having them replaced. Is that right?"

Listens attentively as patient confirms her concern about mercury toxicity from online reading.

"Thank you for bringing this up — I really appreciate you sharing that with me, and I want you to know you are absolutely not alone in wondering about this. It's a question I hear quite regularly, and it's a completely understandable concern. What I'd like to do today is give you accurate, evidence-based information so that by the end of our conversation you can make a truly informed decision. Does that sound okay?"

---

Evidence-Based Explanation of Amalgam Safety

"Let me explain what the science actually tells us, because I think once you understand the details, it may put your mind at ease. You're right that dental amalgam contains mercury — that part is true. However, the mercury in amalgam is elemental mercury, and it's bound in a very stable alloy with silver, tin, and copper. This is fundamentally different from methyl-mercury, which is the organic form found in contaminated fish and which is genuinely toxic to the nervous system. The chemistry is completely different, and the way your body handles each form is completely different."

"Now, amalgam fillings do release a tiny amount of mercury vapour during chewing and tooth-grinding, but the levels measured are well below any threshold considered harmful by international health authorities — including the World Health Organisation and Australia's own Therapeutic Goods Administration. Decades of high-quality research have not established any causal link between dental amalgam restorations and systemic disease in otherwise healthy individuals. So for a healthy person like yourself, the current evidence simply does not support removing amalgam fillings on health grounds alone."

---

Legitimate Clinical Indications for Replacement

"That said, I want to be clear — there are absolutely situations where replacing an amalgam restoration makes very good clinical sense, and I would not hesitate to recommend it in those circumstances."

"The first is if a filling has failed — for example, if there are cracks in the restoration, leaking margins, or secondary decay developing underneath it. Second, if the tooth needs a crown anyway, it makes sense to address the filling at the same time. Third, if you were pregnant or breastfeeding — as a precautionary measure, not because of proven harm, the recommendation is to avoid both placing and removing amalgam during that time. Fourth, if you have a known hypersensitivity to mercury, which is rare but does occur and typically presents as an oral lichen planus pattern on the cheek tissue next to the filling. And finally, if a filling is causing galvanic sensitivity or contributing to a cracked tooth syndrome, that would also be a sound reason to replace it."

---

Risks of Replacing Functional Amalgam — The Key Inflection Point

"Now here is something I feel is really important for you to understand, because many patients are surprised by this. Replacing an amalgam filling that is currently working perfectly well is not a risk-free procedure — in fact, in some ways it carries more risk than leaving it alone."

"During the removal process, mercury vapour exposure is actually at its highest point — significantly higher than anything that occurs during normal daily function of an intact filling. That is why, if we ever do need to remove amalgam for legitimate clinical reasons, we use a rubber dam to protect your airway, high-volume evacuation, and we minimise drilling time as much as possible. Beyond the mercury issue, removing a large, deep amalgam also risks weakening the remaining tooth structure, and in a very deep cavity, there is a risk of exposing the nerve — which could mean you'd need a root canal treatment that could have been entirely avoided. There's also the practical reality that composite resin restorations in large posterior cavities don't always wear as well or last as long as a well-placed amalgam, so you may face earlier retreatment down the track."

---

Clinical Assessment & Individualised Plan

"So what I'd like to propose is this: let me examine each of your amalgam restorations individually today. I'll be looking for any signs of failure — cracking, leaking margins, recurrent decay, or any symptoms the tooth is giving you. Any filling that shows clinical or radiographic evidence of failure, I would recommend replacing regardless, and I'd use composite or another tooth-coloured material. For any fillings that are clinically sound and functioning well, my recommendation is to monitor them at your regular check-ups rather than replace them proactively."

"This way, we're making each decision based on the actual condition of each tooth — not a blanket approach either way. How does that sound to you? Do you have any questions before we take a look?"

Listens to patient, addresses any remaining concerns respectfully, then proceeds to clinical examination with appropriate radiographs.

"Thank you for trusting me with this today. I want you to feel completely comfortable with whatever we decide together."

R3
Dental Erosion in an Athlete (Dietary + Lifestyle Assessment)
Category:** Restorative / Preventive | **Time:** 11 min | **Difficulty:** Exam-ready

CASE SUMMARY

22-year-old competitive cyclist presents with sensitivity and visible erosion on palatal surfaces of upper anteriors and occlusal surfaces of posterior teeth. Athlete's diet: sports drinks during training, lemon water first thing in the morning, protein shakes. Does NOT have reflux symptoms (extrinsic erosion, not GERD).

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

History — INFLECTION 1: The acidic exposure pattern

"Can you walk me through a typical training day — what you eat and drink from when you wake up to when you go to bed, especially around training sessions?"

Why this matters: Athletes often don't realise that sports drinks, energy gels, protein shakes, lemon water, and kombucha are all acidic. The candidate must probe frequency and duration of exposure.

Key findings:

  • Sports drink sipped throughout 3-hour rides (prolonged acid bath)
  • Lemon water first thing = acid on dehydrated, low-salivary-flow teeth first thing in morning
  • Brushing immediately after acidic food/drink (accelerates erosion — candidates must know NOT to do this)

Diagnosis (1.5 min)

"What I'm seeing is called dental erosion — the acid from your diet is gradually dissolving the surface of your teeth. This is different from cavities (which are caused by bacteria) — it's a chemical process. The pattern we see on your palatal surfaces and the cupping on your back teeth fits with a pattern of repeated acid exposure from your diet."

Dietary counseling — INFLECTION 2

"Here's what I'd like to address:

  1. Sports drinks during training: Try to switch to water where possible. If you need electrolytes, drink the sports drink in one go rather than sipping over hours. Every sip is an acid attack — sipping over 3 hours is 3 hours of constant acid on your teeth.
  2. Lemon water first thing: This is one of the worst combinations — low salivary flow in the morning + acid = maximum erosion. Switch to plain water or use a straw.
  3. Wait 30–60 min before brushing after acid — brushing on acid-softened enamel removes more structure. Rinse with water or a fluoride mouthwash instead, then brush later.
  4. Casein/milk protein after training — milk or cheese can help neutralize acid and buffer the mouth"

Treatment plan (2 min)

  • Sensitivity: high-concentration fluoride toothpaste (5000 ppm — Clinpro or Tooth Mousse) applied nightly
  • Fluoride varnish applications 2–4× per year
  • Monitor: study models and photos at 6 months to track progression
  • Restorative: only if erosion reaches dentine and causes pain or functional issues — then composite build-ups or veneers. No immediate restorative treatment if erosion is still superficial.

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Takes detailed acid exposure history (training diet, timing, duration)
  2. ✅ Identifies sipping sports drinks as the main culprit (prolonged low-grade acid)
  3. ✅ Explains erosion mechanism (chemical, not bacterial)
  4. ✅ Counsels on NOT brushing immediately after acid (counter-intuitive but critical)
  5. ✅ Proposes practical alternatives (water, straw, casein, timing changes)
  6. ✅ High-fluoride toothpaste + monitoring before any restorative intervention

TG4 ALERTS

Do NOT brush immediately after acidic food/drink — TG4: wait 30–60 min or rinse with water/fluoride mouthwash first. Brushing on softened enamel accelerates erosion.
High-fluoride toothpaste (5000 ppm) — Prescription-strength toothpaste for erosion management. Recommend nightly application after brushing.
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • "Distinguish erosion from attrition and abrasion before proceeding: erosion is smooth, cupped/concave surfaces, often on palatal surfaces of upper anteriors (intrinsic) or buccal/occlusal surfaces (extrinsic). Attrition is flat, facetted, matching wear on opposing teeth. They often coexist."
  • "The critical question is frequency and contact time, not volume: sipping a sports drink throughout a 90-minute session keeps the oral pH below 5.5 continuously. One bottle consumed in 5 minutes allows remineralisation between acid exposures."
  • "Protective measures (TG4-informed): wait 30 minutes before brushing after acid exposure, use a soft toothbrush, use fluoride toothpaste 1450ppm, consider CPP-ACP products (Tooth Mousse) which promote remineralisation, rinse with water immediately after sports drink."
  • "Screen for GORD or disordered eating if palatal erosion is prominent — the distribution of erosion guides the source. Palatal erosion in a fit, healthy athlete warrants a brief, sensitively phrased screen."
Patient Reframes
  • "It's not about how much sports drink you have — it's about how long it stays in contact with your teeth. Sipping one bottle over a whole session is far more damaging than drinking it quickly, because the acid never lets your saliva remineralise the enamel."
  • "The acid in sports drinks essentially dissolves enamel — it's not decay, it's a chemical process. Once enamel is lost, the body can't grow it back. What we can do is stop the process and protect what's left."
  • "Water is the best drink during training — it hydrates just as effectively for most sessions under 60 minutes. Sports drinks are marketed heavily but the benefit for recreational athletes is limited."
Curveball Deflectors
  • "But I clean my teeth straight after training." → "I know that seems logical — but brushing immediately after acid exposure can actually accelerate erosion because the enamel is softened. The advice is counterintuitive: rinse with water, wait 30 minutes, then brush."
  • "Are you sure it's from sports drinks? I eat really healthily." → "Healthy diets can still cause erosion — citrus fruits, kombucha, sparkling water with lemon, and sports drinks all have a low pH. I'd also want to rule out an acid reflux component, because the pattern of wear on your back teeth could suggest that too. Can I ask a few questions about heartburn?"
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ▶
STAGE: Opening and Establishing Rapport

"Hi, I'm Dr. Chen — lovely to meet you. Please come in and take a seat. So I can see from your notes that you've been having some sensitivity with your teeth. Before I have a look, I'd love to chat with you for a little while to understand what's been going on. Is that okay?"

Pauses, listens attentively.

"How long has the sensitivity been bothering you, and whereabouts in your mouth do you mainly notice it?"

Allows the patient to respond, then transitions smoothly.

"Thanks for telling me that. I also understand you're a competitive cyclist — that's impressive. I'm going to ask you some questions about your training and diet that might sound a bit unusual for a dental visit, but I promise there's a very good reason, and it's going to be really relevant to what's happening with your teeth."

---

Detailed Dietary and Lifestyle History

"Can you walk me through a typical training day — what you eat and drink from the moment you wake up right through to when you go to bed, especially around your training sessions? I'm interested in everything — drinks, snacks, shakes, anything."

Listens carefully, probing where needed.

"You mentioned lemon water first thing in the morning — is that something you do every day? And do you drink it straight from a glass, or do you use a straw? And how soon after that do you brush your teeth?"

Pauses for response.

"And during your rides — what are you drinking? How long are your typical training sessions, and are you sipping the sports drink throughout, or taking it all in one go?"

Listens attentively.

"So you're sipping it over a three-hour ride. Okay, that's really important — I'll come back to that in a moment. What about after training — are you having protein shakes? What brand, and do you mix it with milk or water?"

Continues history.

"Do you ever experience heartburn, acid reflux, or a sour taste in the back of your throat? Any vomiting related to training or otherwise?" Confirms no reflux symptoms. "Good, thank you for that."

"And when you brush, do you tend to brush straight after eating or drinking, or do you wait a while?"

---

Clinical Findings and Diagnosis Explanation

"Thank you — that's been really helpful. Let me now have a look inside your mouth."

Conducts visual examination. Notes cupped occlusal surfaces on posterior teeth and loss of surface detail on the palatal surfaces of the upper anterior teeth. No active carious lesions. Enamel appears smooth and glazed in affected areas.

"Okay, so I can see exactly what's causing your sensitivity, and I want to explain it clearly. What you have is called dental erosion. Now, this is different from a cavity. A cavity is caused by bacteria producing acid as a by-product of eating sugars — it's a bacterial process. Erosion is a purely chemical process — it's acid from your diet directly dissolving the surface of your enamel. No bacteria involved at all.

The pattern I can see is really characteristic — there's some thinning and cupping on the biting surfaces of your back teeth, and there's surface loss on the inner surface of your upper front teeth. That pattern fits perfectly with repeated acid exposure from the foods and drinks you've described. The good news is we've caught this at a stage where we don't need any fillings or major work right now — but we do need to make some changes to stop it progressing."

---

Dietary Counselling and Behavioural Advice

"Let me go through the three main things I want you to change, because these will make the biggest difference.

First, the sports drinks during your rides. Every single sip is an acid attack on your teeth. When you sip continuously over three hours, your teeth are essentially bathed in acid for three hours — your saliva never gets a chance to neutralise and remineralise the enamel. Where possible, I'd encourage you to switch to plain water during training. If you genuinely need the electrolytes for performance, try to drink the sports drink in one go rather than sipping, and then rinse with water straight afterwards. That dramatically reduces the duration of acid exposure.

Second, the lemon water first thing in the morning. This one is actually quite damaging because your saliva flow is at its lowest when you first wake up — your natural buffering capacity is minimal. Starting the day with acid on a dry mouth is one of the worst combinations we see for erosion. I'd suggest switching to plain water in the morning. If you do have something acidic, use a straw to direct it away from your teeth, and rinse your mouth with plain water straight after.

Third — and this one surprises a lot of people — please do not brush your teeth immediately after having anything acidic. When acid softens the enamel surface, brushing at that point physically removes the softened structure. You're essentially scrubbing away your own teeth. Instead, rinse thoroughly with plain water or a fluoride mouthwash straight after acid exposure, and then wait at least thirty to sixty minutes before brushing. I know that feels counterintuitive, but it is genuinely important.

One more positive suggestion — having milk, cheese, or a casein-based protein shake after training can actually help neutralise the acid in your mouth and promote remineralisation. So if you can switch your post-training shake to one mixed with milk rather than water, that would be beneficial."

---

Treatment Plan and Monitoring

"In terms of what I'd like to start doing for you clinically — I'm going to apply a professional fluoride varnish today. This will help protect the exposed surfaces and reduce your sensitivity. I'll recommend we do this every three to four months going forward.

For home care, I want you to use a high-concentration fluoride toothpaste — specifically one containing five thousand parts per million of fluoride. You can get this on prescription — brands like Clinpro or Tooth Mousse Plus are good options. Apply it last thing at night after brushing, leave it on without rinsing, and let it work overnight. This is your most important home-care step.

I'd also like to take some clinical photographs and study models of your teeth today. We'll use these as a baseline, and at your six-month review we can compare and objectively see whether the erosion is stable or progressing. That's our monitoring strategy.

In terms of restorative treatment — at this stage I don't think you need any fillings or veneers. We only consider those options if erosion reaches the deeper layer of the tooth called dentine, or if you're getting pain that's affecting your daily life or your ability to eat. Right now, prevention is our best treatment."

---

Safety Net and Closing

"So just to summarise: we're looking at some dietary timing changes, switching from sipping sports drinks to bolus drinking where possible, avoiding brushing straight after anything acidic, and starting the high-fluoride toothpaste nightly. I'll give you a written summary of everything we've discussed today so you have it as a reference.

If your sensitivity gets significantly worse, or you notice any sharp edges, chipping, or new sensitivity to cold or sweet foods, I want you to come back and see me straight away rather than waiting for your review.

Do you have any questions about anything we've discussed? I know there's a lot to take in."

Listens to patient's response, addresses any concerns warmly and clearly.

"You're doing the right thing by coming in early. With these changes and regular monitoring, we can absolutely keep your teeth stable and protect them for the long term. I'll see you back in six months — or sooner if you need me."

R4
Behaviour Management for Uncooperative Child (4-Year-Old, Carious Molars)
Category:** Restorative / Pediatric | **Time:** 11 min | **Difficulty:** Exam-ready

CASE SUMMARY

4-year-old with grossly carious primary molars, uncooperative and crying during exam. Mother frustrated and wants "them all out under general anaesthetic." Candidate must discuss behaviour management techniques, consent considerations, and GA vs. in-chair options.

CANDIDATE BRIEF

A 4-year-old girl presents with grossly carious 64, 65 (upper left primary first and second molars). She is crying and will not open her mouth for the examiner. Her mother says she "has been like this for every dentist appointment" and is asking for everything to be done under general anaesthetic. Medical history: healthy, no allergies.

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

Address the mother first — INFLECTION 1

"I can see this has been stressful for both of you. Let me explain how we can approach this, and we'll work together to find the right solution."

Behaviour management ladder (2.5 min)

"Before going straight to general anaesthetic, we typically work through a series of approaches to see what the least invasive option is that works for her:

  1. Tell-show-do: I explain what I'm going to do, show her with a model or my finger, then do it. This builds trust.
  2. Non-pharmacological approaches: lots of praise, distraction (favourite music or show on iPad), reward charts, taking breaks
  3. Relative analgesia (nitrous oxide/happy gas): gentle sedation that keeps her awake and cooperative but relaxed — very safe, reversible within minutes. Best option to try first if simpler approaches fail
  4. Oral sedation (midazolam): prescribed by GP or specialist, taken before the appointment. Works for some children. Requires monitoring
  5. General anaesthetic: if all else fails, or if the number/complexity of teeth is too great to manage in the chair safely — then GA is appropriate"

Silver Diamine Fluoride as interim — INFLECTION 2

"While we're working toward any of these, Silver Diamine Fluoride is something I can apply today — no drilling, no injection, just a liquid on the teeth. It arrests the decay and buys us time. It does stain the decayed area black, but for a child this young with this many teeth affected, it's a valuable option while we plan treatment."

GA discussion (1.5 min)

"GA does have real risks — it requires a fasting period, hospital admission, and anaesthetic risk (even in healthy children). It should be reserved for cases where all in-chair approaches have failed, or where the number of teeth and complexity of treatment genuinely can't be done safely in the chair. We're not at that point yet — let's try nitrous first."

Consent considerations

"One important note: for a child this young, all treatment decisions require your informed consent as her parent/guardian. I'll make sure you understand each option before we proceed with anything."

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Validates mother's frustration without dismissing it
  2. ✅ Presents behaviour management ladder (TDD → N2O → oral sedation → GA)
  3. ✅ Discusses SDF as interim measure today (no drilling)
  4. ✅ Explains GA risks honestly — reserve for true failures of in-chair management
  5. ✅ Confirms parental consent required for all treatment decisions

TG4 ALERTS

N2O safety — TG4: do NOT use N2O if child is on diazepam (GABA interaction). Check medications before use.
GA risks in children — Not trivial. Fasting, hospital, anaesthetic agent, post-op recovery. Use when clinically appropriate, not as first-line.
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • "Behaviour management hierarchy: non-pharmacological first — Tell-Show-Do, positive reinforcement, distraction, voice control (firm single-word instruction, not shouting), stop-signal (child-controlled). Advance to pharmacological only after non-pharmacological approaches have been optimised or are clearly insufficient."
  • "Pharmacological options (graduated): oral midazolam pre-medication (0.2–0.5mg/kg, max 15mg, given 30–45 min before appointment), inhalational sedation (nitrous oxide — excellent safety profile for cooperative children who can accept the mask), IV sedation or general anaesthesia for extensive treatment or genuinely unmanageable anxiety."
  • "GA referral indications: extensive caries requiring multiple quadrant treatment, age <3 years, severe dental anxiety that has failed other approaches, medical or behavioural conditions that preclude cooperative treatment."
  • "Document consent from the parent for the behaviour management approach chosen, including any pharmacological adjuncts and their risks."
Patient Reframes
  • "I know it's upsetting to see your child distressed in the dental chair — and I want to be honest: some children at this age are not developmentally ready for cooperative treatment. That doesn't mean nothing can be done; it means we need to match the treatment approach to where your child actually is."
  • "Our goal isn't just to get the treatment done today — it's to make sure your child doesn't leave with a fear of the dentist that follows them for life. Sometimes a gentler, slower approach now saves years of anxiety later."
Curveball Deflectors
  • Parent: "Just do it while I hold her down." → "I understand the impulse — you want this sorted. But physical restraint without the child's cooperation is not consistent with current best practice and can cause psychological harm. It also makes future dental visits much harder. Let me walk you through what I'd like to try first."
  • Parent: "Why can't you just do it quickly without the fuss?" → "I wish it were that simple. Working in the mouth of a distressed, moving child safely requires cooperation. I could rush it — but I'd risk causing harm, either physically or to her relationship with dental care. The approach I'm proposing is slower but it's much safer and kinder."
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ▶
STAGE: Opening and Empathy

Approaches the mother warmly, crouches to the child's level briefly, then turns attention to the mother.

"Hello, I'm the dentist. Thank you both for coming in today — I can see this has been a bit of a tough morning, and I really appreciate you staying. It looks like someone is feeling pretty nervous right now, and that is completely okay. We see this with lots of four-year-olds."

Turning to the mother directly: "And I can hear how frustrated and worried you are — this is not easy when you just want your daughter to feel better and get the help she needs. I want to reassure you that we are absolutely going to find the right path forward for her today. Let me walk you through how I like to approach this, and we can make a decision together."

Invites the mother to sit, ensures the child is settled with a toy or distraction in the room.

---

Behaviour Management Ladder

"Before we talk about general anaesthetic, I want to explain that in paediatric dentistry we always work through a ladder of approaches — starting with the gentlest option and stepping up only if needed. This protects your daughter from unnecessary risk while still getting her the care she needs.

The first approach is something called Tell-Show-Do. I tell her exactly what I'm going to do in simple words she understands, I show her — perhaps using a model or just my finger — and then I do it gently. Children often surprise us once they feel in control and know what to expect.

Alongside that, I use lots of positive reinforcement — praise, a sticker chart, her favourite music or a show on an iPad as distraction. These are simple but genuinely effective for many children her age.

If those approaches aren't quite enough, the next step is relative analgesia — what we call happy gas, or nitrous oxide. It's a gentle inhaled sedation that keeps her fully awake and breathing on her own, but helps her feel calm and relaxed. It works within a few minutes and wears off completely within minutes of stopping. It is very safe and reversible, and it is my preferred first pharmacological step.

One important check before using nitrous oxide — I need to confirm she is not taking any diazepam or benzodiazepines, because combining those medications with nitrous oxide carries a real risk of respiratory depression and is contraindicated. You have mentioned she has no medications, so we are clear on that.

If nitrous oxide is not sufficient, the next step would be oral sedation with midazolam, prescribed in consultation with her GP or a specialist. It is taken before the appointment and requires monitoring throughout. It works well for some children but requires a higher level of preparation.

General anaesthetic is the final step on that ladder, and I do want to discuss it with you — but I would like to explain why we reserve it."

---

Silver Diamine Fluoride as Interim Measure Today

"Now, here is something important and practical — something I can actually do for her today, right now, without any drilling, no injection, and no need for her to do anything difficult.

It is called Silver Diamine Fluoride. It is a liquid I paint directly onto the decayed areas of the teeth. It arrests the decay — it essentially stops it from progressing further — and it buys us valuable time while we plan the definitive treatment together.

I do need to be honest with you about one thing: Silver Diamine Fluoride stains the decayed part of the tooth black permanently. For adult front teeth, that can be a cosmetic concern. But for a four-year-old with grossly carious back molars that she will eventually lose anyway, this is a very reasonable trade-off. It protects her from pain and infection while we work toward a longer-term solution. I would recommend this as our starting point today."

---

General Anaesthetic — Honest Discussion

"Now, about general anaesthetic — I hear you, and I want you to know I am taking your request seriously. GA absolutely has a role in paediatric dentistry, and for the right child in the right circumstances it is the correct choice.

However, GA carries real risks that are not trivial even in healthy children. She would need to fast beforehand, be admitted to hospital, receive an anaesthetic agent, and go through a post-operative recovery period. There are risks of airway complications, post-anaesthetic agitation, nausea, and rarely more serious events. We only recommend GA when in-chair approaches have genuinely failed, or when the number and complexity of teeth requiring treatment makes it unsafe or unrealistic to manage in the chair — even with sedation.

At this point, we have not yet tried nitrous oxide, we have not applied Silver Diamine Fluoride, and we have not given Tell-Show-Do a proper opportunity to build her trust. I would not feel I was acting in her best interest if I referred straight to GA today without working through those steps first. If we try these approaches and she remains unable to cooperate, or if the treatment complexity demands it, then GA becomes absolutely appropriate and I will support that referral fully."

---

Consent and Closing Plan

"One final and important point — because she is four years old, every decision about her treatment requires your informed consent as her parent and guardian. I will make sure I explain each step clearly before we proceed with anything, answer all your questions, and document your agreement. Nothing happens without your understanding and approval.

So here is what I would like to propose today: I would like to apply Silver Diamine Fluoride to the affected teeth right now — that can happen gently, without distressing her further. Then I would like to book her for a second appointment with nitrous oxide available, give Tell-Show-Do a proper chance, and reassess from there. Does that feel like a reasonable starting point for you?"

Pauses, listens to mother's response, addresses any remaining concerns.

"Thank you for trusting me with her care. We are going to get there together."

R5
Missing Upper Lateral Incisor — Options Counseling
Category:** Restorative / Oral Medicine | **Time:** 11 min | **Difficulty:** Exam-ready

CASE SUMMARY

19-year-old, congenitally absent upper left lateral incisor (22), canine has drifted mesially. Orthodontically treated but gap remains (space created by ortho). Patient wants the gap filled. Candidate must counsel on implant, resin-bonded bridge, conventional bridge, and space closure options.

CANDIDATE BRIEF

A 19-year-old female presents asking about options for replacing her missing upper left lateral incisor (22). She has completed orthodontic treatment to open/maintain the space. She is healthy, non-smoker, no medical history of note.

EXAMINER CONTEXT

Patient is focused on aesthetics and wants the "best option." Will ask "Which one would you get?" Will specifically ask about implants — she's heard they're the gold standard. Hidden concern: cost.

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

Examination findings (1 min)

"The space looks adequate — let me measure. The adjacent teeth, bone volume, and gum health look good."

Counselling on options (4 min) — INFLECTION 1: Complete, honest, patient-centred

Option 1 — Implant (gold standard, but timing matters):

"An implant is generally considered the best long-term option because it doesn't involve the adjacent teeth and it preserves bone. However — and this is important — at 19, your facial bones are still growing and developing. Placing an implant now could cause it to look 'submerged' in a few years as the surrounding bone grows. The standard recommendation is to wait until around 18–20 in females, 21–22 in males. We'd want a CBCT to assess bone volume and confirm you're ready. It's a surgical procedure, usually done with local anaesthetic, takes several months total (implant + healing + crown). Cost: approximately $3,500–$5,000 per implant."

Option 2 — Resin-bonded bridge (Maryland bridge):

"This is a conservative option — a porcelain tooth attached to a thin metal or ceramic 'wing' that's bonded to the back of the adjacent tooth with minimal preparation. It's much less invasive than a conventional bridge, doesn't require crowning adjacent teeth, and is fully reversible. It can be done now, is less expensive (~$1,500–$2,000), and is often used as a transitional solution for young patients until they're ready for an implant."

Option 3 — Conventional bridge:

"A bridge involves crowning both adjacent teeth and suspending an artificial tooth between them. I generally don't recommend this as first-line for a young, healthy patient — you'd be permanently altering two perfectly healthy teeth for the sake of replacing one missing tooth."

Option 4 — Space closure with orthodontics:

"This means moving your canine into the lateral position and reshaping it with composite. This is done — it works — but it requires careful planning and the canine is typically larger and yellower than a lateral, so the aesthetics can be tricky."

INFLECTION 2: "Which would you get?"

"Honestly — at your age, I'd recommend starting with a Maryland bridge now to fill the gap while your bone continues to develop, and then reassessing for an implant in 2–3 years. That gives you the least invasive, most conservative path to a long-term great result."

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Assesses bone, space, adjacent teeth, and growth status before recommending
  2. ✅ Explains implant timing consideration (skeletal maturity) — critical for 19yo
  3. ✅ Presents all four options with honest pros/cons
  4. ✅ Recommends Maryland bridge as transitional option (evidence-based for young patients)
  5. ✅ Does NOT recommend conventional bridge (tooth destruction principle)
  6. ✅ Addresses cost when patient raises it

TG4 ALERTS

Implant timing in young patients — Facial growth continues until ~18–20 in females, ~21–22 in males. Premature implant placement can cause implant submergence as surrounding bone grows. CBCT + growth assessment required.
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • "Three evidence-based options for congenitally missing upper lateral incisor: (1) implant, (2) resin-bonded cantilever bridge off the canine (Maryland bridge), (3) space closure with orthodontics and canine reshaping. Each has a specific patient profile."
  • "Implant timing: skeletal growth must be complete. For females: 18–20 years minimum; males: 20–22 years. Premature implant placement results in infra-occlusion as surrounding bone continues to grow. Serial clinical and cephalometric assessment guides timing."
  • "Resin-bonded bridge (RBB): cantilever design off canine — single wing, single abutment tooth. Evidence: 10-year survival rates ~80–90%. Advantage: minimal tooth preparation, reversible. Most appropriate for young patients while awaiting implant eligibility, or as definitive treatment if implant is not preferred."
  • "Orthodontic space closure: move canine mesially into lateral position, reshape to mimic lateral incisor profile. Works best when canines are naturally slender. Avoids prosthetic replacement entirely — but requires ortho treatment and possibly composite/veneer on canine."
Patient Reframes
  • "The good news is you have three solid options — and there's no urgency to choose today. We have time to plan this properly, and the right answer depends on your age, your bite, what your neighbouring teeth look like, and what matters most to you."
  • "An implant is the gold standard long-term replacement — but you have to wait until your jaw has finished growing, which is a few more years. In the meantime, a temporary bridge gives you a tooth in that space without committing to anything permanent."
Curveball Deflectors
  • "I want an implant now." → "I completely understand — an implant is the ideal long-term option. The issue is timing: if we place it before your jaw finishes growing, the implant stays in the same position while the surrounding bone continues to move, and you end up with a tooth that's too high. We're talking a couple of years' wait. In the meantime, I can give you a really good temporary option."
  • "Which one would you get?" → "Honestly? If I were your age and waiting for an implant — a resin-bonded bridge. It protects the space, looks natural, and if it ever needs to come off, nothing has been permanently changed. But let's make sure you understand all three options before you decide."
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ▶
STAGE: Opening & Clinical Assessment

"Hi, come on in — I'm Dr. Chen. Great to meet you. So I understand you've just finished your orthodontic treatment and you're here today to talk about options for filling in that gap where your upper left lateral incisor never developed. Is that right? Wonderful. Before I go through all your options, I'd like to have a quick look in your mouth so I can give you the most accurate advice possible. Is that okay?"

Examines the space at site 22. Notes mesial drift of canine has been corrected orthodontically and adequate space has been reopened.
