Measures the mesiodistal width of the space with a probe — approximately 6–7 mm. Assesses gingival health, which appears healthy with no recession. Palpates the ridge for adequate buccopalatal width. Notes adjacent teeth 21 and 23 are sound, unrestored, and vital.

"The space looks really good — your orthodontist has done a great job opening it back up to a proper width. Your gums are healthy, the adjacent teeth are in excellent condition, and the bone ridge feels like it has good volume. That actually puts you in a very favourable position because all four of the options I want to discuss with you are genuinely on the table."

---

Implant — Gold Standard With Important Timing Caveat

"So let me walk you through the options one by one, starting with what is generally considered the best long-term solution — a dental implant. An implant is a small titanium screw we place into the jawbone, and after it integrates — usually over three to four months — we attach a crown on top. The big advantage is that it doesn't involve your adjacent teeth at all, and it actually preserves the bone in that area long-term.

Now — and this is the most important thing I need to tell you — at nineteen, your facial skeleton is still completing its growth. In females, we generally expect growth to be complete around eighteen to twenty years of age. If we place an implant before that's confirmed, what can happen is the surrounding bone continues to grow slightly but the implant doesn't move with it — so it can appear to 'sink' or look submerged compared to the neighbouring teeth over time. It's a well-documented problem and it's why I wouldn't place an implant today without first taking a CBCT scan to assess your bone volume in three dimensions and confirming your growth has truly finished — we can cross-reference that with your orthodontist's records and cephalometric data.

In terms of the process — it's done under local anaesthetic, entirely in the dental chair. Total treatment time from surgery to final crown is typically four to six months. Cost is in the range of thirty-five hundred to five thousand dollars all inclusive. It is genuinely the gold-standard long-term result."

---

Resin-Bonded Bridge & Space Closure Options

"The second option is a resin-bonded bridge — sometimes called a Maryland bridge. This is a porcelain tooth attached to a very thin metal or ceramic wing, which bonds onto the back of your canine with minimal tooth preparation. It's completely reversible, we preserve your adjacent teeth entirely, and it can be placed right now — today if we wanted to start the process. Cost is typically around fifteen hundred to two thousand dollars. The main limitation is that occasionally the bond can come loose, but modern technique makes these very reliable, particularly when there's only one wing on the canine side.

The third option is a conventional bridge — that's where we crown both the canine and the central incisor either side, grind them down significantly, and suspend an artificial tooth between them. I have to be honest with you: I genuinely don't recommend that approach for a young, healthy patient like you. We'd be permanently and irreversibly cutting into two perfectly healthy, untouched teeth just to replace one missing tooth. That's a significant sacrifice, and I don't think it's the right choice here.

The fourth option is orthodontic space closure — moving your canine further forward into the lateral position and reshaping it with composite resin to look more like a lateral incisor. It works, and some patients are very happy with it. The challenge is that canines are naturally a bit larger and tend to be more yellow in shade than lateral incisors, so achieving ideal aesthetics takes careful planning and some ongoing composite work. It's something to discuss with your orthodontist if you wanted to pursue it."

---

Personal Recommendation & Shared Decision-Making

"So — and I want to be transparent with you — if you asked me what I would recommend for you personally right now, here's my honest answer. I would start with a Maryland bridge in the short term. It fills the gap beautifully, preserves all your healthy tooth structure, costs a fraction of an implant, and it gives your bone another two to three years to finish developing. Then, at around twenty-one or twenty-two, we reassess with a CBCT, confirm your growth is complete, and if everything looks good, we transition to an implant for the long-term result. The Maryland bridge can actually serve as your temporary restoration while the implant heals, so nothing is wasted.

That pathway gives you the most conservative, least invasive route to an outstanding long-term outcome."

---

Questions, Costs & Safety Net / Closing

"Does that make sense? I know that's a lot of information. Do you have any questions about any of the options — cost, timing, what the procedures actually involve?

If cost is a factor, the Maryland bridge now is genuinely excellent value and clinically appropriate — it's not a compromise, it's actually the evidence-based recommendation for your age group. And we can always revisit the implant conversation down the track when the timing is right.

What I'd suggest as our next step is: I'll take some study photographs and measurements today, write a brief letter to your orthodontist to let them know we've had this discussion and to get their growth assessment records, and then you go home, think it over, perhaps talk to your family, and come back to me when you're ready to proceed. There's no urgency — the space is beautifully maintained and there's no harm in taking a week or two to decide.

I'll also give you a printed summary of the four options with approximate costs so you've got something to refer back to at home. Any other questions at all? Wonderful — it was really lovely meeting you today."

R6
Peg Lateral / Microdontia (Diazepam + N2O Risk)
Category:** Restorative | **Time:** 11 min | **Difficulty:** Exam-ready

CASE SUMMARY

Patient with peg-shaped upper right lateral incisor (12) presents wanting cosmetic improvement. Also mentions extreme anxiety and asks about "happy gas." Medical history reveals they are on diazepam 5mg BD prescribed by GP for generalized anxiety disorder. Candidate must address the diazepam + N2O interaction AND counsel on composite resin veneer vs. porcelain veneer vs. crown.

CANDIDATE BRIEF

25-year-old patient with a peg-shaped upper right lateral incisor wants it "made to look normal." They are extremely anxious about dental work and request nitrous oxide sedation. Medical history: generalized anxiety disorder, on diazepam 5mg twice daily prescribed by GP.

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

The diazepam + N2O contraindication — INFLECTION 1: CRITICAL TG4 point

"Thank you for mentioning the diazepam — that's really important. Unfortunately, I can't safely use nitrous oxide (happy gas) in the same appointment if you're taking diazepam. Both diazepam and nitrous oxide work on the same receptor in the brain — called GABA. When both are acting at the same time, it creates an additive sedation effect that can cause significant breathing difficulty. It's a safety risk I'm not able to take.

What I CAN do:

  • If your anxiety is significant, we could look at alternative anxiolysis strategies — oral sedation with a different drug class, or IV sedation with a specialist
  • I can also discuss with your GP whether diazepam is appropriate on the day of treatment, or whether it should be timed differently
  • For simple composite work like this, many patients find that once they're comfortable in the chair and we take our time, they're okay — can we try that first?"

Cosmetic treatment options (2.5 min) — INFLECTION 2

Option 1 — Direct composite resin buildup:

"The most conservative approach — I add tooth-coloured resin to reshape the tooth. No drilling needed (or very minimal), reversible, can be done in one appointment, costs ~$300–$600. Results can be excellent with skill. Downside: composite can chip or stain over years and may need occasional touching up."

Option 2 — Porcelain veneer:

"A thin porcelain shell bonded to the front of the tooth. More durable and stain-resistant than composite, more natural-looking long-term. Requires a small amount of enamel preparation. More expensive (~$1,500–$2,000), two appointments, not as easily reversible."

Option 3 — Crown:

"For a peg lateral, a crown is overkill — it involves drilling down all sides of the tooth for minimal benefit over a veneer. I wouldn't recommend it unless there were structural reasons."

Recommendation

"My suggestion would be direct composite first — it's reversible, minimal intervention, and if you're happy with the result, we don't need to go further. If over time you want something more permanent, we can revisit veneers."

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Identifies and clearly explains the diazepam + N2O contraindication (GABA mechanism)
  2. ✅ Offers alternative anxiety management strategies
  3. ✅ Presents composite, veneer, and crown options with honest pros/cons
  4. ✅ Recommends conservative (composite) as first-line per minimal-intervention principles
  5. ✅ Does NOT proceed with N2O

TG4 ALERTS

Diazepam + N2O = CONTRAINDICATED — TG4: both act on GABA receptors. Combined effect causes additive CNS depression with respiratory risk. Do NOT use together.
Minimal intervention for peg lateral — Crown preparation is overly destructive for a peg lateral. Composite or veneer is appropriate.
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • "Peg lateral treatment options in order of invasiveness: composite resin build-up (most conservative, reversible, excellent aesthetics achievable), porcelain veneer (minimal preparation, high aesthetics, less reversible), full crown (only if there is existing damage, caries, or structural insufficiency)."
  • "Diazepam + nitrous oxide interaction: both are CNS depressants. Combined use produces additive/synergistic sedation — the patient may become more deeply sedated than intended, with potential airway risk. In general practice without full monitoring and resuscitation capability, this combination should be avoided. If the patient requires sedation, refer to a sedation-trained practitioner."
  • "The restorative approach for peg lateral: use a silicone index from a diagnostic wax-up to guide composite placement. Freehand composite on a peg lateral without a guide risks an asymmetrical or bulbous result."
Patient Reframes
  • "The composite build-up is actually the smartest starting point — it's the most reversible option, it looks excellent when done well, and if you later want a veneer, that's still possible. We're not burning any bridges."
  • "The gas and the tablet you take — both relax you, but together they relax you more than either alone. In this setting, that's not safe. I want to offer you alternative ways to manage your anxiety that don't combine those two."
Curveball Deflectors
  • "Can I have the gas today?" → "Normally I'd say yes — but because you've taken diazepam today, the two together produce a deeper level of sedation than I can safely manage here. It's not a permanent no — it's a 'not together, and not today'. I can use the gas at a separate appointment when the diazepam hasn't been taken."
  • "What's the most natural-looking option?" → "Honestly, composite resin done well is hard to distinguish from the real thing — particularly for a peg lateral, which has a simple shape to mimic. I'd start there. If after a year you're not happy, we can talk about veneers."
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ▶
STAGE: Opening and History

"Hi, come on in and take a seat — make yourself comfortable. I'm Dr. Chen, one of the dentists here today. Before we look at your tooth, I'd love to just have a chat and find out a little more about what's brought you in. Is that okay?"

Pauses and allows patient to respond.

"So you're wanting to improve the appearance of your upper right front tooth — the one that looks a little smaller and more pointed than the others. Absolutely, that's something we can definitely help with. Now, I also see on your health history form that you've mentioned feeling quite anxious about dental visits, and you've asked about nitrous oxide — happy gas. I want to make sure we address both of those things today, so thank you for being upfront."

"Can I just confirm your medical history with you? You're taking diazepam — five milligrams, twice a day — prescribed by your GP for generalised anxiety disorder. Is that correct? Are you on any other medications, supplements, or do you have any allergies we should know about? Any other medical conditions?"

Listens carefully and confirms no other significant history.

"That's really helpful — thank you. I want to make sure everything we plan today is completely safe for you, so what you've just told me is very important."

---

Addressing the Diazepam and Nitrous Oxide Contraindication

"Now, I do need to talk to you about the happy gas request, because this is really important for your safety. Unfortunately, I'm not able to use nitrous oxide on the same day that you've taken your diazepam — and I want to explain exactly why, because I know that might be disappointing to hear."

"Both diazepam and nitrous oxide work on the same receptors in the brain — they're called GABA receptors. GABA is essentially your brain's natural calming system. Diazepam activates those receptors, and nitrous oxide does the same thing. When both are working at the same time, the effects don't just add up — they can combine to cause significant sedation, and more seriously, they can suppress your breathing. That's a safety risk I'm simply not able to take, and it's not something I'm willing to compromise on."

"So nitrous oxide is contraindicated while you're taking diazepam — that's a firm boundary based on current clinical guidelines."

"What I absolutely can do is make sure this appointment is as comfortable as possible for you in other ways. For someone with significant dental anxiety, we have a few options. First, I'll take things at your pace — no rushing, full control always with you, we stop whenever you need. Second, if after trying that you feel you'd benefit from something stronger, I can refer you to a specialist for IV sedation, which is a different drug class and is managed safely in that context. Third, I'd also like to write to your GP — with your permission — to have a conversation about your anxiety management on the day of dental treatment, and whether the timing of your diazepam could be adjusted safely. For what we're actually doing today — which is quite conservative and gentle — many patients with anxiety find that once they're settled in the chair, we can get through it together comfortably. Shall we give that a try?"

---

Diagnosis and Treatment Options

"Now let's talk about your tooth. The upper right lateral incisor — the second tooth from the middle on the upper right — has a condition called microdontia, sometimes called a peg lateral. It's a variation in how the tooth developed, and it's actually quite common. The tooth is fully healthy — it's just smaller and more conical in shape than we'd expect. The good news is there are several excellent ways to make it look completely natural."

"I want to walk you through three options so you can make an informed decision."

"The first option is a direct composite resin build-up. This is where I use a tooth-coloured resin material — the same material used for white fillings — and I sculpt it directly onto your tooth to reshape it into a normal-looking lateral incisor. In most cases this requires no drilling at all, or only the very minimum. It's done in a single appointment, it's fully reversible if you ever change your mind, and it typically costs in the range of three hundred to six hundred dollars. The results can be genuinely excellent. The main thing to be aware of is that composite can chip or pick up some staining over time, so it may need a small touch-up every few years."

"The second option is a porcelain veneer. This is a very thin shell of porcelain that is custom-made in a laboratory and bonded to the front surface of your tooth. Porcelain is more resistant to staining and generally looks very lifelike long-term. It does require a small amount of enamel to be prepared from the tooth surface — so it's less reversible than composite — and it involves two appointments. The cost is typically in the range of fifteen hundred to two thousand dollars."

"The third option people sometimes ask about is a crown. For a peg lateral like yours, I would not recommend a crown. A crown involves cutting down the entire tooth on all sides, which is far more destructive than necessary when the tooth itself is healthy. That level of intervention isn't justified here."

---

Recommendation and Shared Decision-Making

"My strong recommendation for you — and this aligns with best practice for minimal intervention dentistry — is to start with the direct composite resin build-up. It's conservative, it's reversible, it can be done in one visit, and the results for a peg lateral are often outstanding. If in a few years you decide you'd like something more permanent, we can always revisit porcelain veneers at that point. We haven't lost anything by starting with composite."

"Does that approach make sense to you? Do you have any questions about either of the options I've described? Take your time — there's no pressure today."

---

Safety Net and Closing

"Before we wrap up — I want to make sure you feel completely supported going forward. I'll write a brief letter to your GP today, with your permission, to let them know about our appointment and to ask whether there's anything we can do collaboratively around your anxiety management before future dental visits. That's really important, and your GP is the right person to be involved in that conversation."

"If you decide you'd like to go ahead with the composite build-up, my nurse will help you book an appointment. I'd suggest we allow about an hour — there's no need for any injections unless you feel you need them, and we'll take the whole thing at whatever pace feels right for you."

"If at any point before that appointment you have questions, concerns, or you just want to talk through things again, please don't hesitate to call us. We're here to support you."

"It was really lovely meeting you today. You've done the right thing coming in, and I want you to know we'll look after you well. Take care."

R7
Small Gap Replacement — Bridge vs. Implant vs. Denture Counseling
Category:** Restorative / Prosthodontics | **Time:** 11 min | **Difficulty:** Exam-ready

CASE SUMMARY

35-year-old patient presents after extraction of tooth 35 (lower left second premolar) 3 months ago. Gap is now healed. Wants to know about replacement options. Bone volume appears adequate on OPG. Adjacent teeth are healthy and unrestored.

CANDIDATE BRIEF

Your task: Counsel the patient on all appropriate replacement options (implant, bridge, denture, no replacement) with honest pros, cons, cost, and your clinical recommendation.

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

Clinical assessment (1 min)

Bone volume (OPG — adequate), adjacent teeth (unrestored, healthy), occlusion, oral hygiene, medical history (no contraindications).

Counselling on options — INFLECTION 1: All options, honest

Option 1 — Dental implant (first-line recommendation):

"An implant replaces the root of the missing tooth with a titanium screw, then a crown on top. It's the most natural-feeling replacement, doesn't involve your adjacent teeth, and preserves the bone underneath (which shrinks when there's no tooth root). It lasts decades with good care. Cost is typically $4,000–$5,500 all up. Takes about 3–6 months from placement to final crown."

Option 2 — Three-unit bridge:

"We crown both adjacent teeth (34 and 36) and hang a false tooth between them. It's fixed (you can't remove it), typically quicker than an implant (~3 weeks, 2 appointments), and less expensive (~$2,500–$3,500). The downside: we permanently alter two healthy, unrestored teeth. For a young patient with healthy adjacent teeth, I'd be reluctant to recommend this."

Option 3 — Partial denture:

"A removable partial denture is the least expensive option (~$800–$1,500). It's removable, so you take it in and out. It doesn't involve the adjacent teeth. Downside: the bone underneath continues to shrink, it can feel bulky, and some people find it less comfortable. For a 35-year-old in good health, I'd only recommend this if cost is a major barrier or if you want a transitional option while planning an implant."

Option 4 — No replacement:

"Leaving the gap — the opposing tooth (25) may over-erupt over time, adjacent teeth may drift, and you'll lose bone in that area. For a posterior tooth in a young person, I'd recommend against this long-term."

Recommendation (1 min) — INFLECTION 2

"Given you're 35, healthy, with good adjacent teeth that are unrestored — an implant is my clear recommendation. It's the most conservative option for adjacent teeth, lasts the longest, and is the gold standard. If cost is a consideration right now, a partial denture as a transitional option is fine, but let's plan toward an implant."

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Presents all four options with honest pros, cons, cost, and timing
  2. ✅ Recommends implant as first-line for young patient with unrestored adjacent teeth
  3. ✅ Explains WHY bridge involves sacrifice of healthy teeth (key ethical point)
  4. ✅ Discusses bone resorption consequences of doing nothing
  5. ✅ Reaches shared decision based on patient's values and circumstances
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • "Present all three options systematically before advocating: implant (gold standard, no adjacent tooth involved, bone preservation), resin-bonded bridge (conservative of adjacent teeth, lower cost, reversible, 10-year survival ~85%), conventional bridge (requires preparation of adjacent teeth — only justified if abutments already need crowning), RPD (removable, lowest cost, most invasive on soft tissue, least preferred for single tooth)."
  • "Key decision drivers: age of patient (implant preferred in younger patients who have decades ahead), bone volume (CBCT/OPG to assess if implant suitability uncertain), adjacent tooth status (existing restorations or planned crowns tilt toward conventional bridge), patient finances and compliance."
  • "Implant cannot be done same-day as extraction in a compromised socket — typically 3 months after extraction for bone healing, unless immediate implant placement criteria are met (intact socket walls, no infection, adequate primary stability)."
Patient Reframes
  • "There's no universally 'best' option here — the right choice depends on your specific situation. My job is to explain each one honestly, including the downsides, so you can decide what fits your life."
  • "An implant is the most like having a natural tooth back — it's independent, doesn't involve the teeth next to it, and preserves the bone. But it takes longer and costs more upfront. Whether that trade-off is worth it is genuinely a personal decision."
Curveball Deflectors
  • "Just give me the cheapest option." → "The cheapest short-term option is often the most expensive long-term. A denture for a single tooth, for example, accelerates bone loss under the gap — which makes future options harder and more expensive. I'd want you to understand those downstream costs before choosing on price alone."
  • "Which one lasts the longest?" → "Implants have the best long-term data — 95%+ survival at 10 years in good bone with good hygiene. But I want to be honest: a well-maintained bridge or denture can also last many years. The difference is more about bone preservation and the teeth next to the gap than about the prosthetic lifespan."
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ▶
STAGE: Opening and Clinical Assessment

"Good morning! I'm Dr. [Name]. Thanks for coming in today. So it's been about three months since we took out your lower left back tooth — the second premolar — and you'd like to talk about your options for replacing it. Is that right? Great. Before I go through everything with you, I just want to ask a couple of quick questions and have a look at your X-ray."

Reviews the OPG — notes adequate bone volume at the 35 site, healthy and unrestored adjacent teeth 34 and 36, no pathology. Checks the occlusion and notes the opposing tooth 25 is currently in normal position. Confirms no medical contraindications — patient is 35, healthy, no medications, non-smoker, good oral hygiene.

"Your X-ray shows the bone in that area looks healthy and there's a good amount of it — which is great news. Your two neighbouring teeth are in excellent condition — no fillings, no crowns. And the tooth above the gap is sitting in a normal position at the moment. So you're actually in a really good situation because we have several solid options to discuss. I'll take you through all of them honestly — including the pros, the cons, the costs, and then I'll give you my recommendation. Does that sound okay?"

Option One — Dental Implant

"The first option — and the one I'd recommend for someone in your situation — is a dental implant. Here's how it works: we place a small titanium screw into the bone where your tooth root used to be. That screw acts as an artificial root. Once it bonds with the bone over about three to four months, we attach a custom-made crown on top. The result looks, feels, and functions just like a natural tooth.

The biggest advantage for you is that we don't touch your neighbouring teeth at all — they stay completely untouched. The implant also preserves the bone underneath, because the titanium root keeps stimulating the bone the same way a natural tooth would. Without a root there, that bone slowly shrinks away over time. An implant lasts decades — potentially a lifetime — with good care and regular check-ups.

The downsides are cost and time. All up, we're typically looking at around four thousand to five thousand five hundred dollars from the surgical placement through to the final crown. The process takes roughly three to six months start to finish — the implant needs time to integrate with the bone before we load a crown onto it. There are two main appointments, plus a review. For a 35-year-old who's healthy with plenty of bone — this is genuinely the gold standard."

Options Two, Three, and Four

"The second option is a three-unit bridge. We crown both neighbouring teeth — 34 and 36 — and suspend an artificial tooth between them, all in one fixed piece. It's cemented in permanently, so you don't remove it. It's quicker — around two to three weeks and two appointments — and less expensive, typically two thousand five hundred to three thousand five hundred dollars.

The significant downside, and I want to be honest with you here, is that we have to permanently cut down and crown two perfectly healthy, unrestored teeth to make that bridge work. Those teeth will always need crowns from that point on. For a 35-year-old with beautiful, untouched neighbouring teeth, I'd find it very difficult to recommend that. It's simply too much of a sacrifice of healthy tooth structure.

The third option is a removable partial denture. This is a plate you take in and out yourself. It doesn't require any work on the adjacent teeth, and it's the most affordable option — roughly eight hundred to fifteen hundred dollars. The downside is comfort — some patients find it bulky or awkward — and importantly, it doesn't stop the bone from shrinking underneath because there's no root in the bone. For a 35-year-old, I'd only suggest this as a transitional option while you're planning toward an implant, or if cost is a significant barrier right now.

The fourth option is to leave the gap. I do need to mention it, but I'd recommend against it long-term. The tooth above — your upper left second premolar — will begin to over-erupt into the space. Your lower neighbouring teeth may drift. And you'll continue to lose bone in that area, which could actually compromise your implant options later on."

Recommendation and Shared Decision

"So, putting it all together — given that you're 35, you're in excellent health, your bone volume is good, and your neighbouring teeth are completely unrestored — an implant is my clear first recommendation. It's the most conservative option for those adjacent teeth, it preserves your bone, and it gives you the best long-term outcome. It genuinely is the gold standard for single tooth replacement in your circumstances.

If the upfront cost is a concern right now, that is completely understandable. A partial denture as a temporary measure is perfectly reasonable — we can fit one relatively quickly while you plan and save for the implant. I wouldn't recommend the bridge given your healthy adjacent teeth, and I'd encourage you not to leave the gap long-term.

I want this to be your decision — you know your circumstances best. Do you have any questions about anything I've gone through? And is cost something we should factor into our planning today?"

Listens to patient's response, addresses concerns, and confirms agreed next step — whether that is implant referral, temporary denture, or further discussion.

"Wonderful. I'll prepare a referral summary for an oral surgeon or implantologist to assess you for the implant placement. In the meantime, if you'd like, we can take impressions for a transitional partial denture today. Let's get you sorted."

R8
Trauma — Lateral Luxation Splinting (Hockey Injury, 12-Year-Old)
Category:** Restorative / Trauma | **Time:** 11 min | **Difficulty:** Exam-ready

CASE SUMMARY

12-year-old presented by parent after hockey puck hit to the face. Upper left central incisor (21) is displaced laterally (lateral luxation). Root formation appears incomplete on PA. Parent and child are anxious. Candidate must diagnose, manage (reposition + splint), and explain the plan.

CANDIDATE BRIEF

12-year-old patient brought in immediately after trauma. Tooth 21 is displaced — moved laterally and locked into the alveolar bone in displaced position. PA shows intact roots, open apex, no fracture. Parent asks "Will the tooth survive?"

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

Triage & Empathy (1 min)

"I can see this is very stressful. Let's take care of this together — a tooth displaced like this can often be saved if we act quickly. Let me explain what I need to do."

Diagnosis (1 min) — INFLECTION 1: Identify as lateral luxation, not avulsion

"The tooth hasn't come out (that would be avulsion) — it's been pushed sideways and has locked into the bone in a displaced position. This is called a lateral luxation. Because the tooth hasn't left the socket, and because it appears to have an open apex (the root isn't fully formed), the blood supply has a better chance of recovering."

Management (2.5 min)

  1. Local anaesthetic
  2. Gentle digital repositioning (push back into position — may hear/feel a click as it unlocks)
  3. Flexible splint: resin composite splint bonded across adjacent teeth (not rigid — flexible splints allow physiological movement and better pulp recovery)
  4. Splint for 2–4 weeks
  5. Chlorhexidine rinse, soft diet, avoid biting on the tooth

Answering "Will the tooth survive?" — INFLECTION 2

"Honestly — the prognosis is guarded but hopeful. Because your daughter's root isn't fully formed, the nerve and blood supply inside the tooth has a better chance of recovering than in an adult. There are two possible outcomes:

  1. The blood supply recovers — the tooth heals normally
  2. The blood supply is disrupted — the tooth's nerve dies over weeks/months, and we'd see changes on the X-ray. We'd then need root canal treatment to save the tooth

We'll monitor with X-rays at 3 weeks, 3 months, 6 months, and 1 year. The first sign that things are going well is that the tooth responds normally to vitality testing."

Safety-netting (1 min)

"If in the next 1–2 weeks you notice the tooth going dark grey/pink, or the gum above the tooth becomes red and swollen, or there's a pimple above the tooth — come in immediately. Those are signs of pulp necrosis."

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Correctly identifies lateral luxation (not avulsion)
  2. ✅ Notes open apex as positive prognostic factor
  3. ✅ Repositions and applies flexible (not rigid) splint
  4. ✅ Honest prognostic conversation — "guarded but hopeful"
  5. ✅ Explains monitoring schedule and what to watch for
  6. ✅ Specific safety-netting (discolouration, gum pimple = pulp necrosis)

TG4 ALERTS

Flexible splint, NOT rigid — TG4/IADT guidelines: rigid splinting increases risk of external root resorption and ankylosis. Flexible splint allows physiological movement.
Open apex = better prognosis — Immature teeth with open apices have greater potential for revascularisation after trauma.
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • "Lateral luxation management: local anaesthetic, digital repositioning (push apically and labially), confirm position clinically and radiographically, flexible splint for 2–4 weeks (not rigid — rigid splinting increases ankylosis risk). IOPA periapical radiograph is standard; CBCT is not routinely required for uncomplicated luxation."
  • "Prognosis is age-dependent: open apex (immature root, child) — excellent pulp survival potential, revascularisation possible. Closed apex (adult) — pulp necrosis likely within weeks to months, requiring RCT. Monitor for colour change (grey-black = necrosis), loss of sensibility testing response, and periapical pathology."
  • "Tetanus status: a penetrating oral wound in a sports injury warrants checking tetanus immunisation status. Standard childhood vaccination covers most patients, but document and confirm."
  • "Sports mouthguard: mandatory post-healing. A custom-fitted mouthguard provides 8–10× more protection than a boil-and-bite type. Refer to the dentist for a custom guard once healing is confirmed."
Patient Reframes
  • "The good news — and I mean genuine good news — is that at 12, the root isn't finished forming yet. That means the blood supply has a much better chance of re-establishing itself than it would in an adult tooth. His age is working in his favour."
  • "The splint keeps the tooth still while the supporting tissue heals — it's not because the tooth is fragile, it's because we need to give the socket time to reattach properly."
  • "We'll monitor the tooth regularly over the next year — what I'm watching for is any colour change or sign that the nerve has been lost. If that happens, we have treatment options. But let's not assume the worst yet."
Curveball Deflectors
  • "Will the tooth survive?" → "At his age, the chances are genuinely good — I'd say more likely than not that the pulp survives because of the open root apex. But I can't promise that, and I'd be doing you a disservice if I did. What I can tell you is that we're doing everything right to give it the best chance."
  • "Should he have come sooner?" → "Ideally yes — a 30-minute window is important for avulsed teeth, though for luxation the timing is more forgiving. You're here now, and that's what matters. Let's focus on what we can do from this point."
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ▶
STAGE: Triage & Empathy

Greets the parent and child warmly, crouches to the child's level, and speaks calmly.

"Hi there — I'm Dr. Chen, one of the dentists here. You must both be feeling pretty shaken up right now, and I completely understand that. I want you to know we're going to look after you very well today. The most important thing is that you came in straight away — that gives us the best possible chance of saving this tooth. Can I ask your name? Lovely, thanks. And Mum, are you happy for me to explain everything to both of you together as we go? Perfect."

Performs a brief extra-oral inspection, noting no facial swelling or obvious jaw asymmetry. Then gently retracts the lip to examine tooth 21.

"I can see that the upper left front tooth has been knocked sideways — I know it looks quite alarming, but I want to reassure you straight away: the tooth is still in the socket. That is actually really important and really good news. Let me take a quick X-ray so I can see the root clearly, and then I'll explain exactly what's happened and what we're going to do."

---

Diagnosis

Reviews the periapical radiograph. Notes no root fracture, intact socket walls, and an open apex on tooth 21.

"Right — I've had a good look at the X-ray, and here's what I can tell you. The tooth has been pushed sideways and is now locked into the surrounding bone in a displaced position. The technical name for this is a lateral luxation. Importantly, it is not an avulsion — the tooth has not come out of the socket. That distinction matters a great deal for the outcome.

Now, here's the other piece of very good news on the X-ray: the root of this tooth is not yet fully formed — you can see the tip of the root is still open. In children around your daughter's age, that open apex means the blood vessels supplying the nerve inside the tooth have a much better chance of recovering after an injury like this, compared to an adult tooth with a fully closed root tip. So we're actually in quite a favourable situation."

---

Repositioning & Splinting

"Before I do anything, I'm going to give a small injection of local anaesthetic to completely numb the area so this is comfortable for you. It might sting just for a moment at the very start, and then everything will go numb. Is that okay?"

Administers local anaesthetic via infiltration to the buccal and palatal aspects of 21. Waits for full anaesthesia.

"I'm now going to gently use my fingers to guide the tooth back into its correct position. There may be a small clicking sensation as it moves back — that's completely normal, it just means it's unlocking from the bone and returning to where it should be. Are you doing okay? Wonderful."

Performs gentle digital repositioning with firm apical and labial pressure. Notes audible click as tooth disengages. Confirms correct position visually and with gentle digital palpation of the labial plate. Takes a confirmatory periapical radiograph.

"The tooth is back in its correct position — that has gone really well. Now I need to hold it steady while it heals, and I do that with a splint. I'll bond a thin, flexible wire across the front of this tooth and the two teeth on either side of it using a tooth-coloured bonding material. It's called a flexible splint, and it's very important that it is flexible — a rigid splint would actually hinder healing. The flexibility allows the tooth to have tiny, natural micro-movements, which encourages the blood supply to recover. The splint will stay in place for two to four weeks."

Places a flexible composite-and-wire splint bonding across teeth 11, 21, and 22. Checks occlusion. Adjusts if necessary.

"I'd like you to rinse twice daily with a chlorhexidine mouthwash — we'll give you a bottle to take home. Please eat only soft foods for the next two to four weeks, and avoid biting directly onto this tooth. No hard fruits, crusty bread, or contact sport until the splint comes off."

---

Prognostic Conversation

"Now, I know the big question on your mind, Mum — will the tooth be okay? I want to be completely honest with you, because I think that's what you deserve. The prognosis is guarded, but genuinely hopeful.

There are two possible pathways from here. The most positive outcome is that the blood supply inside the tooth recovers fully — the tooth heals, the root continues to develop, and everything is normal. Because the root tip is still open, this is a real and realistic possibility. The second outcome is that, despite our best efforts, the blood supply is disrupted and the nerve tissue inside the tooth slowly dies over the coming weeks or months. If that happens, we would see changes on the X-ray — we would not simply wait and hope — and we would then carry out root canal treatment to remove the dying tissue and seal the root. Root canal treatment at that stage is very successful and would still allow us to keep the tooth long-term.

So the tooth is not lost. We are very much in a 'watch carefully and act if needed' situation, and I will be watching very closely."

---

Monitoring Schedule & Safety Net / Closing

"Here is our review plan. I'd like to see you at three to four weeks to remove the splint and do vitality testing. Then again at three months, six months, and twelve months, with X-rays at each visit. The first reassuring sign that things are going well is if the tooth responds normally when we test it with a cold stimulus. That tells us the nerve is alive.

Now — the most important part before you go. I need you to watch for three specific warning signs at home. First, if the tooth changes colour — particularly if it goes dark grey or has a pinkish tinge. Second, if the gum above the tooth becomes red, swollen, or tender. And third, if a small pimple appears on the gum just above the tooth. Any one of these signs means please call us immediately and come in that same day. These signs would tell us the nerve tissue has broken down and we need to act quickly to protect the root.

Do you have any questions at all? You have both done exactly the right thing coming in so promptly — that truly gives this tooth the best possible chance. We'll see you back in three to four weeks, and please don't hesitate to call us in the meantime."

R9
Crown/Onlay Planning for Endodontically-Treated Molar
Category:** Restorative | **Time:** 11 min | **Difficulty:** Exam-ready

CASE SUMMARY

Patient had RCT completed on tooth 46 six months ago. Tooth has a large access cavity and failing MOD amalgam. Candidate must explain why cuspal coverage is essential for long-term survival of RCT teeth, present crown vs. onlay options, and plan appropriately.

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

Explain why RCT teeth need cuspal coverage — INFLECTION 1

"After a root canal treatment, the tooth becomes more brittle. This is because:

  1. We removed the pulp, which provided moisture and sensory feedback to the tooth structure
  2. The tooth now has a large access cavity through the biting surface, and possibly a large existing filling that has further weakened it
  3. Without coverage over the cusps, the tooth is very likely to crack under chewing forces — and a crack usually means loss of the tooth

Research shows RCT teeth are significantly more likely to survive long-term when protected with cuspal coverage."

Crown vs. Onlay — INFLECTION 2

"You have two main options:

Onlay (indirect partial coverage):

Covers the biting surface and cusp tips, preserving more of your own tooth structure on the sides. Requires less drilling. Very strong when bonded with modern materials. Recommended when there's still adequate tooth structure remaining on the sides.

Full crown:

Covers the entire tooth. More preparation required, removes more tooth structure. Necessary when there's significant breakdown or crack risk on the sides of the tooth.

Looking at your tooth — the sides appear intact and there's enough structure. I'd lean toward an onlay as the more conservative option, but let me take impressions and have a closer look before confirming."

Material options

  • Zirconia: very strong, good for back teeth with high bite forces, slightly less conservative preparation
  • Lithium disilicate (e.max): excellent aesthetics, strong, bonds well
  • Gold: most biocompatible, last longest of all, but aesthetic concerns for most patients

Plan

  1. Access cavity build-up (core build)
  2. Impression + CBCT if uncertain about remaining structure
  3. Temporary crown while permanent fabricated (2–3 weeks)
  4. Fit, adjust, cement

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Explains why RCT teeth need cuspal coverage (brittleness + access cavity)
  2. ✅ Explains crack risk without coverage
  3. ✅ Presents onlay vs. crown with honest pros/cons
  4. ✅ Applies minimal intervention principle (onlay where possible)
  5. ✅ Discusses material options (zirconia, e.max, gold)
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • "The ferrule principle: minimum 2mm of sound circumferential dentine above the finish line of the crown preparation is required for crown retention and fracture resistance. Without adequate ferrule, even a post-and-core will not provide a retentive crown — the restoration will fail."
  • "Endodontically treated molar with MOD cavity: the remaining cusps are unsupported and at high risk of catastrophic fracture. Cusp coverage is mandatory — onlay (if <4 cusp coverage needed) or full coverage crown (>4 cusps or inadequate tooth structure). A simple direct composite filling is inappropriate."
  • "Post-and-core: indicated only when coronal structure is insufficient to retain a core — not routinely for all endodontically treated teeth. A post provides retention for the core, not strength for the tooth or the crown. A well-retained core with adequate ferrule is always preferable to a post."
  • "Material choice for posterior crown: zirconia (excellent strength, minimal preparation, good for bruxers), PFM (proven longevity, can be used in limited occlusal clearance), EMAX (excellent aesthetics, but limited in very high load areas like second molars)."
Patient Reframes
  • "The root canal has dealt with the infection — now we need to deal with the structural problem. Back teeth that have had root canals are more brittle than living teeth because they lose some moisture over time, and the large filling that was there means the walls of the tooth are unsupported. A crown wraps around the whole tooth and protects it from cracking."
  • "A crack in a back molar is often catastrophic — you can lose the tooth entirely in one bite. The crown is preventing that scenario, not just cosmetic."
Curveball Deflectors
  • "Do I really need a crown? Can't you just fill it?" → "A large composite filling in a back tooth that's had root canal treatment is one of the most common ways to lose that tooth — the cusps are unsupported and can fracture under chewing forces. I've seen it happen many times. The crown is protective, not just restorative."
  • "How long will the crown last?" → "With good home care and regular reviews, a well-made crown on a properly root-treated tooth has a 10–15+ year lifespan in most studies — often longer. What fails crowns is usually decay at the margins or a fracture of the underlying tooth. Both are things we can prevent with maintenance."
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ▶
STAGE: Opening & Orientation

Candidate greets the patient warmly and establishes rapport.

"Hello, come on in and take a seat. My name is Dr. Chen — lovely to meet you. So today I'd like to have a chat about your lower right molar, tooth 46, the one that had the root canal treatment completed about six months ago. I want to talk you through where things stand and what our next step should be to make sure that tooth stays healthy and functional for as long as possible. Does that sound okay with you?"

Pauses to allow patient to respond, nods and listens actively.

"Great. Now before I explain anything, can I just ask — how has the tooth been feeling? Any pain, sensitivity, or discomfort when you bite down on that side?"

Allows patient to answer, acknowledges their response.

"Good to know. And are you aware that the tooth still has that old filling in it — the large silver filling that was there before the root canal? Have you noticed any issues with it — any movement, rough edges, anything like that?"

Listens attentively and nods.

---

Why RCT Teeth Need Cuspal Coverage

"So let me explain something important about teeth that have had root canal treatment, because it really does shape everything we're about to discuss. After a root canal, the tooth actually becomes significantly more brittle over time. I want to help you understand why that happens.

During root canal treatment, we remove the pulp — that's the living tissue inside the tooth, the nerves and blood vessels. That pulp wasn't just responsible for sensation; it also delivered moisture and nutrients to the surrounding dentine, which helped keep the tooth flexible and resilient. Once that's gone, the tooth structure becomes drier and more prone to fracture.

Now, on top of that, your tooth 46 has a large opening through the biting surface — that's the access cavity we created to do the root canal — and it still has that old, large MOD amalgam filling, which means it spans from the back surface right through to the front surface of the tooth. Between those two things, a significant amount of the internal structure has already been removed. The cusps — those are the raised points on the biting surface — are now unsupported and sitting under considerable stress every time you chew.

Research is very clear on this: without coverage over those cusps, RCT teeth are at a dramatically higher risk of catastrophic vertical fracture. And I want to be honest with you — if that tooth cracks vertically down into the root, we are usually looking at losing the tooth entirely. That's something we very much want to avoid. Cuspal coverage has been shown to significantly improve the long-term survival of root-canal-treated molar teeth, and that is why it is the standard of care."

---

Crown vs. Onlay — Presenting the Options

"So, you have two main options for protecting this tooth, and I want to walk you through both of them honestly so we can decide together what suits you best.

The first option is an onlay. This is what we call an indirect partial coverage restoration — it covers the entire biting surface and protects the cusp tips, but it preserves the natural tooth structure on the sides of the tooth, which means less drilling is required. When we bond a modern onlay into place, it actually reinforces the tooth from within. It is a very strong, conservative approach, and it is my preferred starting point when there is still adequate tooth structure on the sides.

The second option is a full crown. A crown wraps around the entire tooth — top, sides, and all. It requires more preparation, which means removing more of your natural tooth structure to create space. We typically recommend a crown when there has been significant breakdown on the sides of the tooth, or when there is a crack risk extending beyond what an onlay can protect.

Looking at your tooth today, the walls on the sides appear to be reasonably intact. On that basis, I am leaning toward recommending an onlay as the more conservative and appropriate option. That said, I do want to take a proper impression and, if needed, a CBCT scan to assess the remaining structure more accurately before I give you a definitive recommendation."

---

Material Options

"Now, in terms of what the onlay or crown would actually be made from — you have a few excellent options, and they each have their own strengths.

The first is zirconia. This is an extremely strong ceramic, very well suited to back teeth where bite forces are highest. It is tooth-coloured, so it looks natural, and the preparation required is slightly less conservative than some other ceramics.

The second option is lithium disilicate — you may have heard of the brand name e.max. This material combines outstanding aesthetics with very good strength, and crucially, it bonds very well to tooth structure, which actually adds to the reinforcement of the tooth. For an onlay in particular, this is often my first choice.

The third option is gold. I know many patients are not keen on the appearance, but I always mention it because gold is the most biocompatible material we have, it is extremely kind to the opposing teeth, and it has the longest clinical track record of any indirect restoration. If aesthetics are less of a concern for a tooth this far back, gold is a genuinely excellent choice."

---

Treatment Plan

"So, here is what I am proposing for your treatment plan. We would start by placing a core build-up — that means filling in the access cavity and the old amalgam space with a strong composite material to give us a solid, predictable foundation to work from.

From there, I will take an impression of the tooth, and we will send that to our dental laboratory where a skilled technician will fabricate your restoration. In the meantime, we will place a temporary crown over the tooth to protect it — that phase typically takes around two to three weeks.

Once the permanent restoration comes back from the lab, we bring you in for the fit appointment, check the bite carefully, make any adjustments needed, and then cement it permanently into place.

Does that all make sense? Do you have any questions about anything I have explained — the reason for doing this, the options, or what the process will involve?"

---

Safety Net & Closing

"Wonderful. A couple of important things to keep in mind while we get this organised. Please do be careful on that side — try to avoid very hard or crunchy foods until we have the definitive restoration in place, because the tooth is at its most vulnerable right now.

If at any point you notice a sharp pain when biting, a sudden change in the way the tooth feels, or if part of the tooth feels like it has moved or broken, please contact us straight away and we will see you as a priority.

Once we have the onlay or crown in place, the long-term outlook for this tooth is genuinely very good. With good oral hygiene and regular check-ups, we are aiming for many, many years of function.

I'll get my nurse to take some photos and an impression today so we can get things moving. Thank you so much for coming in — you're doing exactly the right thing by getting this sorted."

PR1
Complete Denture Patient — Denture Not Fitting, Multiple Problems
Category:** Prosthodontics | **Time:** 11 min | **Difficulty:** Exam-ready

CASE SUMMARY

Edentulous patient, 72-year-old, presents with loose upper denture (worn for 8 years), sore ridge, and angular cheilitis. Combination syndrome present (upper complete denture opposing natural lower front teeth). Candidate must assess, diagnose, and manage comprehensively.

CANDIDATE BRIEF

72-year-old edentulous upper arch, lower anterior teeth (33–43) remaining, wearing an upper complete denture for 8 years. Presenting complaints: loose upper denture, sore ridge, and cracking at corners of mouth. Your task: assess, diagnose, and plan management.

EXAMINER CONTEXT

Patient is embarrassed about the denture falling out in social situations. Is anxious about cost of new denture. Has not been to a dentist for 5 years.

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

History (2 min)

  • How long worn, when looseness started, diet changes
  • Denture hygiene: "Do you take it out at night? How do you clean it?"
  • Medical history: diabetes, xerostomia-causing medications (antihistamines, antidepressants, antihypertensives)
  • "Have you noticed any changes to the shape of your face?"

Examination (1.5 min)

  • Denture fit, retention, stability (border seal, flange extensions)
  • Ridge assessment: upper anterior ridge — check for fibrous/flabby tissue (classic combination syndrome finding)
  • Opposing lower teeth: overeruption or periodontal issues
  • Soft tissue: angular cheilitis (corners of mouth)
  • Palate: denture stomatitis signs

Diagnosis — INFLECTION 1: Combination syndrome

"What's happened here is called combination syndrome. When you have natural teeth in the bottom front and a complete denture on top, the bite forces get distributed unevenly. Over time, the upper front part of the jaw loses bone, while the lower back (where there are no teeth) also loses bone. This causes the denture to rock and become loose, and it also changes the shape of your face — the typical result is that your upper lip starts to fold inward a bit."

Angular cheilitis management

"The cracking at the corners of your mouth — this is called angular cheilitis, and it's very common with dentures that have lost their vertical height. When the bite collapses, the corners of your mouth get folded and become moist, which allows fungal and bacterial growth. We treat it with miconazole cream for the corners and address the root cause — the denture."

Management plan (2 min) — INFLECTION 2

  1. Antifungal treatment for angular cheilitis and any denture stomatitis (miconazole cream to corners + denture stomatitis treatment)
  2. Reline the existing denture short-term (tissue conditioner first if ridge is sore)
  3. Discuss new upper complete denture
  4. Periodontal assessment and treatment of lower anteriors
  5. Consider implant-retained overdenture if patient interested and financially able (better retention, bone preservation)
  6. TG4: Dry storage overnight

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Diagnoses combination syndrome with explanation
  2. ✅ Angular cheilitis: antifungal cream + vertical dimension correction
  3. ✅ Denture stomatitis: dry storage + antifungal
  4. ✅ Plans tissue conditioning before impressions for new denture
  5. ✅ Mentions implant overdenture as an option
  6. ✅ Addresses the lower anterior teeth (often neglected but integral to the problem)

TG4 ALERTS

Denture dry storage overnight — TG4: reduces Candida colonization. Patient likely soaking in water (moist = Candida growth). Correct this as part of angular cheilitis and denture stomatitis management.
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • "Systematic denture assessment: (1) Extra-oral — VDO, facial support, aesthetics. (2) Intra-oral — ridge assessment (bone volume, muscle attachments, undercuts), soft tissue health (denture stomatitis? — treat before new denture). (3) Denture assessment — fit (border seal, extension), retention (suction, post-dam), stability (balanced occlusion, occlusal scheme), aesthetics."
  • "Denture stomatitis (Candida albicans under denture base): treat with miconazole gel applied to the fitting surface of the denture TID for 2 weeks, AND advise denture removal at night, and soaking in dilute sodium hypochlorite (not bleach-strength) to disinfect the denture. Do not reline onto an infected mucosa."
  • "Implant-retained overdenture discussion: mandatory to raise with edentulous patients, particularly mandible. Two implants supporting a mandibular overdenture is the minimum standard of care (McGill Consensus Statement). It dramatically improves stability, retention, and quality of life, and preserves alveolar bone."
  • "Bone resorption is inevitable under a conventional denture: it continues at ~0.5mm/year on average. Relining is a temporary solution; bone loss is permanent. Implants preserve bone — this is the long-term argument for overdentures."
Patient Reframes
  • "Dentures need to be remade or relined periodically because your jaw bone changes shape underneath them — that's not a sign of poor quality work, it's the nature of wearing a denture on living tissue."
  • "I want to mention an option that not everyone knows about: implant-supported dentures. Two small implants in the lower jaw completely change how a denture functions — it clicks in and stays put. The evidence is strong that it improves quality of life significantly. It costs more upfront but many patients say it's transformative."
Curveball Deflectors
  • "Why do my dentures keep falling out?" → "Several possible reasons — let me check each one. The lower denture is inherently harder to retain than the upper because there's less surface area and the tongue and cheeks can dislodge it. Ridge resorption reduces the suction we can achieve. Occlusal balance affects how the denture sits under load. Let me assess each factor."
  • "The last dentist made them perfectly — why are they failing now?" → "They probably were excellent when they were made. The problem is that the ridge underneath has continued to resorb since then, so the fit that was accurate two years ago is no longer accurate today. That's not a reflection on the quality of the previous work."
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ▶
STAGE: Opening and History

"Hello, come in and take a seat. My name is [Candidate Name], I'm the dentist today. How are you feeling? You've come in today about your upper denture — is that right? Before I take a look, I'd love to hear more about what's been bothering you."

"You've had this upper denture for about eight years now — when did you first notice it starting to feel loose? And has the soreness in your mouth been there for a while, or did it come on more recently?"

"Can you tell me a little about how you clean your denture each day? Do you take it out at night, or do you sleep in it? And when you do take it out, where do you store it — do you leave it in a glass of water, or somewhere else?"

"Have you noticed any changes to your face — perhaps your lips look a bit different, or your chin feels closer to your nose than it used to?"

"Are you managing to eat comfortably? Has your diet changed — softer foods, avoiding anything crunchy?"

"Now, a few important health questions. Do you have diabetes, or any conditions that are being managed with tablets? Some medications — including certain blood pressure tablets, antihistamines, or antidepressants — can cause a dry mouth, which can affect how well a denture fits and can contribute to that soreness. Does your mouth ever feel dry?"

---

Examination

Inspects the corners of the mouth. Notes erythema and fissuring bilaterally — consistent with angular cheilitis.

Examines the upper denture in situ: assesses retention by lifting posteriorly — minimal resistance. Border seal is inadequate. Flanges appear under-extended. Denture rocks under digital pressure — poor stability.

Removes the upper denture. Examines the upper anterior ridge: notes a compressible, mobile, flabby tissue replacing the alveolar bone in the anterior maxilla. Posterior ridges are resorbed but firm.

Examines the palate: erythematous mucosa beneath the denture — diffuse type II denture stomatitis noted.

Examines the lower arch: natural lower anterior teeth 33 to 43 present, with evidence of overeruption and mild to moderate periodontal recession. No lower posterior teeth present.

---

Diagnosis and Explanation — Combination Syndrome and Angular Cheilitis

"Thank you for letting me examine you. I want to explain what I've found, and I think once I explain it, a lot of what you've been experiencing will make sense."

"What's happened here is something called combination syndrome. When you have natural teeth only in the lower front, and a complete denture on top, the biting forces get distributed very unevenly. Over time, the bone under the upper front part of your denture gets resorbed — it actually shrinks away — while the back of the lower jaw, where there are no teeth, also loses bone. This is why your denture rocks forward and feels loose. It also explains why the shape of your face has changed — the vertical height of your bite has collapsed, and that causes your upper lip to fold inward and the corners of your mouth to drop down."

"Those cracked, sore corners of your mouth are called angular cheilitis. When the bite collapses, the corners of the mouth become folded and stay moist — that moist environment allows a fungal organism called Candida to grow there. That's what's causing the cracking and soreness."

"I've also noticed that the skin of your palate under the denture is quite red and inflamed — this is called denture stomatitis, and it's also related to Candida. It's very common when a denture is stored in water overnight, because that keeps the surface moist and allows the fungus to thrive."

---

Management Plan

"So here's what I'd like to do for you, step by step."

"For the corners of your mouth, I'm going to recommend miconazole cream — a small amount applied to each corner two to three times daily. That will treat the Candida directly. But we also need to address the underlying cause, which is the collapsed bite."

"For the stomatitis under your denture, the most important change you can make tonight is this: please stop storing your denture in water. According to current best practice, dentures should be stored dry overnight — this significantly reduces Candida colonisation on the denture surface. I'd also ask you to clean the fitting surface of the denture thoroughly each day."

"Now, your ridge at the front of the upper jaw has become quite soft and moveable — we call that flabby tissue — and this means I can't take a final impression for a new denture just yet. First, I want to place a tissue conditioner inside your existing denture. Think of it as a soft, cushioning liner that allows the tissues to recover and the inflammation to settle over the next two to four weeks. Once the ridge is healthier, we can take accurate impressions."

"After that, we will make you a new upper complete denture, carefully restoring your bite to a proper vertical height. This will take the tension off the corners of your mouth and form part of the long-term management."

"Your lower front teeth are also an important part of this picture. They are the reason the combination syndrome has developed, and I've noticed they've drifted slightly and the gums have receded. I'd like to do a full periodontal assessment of those teeth and provide any treatment needed to stabilise them."

"Finally, I want to mention that if you are open to it and it is financially feasible, implant-retained overdentures are an excellent long-term option. Even two implants in the upper jaw can dramatically improve denture retention and slow down further bone loss. I'm happy to discuss that in more detail at a future visit."

---

Safety Net and Closing

"I know that's quite a lot of information, so please stop me if anything is unclear. The most important things to start today are: switch to dry storage of your denture overnight, and begin the miconazole cream at the corners of your mouth."

"I'd like to see you again in two to four weeks to review how the tissues are responding to the tissue conditioner, and then we'll move forward with planning the new denture from there."

"Do you have any questions? Is there anything you'd like me to go over again? You're doing the right thing coming in — these issues are very treatable, and we'll get you comfortable again."

PR2
Implant Assessment — Warfarin + Prosthetic Heart Valve
Category:** Prosthodontics / Oral Surgery | **Time:** 11 min | **Difficulty:** Exam-ready

CASE SUMMARY

Patient requests implant for missing tooth 46. Has prosthetic mitral valve (warfarin, INR 2.5). Candidate must assess implant suitability, address warfarin management for implant surgery, and discuss antibiotic prophylaxis requirement.

CANDIDATE BRIEF

55-year-old patient, missing tooth 46 (lost 18 months ago), requests dental implant. Medical history: prosthetic mitral valve (on warfarin, INR 2.5 checked last week). Healthy otherwise, non-smoker.

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

Implant suitability assessment (2 min) — INFLECTION 1

  • Bone volume and density: OPG + CBCT
  • Ridge height (especially inferior alveolar nerve proximity for lower posterior)
  • Oral hygiene (OH must be good — implants fail with poor OH)
  • Smoking (no smoking here — good prognostic factor)
  • Occlusion, parafunctional habits (bruxism)
  • Medical fitness for surgery (warfarin, cardiac history)

Warfarin management for implant surgery (1.5 min) — INFLECTION 2

"For implant surgery — which is more involved than a simple extraction — we need to review your INR. The general approach is the same: we do NOT stop warfarin.

  • If INR is within therapeutic range (2.0–3.0), implant surgery can typically proceed with local haemostasis
  • We use resorbable sutures, haemostatic agents, and careful surgical technique
  • I'll coordinate with your cardiologist to confirm they're comfortable proceeding"

Antibiotic prophylaxis — INFLECTION 3

"With your prosthetic heart valve, you DO require antibiotic prophylaxis before the implant surgery — this is the same as for an extraction. Amoxicillin 2g orally 30–60 minutes before the procedure."

Implant procedure explanation (1.5 min)

"If everything checks out:

  1. CBCT to confirm bone dimensions
  2. Surgical placement of titanium implant under local anaesthetic (one appointment, ~45 min)
  3. 3–6 months healing (osseointegration)
  4. Abutment placement
  5. Final crown

Total: 5–8 months from start to finish."

Post-op care for cardiac patient

  • Antibiotic prophylaxis as above
  • Local haemostasis (no aspirin, warfarin continued as usual)
  • Review in 1 week
  • Longer follow-up given cardiac complexity

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Performs comprehensive implant assessment (bone, OH, occlusion, medical fitness)
  2. ✅ Warfarin: continue, coordinate with cardiologist, local haemostasis
  3. ✅ Prosthetic valve = antibiotic prophylaxis required (amoxicillin 2g pre-op)
  4. ✅ Explains procedure and timeline clearly
  5. ✅ Plans appropriate follow-up
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • "Prosthetic heart valve = high-risk cardiac condition → antibiotic prophylaxis required before implant surgery (which breaches the mucosa). Regimen: amoxicillin 2g orally 30–60 min before. If penicillin-allergic: clindamycin 600mg."
  • "Warfarin management for implant surgery: INR check ideally within 24–72 hours of the procedure. INR <3.5 — proceed with local haemostatic measures. Do NOT stop warfarin. Coordinate with cardiologist — they may have specific INR target ranges for the prosthetic valve type."
  • "Implant placement in anticoagulated patients: expect greater intra-operative bleeding, manage with oxidised cellulose, tranexamic acid irrigation, sutures with good primary closure. Advise patient to monitor post-operatively."
  • "Pre-implant workup: CBCT to assess bone volume and proximity to anatomical structures, OPG, medical history including duration on warfarin, INR stability, cardiologist letter if needed."
Patient Reframes
  • "The warfarin protects your prosthetic valve from clot formation — stopping it for dental work creates more risk than the dental bleeding does. We manage the bleeding locally, and you stay protected."
  • "The antibiotic you'll take before the procedure is a single dose — not a course. It's specifically to prevent bacteria from the procedure reaching your heart valve during the moment the gum is disturbed."
Curveball Deflectors
  • "My cardiologist said I can't have dental work done." → "I'd like to speak with your cardiologist directly if possible — because unmanaged dental disease (infection, bleeding gums) also creates bacteraemia that's a risk to your valve. In most cases, we can find a safe way to proceed together. Can I write to them to explain the planned procedure and our precautions?"
  • "Do I need to stop the warfarin for the implant?" → "No — the current evidence and guidelines recommend continuing warfarin at therapeutic levels for dental surgical procedures, including implants. We manage the bleeding locally. Stopping warfarin for this procedure is more dangerous than the bleeding risk we can control."
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ▶
STAGE: Opening and Initial Assessment

"Good morning, I'm Dr. [Name]. It's lovely to meet you. I understand you're interested in having a dental implant to replace your missing lower right molar — is that right? Before we talk about the implant itself, I'd like to ask you a few questions and go through your medical history carefully, because that will really guide how we plan your treatment. Is that okay?"

Candidate reviews the medical history form and confirms: prosthetic mitral valve, warfarin therapy, INR 2.5 measured one week ago, non-smoker, otherwise healthy.

"Thank you for bringing your medical details. So you have a prosthetic mitral valve and you're taking warfarin — that's really important information, and I'll come back to that in detail shortly. First, can I ask — how long have you been missing that lower molar? And how has your eating been since you lost it? Have you noticed the teeth around the space shifting at all?"

Patient confirms tooth lost 18 months ago, no shifting noticed, eating manageable but prefers left side.

"Good. And at home, how do you find your brushing and flossing routine? Any bleeding when you brush? Any loose teeth or gum problems we should know about?"

Implant Suitability Assessment

"So, implants are an excellent option for replacing a single missing tooth, and you're actually a good candidate on several fronts — you're a non-smoker, which is one of the most important prognostic factors for implant success, and it sounds like your oral hygiene is well maintained. Those are both really positive signs."

"However, because this tooth is in the lower jaw, there's an important nerve called the inferior alveolar nerve that runs through the jawbone just below where your tooth used to be. Before we can commit to an implant, I need to take some specialised imaging. I'll start with an OPG — a panoramic X-ray — to get an overview of the bone height and the nerve position. Then I'll arrange a CBCT scan, which gives us a three-dimensional picture of the bone. That tells us the exact height, width, and density of the bone available, and precisely how far the nerve sits from the proposed implant site. We need a minimum of about ten to twelve millimetres of bone height above the nerve, and adequate width — roughly six millimetres — to safely place an implant."

"I'll also examine your bite carefully today. Do you ever wake up with a sore jaw, or has anyone told you that you grind your teeth at night? Grinding — or bruxism — places very high forces on implants and can affect their long-term success, so that's something we'd need to manage, possibly with a night guard."

Warfarin Management — Inflection Point

"Now, let's talk about your warfarin. This is a very common question, and I want to reassure you — the current evidence-based approach, which our guidelines support, is that we do NOT stop your warfarin before implant surgery. Stopping warfarin puts you at serious risk of a blood clot forming on your prosthetic valve, and that risk is far greater than any bleeding risk during the procedure."

"Your INR was checked last week at 2.5, which sits nicely within your therapeutic range of 2.0 to 3.0. Ideally, I'll ask you to have another INR check within 24 hours of the surgery date, just to confirm it's still in range on the day. As long as it is, we can proceed safely."

"During the surgery itself, I'll use careful technique, place resorbable sutures, and use local haemostatic agents — such as a small piece of absorbable gelatin sponge — to control any bleeding at the site. I will also be in contact with your cardiologist before we proceed, to let them know what we're planning and to confirm they're comfortable with the timing and approach. That coordination between us is really important for your safety."

Antibiotic Prophylaxis — Inflection Point

"Now, because you have a prosthetic heart valve, you do require antibiotic prophylaxis before the implant surgery. This is the same recommendation that applies to your extractions — the implant placement creates a pathway for bacteria to enter the bloodstream, and we want to protect your valve from a serious infection called infective endocarditis."

"The antibiotic we use is amoxicillin, two grams taken orally, thirty to sixty minutes before the procedure. If you have a penicillin allergy, we would discuss an alternative — but as you have no allergies listed, amoxicillin is the appropriate choice. I'll write you a script for this in advance so everything is ready on the day."

Procedure Explanation and Timeline

"So, assuming the CBCT confirms adequate bone and everything checks out medically, here is what the process looks like. At the first surgical appointment — which takes around forty-five minutes under local anaesthetic — I place a small titanium implant into the jawbone. You won't feel pain during the procedure, though you may feel some pressure. Afterwards, I'll prescribe paracetamol one gram every four to six hours for pain relief. We avoid ibuprofen in your case given that you're on warfarin, as the combination increases bleeding risk."

"The implant then undergoes a process called osseointegration — the bone grows around and bonds to the titanium. This takes three to six months. After that, a small connector piece called an abutment is attached, and finally, your custom-made crown is fitted. From start to finish, you're looking at approximately five to eight months."

Follow-Up, Safety Netting, and Closing

"I'll review you one week after the implant placement to check healing, remove any sutures if needed, and make sure there's no sign of infection or bleeding concerns. Given your cardiac history, I'll keep your cardiologist informed at each stage of treatment."

"Before we finish today — do you have any questions at all? About the imaging, the warfarin, the antibiotic, or the procedure itself? I want to make sure you feel completely informed and comfortable before we move forward. Once the CBCT is done, I'll sit down with you again and we can look at the images together and finalise the plan. How does that sound?"

PR3
Ulcer on Lower Ridge — New vs. Existing Denture
Category:** Prosthodontics / Oral Medicine | **Time:** 11 min | **Difficulty:** Exam-ready

CASE SUMMARY

Patient wearing existing lower partial denture presents with a 10-day non-healing ulcer on lower alveolar ridge (lingual flange area). Candidate must distinguish traumatic ulcer from other causes (aphthous, malignancy), adjust denture if traumatic, and safety-net for non-healing ulcers.

CANDIDATE BRIEF

68-year-old presents with a painful ulcer on the lower alveolar ridge, present for 10 days, "started when I got the new denture fitted." Denture is 3 weeks old. Ulcer is 7mm × 5mm, irregular margins, base appears yellowish, surrounded by erythematous halo.

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

History (1.5 min) — INFLECTION 1: Timeline + denture correlation

  • "When exactly did the ulcer start — was it right after getting the new denture, or did it come on gradually?"
  • "Has it changed in size or shape since you first noticed it?"
  • "Any similar ulcers in the mouth before?"
  • "Any general health changes, new medications, stress?"
  • Medical history: any immunosuppression, previous oral cancer, smoking/alcohol history

Examination (1.5 min)

  • Site, size, margins (smooth = traumatic/aphthous; irregular/rolled = malignancy red flag)
  • Base (yellow/grey = fibrin — normal for traumatic ulcer; indurated = red flag)
  • Any palpable lymphadenopathy (red flag for malignancy)
  • Denture fit: is the lingual flange overextended in that area? Is the denture rubbing?

Diagnosis — INFLECTION 2: Traumatic ulcer vs. red flags

"Based on the timing (started with the new denture), the location (directly under the denture flange), and the appearance, this looks like a traumatic ulcer caused by the denture rubbing. These are the most common ulcers in denture patients.

However, I need to be honest: any ulcer that hasn't healed in 2–3 weeks needs to be taken seriously. 10 days is still within the expected healing window for a traumatic ulcer, but if it's not resolved in another 1–2 weeks after we adjust the denture, we need to biopsy it."

Management

  1. Adjust/relieve the denture in the area causing irritation (pressure point indicator paste to identify exact spot)
  2. Advise patient to leave denture out overnight (or as much as possible)
  3. Chlorhexidine rinse 0.2% twice daily
  4. Review in 2 weeks
  5. If not healed at 2 weeks → biopsy regardless of appearance
