Safety-netting — INFLECTION 3

"I want to be clear: the 2-week rule applies to all oral ulcers. If this hasn't healed completely by then, we will take a small sample (biopsy) to make sure it's not something more serious. Please come back sooner if it gets bigger, more painful, or you feel a lump in your neck."

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Correlates ulcer onset with new denture fitting
  2. ✅ Examines denture for the causative pressure point
  3. ✅ Identifies red flags (irregular margins, induration, >3 weeks non-healing)
  4. ✅ Adjusts denture as primary treatment
  5. ✅ Explicit 2-week rule and biopsy plan if not healed
  6. ✅ Lymphadenopathy check (malignancy screen)

TG4 ALERTS

2-week rule for oral ulcers — Any ulcer persisting beyond 2–3 weeks must be biopsied. Squamous cell carcinoma can mimic traumatic ulcer. Do NOT reassure and dismiss without review.
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • "Denture-related ulcer differential: (1) denture-induced traumatic ulcer (most common — localised, oval, at site of pressure, resolves within 2 weeks of denture adjustment), (2) non-specific traumatic ulcer (bone spur, sharp food), (3) recurrent aphthous ulcer, (4) squamous cell carcinoma."
  • "Red flags requiring urgent referral: ulcer present >2 weeks without healing, indurated (firm) base, raised or rolled borders, painless (SCC is often painless), associated lymphadenopathy, patient with tobacco/alcohol history, floor of mouth or ventral tongue location."
  • "Do not simply adjust the denture and discharge — always arrange a review in 2 weeks. If the ulcer has not healed in 2 weeks, refer urgently regardless of the appearance. This is non-negotiable."
  • "New denture ulcer vs existing denture ulcer: new denture = sore spots expected in first 24–72 hours, adjust the denture using pressure indicator paste to identify the contact point. Existing denture = the denture has changed or the ridge has changed — investigate why."
Patient Reframes
  • "A sore spot under a denture is very common and usually very easy to fix — we identify the pressure point precisely and adjust it. But because any ulcer that hasn't healed in two weeks needs to be checked, I want to see you again in a fortnight to confirm it's resolved."
  • "I'm not worried about this today — but the only way to be certain is to monitor it. Most of these are exactly what they look like: a pressure sore from the denture. The rare ones that aren't are much easier to treat when found early."
Curveball Deflectors
  • "It's nothing serious, is it?" → "Almost certainly not — the location and appearance are consistent with a pressure sore from the denture. But I'd be doing you a disservice if I dismissed any oral ulcer without a follow-up. We adjust the denture today and I need to see you again in two weeks. If it's healed, great. If it hasn't, I refer you."
  • "Just adjust the denture and it'll be fine." → "I'll definitely adjust it — that's the most likely solution. And I want to confirm it's worked by seeing you again in two weeks. It takes 30 seconds to check, and it means we're not missing something we'd wish we hadn't."
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ▶
STAGE: Opening & History

"Good morning, I'm Dr. [Name]. Please come in and take a seat. I understand you've got a sore area in your mouth that's been bothering you — I'll do my best to help you today. Before I take a look, I'd like to ask you a few questions first, if that's alright."

"So, you mentioned a painful ulcer on your lower gum. Can you tell me, when exactly did you first notice it — was it right after getting your new denture fitted three weeks ago, or did it come on more gradually over time?"

Pauses and listens attentively.

"And has the ulcer changed at all since you first noticed it — has it grown bigger, changed shape, or become more or less painful?"

"Have you ever had a similar ulcer in your mouth before — either under a denture or anywhere else?"

"Any ulcers elsewhere on your body, skin rashes, or eye problems?" Pauses. "Any recent changes to your general health — have you been under more stress than usual, or started any new medications recently?"

"Do you have any medical conditions I should know about — anything like diabetes, or are you on any medications that lower your immune system, such as steroids or chemotherapy?"

"I also want to ask — and please don't be offended, it's a routine question I ask all my patients — do you smoke or drink alcohol, and if so, roughly how much?"

"Have you ever had any treatment for mouth cancer or any growths in your mouth previously?"

"Thank you, that's really helpful. Now I'd like to have a good look at the area."

---

Examination

Puts on gloves, mask, and eye protection. Examines the ulcer under good lighting with a mouth mirror and probe.

"I can see the ulcer on the lingual aspect of the lower alveolar ridge — it measures approximately seven millimetres by five millimetres. The margins appear somewhat irregular, and the base has a yellowish fibrinous slough, which is fairly typical of a traumatic ulcer. The surrounding tissue has an erythematous halo around it."

Gently palpates the base of the ulcer with a gloved finger.

"I'm just feeling around the ulcer now — I'm checking whether the base feels firm or hard underneath, which we'd call induration. At this stage it feels soft, which is reassuring."

Palpates the submandibular and cervical lymph nodes bilaterally.

"I'm now feeling the glands in your neck — I want to make sure there's no swelling there. They feel soft and non-tender at the moment, which is a good sign."

Examines the lower partial denture, paying close attention to the lingual flange extension in the region of the ulcer.

"I'm now looking closely at your denture — specifically at the flange on the inside of the lower gum where the ulcer is sitting. I can see the lingual flange is slightly overextended in this area, which means it's likely been pressing and rubbing on the gum tissue and creating this sore."

---

Diagnosis & Explanation

"Thank you for your patience. I'd like to explain what I think is going on."

"Based on everything — the timing of the ulcer starting shortly after your new denture was fitted, the location directly underneath where the denture flange sits, and the appearance of the ulcer itself — my assessment is that this is most likely a traumatic ulcer caused by the denture rubbing and putting pressure on that area of your gum. These are actually the most common type of ulcer we see in people who wear dentures, and they're very treatable."

"That said, I want to be completely honest with you. Any ulcer in the mouth that hasn't healed within two to three weeks needs to be taken very seriously, because occasionally ulcers can represent something more significant. You're ten days in, so we're still within the expected healing window. However, if this ulcer has not healed completely within the next one to two weeks after we adjust the denture today, I will need to take a small tissue sample — a biopsy — to be absolutely certain of what we're dealing with. I'd rather be thorough than make assumptions."

---

Management Plan

"So here's what I'm going to do today. Firstly, I'll adjust your denture in the area that's causing the irritation. I'll use a pressure-indicating paste — a special material I apply to the inside of the denture — which will show me exactly where the denture is pressing too hard on your gum. I'll then carefully reduce that area with a slow-speed handpiece so the denture no longer rubs on the ulcer."

Performs the denture adjustment with pressure indicator paste and acrylic bur. Polishes the adjusted area smoothly.

"I've now smoothed off that area. The denture should feel much more comfortable. I'll ask you to put it back in and tell me how that feels."

"In addition to the adjustment, I'd like you to take the denture out overnight — and in fact, as much as you comfortably can during the day if possible. Leaving the gum tissue free of the denture gives it the best chance to heal, and as a general rule for denture hygiene, dry overnight storage is recommended rather than storing in water."

"I'd also like you to rinse your mouth with chlorhexidine mouthwash — the 0.2% strength — twice a day after meals. Just hold it gently around the ulcer for about thirty seconds each time, then spit it out. You can get this over the counter at any pharmacy."

"For pain relief, paracetamol one gram every four to six hours as needed should be sufficient — please don't exceed four grams in twenty-four hours."

"I'd like to see you back here in two weeks. If the ulcer is completely healed by then, wonderful. If it is not fully healed — regardless of how it looks — I will arrange a biopsy that same appointment. There are no exceptions to that two-week rule."

---

Safety Netting & Closing

"Before you go, I want to be very clear about when to come back sooner — please don't wait for the two-week appointment if any of the following happen: if the ulcer becomes noticeably larger, if the pain suddenly gets much worse, if you feel a lump or swelling appearing in your neck, or if you develop difficulty swallowing or speaking. Any of those things, please call us immediately and we'll see you the same day."

"Also, because I mentioned it earlier — if you are a smoker, I'd gently encourage you to consider quitting. Smoking significantly slows down healing and increases the risk of serious conditions in the mouth. We can refer you to support services that are very effective."

"Do you have any questions about what I've explained today? I know it's a lot of information."

Pauses and listens.

"You're doing the right thing by coming in. Most of the time these ulcers settle beautifully once the denture is adjusted, and I'm confident we've addressed the cause today. I'll see you in two weeks — and please don't hesitate to ring us before then if you're worried. Take care."

PR4
Implant-Retained Overdenture Counseling (Edentulous Patient)
Category:** Prosthodontics | **Time:** 11 min | **Difficulty:** Exam-ready

CASE SUMMARY

75-year-old edentulous patient (complete dentures for 15 years, lower denture very loose). GP has referred for "implant assessment." Patient has not heard of implant overdentures and is nervous about surgery. Candidate must counsel on the option, benefits vs. risks, and decide if patient is suitable.

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

Opening (1 min)

"Your GP has mentioned implants might help your denture — let me explain what that means and see if it's suitable for you."

Current situation assessment (1.5 min)

"Why is your lower denture loose?

  • Bone resorption: after teeth are removed, the jaw bone shrinks over time. After 15 years without teeth, there's likely been significant bone loss
  • Nothing anchors the lower denture — it sits on soft tissue only
  • The upper denture (resting against the palate) usually stays better because of suction; the lower has no palate to suction to"

Explaining implant-retained overdenture — INFLECTION 1

"An implant-retained overdenture means we place two to four small titanium implants into your lower jaw — that's a minor surgical procedure under local anaesthetic. Your existing denture (or a new one) is then modified to 'clip on' to those implants. The denture still comes out for cleaning — it's removable — but when it's in, it locks firmly into place. You can speak and eat without it moving.

Research consistently shows this is one of the most life-changing prosthodontic procedures for edentulous patients. It significantly improves chewing ability, confidence, and quality of life."

Risks and suitability (1.5 min) — INFLECTION 2

  • Bone volume: CBCT required to check if there's enough bone for implants (2 implants minimum for lower overdenture)
  • Medical history: well-controlled conditions are fine; uncontrolled diabetes, bisphosphonates, or cancer treatment (radiotherapy to jaw) are relative contraindications
  • Smoking: reduces implant success significantly
  • Surgical risk: minor procedure, local anaesthetic, short recovery

If patient is worried about surgery:

"The procedure for 2 implants takes about 45–60 minutes. Most patients are surprised by how manageable it is. It's a lot less involved than you might imagine."

Cost & process (1 min)

"Typically: 2 implants + overdenture modification: ~$5,000–$7,000. If a new denture is needed too, add ~$1,500–$2,000. It's a significant investment, but for many patients it's life-changing. We can discuss payment plans."

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Explains why lower dentures are inherently less retentive than upper
  2. ✅ Explains implant overdenture mechanism clearly (clips on, still removable)
  3. ✅ Orders CBCT for bone assessment before committing
  4. ✅ Discusses contraindications (uncontrolled diabetes, bisphosphonates, radiotherapy)
  5. ✅ Addresses surgical anxiety honestly and reassuringly
  6. ✅ Provides cost context
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • "McGill Consensus Statement (2002): a 2-implant mandibular overdenture should be the minimum standard of care for the edentulous mandible. This is not a luxury item — it's evidence-based best practice."
  • "Attachment systems: (1) Ball/stud (simplest, low maintenance, some lateral movement), (2) bar-retained (more stability, more complex, higher maintenance), (3) Locator (most commonly used currently — self-aligning, low profile, good retention). Choice depends on inter-arch space and ridge morphology."
  • "Bone preservation argument: conventional dentures cause bone resorption; implants transmit load to bone which stimulates it. Patients who have implants placed earlier preserve more ridge long-term. This is the strongest long-term argument."
  • "Pre-implant assessment: CBCT for bone volume (particularly height of mandibular canal), medical clearance, smoking status (relative contraindication — increases failure rate, not absolute)."
Patient Reframes
  • "Research consistently shows that implant-supported dentures significantly improve quality of life — patients can eat what they want, speak confidently, and don't worry about the denture moving. The two implants act like anchors: the denture clicks in and stays put."
  • "There's also a long-term bone argument: conventional dentures cause the jawbone to shrink over time because there's no tooth root stimulating it. Implants actually preserve the bone. So two implants now can protect the jaw structure for decades."
  • "The procedure for two implants in the lower jaw is relatively straightforward — it's done under local anaesthetic, takes about an hour, and most patients are surprised by how manageable it is."
Curveball Deflectors
  • "I've had dentures for years and they're fine." → "I'm glad they've worked for you — and I'm not suggesting they're failing. I raise implants because the evidence is strong enough that I'd be remiss not to mention the option. If you're genuinely happy with your current dentures, that's a completely valid choice. I just want you to have heard about the alternative."
  • "How much does it cost?" → "The implants themselves are a significant upfront investment — typically $3,000–5,000 per implant in Australia. But many patients find it's cost-effective over the long term when you factor in relining, remaking dentures, and the benefit to quality of life. I can refer you for a specialist consultation where the costs are detailed."
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ▶
STAGE: Opening

Greet the patient warmly and establish rapport immediately.

"Good morning, come in and take a seat. My name is Dr. [Name] — I'm the dentist here today. Your GP has referred you for an implant assessment, which I'm very glad to hear. Before we talk about any treatment at all, I'd love to hear a bit about how your dentures have been going for you. Is that okay?"

Allow the patient to respond. Listen actively, then continue: "So you've had your complete dentures for about 15 years now, and the lower one in particular has become quite loose and uncomfortable — that makes complete sense, and you are definitely not alone in that experience. Today I want to explain what an implant-retained overdenture is, whether it might suit you, and answer any questions or worries you have, including about the surgical side of things. There's no commitment today — this is purely information and assessment. Does that sound okay?"

---

Understanding the Problem — Why the Lower Denture Loosens

"I want to start by explaining why this has happened, because once you understand the reason, the solution makes a lot more sense."

"When teeth are removed, the jawbone underneath no longer has roots stimulating it, so over time it naturally shrinks — we call this bone resorption. After 15 years, there has very likely been significant bone loss in your lower jaw. Your lower denture is essentially resting on soft tissue — your gums — with nothing anchoring it in place. Every time you chew or speak, it can shift or lift."

"Now, people often ask: why does the upper denture stay in better? That's a great question. The upper denture covers your entire palate, and that large surface area creates a suction effect — almost like a suction cup. The lower jaw has no palate, so there's no suction possible. The lower denture has always been the harder one to retain, and bone loss over time only makes that worse. So what you're experiencing is not a fitting problem with your current denture — it's a biological reality of long-term tooth loss."

---

Explaining the Implant-Retained Overdenture

"So this is where implants come in, and I want to be really clear about what this involves so you have a full picture."

"An implant-retained overdenture means we place two to four small titanium implants — they're like tiny screws, roughly the diameter of a matchstick — directly into your lower jawbone. This is done in the chair under local anaesthetic. Your existing denture, or a new one if needed, is then modified to clip onto those implants using small attachments, a bit like press-studs. The denture is still completely removable — you take it out at night for cleaning — but when it's in your mouth, it locks firmly and securely into place."

"The difference patients describe is remarkable. You can chew food you haven't been able to eat in years — steak, apples, crusty bread. You can speak without worrying the denture will move. You don't need adhesives. The research on this is very clear: a two-implant lower overdenture is consistently shown to be one of the most life-changing prosthodontic treatments we can offer. It significantly improves chewing ability, confidence, and quality of life. The McGill Consensus — an international expert statement — actually recommends it as the minimum standard of care for edentulous lower jaws."

---

Addressing Surgical Anxiety and Assessing Suitability

"Now, you mentioned you're a little nervous about surgery, and I completely understand that. Can I reassure you about what the procedure actually involves?"

"For two implants, the appointment typically takes around 45 to 60 minutes in the chair — similar to having a tooth out, but a bit longer. You'll be numb with local anaesthetic, so you won't feel pain during the procedure. Afterwards there's some mild soreness for a few days, managed easily with paracetamol one gram every four to six hours. Most of my patients tell me afterwards they were genuinely surprised by how manageable it was."

"To assess whether implants are suitable for you specifically, I need to ask a few important questions. Do you have diabetes, and if so, is it well controlled? The reason I ask is that uncontrolled diabetes — an HbA1c above eight percent — significantly increases infection risk and slows healing around implants. Well-controlled diabetes is absolutely fine."

"Have you ever taken medication for osteoporosis — tablets or injections such as alendronate or zoledronic acid? These are called bisphosphonates, and they can affect how jaw bone heals after surgical procedures, so we need to know about them. Similarly, have you ever had radiotherapy to your head or neck area? That can also affect bone healing."

"And I do need to ask — do you smoke? I ask because smoking reduces implant success rates considerably, and it's something I always raise, because support to quit is available and makes a real difference."

"To confirm there is sufficient bone volume to place the implants safely, I will need to arrange a CBCT scan — that's a three-dimensional x-ray of your jaw. It takes only a few minutes and is low-dose. Without that scan, I cannot confirm you are suitable or plan the implant positions accurately."

---

Cost, Process, and Closing

"I want to be transparent about cost, because it's an important part of the decision."

"Typically, two implants with modification of an existing overdenture costs in the range of five thousand to seven thousand dollars. If your current lower denture needs replacement as well — which is often the case after this length of time — that adds approximately fifteen hundred to two thousand dollars. I won't pretend that's a small amount. However, for most patients, the improvement to daily life is profound, and we can discuss payment plan options to make it more manageable."

"So here is what I'd suggest as our next step: we take the CBCT scan to assess your bone, I review your medical history in full, and then I can give you a personalised recommendation and a detailed written treatment plan with exact costs — no obligation. Does that feel like a comfortable way forward for you?"

"Do you have any questions at all — about the procedure, the healing, anything I've said today? There are no silly questions here. I want you to feel completely informed."

Allow the patient to respond, answer any questions, and close warmly: "You're in very good hands, and whatever we decide together, our goal is simply to give you a denture you can rely on and a smile you feel confident in. I'll organise that scan referral for you today."

PR5
Aesthetic Complaint — Old Crowns, Patient Wants Veneers
Category:** Prosthodontics / Communication | **Time:** 11 min | **Difficulty:** Exam-ready

CASE SUMMARY

40-year-old patient unhappy with appearance of front teeth (crowns on 11, 21 placed 12 years ago, now showing grey margin, slightly darker than adjacent teeth). Wants porcelain veneers on all upper front teeth. Candidate must assess, explain options, and manage expectations.

CANDIDATE BRIEF

Patient presents unhappy with the appearance of their upper front crowns (11, 21). The crowns are 12 years old, metal-ceramic type, with visible grey gingival margins and colour mismatch. Adjacent teeth (12, 22, 13, 23) are natural, slightly yellowed. Patient has seen an advertisement for "porcelain veneers" and wants 6 on the upper front teeth.

EXAMINER CONTEXT

Patient has unrealistic expectations of what veneers can achieve. They've been told they need "all-ceramic crowns" by another dentist but didn't understand the difference. They want to understand all their options and their budget is limited (~$3,000–$4,000 total).

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

Examination & Assessment (1.5 min)

  • Crown margins: grey/dark line = porcelain-fused-to-metal (PFM) margins showing, or gingival recession exposing metal
  • Crown colour: outdated shade, not matching current natural teeth shade
  • Crown integrity: any fracture, caries, or perio issues? (if crowns structurally sound, replacement may be elective)
  • Natural adjacent teeth: shade, condition, patient's expectations

Explaining the problem honestly — INFLECTION 1

"The grey line you're seeing at the gum margin is where the metal part of the crown meets the gum — the gum has receded a little over the years, exposing it. The colour mismatch is because the shade of these crowns was matched 12 years ago, and your natural teeth have yellowed slightly since then (which is normal)."

Options (2.5 min) — INFLECTION 2

Option 1 — Replace the two crowns with all-ceramic (zirconia or e.max):

"This addresses the root problem: the existing crowns are showing their metal base. Replacing them with all-ceramic crowns removes the grey margin issue and allows us to match the colour. Cost: ~$1,500–$2,000 per crown = $3,000–$4,000 for both. This fits your budget."

Option 2 — Veneers on the adjacent teeth:

"If we replace the crowns but the adjacent natural teeth look yellow by comparison, we could then add veneers to 12, 22 (and possibly 13, 23) for a more uniform look. But this adds significant cost and involves removing enamel from healthy teeth — which I'd want to weigh carefully."

Option 3 — Whitening first:

"Before doing anything cosmetically, I'd recommend tooth whitening on the natural teeth first — it's non-invasive and inexpensive (~$400–$600 in-chair or take-home). Once we get the natural teeth to a target shade, we can match the new crowns to that shade. This gives the best aesthetic result."

Managing expectations on veneers — INFLECTION 3

"I want to address the veneers on all 6 teeth — I'd need to examine more closely, but porcelain veneers on teeth that are already crowned would mean adding another layer of porcelain over existing crowns, which isn't usually how it works — crowns already cover the whole tooth. What you might have seen advertised as 'veneers on everything' is usually composite resin cosmetic work or a full smile makeover involving multiple crowns. Let me show you the difference."

Recommended plan

  1. Whiten natural teeth to target shade
  2. Replace the 2 PFM crowns with all-ceramic at the whitened shade
  3. Reassess whether additional veneers are needed
  4. Total estimate within budget

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Explains grey margin issue correctly (metal exposure from gingival recession)
  2. ✅ Recommends whitening natural teeth BEFORE shade-matching new crowns
  3. ✅ Presents all-ceramic crown replacement as the primary solution
  4. ✅ Manages veneer expectation honestly (veneers ≠ crowns, different indication)
  5. ✅ Works within patient's budget
  6. ✅ Minimal intervention principle: doesn't recommend veneers on all 6 unnecessarily
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • "Assess the existing crowns first before any discussion of veneers: check crown margins (open margins = decay risk), occlusal contacts (heavy contacts = fracture risk), gingival health around crown margins, pulp status, radiographic bone levels. Do not agree to 'redo everything' without this information."
  • "Veneers on crowned teeth: generally not appropriate — the existing crown has already reduced the tooth. Adding a veneer on top creates a layered structure with more failure risk and more bulk. If crowns are failing, they should be replaced, not veneered."
  • "Biological cost of veneers: irreversible tooth preparation, risk of pulp irritation, increased risk of fracture with thin enamel remaining. Composite bonding is the minimally invasive alternative — no preparation required, reversible, less expensive."
  • "Provisional restorations and diagnostic wax-ups: always use these before committing to irreversible treatment. 'Try-ins' in composite allow the patient to see the result before the final decision. This protects both patient and clinician."
Patient Reframes
  • "Before we change anything, I want to look at what's currently there — the existing crowns, the bite, the gum health. Any cosmetic change needs to start with a stable foundation. Once I have the full picture, I can tell you exactly what's realistic."
  • "The most important thing I want you to understand is that veneers and crowns involve permanently removing tooth structure. Once that's gone, it's gone. I want to show you what we can achieve before you commit to anything irreversible."
Curveball Deflectors
  • "I just want them whiter and more even." → "Those are very achievable goals — and the least invasive route to them might be professional whitening first, then assessing whether any reshaping or bonding is needed. We can often get a dramatic improvement without touching the tooth structure at all."
  • "The crowns were done 10 years ago — they should be replaced anyway." → "Age alone isn't a reason to replace crowns — if they're functional and the margins are intact, there's no clinical indication to replace them. Replacing crowns unnecessarily means more drilling, more risk, and more cost. Let me assess them properly first."
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ▶
STAGE: Opening & Presenting Complaint

"Good morning, I'm Dr. [Name], one of the dentists here. It's great to meet you. Please take a seat and make yourself comfortable. Before I take a look, I'd really like to hear what's been bothering you in your own words — what brings you in today?"

Listens attentively as patient describes dissatisfaction with the appearance of the upper front teeth — the dark line at the gum, the colour mismatch, and their interest in porcelain veneers after seeing an advertisement.

"Thank you for explaining that so clearly. I can absolutely understand why that's bothering you — it's very much in your smile line and it's something you see every day. I'm going to have a close look at everything today, and then we'll have an honest conversation about what's going on and what the best options are. Does that sound okay?"

---

Examination & Assessment

Examines teeth 11 and 21 with a mirror and probe. Notes visible grey gingival margin, slight gingival recession of approximately 1 mm, no mobility, no tenderness to percussion, probing depths within normal limits. Crowns are structurally intact with no evidence of caries or fracture at the margins. Shade of existing crowns is noticeably lighter and more opaque than the adjacent natural teeth 12, 22, 13, and 23, which have yellowed naturally over time. No periodontal concerns noted on adjacent teeth.

"I've had a thorough look now and I have a really clear picture of what's happening. Let me explain it to you."

---

Explaining the Problem Honestly

"The grey line you can see at the gum is where the metal base of your crown meets the gum line. The crowns you have are a type called porcelain-fused-to-metal — they have a metal core inside with porcelain baked on top. Over the past twelve years, the gum has receded very slightly, which is completely normal with age and brushing, but it's enough to expose a tiny sliver of that metal rim — and that's the dark line you're seeing. The crowns themselves are structurally sound — there's no decay, no cracks — but aesthetically, that metal edge is now visible and it's not going away on its own."

"The colour mismatch is a separate issue. When these crowns were made twelve years ago, they were shade-matched beautifully to your teeth at the time. But natural teeth do yellow gradually over the years — again, completely normal — and the porcelain in a crown doesn't change colour with time. So now there's a noticeable difference between the crowns, which have stayed the same, and your natural teeth, which have shifted warmer and more yellow. That's what's creating that slightly artificial look."

---

Options & Recommendation

"Now, I want to address the veneers question directly, because I think it's really important you understand the difference. A veneer is a thin shell of porcelain bonded to the front of a natural tooth — it's a wonderful option for natural teeth, but it can't simply be placed over an existing crown. The crown already covers the whole tooth. So adding a veneer on top of a crown isn't how it works clinically. What you may have seen advertised is often a full smile makeover that combines multiple types of restorations. I want to make sure we're doing what's right for your teeth, not just what sounds appealing."

"Here's what I'd actually recommend. First — and this is the most important step — I'd suggest whitening your natural teeth before we do anything else. In-chair whitening or a take-home tray system, costing approximately four to six hundred dollars, will lift those adjacent teeth to a brighter, more uniform shade. The reason we do this first is critical: once we settle on your new target shade after whitening, we can then have the new crowns made to exactly match it. If we do the crowns first and whiten afterwards, the crowns won't change colour and we end up back where we started."

"Once the natural teeth have reached a stable shade — usually two to four weeks after whitening — we replace the two existing crowns on teeth eleven and twenty-one with all-ceramic crowns. Modern all-ceramic options, such as lithium disilicate or zirconia, have no metal at all, so there's no grey margin possible, the light passes through them naturally, and the aesthetics are genuinely excellent. The cost per crown is approximately fifteen hundred to two thousand dollars, so we're looking at three to four thousand dollars for both."

"After that, we step back and reassess together. In many cases, once the natural teeth are whitened and the new crowns are in at that shade, the overall result is very harmonious and nothing further is needed. If at that point you feel the canines or lateral incisors still look uneven or you'd like them refined, we could then discuss veneers on those teeth — but I'd never recommend removing enamel from perfectly healthy teeth unless there's a clear benefit, and I'd want you to see the result of the first two steps before committing to anything further."

---

Safety Net & Closing

"So to summarise the plan: step one is whitening your natural teeth to your desired shade — non-invasive, reversible, and inexpensive. Step two is replacing the two crowns with all-ceramic restorations matched to that new shade. Step three is a review, and we reassess from there. This approach gives you the best aesthetic outcome, keeps things as conservative as possible, and works within a sensible budget."

"I do want to take a full set of periapical radiographs of those crowned teeth today just to confirm there's nothing going on underneath that we can't see clinically — things like root canal health or bone levels — before we commit to the treatment plan. That's just good practice."

"Do you have any questions about anything I've explained? I know it's a lot to take in, and I'm very happy to go over any part of it again. There's absolutely no pressure — this is elective treatment and the decision is entirely yours."

PR6
Denture Adjustment — Patient Complaint (Poor Retention + Sore Spots)
Category:** Prosthodontics / Communication | **Time:** 11 min | **Difficulty:** Exam-ready

CASE SUMMARY

Patient with newly made full upper denture (2 weeks old) complaining of 3 sore spots, poor retention, and clicking when talking. Communication station: candidate must manage the complaint appropriately, examine, adjust, and set realistic expectations.

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

Opening & validation (1 min)

"I'm sorry to hear you're finding the denture uncomfortable — let's go through everything carefully. New dentures almost always need adjustments in the first few weeks, so please don't be disheartened."

History (1.5 min) — INFLECTION 1: Get specific details

  • Sore spots: where exactly, when do they occur (eating/speaking/constant)?
  • Clicking: when? (often indicates loss of border seal or incorrect occlusal vertical dimension)
  • Retention: comes out when? (eating, speaking, yawning)
  • "Have you been wearing it consistently or leaving it out?" (if left out, mucosa hasn't adapted)

Examination (1.5 min)

  • Pressure relief paste (PIP) or articulating paste: identify exact sore spots on denture flange
  • Border seal: check peripheral seal
  • Occlusion: check in maximum intercuspation and lateral excursions (clicking often = premature contact)
  • Retention: check after applying digital pressure/suction

Management — INFLECTION 2: Adjustment vs. remake decision

Sore spots: relieve denture with acrylic bur in the identified area. Show patient the spot. Explain.

Clicking: check for balancing side interference or occlusal premature contact → adjust.

Poor retention: if border seal adequate → may need time to adapt; if border seal deficient → consider relining or adding compound to flange.

Setting realistic expectations (2 min) — INFLECTION 3

"New dentures almost always require 2–3 adjustment visits in the first month. This is completely normal and expected — it's not a sign the denture was made badly. Your mouth is adapting to the new appliance, and the bite and pressure points often need fine-tuning.

Dentures also take time to learn to use — just like any new skill. The muscles of your lips, tongue, and cheeks need time to learn to stabilise the denture. Most patients feel significantly more comfortable at the 4–6 week mark.

If after 3–4 adjustment visits problems persist, we'll reassess whether a reline or partial remake is needed."

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Validates complaint without being defensive
  2. ✅ Uses pressure relief paste to identify exact sore spots
  3. ✅ Investigates cause of clicking (premature contact most likely)
  4. ✅ Adjusts appropriately with clinical evidence (no guessing)
  5. ✅ Sets realistic expectations (2–3 adjustment visits normal)
  6. ✅ Distinguishes normal adaptation period from genuine problem requiring remake
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • "Systematic approach to denture complaints: (1) identify the specific symptom — retention (won't stay in), stability (rocks when chewing), comfort (sore spots), aesthetics. Each has a different cause and a different fix. Do not adjust blindly."
  • "Retention vs stability: retention is how well the denture resists displacement at rest (border seal, post-dam, anatomical undercuts). Stability is resistance to movement during function (balanced occlusion, adequate ridge). These are different problems with different solutions."
  • "Sore spots: use pressure indicator paste (PIP) to identify precise contact points. Adjust those points — not by grinding randomly, but by targeted relief where the paste transfers to the tissue. Document which adjustments were made."
  • "Denture adhesive: short-term adjunct only. If a patient relies on adhesive for a denture that's less than 5 years old, the denture needs assessment and likely relining — not more adhesive."
Patient Reframes
  • "I can fix most of what you're describing — but I need to understand exactly which part of the problem bothers you most, because 'it doesn't fit' can mean five different things with five different solutions."
  • "The paste I put on the fitting surface shows me precisely where the pressure is — so instead of guessing which spot to adjust, I'm adjusting exactly the right place. This is much more effective than 'grinding a bit off' and hoping."
Curveball Deflectors
  • "The other dentist said nothing can be done." → "Sometimes that means the ridge has resorbed to the point where conventional adjustments won't achieve much — in which case relining or remaking is the next step. Let me assess where we are and give you my honest assessment of the options."
  • "Just give me more adhesive." → "Adhesive masks the underlying fit problem temporarily — and if you're using a lot of it, that's a signal that the denture needs clinical attention. It's not harmful, but it's not a fix. Let me find out why it's not retaining and address that properly."
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ▶
STAGE: Opening & Validation

Greets the patient warmly, shakes hands, and makes comfortable eye contact.

"Hello, my name is Dr. [Name], lovely to meet you. Please come in and take a seat — make yourself comfortable. Now, I understand you've been having some difficulties with your new upper denture, and I'm really glad you've come back to see me. I'm sorry to hear it hasn't been entirely comfortable — that must have been quite frustrating, especially when you were looking forward to using it. I want you to know that this is exactly the right thing to do, coming back in. New dentures almost always need a few adjustments in the first couple of weeks, so please don't be disheartened at all. We are absolutely going to sort this out together. Let me ask you a few questions first, and then I'll take a careful look."

---

History Taking

"Can you tell me, in your own words, what's been bothering you most? Let's start with the sore spots — whereabouts in your mouth are you feeling the soreness? Is it more towards the front, on the sides, or further back? And when does the soreness happen — is it there all the time, or mainly when you're eating or speaking?"

Listens attentively, nods, and takes brief notes.

"And the clicking sound you mentioned — when do you notice that happening? Is it mainly when you're talking, or also when you're chewing? Does the denture feel like it's shifting or moving when that happens?"

"Now, with the retention — tell me more about when it tends to come loose. Is it when you're eating, when you open your mouth wide, or even just when you're speaking? Has it ever fallen out completely?"

"Have you been wearing the denture consistently throughout the day, or have there been times when you've left it out for a while? That's a completely fine thing to do — I just want to understand how it's been going. And are you storing it dry overnight, out of water, as we discussed?"

"How has eating been overall? Are you managing soft foods at this stage? And has the denture caused any problems with your speech — aside from the clicking?"

---

Clinical Examination

"Thank you — that's really helpful. I'd like to have a close look now, both at the denture itself and at your mouth, so I can work out exactly what's going on and where. Is that alright?"

Asks patient to remove the denture. Examines the oral mucosa carefully under good lighting, noting any erythematous or ulcerated areas on the ridge, palate, and flanges.

"I can see there are a couple of areas in your mouth that look a little irritated — that tells me the denture is pressing in specific spots, and that's very fixable."

Applies pressure indicator paste evenly to the fitting surface of the denture.

"I'm going to put a thin layer of this indicator paste on the inside of the denture — it's completely safe. When you put the denture in and bite together gently, and then move your jaw side to side, the paste will show me exactly where it's pressing too hard."

Patient seats denture. Examines the paste distribution carefully.

"Yes — I can see three clear pressure spots here, here, and here. That matches exactly what you've been feeling."

Seats the denture and checks occlusion with articulating paper in maximum intercuspation and lateral excursion to identify premature contacts causing the clicking. Checks peripheral border seal by digital pressure on the denture and assessing displacement.

---

Adjustment & Explanation

Selects appropriate acrylic adjustment bur and relieves the three identified pressure areas on the fitting surface of the denture.

"I'm going to use a small bur — a polishing tool — to gently remove a tiny amount of the acrylic in those precise spots. I'm only working in the areas the paste showed me, so there's no guesswork involved. I'll have you try it again afterwards and we can check with the paste a second time to make sure we've resolved it properly."

Re-applies paste, patient reseats denture, confirms improvement.

"Excellent — that's looking much better. Now regarding the clicking, the articulating paper showed me a small premature contact on the back left side — that's where the teeth are meeting a fraction early, which tips the denture and breaks the seal. I'm going to adjust that contact very carefully."

Makes occlusal adjustment. Rechecks with articulating paper.

"And with the retention — the border seal is actually intact, which is reassuring. Part of what you're experiencing is simply that the muscles of your cheeks, lips, and tongue are still learning to help stabilise the denture. That takes time and is completely normal."

---

Setting Realistic Expectations & Safety Net

"I want to take a moment to explain what you can expect over the coming weeks, because I think it will help you feel a lot more confident about how things are going. Most patients with a new full denture need two to three adjustment visits within the first month — that is completely normal and expected, and it is not a sign that the denture was made poorly. Your mouth is adapting to a new appliance, and the pressure points and bite almost always need some fine-tuning after the initial fitting."

"The muscles of your lips, tongue, and cheeks take time to learn how to stabilise the denture — it really is a bit like learning a new skill. Most of my patients tell me they feel significantly more comfortable and confident by the four to six week mark."

"Please keep wearing the denture consistently during the day — that actually helps your mouth adapt more quickly. And do continue storing it dry overnight, out of water — that's important for keeping it clean and reducing any risk of irritation."

"If at any point a new sore spot appears before your next visit, do come back in — please don't put up with pain, because adjustments are a normal part of this process and there's no reason to suffer. If after three or four adjustment visits we find things still aren't settling, we'll reassess together. At that point, a reline to improve the fit of the fitting surface might be the right next step — but I don't anticipate we'll need that."

"Do you have any questions at all? Is there anything I've explained that you'd like me to go over again? You're doing really well, and I'm confident we're going to get you very comfortable with this denture. Let's book you in again in one week's time."

PR7
Implant Failure — Patient Concerned Implant Is Loose
Category:** Prosthodontics | **Time:** 11 min | **Difficulty:** Exam-ready

CASE SUMMARY

Patient presents 4 months after implant placement (lower molar 46, another practice) feeling the implant is "wobbly." Clinical assessment: mobility of crown, check whether it's the crown, the abutment screw, or the implant itself that's moving.

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

History (1.5 min)

  • When was implant placed? (4 months — early; osseointegration typically 3–6 months)
  • When did mobility start?
  • Any pain, bite issues, recent trauma?
  • General health: smoking, diabetes, bisphosphonates?

Clinical examination — INFLECTION 1: Distinguish three types of mobility

"Let me check the implant carefully. Mobility can come from three different places:

  1. The crown is loose (most common and simplest fix): the crown has come loose from the abutment or the abutment screw has loosened. I can see if there's any give at the crown-abutment junction with a tool. Fix: tighten the screw, possibly re-cement
  2. The abutment is loose (also common): similar fix — tighten the abutment screw
  3. The implant itself is mobile (most serious): this means osseointegration has failed. The implant is moving inside the bone."

If implant itself is mobile — INFLECTION 2: Explantation decision

"Unfortunately, a mobile implant cannot be saved. An implant that hasn't integrated with the bone will continue to cause bone loss if left. The recommended management is:

  1. Remove the failed implant
  2. Allow the site to heal (3–6 months)
  3. Assess bone volume and reassess for re-implantation
  4. Investigate why it failed (poor OH, smoking, uncontrolled diabetes, poor healing, insufficient bone)"

Communication — referring back to placing dentist

"This implant was placed by another practice, so I'll write a referral back to them with my findings. They'll need to know about this, as they will have records of the placement details. You're also entitled to seek a second opinion if you wish."

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Distinguishes crown, abutment, vs. implant mobility (three different problems, three different solutions)
  2. ✅ Correctly states that a mobile implant = implant failure, requires explantation
  3. ✅ Investigates cause of failure to prevent recurrence
  4. ✅ Refers back to placing dentist appropriately
  5. ✅ Informs patient of right to second opinion
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • "Before anything else, I need to distinguish two different types of looseness: the prosthetic component (crown, abutment, or screw) being loose — which is a simple fix — versus the implant itself moving in the bone, which means osseointegration failure and a completely different management pathway."
  • "To test implant stability I use percussion and direct digital pressure. Any rotational or translational movement of the implant body itself = failed osseointegration. That implant needs to come out."
  • "Late implant failure causes: peri-implantitis (most common), occlusal overload, bruxism, smoking, systemic disease progression. Once I know the cause, I can address it before planning replacement."
  • "If the implant is removed: allow 3–6 months for bone healing and assess bone volume before considering re-implantation. CBCT guides the planning for the second attempt."
Patient Reframes
  • "There are actually two different types of looseness — the crown or connector being loose is a quick fix I can sort today. If the implant itself is moving in the bone, that tells us something different has happened, and I want to walk you through what that means."
  • "Even if the implant has failed, you haven't lost your options. Once it's healed, we can assess whether another implant is possible, or consider alternatives. This is a setback, not a dead end."
Curveball Deflectors
  • "Why did this happen? The implant was expensive." → "I understand the frustration — that's a legitimate concern. Once I've determined what's happened clinically, I'll explain what caused it and what our options are. Some causes relate to healing biology we can't fully predict; others are addressable."
  • "Can't you just tighten it?" → "If it's the abutment screw that's loose, yes — absolutely, that's a 5-minute fix. If the implant itself is mobile, tightening won't help because there's no longer bone holding it. I need to determine which situation we're dealing with before I do anything."
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ▶
STAGE: Opening & Introduction

"Hello, come in and take a seat — my name is Dr. [Name], I'm the dentist here today. Before we begin, can I just confirm your name and date of birth for our records? Thank you. I understand you're feeling a bit worried about your implant — that it feels like it might be moving. I completely understand that's unsettling, especially after going through the process of having it placed. What I'd like to do today is have a thorough chat about what you've been experiencing, then take a careful look at the implant so we can work out exactly what's happening. Does that sound okay to you?"

---

History Taking

"So, let's start from the beginning. You mentioned the implant feels wobbly — when exactly did you first notice that sensation? And can you recall when the implant was placed? Four months ago, you said — and it was done at another practice. Thank you for letting me know.

Now, is the wobbling something that's been there since the beginning, or did it start more recently? Has it been getting worse? Any pain around the implant site — either constantly or when you bite down? Have you had any trauma to that area recently — perhaps a knock, biting something hard, or a fall?

How has your bite been feeling? Any discomfort on chewing, or does it feel like the implant is catching on something differently than before?

Now I need to ask a few questions about your general health, because these can really affect how an implant heals. Are you a smoker, or have you smoked in the past? Do you have diabetes, and if so, has it been well-controlled recently? Are you taking any medications — in particular, have you ever taken bisphosphonates, which are medications for osteoporosis or bone conditions? Any other significant medical history I should know about?

Thank you — that's really helpful. Let me now take a careful look at the implant itself."

---

Clinical Examination — Distinguishing the Source of Mobility (Inflection 1)

Examines the implant systematically. Uses a mirror and probe. Applies gentle lateral force to the crown with two instrument handles. Observes movement at the crown, the abutment junction, and then at the gingival margin to detect movement of the implant body itself. Takes a periapical radiograph to assess bone levels around the implant.

"So I've had a careful look, and I want to explain what I've found — and why it matters, because the location of the movement makes a very big difference to what we do next.

There are actually three different places where movement can come from with an implant, and each one means something quite different. The first, and most common — and most reassuring — is that the crown itself has simply come loose from the abutment, or the small screw that holds everything together has loosened over time. In that case, I can see movement at the crown-abutment junction, but the implant underneath is completely stable in the bone. That's a straightforward fix — I tighten or replace the screw and, if needed, re-cement the crown.

The second possibility is that the abutment — the connector piece between the implant and the crown — has loosened from the implant body. Again, this is fixable — I can access and tighten that abutment screw.

The third possibility — and the most serious one — is that the implant body itself is moving inside the bone. That means the implant has not properly fused with the jawbone, a process we call osseointegration. At four months, that process should be well established or nearly complete, so movement of the implant itself is a significant concern."

---

Diagnosis & Management — Failed Osseointegration (Inflection 2)

"Based on my examination today, what I'm finding is that the movement appears to be coming from the implant body itself, and on your X-ray I can see bone loss around the implant. I want to be honest with you, because I think that's the most respectful thing I can do — an implant that is moving within the bone cannot be saved. If we leave it in place, it will continue to cause progressive bone loss in that area, which would actually make future treatment more difficult.

The recommended course of action is to remove the implant — this is called explantation. The procedure itself is generally straightforward. After removal, we allow the site to heal for approximately three to six months. During that time, we can assess the bone volume that remains, and once you've healed well, we can discuss whether re-implantation is appropriate.

But I also want to understand why this happened, so that if we do replace the implant, we give it the best possible chance. Implant failure at this stage can be related to smoking — which significantly reduces blood supply and healing — uncontrolled blood sugar in diabetes, poor oral hygiene around the implant during healing, insufficient bone at placement, or occasionally early loading before the implant had time to integrate. Understanding the cause helps us prevent it from happening again."

---

Referral, Patient Rights & Safety Net / Closing

"Now, because this implant was placed at another practice, I want to handle this carefully and professionally on your behalf. I'll write a detailed referral letter back to the treating dentist, outlining my clinical findings, the radiographic findings, and my assessment. They'll have the original placement records — the implant brand, dimensions, and the surgical notes — all of which are important for planning your next steps. They have a responsibility to follow this up with you.

You are also absolutely entitled to seek a second opinion at any time — for example, from an implant specialist or oral surgeon — and I encourage you to do so if it would give you greater confidence. I can provide you with a copy of today's findings to take with you.

In the meantime, please avoid placing heavy chewing forces on that side, and if you notice any pain, swelling, or the implant feels like it's moving more, please contact us straight away — don't wait.

Do you have any questions at all? I know this isn't the news you were hoping for, and I'm sorry for that. My priority is to make sure we get the best possible outcome for you from here. We'll get through this together."

PR8
Combination Syndrome + Osteoporosis Medication Clearance
Category:** Prosthodontics / Oral Medicine / Communication | **Time:** 11 min | **Difficulty:** High

CASE SUMMARY

A 68-year-old woman is referred by her GP for dental clearance before commencing anti-resorptive medication (bisphosphonate or denosumab) for osteoporosis. She has only four remaining mandibular teeth — the lower central incisors (31, 41) — both grade 2 mobile, with a classic combination syndrome presentation: flabby maxillary anterior ridge, good posterior ridge support, and mild denture stomatitis under her existing upper complete denture. She is deeply resistant to extraction and has seriously considered flying overseas to have the procedure done, believing this will sidestep the need. The candidate must recognise combination syndrome, explain the MRONJ risk timeline clearly, and use motivational interviewing to guide her toward accepting extraction before the medication window closes.

CANDIDATE BRIEF

Mrs. Okonkwo, 68, is referred by Dr. Patel (GP) with a referral letter requesting dental clearance before commencing alendronate 70mg weekly for newly diagnosed osteoporosis. She wears an upper complete denture and retains only 31 and 41. On examination: 31 and 41 are grade 2 mobile (horizontal and vertical) with generalised bone loss to the apical third on periapical X-ray; the upper anterior ridge is soft, compressible, and fibrous (flabby ridge); mild erythema covers the upper denture-bearing mucosa consistent with denture stomatitis; the posterior ridges are well-preserved. Mrs. Okonkwo says: "My GP wants me to have those two teeth out first but I've had them all my life. A friend told me if I get it done overseas the Australian rules don't apply and I won't have to do it." Your task: assess, diagnose, address the MRONJ risk, and use motivational interviewing to work through her resistance.

EXAMINER CONTEXT

Mrs. Okonkwo is distressed and fixed on the idea of keeping her lower teeth. She becomes tearful when extraction is raised. She has clearly researched "getting work done in Bali" and believes this is a genuine workaround. She respects clinical authority but will not be rushed. She will engage meaningfully if the candidate takes time to explain what MRONJ is in plain language and what it looks like. If the candidate connects the medication to her long-term quality of life (fracture prevention) and shows genuine empathy for her attachment to her teeth, she shifts toward accepting the recommendation. If the candidate is dismissive, she becomes defensive and closes down. She will directly ask: "Can I start the medication while I still have the teeth and just keep coming for check-ups?"

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

Opening — acknowledge the referral context (0.5 min)

"Thank you for coming in, Mrs. Okonkwo. Your GP has written to me about the medication they'd like to start for your bones, and they've asked me to check your teeth first. Before we talk about any of that, can I have a look at your mouth?"

Clinical examination (1.5 min)

  • Lower anteriors 31, 41: grade 2 mobility (horizontal ≥1mm, some vertical), generalised severe bone loss on periapical X-ray — hopeless prognosis
  • Upper ridge: anterior segment soft and compressible (flabby ridge — fibrous hyperplasia caused by the lower teeth continuing to erupt against the upper denture/soft tissue over years)
  • Upper denture: mild diffuse erythema over fitting surface area = denture stomatitis (Candida)
  • Posterior ridges: well-formed, good bone support
  • Existing upper complete denture: poor retention (likely time for replacement)

Naming what you see — INFLECTION 1: Combination syndrome

"Mrs. Okonkwo, I can see a few things happening in your mouth that are related to each other. The two front teeth you've kept in your lower jaw — they've been working really hard over the years, biting against the front of your upper denture. Over time, that constant pressure has caused the bone and gum tissue at the front of your upper jaw to become soft and spongy — what we call a flabby ridge. Your lower teeth themselves have become loose — the bone that holds them has reduced significantly. I also noticed some redness under your upper denture, which suggests a mild fungal infection called denture stomatitis. This is a very common pattern we call combination syndrome."

Why the GP referral matters — INFLECTION 2: Explain MRONJ in plain language

"Now, let me explain why Dr. Patel has asked you to see me before starting the bone medication.

The medication she wants to start — alendronate — is an anti-resorptive drug. It works by slowing down bone breakdown, which is wonderful for your skeleton and your fracture risk. But it has one specific effect on the jawbone: it reduces the jaw's ability to heal after any wound — including after a tooth extraction.

If you start this medication and then have those two teeth removed later — either here or overseas — there is a significant risk of developing a condition called MRONJ: medication-related osteonecrosis of the jaw. This is where the jaw bone is exposed and doesn't heal. It can become infected, painful, and in severe cases requires surgery to the jaw itself. It is not reversible. It is one of the more difficult complications in dentistry to manage once it occurs.

The good news is that this risk is dramatically lower — almost eliminated — if we remove those teeth before you start the medication, allow the bone to fully heal, and then give clearance to your GP to proceed. That healing window is the key."

Answer her direct question — INFLECTION 3: "Can I start medication and just monitor?"

"I understand why you're hoping we can find a way around this. But I have to be honest with you: starting the medication while the teeth are still there and mobile means that when they do eventually need to come out — and they will, because the bone holding them is almost gone — you'll be on active medication and the extraction risk will be much higher. The window to do this safely is now, before you start. Waiting or monitoring isn't a safe alternative."

Address the overseas plan — INFLECTION 4: Motivational, not dismissive

"I want to talk about what you said about going overseas. I completely understand the instinct — if there's a way to keep your teeth and still move forward with your bone treatment, you'd take it. But here's what I want you to know: the MRONJ risk doesn't change based on where the extraction happens. It's a biological effect of the medication on your jawbone — Australian rules have nothing to do with it. If the extraction is done overseas after you've started the medication, the risk is exactly the same. And managing a jaw complication overseas, or when you return, adds a whole other layer of difficulty."

(Pause. Let this land. Don't rush to the next point.)

"How are you feeling about what I've just explained?"

Empathy and autonomy (1 min) — INFLECTION 5

"I want to say something important: I understand that those teeth have been part of you for your whole life, and the idea of losing them feels like losing something real. That's not nothing. What I'm asking you to do is hard. But I'm asking because the alternative — the medication causing your jaw bone to fail — is genuinely worse. And I'll be here to make sure that when the teeth do come out, we have a good plan for replacing them so you're not without something to bite with."

Prosthodontic plan post-extraction (1 min)

"Once those two teeth are removed and the area has healed — typically 3 months — I'll review you and we can plan your lower denture. At that point, we should also look at whether your upper denture needs to be remade, given the flabby ridge changes and the denture stomatitis. Ideally we'd make both dentures at the same time."

Consider mentioning implant-retained overdenture for the lower as a long-term option, if resources allow.

Denture stomatitis today (0.5 min)

"For the redness under your upper denture — I'd like to start you on an antifungal gel: miconazole gel applied to the fitting surface of your denture twice daily for 2 weeks. Also, please take your denture out overnight and soak it in a diluted antiseptic solution. This reduces the fungal load significantly."

Clearance letter to GP (0.5 min)

"Once the extractions are done and I've confirmed healing at your 3-month check, I'll write to Dr. Patel directly to confirm you're clear to start the medication. That's what she's waiting for."

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Names combination syndrome by its components (flabby ridge, retained lower anteriors, loss of anterior maxillary bone support, preserved posterior ridges)
  2. ✅ Grades lower tooth mobility correctly (grade 2 = horizontal movement + some vertical = hopeless prognosis)
  3. ✅ Explains MRONJ in plain language — not jargon, not rushed
  4. ✅ Directly answers "Can I start medication and monitor?" — No, the extraction risk is highest AFTER starting; the window is NOW
  5. ✅ Addresses the overseas plan factually and non-judgmentally (MRONJ is biological, not jurisdictional)
  6. ✅ Uses motivational interviewing — empathy, autonomy, explores her resistance rather than overriding it
  7. ✅ Treats denture stomatitis (miconazole gel to denture fitting surface; denture out at night)
  8. ✅ Plans new upper and lower dentures post-healing, with implant overdenture mentioned as an option
  9. ✅ Provides clearance letter to GP only after confirmed healing (3-month review)

TG4 ALERTS

MRONJ and anti-resorptive medications — TG4: alendronate, zoledronic acid, and denosumab all increase MRONJ risk. Risk is significantly lower (approaches baseline) when extractions are completed and healed BEFORE starting medication. Dental clearance = extract all hopeless teeth + confirm healing (typically 3 months for bisphosphonates; longer if IV bisphosphonates or denosumab planned).
Denture stomatitis — TG4: first-line treatment is miconazole oromucosal gel applied to the fitting surface of the denture twice daily for 2–4 weeks. Patient must also remove denture overnight and soak in antiseptic (diluted chlorhexidine or sodium hypochlorite). Address denture hygiene habits as these are the underlying cause.
Grade 2 mobile teeth — Grade 2 = horizontal mobility >1mm. Grade 3 = vertical (axial) mobility present. Both grades typically indicate hopeless prognosis. Do NOT monitor and hope — especially in context of pending anti-resorptive therapy.
