STAGE: Opening — Acknowledging the Referral and Establishing Rapport

"Mrs. Okonkwo, thank you so much for coming in today. I've had a chance to read the referral letter from Dr. Patel, and I understand she's planning to start you on some medication for your bones and wanted me to check your teeth first before that happens. That's exactly the right sequence, and I'm really glad you came. Before we talk about any of that, would it be alright if I have a good look at your mouth? I'd like to examine your teeth and your gums, and also have a look at how your upper denture is sitting."

Conducts a thorough clinical examination. Assesses mobility of lower central incisors 31 and 41 — notes horizontal movement greater than one millimetre and detects axial, vertical movement. Records grade 2 to grade 3 mobility — clinically hopeless prognosis. Reviews periapical radiographs — confirms generalised bone loss extending to the apical third of both roots. Palpates the upper anterior ridge — soft, compressible, fibrous tissue confirmed. Assesses upper denture-bearing mucosa — diffuse mild erythema consistent with denture stomatitis. Notes posterior ridges bilaterally are well-formed with preserved bone support. Removes upper denture to assess fit and retention — retention is poor.

---

Clinical Findings — Naming Combination Syndrome

"Thank you for letting me have a look, Mrs. Okonkwo. I can see a few things happening in your mouth, and they're all connected to each other, so I'd like to walk you through what I've found.

The two front teeth you have in your lower jaw — they've been doing a remarkable job holding on. But over the years, they've been pressing up against the front of your upper denture with every bite. That constant pressure from below has caused the bone and tissue at the front of your upper jaw to gradually change — the tissue there has become soft and spongy rather than firm. We call that a flabby ridge, and it's a real challenge for denture stability going forward.

At the same time, those two lower teeth themselves have become quite loose. When I tested them, they moved more than a millimetre from side to side, and there was also some movement when I pushed upward — that tells me the bone supporting them has reduced very significantly. I could see this clearly on the X-ray as well, where the bone loss has extended almost to the root tips.

I also noticed some redness across the area under your upper denture — that's a mild fungal infection called denture stomatitis. It's caused by Candida, a yeast, and it's extremely common under dentures, especially if the denture is worn overnight.

On the positive side, your back ridges — the areas where your back teeth used to be — are in very good shape. There's good bone support there.

This overall picture — the flabby front ridge on top, the two remaining lower front teeth causing that pressure, and the preserved back ridges — is a pattern we recognise in dentistry. It's called combination syndrome. It tells us quite a lot about what your mouth has been doing over the years, and it's important for planning what comes next."

---

Explaining MRONJ — Why the Timing Matters Completely

"Now I want to explain something important, because this is really the heart of why Dr. Patel has sent you to me before starting the bone medication.

The medication she has in mind — alendronate, taken as a tablet once a week — is excellent for your skeleton. It works by slowing down the natural process of bone breakdown, and for someone with osteoporosis, that significantly reduces the risk of fractures. It's a very widely used and effective medication.

However, it has one specific effect on the jawbone that we have to take seriously. Once alendronate is in your system, it accumulates in the bone throughout your body, including your jaw. Over time, it reduces the jaw's ability to heal after any wound — including after a tooth extraction. So if those two teeth were removed after you've started this medication, there is a meaningful risk of developing a condition called MRONJ — medication-related osteonecrosis of the jaw. What that means in plain language is that the jawbone becomes exposed through the gum, and simply does not heal. It can become infected, it can be painful, and in serious cases it requires surgical removal of the affected bone. Once it occurs, it is not reversible and it is genuinely one of the most difficult complications we manage in dentistry.

Here is the crucial thing, Mrs. Okonkwo: this risk is dramatically reduced — it approaches the background risk in the general population — if we remove those teeth first, allow your jaw to fully heal, and then give Dr. Patel the all-clear to start the medication. That healing window is typically around three months. The window we have right now, before you start, is genuinely the safest and best time to do this."

---

Addressing Her Resistance — The Overseas Plan and Motivational Dialogue

"I want to gently address something you mentioned — the idea of having the teeth removed overseas so that, as you said, the Australian rules wouldn't apply.

I completely understand the instinct behind that. If there were a way to keep those teeth and still safely start your bone treatment, you would absolutely take it — and so would I. But I have to be honest with you about something important: the MRONJ risk has nothing to do with where in the world the extraction happens. It is a biological effect of this medication on your jawbone. The medication changes how your jaw heals, and that is true whether the extraction happens here, in another country, or anywhere else. Australian guidelines aren't creating this risk — the pharmacology of the medication is. And managing a jaw complication while you're overseas, or returning home with an unhealing wound, would add a very serious layer of difficulty to an already difficult situation.

I also want to answer directly the question of whether we could simply start the medication now and monitor those teeth. I understand why that sounds appealing — but the honest answer is no, that's not a safe path. Those teeth are already at a hopeless stage — the bone holding them is almost gone. It's not a matter of if they'll need to come out, it's a matter of when. If that moment arrives after you've been on alendronate for months or years, the extraction risk is substantially higher than it is today.

The window to do this safely is right now."

Pauses. Allows silence. Maintains eye contact.

"How are you feeling about what I've just explained?"

Listens fully to her response. Validates without dismissing.

"I hear you. And I want to say something sincerely — those teeth have been part of you your whole life, and being asked to let them go is genuinely hard. That's not a small thing, and I'm not treating it as one. What I'm asking of you is difficult. But I'm asking because the alternative — the medication causing your jawbone to fail — is something I cannot in good conscience allow you to walk into without understanding it fully. And I will be with you through every step of what comes next."

---

Management Plan — Treatment and Prosthodontic Planning

"So here is what I'd like to do for you, step by step.

First, I'd like to arrange the extractions of those two lower front teeth as soon as we can schedule them. We'll make sure you're comfortable — local anaesthetic is all you'll need — and we'll take good care of the sites afterward.

For the redness under your upper denture — the denture stomatitis — I'd like to start treatment for that today. I'm going to recommend miconazole oromucosal gel, applied directly to the fitting surface of your upper denture twice daily for two to four weeks. This treats the Candida on the denture itself, which is where it lives and reinfects the tissue. I'd also ask you to please take your denture out overnight — this alone makes an enormous difference — and soak it in a diluted chlorhexidine solution. The tissue needs time to breathe and recover each night.

After the extractions, I'll see you again at around three months. By that point, the extraction sites should be well healed, and I'll be able to confirm that to Dr. Patel in writing — a formal clearance letter — so she can safely start your alendronate.

At that same three-month review, we'll start planning your new lower denture. And given the changes to your upper ridge — the flabby tissue at the front — your upper denture should also be remade. Ideally, we'd construct both dentures together, which gives us the best chance of getting the bite and the fit right for you.

I'd also like you to know that, depending on your circumstances, there is

S10
Third Opinion — Re-RCT vs. Extraction (Tooth 25, Fosamax 5 Years)
Category:** Oral Surgery / Restorative / Communication | **Time:** 11 min | **Difficulty:** High

CASE SUMMARY

Mrs. Caldarin, 58, presents for a third opinion regarding tooth 25 (upper left second premolar), which was root-treated approximately 3 years ago. Dentist 1 recommended re-RCT, crown lengthening, post and core, and a crown to save the tooth. Dentist 2 recommended extraction. She has been sitting on this decision for a month, is anxious, and wants an honest, clear recommendation. She has been taking Fosamax (alendronate) 10mg daily for osteoporosis for 5 years. Smoking is a hidden agenda — she smokes 10 cigarettes/day and will only disclose this if directly asked. The IOPA shows: tooth 25 root canal filled with gutta-percha, large composite coronal restoration, apical widening (periapical radiolucency consistent with persistent/recurrent apical periodontitis), and secondary caries visible at the distal margin of the restoration, extending sub-gingivally.

CANDIDATE BRIEF

Mrs. Caldarin, 58, arrives with a folder of notes from two previous dental opinions. She is frustrated and anxious. She says: "Dentist 1 wants to do a re-root canal, crown lengthening, and a post and crown — it sounds like a lot of work. Dentist 2 just said to pull it out. I don't know who to trust or what's right for me. I just want someone to give me a straight answer."

Medical history (volunteered): taking Fosamax 10mg daily for osteoporosis for 5 years.

Hidden agenda: smokes 10 cigarettes/day — will not volunteer this unless asked.

An IOPA is available. Your task: review the X-ray, examine the tooth, give an honest independent assessment of restorability, counsel on MRONJ risk relevant to either pathway, and help her reach an informed decision.

IOPA FINDINGS

IOPA — Tooth 25 (UL Second Premolar)
Key findings
Adequate GP obturation
2° caries, distal, ~2mm sub-gingival
Periapical radiolucency ~3mm
Ferrule zone — key decision
CR ratio ~1:1.5 (acceptable)
Periodontal bone: WNL

Key X-ray summary for exam: Adequate obturation but persistent periapical pathology = re-RCT is clinically indicated IF the tooth is restorable. Restorability is the central question — determined by the ferrule, not the X-ray.

EXAMINER CONTEXT

Mrs. Caldarin will initially say "I just want to keep the tooth if possible." She becomes more engaged once the candidate explains the restorability concept using non-jargon language. She will ask: "Why did two dentists give me opposite advice?" — candidate must explain honestly that restorability hinges on clinical findings that can differ in interpretation. She will NOT volunteer smoking unless directly asked about lifestyle. If the candidate does not ask, the examiner will note the omission. When smoking is revealed, she will be defensive ("I only smoke a little") — candidate should address the relevance calmly. She will ask: "Does the bone tablet cause problems with the extraction?"

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

Opening — acknowledge the difficulty (0.5 min)

"Mrs. Caldarin, thank you for bringing your records. I can hear how frustrating it's been to get different advice — that's a really difficult position to be in. My job today is to give you my honest, independent assessment. Can I start by having a look at the X-ray and then examining the tooth?"

IOPA interpretation — INFLECTION 1: Read it systematically

"Looking at the X-ray: the root canal filling looks technically adequate — the filling goes close to the tip of the root. But I can see two important things: there's a dark area at the tip of the root — that's the infection that the root canal was supposed to treat, and it hasn't resolved. It's called a periapical lesion. And I can see decay starting under the edge of the filling on the back surface of the tooth, extending below the gum line.

These two findings explain why both your previous dentists flagged this tooth — the root canal appears to have failed, and there is new decay undermining the existing restoration."

Examination — the restorability assessment — INFLECTION 2: Ferrule is the decision-maker

Probe and assess:

  • How far does the caries extend sub-gingivally? Estimate from probing.
  • How much sound tooth structure remains above the bone crest?
  • Is there ≥2mm of sound dentine circumferentially above the crest to achieve a ferrule?

"The key question is: after we remove all the decay, is there enough healthy tooth left above the gum and bone to build a crown that will hold? We need at least 2mm of healthy tooth structure all the way around — what we call a 'ferrule.' Without it, even the best crown will eventually fail."

Restorability outcomes (1.5 min)

Present as a genuine fork in the road, based on clinical findings:

If ferrule IS achievable:

"Based on what I can see, there is enough tooth to work with, but it is borderline. Here is what Dentist 1 proposed:

  1. Re-RCT: retreating the root canal to clear the infection at the tip. This can be done by an endodontist (specialist) — success rate is around 70–85%.
  2. Crown lengthening: a minor surgical procedure to expose 2mm of sound tooth above the bone, so the crown has something to grip. 6–8 weeks healing time before crowning.
  3. Post and core: a post placed into the root canal to help retain the crown build-up.
  4. Crown: final restoration.

This is significant treatment. Cost is substantial. But IF it works, you keep the tooth."

If ferrule is NOT achievable:

"If the decay goes too deep, no amount of crown lengthening will help — the crown-to-root ratio and the bone level set a limit. In that case, extraction is the right answer — not because the dentist gave up, but because saving it would guarantee a future failure."

Why two dentists gave different advice — INFLECTION 3

"I want to answer your question about why you got different advice. This tooth is on the border of restorability. Both dentists may have been right from what they saw. Dentist 1 believed there was enough tooth to save it; Dentist 2 felt the risk wasn't worth it. This is genuinely a judgment call — it's not that one dentist was incompetent. My job is to give you the clearest picture I can from today's examination, and then support your decision."

Smoking — INFLECTION 4: Must ask

"Before we talk about the best pathway, I need to ask about a few lifestyle factors. Do you smoke?"

(If yes):

"Thank you for telling me. Smoking affects this decision in two ways. First, if we try to save the tooth — re-RCT and crown lengthening — healing after the crown lengthening surgery takes longer and is less predictable in smokers. Second, if we go with extraction — and if you later want an implant to replace the tooth — smoking significantly reduces implant success rates (from ~95% to ~80% in moderate smokers, lower in heavy smokers). I'm not going to tell you what to do about smoking, but I want you to have that information because it's clinically relevant."

Fosamax and MRONJ — INFLECTION 5: Address the "bone tablet" question

"Yes — the medication you're taking for your bones is relevant, and I'm glad you mentioned it. Alendronate — Fosamax — is a bisphosphonate. It works by reducing bone breakdown, which is great for your skeleton. But it has a specific effect on the jaw: if the jawbone is disrupted — by an extraction — it can be slower to heal, and in some cases the bone can become exposed and fail to close over. This is called MRONJ — medication-related osteonecrosis of the jaw.

The risk with oral alendronate at your dose over 5 years is low — estimated at less than 0.1%. But it is real, and I need to explain it before we proceed with extraction.

If saving the tooth: There is no extraction, so the MRONJ risk is minimal. Periodontal probing and crown lengthening carry a much lower risk than extraction.

If extracting: We manage it by keeping the socket as clean as possible, using resorbable sutures to close the site, and monitoring healing closely. We do NOT stop the Fosamax — current evidence does NOT support a drug holiday for low-risk oral bisphosphonate."

Shared decision — INFLECTION 6

"Here is my honest recommendation based on today's examination: [state based on your ferrule assessment]. I'll support whatever decision you make, but I want you to make it with the full picture. The re-RCT pathway is a longer, more expensive road with a meaningful chance of success. The extraction pathway is simpler and more predictable — but you do lose the tooth and face decisions about replacement."

Replacement options if extraction

  • Implant: best long-term replacement — but smoking reduces success; discuss
  • Bridge: requires crown prep on teeth 24 and 26 — conservative issue
  • Partial denture: removable, least invasive, lower cost
  • No replacement: acceptable for a premolar in some patients (discuss tipping/supraeruption of opposing)

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Reviews the IOPA systematically: obturation quality, periapical pathology, secondary caries, bone levels
  2. ✅ Identifies ferrule as the central restorability criterion (≥2mm circumferential sound dentine)
  3. ✅ Explains why two dentists gave different advice — borderline case, not incompetence
  4. ✅ Gives an honest independent opinion, neither validating nor dismissing previous dentists
  5. ✅ Asks about smoking — it is a hidden agenda and must be directly elicited
  6. ✅ Addresses smoking's impact on both crown lengthening healing AND future implant success
  7. ✅ MRONJ counseling specific to ALREADY ON bisphosphonate (vs. about to start — different from PR8)
  8. ✅ Does NOT recommend stopping Fosamax (drug holiday not recommended for low-risk oral bisphosphonate — TG4)
  9. ✅ Presents replacement options with honest trade-offs if extraction chosen

TG4 ALERTS

MRONJ — oral bisphosphonate, already taking — TG4: for patients already on oral bisphosphonate (low MRONJ risk category), do NOT routinely stop the medication pre-extraction (drug holiday not recommended). Use local haemostatic measures: primary closure with resorbable sutures, chlorhexidine rinse post-op, monitor healing at 1 and 2 weeks.
Re-RCT vs. extraction — restorability framework — The decision must be based on: (1) ferrule ≥2mm circumferential, (2) crown-to-root ratio acceptable after crown lengthening, (3) strategic value of tooth, (4) patient factors (compliance, smoking, cost). If ferrule cannot be achieved after crown lengthening without compromising adjacent teeth or bone, extraction is indicated regardless of RCT quality.
Smoking and dental healing — Smoking impairs healing after any surgical procedure (crown lengthening, extraction) via vasoconstriction and reduced immune response. Also significantly reduces implant osseointegration success. Must be disclosed to patient as it affects both the save and the replace pathways.

"Mrs. Caldarin, thank you so much for coming in today, and thank you for bringing all of your records — that's really helpful. I can hear how exhausting and frustrating the last month has been. Getting two completely different pieces of advice from two dentists you trusted is genuinely difficult, and I want you to know I think it was the right thing to seek a third opinion. "Before I do anything else, can I have a look at the X-ray you've brought, and then I'd like to examine the tooth directly?"

IOPA Interpretation and Clinical Examination

Reviews the radiograph systematically, noting the following aloud to the patient.

"Right, so I'm looking at your X-ray now — the upper left second premolar, tooth 25. Let me walk you through what I can see, because I want this to make sense to you, not just to me."

"The root canal filling itself actually looks technically reasonable — it appears to go close to the tip of the root, which is what we aim for. So the original root canal wasn't badly done. But here are two things that concern me. First, I can see a dark area at the very tip of the root — this is an area of infection that the root canal was supposed to resolve, and it hasn't. We call it a periapical lesion, and it tells me the root canal has not fully succeeded. Second — and this is equally important — I can see decay starting underneath the edge of your filling on the back surface of the tooth, and it appears to be extending below the gum line. That is new decay undermining the existing restoration. So we have two separate problems: a persistent infection at the root tip, and new decay threatening the foundation of the tooth."

Proceeds to clinical examination — probing all six points around tooth 25, assessing the extent of subgingival caries, and estimating remaining sound tooth structure above the alveolar crest.

"Now I'm going to probe around the tooth very gently to measure how far down that decay goes and how much healthy tooth is left above the bone. This tells me whether saving the tooth is structurally realistic. Bear with me — this may be slightly uncomfortable."

---

Restorability Assessment — The Ferrule Conversation

"Right. Here is the central question — and this is actually the reason the two dentists gave you different answers. After we remove all the decay, is there at least two millimetres of healthy tooth structure remaining all the way around the tooth, above the bone level? We call this the 'ferrule.' Without it, even the most beautifully made crown will eventually fail, because it has nothing solid to grip. It's like trying to put a lid on a jar with no rim."

"Based on what I can see today, the decay at the distal margin is extending close to — and possibly below — the bone crest on that surface. This puts this tooth in the borderline category for restorability. It is not impossible to save, but it is genuinely on the margin."

"If we decide to try to save it, here is the full pathway Dentist 1 proposed, and I want to be honest about what each step involves. First, re-root canal treatment — retreating the canal to clear the persistent infection at the root tip. Done by a specialist endodontist, the success rate is approximately seventy to eighty-five percent. Second, crown lengthening — a minor surgical procedure to surgically move the gum and bone down to expose at least two millimetres of sound tooth above the bone, giving the crown something to hold onto. This needs six to eight weeks of healing before we can crown the tooth. Third, a post placed into the root canal to help retain the core build-up, and finally a full crown. This is a significant treatment pathway — it is time-consuming, it has real cost, and it carries no guarantee. But if it works, you keep your own tooth."

"If the decay extends too deeply for crown lengthening to solve the ferrule problem — or if you decide the time, cost, and uncertainty are not worth it — then extraction is a completely valid choice. That's not giving up. That's being realistic."

---

Why Two Dentists Disagreed — and the Smoking Question

"I want to answer your question directly: why did two dentists give you opposite advice? This tooth sits right on the borderline of restorability. Dentist 1 believed there was enough tooth structure to justify the save pathway. Dentist 2 looked at the same tooth and concluded the risk and complexity weren't justified. Both of those positions are clinically defensible. Neither dentist was incompetent or wrong — this is a genuine judgment call, and borderline teeth are genuinely hard. My job is to be as precise as I can with today's examination and give you my honest view."

"Before I give you my recommendation, I need to ask you about something important. Do you smoke at all, or have you smoked in the past?"

If patient discloses smoking ten cigarettes per day: "Thank you for telling me — I know that's sometimes a sensitive thing to mention, and I'm not here to judge you. But it is clinically relevant, and here's why it matters for both pathways. If we try to save the tooth — the crown lengthening is a surgical procedure, and smoking reduces blood flow to healing tissues, which means slower and less predictable healing after surgery. If we extract the tooth and you later consider an implant to replace it, smoking reduces implant success rates significantly — from around ninety-five percent in non-smokers to closer to eighty percent in moderate smokers, and lower with heavier use. So smoking affects both the save option and the replace option. I want you to have that information."

"On that note — and I say this briefly and without pressure — if you're ever open to support with smoking, even cutting down, that's something I'm happy to discuss or refer you for. The evidence is clear that even brief advice makes a difference."

---

MRONJ Counselling — Fosamax and Extraction Risk

"Now — the medication you mentioned, Fosamax, alendronate — this is important and I want to explain it carefully, because it affects the extraction pathway specifically."

"Alendronate is a bisphosphonate. It works by slowing down the cells that break down bone, which is exactly what you want for osteoporosis — it protects your skeleton. However, bisphosphonates have a particular effect on jawbone. When the jawbone is disrupted by an extraction, the healing can sometimes be impaired, and in a small number of cases the bone can become exposed and fail to close over. This condition is called MRONJ — medication-related osteonecrosis of the jaw — and it is serious when it occurs."

"Now, here is the reassuring part. The risk with oral alendronate at your dose, even after five years, is low — estimated at less than one in a thousand, so less than 0.1 percent. You are not in a high-risk category. You are not on an intravenous bisphosphonate, you are not having cancer treatment, and your dose is standard."

"One thing I want to be very clear about: I will not be advising you to stop your Fosamax before any procedure. Stopping and restarting bisphosphonates — what some people call a 'drug holiday' — is not recommended for patients in your risk category. The evidence does not support it, and your bone health matters. What we do instead, if we proceed to extraction, is manage the socket carefully — we close it with dissolving stitches to encourage primary healing, we use a chlorhexidine rinse in the days after, and I monitor your healing closely at one week and two weeks. If we save the tooth, the MRONJ risk is minimal, as we are not extracting."

---

Shared Decision and Replacement Options — Closing

"So here is my honest clinical recommendation, based on today's examination. The decay on the distal surface is extensive and subgingival, the periapical lesion confirms the root canal has not succeeded, and the ferrule is borderline. In my assessment, if crown lengthening can achieve two millimetres of sound tooth circumferentially — and that is something I would want confirmed — then the save pathway is technically possible but carries meaningful risk of eventual failure. If the decay extends to a level where crown lengthening cannot achieve that ferrule, then extraction is the right answer, and it is not a lesser outcome — it is the correct one."

"If extraction is the path, I want you to know your replacement options. A dental implant is the gold standard

PR9
Broken Denture Teeth — Metal RPD, Reduced Vertical Dimension
Category:** Prosthodontics / Communication | **Time:** 11 min | **Difficulty:** Exam-ready

CASE SUMMARY

Mr./Mrs. Cooper presents upset and distressed: the acrylic teeth on their metal partial denture fractured overnight. The denture was provided by your colleague 6 months ago. On examination you identify reduced occlusal vertical dimension (OVD) and angular cheilitis at both corners of the mouth. The patient is slightly agitated — partly about the inconvenience, partly implying the denture was substandard. The candidate must manage the patient's frustration, diagnose the root cause (collapsed VD causing excessive occlusal load and fatigue fracture of the acrylic teeth), and present a clear short-term and long-term management framework.

Examiner variations — read before the station:

  • Variation A (Commissioner / Senior Public Official): Patient has an important public-facing event in 3 days. They are not aggressive but there is a clear undercurrent of "this needs to be fixed today — I have professional obligations." Manages upward expectations without over-promising.
  • Variation B (Sales Representative): Patient's income depends on face-to-face client interactions. They are distressed about appearance more than anything else. Will specifically say: "I can't see clients like this."
  • Standard variation: Patient is generally upset and frustrated. Will ask: "Is this the dentist's fault? Should this have happened after only 6 months?"

CANDIDATE BRIEF

Mr./Mrs. Cooper, medically fit and well, presents holding their metal partial denture. Two acrylic posterior teeth have fractured off the metal framework. The denture was made by your colleague 6 months ago. The patient says: "I woke up this morning and found these two teeth on my pillow. This is really embarrassing — I have [an important event / client meetings] coming up and I can't be walking around like this."

On examination:

  • Metal RPD: two acrylic posterior teeth (lower left) fractured cleanly at the junction with the metal framework — classic fatigue fracture pattern
  • Reduced occlusal vertical dimension: the patient's face height at rest and on occlusion is reduced; inter-occlusal rest space is greater than normal (~5–6mm vs ideal 2–3mm)
  • Angular cheilitis: bilateral, fissured erythema at the corners of the mouth
  • Existing denture fit: metal framework seats well; clasps still retentive

Key question to ask in the history: "Have you had dentures before? How long have you been wearing partial dentures, and what were your previous dentures like?"

EXAMINER CONTEXT

Patient is not aggressive but is visibly frustrated and slightly flustered. Will use phrases like "This really shouldn't have happened after 6 months" and "Was this made properly?" — the candidate must address this without dismissing the concern and without criticising the colleague's work. The patient will become calmer and more cooperative if the candidate:

  1. Acknowledges their frustration genuinely
  2. Explains what happened in plain language (why the teeth broke)
  3. Gives a concrete short-term fix timeline

The patient will push for "Can you just glue them back on today?" — the candidate must explain why chair-side gluing is not appropriate and that a same-day lab repair is the correct short-term solution. For the commissioner/sales variation: this urgency is legitimate and the candidate should actively problem-solve the timeline (call lab, same-day if possible, document the effort).

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

Opening — de-escalate immediately (0.5 min) — INFLECTION 1

"Mr. Cooper, I can hear how stressful this is — especially with what you have coming up. Let me have a proper look and I'll tell you exactly what we're dealing with and what we can do about it today."

Sit down. Make eye contact. Do not start examining before acknowledging the patient's emotional state.

History — INFLECTION 2: Ask about previous dentures

"Before I look, I want to ask you a few questions.

  • When did you first start wearing partial dentures? How long have you been in a denture?
  • What were your previous dentures like — similar design, or different?
  • Did you notice any changes to how the bite felt before this happened — anything feeling lower, teeth meeting differently?
  • Do you clench or grind at night? Has anyone told you that?
  • How do you clean and store the denture?"

Why previous denture history matters: If the patient has had partial dentures for many years, the vertical dimension may have been gradually collapsing over successive dentures — each one made to the collapsed state rather than the correct OVD. This is a systemic problem, not a one-off fracture.

Examination (1.5 min)

  • Metal framework: seats well, clasps retentive, no metal fatigue or cracks
  • Fracture site: clean fracture at acrylic-metal junction — consistent with fatigue fracture from excessive occlusal force
  • OVD: reduced (face height reduced; inter-occlusal rest space ~5–6mm); confirm by asking patient to swallow and close naturally, then compare to measured lower face height
  • Angular cheilitis: bilateral commissures — fissured, erythematous, crusted at corners

Explain what happened — plain language — INFLECTION 3

"Let me explain what I've found and why this happened — because once you understand it, the solution will make more sense.

The metal part of your denture is completely fine — that's intact. What broke are the artificial teeth, which are made of acrylic — a plastic material. Acrylic teeth fracture for one main reason: they're being asked to absorb more force than they're designed for.

When I look at your bite, your face height — the distance between your upper and lower jaws when you bite — is reduced compared to where it ideally should be. We call this the vertical dimension. When the vertical dimension decreases, your teeth meet harder and with more leverage. Over time — especially overnight when many people clench or grind unconsciously — this creates a fatigue fracture in the acrylic. It's like bending a paperclip back and forth until it snaps. It doesn't break in one go — it cracks gradually and then fails all at once."

Address the colleague question — INFLECTION 4

"You asked whether this should have happened. I want to be honest with you without speculating about decisions I wasn't part of. What I can tell you is that the reduced vertical dimension is something that needs to be addressed going forward — whether it was present when the denture was made or developed since then. My focus today is making sure we fix this properly for you."

Do NOT say: "The other dentist made a mistake." Do NOT dismiss the concern: "These things just happen." Find the middle: acknowledge the situation, own the solution, don't assign blame.

Short-term management — INFLECTION 5

"Here's what we can do today:

Immediate / same-day:

  • I'm going to take your denture and send it to our dental laboratory right now for a same-day repair — they'll rebond the fractured teeth back onto the framework using proper dental acrylic. This is the correct repair: chair-side super-glue or DIY adhesives are not appropriate — they don't hold under occlusal load, can distort the fit, and can be toxic if ingested.
  • Turnaround: most labs can do a same-day repair if we get it there by [time]. Let me call them now while you wait.
  • You'll have your denture back [today / tomorrow morning].

In the meantime:

  • I can provide you with a denture adhesive if you need to wear it for a short period, but the repair is the priority.
  • For the angular cheilitis: I'll give you a miconazole cream — apply a small amount to the corners of your mouth twice daily. This treats both the fungal and bacterial components."

For commissioner/sales variation:

"I understand you have [event/meetings] in [X days]. Let me call the lab right now and confirm the turnaround. If same-day isn't possible today, I'll personally follow up to make sure it's ready first thing tomorrow morning."

Long-term management — INFLECTION 6

"Once the immediate repair is done, I want to have a proper conversation about the bigger picture — because if we just repair the teeth and send you on your way, they'll fracture again. The root cause hasn't been addressed.

What I'd recommend:

  1. Restore the correct vertical dimension: We need to determine your correct bite height. This involves taking records over a few appointments and gradually re-establishing the correct OVD. This is sometimes done with an occlusal splint first to allow the muscles to adapt, then progressively in the prosthesis.
  1. New RPD at the correct OVD: Once we've confirmed the correct vertical dimension, we make a new metal partial denture incorporating it. The new acrylic teeth will be set at the correct height, and the occlusal forces will be distributed properly — dramatically reducing fracture risk.
  1. Consider implant support (if appropriate): If budget and bone allow, implant-retained abutments for the partial denture dramatically reduce movement and occlusal leverage on acrylic teeth.
  1. Address parafunction: If there is nocturnal clenching or bruxism, an occlusal splint worn at night protects the denture teeth from fatigue fracture.
  1. Correct angular cheilitis: Will resolve with the combination of antifungal cream AND restoration of correct VD — the corners of the mouth will no longer be folded once the face height is restored."

Summary check (0.5 min)

"So — immediate priority: repair today, back to you ASAP. Longer term: we need to look at the vertical dimension and make a plan for a new denture that addresses the root cause. Does that make sense? Do you have any questions?"

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ De-escalates the patient's frustration before examining — empathy first
  2. ✅ Asks about previous denture history — establishes whether VD has been collapsing progressively over multiple dentures
  3. ✅ Examines OVD explicitly (inter-occlusal rest space, face height), not just the broken teeth
  4. ✅ Explains the fatigue fracture mechanism in plain language (paperclip analogy)
  5. ✅ Manages the colleague question diplomatically — no blame, no dismissal
  6. ✅ Short-term: lab repair (same-day where possible), not chair-side adhesive
  7. ✅ Calls the lab in front of the patient for urgent cases — demonstrates active problem-solving
  8. ✅ Long-term: new RPD at correct OVD; addresses bruxism; angular cheilitis resolves with VD correction
  9. ✅ Angular cheilitis: miconazole cream + root cause (VD correction)
  10. ✅ Adapts urgency appropriately for commissioner/sales variation without over-promising

TG4 ALERTS

Angular cheilitis in denture patients — TG4: primary treatment is miconazole cream (antifungal + antibacterial) to the affected commissures, twice daily for 2–4 weeks. However, if the root cause is reduced vertical dimension, topical treatment alone will not prevent recurrence — the VD must be corrected.
Chair-side denture repair with super-glue or DIY adhesives — Contraindicated. Cyanoacrylate adhesives (super-glue) do not bond adequately under occlusal load, can distort the denture base, alter the fit surface, and are potentially toxic if ingested. Always use a dental laboratory for denture repairs.
Reduced OVD and fatigue fracture — Acrylic denture teeth fracture when OVD is insufficient because the occlusal forces are concentrated and the acrylic has insufficient room to absorb them. Repairing without correcting OVD will result in repeat fracture.

INFLECTION POINTS

PointWeakStrong
OpeningGoes straight to examining the dentureAcknowledges frustration first: "I can hear how stressful this is — let me have a look and tell you exactly what we can do today"
Denture history"How long have you had this denture?" (only asks about the current one)"Have you had partial dentures before this one? How long have you been in a denture?" — establishes whether VD has been collapsing over successive dentures
Explaining the fracture"The teeth just broke — these things happen"Explains fatigue fracture mechanism: reduced VD → excessive force → repeated stress → acrylic fracture. Uses the paperclip analogy.
Colleague question"I can't comment on what the other dentist did" (dismissive) OR "They should have caught the reduced VD" (critical)"Without being there I can't speculate — what I can tell you is what needs to happen going forward and I'll make sure we get this right"
Short-term fix"I'll glue them back on now""Lab repair only — I'm calling the lab right now to get this done today"

BETTER PHRASES

  • Instead of: "These things happen with dentures" → "The teeth fractured because of the reduced bite height — that's the root cause, and it's fixable."
  • Instead of: "The other dentist should have checked the vertical dimension" → "I want to focus on making sure we get the right outcome for you going forward."
  • Instead of: "I'll glue it back on" → "A proper laboratory repair is the only reliable fix — I'm going to call them now and sort out the fastest turnaround we can manage."
  • Instead of: "Come back in a few weeks for a new denture" → "Let me walk you through the two stages — what we do today and what we plan for the longer term so this doesn't happen again."

EXAM VARIATIONS CHEAT SHEET

Sales representativeAppearance = livelihood, distressed about aestheticsValidate the aesthetic concern; reassure that lab repair will restore appearance; interim adhesive if gap before repair

KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • "Systematically: why did the teeth break? Occlusal overload (most likely), reduced VDO causing overclosure, material fatigue, poor bonding to denture base, parafunction. Identify the cause before the repair, or it repeats."
  • "Reduced VDO: assess clinically — reduced facial height, overclosure, deepening nasolabial folds; confirm with mounted study models and provisional VDO trial. Do not increase VDO without a trial period (Lucia jig or occlusal splint at proposed VDO for 4–6 weeks)."
  • "If VDO change is indicated: remount, new record at proposed VDO, gradual rehabilitation — do not change VDO and restore permanently in the same appointment."
  • "Metal RPD with broken teeth: repair is possible short-term, but if underlying VDO or occlusion is unaddressed, it's a temporary fix. Full assessment first."
Patient Reframes
  • "The broken teeth are a symptom — they're telling us the bite relationship has changed over time and those teeth are taking more force than they're designed for. Repairing without fixing the cause means they'll break again, possibly sooner."
  • "I'm going to do a temporary repair today so you have function — and then I want to take some measurements of your bite to understand the bigger picture before we plan the permanent fix."
Curveball Deflectors
  • "Just glue them back on." → "I can do a temporary repair — and I will — but if I only do that and send you home, we'll be here again in a few months for the same reason. Can I take 10 minutes to look at why they broke before I repair them?"
  • "Is this my fault?" → "No — this is a mechanical issue with the bite relationship, not anything you've done wrong. Denture teeth wear and can break when forces aren't distributed evenly. It's something we can fix with the right assessment."
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ▶
STAGE: Opening — De-escalation and Acknowledgement

Candidate enters the room, sits down at eye level with Mr. Cooper, and makes direct, calm eye contact before reaching for any instrument or the denture.

"Mr. Cooper, thank you for coming in — and I'm sorry you're having such a stressful morning. I can hear how upsetting this is, especially with what you have coming up. I want you to know that you've absolutely done the right thing by coming straight in. What I'd like to do is ask you a few questions first, then have a proper look, and then I'll tell you exactly what's happened and what we're going to do about it — including what we can sort out for you today. Does that sound okay?"

Pauses and waits for the patient to settle. Does not begin examination. Does not look at the denture until after history is complete.

---

History

"Before I examine the denture, I'd really like to understand the full picture — it'll help me give you the right answer. So firstly, have you worn partial dentures before this one? And if so, how many years have you been in a partial denture altogether? I ask because it helps me understand how your bite has changed over time."

Listens carefully. Follows up:

"What were your previous dentures like — were they a similar design, or different? And when you were wearing those earlier ones, do you remember your bite feeling solid and even, or did things feel like they were gradually getting lower or flatter over the years?"

"In the lead-up to this happening — did you notice anything changing with your bite on this current denture? Any feeling that your teeth weren't meeting the way they used to, or that things felt a little flat?"

"Do you clench or grind your teeth at night? Has anyone — a partner, a previous dentist — ever mentioned that to you?"

"How do you clean your denture, and do you leave it out at night or sleep in it?"

Records answers. Notes that if the patient has worn multiple successive partial dentures over many years, the vertical dimension may have been collapsing progressively across each new prosthesis — each one constructed to the already-reduced bite height rather than the correct dimension.

---

Examination and Diagnosis

Receives the denture. Examines it systematically, narrating findings aloud to keep the patient engaged and informed.

"Right — let me have a careful look at this. The metal framework — the chrome base — that is completely intact. No cracks, no distortion, the clasps are all in good shape. So the underlying structure is fine."

Seats the denture in the patient's mouth and assesses framework fit and clasp retention — both satisfactory.

"What I can see very clearly is that these two posterior teeth have fractured cleanly right at the junction between the acrylic tooth and the metal framework. That's a very specific fracture pattern — and it tells me something important about why this happened."

Asks the patient to swallow gently and close naturally. Assesses lower face height and inter-occlusal rest space by observation and measurement.

"I'm now looking at your bite — the distance between your upper and lower jaws. When you're at rest, that gap should ideally be somewhere around two to three millimetres. What I'm seeing is closer to five or six millimetres. And when you close, your face height — the vertical distance here — is reduced compared to where it should be. That's called the occlusal vertical dimension, and it's sitting lower than it needs to be."

Examines the commissures of the mouth.

"I can also see some redness and cracking at both corners of your mouth — that's called angular cheilitis, and it's directly related to what I've just found in your bite. I'll come back to that in a moment."

---

Explanation — What Happened and Why

"Mr. Cooper, let me explain what's caused this — because once you understand it, everything else I'm going to suggest will make complete sense."

"The metal part of your denture is fine. What broke are the acrylic teeth — the plastic artificial teeth bonded onto the framework. Acrylic teeth are strong, but they have a limit. They fracture for one main reason: they're being asked to absorb more force than they were designed for. When the vertical dimension — your bite height — is reduced, your jaws close harder and with more mechanical leverage. The forces concentrate right at that acrylic-to-metal junction. Over time — particularly overnight, when many people clench or grind without even realising it — this creates what we call a fatigue fracture. Think of it like bending a paperclip back and forth. It doesn't snap straight away — it weakens a little each time, and then one day it fails all at once. That's what's happened here."

"Now — you asked a very fair question: should this have happened after only six months? I want to be honest with you, and I also want to be fair. I wasn't present when this denture was made, so I can't speculate about decisions I wasn't part of. What I can tell you clearly is that the reduced vertical dimension is the underlying cause — and that is something we need to address going forward, regardless of how it developed. My focus today is making sure we fix this properly for you and making sure it doesn't happen again."

Does not assign blame to the colleague. Does not dismiss the patient's concern with "these things just happen."

---

Short-Term Management Plan

"Here is exactly what we're going to do right now."

"I'm going to call our dental laboratory this moment — while you're sitting here — and get your denture booked in for a same-day repair. The lab will rebond those fractured teeth back onto the framework using proper dental acrylic and the correct bonding technique. That is the right way to repair this. I want to be very clear: chair-side super-glue or over-the-counter denture adhesives are not appropriate here — they don't hold under biting force, they can distort the fit surface of your denture, and some are potentially harmful if accidentally ingested. We do this properly."

Picks up phone and calls the laboratory in front of the patient, confirming drop-off time and expected turnaround.

"Most laboratories can turn this around same-day if we get it there this morning. I'll confirm the exact time now. You'll either have it back this afternoon, or — at the very latest — first thing tomorrow morning. I'll personally follow up to make sure."

"For the corner-of-the-mouth cracking — the angular cheilitis — I'm going to give you a miconazole cream. Apply a small amount to both corners of your mouth twice daily. Miconazole is ideal here because it treats both the fungal and bacterial components, which are both usually present. Use it for two to four weeks. I do want to be transparent with you though: the cream will treat the symptoms, but the reason those corners are folding and staying moist is because your face height is reduced. Once we address that properly, the angular cheilitis should resolve for good."

---

Long-Term Management and Closing

"Once the repair is done and you're comfortable again, I want us to sit down and talk through the bigger picture — because if we simply send you on your way with repaired teeth and don't address the vertical dimension, those teeth will fracture again. We'd be treating the symptom, not the cause."

"What I'm recommending longer term is this: first, we take proper records over a couple of appointments to establish your correct bite height. Sometimes we use an occlusal splint initially — a guard that gradually re-trains the jaw muscles to function at the correct dimension before we build it into a prosthesis. Once we've confirmed the right position, we construct a new metal partial denture at the correct vertical dimension. The teeth will be set at the right height, the forces will be properly distributed, and the fracture risk drops dramatically."

"If you are grinding or clenching at night, a protective occlusal splint worn overnight will also significantly reduce the fatigue loading on the denture teeth between now and then."

"And as I mentioned — once the face height is restored, those corners of your mouth will no longer fold inward, and the angular cheilitis should clear up and stay away."

"So — to summarise where we're at: today, we get the denture repaired and back to you as quickly as possible. From there, we make a proper plan to address the vertical dimension so this doesn't happen again. You have the miconazole for the corners of your mouth in the meantime."

"I know this morning has been really stressful, and I appreciate your patience. Do you have any questions about anything I've said? Is there anything you'd like me to go over again?"

OM1
Oral Ulcer — Aphthous vs. Squamous Cell Carcinoma
Category:** Oral Medicine | **Time:** 11 min | **Difficulty:** Exam-ready

CASE SUMMARY

55-year-old male smoker presents with a 3-week non-healing ulcer on the lateral border of the tongue. Painless. Has been smoking 20/day for 30 years and drinks alcohol socially. Partner noticed it and urged him to come in.

CANDIDATE BRIEF

A 55-year-old male presents with a painless ulcer on the right lateral border of the tongue, present for 3 weeks. He only came in because his partner insisted. Smokes 20/day for 30 years, drinks 3–4 standard drinks most evenings. Your task: take a history, examine, give a differential diagnosis, and explain your management plan.

EXAMINER CONTEXT

Patient is dismissive — "It's probably nothing, I've had mouth ulcers before." He hasn't seen a dentist in 7 years. Only came in because his partner "nagged" him. Will not volunteer smoking or alcohol history unless asked directly. Will become more engaged and visibly worried once the candidate explains the serious differential.

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

Opening & Rapport (1 min)

"I'm glad you came in today — and tell your partner thank you for the nudge. Let's take a thorough look at this. Can I ask a few questions first?"

History (2 min) — INFLECTION 1: Risk factors

  • HOPC: "How long has it been there? Has it changed in size? Is it painful or painless?" (Painless = more concerning than painful — SCC is often painless; aphthous is typically very painful)
  • Smoking: "Do you smoke? How many a day, for how long?"
  • Alcohol: "How much do you typically drink in a week?"
  • Previous ulcers: "Have you had ulcers like this before? Do they usually come and go?" (Recurrent, healing in 2 weeks = aphthous pattern; this doesn't fit)
  • Dentures/trauma: any sharp tooth or denture rubbing?
  • General health: weight loss, fatigue, dysphagia, lumps in neck?

Examination (1.5 min)

  • Site: lateral border of tongue (HIGH-RISK site for SCC)
  • Size: 12mm × 8mm
  • Margins: irregular, slightly raised/rolled margin
  • Base: indurated (firm) when palpated
  • Surrounding tissue: erythematous halo, no vesicles
  • Cervical lymphadenopathy: palpate submandibular and cervical chain — any palpable node?

Diagnosis — INFLECTION 2: Name the serious differential clearly and honestly

"I need to be honest with you about what I'm seeing. This ulcer has several features that concern me:

  • It's been there for 3 weeks without healing
  • It's on the side of the tongue — which is one of the highest-risk sites for oral cancer
  • It has irregular, raised edges
  • It feels firm underneath
  • You've been smoking for 30 years and drink regularly, which are the two biggest risk factors for mouth cancer

I am not saying this IS cancer — but I am saying I cannot rule it out without a biopsy, and this absolutely needs one. A traumatic or aphthous ulcer doesn't look like this."

Management — INFLECTION 3: Biopsy urgency

"Here is what needs to happen:

  1. I'll refer you TODAY for an urgent biopsy — I'll write a referral to an oral medicine specialist or oral and maxillofacial surgeon marked URGENT
  2. In Australia, a 2-week wait pathway exists for suspected oral malignancy — this should happen quickly
  3. Do NOT wait and see. Waiting more time on a lesion like this could mean the difference between an early-stage cancer that's highly curable, and a late-stage one that's not."

Lifestyle (1 min)

"And regardless of what the biopsy shows — smoking and alcohol are the biggest drivers of this. If you've ever had a reason to quit, this is it. I can support you in that or refer you to your GP."

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Asks specifically about smoking, alcohol, duration, and change in ulcer character
  2. ✅ Examines correctly: site, size, margins (rolled/irregular = red flag), induration, lymphadenopathy
  3. ✅ Identifies high-risk features: painless, 3+ weeks, lateral tongue, induration, rolled margins
  4. ✅ Names the serious differential (SCC) clearly and honestly without causing unnecessary panic
  5. ✅ Recommends urgent biopsy referral (not watchful waiting)
  6. ✅ Counsels on smoking and alcohol cessation
  7. ✅ Does NOT reassure prematurely ("It's probably nothing")

TG4 ALERTS

2-week rule — non-negotiable — Any ulcer not healing at 2–3 weeks must be biopsied. Do not reassure without histological confirmation.
Painless ulcer on lateral tongue — Squamous cell carcinoma is often painless in early stages. Painlessness is NOT reassuring — it is a red flag.
Smoking + alcohol = multiplicative risk — Together, they increase SCC risk up to 30× more than either alone.

INFLECTION POINTS

PointWeakStrong
Smoking/alcohol historyNot askedSpecifically probes smoking pack-years and alcohol units; links to cancer risk
Naming the differential"Let's just watch it for a bit longer""This has features I can't ignore — I need to refer you for a biopsy urgently"
IndurationNot examinedPalpates the base; identifies firmness as a significant red flag
Urgency"We'll refer you in a few weeks""URGENT referral today — 2-week pathway for suspected malignancy"

COMMON PITFALLS

  • ❌ Telling patient "it's probably just a canker sore, come back in 2 weeks"
  • ❌ Not examining cervical lymph nodes
  • ❌ Not naming SCC as a differential (candidates often hedge; examiners want them to name it)
  • ❌ Referring routinely (not urgently) for a lesion with multiple red flags
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • "Systematic ulcer assessment: site, size, shape, border (flat vs rolled), base (flat vs indurated), duration, number, associated lymphadenopathy, patient history (tobacco, alcohol, previous oral cancer, immunosuppression)."
  • "SCC red flags: >2 weeks duration, indurated base, rolled or everted border, painless, floor of mouth/ventral tongue/lateral tongue/retromolar trigone location, lymphadenopathy, tobacco or high alcohol use."
  • "Urgent 2-week pathway referral to oral medicine or OMFS: any ulcer with red flags. Do not biopsy and manage yourself — referral ensures specialist assessment, appropriate biopsy, and histopathology review."
  • "Classic aphthous: small, round, yellow-grey base, red halo, very painful, heals in 10–14 days without scarring. Manage with triamcinolone paste, chlorhexidine mouthwash; investigate systemic cause if recurrent (FBC, iron, B12, folate, coeliac screen)."
Patient Reframes
  • "Most mouth ulcers are completely benign — the vast majority of what I see every week is aphthous ulceration. I'm referring you because the duration and appearance of this one are different from a typical aphthous ulcer, and I want a specialist to confirm that."
  • "Getting a specialist to look at this is the fastest way to get certainty — and if it's nothing, which I hope it is, you'll know that definitively rather than wondering."
Curveball Deflectors
  • "I've had ulcers all my life — this is normal for me." → "Recurrent aphthous ulcers are very common — and this may well be another one. But the duration and some features today are outside what I'd expect from your typical pattern. Two weeks to see a specialist is worth it for certainty."
  • "Do I need a biopsy today?" → "Not from me — the biopsy is better done by the specialist who will also review the histopathology and manage any follow-up. I'm referring you through the urgent pathway, which means a 2-week appointment."
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ▶
STAGE: Opening & Rapport

Candidate greets the patient warmly, makes eye contact, and ensures patient is comfortable.

"Good morning, Mr. Davies. I'm Dr. Chen — I'm the dentist you'll be seeing today. Thank you so much for coming in. I understand your partner encouraged you to make this appointment. I'm really glad you did. Before I take a look, would it be alright if I asked you a few questions first? It'll help me understand what's been going on." Pauses, ensures patient is settled. "Take your time — there are no wrong answers here."

---

History

"So, tell me in your own words — what have you noticed in your mouth?"

Listens attentively to patient's description, then follows with targeted questions.

"How long has this ulcer been there? And has it changed at all in that time — has it grown, or does it look different from when you first noticed it?"

"Now, this is an important question — does it hurt? Is there any pain or discomfort from it at all?" Notes that the patient reports it is painless. "I see. And have you had ulcers like this before — ulcers that tend to come and go, maybe healing within a week or two?" Notes patient denies recurrent ulcers.

"I need to ask you about a couple of habits, and I want you to know there's no judgment here — this is purely to help me understand your health. Do you smoke? How many cigarettes a day, and for roughly how long?" Notes patient reports 20 cigarettes per day for 30 years — a 30 pack-year history.

"And alcohol — how much would you typically drink across the week?" Notes patient reports three to four standard drinks most evenings.

"Have you noticed any difficulty swallowing? Any unexplained weight loss recently, or feeling more tired than usual?" Notes patient denies these. "Any lumps or swelling that you've noticed in your neck or under your jaw?" Notes patient is unsure.

"Do you wear a denture, or do you have any sharp or broken teeth that might be rubbing against your tongue?"

---

Examination

"Thank you for telling me all of that. I'd now like to have a thorough look inside your mouth, and I'll also gently feel along your neck. Please let me know if anything is uncomfortable."

Conducts full extraoral and intraoral examination systematically.

Palpates submandibular and cervical lymph nodes bilaterally. Notes a firm, non-tender, approximately one-centimetre node palpable in the right submandibular region.

Inspects intraoral tissues. Identifies ulcer on the right lateral border of the tongue — approximately twelve millimetres by eight millimetres in dimension. Margins are irregular and raised with a rolled border. The base of the ulcer appears granular. No surrounding vesicles are present. An erythematous halo borders the lesion.

Performs bimanual palpation of the ulcer base. Notes induration — the tissue feels firm and indurated beneath the surface.

Records findings. Steps back calmly and reassuringly before speaking.

---

Diagnosis & Honest Explanation

"Mr. Davies, I want to be straightforward with you, because I think you deserve honesty. What I'm seeing today concerns me, and I want to explain why."

"This ulcer has been present for three weeks without any sign of healing. It sits on the side of your tongue, which is one of the highest-risk sites in the mouth for a particular type of cancer called squamous cell carcinoma — oral cancer. The edges of the ulcer are raised and irregular — what we call rolled margins — and when I palpated underneath it, the tissue feels firm and indurated rather than soft. I also felt a small firm lymph node under your jaw on the right side."

"I also need to mention — and I know this might seem counterintuitive — that this ulcer is painless, and that is actually more concerning, not less. Painlessness in an ulcer like this is a red flag, not a reassurance."

"Now, I am not telling you this is definitely cancer. I cannot make that diagnosis — only a biopsy and laboratory analysis can do that. What I am telling you is that I cannot rule it out, and I would not be doing my job if I didn't act on this today."

"Your smoking history and the amount of alcohol you drink are the two biggest risk factors for oral cancer, and together they increase the risk significantly — far more than either would alone."

---

Management Plan

"So here is exactly what is going to happen. I am going to write an urgent referral today — right now, before you leave — to an oral medicine specialist and oral and maxillofacial surgeon. This referral will be marked urgent, and in Australia there is a two-week pathway for suspected oral malignancy. That means you should be seen and have a biopsy arranged within two weeks."

"An incisional biopsy — where a small piece of tissue is taken from the ulcer — is the only way to know for certain what this is. Once we have that result, we will know what the next step is. If it is something benign, that is excellent news. If it is something that requires treatment, then finding it now, at this stage, gives you the very best chance of a good outcome."

"Please do not wait on this. Please do not put this appointment off. The difference between an early-stage oral cancer and a late-stage one can be the difference between very effective treatment and something far more difficult to manage."

"I'll also write a letter to your general practitioner today so they are in the loop."

---

Lifestyle Counselling & Safety Net / Closing

"I also want to talk about smoking and alcohol — not to lecture you, but because this is genuinely important. Regardless of what the biopsy result shows, both smoking and alcohol are direct drivers of lesions like this. Quitting smoking — even now, even after thirty years — reduces your risk significantly and improves healing. I can provide you with brief cessation advice, or refer you to your GP or Quitline on 137 848, who can support you with nicotine replacement or other options."

"In terms of what to watch for before your specialist appointment — if this ulcer grows, if it starts bleeding, if you develop new swelling in your neck, or if you have any difficulty swallowing, please contact us or go to your nearest emergency department immediately. Don't wait for the appointment in that situation."

"You've done exactly the right thing by coming in today — and I mean that sincerely. Your partner was right to push you, and you were right to listen. Do you have any questions for me at all before we get that referral written?"

Allows patient time to respond. Provides written information, confirms referral is being sent urgently, and arranges a follow-up contact within one week to confirm the specialist appointment has been received.

OM2
Oral Lichen Planus (White Striations + Burning Gums)
Category:** Oral Medicine | **Time:** 11 min | **Difficulty:** Exam-ready

CASE SUMMARY

52-year-old female presents with burning gums and white lacy streaks (Wickham's striae) on bilateral buccal mucosa. Present for 4 months. Stressful period at work. No ulceration currently. Anxious patient, wants to know if it's cancer.

CANDIDATE BRIEF

A 52-year-old female presents complaining of burning gums and white lines inside both cheeks for 4 months. No trauma, no new medications. She is worried because her sister had oral cancer and wants to know if these white patches are dangerous.

EXAMINER CONTEXT

Patient is anxious. Will directly ask "Is this cancer?" — candidate must answer honestly but reassuringly. She's been under significant work stress and sleep-deprived. Will not volunteer stress unless asked. Medical history: no medications currently, no systemic disease.

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

History (2 min) — INFLECTION 1: Bilateral = unlikely malignant

  • Site: bilateral buccal mucosa (bilateral = strongly suggests systemic/immune cause, not malignancy)
  • Duration: 4 months, stable
  • Symptoms: burning sensation, not ulcerated currently
  • Aggravating: stress, spicy food, acidic food
  • Medications: current and recent (some medications cause lichenoid reactions — NSAIDs, beta-blockers, antimalarials)
  • Stress history: "How have you been generally? Any major stressors?"
  • Family history: sister's oral cancer (patient's primary fear — must be addressed)

Examination (1.5 min)

  • Bilateral buccal mucosa: fine white lacy network (Wickham's striae) — bilateral and symmetrical
  • No ulceration, no erythroplakia, no induration
  • Gingivae: desquamative gingivitis possible in erosive OLP
  • Skin and nails: any skin lesions (OLP can be part of systemic lichen planus)

Diagnosis — INFLECTION 2: Name it, explain it, address the cancer fear

"What I'm seeing is a pattern called oral lichen planus. Let me explain what that is, and then let me address your concern about cancer directly.

Oral lichen planus is an immune condition — your immune system is reacting against the cells lining your mouth. We're not entirely sure why it happens, but stress, certain medications, and genetic factors can all play a role. The classic appearance is exactly what you have: fine, lacy white lines on both cheeks. It often causes a burning sensation and can flare with stress, spicy food, or acidic foods.

Is it cancer? No — this pattern, particularly being bilateral and lacy, is not cancer. However — and I want to be completely honest with you — oral lichen planus does carry a very small increased risk of developing into cancer over many years, about 1–2% lifetime risk. That's why we monitor it regularly and biopsy any areas that change. Right now, I'm not concerned, but we will keep a close eye on it."

Management (2 min) — INFLECTION 3: Multi-pronged

"Management has several parts:

  1. Confirm the diagnosis: I'll arrange a biopsy of the white area — even though I'm fairly confident this is OLP, a biopsy gives us certainty and a baseline
  2. Manage symptoms:
  • Corticosteroid mouthwash (betamethasone or triamcinolone in Orabase) — reduces inflammation and burning during flares
  • Avoid known triggers: spicy food, acidic foods, alcohol-based mouthwash
  1. Address stress: OLP commonly flares with stress — if stress is a significant factor, speaking with your GP about stress management or counselling may help
  2. Review every 6 months — photos taken today for comparison; biopsy of any new ulcerated or erythematous areas immediately
  3. Smoking: if you smoke, cessation reduces cancer risk significantly"

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Identifies bilateral white striations as a hallmark of OLP (not malignancy)
  2. ✅ Asks about medications (lichenoid reactions)
  3. ✅ Addresses cancer fear directly and honestly (small real risk, not nil)
  4. ✅ Explains immune mechanism in plain language
  5. ✅ Plans biopsy for diagnostic confirmation
  6. ✅ Prescribes topical steroid for symptom management
  7. ✅ 6-monthly monitoring plan; biopsy any new changes

TG4 ALERTS

OLP malignant transformation risk — ~1–2% lifetime risk. Monitoring is not optional. Biopsy any erosive, erythematous, or new ulcerated areas immediately.
Topical corticosteroids for OLP — TG4: first-line for symptomatic OLP. Betamethasone mouthwash or triamcinolone paste. Systemic steroids for severe erosive OLP only.

INFLECTION POINTS

PointWeakStrong
Bilateral = reassuringDoesn't comment on bilateral nature"The fact that this is on BOTH sides simultaneously makes malignancy very unlikely — cancer is almost always one-sided"
Cancer questionVague reassurance ("it's fine")Honest: "This is not cancer, but it does carry a very small long-term risk — that's why we monitor it"
BiopsyNot mentionedPlanned for diagnostic certainty and baseline
Stress linkNot exploredAsks about stress; explains OLP-stress link; suggests GP for stress management
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • "OLP clinical features: bilateral symmetry (key diagnostic feature), reticular/striae pattern (Wickham's striae) predominantly on buccal mucosa; erosive/atrophic form causes burning and soreness; bullous type least common."
  • "Malignant transformation: approximately 1% lifetime risk, higher with erosive type. This makes periodic specialist review mandatory — not optional. Refer to oral medicine for diagnosis confirmation and ongoing monitoring."
  • "Lichenoid reaction: clinically identical but unilateral, or associated with a drug/dental material. Screen medication list (NSAIDs, antimalarials, ACE inhibitors, beta-blockers) and note any adjacent restoration."
  • "Management: topical corticosteroids for erosive areas (triamcinolone paste, betamethasone mouthwash); avoid SLS-containing toothpaste; manage stress; a flare does not mean transformation — educate the patient."
Patient Reframes
  • "OLP is a chronic condition, but manageable. For most people with the reticular type, it causes minimal trouble and stays stable. The erosive form needs more treatment, but we have effective options."
  • "The 1% transformation risk sounds frightening in isolation — but it means 99% of patients with OLP never develop cancer. We monitor because early detection makes all the difference, not because transformation is likely."
Curveball Deflectors
  • "Is it because of stress?" → "Stress can trigger flares — but it doesn't cause OLP. This is an immune-mediated condition. Managing stress is sensible general advice, but I want to be accurate: the underlying cause is immunological."
  • "I looked it up and it said it turns into cancer." → "The small transformation risk is real, which is why I'm referring you to a specialist for monitoring. But 'can transform' and 'commonly transforms' are very different. The 1% figure means regular review catches anything early — which is exactly what we're doing."
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ▶
STAGE: Opening & Initial Rapport

"Good morning, I'm Dr. Chen. Please come in and take a seat. Before we get started, I just want to let you know we have about eleven minutes together today, and I really want to make sure I address everything that's on your mind. Can you start by telling me in your own words what's been bothering you?"

Listens attentively without interrupting. Patient describes burning gums and white lines inside both cheeks for around four months.

"Thank you for telling me that. I can hear that this has been worrying you, and I want you to know we're going to work through this carefully together."

---

History Taking

"Let me ask you a few more questions so I can build a complete picture. Firstly, are the white lines on one side or both sides of your mouth?" Confirms bilateral buccal mucosa. "And have they changed at all — grown, ulcerated, or bled — since you first noticed them?" Confirms stable, no ulceration.

"On a scale of one to ten, how bad is the burning sensation? Does anything make it worse — spicy food, acidic drinks, or citrus?" Confirms aggravated by spicy and acidic foods. "And have you noticed it flares when you're under pressure at work?" Patient confirms significant work stress over the past four to five months.

"Are you taking any regular medications — including anything over the counter, like anti-inflammatories, blood pressure tablets, or antimalarials? I ask because some of those can cause a very similar reaction inside the mouth." Documents no current medications. "Any new dental materials, mouthwashes, or toothpastes introduced around the time this started?"

"You mentioned your sister had oral cancer — and I imagine that's been sitting heavily on you. We will absolutely come back to that. Before we do, is there any history of skin rashes, particularly on your wrists or lower legs, or changes to your nails?" Screening for systemic lichen planus.

---

Examination & Findings

Dons gloves. Examines extra-orally — no lymphadenopathy, no skin lesions visible on wrists.

Intra-oral examination: bilateral buccal mucosa shows a fine, lacy white network — classic Wickham's striae — symmetrically distributed. No ulceration, no erythroplakia, no induration on palpation. Gingivae show mild diffuse erythema consistent with early desquamative gingivitis. No lesions on tongue, floor of mouth, or palate.

"Thank you for your patience with the examination. I've seen everything I need to and I'd like to explain what I've found."

---

Diagnosis & Addressing the Cancer Fear

"What I'm seeing is a condition called oral lichen planus. Let me explain what that is — and then let me address your concern about cancer directly, because I know that's what's most on your mind.

Oral lichen planus is an immune condition. Your own immune system is reacting against the cells lining your cheeks, and we're not entirely sure why it happens — but stress, genetics, and occasionally certain medications can all play a role. The classic appearance is exactly what you have: fine, lacy white lines on both cheeks, which we call Wickham's striae. The key word there is both cheeks. Because it's bilateral and symmetrical, that pattern is very strongly associated with an immune condition rather than anything dangerous.

Now — is it cancer? No, it is not cancer. But I want to be completely honest with you, because I think you deserve that. Oral lichen planus does carry a very small increased lifetime risk of developing into cancer — around one to two percent over many years. That's real, and it's why we don't just leave this alone. We monitor it regularly, we document it with photographs, and we biopsy any area that changes — becomes red, ulcerated, or feels firm. Right now, looking at your mouth today, I am not concerned. But we will keep a very close eye on it, and that is a promise."

---

Management Plan

"So here is exactly what we're going to do, in a few steps.

First, I would like to take a small biopsy of the affected area. Even though I am confident in this diagnosis, a biopsy gives us absolute certainty and a written baseline — it's the right thing to do. The procedure is straightforward under local anaesthetic.

Second, to manage your burning, I'll prescribe a topical corticosteroid. The first-line treatment is a betamethasone mouthwash — you rinse and spit with it, you don't swallow it — which reduces the inflammation and gives relief during flares. Triamcinolone paste applied directly to the gum is another option if the gum burning is particularly troublesome.

Third, we'll address your triggers. Avoiding spicy and acidic foods, and switching to an alcohol-free mouthwash, can make a meaningful difference day to day.

Fourth — and this matters — the stress connection is real. I'd encourage you to speak with your GP about stress management strategies or counselling, because flares often track closely with periods of high stress.

Finally, I'll see you every six months for monitoring. I'll take photographs today so we have a reference point. If at any point between visits you notice a new sore, an area that bleeds, or any change in how the white lines look, I want you to come in straight away — don't wait for your scheduled appointment."

---

Safety Net & Closing

"Do you have any questions about anything I've explained — the biopsy, the medication, or the monitoring plan?"

Allows patient to respond. Addresses any residual anxiety calmly.

"I know your sister's experience has made this very frightening, and it makes complete sense that you came in. You did exactly the right thing by not ignoring it. We've caught this early, we know what it is, and we have a clear plan. You are not alone with this — we'll manage it together. I'll organise the biopsy referral and get the prescription ready for you before you leave today. Take care, and please don't hesitate to call the practice if anything changes before we next see you."

OM3
Leukoplakia / Erythroplakia — Biopsy Decision
Category:** Oral Medicine | **Time:** 11 min | **Difficulty:** Exam-ready

CASE SUMMARY

White patch on the floor of mouth of a 60-year-old male smoker, present for 6 weeks. No symptoms. Irregular margins. Candidate must distinguish from other white lesions, know when to biopsy, and urgently refer.

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

History (1.5 min)

  • Duration: 6 weeks (beyond the 2-week rule — must biopsy)
  • Symptoms: asymptomatic (concerning — malignancy is often painless)
  • Risk factors: smoking (20/day), alcohol (daily)
  • Denture trauma, sharp tooth, cheek biting — any local cause?

Examination (1.5 min)

  • Site: floor of mouth (HIGH-RISK: floor of mouth + ventral tongue = highest SCC risk in oral cavity)
