  • Appearance: white patch, cannot be wiped off (rules out candidiasis)
  • Margins: irregular
  • Surface: homogeneous white vs. mixed white/red (erythroleukoplakia = highest risk)
  • Induration on palpation?
  • Lymphadenopathy?

Differential diagnosis (1.5 min) — INFLECTION 1

"There are several possible explanations for a white patch like this:

  • Frictional keratosis / traumatic white patch — caused by rubbing or trauma; usually resolves when the cause is removed
  • Candidiasis — can be wiped off; looks more diffuse/creamy; responds to antifungal
  • Leukoplakia — white patch with no other identifiable cause; can't be wiped off; on the spectrum from benign to pre-malignant
  • Erythroplakia — red patch or mixed red-white (your higher-risk version) — highest rate of dysplasia
  • Squamous cell carcinoma — established malignancy

Given this is on the floor of the mouth in a heavy smoker, has irregular margins, and has been present 6 weeks — leukoplakia with possible dysplasia or early malignancy is what I need to rule out."

Management — INFLECTION 2: No "watchful waiting" here

"I want to be upfront — a white patch on the floor of the mouth in a smoker of your age is not something I can monitor and review in a few months. This needs an urgent biopsy.

Here is the plan:

  1. Urgent referral to oral medicine or OMFS for incisional biopsy
  2. While we wait — do NOT remove the patch ourselves or try to rub it off
  3. The biopsy will tell us if there is dysplasia (pre-cancerous change) or established cancer
  4. If dysplasia: management depends on grade — mild = monitor; severe = excision
  5. If cancer: prompt specialist management (surgery ± radiotherapy)"

Smoking cessation (1 min)

"Regardless of the biopsy result, stopping smoking is the most powerful thing you can do to reduce progression and improve outcomes."

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Cannot wipe off = not candidiasis
  2. ✅ Floor of mouth = highest-risk site
  3. ✅ Erythroleukoplakia > leukoplakia in malignant potential
  4. ✅ Urgent biopsy referral (not watchful waiting)
  5. ✅ Smoking cessation as key intervention

TG4 ALERTS

Erythroplakia — Red patches carry higher rate of dysplasia and malignancy than white patches. Any red oral lesion that can't be explained = urgent biopsy.
Floor of mouth — Highest-risk anatomical site in oral cavity for SCC due to pooling of carcinogens in saliva.
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • "Leukoplakia: white patch not attributable to any known cause, cannot be rubbed off. ~15–20% have dysplastic changes on biopsy. Erythroplakia: red patch — 40–60% have dysplasia or carcinoma. Any erythroplakia warrants urgent biopsy."
  • "Biopsy indications for leukoplakia: any red area within the patch, nodularity, floor of mouth or ventral/lateral tongue, tobacco user, >2 weeks not resolving after removing possible causative factors."
  • "Do not reassure and review in 3 months for a suspicious lesion. Refer to oral medicine or OMFS for biopsy. The biopsy site selection and histopathology management should be in specialist hands."
  • "Non-dysplastic leukoplakia: can be monitored with 3-monthly review and clinical photography — but requires patient education about red flags and return visit triggers."
Patient Reframes
  • "I'm not telling you this is cancer — I'm telling you it needs to be checked by a specialist because a small proportion of white patches do have early changes we need to know about. The biopsy tells us definitively."
  • "Biopsy sounds daunting but it's a minor procedure — local anaesthetic, a small sample of tissue, a stitch. The information it gives us is far more valuable than continuing to watch and wonder."
Curveball Deflectors
  • "I had this checked before and they said it was fine." → "When was that, and was it biopsied or visually observed? Lesions can evolve over time, and 'fine on inspection' isn't the same as 'fine on histopathology.' Today's appearance warrants a fresh assessment."
  • "Can't you just remove it?" → "Excision is a treatment option — but it's done after biopsy to confirm the diagnosis, not instead of it. The specialist will determine the extent and whether full excision is appropriate based on the histology."
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ▶
STAGE: Opening and Initial History

"Good morning, Mr. Thompson. I'm Dr. Chen, one of the dentists here today. Please take a seat and make yourself comfortable. Before I examine you, I'd like to ask you a few questions about what's been going on. Is that alright with you?"

"You've come in today about something you've noticed in your mouth — can you tell me in your own words what you've seen or felt?"

After the patient describes the white patch: "And how long have you been aware of this? Six weeks — thank you. Has it changed in size or appearance at all since you first noticed it? Has it caused you any pain, soreness, burning, or difficulty swallowing?"

Notes that the lesion is asymptomatic and has been present for six weeks — well beyond the two-week threshold for watchful waiting.

"Have you noticed any lumps in your neck, or any unexplained weight loss or fatigue recently?"

"Now I'd like to ask about some habits that can affect the mouth. Do you smoke? How many cigarettes a day, and for how many years? And do you drink alcohol — how often, and roughly how much?" Notes heavy smoking at 20 cigarettes per day and daily alcohol use — two major independent risk factors for oral malignancy.

"Do you wear a denture? Any sharp teeth that might be rubbing in that area? Have you ever noticed yourself biting your cheek or lip?"

Clinical Examination

"Thank you for that. I'd now like to have a careful look inside your mouth. I'll be gentle."

Examines the floor of the mouth systematically under adequate light. Notes a white patch on the floor of the mouth that cannot be wiped off with gauze — this immediately rules out pseudomembranous candidiasis. Assesses the margins, which are irregular. Notes whether the surface is uniformly white or contains any red components — any mixed red-and-white appearance would indicate erythroleukoplakia, which carries the highest risk of dysplasia. Palpates gently for induration or fixation.

Palpates the submental and submandibular lymph nodes bilaterally. Notes their size, consistency, tenderness, and mobility.

"That all looks as comfortable as it can be. Thank you for bearing with me."

Differential Diagnosis — First Inflection Point

"Mr. Thompson, I want to go through with you what a white patch like this could mean, and then I'm going to be very honest with you about what I think needs to happen next."

"There are a few possible explanations for a white patch in the mouth. The first is something called frictional keratosis — a thickening of the lining caused by rubbing, from a denture edge or a sharp tooth. Those patches usually settle once the cause is removed. The second is oral thrush — a fungal infection that looks white and creamy and, crucially, can be wiped off with a piece of gauze. This patch cannot be wiped off, so thrush is not the explanation here."

"The third possibility, and the one I'm most concerned about, is leukoplakia — a white patch with no other identifiable cause, which sits on a spectrum from completely benign through to pre-cancerous change, which we call dysplasia. Beyond that, at the most serious end, we have to consider early squamous cell carcinoma. There is also a related condition called erythroplakia — a red patch, or a mixed red-and-white patch — which actually carries a higher rate of dysplasia and established cancer than a purely white patch."

"Given that this patch is on the floor of the mouth — which is the highest-risk site in the entire oral cavity because carcinogens from tobacco pool in saliva there — combined with irregular margins, six weeks' duration, and your smoking history, I cannot reassure you that this is harmless without a tissue biopsy."

Management Plan — Second Inflection Point

"Mr. Thompson, I want to be upfront with you. This is not a situation where I can ask you to come back in a couple of months and see how things look. That would not be the right approach here, and it would not be safe."

"What I am going to do today is refer you urgently to a specialist — either an oral medicine specialist or an oral and maxillofacial surgeon — for an incisional biopsy. That means they take a small sample of tissue from the lesion under local anaesthetic and send it to a pathologist, who examines it under a microscope and tells us exactly what we are dealing with."

"I want to be very clear — please do not rub or scratch at the patch yourself in the meantime, and I will not be attempting to remove it here today. The biopsy needs to be taken from the most representative area, and that is the specialist's job."

"The result will guide everything that follows. If it shows mild dysplasia — early pre-cancerous change — the approach is careful monitoring with regular review. If it shows severe dysplasia, excision is recommended. If it shows established malignancy, you will be referred promptly for specialist oncological management, which may involve surgery, radiotherapy, or both."

"I know this is a lot to take in. Do you have any questions at this stage, or is there someone who might come with you to the specialist appointment?"

Smoking Cessation and Safety Net

"Before we finish, I want to talk about something that is within your control right now, regardless of what the biopsy shows. Stopping smoking is the single most powerful thing you can do to reduce the risk of this lesion progressing and to improve your outcome whatever the result."

"I know that's easier said than done, and I'm not here to lecture you. What I would like to do is refer you to the Quitline — the number is 13 7848 — and your GP can also help with nicotine replacement or medication to support cessation. Brief advice combined with support genuinely improves quit rates, and now is a meaningful time to act on it."

"In terms of what to watch for — if you notice any change in the patch, any ulceration, any bleeding, any swelling in your neck, or any difficulty swallowing before your specialist appointment, please contact us or go to your nearest emergency department immediately. Do not wait."

"I'm going to write the referral letter now, marked urgent, and I'll also give you a copy to keep. Do you have any final questions for me today? You've handled this very well, and we are going to move on this quickly."

OM4
Angular Cheilitis + Iron Deficiency Anaemia
Category:** Oral Medicine | **Time:** 11 min | **Difficulty:** Exam-ready

CASE SUMMARY

45-year-old female with cracking at the corners of her mouth for 3 months, fatigue, and pale conjunctiva. Recent dietary changes (vegan for 1 year). Candidate must identify angular cheilitis, explore nutritional deficiency, and refer appropriately.

CANDIDATE BRIEF

45-year-old female presents with bilateral cracking and soreness at the corners of her mouth for 3 months. She also mentions feeling tired a lot. She's been vegan for 1 year. Your task: assess, diagnose, and manage.

EXAMINER CONTEXT

She hasn't connected her fatigue and mouth changes to her dietary change. Will reveal she's been vegan only if specifically asked about diet. No iron or B12 supplementation since going vegan.

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

History (2 min) — INFLECTION 1: Diet is the key

  • Angular cheilitis history: bilateral, duration, previous episodes
  • Dentures? (denture wearers common), denture fit?
  • Fatigue: duration, exercise tolerance, breathlessness
  • Diet: "Have you made any changes to your diet recently?" (She'll reveal vegan for 1 year)
  • Supplements: "Are you taking any iron or B12 supplements?"
  • Menstrual history: heavy periods? (iron loss)
  • Medication: any immunosuppression?

Examination (1.5 min)

  • Angular cheilitis: bilateral, fissured, crusted corners — erythema
  • Oral mucosa: check for candidiasis (white patches), atrophic glossitis (smooth, red, sore tongue — iron/B12 deficiency)
  • Eyes: pale conjunctiva (anaemia)
  • Nails: koilonychia (spoon-shaped nails — iron deficiency)

Diagnosis — INFLECTION 2: Connect the dots

"The cracking at the corners of your mouth — called angular cheilitis — has several possible causes. In your case, I'm thinking about nutritional deficiency specifically:

You've been vegan for a year without supplementation. Plant-based diets are low in iron and B12 — both of which are essential for healthy skin and mouth tissue. Iron deficiency in particular causes angular cheilitis, a smooth sore tongue, and fatigue — which you're also describing. Combined with the pale inner eyelids I noticed, I'm concerned about iron deficiency anaemia.

B12 deficiency can develop silently over 2–3 years on a vegan diet because the body has stores, but once depleted, it causes nerve damage and anaemia."

Management (2 min)

  1. Local treatment: miconazole cream to the corners (fungal component common in angular cheilitis)
  2. Blood tests: FBC, iron studies, serum ferritin, B12, folate — refer to GP for these
  3. Dietary counselling: iron-rich plant foods (legumes, fortified cereals, dark leafy greens) + vitamin C to improve absorption; B12 supplementation is essential on a vegan diet
  4. GP referral: if iron deficiency confirmed, supplement with iron (ferrous sulfate 325mg daily); if B12 deficient, B12 injections or high-dose oral supplementation
  5. Review in 6 weeks once supplementation started

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Identifies vegan diet as key risk factor for iron/B12 deficiency
  2. ✅ Links angular cheilitis + fatigue + pale conjunctiva to systemic deficiency
  3. ✅ Examines for atrophic glossitis, pale conjunctiva, koilonychia
  4. ✅ Local treatment (antifungal) + systemic investigation (bloods)
  5. ✅ Refers to GP for blood tests and supplementation
  6. ✅ Dietary counselling appropriate to vegan lifestyle (not "eat meat")

TG4 ALERTS

Angular cheilitis: treat locally AND investigate systemically — Miconazole cream treats the fungal/bacterial component, but if nutritional deficiency is the root cause, topical treatment alone will not prevent recurrence.
B12 deficiency on vegan diet — Cannot be obtained from plant foods alone. Supplementation is mandatory, not optional. Deficiency causes irreversible nerve damage if untreated.
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • "Angular cheilitis causes: Candida albicans (most common), Staphylococcus aureus, or polymicrobial. Contributing factors: loss of vertical dimension (commissure folds collect moisture), iron or B12 deficiency, immunosuppression, denture stomatitis."
  • "Systemic screen: FBC (anaemia), iron studies, B12, folate, fasting glucose. Angular cheilitis + pallor + smooth glossitis = iron deficiency anaemia triad — refer for haematology workup and investigate cause (GI blood loss, malabsorption)."
  • "Treatment: miconazole cream topically (antifungal AND antibacterial) to commissures; address VDO if denture-related; iron/B12 supplementation once confirmed on bloods."
  • "Coeliac disease association: iron deficiency that doesn't respond to supplementation warrants anti-tTG antibody testing — dental presentation can be the first flag for undiagnosed coeliac."
Patient Reframes
  • "The sores at the corners of your mouth often reflect what's happening internally — particularly nutritional levels. I want to treat the local infection with a cream, but I also want to check some blood tests to make sure we're not missing an underlying cause."
  • "If it's a nutritional deficiency, the cream alone won't prevent it coming back — so the blood test is the part that actually fixes it long term."
Curveball Deflectors
  • "I just need a cream." → "I'll prescribe one — miconazole, which covers the most likely cause. But if there's an underlying nutritional deficiency or denture issue driving it, the cream treats the symptom and it returns. Bloods take one visit to exclude that."
  • "I've had this for years." → "Chronicity actually increases the importance of checking the systemic causes — a persistent angular cheilitis that keeps returning despite treatment is more likely to have an underlying driver like anaemia or a denture VDO issue than an acute episode."
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ▶
STAGE: Opening and Initial History

"Good morning, I'm Dr. Chen. Please come in and take a seat. How are you today?" Pauses and allows patient to settle. "I understand you've come in with some soreness at the corners of your mouth — is that right? And you've been experiencing some tiredness as well? I'd like to ask you a few questions to understand what's been going on, and then take a look in your mouth and at a couple of other areas. Is that okay?"

"Can you tell me more about the cracking at the corners of your mouth? How long has this been bothering you?" Allows patient to describe three months of bilateral soreness. "Is it both corners, or just one side?" Confirms bilateral. "Has this ever happened to you before, or is this the first time?" Allows response. "Would you describe it as painful, or more of a burning or stinging sensation, particularly when you eat or open your mouth wide?"

"Do you wear dentures or a partial denture at all?" Confirms no dentures. "Have you noticed any white patches or redness anywhere else inside your mouth, or a sore, smooth tongue?" Allows response.

"Now, you mentioned feeling tired — how long has the fatigue been going on? Are you getting breathless doing things you'd normally manage easily, like climbing stairs?" Allows response. "Have your periods been particularly heavy recently?" Allows response regarding menstrual history.

"Have you made any recent changes to your diet?" Pauses attentively as patient reveals she has been vegan for one year. "That's really helpful to know. Are you taking any nutritional supplements — anything like iron, B12, or folate?" Confirms no supplementation. "Are you on any regular medications, including anything for your immune system?" Confirms no immunosuppressants.

---

Clinical Examination

"Thank you for telling me all of that. I'd like to examine the corners of your mouth, inside your mouth, and briefly check your eyes and hands. I'll be very gentle."

Examines the commissures bilaterally. Notes erythematous, fissured, crusted angular lesions with no obvious white plaques at the commissures themselves.

Examines the oral mucosa. Notes atrophic glossitis — the tongue is smooth, erythematous, and depapillated, consistent with iron or B12 deficiency. No discrete white patches elsewhere.

"I'm just going to have a gentle look at your inner eyelids." Gently everts the lower eyelids bilaterally. Notes markedly pale conjunctiva consistent with anaemia.

"May I have a look at your fingernails?" Examines nails and notes koilonychia — spoon-shaped nails bilaterally — consistent with iron deficiency.

---

Diagnosis and Explanation

"Thank you. I have a clear picture now and I'd like to explain what I think is happening."

"The cracking and soreness at the corners of your mouth is a condition called angular cheilitis. It's very common, and it can be caused by a number of things — but in your case, I believe the underlying cause is a nutritional deficiency, specifically iron and possibly vitamin B12."

"Here's why I'm connecting these things. You've been following a vegan diet for a year without taking any supplements. Plant-based diets are naturally very low in iron and contain virtually no vitamin B12 — B12 simply cannot be obtained from plant foods. Iron deficiency causes the skin and mucous membranes to break down, which is why the corners of your mouth are cracking. It also explains your smooth, sore tongue, your fatigue, and the pallor I noticed in your inner eyelids. The shape of your nails — slightly spoon-shaped — is another classic sign of iron deficiency."

"B12 deficiency can develop silently over two to three years on a vegan diet because your body has stored reserves. Once those stores are depleted, it causes a specific type of anaemia and, importantly, can lead to irreversible nerve damage if it goes untreated. So we do need to address this now."

"The angular cheilitis also often has a fungal component — a yeast called Candida can colonise those cracked corners — so we will treat that locally as well."

---

Management Plan

"There are two parts to managing this — a local treatment for the corners of your mouth, and a systemic investigation with your GP."

"For the local treatment, I'd like you to apply miconazole cream — an antifungal cream — to the corners of your mouth two to four times daily after meals and at night. Apply a small amount with a clean fingertip. This will treat the fungal and bacterial component. However, I want to be clear: if we don't address the nutritional deficiency, the angular cheilitis will keep coming back, because the root cause hasn't been treated."

"I'm going to write you a referral letter to your GP today. I'd like them to arrange blood tests including a full blood count, iron studies, serum ferritin, serum B12, and folate. If iron deficiency anaemia is confirmed, your GP will likely prescribe ferrous sulfate 325 milligrams daily. If your B12 is low, you'll need either B12 injections or high-dose oral B12 supplementation — your GP will guide you on which is most appropriate."

"In the meantime, I'd like to discuss your diet. I completely respect your choice to follow a vegan lifestyle, and there are good plant-based sources of iron — legumes like lentils and chickpeas, fortified breakfast cereals, tofu, and dark leafy greens like spinach and kale. Eating these alongside foods rich in vitamin C — like citrus fruit or capsicum — significantly improves iron absorption. However, there is no reliable plant-based source of B12. Supplementation is not optional on a vegan diet — it is essential to prevent permanent nerve damage."

---

Safety Net and Closing

"I'd like to see you back here in six weeks to check how the angular cheilitis is responding and to review your blood test results once you've had them done."

"In the meantime, if the soreness at the corners of your mouth significantly worsens, if you develop any difficulty swallowing, if the white patches spread inside your mouth, or if your tiredness and breathlessness become much worse — please don't wait for your follow-up. Contact your GP promptly."

"Do you have any questions about anything I've explained today? I know that's quite a lot of information." Allows patient to respond and addresses any concerns. "I'll prepare your GP referral letter now, and I'll also write down the name of the miconazole cream so you can get it from the pharmacy today. Thank you for coming in."

OM5
Burning Mouth Syndrome / Xerostomia
Category:** Oral Medicine | **Time:** 11 min | **Difficulty:** Exam-ready

CASE SUMMARY

62-year-old female, 8-month history of constant burning sensation in the tongue and lips with no visible lesions. Dry mouth. Multiple medications including amitriptyline and amlodipine. Post-menopausal. Candidate must diagnose burning mouth syndrome, identify contributing medications, and manage.

CANDIDATE BRIEF

62-year-old female presents with an 8-month history of burning and tingling in her tongue and lips. Examination shows no visible abnormality. She is post-menopausal and takes amitriptyline 50mg (depression), amlodipine 5mg (hypertension), and a proton pump inhibitor. She also complains of a dry mouth. Your task: assess and manage.

EXAMINER CONTEXT

Patient is frustrated — she's been to three doctors and told "nothing is wrong." Wants someone to validate her symptoms. Will ask "Is this all in my head?" Must be handled sensitively.

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

History (2 min) — INFLECTION 1: Pattern recognition

  • Burning character: constant or intermittent? Better in morning or worse? (BMS classic: better in morning, worse as day goes on, absent at night — opposite of neuropathic pain)
  • Trigger-free: not triggered by specific foods? (if certain foods = contact allergy, not BMS)
  • Dry mouth: onset, saliva reduction, difficulty swallowing dry food, waking at night to drink?
  • Medications: "Can I go through all your medications?" (Amitriptyline = xerostomia; amlodipine = gingival overgrowth but not BMS directly; PPIs may affect B12 absorption long-term)
  • Menopausal status and HRT?
  • Anxiety, depression, major life stressors?
  • Sleep: quality, snoring?

Examination (1.5 min)

  • Oral mucosa: all normal (NO visible lesion = key to BMS diagnosis)
  • Salivary flow: reduced (check under tongue for saliva pool)
  • Exclude: candidiasis (wipe test), OLP, geographic tongue, denture issues

Diagnosis — INFLECTION 2: Acknowledge the frustration, explain the condition

"I want to be the first person to tell you — your symptoms are absolutely real. They are not in your head. Burning mouth syndrome is a recognised medical condition involving changes in the way the nerves in your mouth and tongue send signals to the brain. It often has no visible cause, which is why examination looks normal — but that doesn't mean nothing is wrong.

It's more common in post-menopausal women, and it can overlap with dry mouth, depression, and anxiety — all of which you're managing. Your amitriptyline is likely contributing to the dry mouth, which in turn makes the burning worse.

This is manageable — not always curable, but definitely manageable."

Management (2 min)

  1. Address xerostomia: sip water frequently, use saliva substitutes (Biotene), avoid caffeine and alcohol, consider sugar-free gum
  2. Review medications with GP: consider whether amitriptyline dose can be adjusted (it's a known cause of xerostomia)
  3. Topical treatments for BMS: alpha-lipoic acid (some evidence), clonazepam rinse (short-term, specialist initiation)
  4. Psychological support: CBT has evidence for BMS — refer to psychologist or GP
  5. Exclude nutritional deficiency: B12, iron, folate (PPI long-term + no supplementation = B12 deficiency risk)
  6. Review in 6–8 weeks

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Validates the patient's symptoms explicitly ("real, not in your head")
  2. ✅ Identifies classic BMS pattern (worse in evening, better in morning)
  3. ✅ Links amitriptyline to xerostomia (medication side effect)
  4. ✅ Diagnoses BMS as a diagnosis of exclusion after excluding visible pathology
  5. ✅ Multi-modal management (saliva, medication review, CBT, nutritional)
  6. ✅ Refers to GP for medication review; checks B12 given long-term PPI

TG4 ALERTS

Xerostomia from medications — TG4: over 400 medications cause dry mouth. Amitriptyline (TCA), antihistamines, antihypertensives, antipsychotics are common culprits. Always review medication list.
B12 deficiency + PPI — Long-term PPI use reduces B12 absorption. Screen with blood test; supplement if deficient.
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • "BMS diagnosis of exclusion: rule out candidiasis, lichen planus, iron/B12/folate deficiency, diabetes, Sjögren's syndrome, poorly fitting dentures, contact allergy. Once excluded = BMS, a central sensitisation pain condition."
  • "BMS demographics: predominantly postmenopausal women; often described as burning, scalding, or tingling; typically worse during the day (improves with eating or distraction); may have taste disturbance."
  • "Management: low-dose clonazepam 0.5mg sublingually (spit after 3 min) — best evidence; low-dose TCAs (amitriptyline); CBT; alpha-lipoic acid (some evidence). Set realistic expectations — BMS is manageable, not curable in most cases."
  • "Xerostomia: medication review is the first step. TIS National medication database for xerostomic side effect profiles. Saliva substitutes, frequent water sips, pilocarpine 5mg TDS if Sjögren's confirmed and severe."
Patient Reframes
  • "Burning mouth is a recognised medical condition — it's not anxiety, it's not in your head. It's a condition where the pain-signalling pathways become sensitised. The fact that there's nothing visible doesn't mean there's nothing wrong."
  • "The dry mouth is almost certainly from one or more of your medications — it's one of the most common drug side effects we see. There are things we can do to protect your teeth and improve comfort, and I'll also ask your GP whether any substitutes are possible."
Curveball Deflectors
  • "My GP says there's nothing wrong." → "They're likely right that there's no serious systemic disease — which is actually reassuring. BMS is a diagnosis of exclusion, and once we've ruled out the reversible causes, we have specific treatments that help significantly. Your GP and I can work together on this."
  • "Will it ever go away?" → "For some patients, yes — spontaneous resolution occurs in about 30% within 5 years. For others it's ongoing but manageable. I want to be honest: I can't promise it resolves, but I can help you manage it much better than you are now."
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ▶
STAGE: Opening and Initial History

"Good morning, I'm Dr. Chen. Please come in and take a seat. Before we begin, may I confirm your name and date of birth? Thank you. I understand you've been having some discomfort in your mouth — I'd really like to hear all about that in your own words. Take your time."

Listens attentively as the patient describes the burning sensation.

"Thank you for sharing that. I can hear how much this has been affecting you. Eight months is a long time to be dealing with something like this, and I want to make sure we get to the bottom of it today. I'm going to ask you some detailed questions — is that alright?"

"Can you describe the burning sensation for me? Is it constant throughout the day, or does it come and go? And tell me — is it actually worse at any particular time of day, or better at certain times?"

Listens for the classic BMS pattern: better in the morning, progressively worse through the day, and absent or reduced at night.

"That's really helpful. Is it there first thing when you wake up, or does it tend to build up as the day goes on? And when you go to sleep at night — does it actually keep you awake, or does it seem to ease off?"

"Now — does anything in particular trigger it? Certain foods, drinks, or activities? Or is it just always there, sitting in the background?"

"You mentioned it's in the tongue and the lips — is it anywhere else? The roof of your mouth, the gums, or the throat?"

Medication and Medical History

"I'd like to go through all of your medications with you carefully, if that's okay. Can you tell me every medication you're currently taking, including anything you buy over the counter?"

Notes: amitriptyline 50 mg, amlodipine 5 mg, proton pump inhibitor.

"Thank you. How long have you been on the amitriptyline? And the proton pump inhibitor — is that something you've been on for many years?"

"I also want to ask about your dry mouth. When did you first notice your mouth felt dry? Is it difficult to swallow dry food like bread or crackers? Do you find yourself waking up at night to sip water? And has your dentist mentioned anything about decay being worse recently?"

"You mentioned you're post-menopausal — are you currently taking any hormone replacement therapy? And how have you been feeling in yourself emotionally — any anxiety, low mood, or significant stress over the past year or two?"

"How is your sleep in general? Do you snore, or has anyone ever mentioned that you stop breathing during sleep?"

"Any recent changes in taste? Any numbness or tingling elsewhere in your body?"

Examination

Examines all oral mucosal surfaces methodically: buccal mucosa, dorsal and lateral tongue, floor of mouth, palate, and lips.

"I'm going to have a careful look inside your mouth now. I'll be gentle."

Inspects for candidiasis — performs wipe test, which is negative. No erythematous patches, no white lesions, no ulceration, no lichen planus-type striae, no geographic tongue changes. Notes visibly reduced saliva pooling under the tongue. Salivary glands are non-tender and non-enlarged.

"Everything looks completely normal in terms of the visible tissues — no sores, no redness, no infection. I'll explain what that means in a moment."

Diagnosis and Explanation

"I want to take a moment to explain what I think is happening, because I think it's really important you hear this clearly."

"What you have is called Burning Mouth Syndrome. And I want to be the first person to tell you — your symptoms are absolutely real. They are not in your head, and they are not imaginary. This is a recognised medical condition involving changes in the way the nerves in your mouth and tongue send signals to the brain. Because the problem is at the nerve level rather than in the tissue itself, the mouth looks completely healthy on examination — but that absolutely does not mean nothing is wrong. It means we're looking at a nerve-based condition."

"Burning Mouth Syndrome is actually much more common in post-menopausal women, and it often overlaps with dry mouth, depression, and anxiety — all of which are relevant for you. The hormonal changes after menopause can affect how nerves in the mouth process sensation."

"Now, there's something else I want to flag. Your amitriptyline — which is a type of antidepressant — is one of the most common medications to cause a dry mouth. Over four hundred medications can contribute to this, and amitriptyline is well known among them. A dry mouth then makes the burning sensation significantly worse, because saliva is protective. So while the amitriptyline isn't causing the Burning Mouth Syndrome directly, it is very likely making things harder for you."

"I also want to mention your stomach tablet — the proton pump inhibitor. Long-term use can reduce your absorption of Vitamin B12, and a B12 deficiency can itself cause burning and tingling in the mouth. So we'll need to check your B12, iron, and folate levels with a blood test."

Management Plan

"Here's what I'd like to do for you, step by step."

"First, for the dry mouth: sip water frequently throughout the day — small amounts often rather than large gulps. There are saliva substitute products available at the pharmacy, such as Biotene spray or gel, which can help coat and protect the tissues. I'd also ask you to avoid caffeine and alcohol as much as possible, as both make dryness worse. Sugar-free gum can stimulate your natural saliva flow if you still have some salivary gland function."

"Second, I want you to see your GP specifically to discuss the amitriptyline. I'm not suggesting you stop it — that decision belongs with your GP and your mental health — but it's worth asking whether the dose can be reviewed, or whether an alternative with less dry-mouth side effect might be suitable."

"Third, for the Burning Mouth Syndrome itself, there is good evidence that Cognitive Behavioural Therapy — CBT — helps people manage this condition meaningfully. I'll recommend a referral to a psychologist through your GP. There are also some specialist treatments — such as a clonazepam rinse used in short bursts, or alpha-lipoic acid — but those would be initiated by an oral medicine specialist, so I'll arrange a referral for you."

"Fourth, I'll write a referral letter for your GP requesting B12, iron, folate, and full blood count — particularly given the long-term PPI use."

"This condition is not always fully curable, but it is absolutely manageable, and many people achieve significant relief with the right combination of approaches. You don't have to simply live with this."

Safety Net and Closing

"I'd like to see you back here in six to eight weeks to review how things are going and check those blood results. In the meantime, if you develop any visible sores, ulcers, white or red patches, difficulty swallowing, or any unexplained lumps, please come back straight away — don't wait for the appointment."

"I'll also give you a written summary of everything we've discussed today so you can share it with your GP."

"Do you have any questions at all? I know that's a lot of information. How are you feeling about everything we've talked about?"

Listens and responds empathetically.

"You've done exactly the right thing by coming in. This has gone on long enough, and now we have a plan. We'll work through this together."

OM6
Jaw Swelling — Differential Diagnosis (Odontogenic vs. Non-Odontogenic)
Category:** Oral Medicine | **Time:** 11 min | **Difficulty:** Exam-ready

CASE SUMMARY

48-year-old patient presents with a slowly growing firm swelling over the right mandible body. Present for 3 months. Painless. No dental symptoms. Candidate must generate a broad differential and plan investigations.

CANDIDATE BRIEF

48-year-old male presents with a gradually enlarging, firm, painless swelling over the right body of the mandible, present for 3 months. No pain, no dental symptoms, no overlying skin changes. Your task: take a history, examine, generate a differential, and plan investigations.

EXAMINER CONTEXT

Patient is not anxious about it — "It came up gradually, I thought it would go away." No previous dental or medical history of note. Non-smoker, minimal alcohol. Will reveal on direct questioning that he had a tooth extracted in that region about 4 months ago.

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

History (2 min) — INFLECTION 1: Timeline after extraction

  • HOPC: rate of growth (slow = more likely benign/cyst; rapid = infection or malignancy), painful vs. painless
  • Dental history: "Did you have any dental work in that area recently?" (He'll reveal an extraction 4 months ago)
  • Systemic symptoms: weight loss, night sweats, fatigue, fever (if yes = lymphoma, metastasis)
  • Medical history: previous cancer, medications, immunosuppression

Examination (1.5 min)

  • Extraoral: site, size, consistency (firm = bone? Cyst? Hard = malignancy, bone?), skin overlying (normal), lymphadenopathy
  • Intraoral: any expansion of buccal or lingual cortex, gum appearance, any fistula, adjacent teeth vitality

Differential Diagnosis (2.5 min) — INFLECTION 2: Breadth is the inflection point

"Given the history and examination, let me walk you through the possibilities:

Odontogenic (from tooth-related structures):

  • Residual radicular cyst — from the extracted tooth's old infection; can expand slowly after extraction
  • Dentigerous cyst — from a retained unerupted tooth
  • Keratocystic odontogenic tumour (KCOT) — more aggressive growth, can recur
  • Ameloblastoma — slow-growing, locally invasive odontogenic tumour

Non-odontogenic:

  • Fibrous dysplasia — developmental bone condition, usually young adults
  • Osteoma — benign bone growth (think Gardner syndrome if multiple)
  • Central giant cell granuloma
  • Osteosarcoma — rare but must be excluded (rapid growth would raise suspicion)
  • Lymphoma — if associated with night sweats, weight loss, lymphadenopathy
  • Metastatic disease — if history of prior cancer"

Investigations (2 min)

  1. OPG: first-line — assess extent, relationship to IAN, cortical destruction, internal structure
  2. CBCT: better 3D assessment of cortical expansion and root relationships
  3. Aspiration: if cystic appearance — aspirate to confirm cyst fluid, cholesterol crystals (confirm odontogenic cyst)
  4. Blood tests: if lymphoma suspected — FBC, LDH, ESR
  5. Incisional biopsy: if imaging suggests aggressive or non-cystic lesion
  6. Specialist referral: OMFS or oral medicine

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Connects timeline to recent extraction (residual cyst as strong differential)
  2. ✅ Generates both odontogenic AND non-odontogenic differential (breadth = inflection point)
  3. ✅ Asks about systemic symptoms (screens for lymphoma/malignancy)
  4. ✅ Plans appropriate staged investigations (OPG → CBCT → aspiration/biopsy)
  5. ✅ Knows when to refer to specialist

TG4 ALERTS

Painless mandibular swelling — Painlessness does not equal benign. Osteosarcoma and lymphoma are often painless initially. Adequate investigation is non-negotiable.
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • "Differential for jaw swelling: odontogenic (abscess, cyst, osteomyelitis), salivary gland (obstruction, sialadenitis, tumour), lymph node enlargement (reactive, lymphoma), vascular, bone pathology (ameloblastoma, OKC, fibrous dysplasia), metastasis."
  • "Key discriminators: duration and growth rate (rapid = infection or malignancy; slow and painless = cyst or benign tumour), fluctuance (cystic/infectious), associated teeth, fever and trismus (acute infection), weight loss and night sweats (lymphoma)."
  • "Radiographic approach: OPG first for bony assessment; CBCT for detailed bone pathology; ultrasound to differentiate cystic vs solid and assess salivary gland; CT/MRI for soft tissue extent."
  • "Urgent referral triggers: rapid enlargement, hard and fixed on palpation, associated lymphadenopathy, weight loss, failure to respond to antibiotics, crossing midline."
Patient Reframes
  • "There are several explanations for this swelling — some are straightforward dental causes, some are less common. I'm going to work through this systematically so we get the right answer, not just the most common one."
  • "I need to examine you carefully and get some imaging before I can tell you what this is. I know uncertainty is uncomfortable — but reaching for a diagnosis before I have the information would be doing you a disservice."
Curveball Deflectors
  • "Is it cancer?" → "That's on the differential — and I won't dismiss your concern. It's also one of the less likely causes. What I need to do now is take a careful history, examine you properly, and get the right imaging. Then I'll have a much better answer for you."
  • "Should I be worried?" → "I want you to take this seriously enough to follow through with the investigations — but I don't want you to catastrophise before we have the facts. Most jaw swellings have benign causes. Let's find out what this one is."
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ▶
STAGE: Opening and History — HOPC

"Good morning, I'm the dentist here today. Please come in and take a seat. Before I examine you, I'd like to ask you a few questions to better understand what's been happening. Is that okay?"

"So you've noticed a swelling on the right side of your jaw — can you tell me when you first noticed it and how it's changed since then?" Candidate listens carefully. Patient reports a slowly growing firm swelling over three months, no rapid change.

"Has it been painful at any point, or has it remained completely painless throughout?" Patient confirms painless throughout. "Has there been any numbness or tingling in your lower lip or chin on that side?" This screens for inferior alveolar nerve involvement.

"I notice this is on the right side of your lower jaw — did you have any dental work done in that area recently?" Patient reveals a lower right molar extraction approximately four months ago. "And before that extraction, was that tooth causing you any pain or infection? Any swelling or pus at the time?" This establishes the link to a potential residual cyst.

"Have you noticed any changes to the overlying skin — redness, warmth, any discharge?" Patient denies. "Any difficulty opening your mouth, swallowing, or speaking?" Patient denies.

"I also need to ask about your general health. Have you had any unexplained weight loss, night sweats, or persistent fatigue over the last few months?" These screen for lymphoma and metastatic disease. "Any fevers?" Patient denies all. "Have you ever been diagnosed with any cancer in the past, anywhere in the body?" Patient denies. "Any medications, particularly long-term steroids or immunosuppressants?" Patient denies. "Any history of similar swellings elsewhere in your body?"

---

Examination

"Thank you. I'd now like to examine you, both outside and inside your mouth. I'll be as gentle as possible."

Conducts extraoral examination. Notes a firm, non-tender swelling over the right body of the mandible, approximately two centimetres in dimension. Overlying skin is normal in colour with no erythema, warmth, or sinus tracts. Palpates the cervical lymph nodes systematically — submandibular, submental, anterior and posterior cervical chains. Notes no palpable lymphadenopathy.

Conducts intraoral examination. Notes buccal cortical expansion in the right mandibular premolar-molar region. Lingual cortex appears intact. Overlying mucosa is intact with no ulceration, erythema, or fistula. Adjacent teeth are present. Conducts sensibility testing on the lower right premolars and molars — all respond within normal limits. Notes the extraction site of the lower right molar has healed clinically.

"The swelling feels bony hard, there is buccal cortical expansion, the overlying mucosa is completely normal, and there is no lymphadenopathy. Importantly, this is painless and slow-growing."

---

Differential Diagnosis

"I'd like to walk you through the possible diagnoses I'm considering, and I want to be thorough here because a painless jaw swelling has a broad differential — painlessness does not equal benign.

Starting with odontogenic causes — those arising from tooth-related structures. My leading differential is a residual radicular cyst. This patient had an extraction four months ago, and a pre-existing periapical cyst can persist and slowly expand after the tooth is removed. This fits the timeline very well. A dentigerous cyst is possible if there is a retained unerupted tooth in the area. A keratocystic odontogenic tumour, or KCOT, must also be considered — it can appear deceptively innocuous on examination but has a significantly higher recurrence rate and more aggressive behaviour. Ameloblastoma is another important odontogenic tumour — it is locally invasive, slow-growing, and classically presents exactly as this patient does.

Moving to non-odontogenic causes: fibrous dysplasia can cause bony expansion, typically in younger adults, and has a characteristic ground-glass appearance on imaging. A central giant cell granuloma presents as a radiolucency and may be asymptomatic. An osteoma is a benign bony overgrowth — if multiple, this raises the possibility of Gardner syndrome. I must also consider osteosarcoma, which is rare but cannot be excluded without imaging — it can present as a painless swelling initially and would demand urgent investigation. Lymphoma can present as painless jaw swelling with or without systemic symptoms. Finally, metastatic disease to the jaw, while uncommon, must be considered — breast, lung, kidney, and prostate are the most common primaries."

---

Investigations

"The investigation plan needs to be staged and systematic.

My first-line investigation is an orthopantomogram, or OPG. This will give me an overview of the entire jaw, show the extent of the lesion, its relationship to the inferior alveolar nerve, any cortical destruction or perforation, the internal structure — whether it is unilocular, multilocular, radiolucent or mixed — and the relationship to adjacent teeth and the extraction socket.

If the OPG raises concern about cortical expansion, root displacement, or an aggressive pattern, I would proceed to cone beam CT. CBCT provides three-dimensional assessment of cortical integrity, bucco-lingual expansion, and more precise anatomical relationships without the radiation dose of a medical CT.

If imaging suggests a cystic lesion, I would perform an aspiration. A straw-coloured aspirate with cholesterol crystals supports an odontogenic cyst. A bloody aspirate would raise concern for a vascular lesion or central giant cell granuloma.

If imaging suggests an aggressive, non-cystic, or destructive lesion, I would arrange an incisional biopsy to obtain a histopathological diagnosis before any definitive treatment.

If systemic features suggested lymphoma, I would request a full blood count, LDH, and ESR as part of the workup.

Regardless of findings, this patient requires referral to an oral and maxillofacial surgeon or oral medicine specialist for co-management and definitive treatment planning."

---

Safety Net and Closing

"I want to be very transparent with you. A slowly growing, painless jaw swelling always requires full investigation — the fact that it is not painful is actually not reassuring on its own, because some serious conditions, including certain bone tumours, begin this way.

We will start with the OPG today, and I will review those results with you and discuss next steps very shortly. If anything on imaging suggests we need to act more quickly, I will fast-track your referral.

In the meantime, please come back immediately — do not wait for your next appointment — if the swelling grows rapidly, if you develop numbness in your lip or chin, if you have difficulty breathing or swallowing, or if you develop fever or night sweats.

Do you have any questions for me at this stage? I want to make sure you feel informed and comfortable with what we're doing." Candidate ensures patient understanding and closes the consultation professionally.

OM7
Oral Manifestations of HIV / Immunosuppression
Category:** Oral Medicine | **Time:** 11 min | **Difficulty:** Exam-ready

CASE SUMMARY

35-year-old HIV-positive patient (on ART, CD4 200, detectable viral load) presents with white plaques on the tongue and buccal mucosa that can be wiped off. Candidate must diagnose oral candidiasis, link to immune status, manage appropriately.

CANDIDATE BRIEF

35-year-old male, known HIV-positive (CD4 200, viral load detectable — currently poorly controlled). Presents with white plaques on the dorsum of tongue and buccal mucosa that he noticed 2 weeks ago. Occasionally wipe off leaving a red, sore base. Your task: assess and manage.

EXAMINER CONTEXT

Patient is aware of his HIV status. He has not been taking his ART consistently for the past 3 months due to side effects. Is worried the mouth problem means his HIV is "getting worse." Will ask: "Does this mean my HIV is out of control?"

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

History (1.5 min)

  • Duration, progression of white plaques
  • Wiping off (wipes = candidiasis; doesn't wipe = OLP, leukoplakia)
  • ART compliance: "How have you been going with your HIV medications?"
  • Systemic symptoms: fever, weight loss, dysphagia (oesophageal candidiasis red flag)
  • Other conditions or recent infections?

Diagnosis — INFLECTION 1: Name it and link it to immune status

"The white plaques that wipe off and leave a red, sore base — this is oral candidiasis. It's a fungal infection caused by Candida, which normally lives in the mouth in small amounts. When your immune system is strong, it keeps it under control. When the immune system is weaker, Candida overgrows.

In your case, your CD4 count of 200 — which is getting into the range where infections like this become more common. With your viral load currently detectable, it means the virus is actively working against your immune system right now."

Addressing "Is my HIV getting worse?" — INFLECTION 2

"I want to answer your question directly: yes, oral candidiasis in someone with HIV does tell us that your immune system is under stress right now. It's an opportunistic infection — it takes advantage of a weakened immune system. The good news is this is very treatable, and getting your ART back on track is the most important thing we can do."

Management (2 min)

  1. Antifungal treatment:
  • Nystatin mouthwash or lozenges — first-line for mild/moderate oral candidiasis
  • Fluconazole 150mg orally — if nystatin insufficient or moderate-severe
  • Duration: 7–14 days
  1. Address ART non-compliance — this is the root cause:
  • Warm, non-judgmental approach: "Can I ask what's been making it hard to take your medications?"
  • Refer back to HIV specialist/GP for ART review — if side effects are the issue, there may be alternative regimens
  1. Oesophageal candidiasis screen: "Any difficulty swallowing or pain when swallowing?" If yes → urgent referral (oesophageal involvement = systemic antifungal, specialist)
  2. Denture hygiene: if wearing dentures — dry storage, antifungal cream on denture

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Diagnoses oral candidiasis correctly (wiping off = diagnostic)
  2. ✅ Links to immune status (CD4 200 = immunocompromised threshold for opportunistic infections)
  3. ✅ Answers the patient's direct question honestly ("yes, it tells us your immune system is under stress")
  4. ✅ Non-judgmental approach to ART non-compliance
  5. ✅ Screens for oesophageal involvement (dysphagia)
  6. ✅ Prescribes nystatin/fluconazole appropriately
  7. ✅ Refers back to HIV specialist for ART review

TG4 ALERTS

Fluconazole interactions — TG4: fluconazole interacts with several ART medications. Check interactions before prescribing or confirm with HIV specialist.
Oesophageal candidiasis — Dysphagia or odynophagia in an HIV patient with oral candidiasis = oesophageal involvement until proven otherwise. Requires systemic antifungal + specialist referral.
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • "Classic oral HIV manifestations: pseudomembranous candidiasis (removable white plaques), erythematous candidiasis (red patches), oral hairy leukoplakia (lateral tongue, non-removable, EBV-driven), Kaposi's sarcoma (purple macular/nodular, palate or gingiva), severe aphthous ulceration, recurrent HSV."
  • "CD4 <200: threshold for opportunistic infections — oral candidiasis, severe HSV, KS are more prevalent. Oral findings may be the first presentation of HIV or of worsening immune status."
  • "HIV testing: offer sensitively and with consent — 'Some of what I'm seeing can be associated with immune system changes. I'd like to suggest some blood tests with your permission.' This is not diagnosing HIV — it's opening the pathway."
  • "Modern ART: patients on effective ART with undetectable viral load have near-normal immune function. Do not conflate HIV status with immunocompromise — ask for current CD4 and viral load."
Patient Reframes
  • "Some of what I'm seeing in your mouth can sometimes be a sign that the immune system is under stress. That's important information — but it's also something we can investigate and address. With your permission, I'd like to arrange some blood tests."
  • "Having this finding doesn't mean something terrible — it means we've found something worth investigating, and finding it now is much better than finding it later."
Curveball Deflectors
  • "Are you saying I might have HIV?" → "I'm saying these findings are associated with immune changes — which can have several causes. HIV is one possibility, but so are medications, other immune conditions, and diabetes. I'd like to do blood tests to find out what's driving this."
  • "I don't want a blood test." → "That's your right, and I'll respect it. I do want to make sure you understand what I'm seeing and why I'm recommending it. If you change your mind, the offer stands."
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ▶
STAGE: Opening and History

"Hi, come on in. I'm the dentist here today — thanks for coming in. Before I take a look, I'd like to ask you a few questions if that's okay. I can see from the notes you've noticed some white patches in your mouth over the last couple of weeks. Can you tell me a little more about that — where exactly you're seeing them, and when you first noticed them?"

Listens as patient describes white plaques on the tongue and inside of the cheeks, present for approximately two weeks.

"Have you noticed whether they wipe off at all — like if you rub them with your tongue or a cloth, do they come away? And when they do come off, does the area underneath look red or feel sore?"

Listens. Patient confirms plaques wipe off, leaving a red, tender base.

"Are you having any difficulty swallowing — or any pain when you swallow, like food getting stuck or a burning sensation going down?"

Listens. Patient denies dysphagia for now — note for monitoring.

"Any fever, night sweats, or unintended weight loss recently?"

Listens.

"Now, I can see from your records you're HIV-positive and you're on antiretroviral therapy. How have you been going with taking your HIV medications? Are you managing to take them every day as prescribed?"

Listens. Patient admits he has been inconsistent with his ART over recent months.

"I appreciate you telling me that — it's really important information and it helps me understand what's going on. Has anything made it difficult to stay on top of them — side effects, or just the day-to-day of it?"

Listens. Non-judgmental. Notes ART non-compliance.

---

Examination and Diagnosis

Conducts an intraoral examination. Observes white, wipeable plaques on the dorsal tongue and bilateral buccal mucosa. On wiping, erythematous, friable base is revealed. No fixed white lesions. No floor-of-mouth swelling. Cervical lymph nodes noted.

"So I've had a good look inside your mouth, and I want to explain what I'm seeing. The white patches that you've noticed — they wipe off and leave a red, sore base underneath. That's the key finding that tells me exactly what this is. This is called oral candidiasis — it's a fungal infection caused by a yeast called Candida, which actually lives in everyone's mouth in small amounts all the time."

"Normally, when your immune system is working well, it keeps Candida under control and you'd never notice it. But when the immune system is under stress, Candida can overgrow and cause these patches. In your case, your CD4 count is 200 — and that's the range where the immune system starts to struggle to fight off these kinds of infections. They're called opportunistic infections because they take advantage of a weakened immune system."

"With your viral load currently detectable, it means the HIV virus is actively working against your immune system right now. That's why this has appeared."

---

Addressing the Patient's Concern Directly

"I want to answer a question I imagine is on your mind — which is whether this means your HIV is getting worse. I want to be straightforward with you: yes, oral candidiasis in someone with HIV does tell us your immune system is under significant stress at this point in time. It's a signal. The good news — and this is genuinely good news — is that this infection is very treatable, and more importantly, getting your ART back on track is the most powerful thing we can do to bring your immune system back and stop this from happening again."

---

Management Plan

"For the infection itself, I'm going to prescribe you an antifungal medication. We'll start with nystatin — this comes as a mouthwash or lozenges. You hold it in your mouth for as long as you can before swallowing, four times a day, for at least seven to fourteen days. It works directly on the candida in your mouth."

"If the nystatin isn't enough — if things aren't improving within about a week — we can step up to fluconazole, which is a tablet taken orally, 150 milligrams. One important thing I need to flag: fluconazole can interact with some antiretroviral medications, so before I prescribe it, I'd want to check that with your HIV specialist or confirm it's safe with your pharmacist. I don't want to start anything that interferes with your HIV treatment."

"Speaking of which — the most important part of managing this today isn't actually the antifungal. It's getting your ART sorted. I'm going to write a referral back to your HIV specialist or GP today, so they can review your antiretroviral regimen. If the side effects have been making it hard to take them, there may be other options available — medications that suit you better. You deserve to have a regimen that works for your life."

"One more important question — you mentioned swallowing is okay at the moment. I want you to watch for that. If you develop any pain or difficulty swallowing in the next few days — anything that feels like burning going down — please go to your GP or emergency straight away. That could mean the candida has spread to your oesophagus, which needs immediate treatment with systemic antifungals and specialist review. Don't wait on that."

"Do you wear any dentures? If so, it's important to store them dry overnight — not in water — and clean them thoroughly, as candida can live on the denture surface and reinfect the mouth."

---

Safety Net and Closing

"To summarise what we're doing today: I'm treating the oral candidiasis with nystatin mouthwash four times daily for seven to fourteen days. I'm referring you back to your HIV specialist urgently for ART review. And I'm asking you to watch for any swallowing symptoms and come back or go straight to your GP if they develop."

"I know today has involved some confronting information, and I want you to know you can ask me anything. This is very manageable — oral candidiasis clears well with treatment, and once your immune system is better supported, you're much less likely to see this come back. Is there anything you'd like me to clarify before you go?"

ME1
Anaphylaxis — Latex or Local Anaesthetic
Category:** Medical Emergency | **Time:** 11 min | **Difficulty:** Exam-ready

CASE SUMMARY

Patient develops generalised urticaria, facial swelling, bronchospasm, and hypotension 5 minutes after administration of articaine with adrenaline. Your task: diagnose anaphylaxis, manage immediately, and call emergency services.

CANDIDATE BRIEF

You have just administered an IANB with articaine 4% (1:100,000 adrenaline) for extraction. Five minutes later the patient reports feeling "strange," develops widespread hives, and their face begins to swell. Manage this emergency.

EXAMINER CONTEXT

The patient (role-played by examiner) starts with "I feel strange — hot, itchy." They rapidly become more symptomatic. If not managed within 2–3 minutes of role-play time, symptoms progress (wheeze added, BP drops on vital signs check). The key test is whether the candidate acts immediately with adrenaline rather than waiting.

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

Recognition — INFLECTION 1: Diagnose fast, act immediately

"This is anaphylaxis until proven otherwise. I am not waiting."

Recognition criteria (at least 2 of):

  • Skin/mucosal: urticaria, flushing, angioedema
  • Respiratory: bronchospasm, wheeze, stridor
  • Cardiovascular: hypotension, tachycardia, collapse
  • GI: nausea, vomiting, cramping (less common)

Immediate management (memorise this sequence):

Step 1 — Adrenaline FIRST. Nothing else before adrenaline.

"Stop the procedure. Call for help. Lay the patient flat (or in recovery position if unconscious/vomiting; semi-recumbent if breathing difficulty)."

"Administer adrenaline IM — adult dose: 0.5mg (0.5mL of 1:1000 adrenaline) into the lateral thigh. This is the ONLY first-line treatment."

Step 2 — Call 000 immediately.

Step 3 — Oxygen (15L/min, high-flow, non-rebreather mask).

Step 4 — Repeat adrenaline in 5 minutes if no improvement.

Step 5 — IV access if available — saline bolus for hypotension.

Step 6 — Antihistamines and corticosteroids are ADJUNCTS only (not first-line):

  • Promethazine or diphenhydramine
  • Hydrocortisone 200mg IV

(These help prevent biphasic reaction but do NOT replace adrenaline)

Explaining to the role-player (1.5 min) — INFLECTION 2

"We are going to look after you. I am giving you an injection of adrenaline right now — it's the medication that reverses what's happening in your body. I need you to stay still and keep breathing calmly. An ambulance is on the way."

Post-event documentation and biphasic reaction

"Anaphylaxis can have a biphasic reaction — symptoms returning 4–12 hours later. The patient must be observed in hospital for at least 4 hours after anaphylaxis. Document the event and all medications in the patient's record. Report to TGA/practice protocols."

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Recognises anaphylaxis using ≥2 system involvement
  2. ✅ Adrenaline FIRST — correct dose (0.5mg IM, lateral thigh)
  3. ✅ Calls 000 immediately
  4. ✅ High-flow oxygen
  5. ✅ Positions correctly (flat with legs raised, or recovery position if unconscious)
  6. ✅ Repeats adrenaline at 5 min if no improvement
  7. ✅ Antihistamines and steroids as adjuncts only — not first-line
  8. ✅ Warns about biphasic reaction; insists on hospital observation

TG4 ALERTS

Adrenaline is the ONLY first-line treatment for anaphylaxis — TG4: do NOT give antihistamine first. Do NOT wait to see if symptoms improve. Adrenaline IM immediately.
Dose: 0.5mg (0.5mL of 1:1000) for adults. 0.3mg (0.3mL) for 6–12 years. 0.15mg (0.15mL) for <6 years.
Biphasic anaphylaxis — Occurs in 5–20% of cases, 1–72 hours after initial episode. Patient must be observed in hospital.

INFLECTION POINTS

PointWeakStrong
Speed of recognitionHesitates, monitors firstImmediately identifies anaphylaxis and acts
First drug givenAntihistamine or steroidAdrenaline — nothing else before adrenaline
Route and doseIV or incorrect doseIM lateral thigh, 0.5mg (0.5mL of 1:1000)
PositioningSits patient uprightFlat with legs elevated (unless breathing difficulty)
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • "Anaphylaxis definition: acute systemic hypersensitivity involving >1 organ system — urticaria/angioedema PLUS bronchospasm or hypotension. Isolated urticaria = allergic reaction, not anaphylaxis. The management differs."
  • "First actions: STOP the causative agent, call 000, lie patient supine (unless respiratory distress → sitting up), IM adrenaline 0.5mg (1:1000) into lateral thigh — this is not optional. Do not delay adrenaline for IV access or antihistamines."
  • "Second-line after adrenaline: oxygen 8–10L/min, IV fluids for hypotension, chlorphenamine 10mg IV, hydrocortisone 200mg IV, salbutamol for bronchospasm. Adrenaline can be repeated at 5 minutes if no improvement."
  • "Post-event: patient must not be discharged without medical review — biphasic reactions occur in up to 20% of cases, typically 4–8 hours later. Refer to allergist for skin testing and EpiPen prescription."
Patient Reframes
  • "(Post-recovery) You had a serious allergic reaction called anaphylaxis — your blood pressure dropped and your breathing was affected. The adrenaline we gave you is what brought you out of it. You'll need to see an allergy specialist to identify the exact cause and carry an EpiPen going forward."
  • "This is not something to wait and see about — a second exposure to the same allergen can be faster and more severe. Identifying the trigger and having emergency medication with you at all times is essential."
Curveball Deflectors
  • "Shouldn't you give antihistamine first?" → "No — adrenaline is always first-line in anaphylaxis. Antihistamines work over 30–60 minutes and do not treat cardiovascular or respiratory collapse. Delayed adrenaline is the most common preventable cause of anaphylaxis death."
  • "Are you sure it's not just a panic attack?" → "Panic attacks don't cause urticaria, bronchospasm, or measurable hypotension. The clinical picture here meets the criteria for anaphylaxis. We treat it as such and investigate later — that's the safe approach."
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ▶
STAGE: Recognition and Immediate Diagnosis

Candidate observes the patient closely. Notes widespread urticaria across the trunk and arms, rapidly developing facial and lip swelling, audible wheeze on expiration, and a visibly distressed, pale patient reporting feeling "strange" and dizzy. Candidate acts without hesitation.

"This is anaphylaxis. I am not waiting for further confirmation."

Candidate calls out to the dental nurse immediately: "I need help in here right now. Call triple zero — 000 — immediately and tell them we have a suspected anaphylaxis following local anaesthetic administration. Give them our full address."

Candidate stops the dental procedure, removes any instruments from the patient's mouth, and reclines the chair to a fully flat position with the patient's legs elevated to support circulation. If the patient reports difficulty breathing, candidate adjusts slightly to semi-recumbent. "You have involvement of your skin, your face, and your breathing — that is at least three body systems. This meets the criteria for anaphylaxis."

---

Immediate Adrenaline Administration

Candidate moves directly to the emergency kit and draws up adrenaline.

"Adrenaline is the only first-line treatment here. Nothing else comes before this."

Candidate speaks clearly to the patient: "I am giving you an injection of adrenaline right now into your outer thigh. This is the medication that will reverse what is happening in your body. It works very quickly. Please stay as still as you can."

Candidate administers adrenaline 0.5 mg — that is 0.5 millilitres of 1:1000 adrenaline solution — by intramuscular injection into the anterolateral thigh, through clothing if necessary. Notes the time of administration.

"Dose confirmed — 0.5 milligrams intramuscular, lateral thigh, time noted. I will reassess in five minutes. If there is no improvement, I will give a second dose of 0.5 milligrams IM at that point."

---

Ongoing Emergency Management

Candidate instructs the nurse: "Apply high-flow oxygen — fifteen litres per minute via a non-rebreather mask — now."

Candidate continues monitoring the patient's level of consciousness, breathing, and skin colour continuously. If the patient becomes unconscious and stops breathing normally, candidate is prepared to commence CPR.

"I am checking pulse and respiratory rate every sixty seconds. If at five minutes there is no clinical improvement — no reduction in wheeze, no improvement in blood pressure, no resolution of swelling — I repeat the adrenaline at the same dose."

After five minutes with partial improvement noted: "Good — some response to the first dose. I will hold the second dose and continue to monitor closely until the ambulance arrives."

Candidate establishes intravenous access if trained and equipment is available. "If IV access is available and the patient remains hypotensive, I will commence a saline bolus for cardiovascular support."

Once the patient is stabilised and the ambulance is en route, candidate adds adjunct therapies: "Antihistamines and corticosteroids are adjuncts only — they are not first-line and must never replace or delay adrenaline. I can now give hydrocortisone 200 milligrams intravenously, which helps reduce the risk of a biphasic reaction. Promethazine may also be given for urticaria as a secondary measure."

---

Communication with the Patient

Candidate speaks calmly and clearly, maintaining eye contact and a reassuring tone throughout.

"I know this is frightening, and I want you to know we are looking after you. You have had a reaction to the medication I gave you — it is called anaphylaxis. I have already given you the injection that treats it, and an ambulance is on its way. You are in the right place and we are not leaving your side. Try to breathe slowly and steadily. Can you tell me if the tightness in your chest is changing at all?"

Candidate listens to the patient's response and provides ongoing reassurance while continuing clinical monitoring.

---

Post-Event Counselling, Biphasic Warning, and Documentation

Once the ambulance arrives and handover is being prepared, candidate addresses the patient directly:

"I need to tell you something very important before you go to hospital. With anaphylaxis, there is a risk of what we call a biphasic reaction — the symptoms can return anywhere from one to seventy-two hours after the initial episode, even after you feel better. This occurs in roughly five to twenty percent of cases. For this reason, you must be observed in hospital for a minimum of four hours. Please do not leave against medical advice."

"You will need to be reviewed by your doctor or an allergist after this to identify exactly which component triggered the reaction — whether it was the local anaesthetic itself, the preservative, or the latex in our gloves. You should carry an adrenaline autoinjector — an EpiPen — until that allergy workup is complete."

Candidate completes full contemporaneous documentation: time of injection, drug administered, dose, route, symptoms observed, treatment given with timestamps, ambulance handover details, and a note that the event will be reported to the Therapeutic Goods Administration and recorded in the patient's dental record as a serious adverse drug reaction.

ME2
Vasovagal Syncope vs. Hypoglycaemia (Differential)
Category:** Medical Emergency | **Time:** 11 min | **Difficulty:** Exam-ready

CASE SUMMARY

Patient becomes pale, sweaty, and dizzy 2 minutes into an extraction appointment. They have Type 1 diabetes and skipped breakfast due to pre-op nausea. Candidate must differentiate vasovagal syncope from hypoglycaemia and manage correctly.

CANDIDATE BRIEF

Greg Tomkins, 28-year-old, Type 1 diabetic (on insulin), becomes pale, sweaty, and says "I feel like I'm going to faint" 2 minutes into your appointment. He mentioned before sitting down that he felt a bit sick this morning and didn't eat breakfast. Manage this emergency.

EXAMINER CONTEXT

Patient is conscious but drowsy. Pulse is weak and fast (90 bpm). BP 100/65. If asked about insulin: he took his usual morning dose despite not eating. If given glucose (oral juice or gel), he improves noticeably within 2 minutes. If positioned supine, he is a little better but doesn't fully recover without glucose.

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

Immediate action (30 sec)

Stop procedure. Call for assistance. Recline chair to supine. Remove any instruments from mouth.

Assess — INFLECTION 1: Vasovagal vs. Hypoglycaemia

Both present similarly: pallor, sweating, dizziness, tachycardia, low BP. The key differential is:

FeatureVasovagalHypoglycaemia
TriggerAnxiety, pain, needleInsulin taken, no food
OnsetUsually bradycardic first, then tachycardicTachycardia, no bradycardia
RecoveryImproves with supine within 1–2 minDoes NOT fully improve with supine
GlucoseNormalLOW
ConsciousUsually recovers fastMay deteriorate if glucose not given

"This patient took insulin without eating — that's a hypoglycaemic event until proven otherwise."

Check blood glucose (if glucometer available)

If <4 mmol/L = confirmed hypoglycaemia.

Treatment — INFLECTION 2

If conscious and able to swallow:

  • 15–20g fast-acting glucose: 150mL orange juice, 3–4 glucose tablets, or glucose gel
  • Repeat in 15 minutes if not improved
  • Once recovered: give long-acting carbohydrate (biscuit, sandwich) to prevent recurrence

If unconscious or cannot swallow:

  • Do NOT give oral glucose (aspiration risk)
  • 1mg glucagon IM (if available in emergency kit)
  • Call 000

If vasovagal (no history of insulin, improves with supine within 2 min):

  • Supine position, legs elevated, reassure
  • Loosen tight clothing, ensure airway
  • Monitor vitals, offer water when recovered

Deferring treatment

"We will not be proceeding with the extraction today. I want to confirm your blood sugar is stable, make sure you've eaten, and let you rest. I'll speak with your GP about pre-treatment glucose management for next time — likely scheduling you for morning appointments after a proper breakfast."

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Differentiates vasovagal from hypoglycaemia using history + clinical features
  2. ✅ Checks blood glucose when diabetes history present
  3. ✅ Gives oral glucose first-line if conscious and able to swallow
  4. ✅ Knows to use glucagon IM or call 000 if unconscious
  5. ✅ Does not proceed with treatment after episode
  6. ✅ Plans future appointment management (GP, morning appointments, breakfast)

TG4 ALERTS

Hypoglycaemia: insulin taken without food — TG4: most common cause of hypoglycaemia in dental setting. Always ask diabetic patients about food intake and insulin timing before starting treatment.
Do NOT give oral glucose to unconscious patient — Aspiration risk. Use glucagon IM or IV glucose (hospital) instead.
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • "Vasovagal: warning prodrome (pallor, sweating, nausea), bradycardia, precipitated by anxiety/pain/venepuncture. Management: recline flat, elevate legs, airway clear, monitor. Recovery within 1–2 minutes of lying flat = strongly suggests vasovagal."
  • "Hypoglycaemia: diabetic patient, gradual onset, confusion/irritability/tremor/diaphoresis, BSL <3.5 mmol/L confirms. Management: 15g fast-acting glucose if conscious (glucose tablets, juice, cola), repeat BSL in 15 min, follow with complex carbohydrate. Unconscious → glucagon IM."
  • "Key differentiator: BSL measurement within 2 minutes of patient becoming unwell. Vasovagal recovers rapidly with supine position alone; hypoglycaemia does not recover without glucose."
  • "Never discharge a post-vasovagal patient immediately — ensure full recovery, check BSL regardless, ensure someone takes them home."
Patient Reframes
  • "The faint was most likely your body's response to the stress of the appointment — it's common and not dangerous. But I'm also going to check your blood sugar just to be sure, because the two can look similar and the treatment is different."
  • "A light meal before your dental appointment is genuinely helpful — particularly if you're on diabetes medication. Fasting before dental visits is not necessary and can create exactly this kind of problem."
Curveball Deflectors
  • "She's diabetic — is this her diabetes?" → "That's exactly what I'm testing for right now. BSL in 90 seconds will tell us. If it's low, glucose. If she recovers with her legs elevated before we even get the reading, vasovagal is more likely. Both are manageable — I just need to confirm which."
  • "Should I give her food now?" → "Only if she's fully conscious and can swallow safely. Not while she's confused or semi-conscious — aspiration risk. Let me check her BSL first and make sure her airway is protected."
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ▶
STAGE: Immediate Recognition and Action

Stops the procedure immediately. Removes all instruments and the dental dam from Greg's mouth. Reclines the dental chair to a fully supine position and elevates his legs slightly. Calls loudly to the dental assistant: "I need help in here now, please."

"Greg, I'm stopping everything right now. You're safe. I'm reclining the chair so you're lying flat — that's going to help. Just breathe normally for me. Can you hear me clearly? I need you to squeeze my hand if you can."

Ensures the airway is clear and unobstructed. Checks the clock. Loosens Greg's collar. Retrieves the emergency kit and glucometer.

---

Rapid Assessment and Differential Diagnosis

"Greg, I'm going to ask you a few quick questions. Stay with me. Did you take your insulin this morning? And you mentioned you didn't eat breakfast — is that right?"

Notes: Greg confirms he took his morning insulin dose but skipped breakfast due to nausea. He has been supine for approximately 90 seconds and has not improved — still pale, sweating, and reporting dizziness. Heart rate is elevated on palpation. There is no bradycardia.

Narrates clinical reasoning: Both vasovagal syncope and hypoglycaemia share pallor, diaphoresis, dizziness, and nausea. In vasovagal, the typical trigger is anxiety or pain, onset includes an initial bradycardia, and the patient classically recovers within one to two minutes of supine positioning. In hypoglycaemia, the trigger is insulin without adequate carbohydrate intake, the heart rate is consistently elevated with no bradycardia, and the patient does not fully recover with positional change alone. This patient took insulin, skipped breakfast, and is not improving — this is a hypoglycaemic episode until proven otherwise.

Checks blood glucose using glucometer. Reading: 2.8 mmol/L. Confirms hypoglycaemia.
