"Greg, your blood sugar is quite low — that's what's making you feel this way. It's because your insulin had nothing to work with this morning. I'm going to give you something sweet right now to bring it back up. This will help, I promise."

---

Emergency Management — Conscious Patient

Confirms Greg is conscious, alert, and has an intact swallow reflex. He can follow commands and open his mouth on request.

"I'm going to give you some orange juice to drink — about 150 millilitres, roughly half a glass. I need you to drink it slowly but steadily. This is going to raise your blood sugar."

Administers 150 mL of orange juice — equivalent to approximately 15 grams of fast-acting glucose. Notes the time. Continues to monitor Greg's level of consciousness, colour, pulse, and responsiveness at regular intervals.

"You're doing really well, Greg. I'm going to check your blood sugar again in about 15 minutes to make sure it's coming up to a safe level. If it hasn't improved by then, I'll give you another 15 grams of glucose and we'll reassess."

After 15 minutes, blood glucose has risen to 4.6 mmol/L. Greg reports he feels more alert and his colour is returning.

"That's a much better reading — your levels are coming up nicely. Now I want to give you something with longer-lasting carbohydrates to make sure this doesn't drop again. I have some plain biscuits and a small sandwich here — can you manage a few biscuits to start?"

Provides long-acting carbohydrate to prevent rebound hypoglycaemia. Continues monitoring.

---

Management if Unconscious — Contingency

"If at any point Greg had lost consciousness or could no longer swallow safely, I would not give anything by mouth — the risk of aspiration is too high. I would administer one milligram of glucagon intramuscularly from the emergency kit, call triple zero immediately, maintain him in a left lateral recovery position to protect his airway, and continue monitoring his breathing and pulse until the ambulance arrived."

---

Deferring Treatment and Safety Net

"Greg, now that you're feeling better, I want to be very clear — we won't be going ahead with the extraction today. Your body has been through a significant episode, and it wouldn't be safe or fair to proceed. I want you to rest here for at least another 20 minutes before you go anywhere, and please don't drive yourself home."

"Before your next appointment, I'm going to write to your GP and let them know what happened today. We'll coordinate with them around timing your insulin and meals on the morning of dental appointments. Ideally, we'll schedule you for an early morning slot after you've had a proper breakfast and confirmed your blood glucose is in a safe range before you sit in my chair."

"If you feel unwell at any point today — more dizziness, confusion, sweating, or your heart racing — please go straight to your GP or the emergency department. Don't ignore it. Do you have someone who can stay with you this afternoon?"

Documents the episode, blood glucose readings, intervention, and outcome in Greg's clinical notes.

ME3
Asthma Attack in the Dental Chair
Category:** Medical Emergency | **Time:** 11 min | **Difficulty:** Exam-ready

CASE SUMMARY

Known asthmatic patient develops acute bronchospasm during treatment, likely triggered by anxiety + aerosolized LA. Candidate must manage acute asthma using available resources.

CANDIDATE BRIEF

A 24-year-old known asthmatic (mild persistent, on salbutamol PRN + fluticasone daily) develops wheeze, difficulty breathing, and is sitting bolt upright 10 minutes into an appointment. She appears anxious and is breathing rapidly.

EXAMINER CONTEXT

Patient is frightened and says "I can't breathe properly." She has her reliever inhaler in her bag. Oxygen is available chairside. If given salbutamol promptly and positioned upright, she improves within 5 minutes. If not given salbutamol, she worsens over 5 minutes (increased WOB, speaking in single words).

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

Immediate recognition (30 sec)

Stop procedure. Do NOT recline the chair — sit patient UPRIGHT (opposite to vasovagal). Acute asthma = bronchospasm, patient needs upright position to maximise lung expansion.

First-line management — INFLECTION 1

"Get her reliever inhaler (salbutamol blue puffer). If she can't use it herself — spacer device."

Salbutamol administration:

  • 4 puffs (100mcg each) via spacer, inhale separately, 4 breaths per puff
  • Repeat every 20 minutes for up to 3 doses

Call 000 if:

  • Not improving after 2 doses of salbutamol
  • SpO2 <92%
  • Speaking in single words (severe)
  • Cyanosis, exhaustion, silent chest (life-threatening)

Oxygen:

  • 6–8 L/min via face mask if SpO2 <94%
  • Aim SpO2 94–98%

Do NOT use:

  • Nitrous oxide — not appropriate in acute respiratory distress
  • NSAIDs — can worsen aspirin-sensitive asthma

Reassurance (1 min) — INFLECTION 2

"I'm going to help you through this. Try to breathe slowly — in through your nose, out through your mouth. Your puffer is going to help in a minute."

If improving (5 min)

Patient settles, SpO2 >95%, speaking in sentences. Do not continue treatment today. Review trigger (anxiety, aerosol, aspirin). Plan future appointment with: pre-appointment salbutamol (1–2 puffs before starting), anxiolysis options, avoid LA with sulfite preservatives.

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Sit upright — NOT supine (opposite of vasovagal)
  2. ✅ Salbutamol first-line: 4 puffs, spacer, every 20 min
  3. ✅ Oxygen if SpO2 <94%
  4. ✅ Knows escalation criteria (single words, silent chest, cyanosis = 000)
  5. ✅ Avoids NSAIDs in aspirin-sensitive asthma
  6. ✅ Plans future appointment management (pre-treatment salbutamol, anxiety reduction)

TG4 ALERTS

Upright position — NOT supine — TG4: asthma patients need to sit upright to maximise functional residual capacity. Reclining worsens airflow obstruction.
Silent chest — Absence of wheeze in severe asthma is NOT reassuring — it means airflow is so reduced there's no turbulence. It's a life-threatening sign.
NSAIDs in aspirin-sensitive asthma — TG4: avoid NSAIDs and aspirin. Use paracetamol only for pain management.
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • "Severity assessment: mild (wheeze, SpO2 >95%), moderate (SpO2 90–95%, unable to complete sentences), severe (SpO2 <90%, cyanosis, silent chest). Manage according to severity — do not underestimate a 'silent chest' (indicates no air movement)."
  • "Management: upright position, stop all treatment, give patient's own reliever (salbutamol) 4–8 puffs via spacer — can repeat every 20 min; oxygen 8–10L/min; call 000 if no rapid improvement, SpO2 <90%, or no reliever available."
  • "LA is safe in asthmatics: adrenaline in LA at standard concentrations (1:80,000 or 1:100,000) does not trigger bronchospasm. Avoid aspirin-containing analgesics in aspirin-exacerbated asthma. Bisulphite-free LA available for sulphite-sensitive patients."
  • "Triggers in the dental setting: latex (use latex-free gloves), metabisulphite in LA preservative, stress and anxiety, dental aerosols."
Patient Reframes
  • "(Prevention) We'll use bisulphite-free local anaesthetic for you, avoid aspirin in any painkillers, and make sure your reliever is with you before we start. With those precautions in place, dental treatment is safe."
  • "(Post-episode) The episode is over and you're safe. I want to make sure we know your reliever is working and your SpO2 is back to normal before you leave. And I'd like to know whether this happens outside the dental setting too."
Curveball Deflectors
  • "Shouldn't you give adrenaline?" → "Adrenaline is for anaphylaxis — not asthma. For an acute asthma attack, the correct first-line treatment is the patient's own reliever inhaler. Adrenaline in this context can cause cardiac arrhythmias and is not indicated."
  • "I forgot my inhaler." → "Our emergency kit has a salbutamol inhaler and spacer. If this happens again, always bring your reliever — but today, we're covered."
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ▶
STAGE: Immediate Recognition & Positioning

Stops procedure immediately. Places instruments down. Does not recline the chair.

"Okay, I'm stopping everything right now. Just leave all the instruments — we're done with treatment for today."

Moves to the patient's side. Patient is sitting bolt upright, visibly anxious, audible wheeze on expiration, respiratory rate elevated.

"I can hear you're having trouble breathing — I can see you're working hard. I'm going to help you right now. The most important thing is to stay sitting up exactly like you are. Don't lie back — sitting upright is the best position for your lungs right now."

Calls to assistant: "Can you bring me the emergency kit immediately — I need the salbutamol inhaler and the spacer device. And someone please be ready to call 000 if I ask."

Checks whether patient has her own reliever inhaler. "Do you have your blue puffer with you today? In your bag?" If yes, retrieves it. If not, uses the practice's salbutamol from the emergency kit.

---

First-Line Salbutamol Administration

"I'm going to give you your reliever now — salbutamol, your blue puffer. We're going to use a spacer so it gets right into your lungs. I want you to try to breathe as slowly and steadily as you can. In through your nose if you can manage it, out through your mouth."

Attaches inhaler to spacer. Shakes the inhaler.

"I'm going to give you four separate puffs. After each puff, I want you to take four slow, gentle breaths in through the spacer. We'll go one puff at a time — just nice and calm."

Administers salbutamol 100 mcg per actuation — four actuations via spacer, one puff at a time, four breaths per puff. Notes time of first dose.

"That's it — you're doing really well. Just keep breathing. The medication will start to open up your airways within a few minutes. You're safe, I'm right here with you."

Reassesses at two minutes. Checks SpO2, respiratory rate, ability to speak in full sentences.

"Can you tell me — are you feeling any easier at all? Can you try to say a whole sentence for me?"

---

Oxygen & Ongoing Monitoring

Applies oxygen via face mask at 6 to 8 litres per minute. Attaches pulse oximeter.

"I'm going to put some oxygen on as well — it's just going to sit gently over your face. It'll help support your breathing while the salbutamol does its work."

Monitors SpO2, aiming for 94 to 98 percent. Continues to reassess every few minutes.

"Your oxygen level is sitting at 96 percent — that's a good sign. I'm going to stay with you and we'll repeat the salbutamol in 20 minutes if you need it. We can give it up to three times."

Mentally notes escalation criteria: if SpO2 drops below 94 percent, if patient can only speak in single words, if cyanosis or exhaustion develops, or if the chest goes silent — a silent chest means no air movement at all, which is a life-threatening sign requiring immediate ambulance.

---

Escalation Decision & 000 Call Criteria

At five minutes, patient is improving — SpO2 95 percent, speaking in short sentences, wheeze lessening.

"You're looking better — your oxygen is coming up and your breathing is easing. We'll keep the oxygen on and I'll check you again in a few minutes."

Narrates internally: if no improvement after two doses of salbutamol 20 minutes apart, or if patient deteriorates — single words only, cyanosis, silent chest, exhaustion — call 000 immediately.

"If at any point you feel worse — if you can't speak, if you feel faint, you tell me immediately and we'll get an ambulance straight away. There's no hesitation on that."

Does not administer NSAIDs for any pain management. If analgesia is required later, paracetamol 1 gram is the appropriate agent. Aspirin-sensitive asthma is a recognised condition and NSAIDs including aspirin must be strictly avoided in any asthmatic patient unless confirmed tolerant.

---

Recovery & Future Appointment Planning

Patient has settled at eight minutes. SpO2 97 percent, breathing comfortably, speaking in full sentences.

"I'm really glad you're feeling better. We're not going to do any more treatment today — your safety is the priority and your body has had enough of a workout. I'd like you to stay here for at least another 15 minutes so I can make sure you're completely stable before you leave."

"I'd also strongly recommend you don't drive yourself home today — is there someone who can come and collect you? If not, we'll organise that for you."

"Once you're home, please contact your GP or respiratory physician and let them know this happened today. It's worth reviewing your asthma management plan."

Discusses future appointment adjustments: "When we see you next time, I'd like you to take one to two puffs of your salbutamol about 15 minutes before you come in — that helps protect your airways before we start. We'll also talk about ways to reduce anxiety around appointments, whether that's a longer appointment time, more frequent breaks, or a referral for some additional support. I'll also make sure we're using local anaesthetic without sulfite preservatives, as those can occasionally act as a trigger."

"Do you have any questions about what happened today or what to do when you get home?"

ME4
Chest Pain / Angina vs. Acute MI
Category:** Medical Emergency | **Time:** 11 min | **Difficulty:** Exam-ready

CASE SUMMARY

65-year-old patient complains of central chest pain radiating to the left arm during dental treatment. Known angina, but this pain is different (more severe, not relieved by glyceryl trinitrate). Candidate must distinguish stable angina from STEMI and manage accordingly.

CANDIDATE BRIEF

65-year-old male, known stable angina (on GTN PRN + atenolol). During filling of tooth 36, he grips the armrest and says "I've got chest pain — like my usual angina, but it feels worse." Manage this emergency.

EXAMINER CONTEXT

His GTN spray is in his jacket pocket. If given GTN, the pain partially reduces (from 8/10 to 5/10) but does not resolve. If candidate waits longer without calling 000, patient says the pain is now 9/10 and he's "feeling sick." The pain does not fully resolve with one dose of GTN.

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

Immediate action (30 sec)

Stop procedure. Call for help. Sit patient upright (semi-recumbent — not flat, not fully upright). Do NOT recline.

History — 30 seconds

"On a scale of 1–10, how bad is the pain? Where exactly? Does it go anywhere? Is this your usual angina?"

Administer GTN — INFLECTION 1

"GTN spray (400mcg, sublingual): 1–2 puffs under the tongue."

  • If pain resolves within 5 minutes: stable angina. Rest, monitor vitals, do not continue treatment today.
  • If pain NOT resolved in 5 minutes with 2 doses of GTN, OR worse than usual, OR patient looks unwell: treat as ACUTE MI.

If not resolved — INFLECTION 2: STEMI protocol

  1. Call 000 immediately — do NOT wait further
  2. Aspirin 300mg (chew, not swallow) — if not contraindicated (not allergic, no active GI bleed)
  3. Oxygen only if SpO2 <94% (routine O2 in chest pain is no longer recommended — TG4 update)
  4. Reassure and monitor — pulse, BP, respiration
  5. Do NOT leave the patient alone
  6. Do NOT give a second dose of GTN if BP is dropping (GTN drops BP; dangerous if patient is hypotensive)

What NOT to do:

  • Do not give food or drink
  • Do not leave patient to drive themselves to hospital
  • Do not try to finish the filling

Communication (1 min)

"I'm concerned this might be more than your usual angina. We've given you your spray and the pain hasn't fully settled. I'm calling an ambulance right now — please stay as calm as you can. I'll stay with you."

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Semi-recumbent position (not flat, not fully upright)
  2. ✅ GTN first-line for angina
  3. ✅ Recognises non-resolution at 5 min = possible MI → call 000
  4. ✅ Aspirin 300mg chewed for suspected MI (not swallowed)
  5. ✅ Oxygen only if SpO2 <94% (NOT routine)
  6. ✅ Does not leave patient alone
  7. ✅ Does NOT give second GTN if blood pressure dropping

TG4 ALERTS

Oxygen NOT routine in chest pain — TG4: hyperoxia may be harmful in MI. Give O2 ONLY if SpO2 <94%. This is a commonly tested update — many candidates still give routine O2.
Aspirin 300mg — chew, don't swallow — Faster buccal absorption. First-line adjunct for suspected STEMI before ambulance arrives.
GTN contraindicated if hypotensive — BP <90 systolic = do not give GTN (causes further vasodilation and cardiovascular collapse).

INFLECTION POINTS

PointWeakStrong
GTN firstCalls 000 immediately without trialling GTNGives GTN, waits 5 min, calls 000 when not resolved
AspirinNot given300mg chewed, after calling 000
Oxygen"Give 100% O2""Only if SpO2 <94%" — knows the updated TG4 guideline
PositionFlat (vasovagal reflex)Semi-recumbent — best for cardiac output
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • "Angina vs MI distinction: angina relieved by GTN within 3–5 minutes; MI — pain persists >20 minutes, unrelieved by 3 doses GTN, may radiate to jaw/arm/back, diaphoresis, nausea."
  • "Angina management: sit upright, patient's own GTN (spray or tablet), rest, monitor. If resolved in 5 minutes — continue cautiously with GP review same day. If not resolved — treat as MI."
  • "Acute MI: call 000 immediately, 300mg aspirin chewable (if no allergy, no haemorrhagic stroke), oxygen only if SpO2 <94%, GTN if systolic >90mmHg, reassure and keep still. Do NOT give aspirin if haemorrhagic stroke is possible."
  • "Prevention in at-risk patients: morning appointments, good analgesia (pain = adrenaline surge = cardiac stress), maximum 2 cartridges of 1:80,000 adrenaline, avoid adrenaline-impregnated gingival retraction cord."
Patient Reframes
  • "The most dangerous thing for your heart during a dental appointment isn't the local anaesthetic — it's untreated pain. Good anaesthesia and a calm appointment actually protect your heart. The small amount of adrenaline in the injection is safe within the recommended limits."
  • "Dental stress can trigger cardiac events in susceptible people — which is why short appointments, excellent pain control, and morning bookings are our standard approach for patients with cardiac history."
Curveball Deflectors
  • "Is it safe to give me an injection with my heart condition?" → "Yes — adrenaline in local anaesthetic within the recommended dose limits is safe for cardiac patients. The stress response from inadequately anaesthetised dental work releases far more endogenous adrenaline than two cartridges of LA."
  • "Should I stop my aspirin before the appointment?" → "No — stopping aspirin for dental work increases cardiac risk without significantly reducing bleeding risk. We manage bleeding locally. Your cardiologist should be the one to advise any changes to your cardiac medications."
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ▶
STAGE: Immediate Response & Positioning

Stops all dental instruments. Places bur and handpiece aside. Removes rubber dam and suction from patient's mouth.

"Mr. Thompson, I'm stopping everything right now. Please don't worry — I'm right here with you. I'm going to sit you up a little so you're more comfortable."

Positions patient in a semi-recumbent position — backrest at approximately 45 degrees. Does not lay patient flat and does not sit patient fully upright.

"Can you tell me — on a scale of one to ten, how bad is this pain right now?"

Calls to the dental assistant: "I need you to bring me the emergency kit immediately, and stay in this room with me."

---

Rapid Focused History

"Mr. Thompson, I need to ask you a few quick questions. Where exactly is the pain? Does it go anywhere — down your arm, your jaw, your shoulder?"

Listens as patient confirms central chest pain radiating to the left arm.

"Is this your usual angina pain, or does this feel different to you?"

Listens as patient confirms it feels worse than his normal angina.

"On your one to ten scale, where is your normal angina — and where is this right now?"

"Have you taken your GTN spray at all today? Do you have it with you?"

Notes the patient's colour, breathing rate, level of distress, and whether he is diaphoretic. Notes the patient appears pale and sweaty.

---

GTN Administration & First Assessment (Inflection Point 1)

"I'm going to give you your GTN spray now — this is the same medication you use at home. Open your mouth slightly for me. I'm going to spray it under your tongue."

Administers glyceryl trinitrate 400 micrograms, one puff sublingually. Notes time.

"Try to keep that under your tongue. I'm going to watch you closely for the next five minutes. Please let me know straight away if the pain gets worse, if you feel dizzy, or if you feel sick."

Monitors patient continuously. Checks pulse and respiratory rate. Does not leave the room.

At five minutes: pain has not resolved. Patient reports pain is still seven out of ten. Remains diaphoretic.

"Mr. Thompson, the spray hasn't settled your pain the way it normally would. I'm now going to treat this as a heart attack until we know otherwise — that is the safest thing I can do for you."

---

STEMI Protocol — Acute MI Management (Inflection Point 2)

Directs assistant: "Call triple zero now — tell them we have a sixty-five-year-old male with severe central chest pain not responding to GTN, possible acute MI. Give them our address."

"Mr. Thompson, I'm calling an ambulance right now. I want you to stay as calm as you can. I am not leaving your side."

Retrieves aspirin from emergency kit.

"I'm going to give you an aspirin tablet — three hundred milligrams. I need you to chew it slowly, not swallow it whole. Are you allergic to aspirin? Do you have any stomach ulcers or active bleeding?"

Confirms no contraindications. Administers aspirin 300 mg — instructs patient to chew.

Checks oxygen saturation with pulse oximeter. Notes SpO₂ is 93%.

"Because your oxygen reading is a little low — below ninety-four percent — I'm going to give you some oxygen through a mask. This will help support your heart."

Applies oxygen via non-rebreather mask at 4 to 6 litres per minute, titrating to achieve SpO₂ of 94 to 98%. Reminds assistant: oxygen is NOT given routinely — only because SpO₂ is below 94 percent, as per TG4 guidelines. Hyperoxia can be harmful in MI.

Does NOT administer a second dose of GTN. Notes patient appears hypotensive — BP felt to be dropping on pulse assessment. GTN is contraindicated if the patient is or becomes hypotensive, as it will further reduce blood pressure and risk cardiovascular collapse.

Continues monitoring pulse rate, respiratory rate, and level of consciousness every two minutes. Does not offer food, water, or any further dental treatment.

---

Communication, Reassurance & Handover

"Mr. Thompson, I know this is frightening, and I want you to know you're in safe hands. We've given you aspirin and oxygen, and the ambulance is on its way. The most important thing right now is that you stay still and try to breathe calmly."

"Is there someone I can call for you — a family member or your carer?"

When paramedics arrive, provides clear verbal handover: "This is Mr. Thompson, sixty-five years old, known stable angina on atenolol and GTN as needed. He developed central chest pain radiating to the left arm during dental treatment at approximately eleven-fifteen. Pain was rated eight out of ten, worse than his usual angina. One dose of GTN 400 micrograms was given sublingually at eleven-fifteen — no resolution at five minutes. Aspirin 300 milligrams was chewed at eleven-twenty-two. Oxygen commenced at four litres per minute — SpO₂ was 93 percent, now reading 96 percent. No second GTN given — concerned about hypotension. He has not lost consciousness. No known aspirin allergy."

Documents time of onset, all medications given with doses and times, vital sign observations, and ambulance call time in the clinical notes.

ME5
Seizure / Epileptic Episode in the Dental Chair
Category:** Medical Emergency | **Time:** 11 min | **Difficulty:** Exam-ready

CASE SUMMARY

Known epileptic patient (on sodium valproate) has a generalised tonic-clonic seizure during routine scaling. Patient has never had a seizure in the dental chair before. Candidate must manage the seizure correctly and know when to escalate.

CANDIDATE BRIEF

32-year-old known epileptic (generalised epilepsy, sodium valproate 500mg BD). During routine scaling, she suddenly becomes rigid, then begins rhythmic jerking of all four limbs. Manage this emergency.

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

Immediate management — INFLECTION 1: Do NOT restrain

"Stop immediately. Remove all instruments from the mouth. Do NOT put anything in the mouth — this is a common myth. You cannot swallow your tongue, and forcing objects in risks injury to patient and staff."

Remove instruments. Call for help. Lower the chair to flat position if safe. Turn patient onto their side (recovery position) if possible — reduces aspiration risk.

During the seizure (protect, don't intervene):

  • Protect from injury: move nearby hard items, pad head if possible
  • Do NOT restrain — can cause injury
  • Note the time seizure starts

Post-ictal phase (1.5 min) — INFLECTION 2: Monitoring

After jerking stops (usually 1–3 minutes):

  • Recovery position
  • Airway assessment — look, listen, feel
  • Supplemental oxygen
  • Allow post-ictal confusion to resolve (patient may be drowsy, confused for up to 30 min)
  • Monitor vitals

Call 000 if:

  • Seizure lasts >5 minutes (status epilepticus)
  • Second seizure without regaining consciousness between (status epilepticus)
  • Patient does not regain consciousness within 10 minutes
  • Injury sustained
  • First-ever seizure
  • Pregnancy

Communication when conscious:

"You had a seizure during your appointment. You're safe now, everything is okay. This is a common occurrence for some people with epilepsy. I want to monitor you here for a little while before you leave. Is there someone we can call to come and pick you up? You shouldn't drive today."

Future appointments (1 min)

  • Confirm patient is well-controlled on medication
  • Morning appointments (most seizures occur with fatigue/stress — avoid late afternoon)
  • Ensure patient has taken their medication that day
  • Have midazolam intranasal/buccal available for future appointments in case of seizure

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Removes instruments, does NOT put anything in the mouth
  2. ✅ Does NOT restrain
  3. ✅ Times the seizure
  4. ✅ Recovery position post-ictally
  5. ✅ Oxygen in post-ictal phase
  6. ✅ Calls 000 if >5 min or status epilepticus criteria
  7. ✅ Doesn't let patient drive home
  8. ✅ Plans future appointments appropriately (medication check, morning slot)

TG4 ALERTS

Do NOT put anything in the mouth during a seizure — TG4: no airways, no fingers, no bite blocks. Causes dental and hand injuries; the patient cannot swallow their tongue.
Status epilepticus — Seizure >5 min or no recovery between seizures = 000 + midazolam IM/IV (hospital). Midazolam buccal 10mg can be given in primary care if available.
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • "Seizure management: do NOT restrain. Do NOT put anything in the mouth. Clear the area of hazards, cushion the head, time the seizure. Place in recovery position post-ictally. Oxygen. Call 000 if: >5 minutes, no known epilepsy, first seizure, second seizure, injury, slow recovery."
  • "Post-ictal phase: expected confusion and drowsiness — normal. Monitor until fully orientated. Do not discharge without an escort. Do not drive."
  • "Status epilepticus (>5 min): buccal midazolam 10mg or IM midazolam — dental practices should have this in the emergency kit if treating epileptic patients."
  • "Phenytoin interaction: enzyme inducer — affects doxycycline, metronidazole, ciprofloxacin, carbamazepine. Phenytoin also causes gingival hyperplasia — increased perio care needs."
Patient Reframes
  • "(Post-seizure) Please don't be embarrassed — this is a medical event, not something you chose or caused. You're safe, you're with us, and we managed it correctly. Let's make sure someone can take you home."
  • "The important thing right now is that the seizure has stopped and you're coming round. I want to stay with you until you're fully orientated."
Curveball Deflectors
  • "Should I have given something to bite on?" → "No — that's one of the most persistent myths about seizure first aid. It's dangerous: people don't swallow their tongues during seizures, and forcing something between clenched teeth risks broken teeth and injury to both the patient and the rescuer."
  • "Could it have been caused by the local anaesthetic?" → "Intravascular LA injection can cause CNS excitation at toxic doses — but a true epileptic seizure from a correctly dosed and aspirated injection is very rare. Given the patient has known epilepsy, this is most likely a breakthrough seizure rather than an LA complication."
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ▶
STAGE: Immediate Recognition and Instrument Removal

Narrates immediately stopping all dental work.

"Stop — she's seizing. I need help in here now."

Removes all instruments from the patient's mouth immediately, including scalers, mirrors, and suction tip. Does not attempt to place anything back into the mouth — no airway adjuncts, no bite blocks, no fingers. Calls loudly to the dental assistant.

"Pass me nothing for the airway — do NOT put anything in her mouth. You cannot swallow your tongue. Forcing anything in risks fracturing her teeth, injuring her jaw, and injuring our hands. This is a common myth and we do not act on it."

Activates the emergency call system or instructs the assistant to call 000 on standby. Notes the time on the clock.

"Time check — seizure started at [states the time]. We need to be counting."

Reclines the dental chair to the flat position smoothly, only if this can be done without placing the operator in the path of the jerking limbs. Moves the bracket tray, spittoon arm, and any hard equipment away from the patient's body. Cushions or cradles the head lightly to prevent it striking the headrest during rhythmic jerking.

"Do not hold her down. Do not restrain her limbs. Restraint causes fractures and dislocations. We protect — we do not intervene."

---

During the Seizure — Protect and Monitor

Stands clear, maintains visual observation, and keeps talking calmly to assistant.

"Keep timing. Move the bracket tray fully away. Put your hand between her head and the headrest — just gentle padding, nothing forceful."

Continues to watch the tonic-clonic phase. Notes character of movements — generalised, all four limbs involved, consistent with her known generalised epilepsy and her sodium valproate history.

"She's a known epileptic on sodium valproate 500 milligrams twice daily. This is within her diagnosis. We manage and monitor unless criteria for 000 are met."

Criteria stated aloud for the benefit of the assistant and the examiner.

"We call 000 immediately if the seizure lasts more than five minutes — that is status epilepticus. We also call if she has a second seizure without regaining consciousness between them, if she does not regain consciousness within ten minutes post-ictally, if there is significant injury, or if this were her first-ever seizure. None of those apply yet — we keep timing."

---

Post-Ictal Management

Jerking ceases at approximately ninety seconds to two minutes. Narrates transition to post-ictal care.

"Seizure has stopped. Time noted. Moving her into the recovery position now."

Rolls the patient onto her left side, supporting her head, ensuring her airway is open. Performs airway assessment — look, listen, feel for breath sounds and chest rise.

"Airway is clear, she is breathing. Bringing oxygen now."

Applies oxygen via a non-rebreather mask or simple face mask at 8 to 10 litres per minute.

"She will be confused and drowsy — this is the post-ictal phase and can last up to thirty minutes. We do not rush her. We stay with her, monitor her breathing, and allow her to come around naturally."

Monitors respiratory rate, colour, and level of consciousness continuously. Does not leave the patient unattended.

---

Communication Once the Patient Regains Consciousness

Patient begins to rouse and appears confused. Speaks calmly and directly.

"Hello — can you hear me? You're okay. You're safe. My name is Dr [name] and you're still in the dental chair. You had a seizure during your appointment today. Everything is under control and we're looking after you."

Allows the patient time to process. Does not overwhelm her with information.

"You don't need to worry about anything that happened. This can happen with epilepsy, and you haven't been harmed. I'd like you to rest here for a little while longer so I can make sure you're feeling steady before we think about what's next."

Pauses, then addresses transport.

"Is there someone we can call for you — a family member or a friend who could come and pick you up? It's important that you don't drive today. After a seizure, it's not safe to drive, and I'd like someone to be with you at home."

---

Future Appointments and Follow-Up Planning

Once the patient is stable and conversation is appropriate, addresses ongoing care.

"Before we book your next appointment, I'd like to ask — had you taken your sodium valproate this morning as usual? Skipping doses is one of the most common triggers for breakthrough seizures, so it's something we'll check each time going forward."

"When we see you again, I'll book you in for a morning appointment. Fatigue and stress can lower your seizure threshold, so a morning slot when you're well rested is much safer. We'll also confirm you've taken your medication on the day."

"I'll also make sure we have intranasal or buccal midazolam available in the clinic as part of our emergency kit going forward — the buccal dose is ten milligrams — so that if a seizure were to exceed five minutes, we can act immediately while waiting for the ambulance."

"I'd also recommend you let your neurologist or GP know this happened today. A breakthrough seizure is worth reviewing — it may mean your medication level or regimen needs to be assessed."

Closes warmly.

"You've been very brave today. We'll take good care of you. Is there anything you'd like to ask me right now before we get someone to come and be with you?"

ME6
Hypoglycaemia — Unconscious Diabetic Patient
Category:** Medical Emergency | **Time:** 11 min | **Difficulty:** Exam-ready

CASE SUMMARY

Type 1 diabetic patient becomes unresponsive in the dental chair. Blood glucose 2.1 mmol/L. Candidate must manage unconscious hypoglycaemia correctly.

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

Recognition (1 min)

Patient found unresponsive. DRSABCD:

  • D — Danger (clear)
  • R — Response (none → unconscious)
  • S — Send for help / Call 000
  • A — Airway (open, maintain)
  • B — Breathing (yes)
  • C — Circulation (pulse present, weak and rapid)
  • D — Defibrillation (not needed — pulse present)

Blood glucose check

2.1 mmol/L = severe hypoglycaemia

Management — INFLECTION 1: Do NOT give oral glucose to an unconscious patient

"Patient is unconscious → cannot give oral glucose. Aspiration risk is immediate."

First-line:

  • Glucagon 1mg IM (lateral thigh or deltoid) — if available in emergency kit
  • Call 000 simultaneously

If glucagon not available:

  • 000 and maintain airway until paramedics arrive with IV dextrose

If patient regains consciousness (within 10–15 min of glucagon):

  • Give oral fast-acting glucose (juice, glucose tablets)
  • Then long-acting carbohydrate (sandwich, biscuit)
  • Do not leave alone
  • Call patient's GP or diabetes team
  • Do NOT proceed with dental treatment today

Communication post-recovery — INFLECTION 2

"You had a very low blood sugar episode and lost consciousness briefly. We gave you a glucagon injection which brought your sugar back up. An ambulance is on the way to check on you — this is standard protocol for any episode like this. Do you have someone we can call?"

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ DRSABCD systematic approach
  2. ✅ Do NOT give oral glucose to unconscious patient
  3. ✅ Glucagon 1mg IM as first-line in unconscious hypoglycaemia
  4. ✅ Calls 000 simultaneously
  5. ✅ Oral glucose + long-acting carbs once conscious
  6. ✅ Does not proceed with treatment; arranges GP follow-up

TG4 ALERTS

Never give oral glucose to an unconscious patient — TG4: aspiration risk. Glucagon IM is the only pre-hospital option for unconscious hypoglycaemia. All dental practices should stock glucagon.
Glucagon dose: 1mg IM in adults. Works within 10–15 min. If no response, maintain airway until paramedics.
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • "Unconscious hypoglycaemia: ABC first, call 000. Do NOT give oral glucose to an unconscious patient — aspiration risk."
  • "Glucagon 1mg IM into lateral thigh — standard response. Allow 10–15 minutes for effect (glucagon stimulates hepatic glycogenolysis). Monitor BSL. If no response in 10 minutes → second dose or IV glucose (paramedics)."
  • "Oral glucose gel to buccal mucosa ONLY if patient has a protected airway and semi-conscious gag reflex — not truly unconscious."
  • "Post-recovery: complex carbohydrate meal essential (prevents rebound hypoglycaemia), no driving, GP review same day, do not reschedule dental appointment until diabetes management reviewed."
Patient Reframes
  • "(Post-recovery) Your blood sugar dropped too low — hypoglycaemia. The injection we gave you told your liver to release its own sugar, which is what brought you round. You need to eat something substantial now and see your GP today to review your medication."
  • "Glucagon is in our emergency kit for exactly this reason — you're safe. This is manageable. But I want to make sure we understand why it happened so it doesn't happen again."
Curveball Deflectors
  • "Can't you just put sugar in her mouth?" → "Only if she's conscious enough to swallow safely. She's not responsive enough for that right now — the sugar could go into her lungs. The glucagon injection is the correct treatment here: it stimulates her own liver to release glucose, which is much safer."
  • "She had breakfast this morning." → "Hypoglycaemia can happen even after a meal if the insulin or medication timing is off, or if the dental appointment caused stress-related glucose changes. The BSL reading is what tells us what's happening — let me show you the number."
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ▶
STAGE: Recognition and DRSABCD Assessment

Notices patient is slumped and unresponsive in the dental chair. Steps back immediately.

"Let me make sure the area is safe first — I can see no electrical hazards, no sharps on the floor, the chair is stable. The environment is clear."

Approaches the patient, places hands firmly on both shoulders and calls loudly: "Hello? Can you hear me? Open your eyes! Squeeze my hand!"

No response. Patient is unconscious.

"I need help in here right now — call triple zero immediately, tell them we have an unconscious adult at this address, and bring the emergency kit and AED to me now."

Tilts the head back gently, lifts the chin, and visually inspects the mouth. Airway is open and clear. Looks, listens, and feels for breathing for ten seconds.

"Breathing is present — I can see chest rise and feel air movement."

Checks the carotid pulse for ten seconds.

"Pulse is present — it feels weak and rapid. No defibrillation is needed at this point."

Positions the patient supine with legs slightly elevated to support perfusion. Retrieves the glucometer from the emergency kit and performs a fingertip blood glucose check.

"Blood glucose is 2.1 millimoles per litre. This is severe hypoglycaemia. That is the cause of this loss of consciousness."

---

Critical Decision — Airway Protection and First-Line Treatment

"This patient is unconscious. I absolutely cannot give anything by mouth — no juice, no glucose gel on the tongue, no glucose tablets. The airway is unprotected and the risk of aspiration is immediate. Oral glucose is contraindicated in an unconscious patient."

Opens the emergency kit and retrieves the glucagon kit.

"I have glucagon available. This is the correct first-line treatment for unconscious hypoglycaemia in a pre-hospital setting. I am going to give one milligram intramuscularly now."

Exposes the lateral thigh, identifies the vastus lateralis, and administers glucagon one milligram IM using the reconstituted kit.

"Glucagon one milligram IM has been given to the lateral thigh. The time is noted. Glucagon works by stimulating hepatic glycogenolysis — I expect a response within ten to fifteen minutes. I will continue to monitor the airway, breathing, and circulation every two minutes while we wait for triple zero to arrive."

Maintains a head-tilt chin-lift, monitors chest rise, and rechecks the pulse every two minutes. Places the patient in a left lateral position if any vomiting appears imminent, while maintaining airway patency.

"000 has been called. I am staying with this patient. If there is no response to glucagon within fifteen minutes and paramedics have not yet arrived, I will maintain the airway and continue monitoring until they do — IV dextrose will be their first-line intervention."

---

Recovery and Post-Conscious Management

Patient begins to stir at approximately twelve minutes. Eye contact is re-established and the patient can follow simple commands.

"Welcome back. You are safe. You are in the dental chair. My name is Dr Chen. You had a very low blood sugar and you lost consciousness briefly. I gave you an injection called glucagon which has brought your sugar back up. Can you tell me your name? Can you squeeze my hand?"

Once the patient is fully alert and able to swallow safely, offers oral fast-acting glucose.

"I would like you to have this glass of orange juice now — about 150 to 200 millilitres. Sip it slowly. Once you have had that, I want you to eat something longer-lasting — here is a sandwich — to make sure your blood sugar stays stable."

Rechecks blood glucose at fifteen minutes post-recovery and confirms a rising level.

---

Communication, Safety Net, and Closing

"You had a hypoglycaemic episode — your blood sugar dropped to 2.1, which is well below the safe range. That is what caused you to lose consciousness. The glucagon injection we gave you reversed it, and your sugar is coming back up now. An ambulance is still on its way — that is standard protocol whenever someone loses consciousness, and I would like the paramedics to assess you before you go anywhere."

"We will not be doing any dental treatment today. Your body has had a significant stress response and it is not safe to continue. Is there someone I can call for you — a family member or a carer?"

"I would like you to contact your GP or your diabetes specialist today, or certainly before your next appointment, so they can review your insulin dosing and identify what may have triggered this episode. Please do not drive home — you need someone with you."

Documents the time of onset, blood glucose reading, glucagon dose and route, time of recovery, and all observations in the patient record. Ensures the emergency kit is restocked and the incident is reported as per the practice's emergency protocol.

"Please take care of yourself today. We will be in touch to reschedule once your team has reviewed your diabetes management."

ME7
Stroke Recognition (FAST) + Emergency Response
Category:** Medical Emergency | **Time:** 11 min | **Difficulty:** Exam-ready

CASE SUMMARY

68-year-old patient with hypertension suddenly develops facial droop, arm weakness, and slurred speech during a routine crown appointment. Candidate must recognize stroke using FAST, call 000, and manage correctly.

CANDIDATE BRIEF

68-year-old patient with known hypertension and atrial fibrillation (on warfarin) suddenly stops responding normally during crown try-in. They appear confused, their face looks unequal, and when asked to raise both arms, the left arm drifts down. Speech is slurred. Manage this emergency.

EXAMINER CONTEXT

Patient can respond but is confused and frightened. Left-sided weakness. Slurred speech. Blood pressure (if checked) is 190/110. Denies headache (haemorrhagic stroke has sudden headache; ischaemic less so). Patient is on warfarin — complicates thrombolysis decision, but candidate should not manage that — just call 000 urgently.

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

Recognition — FAST — INFLECTION 1: Say the word "stroke"

"F — Face: is the face drooping? Yes — asymmetric.

A — Arms: can they raise both arms? Yes — left arm drifts down.

S — Speech: slurred? Yes.

T — Time: This is a stroke. Time to call 000 NOW."

Immediate management (first 2 minutes)

  1. Call 000 immediately — state "possible stroke, I need an ambulance urgently"
  2. Time the onset — emergency team will ask; thrombolysis is time-dependent (4.5-hour window for tPA in ischaemic stroke)
  3. Do NOT give aspirin — stroke may be haemorrhagic (warfarin patient), aspirin could worsen bleeding
  4. Do NOT give anything by mouth — dysphagia common in stroke; aspiration risk
  5. Reassure the patient — stay calm, stay with them, position comfortably (semi-recumbent or recovery if unconscious)
  6. Monitor vitals — airway, breathing, pulse until ambulance arrives

INFLECTION 2: Common mistakes

  • Do NOT give aspirin without knowing stroke type (haemorrhagic vs. ischaemic)
  • Do NOT attempt further treatment — stop all dental work
  • Do NOT let patient go to hospital by car

Communication with patient

"Something has happened that means we need to get you to hospital right away. An ambulance is coming. Please stay as still as you can and try not to worry — you're in safe hands."

What to relay to 000/ambulance:

  • Time of onset (exact)
  • FAST findings
  • Medical history (AF, hypertension, warfarin)
  • Current medications

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Uses FAST criteria explicitly and correctly
  2. ✅ States "stroke" aloud — does not hedge
  3. ✅ Calls 000 immediately
  4. ✅ Times onset (crucial for thrombolysis window)
  5. ✅ Does NOT give aspirin (haemorrhagic stroke risk — especially in warfarin patient)
  6. ✅ Does NOT give anything by mouth (dysphagia)
  7. ✅ Relays complete handover to 000/ambulance

TG4 ALERTS

Do NOT give aspirin for suspected stroke — TG4: unless stroke type confirmed as ischaemic by CT, aspirin risks worsening haemorrhagic stroke. In a warfarin patient, this is especially critical.
Thrombolysis window — 4.5 hours from onset for ischaemic stroke. Time of onset is the most critical piece of information to document and relay.
Dysphagia — Stroke commonly causes swallowing difficulty. Nothing by mouth until assessed by hospital team.

INFLECTION POINTS

PointWeakStrong
Recognition"Something seems wrong, let me wait and see"Immediately applies FAST criteria; calls stroke within 60 seconds
AspirinGives aspirin (classic error)"No aspirin — we don't know if this is bleeding or a clot, and this patient is on warfarin"
TimeNot documentedNotes exact time of onset and relays to 000
Handover"Patient unwell, send ambulance""Possible stroke, onset 10:42am, FAST positive, on warfarin, AF, hypertension, 68yo male"
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • "FAST: Face (unilateral drooping, asymmetry when smiling), Arms (unilateral weakness — one arm drifts down when both raised), Speech (slurred, confused, word-finding difficulty), Time — call 000 immediately."
  • "Time is brain: 1.9 million neurons die per minute in untreated stroke. Thrombolysis effective within 4.5 hours of onset. Do not delay emergency call to 'watch and see'."
  • "Do NOT give aspirin until CT confirms stroke type — haemorrhagic stroke makes up ~15% of strokes and aspirin is actively harmful. This decision belongs in hospital."
  • "Position: 30–45 degrees, NOT supine. Do not give food or water (dysphagia risk). Keep patient calm and reassured. Monitor airway, breathing, circulation until ambulance arrives."
Patient Reframes
  • "The combination of facial asymmetry, arm weakness, and speech difficulty is a recognised emergency pattern. I'm calling 000 now. We can work out whether it's truly a stroke in the ambulance — but we don't have time to wait and see."
  • "(To bystander) Every minute matters with a stroke. I'd rather call 000 and be wrong than not call and lose the window for treatment."
Curveball Deflectors
  • "He just looks confused — maybe he's tired." → "The facial asymmetry and arm weakness aren't signs of tiredness. Those are neurological signs that together meet the FAST criteria for stroke. We call 000 now."
  • "Shouldn't you give aspirin?" → "Not yet. About 15% of strokes are caused by bleeding in the brain — and aspirin would make that catastrophically worse. That distinction requires a CT scan in hospital. The right action is emergency services, not aspirin."
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ▶
STAGE: Recognition — Initial Assessment

The patient has become confused mid-procedure during the crown try-in. Calmly but urgently, stop all dental work immediately. Lay down the handpiece. Look directly at the patient.

"Mr. Baxter, can you hear me? I'm just going to check on you right now."

The patient responds with garbled, slurred speech and appears confused. His face looks unequal — there is a visible droop on the left side. Begin FAST assessment immediately, speaking aloud so the dental assistant can hear.

"I'm running through FAST right now. F — Face: Mr. Baxter, can you smile for me?" The patient attempts a smile and the left side of the face droops markedly. "Facial asymmetry — yes, that's positive. A — Arms: Mr. Baxter, I need you to lift both arms out in front of you and hold them there." The patient raises both arms; the left arm drifts downward within seconds. "Left arm drift — positive. S — Speech: Mr. Baxter, can you say 'the sky is blue'?" The patient's response is slurred and unclear. "Slurred speech — positive. T — Time: This is a stroke. Time to act is right now."

---

Immediate Emergency Response — Calling 000

"Sarah, call 000 immediately — tell them we have a 68-year-old male with a suspected stroke. I need the time — note it on the chart right now."

Check the clock. Note the exact time of onset.

"The time is 10:24 am. That is our onset time — it goes on the chart and it goes to the ambulance. Write that down."

Take the phone and speak directly to the 000 operator.

"Hello, this is Dr. [Name] calling from [practice address]. I need an ambulance urgently. I have a 68-year-old male patient who I believe is having a stroke. He has facial asymmetry on the left, left arm drift, and slurred speech — all three limbs of FAST are positive. Onset was approximately 10:24 am. His background includes hypertension and atrial fibrillation, and he is on warfarin. Please send an ambulance immediately."

Stay on the line until the operator confirms the crew is dispatched.

---

Immediate Clinical Management — What To Do and What NOT To Do

Recline the dental chair to a comfortable semi-recumbent position. Do not lay him completely flat if he remains conscious — aspiration risk is real given likely dysphagia.

"Mr. Baxter, something has happened that means we need to get you to hospital right away. An ambulance is coming. Please try to stay as still as you can. You are safe — I am right here with you and I am not going anywhere."

Monitor airway, breathing, and pulse continuously. If the patient loses consciousness, place in recovery position and reassess airway immediately.

Do not give aspirin. This patient is on warfarin with atrial fibrillation. The stroke may be haemorrhagic, and administering aspirin without a confirmed CT diagnosis risks catastrophically worsening a bleed. TG4 is explicit — aspirin is contraindicated in suspected stroke until stroke type is confirmed as ischaemic by imaging.

Do not give anything by mouth — no water, no tablets, nothing. Stroke commonly causes dysphagia and the aspiration risk is significant.

Do not attempt to continue or complete any dental procedure. Do not allow the patient or any family member to drive him to hospital. Ambulance transport only.

---

Monitoring and Handover Preparation

Continue monitoring the patient. Talk to him calmly and reassuringly throughout.

"Mr. Baxter, the ambulance is on its way. I'm going to stay right here with you. Can you squeeze my hand? Good. You're doing really well."

Check pulse rate and rhythm — note it on the chart. This patient has known atrial fibrillation; AF is a major cardioembolic risk factor for ischaemic stroke.

Prepare a written handover note for the paramedics including: exact time of onset (10:24 am), FAST findings and their laterality (left-sided face and arm), known medical history of hypertension and atrial fibrillation, current medications including warfarin, and any known allergies.

---

Paramedic Handover and Closing

When paramedics arrive, hand over clearly and concisely.

"This is Mr. Baxter, 68 years old. Onset of symptoms at 10:24 am — that gives you roughly 22 minutes. He presented with left facial droop, left arm drift, and slurred speech — positive FAST on all three criteria. History of hypertension and atrial fibrillation. He is on warfarin. No aspirin has been given. He has been semi-recumbent and conscious throughout. He has had nothing by mouth."

Hand the written note directly to the paramedic.

"The thrombolysis window is 4.5 hours from onset for ischaemic stroke — time is critical. He needs CT urgently to determine stroke type before any pharmacological intervention."

Stay with the patient until he is transferred to the stretcher.

"Mr. Baxter, these paramedics are going to take excellent care of you. You're in good hands. I'll be in touch with your family."

PD1
Nursing Bottle Caries (1–2 Year Old)
Category:** Pediatric | **Time:** 11 min | **Difficulty:** Exam-ready

CASE SUMMARY

Parent of an 18-month-old presents concerned about brown discolouration on upper front teeth. Child is given a bottle of formula at bedtime and during the night. Classic early childhood caries (ECC) / nursing bottle caries pattern. Candidate must educate the parent without blame and create a realistic prevention plan.

CANDIDATE BRIEF

Parent of an 18-month-old presents after noticing brown/black spots and what look like "holes" in the upper front teeth. The child has a bottle at night and sometimes during the night if unsettled. The lower teeth look fine. Your task: assess, diagnose, educate the parent, and create a prevention plan. Examination is limited to what you can do with a cooperative toddler (quick visual exam, no full charting).

EXAMINER CONTEXT

Parent is a first-time mother, feels guilty, and is defensive. Will say "I didn't know this was a problem" when feeding habits are raised. Will not volunteer the night bottle unless specifically asked about routine. Becomes more engaged when the candidate explains the mechanism without blaming her. Hidden concern: can the teeth be saved, or do they need to come out?

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

Opening & Rapport (1 min)

"Thank you for coming in — I know it can be hard to bring little ones in at this age. You've done exactly the right thing by getting this checked early. Before I have a look, can I ask a few questions?"

History (2 min) — INFLECTION 1: Uncover the feeding pattern gently

  • "What does [child's name] eat and drink during the day?"
  • "What about at bedtime — does he/she have a bottle or breastfeed to sleep?"
  • "Does he/she wake during the night? What do you give to settle them?"
  • "Are you using fluoride toothpaste? When did you start brushing?"
  • "Is there fluoride in your water at home?" (tank vs. tap)

Examination (1 min)

  • Upper front teeth (51, 52, 61, 62): classic nursing bottle caries pattern — upper anteriors most affected, lower anteriors relatively spared (tongue protects lower teeth from pooled milk)
  • Brown/cavitated lesions on labial surfaces, possibly cervical area
  • Lower teeth: assess for caries
  • Quick, gentle — use knee-to-knee position with parent

Diagnosis — plain language, no blame (2 min) — INFLECTION 2

"What I can see is called early childhood caries — it's a very common form of tooth decay in toddlers. Here's how it happens: when a child falls asleep with a bottle, the milk or formula pools around the upper front teeth. Milk contains natural sugars that feed the bacteria in the mouth, and when those bacteria produce acid, it sits against the teeth all night long — because saliva flow decreases during sleep. The lower teeth are protected because the tongue covers them. This is not about your parenting — it's a pattern that many parents don't know about until they see us."

Prevention Plan (2 min) — INFLECTION 3

  1. Stop the bedtime/night bottle: "This is the most important change. The bottle at night is the primary driver. Can we work toward weaning off it? Even switching to water in the bottle overnight is a significant improvement."
  2. Brushing: "Brush twice daily, morning and before bed, as soon as the first tooth appeared — or from now. Use a soft infant toothbrush and a rice-grain-sized amount of low-fluoride children's toothpaste (appropriate for under 2). You brush — don't let them do it themselves at this age."
  3. Fluoride: If tank water: "We'll apply fluoride varnish today — it's the single most effective preventive treatment for children this age. We'll do this every 6 months."
  4. Feeding on demand: "Breastfeeding on demand at night has a similar effect on teeth — it's a tougher conversation because of the feeding relationship, but after the first tooth erupts, we need to start managing it."

What happens to the teeth? — INFLECTION 4

"For the affected teeth — if the decay is limited to the outer layer, we may be able to apply Silver Diamine Fluoride today to arrest the decay. If the decay is deep, we may need to refer for treatment under sedation or general anaesthetic if your child isn't cooperative enough for fillings."

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Takes feeding history without leading or blaming
  2. ✅ Explains nursing bottle caries mechanism in plain language (pooling + acid + sleep)
  3. ✅ Explains why upper more affected than lower (tongue protection)
  4. ✅ Night bottle change as most critical intervention
  5. ✅ Correct toothpaste advice for age <2 (rice-grain, low-fluoride)
  6. ✅ Fluoride varnish for high-risk children
  7. ✅ Addresses parent's concern about tooth fate (SDF arrest vs. GA for fillings)

TG4 ALERTS

Fluoride varnish — TG4: recommended every 6 months for high-caries-risk children. Most effective preventive intervention for ECC.
Toothpaste for under 2 — Rice-grain size, low-fluoride (400–500ppm). Standard adult fluoride toothpaste (1000ppm+) should not be used for infants.

INFLECTION POINTS

PointWeakStrong
Feeding historyAsks generic questionsSpecifically asks about bedtime and night feeding — this is THE key clinical finding
Blame avoidance"You shouldn't have given a bottle at night""Many parents don't know about this — it's not about how much you care, it's about the pattern"
Key change"Cut down on sugary food""The night bottle is the main driver — switching to water overnight is the single most impactful change"
Tooth fate"We'll see how it goes""SDF today to arrest the decay; possible GA referral if restorative treatment is needed"
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • "Nursing bottle caries pattern: upper central incisors affected first and most severely (milk pools around them when bottle is held by sleeping infant); lower anteriors relatively spared (protected by tongue and saliva from submandibular glands)."
  • "Risk factors: nocturnal bottle beyond 12 months with milk/formula/juice, ad libitum breastfeeding beyond 12 months, frequent sugar exposure throughout day, delayed first dental visit."
  • "Management: eliminate nocturnal bottle — transition to water after 12 months; toothbrushing from first tooth eruption with smear of low-fluoride toothpaste (500ppm <2 years); fluoride varnish from first tooth if high risk; early referral to paediatric dentist."
  • "Safeguarding awareness: severe early childhood caries in a very young child warrants assessment of parental capacity and access to care. Document DMFT, photographic record, treatment provided."
Patient Reframes
  • "The pattern of decay I'm seeing is specifically related to the nighttime bottle — it's a very common presentation, and the good news is we can stop it progressing right now by making some changes."
  • "After 12 months, the bedtime bottle can be replaced with water. I know that sounds hard, but many parents tell me it's easier than they expected once they try."
Curveball Deflectors
  • Parent: "All children get cavities." → "Not all children do — and in a 1-year-old, decay at this stage is a sign we need to act now to protect the developing adult teeth underneath. This is preventable."
  • Parent: "They're just baby teeth." → "These teeth won't fall out until age 6–8. In the meantime, untreated abscesses can damage the adult teeth forming below them, and children in dental pain struggle to eat and sleep. We should act now."
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ▶
STAGE: Opening & Rapport

"Hello, come on in — thank you so much for bringing him in today. I know getting a toddler to a dental appointment takes quite a bit of effort, and I want you to know you've done exactly the right thing by having this checked early. My name is Dr. Chen, I'm the dentist here today. Before I have a look at those teeth, would you mind if I asked you a few questions first? It helps me understand what's going on."

Smiles warmly at both parent and child. Offers child a toy or mirror to hold to build comfort. Maintains relaxed, non-judgmental tone throughout.

"And what's his name? Oliver — lovely. Hi Oliver! What a big boy."

---

History

"So you've noticed some brown discolouration and what look like little holes on his upper front teeth — is that right? How long have you noticed that for?"

Listens attentively without interrupting.

"What does Oliver eat and drink during the day? Does he have meals with the family, or mostly formula still?"

Pauses to allow full answer.

"And at bedtime — does Oliver have a bottle to help him settle and go to sleep? What's usually in it — formula, milk, juice?"

"Does he wake during the night at all? And if he does, what do you give him to settle him back down — another bottle?"

"That's really helpful, thank you. Now, what about teeth cleaning — are you brushing his teeth at home? When did you start, and what toothpaste are you using?"

"One more thing — do you have town water at home, or tank rainwater? I ask because fluoride in tap water makes a real difference for little teeth."

---

Examination

"Alright, let's have a look at those teeth. The easiest way to examine a toddler this age is what we call a knee-to-knee position — I'll sit facing you, and if you could sit Oliver on your lap facing you, then gently lay him back so his head rests on my knees. That way he still feels safe with you, and I can get a good look. Is that okay?"

Conducts gentle visual examination. Notes classic nursing bottle caries pattern: brown-to-cavitated lesions on the labial and cervical surfaces of the upper central and lateral incisors — teeth 51, 52, 61, and 62 — with the lower anterior teeth relatively spared. Notes no apparent involvement of lower incisors.

"Good boy Oliver, that was brilliant. All done."

---

Diagnosis — Plain Language, No Blame

"Thank you for letting me have a look. So what I can see is a condition we call early childhood caries — it's actually one of the most common things I see in toddlers this age, and I want to be clear from the start: this is not about anything you've done wrong. Most parents simply aren't told about this until they come in and see it."

"Here's what happens. When Oliver falls asleep with a bottle of formula, the milk pools around the upper front teeth. Milk contains natural sugars, and the bacteria that live in everyone's mouth feed on those sugars and produce acid. Normally saliva washes that acid away, but during sleep our saliva flow drops right down — so the acid sits against the teeth all night. Over weeks and months, that's enough to break down the enamel and cause decay."

"Now, you might wonder why the bottom teeth look fine. That's actually the tongue — it sits over the lower teeth during feeding and sleeping, and physically shields them from the pooled liquid. The upper front teeth have no such protection, which is exactly the pattern I'm seeing today."

"The good news is you've caught this early enough that we have real options."

---

Prevention Plan

"The single most important change we can make is the night bottle. That bottle at bedtime — and especially any bottle during the night — is the primary driver of this decay, because it's happening when his mouth is most vulnerable. I know that's often how little ones settle, and I'm not asking you to do it overnight, but can we work toward weaning him off it over the next two to four weeks? Even if that feels difficult right now, switching to plain water in the bottle overnight would already be a significant improvement — water causes no acid attack at all."

"For brushing: from today, we brush twice daily — morning and last thing before bed. Use a soft infant toothbrush and a rice-grain-sized amount of low-fluoride children's toothpaste — the ones formulated for under-twos, which contain around four hundred to five hundred parts per million of fluoride. Please don't use adult toothpaste on Oliver yet — the fluoride concentration is too high for this age group. And you do the brushing — at eighteen months he simply doesn't have the coordination to do it effectively himself."

"Because you're on tank water at home, Oliver isn't getting fluoride in his drinking water, which puts him in a higher-risk group. So what I'd like to do today is apply a fluoride varnish to his teeth — it takes about thirty seconds, it's completely safe, and it's the most effective preventive treatment we have for early childhood caries. We'll repeat that every six months going forward."

---

Treatment Options & Safety Net / Closing

"For the teeth that are already affected — because the decay appears to be in the early-to-moderate stage — I'd like to apply something called Silver Diamine Fluoride today. It's a liquid we paint onto the affected areas, it arrests the decay and stops it progressing. It will turn the decayed areas dark or black, and I want you to expect that — it looks a little confronting but it means it's working. The healthy tooth structure stays its normal colour."

"If the decay were to progress deeper, or if Oliver becomes distressed and we can't manage things in the chair, we may need to refer for treatment under sedation or general anaesthetic. That's not where we are today, but I want you to know the pathway so there are no surprises."

"I'd like to see Oliver again in six weeks so I can check how the arrested areas look and repeat the fluoride varnish. Between now and then — if you notice a tooth breaking, any swelling near the gum, or Oliver seems to be in pain — please call us straight away and we'll see you the same day."

"You've done a wonderful thing coming in today. Oliver is lucky to have you looking out for him. Do you have any questions for me before we get started?"

PD2
Fissure Sealant Counseling + Application (8-Year-Old)
Category:** Pediatric / Preventive | **Time:** 11 min | **Difficulty:** Exam-ready

CASE SUMMARY

8-year-old with newly erupted first permanent molars (6s), deep fissures, and a high caries risk history. Parent asks what fissure sealants are and whether they're necessary.

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

History (1.5 min)

  • Caries history (previous fillings in baby teeth = high risk)
  • Dietary and OH habits
  • Fluoride access

Examination

  • 16, 26, 36, 46: deep, narrow fissures — stained but not cavitated on probing/laser detection
  • No caries evident in fissures yet — optimal timing for sealants

Explaining fissure sealants (2 min) — INFLECTION 1

"The back molars that have just come through have very deep grooves on the biting surface. These grooves are so narrow that even a single toothbrush bristle can't get into them to clean them. Bacteria and food get trapped in there and cause decay from the inside, even if you're brushing well. A fissure sealant is a thin plastic coating that we paint into those grooves — it fills them in, sealing the bacteria out and making the surface smooth and easy to clean. It's quick, painless, and no needles required."

Evidence base (1 min)

"Studies show fissure sealants reduce caries in permanent molars by up to 70–80% over 5 years. Given your child's history of decay in baby teeth, I'd strongly recommend them."

Procedure explanation (1 min)

"We clean the tooth surface, apply a mild gel for 15 seconds to help the sealant bond, rinse, dry, apply the sealant liquid, and set it with a blue light in about 30 seconds. The whole thing takes under 5 minutes per tooth. Your child will feel a slight pressure but no pain."

Longevity and monitoring (1 min)

"Sealants last 3–5 years on average, sometimes longer. We check them at every 6-monthly visit and top them up if needed. They're not permanent but they're worth it during the high-risk cavity years — ages 6–14."

Cost and alternatives (1 min)

"Cost is typically $30–$60 per tooth. The alternative is to wait and monitor — but if decay starts in those fissures, it often progresses quickly before it's visible, and the filling would cost significantly more."

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Explains fissure anatomy and why brushing can't reach them
  2. ✅ States the evidence base (70–80% caries reduction)
  3. ✅ Explains procedure clearly — no needle, painless, quick
  4. ✅ Discusses longevity and need for monitoring
  5. ✅ Presents cost-benefit compared to eventual filling

TG4 ALERTS

Optimal timing — Apply fissure sealants as soon as the molar is fully erupted and accessible (age 6–7 for first molars, 11–13 for second molars). Don't wait for caries to develop.
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • "Evidence: pit and fissure sealants reduce occlusal caries by ~70–80% in at-risk permanent molars (Cochrane review). Most effective when applied within 2 years of eruption — age 6–8 for first molars, 11–13 for second molars."
  • "Material: resin-based preferred over GIC in cooperative children (superior retention at 2–4 years). GIC acceptable if isolation is challenging. Complete moisture isolation is critical — contamination before bonding = failure."
  • "Application: acid etch 15–30 sec, rinse, dry, apply sealant, light cure, check occlusion (remove high spots), confirm complete coverage of all pits and fissures."
  • "Monitoring: check at every recall for partial loss or complete debonding. Reseal if needed. Evidence shows partial sealants still provide some protection."
Patient Reframes
  • "The grooves on these adult molars are very deep and narrow — the toothbrush bristle physically can't reach the bottom of them no matter how well you brush. The sealant fills those grooves and creates a smooth surface that's easy to clean."
  • "This is one of the most evidence-based preventive treatments in dentistry. For children at caries risk, it's a straightforward way to protect these important teeth for years."
Curveball Deflectors
  • Parent: "Does it contain BPA?" → "Current evidence shows the amount of BPA from sealants is negligible — far below any level associated with health effects. The benefit of preventing decay in permanent molars significantly outweighs any theoretical risk. I can show you the evidence if you'd like."
  • "Will it hurt?" → "Not at all — no needles, no drilling. We paint a liquid on the tooth and shine a special light on it for 20 seconds. Most children find it completely fine."
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ▶
STAGE: Opening and Introduction

Candidate greets the parent and child warmly, ensures both are seated comfortably, and establishes rapport before beginning.

"Hello, I'm Dr. [Name]. It's lovely to meet you both. And what's your name? Eight years old — brilliant. I'm just going to have a little look at your teeth today and have a chat with your mum about how we can keep them really strong and healthy. Is that okay with you? Great, you're doing wonderfully already."

Turning to the parent: "Before I do the examination, I'd like to ask you a few quick questions about Liam's dental history, if that's alright."

---

History Taking

"Has Liam had any fillings before? ... Right, so he's had fillings in a few of his baby teeth — that's really helpful to know. That does tell us he's had some experience with decay, so we want to be extra careful protecting his adult teeth as they come through."

"How often would you say he's brushing? ... And is he using a fluoride toothpaste? ... Good. What about his diet — does he have sugary drinks or snacks during the day, outside of mealtimes? ... Okay, so the occasional juice and some after-school snacks. That's quite typical for his age but worth keeping in mind."

"Is there fluoride in your local water supply, or is he on tank water? ... Right. And has he been having regular check-ups? Wonderful, that's excellent."

---

Clinical Examination

Candidate examines all four first permanent molars — teeth 16, 26, 36, and 46 — using a probe, mirror, and laser detection device.

"I can see that all four of his big adult molars have come through nicely. I'm just going to take a closer look at the biting surfaces."

Notes deep, narrow fissures with mild staining on all four teeth. No cavitation is detected on probing and laser detection values remain within sound tooth thresholds. Records findings carefully.

"Everything looks intact — no holes yet, which is exactly where we want to be. This is actually the perfect time to talk about something called fissure sealants, and I'd like to explain what they are and why I think they'd be really beneficial for Liam."

---

Explaining Fissure Sealants

"The big back molars that have just come through have very deep grooves on their biting surfaces — we call these fissures. These grooves are so narrow that even a single toothbrush bristle cannot get down into them to clean properly. Bacteria and food particles get trapped deep inside and can cause decay from the inside out, even when your child is brushing beautifully twice a day. It's not a failure of brushing — it's simply the anatomy of the tooth."

"A fissure sealant is a thin, tooth-coloured plastic coating that we paint directly into those grooves. It fills them in completely, sealing the bacteria out and turning that rough, grooved surface into a smooth one that's easy to clean. There's no needle involved, no drilling, and no pain — Liam will just feel a little pressure and taste something slightly minty. The whole process takes under five minutes per tooth."

"In terms of the evidence, studies consistently show that fissure sealants reduce the risk of decay in permanent molars by up to seventy to eighty percent over five years. Given that Liam has already had fillings in his baby teeth, his risk of developing decay in these adult teeth is higher than average. For him, I'd strongly recommend sealing all four molars now, while there's no decay present, because this is the optimal window."

"As for the procedure itself: we clean the tooth surface thoroughly, apply a mild conditioning gel for about fifteen seconds to help the sealant bond, rinse it off, dry the tooth completely, paint on the sealant liquid, and then set it with a blue light in about thirty seconds. That's it — done."

---

Longevity, Cost, and Alternatives

"Sealants typically last between three and five years, sometimes longer, depending on how they wear. We check them at every six-monthly visit, and if we see any chips or gaps, we simply top them up. They don't last forever, but they give us protection through the highest-risk years for decay, which are roughly ages six to fourteen — exactly where Liam is right now."

"In terms of cost, you're typically looking at around thirty to sixty dollars per tooth. So for all four molars, that might be one hundred and twenty to two hundred and forty dollars in total. I know that's a consideration, but compare that to the cost of a filling, which can be three hundred dollars or more per tooth, plus the fact that once a tooth has a filling, it's weakened and may need further treatment down the track. Sealants are genuinely one of the most cost-effective things we can do in dentistry."

"The alternative is to monitor and wait — but the concern with that approach is that decay in deep fissures often progresses significantly before it becomes visible on an X-ray or to the eye. By the time we can see it, the damage is already quite advanced. I'd rather we protect now than repair later."

"Do you have any questions at all? ... You're very welcome. I think Liam is going to be absolutely fine — he's already been so brave today. Shall we go ahead and get started?"

PD3
Avulsed Permanent Tooth — Playground Injury (10-Year-Old)
Category:** Pediatric / Emergency | **Time:** 11 min | **Difficulty:** Exam-ready

CASE SUMMARY

Parent phones from school — 10-year-old knocked out upper left central incisor (21) in playground 20 minutes ago. Tooth is in a container of water. Parent is panicking. Candidate must manage the avulsion over the phone then in clinic.

CANDIDATE BRIEF

A parent calls you saying "My son knocked his tooth out at school, someone picked it up and put it in a cup of water — what do I do?" You confirm the tooth is permanent (he's 10). Manage the emergency — first by phone instructions, then as they arrive at your practice 15 minutes later.

EXAMINER CONTEXT

Parent is panicking, speaking fast, not following instructions well. Will ask "Can it be put back in?" repeatedly. Tooth has been in a cup of cold water for 20 minutes (suboptimal storage). If candidate gives correct storage instructions (milk or saliva), parent complies.

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

Phone management — INFLECTION 1: Speed matters, 60-min window

"I need you to listen carefully — we have a chance to save this tooth but we need to act quickly.

  1. Pick up the tooth by the white part (the crown) — NOT by the root. Don't scrub or rinse it
  2. If the tooth is dirty, rinse it VERY GENTLY under cold water for less than 10 seconds — nothing more
  3. Best option: put the tooth in a glass of milk (not water — water damages the root cells)
  4. If no milk: the child can hold the tooth in their mouth, between the cheek and gum — saliva is fine
  5. If neither: wrap it in cling film to keep it moist
  6. Get here NOW — every minute matters"

In-clinic management (5 min) — INFLECTION 2: Replant within 60 min

Examination:

  • Tooth: permanent central incisor, open or closed apex? (closed = better prognosis if replanted)
  • Socket: blood clot present? Gently irrigate socket with saline
  • Extra-oral dry time: 20 min in water (suboptimal — PDL cells stressed but may still viable)

Replantation procedure:

  1. Local anaesthetic
  2. Gently irrigate socket with saline to clear clot
  3. Replant tooth: hold by crown, gentle firm pressure until seated (feel click)
  4. Check occlusion — may need slight adjustment
  5. Flexible splint across adjacent teeth — 7–10 days for uncomplicated avulsion
  6. Antibiotics: amoxicillin 7 days (TG4)

Post-replant instructions (1.5 min)
