"Soft diet for 2 weeks. Chlorhexidine rinse twice daily. Come back in 1 week for splint check, then 2 weeks for splint removal. Then monthly X-rays for 3 months, then 6-monthly for 1 year."

Prognosis discussion — INFLECTION 3

"I want to be honest with you. The tooth has been out for 20 minutes and stored in water — water is not ideal because it damages the root surface cells. We've replanted it, but the most likely outcome is that the root will gradually resorb over months to years. In the best case scenario it stays for several years — long enough for your son to grow to adulthood and then get an implant. Either way, replanting is always worth trying."

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Phone instructions: hold by crown, milk or saliva, not water, come NOW
  2. ✅ Correctly identifies 60-minute replantation window
  3. ✅ Replantation technique: irrigate, seat firmly, flexible splint 7–10 days
  4. ✅ Antibiotics post-replantation (amoxicillin 7 days)
  5. ✅ Honest prognosis discussion (water storage = reduced PDL viability)
  6. ✅ Long-term monitoring schedule (monthly X-rays)

TG4 ALERTS

Storage medium — TG4/IADT: Milk is first-line. Water is damaging (hypotonic — causes cell lysis). Saliva second-best.
Antibiotics post-avulsion — TG4: amoxicillin 7 days (adult 500mg TDS; weight-based in children). Reduces infection and inflammatory resorption risk.
Flexible splint — TG4/IADT: 7–10 days for uncomplicated avulsion. Rigid splinting increases ankylosis and replacement resorption.
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • "Extra-alveolar time is the single most important prognostic factor for avulsed permanent teeth. <60 minutes in appropriate storage = viable PDL cells = good prognosis. Every minute dry kills more periodontal ligament cells."
  • "Storage media in order: HBSS (Hanks BSS, Save-a-Tooth kit) > milk > saline > saliva (buccal vestibule) > water (hypotonic — kills PDL cells, but better than dry storage)."
  • "Replantation protocol: gentle rinse (saline if contaminated), replant in correct orientation, flexible splint (0.016 inch wire + composite) for 2 weeks, tetanus status, amoxicillin 500mg TDS 7 days, patient education on monitoring."
  • "Open apex (immature tooth): revascularisation possible — do NOT do RCT immediately; monitor for vitality; if pulp necrosis confirmed → revascularisation protocol or apexification. This is the main advantage of younger patients."
Patient Reframes
  • "At 10, his root is still forming — that means the blood supply has a real chance of re-establishing itself inside the tooth, which adult teeth can't do. His age is working in his favour here."
  • "Even if complications develop later — which some replanted teeth do experience — replanting now keeps the space and preserves the bone. That matters enormously for any future treatment options."
Curveball Deflectors
  • "Someone said to put it in water." → "Water damages the cells on the root surface because it's the wrong salt concentration. Milk is the best household emergency storage — it's pH-balanced and isotonic enough to keep those cells alive. You've done the right thing getting here quickly."
  • "Will it definitely survive?" → "I can't guarantee it — some replanted teeth do develop complications over months or years. But not replanting is the one decision I know leads to tooth loss. Replanting gives it the best possible chance, and complications can be managed as they arise."
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ▶
STAGE: Phone Assessment — Establishing Urgency

"Hello, this is Dr [Name] speaking. I can hear you're worried — let's work together right now to give your son the best chance of saving this tooth. Can I just ask quickly — how old is your son?" Parent confirms 10 years old. "Good. At 10, this is almost certainly an adult tooth, and the great news is that adult teeth can be put back. But we need to move fast — we have roughly 60 minutes from when the tooth came out, and 20 of those are already gone. I need you to listen very carefully."

Phone Instructions — Immediate First Aid

"First — pick up the tooth, but only touch the white part at the top, the crown. Do not touch the root — that's the pointy end. Do not scrub it, do not use soap, and do not wrap it in tissue or cloth. If it looks dirty, hold it under cold running water for less than ten seconds — no more than that, and nothing else.

Now, here is the most important thing: take the tooth out of that cup of water right now. Water actually damages the cells on the root surface — it will reduce our chances of saving the tooth the longer it sits there. The best thing to store it in is milk — full-fat or skim, either is fine. Put the tooth straight into a glass of milk and bring it with you. If you cannot get milk in the next two minutes, have your son hold the tooth in his mouth, between his cheek and his gum — his own saliva is a safe storage medium. Please do not try to push the tooth back in yourself.

I am clearing my schedule right now. Get in the car and come directly to [practice address]. Every single minute matters — please come immediately."

In-Clinic Examination and Replantation

Parent and child arrive approximately 15 minutes later. Candidate greets them calmly, reassures the child, and moves directly to the dental chair.

"Well done for getting here so quickly. Let me have a look at everything now." Examines tooth: permanent maxillary left central incisor, root appears fully formed suggesting a closed apex — prognosis guarded but replantation is still clearly indicated. Total extra-oral dry time now approximately 35 minutes in water — PDL cells stressed but replantation remains worthwhile.

Examines socket: clot present, soft tissue relatively intact, no alveolar fracture detected on palpation.

"I'm going to numb the area so this is comfortable for you. You'll feel a little pinch first." Administers local anaesthetic — infiltration to buccal and palatal of 21 region, using lignocaine 2% with 1:100,000 adrenaline, aspirating before injection, keeping within the 4.5 mg/kg weight-based maximum.

Gently irrigates socket with sterile saline to remove the clot and any debris. Holds tooth by crown only, orients it correctly, and with gentle, steady pressure seats the tooth into the socket until a tactile click is felt and the crown is level with the adjacent teeth. Checks occlusion — no premature contact detected.

Places a flexible composite-and-wire splint from tooth 22 to 11, ensuring the splint is passive and allows physiological mobility. "We'll leave this splint in place for seven to ten days — not longer, because keeping it rigid for too long can actually cause the root to fuse to the bone, which we want to avoid."

Prescribing and Post-Replantation Instructions

"I'm prescribing amoxicillin for your son. Given his weight I'll calculate the dose carefully — this will be taken three times a day for seven days, and it's important to finish the full course. It helps reduce infection and also reduces the risk of the root breaking down. If he has any rash, hives, or swelling after the first dose, stop immediately and call me or go to emergency."

"For the next two weeks, please keep him on soft foods only — nothing hard, crunchy, or chewy. He should rinse gently with a chlorhexidine mouthwash twice a day — after breakfast and before bed. No contact sport while the splint is in."

"I want to see him back in one week for a splint check and review, and then again at two weeks to remove the splint. After that we'll take X-rays every month for three months, then every six months for a year. These X-rays are essential — they let us catch any root resorption early."

Prognosis Discussion and Closing

"I want to be completely honest with you both, because you deserve to know what to expect. The tooth was stored in water for roughly 35 minutes before arriving here. Water is unfortunately a damaging storage medium — it causes the cells on the root surface to swell and break down, which makes long-term survival harder. The most likely outcome over months to years is that the root will gradually resorb — meaning the body will slowly break it down.

In the best-case scenario, the tooth remains functional for several years — potentially long enough for your son to reach adulthood, at which point a dental implant becomes a very good long-term option. Even a tooth that lasts five or six years is worth having — it maintains the bone, preserves the space, and lets him grow normally.

Replanting this tooth was absolutely the right decision, and you did the right thing by getting here quickly. Do you have any questions at all?" Provides written post-operative instructions and practice contact details. "Please don't hesitate to call us if anything concerns you — any pain, swelling, or darkening of the tooth."

PD4
Molar Incisor Hypomineralisation (MIH)
Category:** Pediatric | **Time:** 11 min | **Difficulty:** Exam-ready

CASE SUMMARY

9-year-old presents with sensitivity and white/yellow/brown patches on first permanent molars and incisor. Parent didn't realise this was a dental condition — thought it was "just staining." Candidate must diagnose MIH, explain it, and plan age-appropriate management.

CANDIDATE BRIEF

A 9-year-old presents with sensitivity (especially to cold and sweet) and visible discolouration on upper and lower first permanent molars and one upper central incisor. The changes include chalky white and yellow-brown areas on the cusps and some breakdown of tooth structure on one molar. Your task: diagnose, explain, and plan management.

EXAMINER CONTEXT

Parent has been blamed by a previous dentist for "not brushing properly." Is defensive. Will reveal the sensitivity significantly affects the child's ability to eat. Child has not had the affected teeth treated yet. Will be relieved when candidate explains this is a developmental condition, not caused by poor OH.

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

History (1.5 min)

  • Sensitivity: cold, sweet, air? How long?
  • Effect on diet/daily life?
  • Brushing history and OH — INFLECTION 1: Establish that OH is adequate, ruling out caries as primary cause
  • Was the child born prematurely or had a serious illness in the first 4 years of life?

Examination

  • First permanent molars (16, 26, 36, 46): demarcated opacities (white, cream, yellow, brown), possible cusp breakdown
  • Upper central incisor: smaller opacity on middle third
  • No widespread caries; plaque control appears adequate

Diagnosis — INFLECTION 2: Name and explain it

"What your child has is called Molar Incisor Hypomineralisation — MIH for short. It's a developmental condition, meaning it happened during the formation of these permanent teeth — before they even came through, between birth and age 3. The result is enamel that is structurally weaker and more porous than normal.

This is NOT caused by poor tooth brushing. Many parents are wrongly told that, and it's not fair."

Management (2 min)

  • Mild: High-fluoride toothpaste (5000ppm), Tooth Mousse (CPP-ACP), fluoride varnish every 6 months, fissure sealants
  • Moderate: Composite resin restoration; premedicate with paracetamol — these teeth are hypersensitive to LA
  • Severe: Stainless steel crown (Hall technique) for full cuspal coverage; or extraction with orthodontic timing if severely compromised

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Correctly identifies MIH as developmental (not caries, not poor OH)
  2. ✅ Explains timing of disruption (birth–3 years)
  3. ✅ Stages management by severity
  4. ✅ Aware of hypersensitivity to LA — premedicate

TG4 ALERTS

High-fluoride toothpaste for MIH — 5000ppm prescription strength for remineralisation. Prescribe specifically — not available OTC for children.
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • "MIH: hypomineralisation affecting 1–4 first permanent molars and/or incisors; enamel has normal thickness but reduced mineral content — appears as creamy/yellow/brown demarcated opacities, chalky texture, prone to post-eruptive breakdown under occlusal forces."
  • "Severity grading: mild (intact surface, opacities only) → moderate (sensitivity, small breakdown) → severe (extensive breakdown, restoration failure, pain affecting function). Severity guides treatment approach."
  • "Restorative challenge: composite and GIC bond poorly to hypomineralised enamel. Stainless steel crown (Hall technique) provides best outcomes for severely affected molars. Composite requires careful technique with extended bonding protocols."
  • "Extraction timing: severely affected FPMs in a patient with good developing second molars — consider strategic extraction timed with second molar eruption (discuss with orthodontist). Avoids repeated restorations that keep failing."
Patient Reframes
  • "This isn't caused by anything you ate or didn't do — it happened when the tooth was forming, before it even erupted, from a disturbance during enamel development. It's not a consequence of brushing or diet."
  • "These teeth are sensitive because the enamel isn't as hard as normal — even cool water can hurt. That's why we need to act quickly; treating them early gives us more options."
Curveball Deflectors
  • Parent: "Why are they this bad already?" → "MIH-affected teeth break down quickly after they erupt because the enamel is soft. That rapid breakdown is unfortunately typical of this condition — it's why acting now while there's tooth structure to work with is important."
  • "Can you just fill them?" → "We can — but I want to be honest: fillings in MIH-affected teeth can fail more quickly than in normal teeth because the surrounding enamel doesn't bond well. I'll use the approach most likely to last and set realistic expectations."
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ▶
STAGE: Opening and History

"Hi, I'm Dr. — lovely to meet you both. And this must be — how are you going today? Nine years old — that's a great age. Don't worry, we're just going to have a chat first before I look in your mouth."

Turning to the parent: "I can see from the notes there's been some sensitivity and some colour changes on a few of the new teeth. I'd love to hear more about that in your own words — when did you first notice something was different?"

Listens to parent describe white, yellow-brown patches and sensitivity. "And has there been any pain or sensitivity with cold drinks, sweet food, or even just breathing in cold air?" Pauses for response. "How long has that been going on — weeks, months?" Pauses. "Is it affecting what he's eating, or has he been avoiding certain foods because of it?"

"Now I want to ask about his brushing routine — who brushes, how often, and what toothpaste are you using?" Listens. Establishes that brushing is twice daily with standard toothpaste and oral hygiene is adequate.

"This is really important — I want to reassure you straight away that this does not look like a problem caused by poor brushing. I'll explain more in a moment. One more question: was there anything significant around the time he was born or in his first three or four years — a premature birth, a serious illness, a high fever that needed hospital care, or any medication for a prolonged period?" Listens and notes response.

---

Clinical Examination

"Alright, let's have a look. I'm just going to count your teeth and check everything carefully — you tell me if anything feels sore."

Examines all four first permanent molars — 16, 26, 36, 46. Notes demarcated opacities ranging from chalky white through cream to yellow-brown, predominantly on the cuspal thirds. Observes structural breakdown on the mesiobuccal cusp of tooth 36. Notes the upper right central incisor has a smaller, well-demarcated white opacity on its middle third. Plaque levels are low. No widespread carious lesions. Periapical radiographs mentally indicated for the affected molars to assess pulpal involvement and root development.

"You've been very brave — well done."

---

Diagnosis and Explanation

Turning to the parent: "So I can tell you exactly what this is, and I want you to hear this clearly — what your child has is called Molar Incisor Hypomineralisation, or MIH for short. It's a developmental condition, meaning the problem happened before these teeth even came through the gum — during the time the enamel was forming, somewhere between birth and around three years of age. Something during that window — it could be an illness, a fever, low oxygen at birth, or sometimes we genuinely never find a specific cause — disrupted the way the enamel mineralised. The result is enamel that is structurally weaker and more porous than normal. It looks different, it can break down, and it causes real sensitivity."

"I want to say this directly: this is NOT caused by poor tooth brushing. Many parents are told that, and it is simply not accurate. Your child's brushing is fine. This was happening before he even had the chance to brush these teeth."

To the child: "Your teeth are just built a little differently on the inside — it's nothing you did wrong."

---

Management Plan

"The good news is we have a clear plan, and it depends on how badly each tooth is affected. I'll walk you through it."

"For all of the affected teeth, I want to start with strengthening straight away. I'm going to prescribe a high-fluoride toothpaste — 5,000 parts per million fluoride. That's prescription strength; you can't buy it over the counter for children, so I'll write that for you today. Use a smear twice a day after normal brushing and don't rinse it off. I'll also apply a fluoride varnish in the chair today and repeat that every six months. I'll also recommend Tooth Mousse — it contains a milk-derived protein called CPP-ACP that helps remineralise weaker enamel — apply it after brushing at night."

"For the molars where the enamel is intact but weakened, I'll place fissure sealants to protect the surface from further breakdown and reduce sensitivity."

"For tooth 36 where there is already some structural loss, I'll need to place a composite resin restoration to rebuild the cusp and cover the exposed, sensitive dentine. Now — and this is very important — teeth affected by MIH are notoriously difficult to get numb. The inflamed dentinal tubules mean local anaesthetic sometimes doesn't work as well as we'd expect. So before we do any restorative work, I'll ask you to give him a weight-appropriate dose of paracetamol about an hour before the appointment — that helps significantly. I'll take my time with anaesthesia and use a slow, careful technique."

"If we find down the track that tooth 36 keeps breaking down despite restorations, the most protective option is a stainless steel crown — it gives full coverage and is extremely durable for children his age. And in the most severe scenario, if a molar is too compromised to save, extraction can be considered — but timing matters, and we'd involve an orthodontist in that decision."

---

Safety Net and Closing

"I'd like to see him every six months minimum — these teeth need close monitoring while he's still growing. If sensitivity gets worse between appointments, or if a tooth chips or breaks, please call us straight away rather than waiting."

"Are there any questions? I know that's a lot to take in." Pauses and listens. "You've done nothing wrong — you brought him in, we've found this, and we have a really solid plan. He's going to be just fine."

PD5
Space Maintainer After Premature Primary Molar Loss
Category:** Pediatric | **Time:** 11 min | **Difficulty:** Exam-ready

CASE SUMMARY

8-year-old's lower left primary second molar (75) was extracted 3 months ago. Adjacent teeth are drifting. Space maintainer discussion required.

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

Examination & History

  • Which primary molar lost (75 = holds space for 35, second premolar, eruption ~11–12 years)
  • How much drift has occurred (measure with calipers)
  • OPG: position of developing 35

Explaining space maintainers — INFLECTION 1

"When a baby tooth is lost early, the teeth on either side drift into the gap, narrowing the space needed for the adult tooth. A space maintainer is a small fixed appliance cemented to the tooth next to the gap — it has an arm that holds the space open until the adult tooth is ready to come through. Think of it as a placeholder."

Types

  • Band-and-loop: most common for single posterior space
  • Lingual arch: if multiple spaces lost bilaterally
  • Removable appliance: less reliable (child must comply)

When NOT to place

  • Drift has already closed most of the space → ortho referral instead
  • Permanent tooth erupting within ~6 months
  • Premolars will be extracted for orthodontic reasons anyway

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Checks OPG for permanent tooth eruption timeline
  2. ✅ Explains the placeholder concept in plain language
  3. ✅ Band-and-loop as standard approach
  4. ✅ Knows the contraindications
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • "Indications: premature loss of primary molar before permanent successor eruption is imminent. Without a space maintainer, mesial drift of the first permanent molar and distal drift of the primary canine/adjacent teeth close the space within weeks to months."
  • "Type: band-and-loop space maintainer for single tooth loss; lingual arch for multiple posterior losses; Nance appliance for bilateral maxillary molar loss."
  • "Timing: place as soon as possible after extraction — ideally at the same appointment or within 2–3 weeks. Delay allows space loss to begin rapidly."
  • "Removal: when the permanent successor is radiographically within 2–3mm of eruption and visible clinically (6-monthly OPG monitoring). Remove too early = space loss recurs; leave too long = impedes eruption."
Patient Reframes
  • "Baby teeth hold space for adult teeth — like bookends on a shelf. Without the tooth, the ones either side move into the gap. The space maintainer acts as that bookend until the adult tooth is ready to come in."
  • "It's a simple wire-and-band device — not orthodontic treatment, just space preservation. The payoff is avoiding orthodontic correction down the line."
Curveball Deflectors
  • "Won't the adult tooth just push things out of the way?" → "Unfortunately not — adult teeth erupt into whatever space is available. If the space has closed, the tooth erupts out of position and needs braces to correct it. The space maintainer prevents that problem from occurring."
  • "How long does it stay in?" → "Until the permanent tooth is close to erupting — we'll check with an X-ray every 6 months. When it's within a few millimetres of breaking through, we remove the maintainer and let the tooth come in naturally."
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ▶
STATION: PD5 — Space Maintainer After Premature Primary Molar Loss

---

Opening and Rapport

"Hello, I'm Dr. [Name]. I'm one of the dentists here today. Are you Mum or Dad? Lovely to meet you. And this must be — what's your name, mate? Great. Come on in and have a seat. Is it okay if I have a chat with both of you today about what's been happening and what we can do to help? Wonderful."

"Now, I understand that one of your back baby teeth was taken out about three months ago — is that right? The lower left one. I want to make sure we look after the space that tooth was holding, so today I'd like to explain what's happening and talk through our options. Before I do, can I ask you a couple of quick questions?"

---

History and Clinical Assessment

"Has anything been bothering you in that area since the tooth came out? Any soreness, or have you noticed anything feeling different when you bite? Good. And are you cleaning that area well with your toothbrush? Excellent."

Examines the lower left quadrant. Notes mesial drift of the lower left first permanent molar (36) and distal drift of the lower left primary first molar (74) into the extraction space. Measures the remaining space with calipers and compares to the contralateral side.

"I can see the teeth on either side of the gap have already started to drift toward each other a little — that's actually quite common when a baby tooth is lost early. That's exactly why I want to speak with you today."

Reviews the OPG. Identifies the developing lower left second premolar (35) at an early stage, with root formation just beginning, indicating the adult tooth is unlikely to erupt for approximately three to four years — well outside the six-month window where intervention would be unnecessary.

"Looking at the X-ray, the adult tooth that belongs in that space — your second premolar — is still developing under the gum and won't be ready to come through until you're around eleven or twelve years old. So we have quite a few years where that space needs to be protected."

---

Explaining the Problem and the Concept of a Space Maintainer

"Let me explain what's happening in simple terms. When a baby tooth is lost early, the teeth on either side tend to drift into the gap — a bit like books on a shelf sliding together when one book is removed. If that happens, there won't be enough room for the adult tooth when it's ready to come through, and that can cause it to come in crooked or become stuck under the gum. A space maintainer is a small fixed appliance we cement onto the tooth next to the gap — it has a little metal arm that sits across the space and holds it open until the adult tooth is ready to come through on its own. Think of it as a placeholder — it doesn't do anything active, it simply keeps the space exactly as it needs to be."

---

Appliance Selection and Treatment Plan

"The type I'd recommend in your situation is called a band-and-loop space maintainer. It's the most commonly used appliance for a single missing back tooth. We fit a small metal band around the tooth next to the gap — in this case, the first permanent molar — and a smooth wire loop extends across to rest against the tooth on the other side. It's fixed in place with dental cement, so you don't need to take it in and out, and it won't get lost. Once we cement it, you'll barely notice it's there."

"I do want to mention that if the space had already closed significantly, a space maintainer wouldn't help — we'd need to refer to an orthodontist to open the space back up first. And if the adult tooth were due to erupt within the next six months or so, we wouldn't place one at all because it would be coming through on its own very soon. In your situation, though, the timing is right and there's still adequate space to maintain, so placing a band-and-loop now is the correct approach."

"To place it, we'll need two appointments — one to take a mould of the teeth, and a second to fit and cement the appliance. Each visit is straightforward and shouldn't be uncomfortable at all."

---

Aftercare, Review, and Safety Net

"Once it's in place, it needs very little maintenance from you. The main thing is to keep cleaning around it carefully — a soft toothbrush and fluoride toothpaste, making sure to brush along the wire and under it where you can. Try to avoid very sticky lollies or chewing gum, as these can pull the band loose. If it ever comes off or feels loose, come and see us straight away, because even a short time without it can allow the teeth to drift."

"We'll check the appliance every six months at your regular visits. When we can see on an X-ray that the adult tooth is close to erupting — typically when its root is about two-thirds formed — we'll remove the space maintainer so the tooth can come through naturally."

"Do you have any questions for me? You're doing a great job looking after your teeth. We'll get you both booked in for the impressions appointment and go from there. Any concerns at all, please don't hesitate to call us."

PD6
Dental Neglect — Safeguarding Concern
Category:** Pediatric / Ethics | **Time:** 11 min | **Difficulty:** Exam-ready

CASE SUMMARY

7-year-old presents with multiple untreated carious teeth, appears thin, has bruising on the arms in multiple stages of healing, and is withdrawn. Mother is defensive. Candidate must manage the appointment and navigate mandatory reporting obligations.

CANDIDATE BRIEF

A 7-year-old girl presents with her mother. Multiple grossly decayed teeth requiring extractions, no dental appointment for 3 years, appears underweight, multiple small bruises on both forearms in varying stages of healing. The mother says "she's just clumsy." The child is very quiet and avoids eye contact. Your task: manage this appointment, including any safeguarding concerns.

EXAMINER CONTEXT

Mother is defensive. The child is quiet and doesn't speak unless spoken to directly. Mother interrupts when you ask the child questions. If the candidate separates the child from the mother, the child says "Mummy says I'm not supposed to talk about home." Bruising has distribution inconsistent with being clumsy (bilateral, multiple healing stages).

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

Clinical assessment (1.5 min) — Complete dental examination fully. Document all findings.

Addressing the bruising — INFLECTION 1: Ask, don't accuse

"I noticed some bruising on [child]'s arms today — as part of my routine, I ask about how children get injuries like this. Can you tell me what happened?"

Listen. Does the explanation fit the distribution and healing stages?

Briefly assessing the child separately — INFLECTION 2

"Would it be okay if I chat with [child] for a minute while you grab a glass of water?"

Open-ended questions: "How are you going? How are things at home?"

Recognising indicators of concern — INFLECTION 3

  • Dental neglect: multiple grossly decayed untreated teeth + 3-year gap
  • Physical: bilateral bruising, multiple healing stages (not consistent with clumsiness)
  • Behavioural: withdrawn, restricted by parent from speaking
  • Parental: dismissive, defensive

"I have a mandatory reporting obligation under Australian law. My role is not to investigate or determine if abuse has occurred — that's the job of child protection authorities. My obligation is to report when there is reasonable suspicion about a child's safety."

Communicating to the parent

Low-to-moderate risk: "I'm required by law to report any concerns I have about a child's wellbeing. I want you to know I'm doing this because I care about [child]'s safety."

High immediate risk: Do NOT inform parent — contact child protection authorities directly.

Documentation

Factual and objective: exact quotes, descriptions of bruising (size, location, colour stage), child's behaviour, parent's responses. No interpretation — only describe.

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Completes dental assessment fully
  2. ✅ Asks about bruising non-judgmentally
  3. ✅ Briefly separates child using age-appropriate language
  4. ✅ Identifies multiple indicators
  5. ✅ States mandatory reporting obligation clearly (reasonable suspicion, not certainty)
  6. ✅ Does NOT investigate themselves
  7. ✅ Documents factually and objectively

TG4 ALERTS

Mandatory reporting — Australian law: report at reasonable suspicion, not certainty. You do not need proof.
Dental neglect is reportable — Untreated grossly decayed teeth in a child with access to care = a form of neglect under child protection law.
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • "Dental neglect = persistent failure to meet a child's basic oral health needs — it is a form of child neglect, not just poor compliance or socioeconomic hardship. It warrants a safeguarding response."
  • "Recognition: severe untreated caries causing pain or infection, multiple extractions under GA, repeated missed appointments with ongoing disease, visible distress not acted upon by carers."
  • "Response: do NOT confront parents accusatorially. Document thoroughly — DMFT, clinical photos (with consent), timeline of presentations. Discuss with senior colleague. In Australia, mandatory reporting obligations vary by state — know your state's threshold."
  • "Referral: most states have a child protection pathway (CPIU or equivalent). The dental team's role is to refer when there are reasonable grounds for concern — not to investigate or judge."
Patient Reframes
  • "(With parent) I can see your child has been in a lot of pain — I want to help sort this out. Can we talk about what's been happening and what's made it difficult to get help sooner?"
  • "I'm not here to judge anyone — I'm here to make sure this child gets the care they need."
Curveball Deflectors
  • "Am I accusing the parents?" → "A safeguarding referral is not an accusation — it's making sure people trained to assess child welfare review the situation. My job is to refer when I have concerns; it's not my job to investigate or reach conclusions."
  • "What if I'm wrong?" → "It's better to refer in good faith and be wrong than not to refer and miss a child in harm. The standard is 'reasonable grounds for concern' — not certainty. AHPRA and child protection legislation protect practitioners who refer in good faith."
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ▶
STAGE: Opening and Clinical Assessment

Greets the child warmly and at eye level before acknowledging the mother. "Hi there — you must be Lily. I'm Dr. Chen, it's really lovely to meet you. And you must be Lily's mum — thank you for bringing her in today." Speaks directly to the child throughout. "Lily, I'm just going to have a look at your teeth today. I'll explain everything I'm doing before I do it, okay? Nothing will be a surprise."

Conducts a full, systematic intraoral examination. Observes and documents multiple grossly decayed primary and permanent teeth, visible pulpal involvement in multiple quadrants, generalised plaque accumulation, and inflamed gingivae. Notes the three-year gap in dental attendance. Records exact tooth numbers, caries staging, and clinical photographs with consent. During the general assessment, observes the child is thin, avoids eye contact, and gives only one-word answers. Notes multiple small bruises on both forearms in varying stages of healing — some yellowish-green, some purple-blue, bilaterally distributed.

"Lily, your teeth have been working really hard and a few of them need some extra help from me. We're going to make a plan to fix that together, okay?"

---

Addressing the Bruising — Non-Judgmental Enquiry

Transitions calmly and without alarm. Addresses the mother in a conversational, non-accusatory tone. "I also do a general health check for all the children I see — it's just part of my routine. I noticed some bruising on Lily's arms today. Can you tell me how she got those?"

Listens carefully. Mother responds: "Oh, she's just clumsy — always bumping into things." Maintains a neutral expression. Notes the explanation — bilateral distribution, multiple healing stages, and the absence of a specific incident — is not consistent with a simple mechanism. Does not challenge or interrogate the mother. "Thank you for telling me. Kids do get bumps and scrapes — I just like to note it down." Documents the mother's exact words verbatim.

---

Brief Separation of the Child

"Lily's been such a great patient — Mum, would it be okay if I just showed Lily how to use the squirty water tool for a minute? There's a water fountain just out in the hallway if you'd like to grab a drink while we finish up." Uses a gentle, natural pretext to create a brief, uncoerced moment alone with the child.

Crouches to child's level. Speaks softly and without leading questions. "Lily, you're doing really well. How are you going overall? Do you like school?" Pauses. "How are things at home?" Observes Lily's response — minimal verbal engagement, avoidance of eye contact, no spontaneous disclosure. Does not press further. "That's okay. I'm here if you ever want to tell me anything — anything at all." Ends the brief interaction warmly before the mother returns.

---

Recognising and Naming the Safeguarding Indicators

Internally consolidates the clinical picture. Dental neglect is established: grossly decayed, untreated teeth across multiple teeth, no dental care for three years in a child old enough to have been brought to a dentist. Physical indicators: bilateral bruising on both forearms in multiple stages of healing — inconsistent with accidental injury from a single mechanism. Behavioural indicators: the child is withdrawn, avoids eye contact, and is reluctant to speak in the parent's presence. Parental indicators: dismissive explanation, defensive posture, appears to discourage the child from speaking independently.

Concludes that there is reasonable suspicion — not certainty, but reasonable suspicion — that this child may be experiencing neglect and possibly physical harm. Under Australian mandatory reporting legislation, reasonable suspicion is the threshold. Proof is not required. The role is to report, not to investigate.

---

Communication with the Mother and Mandatory Reporting

Assesses that this situation does not indicate immediate high-risk danger requiring silent referral. Speaks to the mother calmly and with care, choosing words deliberately. "I want to be completely open with you. As a dentist in Australia, I have a legal obligation to report any concerns I have about a child's wellbeing to the relevant child protection authority. I want you to know that I'm doing this because I genuinely care about Lily's safety — it's not an accusation, and it's not a judgment of you as a parent. My job is simply to make sure Lily is looked after."

Pauses to allow the mother to respond. Remains calm regardless of her reaction. "A child protection worker will be in contact — their role is to support families, not to punish them. I'd encourage you to be open with them."

---

Documentation and Safety Net

Documents immediately and precisely. Records exact tooth numbers and caries staging, clinical photographs, child's weight and general appearance, the location, approximate size, and colour stage of each bruise — for example: "three bruises on the right forearm measuring approximately 1–2 cm, yellowish-green consistent with healing over seven to fourteen days; two bruises on the left forearm, purple-blue consistent with more recent injury." Records the mother's exact words in quotation marks. Records the child's behaviour verbatim and observationally. Uses no interpretive or emotive language — only objective, factual description.

Contacts the statutory child protection authority — in this jurisdiction, the relevant state child protection service — and makes a formal report before the end of the working day. Notifies the practice principal. Retains all documentation securely. "Lily, it was really great to meet you today. I'm going to do everything I can to help you feel better — with your teeth and everything else."

PD7
Child Dental Anxiety — Previous Traumatic Experience
Category:** Pediatric / Communication | **Time:** 11 min | **Difficulty:** Exam-ready

CASE SUMMARY

10-year-old presents extremely anxious after a traumatic extraction experience at another dentist age 6. Refuses to sit in the chair, crying. Candidate must manage anxiety using non-pharmacological behaviour management before any treatment.

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

Greet outside the surgery — INFLECTION 1: Don't start in the chair

Meet the child in the waiting room. Get on their level. Speak to them first, not the parent.

"Hi [name]. Before we go in, can I tell you what we're going to do today? Just a look — nothing else."

Tell-show-do in the waiting room (2 min)

Demonstrate the mirror, light, and suction on yourself or the child's hand before any instruments near the mouth.

Acknowledge the fear — INFLECTION 2

"It sounds like you had a scary experience before. That makes sense. My job today is to show you we can do this slowly and safely, at your pace."

Stop signal + perceived control — INFLECTION 3

"If at any time you want me to stop, raise your hand and I'll stop immediately. Promise."

This is the most important behaviour management tool — perceived control.

Distraction

"What's your favourite show? We can put it on the TV here while I have a quick look."

Positive reinforcement

Praise each small step: "That was really brave. Well done."

Avoid: "Don't worry" (dismisses fear); "It won't hurt" (broken promise risk).

If refusal is complete

"That's okay. We don't have to do anything today. Would it be okay if we just sit in the chair?" Build trust over multiple visits — this is valid dental management.

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Meets child outside surgery, speaks to child first
  2. ✅ Tell-show-do before any instruments
  3. ✅ Acknowledges previous trauma without dismissing
  4. ✅ Establishes stop signal (perceived control)
  5. ✅ Praises each step
  6. ✅ Accepts refusal as valid management

TG4 ALERTS

Never say "It won't hurt" — Say: "I'll do everything I can to keep you comfortable, and if anything feels wrong, raise your hand."
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • "Assess severity first: validated tool (Modified Child Dental Anxiety Scale or Facial Image Scale for younger children); identify the specific fear trigger — injection, drill, smell, loss of control, confinement."
  • "Non-pharmacological hierarchy: tell-show-do, positive reinforcement, distraction, child-controlled stop signal, voice control. Exclude parent if presence increases anxiety in some children."
  • "Pharmacological: oral midazolam pre-medication (0.2–0.5mg/kg, max 15mg, 30–45 min before); inhalational sedation with N2O from age 3–4 if mask-tolerant; IV sedation or GA for extensive treatment or failed outpatient approaches."
  • "Trauma-informed framing: acknowledge the previous experience explicitly. Do not minimise. Build trust incrementally — a desensitisation visit with no treatment is a legitimate and valuable use of an appointment."
Patient Reframes
  • "I want to know what happened before — because if we understand what frightened you, we can do things differently this time. This visit doesn't have to be anything like that."
  • "Our goal isn't just to get treatment done today — it's to make sure you don't leave with a fear of dentists that stays with you for life. Working at your pace now builds something that makes every future visit easier."
Curveball Deflectors
  • Child: "I don't want the needle." → "Tell me more about that — is it the needle itself, or the feeling, or just not knowing what's coming? Because we can put a numbing cream on first so you don't feel anything before the injection."
  • Parent: "She's just being dramatic." → "Children's dental fear is real, even when it looks out of proportion to us as adults. If we force the treatment today, the next visit will likely be worse. Working with her now builds cooperation that pays off for every appointment after this."
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ▶
STAGE: Meeting the Child — Waiting Room Greeting

Candidate walks into the waiting room, crouches down to the child's eye level, and speaks directly to the child before addressing the parent.

"Hi, I'm Dr. [Name]. You must be Liam. It's really good to meet you." Smiles warmly, maintains a calm and unhurried posture. "Mum, thanks so much for bringing Liam in today — I'll make sure I keep you both in the loop the whole time."

Turns back to Liam. "Liam, before we go anywhere, I just want to have a quick chat with you out here — is that okay? I'm not going to do anything to your teeth today without telling you first. Today is just about us getting to know each other."

Pauses to let that land. "Can I ask — how are you feeling right now? A little nervous?" Listens, nods. "Yeah, that makes a lot of sense. I'd probably feel the same way."

---

Acknowledging the Previous Trauma

"Liam, your mum mentioned that you had a really scary experience at the dentist when you were little. I want you to know — that was not okay, and it makes complete sense that you'd feel nervous about coming back. What happened to you would make anyone feel that way."

Maintains eye contact, calm tone — no rushing. "My job today is completely different. We go at your pace. If you ever want to stop, we stop. Full stop. No questions asked."

Turns briefly to the parent. "Would it be alright if I showed Liam a couple of the things we use — right here, before we even think about going into the room?"

---

Tell-Show-Do in the Waiting Room

Candidate opens a small tray brought from the surgery, containing only a mouth mirror and a pen torch.

"Liam, can you see this little mirror? This is all I use to have a look inside your mouth. That's it — just a little mirror, like the ones you use at home, almost. Here — you can hold it." Hands the mirror to Liam. "Feel how smooth it is? Nothing sharp."

Picks up the pen torch. "And this is just a little light — like a torch. I'll shine it so I can see clearly. Want to shine it on your hand? Go ahead." Lets Liam hold and interact with the torch.

"That's the most I'll do today — I promise. Just that mirror, just that light, just a look. If I ever want to do anything more, I'll tell you first and ask if it's okay. Deal?"

Smiles. "You're doing so well already, Liam — I mean it."

---

Establishing the Stop Signal and Perceived Control

"Now — this is the most important thing I'm going to tell you today, so I want you to remember it. If at any point you feel uncomfortable, or you just want a break, all you have to do is raise your hand — like this." Demonstrates raising one hand. "And I stop. Immediately. No matter what I'm doing — I stop. I promise you that."

"Do you want to practise? Go on — raise your hand." Liam raises hand. "Perfect — and I stop." Pauses dramatically. "See? You're in charge, Liam. Not me. That's how we do it here."

---

Distraction, Positive Reinforcement, and Entering the Surgery

"Liam, what's your favourite show at the moment? We've actually got a TV on the ceiling in there — we can put something on while I have my little look. What do you reckon?"

Guides Liam gently toward the surgery — no pressure, walking alongside. "Would it be okay if we just sit in the big chair together first? You don't have to do anything — we can just see what it feels like."

Once seated, immediately praises. "That was really brave, Liam — seriously, well done for giving it a go."

If Liam becomes tearful or refuses to recline: "That's completely okay. We don't have to go back today. Sitting here is more than enough — and that takes real courage." Does not force any procedure.

Turns to parent at close. "We've made really great progress today. Building trust takes time, and Liam has done brilliantly. I'd like to see him again in a couple of weeks — each visit we'll go just one small step further. This is exactly how we manage things, and it works."

"Liam — you were amazing today. I'll see you again soon, yeah?"

OT1
Crossbite with Functional Shift — Early Intervention (9-Year-Old)
Category:** Orthodontics | **Time:** 11 min | **Difficulty:** Exam-ready

CASE SUMMARY

9-year-old with anterior crossbite and mandibular functional shift to the left on closure. Candidate must identify the functional shift, explain urgency, and discuss early intervention options.

CANDIDATE BRIEF

9-year-old referred with "an underbite." Tooth 21 is in crossbite and when the patient closes, the mandible shifts to the left. Skeletal pattern appears mildly Class I. Parent asks: "Does this need treatment now, or can we wait?"

EXAMINER CONTEXT

Parent wants to wait for all adult teeth. Will ask "Won't it correct itself?" Must be clearly advised that this specific situation requires early intervention — the functional shift can cause permanent asymmetric growth.

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

Explain the functional shift — INFLECTION 1: Why it can't wait

"This is different from most orthodontic issues that can wait. When your child bites down, their jaw is being forced to slide to one side every time they bite — thousands of times a day. The jaw is developing asymmetrically. Over time this can cause the jawbone to grow unevenly, creating a skeletal asymmetry that is much harder to treat in a teenager or adult. If we fix this now, while the bone is still adaptable, the jaw can correct itself."

Treatment options — INFLECTION 2

  • Tongue blade therapy: very mild cases only, if displacement is minimal and overbite favourable
  • Removable appliance with inclined plane: tips the upper tooth forward
  • Fixed 2×4 appliance: brackets on upper incisors + first molars; most reliable — my preference
  • Treatment time: 3–6 months for the crossbite. Full orthodontic assessment waits until all adult teeth are through.

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Names and explains the functional shift
  2. ✅ Explains asymmetric growth risk — the reason early intervention is essential
  3. ✅ Appropriate early options presented
  4. ✅ Distinguishes from full orthodontic treatment

TG4 ALERTS

Functional crossbite = early intervention — A crossbite with functional shift must NOT be left to wait for full permanent dentition.
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • "Anterior or posterior crossbite with functional shift: mandible deflects to accommodate premature contact in ICP vs RCP. If left untreated, asymmetric loading during growth can produce facial asymmetry and condylar growth changes."
  • "Functional shift diagnosis: compare tooth positions in RCP (retruded contact position) vs ICP (intercuspal position). If they differ, a functional shift is present."
  • "Early intervention (age 7–10): strongly indicated — this is one of the few truly time-sensitive orthodontic problems. Correction during active sutural growth is simpler, more stable, and avoids surgical correction later."
  • "Treatment: upper removable appliance with Z-spring for anterior crossbite; quad helix or rapid maxillary expansion (RME) for posterior crossbite with narrow maxilla."
Patient Reframes
  • "This is one of the few orthodontic problems where timing really matters — and your child is at exactly the right age. Correcting it now, while the bones are still growing, is much simpler. Waiting until growth is complete may mean surgery."
  • "The crossbite isn't just about how the teeth look — it's affecting how the jaw closes every single time, and that uneven loading can change the way the jaw grows."
Curveball Deflectors
  • Parent: "Can we wait until all adult teeth come in?" → "For most orthodontic problems, yes — waiting is fine. This is a specific exception. The jaw displacement on every bite affects how the bones grow during these years. Waiting until growth is complete makes this significantly harder and sometimes requires surgery."
  • "How long will it take?" → "To correct the crossbite itself, typically 3–6 months with a removable appliance. Then retention until growth is complete. The active phase is short."
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ▶
STAGE: Opening and Initial Assessment

"Hi, I'm Dr. Chen — lovely to meet you both. And this must be our patient! What's your name? Great, nice to meet you. Mum, thank you for bringing her in today. I understand you've been told she has an underbite — I want to have a good look today and explain exactly what's going on, then we can talk through what the best approach is. Is that okay with you both?"

Candidate invites the child to sit in the chair and conducts a brief extraoral examination, observing the face at rest and then asking the child to bite together slowly from open. Candidate notes the mandible deviating to the left on closure and observes tooth 21 in anterior crossbite with the mandible in the final intercuspal position.

"I'm going to ask you to open your mouth a little bit and then very slowly, slowly close all the way together — like you're biting on something soft. Perfect. Now let me have a look inside."

Candidate examines intraorally, confirming tooth 21 is in crossbite, checks for a positive overjet on that tooth in the retruded contact position, assesses the overbite as favourable, and notes the skeletal pattern appears mildly Class I.

---

Explaining the Functional Shift to the Parent

"Thank you for being so patient. I want to take a moment to explain what I've found, because this is actually different from the usual sort of orthodontic concern that can wait until all the adult teeth come through.

What your daughter has is called a functional shift. When she starts to close her mouth, her teeth don't quite fit together cleanly — one of the upper front teeth, this one here, sits behind the lower teeth instead of in front. Because of that, every time she bites down, her jaw is forced to slide across to the left to find a comfortable position. She's doing this automatically, without even realising it.

Now, here is why this matters: she is doing that shift thousands of times every day — every time she swallows, every time she chews, every time she closes at rest. The jaw is still growing at this age, and bone responds to the forces placed on it. If the jaw is being pushed to one side repeatedly over months and years, it can start to grow unevenly. That means the asymmetry that right now is just a muscular habit could become a true skeletal asymmetry — a difference in the shape of the jaw itself — and that is significantly harder and more involved to treat in a teenager or an adult. While the bone is still adaptable, as it is right now at nine years of age, we have the best chance of the jaw correcting itself once we free the bite."

---

Answering the Parent's Question Directly

"So to answer your question directly — no, I would not recommend waiting. Most orthodontic treatment absolutely can wait until the adult teeth are through, and I'll recommend a full orthodontic assessment at that point. But a crossbite with a functional shift is one of the situations where early intervention is genuinely indicated. The window we have right now is the right window to act."

---

Presenting Treatment Options

"There are a few ways we can address this, and I'd like to walk you through them.

The simplest approach is something called tongue blade therapy — where the child uses a flat stick to apply gentle pressure to tip the tooth forward several times a day. I'll be honest with you: this only works in very mild cases where the displacement is minimal and the bite depth is favourable. Based on what I see today, I think we need something a little more reliable.

The second option is a removable appliance — a plate with a small inclined ramp built into it that guides the upper tooth forward when your daughter bites down. It's effective, but it does depend on wearing it consistently, and at this age compliance can vary.

My preference for a case like this is a fixed appliance — what we call a two-by-four appliance. That means brackets on the two upper front teeth and bands on the two upper first molars, with a wire connecting them. Because it's fixed in place, it works around the clock regardless of cooperation, and it's the most reliable way to tip tooth 21 into its correct position. Treatment time for correcting this crossbite is typically in the range of three to six months.

Once this is resolved and we've confirmed the shift has gone — meaning the jaw is closing straight — I'll refer you for a full orthodontic assessment when all the adult teeth have come through. This early treatment doesn't replace full orthodontic care; it simply protects the jaw's growth in the meantime."

---

Safety Net and Closing

"Do you have any questions about anything I've explained? I want to make sure you feel clear on why we're recommending acting now rather than waiting.

If we proceed, I'll take some records — photographs and X-rays — and we'll get started as soon as possible. In the meantime, if you notice any pain when she bites, or if the jaw seems to be clicking or locking, please contact us straight away. Otherwise I'll see you at your next appointment and we'll put a plan in place. You're doing the right thing by having this looked at now."

OT2
Orthodontic Consent — Risks, Benefits, and Relapse
Category:** Orthodontics / Communication | **Time:** 11 min | **Difficulty:** Exam-ready

CASE SUMMARY

14-year-old and parent consenting for full fixed appliance treatment (crowding, Class II Div 1, overjet 8mm). Candidate must obtain consent covering all material risks.

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

Benefits (1 min)

Align teeth, reduce overjet, improve bite, improve aesthetics, easier to clean long-term.

Risks — INFLECTION 1: All 6 material risks

  1. Root resorption — minor shortening in all patients; significant in small %; monitored with X-rays
  2. Decalcification / white spots — irreversible if plaque isn't kept off brackets; brush after every meal
  3. Treatment length — 18–24 months estimated; could be longer
  4. Discomfort — after adjustments (3–5 days); paracetamol helps
  5. Breakage — broken brackets extend treatment; avoid hard/sticky food
  6. Relapse — INFLECTION 2: Most important long-term risk — Teeth drift back without retainers. Retainers are for life. If you stop wearing retainers, teeth will move.

Alternatives (1 min)

  • Clear aligners: removable, more expensive, strict compliance required
  • No treatment: crowding and overjet remain

Retention protocol

Bonded wire on lower anteriors (fixed) + removable upper Essix. Full-time 6 months, then nights for life.

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ All 6 material risks covered
  2. ✅ Relapse emphasised as lifelong concern
  3. ✅ Retention: bonded lower + removable upper, lifelong nights
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • "Informed consent for orthodontics must cover: root resorption (external apical — all patients, risk higher with longer treatment and certain tooth types), white spot lesions/caries around brackets, soft tissue ulceration, TMJ (not proven causative but patients ask), and — most importantly — relapse."
  • "Relapse is universal without retention. Every orthodontic patient must understand this before treatment starts. Retention is a lifetime commitment for lower anterior teeth."
  • "Retention options: bonded fixed retainer (lower anterior — excellent compliance, but needs cleaning, can break), removable Hawley or Essix (upper — compliance-dependent, minimum nightly wear indefinitely)."
  • "Root resorption: mild in most patients (1–2mm at apex), rarely clinically significant. Reassess at 9–12 months mid-treatment with periapical radiographs if treatment is prolonged."
Patient Reframes
  • "The most important thing I want you to understand before we start: orthodontic treatment straightens teeth permanently — but teeth stay straight permanently only with a retainer. Without retention, teeth move. This is not a complication; it's biology."
  • "Root resorption sounds alarming but in most patients it's millimetres at the root tip and has no clinical impact. Significant resorption is rare and monitored."
Curveball Deflectors
  • "Will I need to wear a retainer forever?" → "For the lower front teeth — realistically, yes. Those teeth want to return to their original position throughout life, and a fixed retainer manages that passively. For the upper, nightly removable wear is the standard plan. Most patients accept this easily once the result is there."
  • "I've heard braces cause jaw problems." → "There's no good evidence that orthodontic treatment causes TMJ disorders. TMJ symptoms can coincide with orthodontic treatment simply because both occur in similar age groups. I'll check your jaw joints now and monitor them."
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ▶
STAGE: Opening and Introduction

Candidate introduces themselves to the patient and parent, confirms identities, and establishes a welcoming tone.

"Hi there, I'm Dr. [Name], one of the dentists here. You must be [patient's name] — and you must be Mum or Dad? Lovely to meet you both. Come on in and take a seat. Today I'd like to talk through the orthodontic treatment we've been planning — the braces — and make sure you both feel really well informed before we go ahead. There's quite a bit to cover, but please stop me at any point if something isn't clear. Does that sound okay?"

---

Benefits of Treatment

"So let's start with why we're recommending braces in the first place. Looking at [patient's name]'s teeth, there's quite a bit of crowding, and the top front teeth are sitting quite far forward — we call that an increased overjet, and right now it's measuring about eight millimetres. A normal overjet is around two to three millimetres, so we do want to bring that back.

With a full set of fixed braces on the upper and lower teeth, we'd be aiming to straighten the crowding, reduce that overjet, improve how the top and bottom teeth bite together, and of course improve the overall appearance of the smile. Beyond aesthetics, straight teeth are genuinely easier to clean, which means a healthier mouth long-term. These are really meaningful changes — and at fourteen, the timing is excellent."

---

Material Risks — All Six

"Now I do need to go through the risks with you honestly, because consent means understanding both sides. There are six main risks I want you to know about.

The first is root resorption. Braces place gentle pressure on teeth, and in doing so, the roots can shorten very slightly — this happens to some degree in almost all patients. In a small percentage it becomes significant. We monitor this with X-rays during treatment, and if we see anything concerning, we can pause or adjust what we're doing.

Second is decalcification — you might hear this called white spot lesions. If plaque builds up around the brackets and isn't removed thoroughly, the enamel underneath can become permanently weakened and leave chalky white marks that don't go away. Brushing after every meal, every single day, is essential to prevent this.

Third is treatment length. We're estimating eighteen to twenty-four months, but that's genuinely an estimate. If there are breakages or if teeth don't move as expected, it can take longer.

Fourth is discomfort. After each adjustment appointment, it's very normal to have soreness for around three to five days. Paracetamol — one gram, every four to six hours as needed — is usually enough to manage that.

Fifth is breakage. If a bracket comes off or a wire breaks, it can set treatment back and extend the overall time. We ask patients to avoid hard and sticky foods — things like nuts, hard lollies, crusty bread, and chewing ice — right through treatment.

Sixth — and I want to spend a little extra time on this one because it's the most important long-term risk — is relapse."

---

Relapse — Lifelong Retention

"Relapse means the teeth drifting back towards where they started, and this is the risk that never really goes away. Teeth have a natural tendency to move. Even after two years in braces, once the pressure is removed, the teeth want to drift. This isn't a failure of the treatment — it's simply how teeth behave throughout life.

The only thing that prevents relapse is wearing retainers consistently and permanently. I need to be very direct with you both: retainers are for life. Not just for a year or two — for life. If [patient's name] stops wearing retainers, the teeth will move. It may be gradual, but it will happen.

Here's what the retention plan looks like. On the lower front teeth, we place a thin bonded wire fixed to the back of the teeth — you can't see it, you can't remove it, and it works continuously. On the upper teeth, we provide a removable clear retainer, similar to a mouthguard. For the first six months after braces come off, that upper retainer needs to be worn full-time. After that, every night for life. This is non-negotiable for maintaining the result."

---

Alternatives and Closing Consent

"It's also important I mention the alternatives. Clear aligners — like Invisalign — are another way to straighten teeth. They're removable and less visible, but they require extremely strict compliance, and they tend to be more expensive. They may also be less predictable for correcting a larger overjet like this one.

The other option, of course, is no treatment. The crowding and the overjet would remain as they are. Given the overjet of eight millimetres, there is a higher risk of trauma to the upper front teeth in that case — which is something worth considering at this age.

Do you both have any questions about anything I've covered? I want to make sure you feel completely comfortable before we move forward. If you're happy to go ahead, I'll have you sign the consent form today, and we'll get things started."

OT3
Impacted Upper Canine — Assessment and Management
Category:** Orthodontics / Oral Surgery | **Time:** 11 min | **Difficulty:** Exam-ready

CASE SUMMARY

13-year-old with retained primary canine (63) and clinically absent permanent canine (23). OPG shows 23 palatally positioned. Candidate must explain diagnosis, investigations, and management pathway.

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

Examination

  • 63 retained, root present; 23 not visible in arch, palpable as palatal bulge
  • OPG: 23 palatally positioned, mesially angulated, crown close to root of 12

Diagnosis

"The adult canine is impacted — stuck behind the bone of the palate. If left, it can damage the root of the tooth next to it (the lateral incisor) — called root resorption."

Investigations — INFLECTION 1: CBCT required

"I need a 3D X-ray (CBCT) to see exactly where the canine is, how deep it is, and how close it is to the lateral incisor root. Essential before any treatment planning."

Management options — INFLECTION 2

  1. Surgical exposure + orthodontic traction (preferred): Oral surgeon exposes and bonds a gold chain; braces guide the tooth into the arch over 12–18 months. 80–90% success for palatal canines.
  2. Extraction of impacted canine: If very high, severely angled, or patient declines prolonged treatment. Open/close the space.
  3. Extract primary canine + monitor: Window likely closed at 13yo — active intervention needed.

First step today

Remove the retained primary canine (63); refer for CBCT and orthodontic assessment.

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Palpates palate (clinical bulge = palatal canine)
  2. ✅ Identifies risk to lateral incisor root
  3. ✅ CBCT before treatment planning
  4. ✅ Surgical exposure + traction as preferred option
  5. ✅ Removes primary canine as first step
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • "Palatal vs buccal impaction: CBCT is essential for 3D localisation — management differs. Palatal (most common ~85%) — surgical exposure from the palate, orthodontic traction. Buccal — exposure from the buccal, different vector of traction."
  • "Root resorption of the lateral incisor: present in ~50% of cases at some stage. CBCT shows severity. Mild resorption — monitor; moderate/severe — discuss extraction of the ectopic canine and replacement planning."
  • "Screening protocol: palpate buccally for canine bulge at age 9–10. If not palpable by age 10 → OPG. Early detection significantly improves outcome — sector 1–2 position on OPG = much better prognosis."
  • "Extraction of deciduous canine at age 10–12 can allow spontaneous correction in ~30% of cases if canine is in sectors 1–2. CBCT then OPG follow-up at 12 months."
Patient Reframes
  • "The canine is one of the most important teeth in the mouth — it guides the bite and forms the cornerstone of your smile. We try very hard to bring it into position rather than extract it. The surgical exposure and braces approach takes time, but it preserves a tooth that would be very difficult to replace."
  • "At your age, with the right treatment, the outcome is usually excellent. The key was catching this early."
Curveball Deflectors
  • "Why can't we just leave it?" → "Unerupted canines don't stay still — they continue to move and can destroy the roots of the teeth beside them, silently, over years. The tooth next to it can lose its root before you notice any symptoms. That's why we act."
  • "What if it can't be moved into position?" → "If, after a period of orthodontic traction, the tooth isn't moving or the root resorption on the neighbouring tooth is severe, extraction becomes the plan. Then we discuss either space closure or an implant. But we try the conservative route first."
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ▶
STAGE: Opening and Clinical Examination

"Hello, my name is Dr. Chen. I'm one of the dentists here today. You must be Liam — and is this Mum with you? Lovely, thank you both for coming in. Liam, I understand we've been keeping an eye on your top teeth, and we want to have a good look today to figure out what's happening with one of your adult canine teeth — that's the pointy one near the front. Is that okay with you both? I'll explain everything as I go."

Examines the upper arch. Notes the retained primary canine, tooth 63, still present in the arch. Crown shows wear, and on gentle probing the root appears to be present. The permanent upper left canine, tooth 23, is not visible erupting into the arch.

"Liam, I'm just going to feel along the roof of your mouth — you might feel a little pressure, that's all."

Palpates the palate. A distinct firm bulge is noted palatally in the region of tooth 23, consistent with the crown of the impacted permanent canine lying against the palatal bone. There is no buccal bulge detectable.

"Thank you, Liam, you did really well. I can feel a small lump on the roof of your mouth — that's actually your adult canine tooth sitting underneath the bone. I can see on your X-ray as well that it hasn't come through, so let me explain exactly what's going on."

---

Diagnosis and Explanation

"So Liam, and Mum — what I've found today is that your adult canine tooth on the upper left is what we call impacted. That means it's stuck underneath the bone and the gum, sitting on the palate — the roof of your mouth — instead of coming down into its correct position in the arch. Your baby canine is still sitting there, which is actually blocking the adult tooth's path."

"The concern I have — and I want to be straightforward with you — is that on your OPG, which is the wide X-ray we took, the adult canine is angled quite steeply toward the front of your mouth and its crown appears to be very close to the root of the tooth next to it, your upper lateral incisor. When an impacted canine sits that close, it can slowly dissolve the root of the neighbouring tooth. We call this root resorption, and it can cause that tooth to become loose or even be lost if we don't act. This is why we do need to act now rather than wait."

---

Investigations — CBCT

"Before we can plan any treatment, I need one more piece of information. Your OPG gives me a flat picture, but it doesn't tell me exactly how deep the tooth sits, precisely how close it is to that lateral incisor root in three dimensions, or which direction I need to approach it surgically. For that, I need to arrange a special three-dimensional X-ray called a CBCT — a cone beam CT scan. It gives us a very accurate 3D image of where the tooth is sitting in the bone. Without it, I cannot safely plan your treatment, and the oral surgeon and orthodontist will both need it before they do anything. I want to be clear that this scan is essential — it's not optional at this stage."

---

Management Options

"Once we have that 3D scan, there are a few directions we can take, and I want to explain them both honestly."

"The best option for someone your age, Liam, is surgical exposure and orthodontic traction. A specialist oral surgeon would make a small opening in the gum to uncover the canine, and then bond a tiny gold chain onto it. That chain attaches to braces, and over the following twelve to eighteen months, the orthodontist uses gentle, controlled pressure to guide the tooth down into its correct place in your arch. For palatally positioned canines, this approach works around eighty to ninety percent of the time when we catch it at your age, so the outlook is genuinely good."

"The other option, which we'd only consider if the tooth is in a very difficult position or if treatment isn't possible, is to remove the impacted canine entirely. That would mean either closing the gap with braces or using the space differently — but we'd only go down that path if the scan shows it's truly necessary."

"Waiting and simply monitoring is not appropriate at thirteen. That window has closed, and we do need to act."

---

First Steps and Safety Net / Closing

"So here is what I'd like to do today. I'd like to remove the baby canine — tooth 63 — here in the chair. It's been there long enough and removing it is the right first step. I'll give you a good local anaesthetic so you won't feel any pain, just a little pressure. After that, I'll refer you for the CBCT scan and write a referral letter to both an orthodontist and an oral surgeon who will work together as a team on your treatment."

"After today's extraction, Liam, your mouth may feel a little sore for a day or two. If you need anything for pain, paracetamol at the correct dose for your weight will be the best thing to take — please don't take anything on an empty stomach. A little oozing of blood today is completely normal. If you have heavy or bright red ongoing bleeding that doesn't settle with firm pressure using a gauze pad for twenty minutes, I'd like you to call us or come straight back."

"Do either of you have any questions before we get started? I know it's a lot of information, but I want to make sure you feel comfortable and confident about the plan. You're in really good hands, and at thirteen, Liam, we have excellent timing to get a great result."

OT4
Failed/Relapsed Orthodontic Treatment — Complaint Handling
Category:** Orthodontics / Communication | **Time:** 11 min | **Difficulty:** Exam-ready

CASE SUMMARY

25-year-old who had orthodontic treatment age 16 presents with significantly crowded lower front teeth. Stopped wearing retainer at age 19. Angry and feels treatment "failed." Candidate must handle the complaint and discuss options.

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

De-escalation (1 min)

"I can see you're frustrated, and I appreciate you coming in to talk about this. I want to understand exactly what's happened."

Explain relapse without blame — INFLECTION 1

"Orthodontic relapse is one of the most common situations we see. Teeth have a natural tendency to drift back — influenced by the tongue, lips, chewing, and growth. This isn't unique to you — it happens to everyone if retainers aren't worn. When retainers were stopped at 19, six years without retention caused meaningful crowding."

Address "Did treatment fail?" — INFLECTION 2

"The treatment didn't fail — your teeth were aligned at the end of braces. What happened after is the relapse phase. I also want to acknowledge: information about lifelong retention wasn't always communicated as clearly as it should be — we're much clearer about that now."

Options

  1. Clear aligner refinement — correct current crowding; then strict lifelong retention
  2. Bonded fixed retainer — permanently wires lower front teeth; no compliance required
  3. Accept current position — if mild, functional concern only

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ De-escalates anger with empathy
  2. ✅ Explains relapse mechanism without blaming
  3. ✅ Acknowledges retention communication should have been clearer
  4. ✅ Offers bonded retainer as compliance-free alternative
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • "Acknowledge the disappointment without admitting liability prematurely. Explore what was expected vs what was discussed at consent — specifically: was retention compliance discussed? Is there documentation?"
  • "If relapse is due to non-compliance with retainer: the outcome is an expected consequence of not wearing the retainer, not a failure of treatment. This needs to be communicated clearly but kindly."
  • "If there is a genuine clinical concern (treatment completed with poor result, significant relapse despite compliant retention, inadequate consent documentation): acknowledge, discuss with MDA, offer remedy."
  • "Options: mild relapse — new retainer at current position (may not fully recover original result); significant relapse — retreatment discussion; complex — referral to orthodontist."
Patient Reframes
  • "I can see how frustrating this is — you've invested a lot of time and money, and the result isn't what you were hoping for. Let's work out exactly what's happened and what the options are from here."
  • "My job today is to examine where things are now, review the records, and give you an honest assessment — not to defend any position before I've done that."
Curveball Deflectors
  • "I want a refund." → "That's a conversation I'm willing to have — once I've reviewed the records and examined you today. If we establish that there was a failure in care, that discussion is legitimate. Can we start with understanding what happened clinically?"
  • "I never wore my retainer — I forgot." → "I appreciate the honesty. Relapse without retainer wear is unfortunately expected — it's one of the most important things we go through at the start of treatment. The good news: mild relapse can often be treated again. Let's see where things are."
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ▶
STAGE: Opening and De-escalation

Greets the patient warmly and gestures to the chair. Maintains open body language and calm tone throughout.

"Hello, I'm Dr. [Name]. Thank you for coming in today. I can see from your expression that you're frustrated, and I want you to know that's completely understandable. Please, take a seat and take your time — I genuinely want to hear what's been happening for you."

Allows the patient to speak. Listens actively without interrupting.

"I can hear how upsetting this is. You went through the whole process at sixteen, you put in that time and effort, and now you're looking at your teeth and feeling like it's all come undone. That's really disappointing, and I appreciate you coming in to talk about it rather than just walking away."

---

History and Clinical Assessment

"Can I ask you a few questions so I fully understand the situation? How long did you wear your retainer after the braces came off? And when did you notice the crowding starting to come back?"

Listens carefully. Confirms retainer use stopped at age nineteen, approximately six years ago.

"And is it mainly the lower front teeth that concern you, or the upper teeth as well? Is there any discomfort, or is it purely the appearance that's bothering you?"

Conducts a brief clinical examination of the lower anterior teeth. Notes crowding and rotations consistent with orthodontic relapse. No pain, no mobility, healthy periodontal tissues.

"Thank you — that's really helpful. I'll just have a careful look now, if that's okay."

---

Explaining Relapse — Without Blame

"So I want to explain what's happened here, because I think once you understand the mechanics, it will make a lot more sense. This is called orthodontic relapse, and it's one of the most common things we see in dentistry."

"Here's what happens: teeth have a natural, lifelong tendency to drift. They're influenced by the pressure of your tongue pushing from the inside, your lips pushing from the outside, the forces of chewing, and even the continued slow changes in your jaw as you move through your twenties. None of that stops when the braces come off — it's biology."

"The retainer's job is to hold the teeth against those forces permanently. Not just for a year or two — indefinitely. When retainer wear stopped at nineteen, those natural forces had six uninterrupted years to move things, and that's what's created the crowding you're seeing now. This is not unique to you — it happens to everyone who stops wearing their retainer."
