"Now — I also want to say something honestly. The question of whether the treatment failed — the answer is no. Your teeth were well-aligned when the braces came off. What's happened since is a relapse phase, not a treatment failure."

"However, I also want to acknowledge this: in the past, information about lifelong retention wasn't always communicated as clearly as it should have been. We're much more explicit about that now — we say 'retainers forever' from day one. I'm sorry that message wasn't as clear for you at sixteen. That's something I think is worth acknowledging."

---

Treatment Options

"So let's talk about where we go from here, because there are good options available to you."

"The first option is clear aligner therapy — something like Invisalign or a similar system. This would correct the crowding over roughly six to twelve months, depending on severity. The important thing is that at the end of that, we must commit to strict lifelong retention. I would strongly recommend we build that into the plan from the start this time."

"The second option — and this is one I think suits your situation particularly well — is a bonded fixed retainer. This is a thin wire that we bond permanently to the back surfaces of your lower front teeth. You can't remove it, you don't have to remember to wear it, and it holds those teeth in position twenty-four hours a day. There's no compliance required. For someone who has experienced relapse, this is often the most reliable long-term solution."

"The third option is to accept the current position if the crowding is mild and purely cosmetic. If it's not affecting your bite or your oral health, that's a valid choice too — though I suspect from what you've described it's causing you real distress."

---

Safety Net and Closing

"I want to make sure you leave here today feeling heard and informed — not overwhelmed. Would it be helpful to take some written information home about the aligner option and the fixed retainer, so you can think it through?"

"I'd also suggest we take some photographs and study models today so we have a proper record of where things are now. That way, whichever direction you choose, we're starting from a clear baseline."

"Do you have any questions at all? There's no rush — I want you to feel confident in whatever you decide."

"Thank you for bringing this to me. I know it wasn't an easy conversation to have, and I respect that you came in. Whatever we do next, we'll make sure the retention side of things is airtight."

OT5
Class II Malocclusion — Growth Modification vs. Wait
Category:** Orthodontics | **Time:** 11 min | **Difficulty:** Exam-ready

CASE SUMMARY

11-year-old with significant overjet (10mm), skeletal Class II (retrognathic mandible), mixed dentition. Parent asks whether to treat now or wait.

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

Assessment

  • Overjet 10mm (ideal: 2–3mm); skeletal Class II
  • Growth status: 11-year-old female approaching peak growth (assess CVM or hand bone age)
  • Mixed dentition, first permanent molars present

Explaining the growth window — INFLECTION 1

"We are in a window of opportunity. While the child is still growing, a functional appliance can guide the lower jaw forward — this is called growth modification. It ONLY works while bones are still growing. Once growth stops (usually 14–16 in girls), it's too late. Missing this window means either orthodontic camouflage (possibly extracting upper premolars) or, in severe cases, jaw surgery as an adult."

Options

  • Twin block (removable, worn full-time): functional appliance, 12–18 months
  • Herbst (fixed): no compliance issues
  • After growth modification: full fixed braces to align teeth

Expected outcomes

Overjet reduction from 10mm toward 4–5mm. Not guaranteed — skeletal growth responds variably.

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Identifies skeletal Class II (not just dental)
  2. ✅ Explains growth modification window — the core concept
  3. ✅ Names twin block and Herbst
  4. ✅ Explains consequences of missing the window (camouflage vs. surgery)
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • "Growth modification timing: peak mandibular growth velocity (CS2–CS3 on cervical vertebrae maturation index, or hand-wrist X-ray) — typically age 10–13 in females, 12–14 in males. Twin block works with this growth; after CS4 (growth complete), skeletal effects are lost."
  • "Twin block appliance: bilateral bite blocks open the bite and position the mandible forward; worn full-time including eating; patient compliance is the primary limiting factor."
  • "If growth complete: camouflage orthodontics (premolar extraction to allow upper incisor retraction and lower incisor proclination) or orthognathic surgery for severe skeletal discrepancy (ANB >5°, significant profile concerns)."
  • "Minor Class II: assess functional impact and incisor trauma risk (proclined upper incisors increase risk of trauma). Not every Class II requires treatment."
Patient Reframes
  • "The reason timing matters here is that the appliance works with the jaw's own growth. It redirects growth that's already happening — like steering a river rather than diverting it. Once growth is complete, that opportunity is gone."
  • "If we've missed the growth window, that's not the end of the story — the options change, but options still exist. Let me explain what those are."
Curveball Deflectors
  • "Can't we do it now?" (patient post-growth) → "The growth modification window has closed for you — the jaw has finished growing, so the twin block won't produce skeletal change anymore. What it CAN still do is dental correction. For a bigger change, we'd discuss orthodontics with or without orthognathic surgery."
  • "My child refuses to wear the appliance." → "Compliance is the biggest challenge with functional appliances — and it's real. Let me talk with your child directly about what's making it difficult. Sometimes adjustments to fit or timing make it tolerable; sometimes we decide the window isn't worth forcing."
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ▶
STAGE: Opening and Scene-Setting

"Hello, I'm Dr. Chen — lovely to meet you both. Please come in and take a seat. And this must be Sophie — hi Sophie, great to have you here today. Mum, I understand you've come in with some questions about Sophie's teeth and jaw, and whether now is the right time to do something about it. I'd love to have a proper conversation about that with you both. Is it alright if I ask you a few questions first, and then I'll explain everything I'm seeing and what our options are?"

Takes note that Sophie is an 11-year-old female in mixed dentition. Reviews the clinical findings: overjet measured at 10 millimetres — noting ideal overjet is 2 to 3 millimetres — first permanent molars fully erupted, skeletal Class II relationship confirmed on clinical and radiographic assessment with a retrognathic mandible.

"Sophie, has anyone ever mentioned to you that your lower jaw sits a bit further back than your upper jaw? Have you noticed your top front teeth stick out quite a bit further than your bottom ones?"

---

Clinical Assessment Findings

"Mum, let me explain what I'm seeing here, because I think once you understand the full picture, the question of timing will make a lot more sense. Sophie has what we call a skeletal Class II relationship. That means it's not just her teeth that are out of position — it's actually the relationship between her upper and lower jaws. Her lower jaw is sitting further back than we'd like to see. On top of that, she has a significant overjet — that's the horizontal distance between her top and bottom front teeth — and Sophie's measures ten millimetres. The normal range we aim for is about two to three millimetres, so she's quite a way outside that range.

Now, the really important piece of this puzzle is Sophie's growth status. Sophie is eleven, and based on what I can assess clinically and from her x-rays, she is approaching what we call her peak growth period. For girls, this typically occurs somewhere between eleven and thirteen years of age. This matters enormously, and I want to take a moment to explain exactly why."

---

The Growth Modification Window — Core Concept

"What we are looking at right now is what I call a window of opportunity, and it is genuinely time-sensitive. While Sophie's jaws are still actively growing, we have the ability to guide the growth of her lower jaw forward using a special appliance. This is called growth modification or functional appliance therapy, and it works by harnessing the body's own natural growth potential to reshape the jaw relationship.

Here is the critical point I need you to understand: this approach only works while the bones are still growing. Once Sophie's jaw growth is complete — which in girls typically occurs around fourteen to sixteen years of age — that window closes permanently. If we miss this window, we cannot go back and recapture it. Our options at that point become much more limited and, frankly, more invasive.

If we wait too long and Sophie's growth has finished, we would be looking at either orthodontic camouflage — which would likely mean extracting upper premolar teeth and pulling the top teeth back to make things look better, without actually correcting the underlying jaw discrepancy — or, in more severe cases, jaw surgery as an adult, which carries its own significant risks, recovery time, and cost. Neither of those outcomes is what we want if we can avoid them. So the question isn't really whether to treat — it's whether to act now while we still can."

---

Treatment Options and Appliances

"In terms of what growth modification actually looks like in practice, we have two main appliances I'd recommend considering for Sophie.

The first is called a Twin Block appliance. This is a removable device — two interlocking plastic plates, one for the upper jaw and one for the lower. Sophie would wear it full-time, ideally twenty-two hours a day, removing it only to eat and clean her teeth. The twin block works by positioning the lower jaw forward and encouraging it to grow in that direction. We would expect to use it for approximately twelve to eighteen months. The limitation is that it does require Sophie's cooperation and commitment to wearing it consistently.

The second option is a Herbst appliance. This is a fixed device — it's attached to the teeth and cannot be removed by Sophie herself. The advantage is that there is no compliance issue, because it's working around the clock regardless. This can be a good choice if we have any concerns about a young patient's ability to wear a removable appliance reliably.

After whichever functional appliance phase we complete, Sophie would then move into a full course of fixed braces to align all the teeth beautifully and fine-tune the bite."

---

Expected Outcomes and Realistic Goals

"In terms of what we can realistically expect, growth modification done at the right time can reduce Sophie's overjet significantly — we would be aiming to bring it down from that ten millimetres toward somewhere in the four to five millimetre range, and then the fixed braces would refine it further. I do want to be honest with you though: skeletal growth responds variably between individuals. We cannot guarantee an exact millimetre outcome, and Sophie's genetics play a role in how much her lower jaw will respond. What I can say is that for a motivated eleven-year-old at this stage of development, the evidence strongly supports acting now.

I'd also like to take some records today — we'll look at Sophie's cervical vertebral maturation stage on her lateral cephalogram to confirm exactly where she sits in her growth curve, which helps us plan the timing precisely."

---

Questions and Closing

"Mum, Sophie — does that all make sense? I know that's quite a lot to take in. What questions do you have for me? I want to make sure you feel completely comfortable before we make any decisions together. There is no pressure today, but I do want you to understand that time is genuinely a factor here, and I wouldn't want Sophie to miss the window where we can make the most meaningful difference with the least invasive approach. I'm here to support you both through every step of this."

OT6
Adult Orthodontics — Combined Ortho-Restorative Planning
Category:** Orthodontics | **Time:** 11 min | **Difficulty:** Exam-ready

CASE SUMMARY

35-year-old with moderate crowding, mesially tilted 36 (post-46 extraction), overerupted 47, wants implant for 46 and crown on 37. Candidate must explain the interdisciplinary sequence.

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

The interdisciplinary problem — INFLECTION 1

"If we placed an implant for 46 now, the space is narrowed by the tilted 36 and the overerupted 47. The implant crown would be in a compromised position and the bite would be off. Restoring 37 with a crown now means restoring a tooth that may move later. The correct sequence: ortho first, then restorative."

Ortho phase — INFLECTION 2

  1. Upright 36 — opens the implant space to correct width
  2. Intrude 47 — address supraeruption
  3. Align crowding

Clear aligners or fixed braces both work; 12–18 months in an adult.

Restorative phase

  1. Implant for 46 — correct width, good angulation, excellent prognosis
  2. Crown on 37 — proper position, ideal margins

Managing expectations

"Adult orthodontics is slower than in teenagers. Lifelong retention required. But the result is a properly sequenced bite that makes implant and crown work last significantly longer."

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Identifies tilted molar + overerupted tooth as problems for implant placement
  2. ✅ Ortho must precede restorative — explains why
  3. ✅ Correct sequence: upright → implant → crown
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • "Adult ortho principles: periodontal health must be stable (no active disease, no bleeding on probing) before and throughout treatment. Ortho moves bacteria-laden plaque subgingivally during tooth movement — in a periodontally compromised mouth, this is dangerous."
  • "Combined ortho-restorative planning: establish the final restorative position FIRST (implant site dimensions, final crown position), then plan orthodontic tooth movement to achieve it. Restorative dentist and orthodontist must agree on the endpoint before either starts."
  • "Treatment sequencing: active perio treatment → stability → ortho → interim prosthetics → final restorations → lifelong retention and perio maintenance."
  • "Retention in adults: lifelong fixed retention recommended for most adult cases — biological drift tendency does not decrease with age."
Patient Reframes
  • "Adult orthodontics is completely possible — and increasingly common. It's more of a multidisciplinary planned process than teenage orthodontics, but the biology of tooth movement works the same way."
  • "There's no age limit as long as the supporting structures are healthy. The key is making sure we plan the orthodontic and restorative outcomes together from the beginning, rather than treating them separately."
Curveball Deflectors
  • "Am I too old for braces?" → "No — there's no biological age limit for tooth movement. The key question is gum health, which we've assessed. The treatment takes a little longer in adults and retention is especially important, but the result is just as achievable."
  • "Can I have clear aligners instead of brackets?" → "Clear aligners are an option for many adult cases — particularly when the movements are primarily tipping rather than torque or intrusion. I'd want the orthodontist to assess whether your specific movements are aligner-appropriate."
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ▶
STAGE: Opening and Scene-Setting

"Hi, come on in and take a seat. I'm the dentist here today. Before we get started, could I just confirm your name and date of birth for me? Great, thank you. So today I'd like to go through a treatment plan with you — one that involves a few different steps, and I want to make sure you understand exactly why we're recommending this particular sequence. Is that alright with you?"

Pauses to allow patient to respond, makes eye contact, adopts an open and unhurried posture.

"You've mentioned you'd like an implant where your lower right back tooth was removed — that's the 46 — and you'd also like a crown on the tooth just behind it, the 37. Those are both excellent goals, and we absolutely can achieve them. But I want to be honest with you today: if we went straight to placing an implant and doing that crown right now, we'd be setting you up for a result that won't last nearly as long as it should. Let me explain why."

---

Identifying the Interdisciplinary Problem

"When a back tooth is removed and the space isn't restored promptly, the neighbouring teeth start to move. In your case, the tooth in front of the gap — the 36, your lower left first molar — has tipped forward and is now leaning into the space where the implant needs to go. At the same time, the tooth above that gap — the 47 — has drifted downward because it no longer has anything below it to bite against. That's called supraeruption, and it means the tooth has over-erupted into the space."

"Now, if we placed an implant crown in that space today, the gap is too narrow — the tilted 36 has stolen part of the space — so the implant would be placed at a compromised angle, and the crown on top of it would be in the wrong position. The bite wouldn't be right, and that implant crown would be under incorrect forces every time you chew. That significantly shortens its lifespan. Similarly, if we prep and crown the 37 now, we'd be crowning a tooth that is going to move during orthodontic treatment — so the margins and the fit of that crown would no longer be ideal once treatment is finished. We'd essentially be doing that crown twice."

"The correct approach is: fix the position of the teeth first with orthodontics, then restore. Ortho first, restorative second."

---

Orthodontic Phase — Goals and Duration

"So the orthodontic phase has three specific goals for you. First, we need to upright the 36 — tipping it back to a vertical position so that the implant space is restored to the correct width and the implant can be placed with ideal angulation. Second, we need to intrude the 47 — that means pushing it back up so there's enough vertical clearance for an implant crown of proper height. And third, we'll take the opportunity to address the moderate crowding in your arches, which will also improve your bite overall."

"In terms of how we do the orthodontics, you have options. Clear aligners — which are removable, nearly invisible trays — work well for adults and can achieve all three of those goals. Traditional fixed braces are also effective. Both approaches in an adult patient like yourself typically take around twelve to eighteen months. Adults move teeth a little more slowly than teenagers, so I want to be upfront about that timeframe."

---

Restorative Phase — Implant and Crown

"Once orthodontics is complete and we've confirmed the space is correct — both in width and in height — we move to the restorative phase. The implant for the 46 will now be placed at the ideal position, with correct angulation and excellent bone support. Because the bite is properly aligned, the forces on that implant crown will be distributed correctly, and you can expect a significantly better long-term outcome."

"The crown on the 37 will then be prepared and fitted with the tooth in its final, stable position. The margins will sit correctly, the preparation will be ideal, and the crown will fit and function exactly as it should."

---

Managing Expectations and Retention

"I do want to set some realistic expectations with you. Adult orthodontics takes commitment — whether you choose aligners or braces, you'll need to attend regular adjustment appointments, and the twelve to eighteen months is an estimate based on what I'm seeing clinically. Some people are a little faster, some a little slower."

"Once orthodontic treatment is finished, retention is lifelong. The teeth will need to be held in place with a retainer — usually a thin wire bonded behind the front teeth and a removable night-time retainer — because without retention, teeth will move back over time in adults."

"I know that sounds like a significant journey before you even get to the implant and crown. But I want you to understand that this sequence exists to protect your investment. Done in the right order, that implant and crown should serve you extremely well for many years. Done out of sequence, we'd be compromising the outcome before we even start."

---

Closing and Next Steps

"Do you have any questions about what I've explained today? I'm very happy to go over any part of it again."

Pauses and listens attentively.

"What I'd like to do next is take some detailed records — that means some photographs, moulds or digital scans of your teeth, and an OPG x-ray — so I can plan the orthodontic treatment precisely and share your case with an orthodontic specialist for a collaborative assessment. We'll then give you a written treatment plan with a timeline and cost estimate for each phase so you can make a fully informed decision. How does that sound?"

OT7
Orthodontic Retainer Non-Compliance — Follow-Up
Category:** Orthodontics / Preventive | **Time:** 11 min | **Difficulty:** Exam-ready

CASE SUMMARY

17-year-old at 3-month post-brace recall. Wearing retainer only 5 nights/week instead of full-time. Mild relapse visible. Candidate must address compliance without damaging rapport.

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

Examination first — INFLECTION 1

  • Mild lower anterior crowding returning (0.5–1mm shift)
  • Retainer fits with pressure (confirms relapse started)

Non-confrontational opening

"I can see from examining your teeth and how the retainer fits that there's been a small amount of movement since finishing braces. How have you been going with wearing it?"

Explaining the stakes — INFLECTION 2

"The first 12 months is the highest-risk period — teeth want to move back most during this time. Wearing it 5 nights means 2 nights of freedom for your teeth to shift. The retainer can only hold where teeth currently are — it can't push them back. If relapse continues, additional orthodontic treatment would be needed to fix it."

Problem-solving the specific barrier

  • Forgetting → phone alarm reminder
  • Discomfort → usually settles in 2–3 months; persists with inconsistent wear
  • Losing it → protective case, discuss backup retainer

Offer bonded retainer alternative

"We can also bond a thin wire permanently to the back of your lower front teeth — no remembering required. Many patients prefer this for the lower anteriors."

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Identifies relapse from examination before asking about compliance
  2. ✅ Non-confrontational — asks, doesn't accuse
  3. ✅ Explains why first 12 months is critical
  4. ✅ Problem-solves the specific barrier
  5. ✅ Offers bonded retainer alternative
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • "Non-compliance causes: aesthetics of retainer (visible, uncomfortable), practical barriers (lost, broken, forgotten), lifestyle change (moved out, travelling), low perceived risk ('it's only been a few weeks')."
  • "Early retention (first 2 years): highest relapse risk. Teeth move rapidly without retainer, particularly lower anteriors. Even brief gaps in retainer wear can result in measurable movement."
  • "Assessment: take new impressions/scans, compare to end-of-treatment models. If movement detected: new retainer at current position (may not recover original result). If significant relapse: retreatment discussion."
  • "Prevention going forward: fixed bonded retainer for lower anteriors; replacement Essix/Hawley with reminder system; vivera retainers (aligner-format, durable, replaced annually)."
Patient Reframes
  • "I understand — retainer wear is genuinely the hardest part of orthodontic treatment for most people. Let me look at where things are now and we'll figure out the best way forward from here."
  • "There's no point in guilt — what matters is what we do now. If there's been movement, let's quantify it and make a plan."
Curveball Deflectors
  • "It's only been 3 months — surely that's not long enough to matter." → "Three months is enough for noticeable movement in some patients, especially in the first year or two after treatment. Let me take impressions and compare to your end-of-treatment records so I can show you what's actually happened rather than guess."
  • "The retainer doesn't fit anymore." → "That's a sign there's been movement — the retainer fits the original position, and if the teeth have moved, there's a gap. A new retainer at the current position stops further movement, even if it doesn't recover everything. That's where we start."
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ▶
STAGE: Examination and Opening

Candidate reviews the patient's clinical file, noting the 3-month post-debond review. Conducts an intraoral examination first — assessing lower anterior alignment visually, then seating the removable retainer to assess fit.

"Hi, it's really good to see you again. Congratulations on getting through your orthodontic treatment — your teeth looked fantastic when we finished. I'm just going to have a look at everything today before we chat. Open nice and wide for me."

Examines the lower anterior segment carefully. Notes approximately 0.5 to 1 millimetre of crowding returning at the lower incisors — mild but visible contact point displacement. Seats the removable retainer and notes it fits with noticeable pressure, confirming that some tooth movement has occurred since debond.

"Thank you, that's great. You can take the retainer out now."

"So, I can see from examining your teeth and the way your retainer fits — it's sitting with a bit of pressure — that there has been a small amount of movement since we finished with the braces. It's mild, and we've caught it early, which is really the main thing. How have you been going with wearing the retainer at home?"

Listens attentively and without interruption. Patient reports wearing it approximately five nights per week.

"Okay, thank you for being honest with me about that — I really appreciate it, and it helps me help you. Can I ask what's been making it tricky on the other nights?"

Patient describes forgetting on some nights and occasional discomfort after not wearing it for a day or two.

---

Explaining the Stakes

"I completely understand — life gets busy, and it's easy to forget. I want to explain what's happening inside your mouth on those nights, because I think it will make sense of why this period is so important.

The first twelve months after braces come off is actually the highest-risk window for teeth to move back. The bone and the ligaments around your teeth are still settling into their new positions, and that process takes a full year. Your teeth have a kind of memory — they want to drift back toward where they started.

When you wear the retainer five nights out of seven, you're giving your teeth two full nights where there's nothing holding them in place. Over weeks and months, that adds up, and that's exactly what we're seeing today — a small but real shift.

The important thing to understand is that the retainer can only hold your teeth where they currently are. It cannot push them back to where they were. So the longer this continues, the more movement accumulates, and at a certain point, additional orthodontic treatment would be needed to correct it — and neither of us wants to go back down that road after everything you've already done."

---

Problem-Solving the Barriers

"So let's work out how to make this more manageable for you. You mentioned forgetting — that's actually the most common reason, and there's a really simple fix. Would you be happy to set a phone alarm for the same time each night, say nine o'clock, just as a prompt? Most patients find that within two to three weeks it becomes habit and they don't even need the alarm anymore.

The discomfort you're feeling when you put it back in after a gap — that tightness and pressure — is actually a sign the teeth have moved slightly in that time. If you wear it consistently, that sensation settles down. It's the inconsistency itself that makes it uncomfortable. Wear it every night and that pressure largely disappears within a few weeks.

Do you have a case you keep the retainer in? It's worth having a dedicated case that lives on your bedside table, so it's always in one place. If you're worried about losing it, we can also discuss having a spare retainer made — it's much more straightforward and affordable than retreatment."

---

Offering the Bonded Retainer Alternative

"There is another option I'd like to mention, and some patients your age actually prefer it for the lower front teeth in particular. We can bond a very thin wire — you wouldn't feel it with your tongue after a day or two — permanently to the backs of your lower front teeth. It's completely hidden, and because it's fixed, there's no remembering required at all. It works around the clock.

Many patients choose to have a bonded retainer on the lower teeth and continue with a removable one on the upper, which reduces the daily compliance pressure significantly. It's something worth considering, and I'm happy to go through the pros and cons with you if you'd like."

---

Agreed Plan and Safety Net

"So here's what I'd suggest we do today. I'm going to monitor the current position and note it carefully in your records. I want you to go back to wearing the retainer every single night — full-time overnight — starting tonight. Set that phone alarm, keep the case by your bed.

I'd like to see you again in six weeks rather than waiting three months, just so we can check whether that mild crowding is stabilising. If it is, we're in great shape. If it continues to shift despite full-time wear, we'll have an honest conversation about the bonded retainer or other options.

Any questions at all? You've worked incredibly hard to get this result — a small adjustment to the routine now protects all of that effort. I'm confident we can get this back on track."

CE1
Breaking Bad News — Positive Biopsy Result
Category:** Communication / Ethics | **Time:** 11 min | **Difficulty:** High

CASE SUMMARY

A 58-year-old patient presents to receive the results of a biopsy taken 10 days ago from a white lesion on the lateral tongue. The pathology report shows squamous cell carcinoma. The patient doesn't know what was biopsied — they were told it was "just a check." Candidate must deliver the diagnosis using a structured framework.

CANDIDATE BRIEF

Mr. Watson, 58, has come to review his biopsy results. At his last appointment, you biopsied a 1.5cm erythroleukoplakic lesion on his left lateral tongue — he was told it was a precautionary biopsy, nothing more. The pathology report has returned: squamous cell carcinoma, moderately differentiated. Your task: deliver this result using a structured, compassionate communication framework.

EXAMINER CONTEXT

Mr. Watson is calm initially but becomes visibly shaken after hearing the diagnosis. Will ask "Is it cancer?" — this is the critical moment. Will ask "Am I going to die?" Becomes tearful. Will ask who will treat this. If given information in a slow, structured, compassionate way, will engage. If information is dumped all at once, will shut down and stop listening.

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

Prepare the environment (0.5 min)

Sit down. No desk between you. Tissues visible. Ask: "Did you bring anyone with you today?" — ideally a support person present for bad news. Not always possible, but ask.

Warning shot — INFLECTION 1

"Mr. Watson, I have the results from your biopsy. Before I share them, I want to let you know that the news is more serious than I had hoped. Are you okay for me to continue?"

(Pause. Wait for a nod or verbal cue.)

This is a "warning shot" — it primes the patient psychologically for serious news. It is not optional.

Deliver the diagnosis — INFLECTION 2: Clear, direct, no euphemisms

"The biopsy shows that the tissue has cancer cells — specifically, a type called squamous cell carcinoma. This is a type of cancer that affects the lining of the mouth and tongue."

Do NOT say: "There are some abnormal cells." Do NOT use jargon: "SCC" without explanation.

Pause (0.5 min)

Say nothing. Let it land. The patient needs a moment. Watch. Be present.

Respond to emotion before continuing — INFLECTION 3

If patient asks "Am I going to die?" — "I understand why you're asking that. This is a very serious diagnosis and I'm not going to minimise it. What I can tell you is that we're going to get you to the right specialist as quickly as possible, and that oral cancers, when caught and treated, have treatment options that can make a real difference. I can't give you survival percentages — that's a specialist's conversation. But you are not alone in this."

Outline the next steps — INFLECTION 4

"Here's what happens next: I'm going to urgently refer you to an oral and maxillofacial surgeon who specialises in this. Urgent means within days to 1–2 weeks. They'll assess the tumour and involve an oncology team who will plan the right treatment — which may involve surgery, radiotherapy, or a combination."

Summarise & check understanding (1 min)

"I want to check I've explained this clearly. Can you tell me in your own words what I've shared with you today?"

Safety-netting

"I'm going to call you tomorrow to make sure the referral has been arranged and to check how you're feeling. If you have questions before then, here's my direct number."

Give written information

Cancer Council or oral cancer patient information sheet.

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Checks if support person present
  2. ✅ Uses warning shot before delivering diagnosis
  3. ✅ Clear, direct language — "cancer" not "abnormal cells"
  4. ✅ Pauses after delivery — does not rush
  5. ✅ Responds to emotional needs before clinical detail
  6. ✅ Does NOT give prognosis percentages — defers to specialist
  7. ✅ Urgent referral (days–2 weeks) to OMFS/oncology
  8. ✅ Follow-up call next day
  9. ✅ Written information provided

TG4 ALERTS

Urgent referral for suspected oral cancer — TG4/AHPRA: 2-week urgent pathway to OMFS or head and neck oncology. Document the referral. Follow up to confirm receipt.

INFLECTION POINTS

PointWeakStrong
Warning shotLaunches directly into "The results show cancer""I need to share some serious news — are you ready?" Pause.
Language"There are some concerning cells""The biopsy shows cancer — squamous cell carcinoma"
After deliveryImmediately continues with treatment infoPauses. Watches. Responds to emotion.
Prognosis question"The survival rate is about 60%""I can't give you numbers — that's the specialist's conversation. But treatment options exist."
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • "SPIKES protocol: Setting (private, no distractions), Perception (what does patient already know?), Invitation (ask if they're ready to hear results), Knowledge (warning shot then clear statement), Emotions (acknowledge with empathy, pause), Strategy (what happens next — referral, MDT, support resources)."
  • "Warning shot: 'I have some news about the biopsy result that I need to share with you — and I want to warn you, it's not the news I was hoping for.'"
  • "Do not speculate on prognosis — that belongs with the specialist and MDT. Your role is to deliver the result, provide emotional support, and arrange urgent referral to oral and maxillofacial surgery or head and neck oncology."
  • "Cancer Council Australia: 13 11 20. Ensure the patient does not leave alone if possible. Document the conversation verbatim in notes."
Patient Reframes
  • "I want to be honest with you — and I'll stay here with you through this."
  • "Having this diagnosed means you're now in the system, and the specialists who deal with this are excellent. The earlier this is found, the more options there are — and we caught this."
  • "I know this isn't what you were hoping to hear. Before anything else — how are you feeling right now?"
Curveball Deflectors
  • "How long do I have?" → "That's exactly the question for the specialist team to answer — I'm not the right person to give you a prognosis, and I wouldn't want to guess at something that important. What I can tell you is that getting you to the right people quickly is what we're doing right now."
  • "Could there be a mistake?" → "The biopsy result was reviewed by a pathologist — it's as accurate a test as we have. A second opinion is absolutely your right. But the result is consistent with what I was seeing clinically, which is why I biopsied it."
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ▶
STAGE: Preparing the Environment

Arranges two chairs at the same level with no desk between them. Places a box of tissues within reach. Ensures the door is closed and there are no interruptions. Sits down, makes eye contact, and speaks in a calm, measured tone.

"Mr. Watson, thank you for coming in today. Before we get started, I just want to ask — did you bring anyone along with you? A partner, a family member, a friend?"

If the patient has no support person: "That's okay. I just want to make sure you're as comfortable as possible. If at any point you'd like to pause and call someone, that's completely fine."

---

Warning Shot — Preparing the Patient

"Mr. Watson, I have your biopsy results here and I've had a chance to go through them carefully. Before I share what they show, I want to be honest with you — the news is more serious than I had hoped for. Are you okay for me to continue?"

Pauses. Waits for a nod or verbal response. Maintains steady, warm eye contact. Does not rush.

"I also want you to know that I'm here with you through this conversation, and we're going to talk through everything — what it means, and what happens next. There's no rush."

---

Delivering the Diagnosis

"Mr. Watson, the biopsy result shows that the tissue we sampled from the side of your tongue contains cancer cells. The specific type is called squamous cell carcinoma — it's a form of cancer that arises from the lining cells of the mouth and tongue."

Pauses. Says nothing for several seconds. Allows the information to land. Watches the patient's face and body language without filling the silence.

If the patient becomes visibly distressed: "Take your time. It's okay to sit with this for a moment."

If the patient asks, "Am I going to die?" — "I understand completely why you're asking that. This is a serious diagnosis and I'm not going to minimise it for you. What I can tell you is that you are not facing this alone, and that we are going to get you to the right specialist team as quickly as possible. Oral cancers do have treatment options that can make a real difference, particularly when they're identified and acted on promptly — as yours has been. Giving you specific numbers or statistics is something that belongs in the specialist conversation, because they will have the full picture. What I can promise you is that we are moving on this urgently."

---

Responding to Emotion Before Clinical Detail

"How are you feeling right now? It's completely normal to feel shocked, or frightened, or even a bit numb. Whatever you're feeling is the right response."

Listens attentively. Does not redirect to clinical information until the patient signals readiness.

"When you feel ready, I'd like to explain exactly what we're going to do from here — the steps that are going to happen in the coming days. Would that be okay?"

---

Outlining Next Steps and Urgent Referral

"Here is what happens next, and I want to be very clear about this. I am going to write an urgent referral today — this is not a routine appointment. You will be seen by an oral and maxillofacial surgeon who specialises in exactly this type of diagnosis. Urgent means within days to one to two weeks at most. That specialist will assess the full extent of the lesion and will work alongside an oncology team — cancer specialists — who will map out the right treatment plan for you. That may involve surgery, radiotherapy, or a combination of both. That decision belongs with them, and they are the right people to have that conversation with you."

"I'll also be contacting the Cancer Council on your behalf — they have a support line and patient information that many people find genuinely helpful during this time. I'll give you that written information before you leave today."

---

Checking Understanding, Safety-Netting, and Closing

"Before you go, I want to check that I've explained this as clearly as I can. Is it okay if I ask you to tell me in your own words what I've shared with you today? Just so I know we're on the same page."

Listens carefully. Gently clarifies any misunderstanding without being patronising.

"I am going to personally call you tomorrow — not my receptionist, me — to confirm that the referral has gone through and to check how you're doing. If anything comes up before then, any question at all, here is my direct number."

Hands the patient a written card with the contact number and a Cancer Council patient information sheet.

"Mr. Watson, I know this is an enormous amount to take in. You've done the right thing by coming in, this has been caught and we are acting on it now. You are not going through this alone."

CE2
Consent for a Minor — Parent-Child Conflict
Category:** Ethics / Communication | **Time:** 11 min | **Difficulty:** High

CASE SUMMARY

A 15-year-old presents without a parent requesting extraction of a painful tooth. The candidate must assess whether the young person has sufficient maturity to consent independently (Gillick competence / mature minor doctrine), and navigate the ethical tension between adolescent autonomy and parental consent.

CANDIDATE BRIEF

Jake, 15, has arrived alone. He has a heavily decayed, symptomatic lower right molar (46) that has been causing significant pain for a week. He says his parents are "away" and he "just wants it fixed now." He has tried to call them but got no answer. He is cognitively mature, articulate, and clearly understands the procedure. Your task: assess capacity, manage the consent process, and decide how to proceed.

EXAMINER CONTEXT

Jake is calm, articulate, and clearly understands what extraction means (risks, alternatives). If the candidate explores capacity using appropriate questions (understands, believes, retains, weighs), he demonstrates it convincingly. If the candidate refuses to treat without parental signature without any assessment, they will lose marks. If the candidate treats without any attempt to reach the parent, they also lose marks. The pain is significant but not an immediate life-threatening emergency.

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

Assess Gillick/mature minor competence — INFLECTION 1

"Jake, before anything else, I need to have a quick chat with you about what you understand about the treatment. Is that okay?"

Test the four elements:

  1. Understand — "Can you tell me in your own words what an extraction involves?"
  2. Believe — "Do you believe this applies to your situation — that this tooth needs to come out?"
  3. Retain — (demonstrated by answers to above)
  4. Weigh — "What are the main risks? What happens if we don't do it? Why have you decided extraction is the right choice?"

If Jake passes: he demonstrates Gillick competence — he is capable of consenting independently under the mature minor doctrine recognised in Australian law.

Attempt to contact parents — INFLECTION 2

Even if Jake has capacity, make a genuine documented attempt to contact the parents (try calling — document time, number called, outcome). This is reasonable practice even with a competent minor.

"I've tried calling your parents twice and left a message. I'll document that."

Decision framework

  • Capacity confirmed + unable to reach parents: For a non-emergency procedure that the patient has clearly consented to and understands — you may proceed with a mature minor who demonstrates competence. Document thoroughly.
  • Capacity uncertain: Do not proceed without parental consent. Schedule urgent review, prescribe analgesia and antibiotics to manage pain until a parent can consent.
  • True emergency (airway, haemorrhage, life-threatening infection): Proceed under necessity doctrine without consent.

Documenting (1 min)

"I'll document in detail: that you attended without a parent, the capacity assessment I carried out and its result, the attempts I made to contact your parents, your consent to proceed, and the treatment provided."

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Formally assesses Gillick/mature minor competence (understand, believe, retain, weigh)
  2. ✅ Makes documented attempt to reach parents regardless
  3. ✅ Correctly applies mature minor doctrine to allow treatment if capacity confirmed
  4. ✅ Distinguishes emergency vs. non-emergency doctrine
  5. ✅ Thorough documentation is essential
  6. ✅ Does NOT refuse treatment solely because patient is 15 without any assessment

TG4 ALERTS

Mature minor doctrine (Australia) — A patient under 18 who demonstrates capacity to understand, believe, retain, and weigh information can provide valid consent. Age 14+ in most Australian jurisdictions creates a presumption of competence. Document the assessment.
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • "Gillick/Fraser competence (Australia): a child under 16 can consent independently if they demonstrate sufficient intelligence and maturity to understand the nature, purpose, and consequences of the proposed treatment — assessed on a case-by-case basis."
  • "At 16+: presumptive capacity to consent in most Australian states. Treat as an adult for consent purposes unless there is evidence of incapacity."
  • "Child refuses, parent consents: if child is Gillick competent, their refusal must be respected. A competent child's refusal overrides parental consent."
  • "Parent refuses, child consents: if child is Gillick competent, they can consent to treatment even without parental agreement for treatments that are in their best interest."
Patient Reframes
  • "(To a teenager) This is your mouth and your body — I want to hear what YOU want and what your concerns are."
  • "(To a parent) I understand you want what's best for your child — and so do I. But at this age, their view carries real weight in the decision. Let me speak with them directly."
Curveball Deflectors
  • "Parent says yes, 14-year-old refuses." → "At 14, I need to assess whether this patient is Gillick competent for this specific decision. If they can understand the treatment, the risks, and the consequences, their refusal is legally and ethically significant. I cannot proceed against a competent child's clearly expressed refusal."
  • "The teenager wants it, but the parent says no." → "If this young person is Gillick competent — which I'm going to assess — they can consent independently. Parental refusal does not override a competent minor's consent for treatment that is in their best interest."
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ▶
STAGE: Opening and Rapport

Greets Jake warmly at the door. Invites him to sit. Notes he has attended alone.

"Hi Jake, I'm Dr. [name], one of the dentists here today. Come on in and take a seat. I can see from our notes that you've come in by yourself today — that's absolutely fine, and I want you to know this is a safe space. Before we do anything clinical at all, I'd like to have a proper chat with you first. Is that okay?"

"So Jake, tell me — what's been going on with this tooth?"

Listens attentively as Jake describes a week of significant pain in the lower right back region, pointing to tooth 46. Notes he has tried to contact his parents without success.

"That sounds really uncomfortable — a whole week of pain is a long time. I want to help you sort this out today if we can. I just need to go through a couple of things with you first, so we can do this properly and safely. Does that make sense?"

---

Capacity Assessment — Gillick / Mature Minor

"Jake, in Australia, even though you're fifteen, the law recognises that a young person your age can sometimes make their own medical and dental decisions — as long as I'm satisfied that you genuinely understand what's involved. So I'd like to ask you a few questions — not to test you, but just to make sure we're on the same page. Is that alright?"

**Understand:** "Can you tell me in your own words what a tooth extraction involves — what we would actually do?"

Listens carefully. Jake describes local anaesthetic, loosening the tooth, removing it. Candidate nods.

"That's exactly right. Good. And do you understand there are some risks involved — things like pain after the procedure, swelling, possible infection, or in rare cases, some numbness if a nerve is nearby?"

**Believe:** "Do you feel that what I've just described applies to your situation — that this is actually your tooth we're talking about, and that extraction is genuinely what's needed here?"

Listens as Jake confirms he does.

**Weigh:** "What happens, in your mind, if we don't take this tooth out today — if we just leave it a bit longer?"

Listens as Jake describes ongoing pain, risk of infection getting worse, disruption to school. Candidate acknowledges.

"And why have you decided extraction is the right choice, rather than, say, waiting until your parents are back?"

**Retain:** Satisfied that Jake has demonstrated retention through the consistency and coherence of his answers throughout the exchange.

"Jake, I have to say — you've shown me that you clearly understand what the procedure involves, you believe it applies to your situation, and you've weighed up the pros and cons thoughtfully. That tells me you have the capacity to make this decision for yourself today. In Australian law, this is called the mature minor doctrine, and it means your consent can be valid even without a parent present, provided I've assessed you the way I just have."

---

Attempt to Contact Parents

"Even though I'm satisfied with your capacity, I want to do the right thing and try to reach your parents once more — not because I need their permission, but because it's good practice and I'd like them to know you've been seen. Would you be okay with that, and do you have a number for them?"

Steps briefly to the side. Attempts two calls. Documents time, number called, and that no answer was received. Returns.

"I've tried calling twice and left a message letting them know you're here and being seen. I've noted that in your file. If they call back, I'll be happy to speak with them."

---

Consent Confirmation and Treatment Decision

"So Jake, based on our conversation, I'm satisfied that you have the capacity to consent to this extraction today. This is a non-emergency procedure, and you've given me your informed consent. I'm going to go ahead and treat you. Before I do, let me go over the key points once more — the extraction itself, the risks including post-operative pain and swelling, the aftercare instructions, and what to look out for. Does that all make sense? Do you have any questions for me?"

Confirms Jake's verbal consent. Proceeds to document full consent in the clinical notes.

"I'll be giving you a local anaesthetic — lignocaine — to numb the area completely before we start. You shouldn't feel any pain during the procedure, though you may feel some pressure. Afterwards, I'll give you written aftercare instructions. For pain relief, paracetamol one gram every four to six hours is your first option, and if needed you can alternate with ibuprofen four hundred milligrams every six to eight hours — just make sure you take that with food."

---

Documentation and Closing

"Jake, before we begin, I want you to know exactly what I'm recording in your notes today. I'm documenting that you attended without a parent or guardian, that I conducted a formal capacity assessment covering your ability to understand, believe, retain and weigh the information, and that you demonstrated Gillick competence as recognised under the mature minor doctrine in Australian law. I'm also recording the two attempts I made to contact your parents, the times those calls were made, and that no answer was received. I'm documenting your informed consent to proceed with the extraction of tooth 46, and I'll record the full treatment provided today."

"If anything changes at any point — if you feel unwell, if you have any doubts, or if your parents want to speak with me afterwards — please don't hesitate. You've done really well today, Jake. Alright, let's get you out of pain."

CE3
Informed Consent — Patient Refuses a Recommended Treatment
Category:** Ethics / Communication | **Time:** 11 min | **Difficulty:** Exam-ready

CASE SUMMARY

A 52-year-old presents for review. You have strongly recommended a root canal treatment for an abscessed tooth (26) — the alternative is extraction. After you explain both options, the patient says: "I don't want the root canal. Just pull it out." You believe extraction is the worse option clinically. Candidate must navigate the tension between clinical recommendation and patient autonomy.

CANDIDATE BRIEF

You have diagnosed an acute apical abscess of 26. You have recommended RCT as it is a strategically important molar in a partially dentate arch. The patient, after your full explanation, says "I've made up my mind — just take it out." They are competent, informed, and insistent. Your task: navigate this ethically and clinically.

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

Explore the reason — INFLECTION 1: Ask before accepting the refusal

"I really want to make sure I understand your decision. Can I ask what's making you lean toward extraction over the root canal? Is it cost? Time? Anxiety about the procedure? Or something else?"

Listen fully. The reason matters — it may be addressable.

Address the specific barrier (1 min)

  • If cost: "The root canal is more expensive up front, but extraction plus replacement options cost more long-term — let me explain."
  • If fear: "We can do the root canal under sedation, with breaks whenever you need them."
  • If time: "We can stage it to work with your schedule."
  • If they simply prefer extraction despite full information: proceed to acceptance.

Confirm it is an informed decision — INFLECTION 2

"I want to make sure you're making this decision with the full picture, because it's an irreversible one. May I just summarise the implications of extraction?"

  1. Loss of 26 — significant chewing tooth
  2. Neighbouring teeth and opposing tooth will drift over time
  3. Bone loss in the extraction site
  4. Replacement options: implant, bridge, partial denture (costs, benefits)
  5. If no replacement: further drift, occlusal collapse over years

Accept the decision (1 min) — INFLECTION 3

"I hear you. You've heard all the information, and you've made a considered choice. A competent adult has the right to decline a recommended treatment, even if I believe a different option is better clinically. I respect that."

Do NOT pressure. Do NOT withhold treatment in response. Do NOT say "fine, it's your loss."

Document (1 min)

"I'll document that I recommended RCT, explained the risks of extraction including missing tooth consequences, that you declined RCT, and that you consented to extraction with full understanding. If you're happy to, I'd ask you to sign a note confirming that discussion."

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Explores the reason for refusal (barrier may be addressable)
  2. ✅ Addresses the specific barrier
  3. ✅ Confirms fully informed before accepting (irreversible decision)
  4. ✅ Explicitly accepts patient autonomy — does not pressure or punish
  5. ✅ Documents the discussion and patient's confirmed informed refusal
  6. ✅ Proceeds with extraction (does NOT refuse to treat)
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • "Competent adults have the absolute right to refuse treatment — including life-preserving treatment. The clinician's role is to ensure the refusal is informed, not to override it."
  • "Informed refusal process: explain the diagnosis clearly, outline the consequences of not treating (specific and realistic), confirm the patient understands, document the conversation."
  • "DO NOT: withhold other care as leverage, coerce, use paternalistic language, treat without consent. DO: offer alternatives, address underlying fears or concerns, leave the door open."
  • "If capacity is in doubt: assess using MCAT (understand, retain, weigh, communicate). If capacity confirmed → respect. If capacity in question → involve family, guardian, legal team."
Patient Reframes
  • "I want to make sure you have all the information — and then, whatever you decide, I respect that it's your decision. Let me be specific about what I think will happen if we don't treat this."
  • "You've heard what I think. What's driving your decision? Because sometimes understanding the concern helps me offer something that works better for you."
Curveball Deflectors
  • "But you're the professional — you know what's best." → "I have clinical expertise, and my job is to give you the best information I can. But the decision about what happens to your body is yours. My role is to ensure the decision is informed — not to make it for you."
  • "What if I change my mind later?" → "You can change your mind at any point — my door is open. What I need to do today is make sure you've heard everything relevant to the decision. After that, the timing is yours."
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ▶
STAGE: Opening and Re-establishing the Conversation

"Thank you for coming back in. Before we go any further today, I just want to check in — I know we've covered a lot of information about tooth 26, and I want to make sure you feel completely comfortable with everything we've discussed. You've told me you'd like to go ahead with extraction rather than the root canal treatment. I really do respect that this is your decision, and I'm not here to override it. But I would feel I wasn't doing my job properly if I didn't take a moment to understand your thinking and make sure we've covered everything. Is that okay?"

Pauses and listens. Maintains open, non-pressuring body language.

---

Exploring the Reason for Refusal

"I really want to make sure I understand your decision. Can I ask what's making you lean toward extraction over the root canal? Is it cost? Concerns about the procedure itself, or the time it takes? Or perhaps something else entirely?"

Listens fully without interrupting.

If the patient indicates cost: "That's completely understandable. The root canal does have a higher upfront cost — you're looking at several appointments and the crown that follows. But I do want you to have the full picture, because leaving the space empty, or replacing the tooth later with an implant or a bridge, typically costs more in total than completing the root canal now. It's worth factoring that in."

If the patient indicates fear or anxiety: "I hear you, and that's very common. I want you to know we can manage that. We can take the procedure in stages, we can use longer anaesthetic appointments with breaks whenever you need them, and if anxiety is a significant concern, we can discuss conscious sedation as an option to make the experience as comfortable as possible."

If the patient indicates time constraints: "We can absolutely stage this to work around your schedule. You don't need to complete it all at once — we can plan each appointment around what suits you."

---

Confirming the Decision Is Fully Informed

"I want to make sure you're making this choice with the complete picture, because removing a tooth is an irreversible decision. May I just take two minutes to summarise what that means for you long-term? I'm not trying to change your mind — I just want to make certain you've heard all of it."

"Tooth 26 is one of your upper back molars — it carries a significant load when you chew, and it sits in a really important position in your arch. Once we remove it, the teeth on either side will gradually drift toward the gap, and the lower molar underneath will start to over-erupt — it moves upward into the space over time. That leads to changes in your bite, increased wear on other teeth, and bone loss in that area of your jaw."

"If you want to replace the tooth later, your options are an implant, a bridge, or a partial denture — each has different costs, timelines, and considerations. If you choose not to replace it, over years that drifting and bone loss will continue. I'm not saying any of this to alarm you — I'm saying it because you deserve to make this decision knowing exactly what to expect."

---

Accepting the Decision and Affirming Autonomy

"I hear you. You've listened carefully, you've asked good questions, and you've made a considered choice with full information. As a competent adult, you absolutely have the right to decline a treatment I've recommended, even when I believe clinically it's the better option. I respect that, and I want to be clear — I'm not going to pressure you further, and I'm not going to withhold treatment because you've made a different choice than I would make."

"We will go ahead with the extraction of 26. I'll look after you well, and we'll make sure you're as comfortable as possible throughout."

---

Documentation and Closing

"Before we proceed, I'd like to note everything we've discussed in your records — that I recommended root canal treatment, that I explained the consequences of extraction including tooth drift, bone loss, and replacement options, and that you declined the root canal with full understanding and consented to extraction. I'll ask you to sign a brief note confirming that conversation took place. That protects you and makes sure everything is transparent. Are you comfortable with that?"

"Is there anything else you'd like to ask before we get started? Any questions at all — about the extraction itself, aftercare, or anything we've talked about today?"

Conducts extraction. Following procedure: "After the extraction, bite firmly on the gauze for about 20 minutes. Some oozing over the next day or two is completely normal. Take paracetamol one gram every four to six hours as needed for pain. If you experience bright, ongoing bleeding, significant swelling, or anything that concerns you, please call us immediately. And whenever you're ready down the track, we're happy to discuss replacement options for that tooth."

CE4
Language Barrier — Working with an Interpreter
Category:** Communication | **Time:** 11 min | **Difficulty:** Exam-ready

CASE SUMMARY

An 80-year-old Vietnamese-speaking patient presents with a family member who offers to interpret. The candidate must navigate the use of an interpreter appropriately — including recognising the problems with using family members as interpreters for consent and complex clinical discussions.

CANDIDATE BRIEF

Mrs. Nguyen, 80, has come with her 45-year-old son David, who speaks English fluently. Mrs. Nguyen speaks no English. David says he will "translate everything." You need to obtain consent for a complex extraction (retained root, close to inferior alveolar nerve). Your task: manage the consultation, including the interpreter dynamics.

EXAMINER CONTEXT

David is well-intentioned but will paraphrase, summarise, and omit details when asked to translate complex information. He says "I know Mum better than you do" when challenged. He downplays risks because he "doesn't want to worry her." If the candidate raises concerns about using a family interpreter for consent, the examiner may offer a professional interpreter option (telephone interpreter service available in Australia).

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

Acknowledge and thank David — INFLECTION 1

"Thank you for being here, David. Your support for your mother is wonderful. I want to be upfront about how I'd like to work today."

Explain the interpreter issue — INFLECTION 2

"For routine visits, a family interpreter is often perfectly fine. However, today I need to discuss a surgical procedure, its risks, and get your mother's consent — that's a situation where the standard of practice is to use a trained interpreter, for her protection and mine. A trained interpreter is bound by professional standards to translate exactly what is said, without summarising or filtering."

Offer the solution (TIS — Telephone Interpreter Service) — INFLECTION 3

"We have access to a free telephone interpreter service called TIS — Translating and Interpreting Service — it's a government service available in Australia for health consultations. With your permission, I'd like to call them now and conduct the consultation that way. It will take about 10 minutes to set up."

"David, I'd still love for you to be present for support — you know your mother and can provide important context. But the formal interpretation will come from the professional."

Consultation with the interpreter

When the interpreter is on the phone:

  • Speak in short sentences. Pause frequently.
  • Speak TO the patient, not "tell her that..."
  • "Mrs. Nguyen, I'm going to explain the procedure. Please tell me if anything isn't clear."
  • Check understanding: "Can you tell me in your own words what we've discussed?"

Document

"I'll note in the file that a TIS interpreter was used, the interpreter's ID number, and that consent was obtained through professional interpretation."

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Acknowledges David's presence warmly, does not exclude him
  2. ✅ Explains the problem with family interpreters for consent (paraphrasing, conflict of interest, filtering)
  3. ✅ Offers TIS as the solution (free, government-backed, professional)
  4. ✅ Speaks to the patient directly during interpretation (not "tell her that")
  5. ✅ Checks understanding in the patient's own words
  6. ✅ Documents interpreter ID and method

TG4 ALERTS

Professional interpreter for consent — Use TIS (131 450) for complex or consent conversations. Family interpreters are acceptable for routine questions but not for informed consent where risk discussions occur. Document interpreter use.
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • "Professional interpreter is mandatory for high-stakes clinical conversations — consent, diagnosis, treatment planning, results. Family members as interpreters are inappropriate: confidentiality risks, accuracy issues, role confusion, potential for bias or withholding."
  • "TIS National (13 14 50): Australian Government Translating and Interpreting Service — free for eligible patients and healthcare providers. Available over the phone immediately."
  • "Working with an interpreter: speak to the patient, not the interpreter. Short sentences. Confirm understanding after each step. Use teach-back ('Can you explain back to me what we've decided?')."
  • "When no interpreter is available: manage acute emergency with available communication aids (visual, pointing, phone translation apps for simple concepts). Rebook for the full consent conversation with a booked interpreter."
Patient Reframes
  • "I want to make sure I explain everything properly to you — so I'm going to call the phone interpreter service now. It takes about 2 minutes to connect, and it means nothing important gets missed."
  • "(Framing for patient) Everything we discuss is completely confidential — the interpreter follows strict professional rules, just like I do."
Curveball Deflectors
  • "His son is here and offers to translate." → "I appreciate that — and I'll use him for logistics. But for the clinical conversation about diagnosis and treatment, I need a professional interpreter. It's not about doubting him; it's about making sure nothing clinical gets misunderstood or omitted, and protecting everyone in the room."
  • "There's no interpreter available." → "I can manage the acute problem today with available communication tools. For the full treatment planning conversation — where accurate consent is essential — I'll rebook with a professional interpreter arranged in advance."
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ▶
STAGE: Opening — Welcoming Mrs. Nguyen and David

Greets both warmly, makes eye contact with Mrs. Nguyen first, smiles and nods respectfully.

"Good morning. You must be Mrs. Nguyen — welcome, it's lovely to meet you." Turns to David. "And you're David, Mrs. Nguyen's son — thank you so much for bringing her in today. It's clear you care deeply about your mother, and having family support here really does make a difference."

"David, before we begin, I'd like to have a quick conversation with you about how we'll run today's appointment. Is that okay?"

---

Addressing the Interpreter Dynamics

"David, for a routine check-up or a straightforward conversation, having a family member help with translation is perfectly fine, and I'd normally welcome that. But today is a little different. I need to discuss a surgical procedure with your mother — a complex tooth extraction — including the risks involved, and I need to obtain her consent. For that kind of conversation, the professional standard of care in Australia is to use a trained interpreter."

Pauses, maintains a warm and non-confrontational tone.

"The reason isn't a reflection on you at all — it's about protecting your mother. A trained professional interpreter is bound by a strict code of conduct to translate every word exactly as it is said, without summarising, paraphrasing, or making decisions about what to include or leave out. When we're discussing surgical risks — things like nerve proximity and the possibility of altered sensation — every word matters. There's also the question of emotional pressure. It can be genuinely difficult for a family member to relay concerning information to someone they love, and that's an unfair position to put you in."

"I hope that makes sense. Does that feel reasonable to you?"

---

Offering the Solution — TIS

"What I'd like to do is use a service called TIS — the Translating and Interpreting Service. It's a free Australian Government telephone interpreter service available specifically for health consultations, and we can call them right now on 131 450. It usually takes about ten minutes to connect with a Vietnamese interpreter. The interpreter introduces themselves, provides an ID number, and then we simply conduct the consultation through the phone."

"David, I'd very much like you to stay in the room throughout — your mother knows you, trusts you, and you can provide important background information if I need it. But the formal interpretation will come from the professional on the phone. That way your mother is fully protected, and you're not put in an uncomfortable position either."

Waits for David's agreement, then proceeds to call TIS.

---

Conducting the Consultation Through the Interpreter

Once the interpreter is connected and has introduced themselves, the candidate notes the interpreter's name and ID number on the file. Speaks clearly, in short sentences, directly to Mrs. Nguyen throughout.

"Mrs. Nguyen, thank you for your patience. I have a Vietnamese interpreter on the phone who will help us communicate today."

"Mrs. Nguyen, I'd like to explain what I found on your X-ray and what I'm recommending. The tooth at the back of your lower jaw has a retained root — that means part of the root is still in your gum. It needs to be removed with a small surgical procedure."

Pauses after each sentence to allow interpretation.

"The root is sitting close to an important nerve called the inferior alveolar nerve. Because of this, there is a small risk — around one to two percent — of temporary altered sensation in your lower lip and chin after the procedure. In very rare cases, this can be permanent. I want to make sure you understand this before we go ahead."

"Do you have any questions so far, Mrs. Nguyen?"

---

Checking Understanding and Obtaining Consent

"Mrs. Nguyen, to make sure I've explained this clearly, could you tell me in your own words what the procedure involves and what the main risk is that we discussed?"

Listens carefully to the interpreted response. If the patient's summary is incomplete, gently clarifies and rechecks.

"That's exactly right. You've understood this very well."

"Are you happy to proceed with the extraction today, knowing what we've discussed?"

Once verbal consent is confirmed, has the consent form signed with the interpreter still on the line to interpret each line of the form as required.

---

Documentation and Closing

Records in the clinical notes: TIS interpreter used for consent discussion, interpreter's name and ID number documented, Vietnamese language, informed consent obtained for surgical extraction of retained root with IAN proximity risk explained.

"Mrs. Nguyen, you've been wonderful today. I'll take very good care of you."

Turns to David. "David, thank you for your understanding. Your mother was able to make a fully informed decision today, and that's the best outcome for everyone. If you have any questions after today, please don't hesitate to call us."

CE5
Aggressive / Abusive Patient — Boundary Management
Category:** Communication / Ethics | **Time:** 11 min | **Difficulty:** Exam-ready

CASE SUMMARY

A 42-year-old patient becomes verbally abusive during a consultation after waiting 25 minutes. He uses profanity toward the receptionist and is now in your surgery being verbally aggressive toward you. Candidate must de-escalate without capitulating, enforce professional boundaries, and decide how to proceed.

CANDIDATE BRIEF

Mr. Reid, 42, has a dental emergency appointment after waiting 25 minutes. He enters your surgery still agitated, says "This is a f***ing joke — I've been in pain all week and you can't even be bothered to see me on time." He is standing rather than sitting, loud, and continues to use profanity. Your task: de-escalate and manage the consultation professionally.

EXAMINER CONTEXT

Mr. Reid is angry about the wait but is in genuine pain. If the candidate de-escalates skillfully (acknowledges the wait, validates the pain, sets firm boundaries), he calms down sufficiently for the consultation to proceed. If the candidate becomes defensive or dismissive, he escalates. If the candidate asks him to leave without any attempt at de-escalation, they lose marks.

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

Immediate — physical safety (0.5 min)

Stay seated or move to a neutral position (not cornered). Door accessible. Do not stand in a confrontational posture.

Acknowledge the frustration — INFLECTION 1: Name it, don't dismiss it

"Mr. Reid, I can see you're in real pain and you've been waiting longer than you should have. That's not what we want for any patient, and I'm sorry you've had to wait."

(Do not apologise for things that aren't your fault — but DO acknowledge the experience.)

Set the boundary — INFLECTION 2: Clear, calm, one time

"I want to help you, and I'm going to give you my full attention. To do that, I need to ask you to speak to me without profanity. I understand you're frustrated — I'm asking because I need to be able to focus on what's happening with you clinically. Can we do that?"

State it once. Do not argue. Wait.

If he continues to be abusive after the boundary is set — INFLECTION 3

"I hear that you're in significant pain, and I genuinely want to help you. But I'm not able to continue the consultation while I'm being spoken to this way. If you'd like me to help you today, I need us to be able to speak calmly. I'm going to give you a moment, and I'll come back."

Give space. Briefly step out if safe to do so.

If he settles — proceed with full consultation

"Thank you. Now tell me — where is the pain, and how long have you been dealing with this?"

If he escalates to threats or physical aggression

"I need you to leave the clinic. I'm going to call the front desk now. We will arrange an emergency referral so that you can be seen elsewhere today — but I can't provide care in this situation."

After the consultation

  • Incident report filed (practice records)
  • Consider whether to continue seeing this patient (right to dismiss from practice for ongoing aggression, with appropriate notice)
  • Brief the reception team about what happened

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Physical positioning first (safety, access to exit)
  2. ✅ Acknowledges the frustration genuinely — does not dismiss or lecture
  3. ✅ Sets the boundary calmly and clearly, once
  4. ✅ Gives the patient an opportunity to comply
  5. ✅ Steps out if needed (de-escalation space)
  6. ✅ Knows when to end the consultation (threats / physical aggression)
  7. ✅ Incident report and follow-through after the event
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • "De-escalation: remain calm, lower your own voice, do not mirror aggression. Use open body language. Acknowledge the frustration specifically: 'I can see you're very upset — let me understand what's happened.'"
  • "Escalation threshold: if verbal abuse continues after one clear, calm boundary statement → pause treatment, sit patient upright, ensure your exit is clear, have a colleague present."
  • "Right to stop treatment: dental professionals have the legal and ethical right to refuse or discontinue treatment when personal safety or professional respect cannot be maintained. Document everything."
  • "Distinction: anxious patient expressing fear ≠ abusive patient. Fear needs empathy and adjustment. Abuse directed at staff needs a boundary statement and potential discharge from the practice."
Patient Reframes
  • "I want to help you — and I can do that best if we can have a respectful conversation. When you're ready, I'm here."
  • "(After escalation) I need to pause here. I understand you're in pain and frustrated — that's legitimate. But I can't continue treatment while things are this way. Can we take a moment?"
Curveball Deflectors
  • "He's just anxious — be more understanding." → "Dental anxiety is real and I take it seriously. There's a difference between a patient who is frightened and needs reassurance — which I can give — and a patient who is directing abuse at my staff. Both deserve care, but the approach is different."
  • "What if they're in acute pain?" → "Acute pain changes the priority — I'll manage the emergency. And I'll also have a clear, kind conversation about what I need from a future appointment to be able to provide ongoing care."
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ▶
STAGE: Physical Safety & Opening

Before Mr. Reid enters, Candidate ensures the chair is not blocking the exit, positions themselves to the side of the desk rather than behind it, and confirms the door remains accessible. Candidate does not adopt a confrontational stance — arms remain relaxed, posture open and calm.

Mr. Reid enters, standing, visibly agitated. Candidate remains calm, does not raise their voice, and makes deliberate, unhurried eye contact.

"Mr. Reid, come in. I'm Dr. [Name]."

Candidate allows a brief pause, does not immediately speak over him.

---

Acknowledging the Frustration

"Mr. Reid, I can hear that you're in real pain, and I can see you've had to wait longer than you should have today. That is genuinely not what we want for any of our patients, and I'm sorry that was your experience this morning. That wait must have been very hard when you're already dealing with significant pain."

Candidate speaks slowly and evenly, does not mirror the agitation, and does not move toward the patient. Gesture toward the dental chair — calm, open-handed.

"Please, take a seat whenever you're ready. I want to hear exactly what's been happening with you."
