---

Setting the Boundary — Clearly, Calmly, Once

Mr. Reid remains standing and continues to use profanity. Candidate does not flinch, raise their voice, or lecture. After a natural pause, candidate speaks directly and steadily.

"Mr. Reid, I do want to help you today — that's exactly why you're here, and you have my full attention. But I need to ask you one thing: I need you to speak to me without that language. I'm not saying that to dismiss how frustrated you are — I understand you're in pain. I'm asking because I need to be able to focus completely on what's happening clinically with you, and I can do that much better when we're able to talk calmly together. Can we do that?"

Candidate states this once. Does not repeat it immediately. Waits. Holds eye contact without aggression. Gives the patient space to respond.

---

Giving Space — If Behaviour Continues

If Mr. Reid continues to be verbally abusive after the boundary has been stated:

"Mr. Reid, I hear you — you are in significant pain and you've been waiting, and that's genuinely difficult. But I'm not able to continue this consultation while I'm being spoken to this way. That's not good for either of us, and it won't help me help you. What I'd like to do is give you a moment. I'm going to step just outside for two minutes, and when I come back, if you're ready, we'll get started straight away."

Candidate steps briefly outside — leaving the door ajar, informing the nurse or reception staff quietly that they are giving the patient a moment to settle. Candidate returns after approximately two minutes.

If at any point Mr. Reid makes a physical threat or moves aggressively toward the candidate:

"Mr. Reid, I need you to stop. I'm going to ask you to leave the clinic now. We will arrange an emergency referral so that you can be seen somewhere else today — but I cannot provide care in this situation. I'm calling the front desk."

Candidate moves toward exit, contacts reception, and does not attempt to physically intervene.

---

Proceeding With the Consultation — If Patient Settles

Mr. Reid sits. His tone changes. Candidate re-enters, sits, and proceeds naturally and warmly.

"Thank you. I appreciate that. Now — tell me, where is the pain exactly, and how long have you been dealing with this?"

Candidate proceeds with a full history: onset, site, character, radiation, severity, aggravating and relieving factors, any swelling, systemic symptoms, and relevant medical history. Clinical examination follows as appropriate. Candidate treats Mr. Reid with the same standard of care as any other patient — the settled consultation is handled professionally and without residual coldness or distance.

---

After the Consultation — Follow-Through

After Mr. Reid has left, candidate completes a formal incident report documenting the behaviour, the specific language used, the time, and the steps taken — including boundary-setting and any time stepped outside. This becomes part of the practice record.

Candidate approaches the receptionist privately.

"I just wanted to check in with you after what happened earlier. Are you okay? That was not acceptable behaviour, and I want you to know I've documented everything. If you'd like to talk about it, I'm here."

Candidate considers, in discussion with the practice principal, whether continued care of Mr. Reid is appropriate. A patient may be dismissed from a practice for ongoing aggressive behaviour, provided reasonable written notice is given and emergency care remains available during any transition period. This is both an ethical right and a duty of care to staff.

CE6
Reporting a Colleague — Impaired/Incompetent Dentist
Category:** Ethics | **Time:** 11 min | **Difficulty:** High

CASE SUMMARY

A dental nurse comes to you saying she's been concerned about a colleague (Dr. X) for several months — arriving to work smelling of alcohol, seeming confused when doing procedures, making clinical errors. She asks your advice. Candidate must navigate the mandatory reporting obligations under Australian law (AHPRA mandatory reporting).

CANDIDATE BRIEF

You are the practice principal. A dental nurse pulls you aside and discloses that she has noticed concerning behaviour in Dr. X over the past 3 months: arriving with alcohol on his breath, seeming unusually confused during procedures, making several charting errors, and recently anaesthetising the wrong tooth before being corrected. She is scared to speak up because Dr. X is her employer's friend. Your task: advise her and determine your own obligations.

EXAMINER CONTEXT

The nurse is nervous and wants reassurance that "nothing bad will happen to Dr. X." Will resist the idea of reporting if the candidate frames it as punitive. If the candidate explains it as patient safety and a professional obligation, she becomes more receptive. She will ask: "What happens to me if I report?" — the candidate must address whistleblower protections.

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

Acknowledge the courage it took to come to you — INFLECTION 1

"Thank you for telling me. I know this wasn't easy to raise — it takes real courage to speak up about a colleague, especially when you're worried about the consequences. I want you to know you've done the right thing."

Clarify what you've heard (1 min)

"Let me make sure I understand. Over the past 3 months, you've noticed Dr. X appearing to have alcohol on his breath, seeming confused during procedures, making charting errors, and one instance of anaesthetising the wrong tooth. Is that right?"

Explain mandatory reporting (2 min) — INFLECTION 2

"Under Australian law, AHPRA has a mandatory reporting scheme. Health practitioners — including dentists and dental nurses — have a legal obligation to report a registered health practitioner if they have a reasonable belief that practitioner is practising while impaired and that the impairment poses a risk of harm to patients.

What you're describing — intoxication, confusion during procedures, a wrong-site anaesthetic — clearly meets the threshold of a reasonable belief of impairment posing risk. This is not optional. The legal obligation is on both of us."

Explain the purpose — not punishment — INFLECTION 3

"I want to be clear about what this reporting is for. It's not about punishing Dr. X. AHPRA will investigate. If Dr. X has an alcohol or health problem, the outcome may include being directed to treatment and support — not just sanctions. Many practitioners who go through this process come out the other side with help they needed. Patient safety comes first, but this process can also help Dr. X."

Whistleblower protections (1 min)

"Your identity is protected under the mandatory reporting scheme. AHPRA treats reports confidentially. You cannot be disciplined or dismissed for making a mandatory report made in good faith. This is a protected action in law."

Next steps

"I'm going to make a report to AHPRA today. I would encourage you to do the same, separately — both of our reports strengthen the picture. In the meantime, I will speak to the practice owner about restricting Dr. X's clinical duties pending investigation, to protect patients in the immediate term."

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Thanks the nurse for coming forward
  2. ✅ Clarifies and documents the specific concerns heard
  3. ✅ Names AHPRA mandatory reporting obligations correctly
  4. ✅ Identifies the threshold: reasonable belief, impairment, risk to patients
  5. ✅ Frames reporting as patient safety AND support for the colleague
  6. ✅ Explains whistleblower protections
  7. ✅ Initiates their own report and advises interim clinical restrictions

TG4 ALERTS

AHPRA Mandatory Reporting — National Law (Health Practitioner Regulation) requires mandatory reporting when a registered practitioner has a reasonable belief that another practitioner is intoxicated, mentally ill, or physically impaired and this poses a risk of harm to the public. Reports made in good faith are protected.
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • "Mandatory reporting in Australia: under AHPRA's National Law, registered practitioners have a legal obligation to report a colleague if they have a reasonable belief the colleague's conduct represents notifiable conduct — impairment, intoxication, sexual misconduct, or practising in a way that causes significant risk to patient safety."
  • "'Reasonable belief' is the threshold — not certainty. Document specific observations: date, what was seen, who was present, patient impact."
  • "Process: consult your MDA (ADAVB, MDDUS, MDA National) first. Report to AHPRA via the notifiable conduct form. Whistleblower protections apply for good-faith reports."
  • "Do NOT: gossip, confront aggressively, investigate yourself, ignore the situation hoping it resolves."
Patient Reframes
  • "(To affected patient) Your safety is my priority. I'm going to document what I've found carefully, and I may need to report my concerns to the appropriate authority — with or without your involvement."
  • "This is one of the hardest things a clinician has to do — and also one of the most important. The obligation to patients outweighs professional loyalty."
Curveball Deflectors
  • "What if I'm wrong about what I saw?" → "The standard is 'reasonable belief' — not certainty. If a reasonable person in your position, with what you observed, would have concern about patient safety, you have an obligation to report. AHPRA investigates; you provide the information."
  • "Can't I just talk to him first?" → "For minor concerns or an isolated incident, a direct conversation is appropriate — and often the right first step. But if the behaviour continues, or if the risk is serious enough that delay creates patient harm, you have a professional obligation that supersedes the discomfort of that conversation."
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ▶
STAGE: Opening — Receiving the Disclosure

Turns to the dental nurse, maintains calm and private setting. Closes the door or steps away from the corridor.

"Thank you so much for coming to me. I can see this hasn't been easy, and I want you to know straight away — you have done the right thing by speaking up. I'm going to take everything you've told me seriously. Before we go any further, I want you to feel safe in this conversation. What you share with me stays between us as far as is possible, and I'll explain why I say 'as far as possible' in a moment."

---

Clarifying and Documenting the Concerns

"Let me make sure I've understood exactly what you've observed, because the details really matter here. Over the past three months, you've noticed Dr. X arriving at work with what appears to be alcohol on his breath. You've described him seeming unusually confused during clinical procedures. There have been charting errors on multiple occasions. And most recently, there was an incident where he anaesthetised the wrong tooth before being corrected. Is that an accurate summary? Is there anything else you'd want to add — dates, frequency, whether anyone else witnessed these events?"

Listens carefully. Nods. Makes a brief written note.

"I'm writing this down because if we need to report — and I do need to explain that to you shortly — having specific documented observations is important. You are not making accusations. You are recording what you have seen. That is a professional and responsible thing to do."

---

Explaining Mandatory Reporting Obligations

"I want to be completely honest with you about something, because you deserve to know where this goes from here. In Australia, under the National Law that governs AHPRA — the Australian Health Practitioner Regulation Agency — there is a mandatory reporting obligation. This is not discretionary. Both registered health practitioners and, in many circumstances, employers and staff who work alongside registered practitioners, are legally required to report if they hold a reasonable belief that a registered practitioner is impaired and that impairment poses a risk of harm to the public."

"What you have described — arriving smelling of alcohol, confusion during clinical procedures, and a wrong-site local anaesthetic — this clearly meets the threshold of a reasonable belief of impairment posing a risk to patients. This is not a borderline situation. One episode of anaesthetising the wrong tooth alone is a significant patient safety event. The combination of what you've described over three months strengthens that picture considerably."

"So I want to be clear: I have a legal obligation to report this to AHPRA. I will be doing that today. I would also strongly encourage you to make your own separate report. Two independent accounts from different observers carry more weight and provide a fuller picture for investigators."

---

Framing the Purpose — Safety and Support, Not Punishment

"I know the word 'report' can sound frightening, especially because Dr. X is connected to your employer. But I want you to understand what this process is actually designed to do. AHPRA's mandatory reporting scheme exists to protect patients — that is its primary purpose. But it is also designed to protect practitioners like Dr. X. If he is struggling with alcohol dependence or another health condition, AHPRA's investigation may result in him being directed into treatment and support. Many practitioners who go through this process receive the help they needed and return to practice safely. Reporting is not the end of Dr. X's career. Not reporting, and allowing a patient to be harmed — that could be."

---

Whistleblower Protections and Immediate Interim Steps

"Now, your safety. Under the mandatory reporting framework, reports made in good faith are legally protected. AHPRA handles reports confidentially. You cannot lawfully be dismissed, disciplined, or penalised for making a report you genuinely and reasonably believed was necessary. That protection exists specifically for situations like this — where someone is worried about the professional or personal consequences of speaking up. You are protected."

"In terms of what happens next in this practice — today, I will be speaking with the practice owner about placing immediate restrictions on Dr. X's clinical duties pending AHPRA's investigation. I cannot allow a situation where patients continue to be placed at risk while we wait for a formal outcome. That conversation will be difficult, but it is necessary."

---

Closing and Support for the Nurse

"Before you go, I want to acknowledge again how difficult this must have been to carry for three months on your own. You showed real professional courage today. If you need support through this process — if you have concerns about your position here, or you want guidance on making your own report — I will help you with that. We can look at the AHPRA website together and I can walk you through the notification form if that would help."

"Do you have any questions for me right now? Is there anything you are unsure about or worried about that we haven't covered?"

CE7
Ethical Dilemma — Conflict of Interest / Dual Obligation
Category:** Ethics | **Time:** 11 min | **Difficulty:** High

CASE SUMMARY

A dental representative visits the practice and offers the dentist a $500 gift voucher in exchange for agreeing to preferentially recommend their composite resin brand to patients. The candidate is asked to navigate the ethical response.

CANDIDATE BRIEF

You are in your practice when a dental materials representative arrives unexpectedly. He offers a $500 restaurant gift card "as a thank you for your continued support" and mentions that if you recommend their new composite brand to all patients, he could "make it $1000 each quarter." He frames it as a standard industry arrangement. Your task: manage this situation ethically.

EXAMINER CONTEXT

The representative is charming and normalises the offer ("everyone does it"). Will persist if candidate is vague. Will become apologetic if candidate is firm and professional.

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

Decline immediately and clearly — INFLECTION 1

"Thank you for coming in, and I appreciate the gesture — but I have to decline the gift card. I can't accept it."

Do not waffle. Do not say "let me think about it."

Explain the ethical basis — INFLECTION 2

"Here's my concern: accepting payment — even in gift card form — in exchange for directing patients toward a particular product creates a conflict of interest. My obligation as a dentist is to recommend treatments that are in my patient's best interests, based on clinical merit, not on the financial relationship I have with a supplier. If I accept this arrangement, I can no longer be sure that my recommendations are purely clinical."

AHPRA and ADAVB obligations (1 min)

"AHPRA's code of conduct and the ADA's code of ethics both prohibit arrangements where financial incentives influence clinical decisions. Arrangements like the one you're describing — where I receive payment proportional to the recommendations I make — are not standard industry arrangements. They're conflicts of interest."

Offer the legitimate alternative (1 min) — INFLECTION 3

"I'm genuinely open to learning about your products on their merits. If you'd like to set up an appointment to present the evidence base, peer-reviewed data, and clinical performance of your composite resin, I'd be happy to evaluate it honestly. If it performs well and offers value to my patients, I'll use it and recommend it — but based on that clinical assessment."

Document

Make a note of the interaction and the offer declined. This protects you if it ever arises later.

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Declines immediately and clearly — no hesitation
  2. ✅ Explains the conflict of interest framework correctly
  3. ✅ Cites AHPRA code of conduct and ADA code of ethics
  4. ✅ Offers the legitimate pathway (evidence-based product evaluation)
  5. ✅ Documents the interaction
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • "Conflict of interest: a situation where professional judgment could be influenced by personal, financial, or other interests. In dentistry: referral arrangements (kickbacks), financial interest in a recommended product, corporate treatment quotas, family practice objectivity."
  • "Disclosure obligation: if a conflict of interest exists, disclose it to the patient so they can make an informed decision about whether to accept the recommendation."
  • "Corporate practice dual obligation: if employer's instructions conflict with patient best interest (treatment quotas, recommending products regardless of indication), the clinician's obligation is to the patient — not the employer. Document the instruction and your clinical justification."
  • "ADA Code of Ethics: Section on conflict of interest; AHPRA Good Practice guidance analogously applicable."
Patient Reframes
  • "I want to be transparent: I have an arrangement with this laboratory that I want to disclose. I refer to them because I genuinely believe they provide the best service — but you should know that relationship exists so you can ask questions or seek a second opinion if you prefer."
  • "My recommendation needs to be based on what's right for you clinically — not on what generates revenue for this practice. Those two things should always be the same, and when they're not, the clinical recommendation wins."
Curveball Deflectors
  • "Your employer says to recommend this to all patients." → "I can recommend it when it's clinically appropriate. Recommending it to everyone regardless of indication would be a conflict of interest and not consistent with my professional obligations. My recommendation has to be clinically justified."
  • "Isn't everyone in dentistry like this?" → "Conflicts of interest exist in every profession — but that doesn't make them acceptable. My obligation is to disclose them when they exist and to ensure my clinical judgment isn't being distorted by them."
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ▶
STAGE: Opening — Receiving the Representative

Greet the representative professionally and allow him to present. Listen without interrupting.

"Thank you for coming in today — I appreciate you taking the time. Please, go ahead."

Allow the representative to complete his offer, including the $500 gift card for "continued support" and the proposal for $1,000 quarterly in exchange for preferentially recommending his composite resin brand to all patients.

Pause briefly. Respond calmly, without hesitation, and without hostility.

"I appreciate the gesture, and I can see this is framed as a standard arrangement — but I have to be straightforward with you: I can't accept the gift card, and I won't be able to enter the arrangement you're describing. Let me explain why, because I want to be transparent rather than just saying no."

---

Declining and Explaining the Conflict of Interest

"Here is my concern, and it's a professional one, not a personal one. Accepting payment — even in gift card form — in exchange for directing patients toward a particular product creates a direct conflict of interest between my financial interests and my patients' clinical interests. My obligation as a dentist is to recommend treatments based solely on clinical merit — on evidence, on patient need, and on what is genuinely in each individual patient's best interest. The moment I accept a financial benefit tied to a particular recommendation, I can no longer be certain that my clinical judgment is free from that influence. And more importantly, my patients cannot be certain of that either. That matters enormously."

"What you're describing — where the payment scales up depending on how many recommendations I make — is not a courtesy gesture. It is a financial incentive designed to influence prescribing behaviour. That is the definition of a conflict of interest in clinical practice."

---

Professional and Regulatory Obligations

"I also want to be clear that this isn't only my personal view. AHPRA's Good Medical and Dental Practice guidelines, which govern my registration, are explicit: practitioners must not allow financial incentives from third parties to influence clinical decision-making. The ADA's Code of Ethics similarly prohibits arrangements where commercial relationships compromise a practitioner's independence in recommending treatments to patients. These are not suggestions — they are obligations that govern my registration and my ability to practise."

"An arrangement where I receive quarterly payments proportional to the product recommendations I make to patients is not a standard industry arrangement. If it were reported to AHPRA or the ADA, it would likely be investigated as a breach of professional conduct. I'm not willing to put my registration, my patients' trust, or the integrity of this practice at risk."

---

Offering the Legitimate Pathway

"Now — that said, I want to be fair to you and to your product. I am genuinely open to evaluating new materials. That's part of keeping my practice current. What I'm not open to is a financial relationship that compromises how I evaluate them."

"If you'd like to arrange a formal product presentation — peer-reviewed clinical data, independent studies on bond strength, wear resistance, colour stability, and long-term performance — I would be happy to sit down and assess your composite resin on its merits. If the evidence supports it, and it performs well for my patients, I will use it and I will recommend it. But that recommendation will be based entirely on clinical assessment, not on the financial arrangement attached to it. That is the only basis on which I can make recommendations in good conscience."

"Would you like to set up a time to do that?"

---

Closing and Documentation

"Thank you for understanding. I hope that's clear, and I hope it doesn't prevent a productive professional relationship going forward — on the right terms."

Allow the representative to respond, then conclude the meeting professionally.

Following the interaction, make a contemporaneous written note in the practice file recording the date, the representative's name and company, the nature of the offer made — the $500 gift card and the $1,000 quarterly arrangement — and the fact that both were declined and the reasons given. This documentation protects the practice in the event the matter is ever raised again, and demonstrates transparent, accountable professional conduct consistent with AHPRA obligations.

SN1
Capacity Assessment — Patient with Dementia
Category:** Special Needs / Ethics | **Time:** 11 min | **Difficulty:** High

CASE SUMMARY

A 78-year-old with moderate Alzheimer's dementia is brought in by her daughter. The patient needs a complex extraction. The daughter says "Just tell me what needs to happen and I'll consent for her." Candidate must correctly assess whether the patient retains capacity for this decision, and navigate the substitute decision-making process if she does not.

CANDIDATE BRIEF

Mrs. Chen, 78, has moderate Alzheimer's dementia. She lives at home with her daughter. She has a grossly carious, abscessed lower molar (36) causing visible distress (she is touching the area repeatedly). The daughter says "She can't make decisions for herself — just talk to me, I'll sign whatever needs signing." Your task: assess Mrs. Chen's decision-making capacity for this specific procedure, and manage consent appropriately.

EXAMINER CONTEXT

Mrs. Chen is quiet but responds to direct, simple questions. When the candidate explains the procedure in very simple terms ("We need to take out a sore tooth"), she says "Yes, take it out — it hurts." She cannot explain risks in detail, but she can express her preference. Daughter is well-intentioned but is trying to take over the consultation entirely.

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

Speak to the patient directly first — INFLECTION 1

"Hello Mrs. Chen — I'm Dr. [name]. I can see that your mouth is hurting. Can you show me where?"

Engage with her directly before speaking to the daughter. Dignity is fundamental.

Capacity assessment — INFLECTION 2: Capacity is decision-specific, not global

"A diagnosis of dementia does not automatically mean a patient lacks capacity. Capacity is assessed per decision, at the time of the decision."

Ask in simple, direct terms:

  1. "Do you know you've come to the dentist?"
  2. "I'm telling you there's a tooth that's very sore and needs to come out. Do you understand that?"
  3. "If we take the tooth out, it should stop hurting. Does that make sense?"
  4. "Would you like us to fix the sore tooth?"

If she consistently says "yes, take the tooth out — it hurts" = she is expressing a preference AND demonstrating basic understanding. This may be sufficient for a relatively straightforward procedure.

If capacity is confirmed: patient is the primary decision-maker — INFLECTION 3

"Mrs. Chen, thank you. I'm going to take that sore tooth out for you today. We'll make sure it doesn't hurt."

The daughter can still be present for support, but Mrs. Chen's consent stands.

If capacity is NOT confirmed (unable to understand or express a consistent preference)

"Mrs. Chen doesn't appear to have capacity for this specific decision. In that case, I need to make a decision in her best interests, in consultation with her family as substitute decision-makers."

In Australia: check for an Enduring Power of Attorney (health decisions), advance care directive, or appointed guardian. If none exists, the next of kin can be consulted (daughter) — but they do not legally consent; the dentist makes the decision in the patient's best interests.

Best interests framework

"The tooth is causing her visible distress. Treating it is clearly in her best interests. The alternative — not treating — means ongoing pain and potentially systemic infection."

Practical considerations for treatment

  • Short appointments; ideally morning when patients with dementia are most alert
  • Familiar companion in the room for comfort
  • Clear, simple language throughout
  • Consider anxiolytic premedication if very anxious
  • LA only unless cooperation allows — avoid GA unless necessary

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Speaks to the patient directly first — not through the daughter
  2. ✅ States that capacity is decision-specific, not global
  3. ✅ Uses simple language to assess the 4 capacity elements
  4. ✅ Accepts the patient's preference as valid consent if she demonstrates understanding
  5. ✅ Knows the substitute decision-making pathway if capacity absent (EPA, advance directive, next of kin in best interests)
  6. ✅ Practical treatment modifications for patients with dementia

TG4 ALERTS

Capacity is decision-specific — A patient with dementia may retain capacity for some decisions (simple extractions) but not others (complex treatment plans). Assess per decision, per time. Document the assessment.
Substitute decision-making in Australia — Check for Enduring Power of Attorney (health) or advance care directive first. Next of kin consultation second, but they inform rather than legally consent — the practitioner makes the decision in best interests.
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • "Capacity is decision-specific and time-specific. A patient with dementia may lack capacity for a complex multi-stage treatment plan but retain capacity to consent to a simple extraction. Always assess for the specific decision at hand."
  • "MCAT framework: (1) Understand — can they comprehend the information? (2) Retain — long enough to decide? (3) Weigh — can they reason through the options? (4) Communicate — can they express a decision?"
  • "If capacity is absent: best interests principle. Consult family or carers for what the patient would have wanted; advance care directive if available; NCAT/guardianship tribunal in Australia for major irreversible decisions; substitute decision-maker (legally appointed guardian)."
  • "Never assume incapacity based on diagnosis alone. Dementia is a spectrum. Use simpler language, shorter sentences, allow more time, choose a calm moment in the day."
Patient Reframes
  • "I'll speak directly with her first — capacity assessment means finding out what she understands and what she wants, not what others want for her."
  • "Even with dementia, many patients can make some decisions for themselves with the right support. I want to find out what she can decide before anyone decides for her."
Curveball Deflectors
  • "Her son says just do it." → "Unless he's a formally appointed medical guardian, he can't consent on her behalf. If she has capacity for this decision, she consents herself. If she doesn't, family input is valuable context — but legally, we follow best interests principles, not family instructions alone."
  • "She just keeps saying no — can't you override her?" → "If she consistently and clearly refuses, I need to establish whether she has capacity to refuse this specific treatment. If she does — even with dementia — that refusal is legally valid and I cannot proceed. If she lacks capacity, we make the best interests decision with her family."
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ▶
STAGE: Opening — Engaging Mrs. Chen Directly

Walks toward Mrs. Chen, makes gentle eye contact, and speaks at a measured, warm pace. Does not initially address the daughter.

"Hello Mrs. Chen — I'm Dr. [name]. It's lovely to meet you. I can see you've been touching your mouth — that must be really uncomfortable. Can you show me where it's hurting?"

Pauses and observes. Mrs. Chen points to the lower left jaw.

"Thank you for showing me. We're going to have a look and see what we can do to help you feel better today."

Now acknowledges the daughter with a warm nod. "Thank you for bringing your mum in. I'll make sure to include you in our conversation. I'd just like to speak with Mrs. Chen first so I can understand how she's feeling — is that alright?"

---

Capacity Assessment — Decision-Specific, In Plain Language

Turns back to Mrs. Chen and speaks slowly and clearly, one idea at a time.

"Mrs. Chen, do you know where you are today?"

She responds that she is at the dentist.

"That's right — well done. I'm a dentist and I'm here to help you. Now, I've had a look at your tooth down here — the one that's been hurting. It has a big infection in it. That's what's causing all that pain."

Pauses to allow processing.

"Because it's so infected, the best thing I can do is take that tooth out. If I take it out, the pain should go away. Does that make sense to you?"

Observes her response. She nods and says it hurts a lot.

"I know it hurts. Now — if I take the tooth out, there will be a small needle first to make the area numb, so you won't feel the tooth coming out. It might feel a little strange, but it shouldn't hurt. Would you like me to take that sore tooth out and help you feel better?"

Mrs. Chen says clearly, "Yes — take it out, it hurts."

Now addresses the daughter directly, and also ensures the patient can still hear.

"I want to take a moment to explain something important. A diagnosis of dementia does not automatically mean that a person cannot make decisions. Capacity is assessed per decision, at the time of the decision. What I've just done is check whether your mum understands what's wrong, understands what I'm proposing, understands what will happen if we don't treat it, and whether she can express a consistent preference. She has done all of those things. She understands she has an infected tooth, she understands I want to remove it, and she has clearly and consistently told me she wants it out. On that basis, Mrs. Chen has capacity for this specific decision, and her consent is valid."

---

Consent and the Daughter's Role

"Mrs. Chen, thank you. You've been very clear. I'm going to take that sore tooth out for you today and we'll make sure it doesn't hurt at all."

Turns to the daughter. "I understand your instinct to help your mum, and that comes from a wonderful place. Your mum can absolutely have you in the room with her today for support — and I'll keep you informed every step of the way. But because she does have capacity for this decision, she is the one who gives consent. Her voice is the one that counts."

"If at any point during the appointment Mrs. Chen changes her mind or becomes distressed, we stop immediately. That's always her right."

---

If Capacity Were Absent — Substitute Decision-Making Pathway

Explains to the examiner and contextualises for the daughter.

"If Mrs. Chen had not been able to understand or express a consistent preference, the process would be different. In that situation I would first ask whether there is an Enduring Power of Attorney for health decisions, or an advance care directive — these are the legally authoritative documents in Australia. If neither exists, I would consult the next of kin — in this case, her daughter — but I want to be clear: the family member does not legally consent on her behalf. What they do is provide information to help me make a decision in her best interests. The clinical decision remains mine."

"In this case, even without capacity, the best interests analysis is straightforward. That tooth is causing her visible and ongoing distress. It carries a risk of spreading odontogenic infection. Treating it clearly serves her best interests. Not treating it does not."

---

Treatment Modifications and Closing

"To make today's appointment as comfortable as possible for your mum, I'll keep the appointment short and work in the morning when people with dementia are generally most alert. You're welcome to sit beside her throughout. I'll use simple, calm language at every step and tell her exactly what I'm about to do before I do it."

"For pain relief, I'll use local anaesthetic — lidocaine is safe and effective. I won't be using anything like intravenous sedation today as this should be manageable with local anaesthetic alone and your mum's comfort and cooperation."

"Afterwards, for any discomfort, paracetamol one gram every four to six hours is the first-line choice — it's gentle and very effective. I'll write that down for you clearly."

"Mrs. Chen — are you ready? We're going to get you out of pain today." Smiles and proceeds.

SN2
Patient with Intellectual Disability — Behaviour Management
Category:** Special Needs | **Time:** 11 min | **Difficulty:** Exam-ready

CASE SUMMARY

A 25-year-old with moderate intellectual disability (Down Syndrome) presents with his support worker. He needs a scale and clean and review of several carious lesions. He has had previous traumatic dental experiences. Candidate must adapt communication and clinical approach.

CANDIDATE BRIEF

James, 25, has Down Syndrome with moderate intellectual disability. He becomes very anxious in the waiting room. His support worker says "He won't let anyone near his mouth — his last dentist had to give up." He is currently covering his mouth with both hands. Your task: manage this appointment, using appropriate communication and behaviour management strategies.

EXAMINER CONTEXT

James responds well to simple, direct language and visual demonstration. Will uncover his mouth when the candidate shows him the mirror on their own teeth first and makes it feel like a "game." Will refuse if rushed or if instruments are produced without a clear tell-show-do sequence. The support worker knows him well and can help — the candidate should use them as an ally.

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

Engage the support worker as an ally — INFLECTION 1

"Hi, I'm Dr. [name]. It's great you're here with James today. You know him best — can you tell me what has worked before and what tends to upset him? Is there anything I should know about how he communicates?"

Direct communication with James — INFLECTION 2

Get down to his level. Use simple, concrete language. Avoid idioms.

"Hi James! My name is Dr. [name]. I'm going to look at your teeth today. Would that be okay?"

No long sentences. Wait for a response. Match his pace.

Tell-show-do (2 min) — INFLECTION 3

"Look — this is my mirror. See? I'm going to show you what it feels like on your hand first. Ready?"

Show on his hand. Then on his support worker's teeth. Then on his teeth.

No surprises. Narrate every step before doing it.

Gradual desensitisation if still refusing

Start with: "Can we look at your teeth? Just look — no touching today."

If yes: "Now can I touch one tooth with the mirror? Just the mirror."

Progress from there.

Positive reinforcement

"That was great, James! You're doing really well." After each small step.

Avoid: "Good boy" — he is an adult. Use: "Well done" / "Excellent."

For complex treatment: consider referral

If treatment under LA is not feasible with standard behaviour management:

  • Conscious sedation (nitrous oxide)
  • Oral premedication (midazolam or similar — refer to specialist)
  • General anaesthesia (last resort, typically through specialist hospital program)

In NSW/VIC/QLD: refer to a Special Needs Dentistry specialist for comprehensive planning.

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Engages the support worker as a key ally before anything else
  2. ✅ Communicates directly with James — not through support worker
  3. ✅ Adapts language: simple, concrete, slow, wait for response
  4. ✅ Tell-show-do throughout — no surprises
  5. ✅ Uses his name; treats him as an adult (avoids "good boy")
  6. ✅ Praises each small step
  7. ✅ Escalation pathway: nitrous → oral sedation → GA referral
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • "Intellectual disability does not automatically mean incapacity. Assess for the specific procedure. Many patients with mild-moderate ID can consent with appropriate communication adjustments."
  • "Communication strategies: plain language (no jargon), short sentences, concrete examples, visual aids and social stories, allow extra processing time, confirm understanding with teach-back."
  • "Desensitisation programme: structured gradual exposure appointments — waiting room, chair, mirror examination, instrument introduction — before any treatment. Invaluable for long-term cooperation."
  • "GA pathway: reserved for extensive treatment when behavioural approaches have been genuinely tried and failed, or where treatment complexity exceeds what's achievable awake. GA carries real risk and is not a first-line convenience."
Patient Reframes
  • "I'd like to understand how to communicate with you best today — what works well for you?"
  • "We might not do any treatment today. That's okay — today might be about getting comfortable, looking around, and building trust. That's a completely legitimate use of this appointment."
Curveball Deflectors
  • "Just use GA — it's easier." → "GA carries anaesthetic risk and should only be used when other approaches have genuinely been tried and aren't adequate. For this level of treatment, I'd like to try a structured behavioural approach first. It takes more appointments upfront but builds something lasting."
  • "He can't understand anything." → "Patients with intellectual disability often understand more than we assume, especially with the right communication approach. I want to direct my communication to him first — in simple, concrete terms — and see what he can tell me."
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ▶
STAGE: Opening — Engaging the Support Worker

Walks into the waiting room. Makes eye contact with the support worker first, then smiles warmly at James without approaching too closely. Crouches slightly to reduce physical dominance.

"Hi there — I'm Dr. [name], one of the dentists here. You must be James, and you must be his support worker — it's great that you've both come in today. Before we head through, I'd love to spend just a couple of minutes chatting with you, if that's okay."

Turns fully to the support worker and speaks quietly, just out of James's immediate focus.

"You know James best, and that genuinely helps me do my job better. Can you tell me what tends to work well when he's anxious — is there anything that calms him down? And is there anything I absolutely should avoid? Does he communicate mostly with words, or does he use gestures or signs?"

Listens carefully, nods, and acknowledges every piece of information the support worker offers.

"That's really helpful, thank you. I also want to make sure James is involved in every decision today — I'll speak directly to him, and I'd love it if you sat close by so he can see you're right there."

---

Direct Communication with James

Gets down to James's eye level — either crouching or sitting in a low chair at the same height. Uses a calm, warm, unhurried tone. No sudden movements.

"Hi James! My name is Dr. [name]. I'm a tooth doctor. I look after teeth."

Pauses. Waits for a response — eye contact, a nod, any acknowledgement.

"James, it looks like your hands are keeping your mouth safe. That's okay. We're not going to rush. We can just sit here for a minute if you like."

Smiles. Allows silence. Does not try to move his hands.

"Is it alright if I just sit with you for a bit? Just sit — nothing else yet."

---

Tell-Show-Do and Gradual Desensitisation

Picks up the mouth mirror. Holds it clearly in view so James can see it.

"James, look — this is my mirror. It's just a tiny mirror on a stick. That's all it is."

Holds it out toward James so he can look at it, touch it if he wants.

"Can I show you what it feels like? I'll do it on your hand first — just on your hand."

Gently touches the back of the mirror to James's hand. Pauses.

"See? That's all it does. Cool and smooth."

Turns to the support worker.

"Would you mind if I showed James on your teeth for a second? Just so he can see exactly what happens."

Demonstrates briefly on the support worker. Then turns back to James.

"James, did you see that? Just a little look. That's all. Can I have a look at your teeth? Just look — no touching yet, just my eyes."

If James allows even partial opening, narrates every single step before doing it. Never moves without warning.

"I'm going to put the mirror just near the front — just near, nice and slow. Perfect. Well done, James. That was excellent."

Uses praise after every small step — specific and adult-appropriate.

"You're doing so well. That took courage — really well done."

Avoids "good boy" entirely. Uses "well done," "excellent," "that was brilliant, James."

---

Clinical Assessment and Findings

Completes as much of the examination as James tolerates, documenting carious lesions and periodontal status. Does not force any step. If James withdraws at any point, immediately backs off.

"Okay James, we'll stop there. That was really great work today."

Turns to the support worker.

"From what I was able to see, James has a few areas that need attention — some decay on several teeth, and his gums need a clean. I want to be honest with you: completing all of this in a standard appointment may not be realistic in one visit, and that's completely fine. We'll take this at James's pace."

---

Management Plan and Escalation Pathway

"For today, I'd like to keep it as a familiarisation visit — build James's trust, and do a gentle scale in the areas he'll allow. We can schedule subsequent visits for the carious lesions once he's more comfortable here."

Addresses the support worker directly.

"If James continues to find standard appointments very difficult, there are other options we can consider together. The first would be nitrous oxide — happy gas — which takes the edge off anxiety very gently and wears off quickly. If that's not enough, we could arrange oral premedication, and I'd refer James to a Special Needs Dentistry specialist for that planning — they're best placed to coordinate midazolam premedication safely. If the treatment is extensive and none of those approaches work, general anaesthesia through a specialist hospital program is available and can allow us to complete everything at once. That would be the last resort, but it's a real and appropriate option for James."

---

Closing and Safety Net

Speaks directly to James again, warmly.

"James, you did an amazing job today. Really. Thank you for letting me meet you."

To the support worker:

"Please let us know before the next visit if anything has changed — if he's unwell, or more anxious than usual, we can reschedule without any pressure. Our front desk can also give you a social story about visiting the dentist, which some patients find really settles things between visits. We're on James's side here, and we'll go at whatever pace works for him."

SN3
Elderly Patient — Polypharmacy and Dry Mouth
Category:** Geriatric | **Time:** 11 min | **Difficulty:** Exam-ready

CASE SUMMARY

A 74-year-old woman presents with a chief complaint of "dry mouth" and rapidly progressing dental decay over the past 2 years. She is on 8 medications. Candidate must identify xerostomia as drug-related, manage the medications interaction, and design an appropriate caries prevention plan.

CANDIDATE BRIEF

Mrs. Taylor, 74, presents with multiple new carious lesions (cervical and root surface) over the past 2 years, previously having been caries-free for a decade. She reports a persistently dry, uncomfortable mouth, especially at night. She is on: metformin, atorvastatin, lisinopril, amlodipine, sertraline, metoprolol, omeprazole, and oxybutynin. Your task: diagnose, explain, and manage.

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

History (1.5 min)

  • When did dry mouth start? (correlate with any medication change)
  • Diet changes in the past 2 years?
  • Oral hygiene habits unchanged?

Medication review — INFLECTION 1: Identify xerogenic drugs

From her list: amlodipine, sertraline, oxybutynin, metoprolol — all have xerogenic effects. Oxybutynin (anticholinergic) is often the major culprit for dry mouth.

"Several of your medications reduce saliva flow as a side effect — particularly oxybutynin, your sertraline, and your amlodipine. Saliva is your mouth's natural protection — it buffers acid, washes food away, and contains minerals that remineralise teeth. When saliva flow drops significantly, decay accelerates. This is very likely the explanation for why your teeth have been deteriorating."

Management — INFLECTION 2: Don't stop medications without GP

"I'll write a letter to your GP explaining the dental impact of these medications. The GP may consider adjusting doses or substituting to less xerogenic alternatives — but that's a medical decision, not mine. I'll advocate for it."

Immediate dental management (2 min)

  1. Fluoride: Prescription high-fluoride toothpaste (5000ppm) twice daily. Fluoride varnish every 3 months (high caries risk protocol).
  2. Saliva substitutes: Biotene range — gel, spray, mouthwash. Use at night and as needed.
  3. Saliva stimulants: Sugar-free gum (xylitol-based) to stimulate residual salivary function.
  4. Diet: Reduce frequency of fermentable carbohydrates. Sip water frequently (not juice, not fizzy water).
  5. Alcohol-free mouthwash: Alcohol-containing mouthwash dries the mouth further — switch to alcohol-free.
  6. Recall: 3-monthly for now instead of 6-monthly — active decay risk.

Existing decay (1 min)

Restore root surface caries with GIC where possible (fluoride-releasing). Composite for anterior aesthetics. Prioritise stability of the dentition.

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Takes medication history and identifies xerogenic culprits (anticholinergics, antidepressants, antihypertensives)
  2. ✅ Explains the mechanism (reduced saliva = lost caries protection)
  3. ✅ Writes to GP — does NOT unilaterally stop medications
  4. ✅ Correct prescription: 5000ppm fluoride toothpaste, fluoride varnish 3-monthly
  5. ✅ Saliva substitutes and stimulants
  6. ✅ No alcohol mouthwash
  7. ✅ Appropriate recall interval (3-monthly)

TG4 ALERTS

Xerogenic medications — TG4: anticholinergics, tricyclic antidepressants, antihypertensives, antipsychotics are major xerogenic drug classes. Polypharmacy compounds the effect. Do not stop medications — liaise with prescriber.
High-fluoride toothpaste for elderly with root caries — 5000ppm prescription-strength fluoride toothpaste (Colgate Neutrafluor 5000, Clinpro 5000). Dramatically reduces root surface caries incidence.
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • "Xerostomia in older patients: most common cause is medication (antihypertensives, antidepressants, antihistamines, diuretics, antipsychotics). Also: Sjögren's, radiation, dehydration."
  • "Consequences: root caries dramatically increases (root surfaces exposed by gingival recession become vulnerable without salivary buffering), candidiasis, mucosal breakdown, denture retention problems, dysphagia."
  • "Management: increase water intake; sugar-free gum (stimulates saliva flow); saliva substitutes for comfort; high-strength fluoride toothpaste (5000ppm Duraphat) if high caries risk; 3-monthly recalls; CPP-ACP (Tooth Mousse) at night."
  • "Medication review: request GP review — if a less xerostomic alternative exists for any medications, substitution can significantly improve salivary flow. Never change medications yourself."
Patient Reframes
  • "The dry mouth you're noticing is almost certainly a side effect of one or more of your medications — it's one of the most common problems we see with polypharmacy. There's a lot we can do to protect your teeth and improve your comfort."
  • "Your risk of tooth decay has increased significantly because of the dry mouth — not because of anything you've done, but because saliva is what protects teeth. We need to compensate for that loss with some specific tools."
Curveball Deflectors
  • "Can't you just give me a spray?" → "A saliva spray helps with comfort — but it doesn't protect teeth the way real saliva does, because it lacks the minerals and antibacterials. The spray is for symptom relief; I also need you on high-strength fluoride toothpaste and more frequent check-ups."
  • "My GP says I have to stay on all my medications." → "I completely respect that — those medications are managing important conditions. I'm not suggesting stopping any of them. What I'm suggesting is asking the GP whether any less xerostomic alternatives exist within the same drug classes. Sometimes they do."
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ▶
STAGE: Opening and History

"Good morning, Mrs. Taylor. My name is Dr. Chen — I'm your dentist today. Please come in and make yourself comfortable. I understand you've been having some trouble with a dry mouth and some new decay. I'd like to ask you a few questions first, if that's all right."

"Can you tell me in your own words when you first noticed your mouth feeling dry?" Listens attentively. "And would you say it's worse at any particular time — perhaps at night, or when you wake up in the morning?" Notes her confirmation of nocturnal symptoms. "Have you noticed any difficulty swallowing, speaking, or tasting your food?"

"Now, you mentioned some new decay. You'd been cavity-free for quite a while, hadn't you? When did you first notice things changing — was it around the same time the dry mouth started, roughly two years ago?" Pauses to allow response. "Have your diet habits or oral hygiene routine changed at all during that period?" Notes no significant dietary or brushing changes reported. "Are you using any mouthwash at the moment?"

"I'd like to go through your medications now, if you don't mind — this is really important for understanding what's happening. Can you tell me everything you're currently taking, including any over-the-counter medicines?" Reviews the list: metformin, atorvastatin, lisinopril, amlodipine, sertraline, metoprolol, omeprazole, and oxybutynin. "And have any of these been started, or had their dose increased, in the last two to three years?" Notes the temporal correlation carefully.

---

Diagnosis and Explanation

"Mrs. Taylor, I think I have a very clear picture of what's been happening, and I want to explain it to you properly because it's actually quite important."

"Several of your medications reduce the flow of saliva as a side effect. In particular, oxybutynin — which you take for bladder control — belongs to a class of drugs called anticholinergics, and these are well known for significantly reducing saliva production. On top of that, sertraline, your antidepressant, and amlodipine, your blood pressure tablet, also have a drying effect on the mouth. When you're taking multiple medications that each reduce saliva — and you're taking four that do this — the combined effect can be quite severe."

"Now, saliva is actually your mouth's natural defence system. It buffers the acids that bacteria produce, it washes food particles away, and it contains minerals like calcium and phosphate that remineralise your tooth surfaces every day. When saliva flow drops significantly, that protection disappears almost entirely — and decay, particularly on the root surfaces and at the gumline, can progress very rapidly. This explains precisely why teeth that were stable for a decade have now developed multiple new cavities within two years. It is not a failure of your oral hygiene — your mouth has simply lost its natural protection."

"The good news is that once we understand the cause, we can manage it very effectively."

---

Medical Liaison

"Before I talk about what we'll do dentally, I want to be clear about one important thing: I am not going to stop or change any of your medications — that is entirely your GP's decision, and it would be unsafe for me to do that unilaterally. However, I am going to write a detailed letter to your GP explaining the dental consequences we are seeing, and I will ask them to review whether any of these medications — particularly oxybutynin — could be substituted for a less drying alternative, or whether the dose could be adjusted. There are sometimes options that achieve the same medical goal with less impact on saliva. Your GP will weigh that up with your overall health in mind. Does that make sense to you?"

---

Immediate Dental Management

"Now let me tell you what we are going to do from a dental perspective — and there is quite a lot we can do."

"Firstly, fluoride. Because your caries risk is currently high, I am going to prescribe you a high-strength fluoride toothpaste — it contains 5000 parts per million of fluoride, which is significantly stronger than regular toothpaste. The brand is Colgate Neutrafluor 5000. You will use this twice daily — brush thoroughly, spit, and do not rinse afterwards, so the fluoride stays on your teeth. Additionally, I will apply a fluoride varnish here in the chair every three months. The evidence for this in root surface caries prevention in older adults is very strong."

"Secondly, saliva substitutes. There is a range called Biotene — a gel, a spray, and a mouthwash — which is specifically designed for people with dry mouth. Use the gel at night before bed, and the spray as needed throughout the day. These won't replace your own saliva, but they provide significant relief and some protection."

"Thirdly, saliva stimulation. If you still have some salivary function — and you likely do — chewing sugar-free xylitol-based gum after meals will stimulate whatever residual flow you have. Xylitol also has a direct anti-cavity effect."

"Regarding mouthwash — please stop any alcohol-containing mouthwash immediately if you're using one. Alcohol is extremely drying and will make your situation considerably worse. Use only an alcohol-free fluoride mouthwash."

"For diet: sip plain water frequently throughout the day — not fruit juice, not sparkling water, just still water. Reduce how often you have sugary or starchy foods rather than eliminating them entirely — frequency is what drives decay, not just quantity."

---

Restorative Plan and Safety Net

"For the cavities that are already present, I would like to restore the root surface lesions with glass ionomer cement where possible — this material releases fluoride continuously, which gives ongoing protection to the surrounding tooth surface. For any cavities in more visible areas, we can discuss composite resin for aesthetics."

"I'll also chart all existing cavities carefully today so we can monitor whether the prevention plan is working."

"I want to see you back every three months rather than the usual six — at this level of caries activity, we need to monitor closely, apply fluoride varnish, and check that the new lesions are stabilising. Once the situation is under control, we can reassess the recall interval."

"Do you have any questions about anything I've explained? I know it's been a lot of information — I genuinely want to make sure you feel confident about what we're doing and why. The most important message is that we have identified the cause, and we have a very clear plan to protect your teeth going forward."

SN4
Frail Elderly Patient — Treatment Planning Principles
Category:** Geriatric | **Time:** 11 min | **Difficulty:** Exam-ready

CASE SUMMARY

An 82-year-old frail man with multiple comorbidities (heart failure, CKD, type 2 diabetes) presents, brought by his son. His oral health has deteriorated significantly. He has multiple broken teeth, advanced periodontal disease, and is in mild chronic pain. The son wants "everything fixed." Candidate must apply frailty-appropriate, patient-centred treatment planning.

CANDIDATE BRIEF

Mr. Kaur, 82, is brought in by his son. He has NYHA Class II heart failure, CKD stage 3, and poorly controlled type 2 diabetes (HbA1c 9.2%). He is frail (moves slowly, fatigues easily), takes 11 medications including warfarin. His mouth has 12 remaining teeth, most broken at the gumline, advanced periodontitis (6–8mm pockets throughout), and multiple root stumps. He is in mild background pain but not in acute distress. His son says: "Fix everything — whatever it takes. He deserves a full smile." Your task: plan care for this patient.

EXAMINER CONTEXT

The son is emotionally invested and has unrealistic expectations. The patient himself, when asked directly, says "I just want to stop hurting and be able to eat." This is the key — the patient's goals and the son's goals differ. The candidate must navigate this and advocate for the patient's expressed wishes.

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

Establish the patient's own goals — INFLECTION 1

"Mr. Kaur, before we talk about treatment, I'd like to hear from you first. What's been bothering you most? What would you most like to achieve from coming here today?"

His answer ("stop hurting and be able to eat") defines the treatment goals. This is the moral anchor of the consultation.

Frailty-appropriate treatment planning framework — INFLECTION 2

"For Mr. Kaur, the treatment plan needs to balance what is clinically ideal with what is realistic, safe, and meaningful for someone with his overall health. Here are the principles:

  1. Function, comfort, and dignity — not comprehensive ideal dentistry. The goal is quality of life, not a full-mouth rehabilitation.
  2. Minimum intervention — each procedure has a risk-benefit ratio that changes with frailty and comorbidity. A treatment that would be straightforward in a 40-year-old carries greater risks at 82 with heart failure, CKD, and anticoagulation.
  3. Reversibility and simplicity — prefer treatments that are simpler, faster, and easier to adjust.
  4. Safety first — anticoagulation (warfarin): check INR before any extractions (target <3.5 for simple extractions per TG4); liaise with cardiologist for complex surgery. Diabetes: poorly controlled (HbA1c 9.2%) increases infection risk — antibiotic prophylaxis for surgical procedures, advise glycaemic optimisation with GP."

Proposed staged plan — INFLECTION 3

Stage 1 (relieve pain and infection):

  • Identify symptomatic/infected teeth — extract root stumps that are sources of infection or pain
  • Periodontal debridement for active infection — not aggressive surgical perio at this stage
  • Adjust any sharp/broken teeth causing mucosal trauma

Stage 2 (restore function):

  • Simple denture (partial or full) once acute treatment complete — can be constructed quickly, non-invasive
  • NOT: implants, full crown work, surgical perio unless the patient requests it and health allows

Stage 3 (maintenance):

  • 3-monthly recalls; carer-guided OH for home care; fluoride varnish

Address the son — INFLECTION 4

"I'd like to explain what I've shared with your father, and then answer any questions you have. I hear how much you want the best for him — and so does he. He told me his main goals are stopping the pain and being able to eat. That's what I'm planning to achieve. A full reconstruction would involve many long appointments, significant anaesthetic risks given his heart, and a long recovery time — and honestly, for someone of his age and health, the risk-benefit balance doesn't favour it. What I'm proposing will relieve his pain and restore his ability to eat, reliably and safely."

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Asks the patient their goals before discussing treatment
  2. ✅ Uses frailty-appropriate planning framework (function, comfort, dignity; minimum intervention)
  3. ✅ Warfarin: check INR before extractions; target <3.5
  4. ✅ Diabetes: infection risk awareness; liaise with GP
  5. ✅ Staged plan: pain relief first → simple denture → maintenance
  6. ✅ Declines comprehensive treatment (implants/full rehab) with clear reasoning
  7. ✅ Addresses the son respectfully, explains patient's own stated goals

TG4 ALERTS

Warfarin and extractions — TG4: do NOT routinely stop warfarin for simple extractions. Check INR: if <3.5, proceed with local haemostatic measures (sutures, resorbable gauze, tranexamic acid mouthwash). If >3.5 or complex surgery: liaise with prescribing physician.
Diabetes and surgery — TG4: poorly controlled diabetes (HbA1c >9%) significantly increases infection and healing complication risk. Consider antibiotic prophylaxis for surgical procedures. Encourage glycaemic optimisation pre-operatively via GP.
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • "Frailty-informed treatment planning: match treatment intensity to the patient's resilience. For severely frail patients, the goals are pain-free, functional, and infection-free — not comprehensive restorative dentistry."
  • "Minimally invasive approaches: ART (atraumatic restorative technique with GIC), palliative extraction under LA if well-tolerated, oral hygiene instruction adapted for carer delivery, fluoride varnish, chlorhexidine gel for high-risk sites."
  • "Key questions to guide planning: What does this patient value most? What can they tolerate? What is their life expectancy and overall trajectory? What does their carer/family think they'd want? What are the risks of treatment vs no treatment?"
  • "Oral health in aged care: critical for quality of life, nutrition, aspiration pneumonia risk, and pain management. Do not dismiss dental problems in frail elderly — untreated oral pain significantly impairs function and wellbeing."
Patient Reframes
  • "The plan for your teeth isn't about making everything perfect — it's about keeping you comfortable, able to eat, and free of pain. Let's figure out together what matters most to you."
  • "Being 88 doesn't mean dental treatment isn't worth doing. Being pain-free and able to eat matters at every age. The question is which treatments achieve that most safely for you specifically."
Curveball Deflectors
  • "She's 88 — is it really worth treating?" → "That's exactly the right question to ask — and the answer depends on what she's experiencing. Pain and inability to eat affect quality of life at any age. The question is which treatments achieve her goals with acceptable risk. That's what I'm trying to find out."
  • "Just extract everything — it's easier." → "Extracting all remaining teeth in a frail patient carries significant risks and recovery burdens. I'd rather consider what each tooth contributes and what its removal costs. Extracting only what's causing problems is usually a better plan than clearing everything."
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ▶
STAGE: Opening and Establishing the Patient's Own Goals

Candidate enters, introduces themselves warmly, and directs attention first to Mr. Kaur — not the son.

"Good morning, Mr. Kaur. My name is Dr. [Name], and I'm the dentist here today. It's lovely to meet you. I see your son has come along with you — that's wonderful. Before we talk about anything else, I'd like to hear from you directly, if that's alright."

Pauses, makes unhurried eye contact with Mr. Kaur.

"Mr. Kaur, before we talk about treatment, I'd like to hear from you first. What's been bothering you most? What would you most like to achieve from coming here today?"

Listens attentively without interrupting. Mr. Kaur expresses that he wants the pain to stop and to be able to eat properly again.

"Thank you so much for telling me that. Stopping the pain and being able to eat comfortably — those are very clear and very reasonable goals, and that's exactly what I'm going to focus on for you today. You're the one sitting in this chair, so your goals are what matter most to me."

---

Medical History Review and Frailty Assessment

"Mr. Kaur, I've had a chance to look over your medical history before today. I understand you have a heart condition, some kidney changes, and diabetes — is that right? And you're on a number of medications, including a blood-thinning tablet called warfarin. Is that all still current?"

Confirms with Mr. Kaur and his son. Notes Mr. Kaur moves slowly, fatigues easily, and required assistance to be seated.

"I want you to know I'll be keeping all of that in mind as we plan your treatment. Everything I recommend will be chosen with your whole health in mind — not just your teeth in isolation. I'll also be in touch with your GP to make sure we're all working together."

---

Frailty-Appropriate Treatment Planning Explanation

"Now, I've had a good look at your mouth, and I'd like to explain what I've found and what I think we should do — and importantly, why."

Speaks clearly and at a measured pace, facing Mr. Kaur.

"You have twelve remaining teeth, most of which are quite broken down, and the gums around them show significant disease, with deep pockets throughout. A number of the root tips left behind are likely contributing to your background pain. I want to be honest with you about what's realistic and what's right for your situation."

"For someone with your overall health — your heart, your kidneys, your diabetes — the most important principle is this: we focus on what will give you the greatest comfort, function, and dignity, with the least possible risk. That means we are not aiming for a perfect textbook mouth. We are aiming for a mouth that doesn't hurt, that lets you eat, and that is safe to maintain. That is a worthwhile and achievable goal."

"Every procedure we consider carries a risk-benefit balance that changes significantly when someone has heart failure, kidney disease, anticoagulation, and poorly controlled diabetes. Your HbA1c — your diabetes sugar marker — is 9.2%, which tells me your diabetes is not well controlled right now. That significantly increases the risk of infection and poor healing after any surgical procedure. I'll be writing to your GP to discuss optimising that before we do any surgery, because that will make treatment safer for you."

---

Proposed Staged Treatment Plan

"So here is what I'm proposing, in stages. First — and most urgently — I want to relieve your pain and remove any active infection. That means identifying which root stumps are causing problems and extracting those. Before I do any extractions, I'll need to check your INR — that's the measure of how your warfarin is working. According to current guidelines, we do not stop warfarin for simple extractions; we check the level and proceed safely if it is within the therapeutic range, which is generally up to 3.5 for simple procedures. If it is above that, I will liaise with your cardiologist or GP before proceeding. I'll also use local haemostatic measures — a resorbable pack and a suture — to ensure the socket heals well."

"I'll also gently clean around the remaining teeth to manage the active gum infection — not aggressive surgical treatment at this stage, just thorough debridement to settle the infection and reduce your discomfort."

"Once the acute phase is settled and you're more comfortable, Stage Two is restoring your ability to eat. I'd like to make you a simple removable denture — partial or full depending on what teeth remain after treatment. This is non-invasive, relatively quick to construct, and adjustable. It will give you back the function you're looking for."

"I want to be clear about what I am not recommending: implants, extensive crown work, or surgical periodontal treatment. These would require multiple long appointments, significant surgical risk given your heart and kidneys, and a lengthy recovery. The risk-benefit balance does not favour those approaches for you right now, and frankly, they are not necessary to achieve your stated goals."

"Stage Three is long-term maintenance — I'd like to see you every three months. We'll apply fluoride varnish to protect remaining teeth, and I'll work with your son and any carers to establish a simple home care routine that is manageable for you."

---

Addressing the Son and Closing

Turns respectfully to the son.

"I'd like to address what you said when you came in — you want everything fixed, and you want the best for your father. I think that's a beautiful thing, and it's clear how much you care about him. I want to reassure you that I share that goal entirely."

"What your father told me today is that he wants to stop hurting and be able to eat. That is what I am planning to deliver — reliably and safely. A full-mouth reconstruction would mean many long appointments, significant anaesthetic exposure, and serious risks given his heart failure, kidney function, and current diabetes control. For a gentleman of his age and frailty, those risks are simply not justified when a simpler, staged plan can achieve exactly what he is asking for."

"What I'm proposing is not a lesser plan — it is the right plan for the right patient. It is designed around his comfort, his dignity, and his safety."

Turns back to Mr. Kaur.

"Mr. Kaur, do you have any questions about what I've described? Are you comfortable with this approach?"

Listens to Mr. Kaur's response, answers any questions simply and directly.

"We'll take this one step at a time, and I'll be with you every step of the way. You're in safe hands."

SN5
Patient in a Wheelchair — Accessibility and Adaptation
Category:** Special Needs | **Time:** 11 min | **Difficulty:** Exam-ready

CASE SUMMARY

A 45-year-old patient with MS (multiple sclerosis) presents in a power wheelchair. She has limited hand function (splinted) and fatigue that worsens through the day. She needs a comprehensive dental assessment and is asking about options for her poor home oral hygiene. Candidate must adapt the appointment environment and OH advice.

CANDIDATE BRIEF

Ms. Park, 45, has MS with progressive upper limb spasticity and fatigue. She arrives in a power wheelchair and is unable to transfer to the dental chair independently. She reports brushing teeth is increasingly difficult and her OH has deteriorated. She has moderate generalised gingivitis. Your task: adapt the appointment and provide relevant OH instruction.

EXAMINER CONTEXT

Ms. Park is intelligent, self-aware, and has researched adaptive OH devices. She will be frustrated if the candidate speaks to her support worker rather than to her directly. She will be impressed if the candidate knows about powered toothbrushes, floss aids, and the option of treating her in the wheelchair.

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

Speak to the patient directly — INFLECTION 1

Address Ms. Park, not the support worker. She is the patient.

Wheelchair treatment option — INFLECTION 2

"Ms. Park, we have two options for today. We can use our transfer equipment to move you to the dental chair — let me ask what works best for you and whether you've transferred to dental chairs before. Alternatively, we can treat you in your wheelchair, which I can recline using a headrest attachment. Many patients with MS find this more comfortable and less fatiguing. What would you prefer?"

Do NOT assume. Ask. Patient preference guides the decision.

Fatigue management (1 min)

"MS fatigue typically worsens through the day — when is your best time? Morning appointments are usually better. Let's keep this appointment short — 30–40 minutes maximum — and schedule multiple visits rather than one long one."

Adaptive OH advice — INFLECTION 3

"For brushing at home with limited hand function:

  1. Electric toothbrush — removes the need for the fine motor wrist movement of a manual brush. Models with larger grip handles are easier to hold with splinted hands. I'd recommend this strongly.
  2. Modified handles — rubber grip sleeves, foam tubing, or toothbrush holder that attaches to the hand
  3. Flossing aids — floss picks or a Waterpik water flosser — these eliminate the dexterity required to handle regular floss
  4. Timing — brush when fatigue is lowest (morning after rest)
  5. Support worker — can we discuss with the support worker providing assisted brushing on days when fatigue is worst? This is an appropriate and recognised part of carer support."

Referral to occupational therapist

"An OT can formally assess adaptive aids for daily activities including oral hygiene — I'd suggest a referral if you haven't seen one recently."

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Addresses Ms. Park directly, not through the support worker
  2. ✅ Offers wheelchair treatment as a valid option — asks patient's preference
  3. ✅ Schedules morning appointments; keeps them short for fatigue management
  4. ✅ Electric toothbrush as primary recommendation
  5. ✅ Floss picks / Waterpik for interdental cleaning
  6. ✅ Discusses support worker-assisted brushing
  7. ✅ Refers to OT for adaptive devices
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • "Treatment in the wheelchair: many modern dental chairs allow treatment of patients who cannot safely transfer. For those who can transfer, use a safe transfer technique with carer assistance and proper positioning."
  • "Communication first: the patient in the wheelchair is the patient — direct all communication to them. A physical disability does not imply cognitive or communication impairment. Do not speak to the carer over the patient's head."
  • "Adaptations: head and neck support, mouth props for limited opening, high-volume suction, shorter appointments (fatigue), pressure care awareness (no prolonged static position), accessible bathroom."
  • "Practice access assessment: ramp, automatic doors, accessible toilet, adjustable chair height. If the practice is not accessible, consider domiciliary visit or referral to a more accessible practice."
Patient Reframes
  • "I want to make this appointment work well for you — can you tell me what you need in terms of positioning and setup?"
  • "I'm going to direct everything to you today — and if at any point you need me to pause or adjust anything, just let me know."
Curveball Deflectors
  • "Can't we just put her in the dental chair?" → "Transfer from a wheelchair needs to be done safely with the right technique. I'll check with her and her carer about whether she can safely transfer, and how. If she can't, I can treat her in the wheelchair — the outcome is the same."
  • "Does she understand what's happening?" → "I'll find out directly from her. A wheelchair doesn't tell me anything about someone's cognitive capacity. Let me ask her."
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ▶
STAGE: Opening and Direct Engagement

Candidate enters, addresses Ms. Park by name with eye contact, maintaining level positioning — crouching or sitting to avoid standing over the patient.

"Hello Ms. Park, I'm Dr. Chen — it's great to meet you. Thank you for coming in today. Before we get started, I just want to make sure you're comfortable and that today works well for you. I'll be speaking with you directly throughout, so please feel free to ask me anything at any time."

Candidate acknowledges the support worker with a brief nod but directs all subsequent conversation to Ms. Park.

"I understand from your notes that you have MS and that you've been finding oral hygiene a bit more difficult lately. I want to make sure we address that properly today. First, let's sort out the most comfortable way to see you — can I ask about your setup?"

---

Appointment Environment and Wheelchair Decision

"Ms. Park, we have two options for today's appointment, and I'd like you to choose what suits you best. The first option is to transfer you to the dental chair — we have transfer equipment and a trained assistant to help make that as smooth as possible. The second option is that we treat you here in your wheelchair. I have a portable headrest attachment that can support your head, and the chair can be partially reclined to give me good access. Many patients with MS find this significantly less fatiguing and more comfortable overall. Have you transferred to a dental chair before, and if so, how did that go for you?"

Candidate listens attentively.

"There's absolutely no obligation to transfer — treating in the wheelchair is clinically appropriate and I'm very comfortable doing so. What would you prefer?"

Candidate ensures the wheelchair is locked and stable, adjusts the dental light accordingly, and positions the portable headrest before proceeding with examination.

---

Fatigue and Appointment Scheduling
