"I want to ask about your fatigue, because it will shape how we plan your care going forward. Can you tell me — when during the day do you generally feel your best? Most of my patients with MS find mornings are significantly better before fatigue builds through the day."

Candidate listens.

"That's really helpful. From now on, I'd like to schedule your appointments in the morning — ideally before eleven o'clock if that suits your routine. I'd also like to keep each visit to around thirty to forty minutes maximum. Rather than trying to cover everything today, we'll split your care across several shorter appointments. That protects your energy and means you'll get more out of each visit. Does that sound manageable?"

"For today, we'll do a thorough assessment, take any necessary radiographs, and talk through your home hygiene. We'll leave any treatment planning for a follow-up once we've reviewed everything together."

---

Clinical Examination and Findings

Candidate conducts a thorough oral examination, periodontal charting, and appropriate radiographic assessment if indicated.

"Thank you for your patience through the examination, Ms. Park. I can see you have moderately inflamed gums throughout — what we call generalised moderate gingivitis. The good news is that this is reversible with improved plaque control at home, and that's very achievable even with the hand function challenges you're describing. There's no sign of deeper bone involvement at this stage, so we've caught this at a good time."

---

Adaptive Oral Hygiene Instruction

"Now, let me talk through what I'd recommend for home care, and I want to tailor this entirely to your situation with the splints and the spasticity.

My strongest recommendation is an electric toothbrush — specifically an oscillating-rotating type like an Oral-B. This completely removes the need for the wrist rotation required with a manual brush, so your hand simply needs to guide it across each tooth surface. Many models now come with a larger diameter grip handle, which is much easier to hold with splinted hands. This single change will make the biggest difference to your gum health.

If the standard grip is still difficult, rubber foam tubing or a grip sleeve can be fitted over the handle — your pharmacy or an independent living centre will stock these. This is a very simple and inexpensive modification.

For cleaning between your teeth, I'd recommend floss picks rather than conventional floss — they require only one hand and no wrapping. Alternatively, a water flosser such as a Waterpik is excellent for patients with limited dexterity. You fill a reservoir and hold a wand — no fine manipulation needed at all.

On timing — please try to do your brushing first thing in the morning after you've had your medication and rested, while your energy is at its best. Even two minutes then is far more effective than an exhausted attempt later in the day.

I'd also like to have a brief conversation with your support worker — with your permission — about assisted brushing on days when your fatigue is particularly severe. Carer-assisted oral hygiene is a well-recognised and appropriate part of support care, and having a consistent technique demonstrated will make a real difference."

---

Referral, Safety Net, and Closing

"One more suggestion — if you haven't seen an occupational therapist recently, I'd strongly recommend a referral. An OT can do a formal assessment of adaptive aids for daily living activities, including oral hygiene specifically, and they may identify solutions I haven't thought of. I'm happy to write that referral letter for you today.

I'll also write a brief care summary you can share with your support worker so they have clear, written guidance on the brushing technique.

Do you have any questions about anything we've discussed? Is there anything that feels difficult or that you'd like me to explain differently?"

Candidate listens and responds appropriately.

"Thank you so much for your time today, Ms. Park. You've been very patient and I really appreciate you sharing so much detail — it genuinely helps me give you the best care. We'll book your next morning appointment at the front desk, keep it to thirty minutes, and continue from where we've left off today. Please don't hesitate to call us if anything changes or if you have questions in the meantime."

SN6
Stroke Patient with Dysphagia — Oral Care and Aspiration Risk
Category:** Special Needs / Geriatric | **Time:** 11 min | **Difficulty:** Exam-ready

CASE SUMMARY

A 70-year-old patient is 6 months post-stroke with right-sided hemiplegia and moderate dysphagia. He is a nursing home resident. His speech pathologist has restricted him to modified texture food. Candidate must advise on oral care modifications, assess aspiration risk during dental treatment, and adapt the clinical approach.

CANDIDATE BRIEF

Mr. Rao, 70, is a nursing home resident attending with a care worker. He has right hemiplegia, right facial droop, and moderate dysphagia (unable to swallow thin liquids safely — on thickened fluids). He has generalised poor oral hygiene with heavy plaque, mild–moderate gingivitis, and a partially erupted wisdom tooth (48) that is inflamed. Your task: manage his oral care and assess whether the wisdom tooth can be managed in this setting.

EXAMINER CONTEXT

Mr. Rao has some expressive aphasia — communicates with gestures and single words. The care worker helps interpret. If the candidate speaks slowly, clearly, and checks for understanding, Mr. Rao participates in the consultation. He can communicate "yes" and "no" reliably.

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

Aspiration risk — INFLECTION 1: The most important safety consideration

"Mr. Rao has dysphagia — he cannot safely manage thin liquids, which means he is at significant risk of aspirating water, saliva, or dental materials during treatment. This changes how I approach any dental procedure."

Modifications for aspiration risk:

  1. Position — Never fully supine. Treat at 30–45° recline maximum; ideally slightly upright
  2. Suction — High-volume suction in mouth at all times during any wet procedure
  3. Rubber dam — Wherever possible, to isolate the field and prevent liquid pooling
  4. Small water volume — Minimal irrigation; avoid large water flush
  5. Check swallowing — Pause frequently to allow patient to swallow or suction to clear

Oral hygiene instructions for carer — INFLECTION 2

"Good oral hygiene is critical in stroke patients — aspiration of oral bacteria is a leading cause of aspiration pneumonia, which is one of the most serious complications after stroke. Here's what the carer should do:

  1. Brush teeth twice daily using a suction toothbrush (designed for patients who can't spit or rinse)
  2. Brush with a small-head electric toothbrush — easier for a carer to manoeuvre
  3. Position at 30° minimum — never flat
  4. Chlorhexidine gel to toothbrush (instead of rinsing with chlorhexidine, which he can't safely gargle)
  5. Dentures if present: remove, clean, and leave out at night"

The wisdom tooth (48) — INFLECTION 3

"The pericoronitis on 48 is an active infection. Options:

  1. Irrigation under the operculum + chlorhexidine gel — manage the acute infection conservatively in this session
  2. Antibiotics — if systemically unwell or spreading infection (check temperature, lymph nodes)
  3. Extraction — desirable for a chronically recurring problem, but significant aspiration risk. For Mr. Rao, an extraction of 48 should be done in a hospital/specialist setting with appropriate anaesthetic support and aspiration precautions — not in the community setting."

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Identifies aspiration risk as the primary clinical safety issue
  2. ✅ Correct positioning: 30–45° (never supine)
  3. ✅ High-volume suction throughout; minimal irrigation
  4. ✅ Oral hygiene instruction for carer: suction toothbrush, chlorhexidine gel, 30° position, no rinsing
  5. ✅ Links oral bacteria + aspiration pneumonia (the major complication)
  6. ✅ Manages pericoronitis conservatively today; refers for extraction to hospital/specialist

TG4 ALERTS

Aspiration pneumonia in stroke patients — Oral bacteria (especially Gram-negative anaerobes from periodontal disease) are a major source of aspiration pneumonia post-stroke. Regular professional oral care and good home care are evidence-based preventive interventions.
Suction toothbrush — Specialised device combining a toothbrush with low-volume suction. Designed for patients with dysphagia who cannot spit. Essential tool for carer-delivered oral care in stroke, dementia, and similar populations.
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • "Dysphagia post-stroke significantly increases aspiration risk during dental treatment. Water, irrigation fluid, debris, and LA solution can all be aspirated — this is a serious risk, not a theoretical one."
  • "Positional adaptations: never supine — treat at 45–60 degrees minimum or as upright as possible. Gravity helps prevent fluid from reaching the posterior pharynx."
  • "Technique adaptations: high-volume suction by assistant at all times, placed before any water is used; minimise irrigation water; avoid gel-based products that pool; use rubber dam where possible; dry techniques for examinations."
  • "Communication: assess aphasia type (expressive — understands but can't speak; receptive — can speak but doesn't understand; mixed). Adapt accordingly — yes/no questions, written communication, speech pathology aids."
Patient Reframes
  • "I want to make the appointment as safe as possible for you — and that means adjusting how I work, particularly with water. I'll talk you through everything as I go so nothing is a surprise."
  • "The adjustments I'm making aren't complicated — mostly position and suction. They mean I can do the treatment safely without the aspiration risk."
Curveball Deflectors
  • "Can't you just use less water?" → "Reducing water helps — but it's the suction technique that makes the real difference. The key is having the suction positioned and active before any water is introduced. I'll make sure my assistant is on suction throughout, and we'll keep you upright the whole time."
  • "She wants to lie flat — she's more comfortable." → "I understand the comfort preference — but lying flat with a swallowing difficulty during dental treatment is a genuine aspiration risk. A slight recline at 45 degrees is the safest position I can offer. If there are ways to make that more comfortable for her, let's work that out."
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ▶
STAGE: Opening and Orientation

Candidate enters, greets the patient and care worker warmly, and confirms identity.

"Good morning, Mr. Rao. My name is Dr. [Name], and I'm the dentist today. It's lovely to meet you. I can see you've come in with your care worker — that's wonderful, and I'll make sure to include you both in our conversation today. Mr. Rao, I understand you've had a stroke, and I want to make sure everything we do today is safe and comfortable for you."

Candidate directs speech toward Mr. Rao throughout, turning to the care worker for clarification where needed.

"Before I examine your mouth, I'd like to ask a few questions to make sure I understand your health background. Is that alright?"

Confirms: six months post-stroke, right hemiplegia and facial droop, moderate dysphagia, restricted to thickened fluids by the speech pathologist, residing in a nursing home, attending for oral assessment and a sore back tooth.

"Thank you. And when you say Mr. Rao is on thickened fluids — he cannot swallow thin liquids safely at all? Has he had any episodes of choking or chest infections recently?"

Notes response. Confirms no recent pneumonia. Proceeds to examination.

---

Clinical Examination and Aspiration Risk Assessment

Examines the oral cavity with Mr. Rao seated at approximately 35 to 40 degrees — not fully reclined.

"I'm going to have a look inside your mouth now, Mr. Rao. I'll be very gentle."

Notes generalised heavy plaque accumulation, mild-to-moderate generalised gingivitis, and inflamed pericoronal tissue around tooth 48 with visible plaque and food debris beneath the operculum. No purulent discharge. No lymphadenopathy. Checks temperature — afebrile.

Turns to the care worker to summarise findings.

"Mr. Rao has some significant gum inflammation throughout his mouth, and the wisdom tooth at the back on the lower right is causing a localised infection in the gum tissue. I want to talk to you both about the most important safety issue first, because it changes everything about how we treat him."

---

Aspiration Risk — Primary Safety Issue

"The most critical safety consideration for Mr. Rao today is his dysphagia. Because he cannot safely swallow thin liquids, he is at significant risk of aspirating — breathing in — water, saliva, or dental materials into his lungs during dental treatment. This is not a minor concern. Aspiration of oral bacteria, particularly the harmful bacteria we find in infected or inflamed gums, is one of the leading causes of aspiration pneumonia after stroke. Aspiration pneumonia is a serious, potentially life-threatening complication, and it is directly linked to poor oral hygiene in stroke patients."

"So the first thing I want to address is how we work safely around this risk. I'll never position Mr. Rao flat on his back. I'll treat him at 30 to 45 degrees recline at most — ideally slightly more upright than that. I will have high-volume suction in the mouth at all times during any wet procedure, to immediately clear water, saliva, or debris before he has any opportunity to inhale it. I'll use a rubber dam wherever possible to isolate the working field. I'll use the absolute minimum volume of water for irrigation — no large rinses — and I'll pause frequently to allow suction to clear his mouth before we continue."

---

Oral Hygiene Instruction for the Care Worker

"Now, the most powerful thing we can do to protect Mr. Rao from aspiration pneumonia long-term is to keep his mouth as clean as possible every single day. This is where you play a critical role."

Addresses the care worker directly.

"Mr. Rao needs his teeth brushed twice daily. The tool I recommend is a suction toothbrush — it is specially designed for patients who cannot spit or rinse safely. It brushes and removes fluid simultaneously. You can use a small-headed electric toothbrush with it, which is easier for you to control and more effective at removing plaque. Please always keep him at 30 degrees minimum — never brush his teeth with him lying flat."

"Instead of a chlorhexidine mouthrinse — which he cannot gargle safely — apply chlorhexidine gel directly onto the toothbrush. This delivers the antibacterial benefit without any swallowing risk. If Mr. Rao has a denture, remove it after meals, clean it thoroughly, and store it dry overnight. Dry storage reduces the build-up of Candida and plaque on the denture surface."

"I would also strongly recommend that Mr. Rao receives professional dental cleaning at regular three-monthly intervals — this is evidence-based care for stroke patients in residential facilities."

---

Management of Tooth 48 — Pericoronitis

"Now, regarding the wisdom tooth. Mr. Rao has pericoronitis — an infection of the gum flap overlying the partially erupted lower right wisdom tooth. Today, because there is no sign of spreading infection, no pus, no swelling of the face or neck, and he is afebrile, I can manage this conservatively and safely in the chair."

"I will gently irrigate beneath the operculum using warm saline or chlorhexidine solution, using the fine tip of a syringe, and I will apply chlorhexidine gel under the flap. I will do this with high-volume suction in situ throughout. I'll also give him oral hygiene instructions for the area — though in practice, his care worker will carry these out."

"In terms of antibiotics — Mr. Rao is systemically well today, so antibiotics are not indicated at this visit. I'll review him in one week."

"However, I want to be clear about the longer-term plan. Extraction of tooth 48 is absolutely the definitive treatment for recurrent pericoronitis, and I would strongly recommend it. But this extraction should not be performed here in the community setting. The aspiration risk during a surgical procedure of this nature — with irrigation, blood, and debris in the airfield — is too significant without appropriate anaesthetic support and hospital-level suction and airway management. I will write a detailed referral to the oral surgery department at a hospital with full documentation of his dysphagia, positioning requirements, and aspiration precautions."

---

Safety Net and Closing

"Mr. Rao, I want to make sure you both know what to watch for. If the tooth becomes more painful, if swelling develops in the jaw or neck, if Mr. Rao develops a fever, has trouble opening his mouth, or has any difficulty breathing, please go to the emergency department immediately — do not wait for a dental appointment."

"I'll provide you with written care instructions for the suction toothbrush technique and the chlorhexidine gel routine. I'll also write a referral letter to the hospital oral surgery team today, clearly outlining his stroke history, dysphagia, aspiration risk, and the need for careful positioning and airway management during the extraction."

"Do you have any questions at all? You've both been wonderful today — thank you for coming in."

M9-1
Drug-Seeking Behaviour — Opioid Request for Dental Pain
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ▶
STAGE: Opening & Focused History

Candidate enters, offers hand, makes eye contact, and sits at the same level as the patient — no desk barrier if possible.

"Hello, I'm Dr. [Name]. I'm one of the dentists here today. I understand you've come in without an appointment — that's completely fine. Can I ask your name? And is it all right if I call you by your first name?"

"Thank you for coming in. I can see you're not comfortable, and I want to do everything I can to help you today. Before I do anything, I just need to ask you a few questions so I understand exactly what's going on. Is that okay?"

"Can you tell me what's been happening with your tooth? Which side is it on, and how long have you been in pain?"

Listens fully. Patient describes lower right dental pain, diagnosis of irreversible pulpitis, root canal planned with regular dentist who is away.

"On a scale of zero to ten, how would you rate the pain right now? And can you describe it — is it a constant throbbing, or does it come and go? Does it wake you at night?"

"Have you noticed any swelling in your face or jaw, difficulty swallowing, or fever? Have you felt unwell at all?"

"What have you already tried for the pain, and in what doses? How often have you been taking the paracetamol and ibuprofen?"

"I'd also like to ask about your general health and your medications — this is really important for your safety. Are you taking any medications regularly, including patches, creams, or anything prescribed by another healthcare provider?"

Patient mentions the pain patch prescribed by her physiotherapist.

"Thank you for telling me about the patch — that's really important. Can you tell me what the patch is called, or what's written on the packet? Is it a buprenorphine patch or a fentanyl patch by any chance?"

Candidate notes confirmed opioid-containing patch — flags opioid-opioid interaction risk internally.

"Do you have any allergies to medications? And is there any chance you could be pregnant?"

---

Decline the Opioid Request — Clearly and Kindly

"Thank you for being so open with me. I can hear how much pain you're in, and I genuinely want to help you get through this. I do need to be honest with you about something, though, because I think it's important."

"I'm not able to prescribe opioid medications — fentanyl, oxycodone, or tramadol — for dental pain today. I want to explain why, because I think you deserve a proper reason rather than just a refusal."

"There are actually two important reasons. First, the patch you're already wearing contains an opioid, and adding another opioid on top of that — even in tablet form — carries a real risk of serious side effects, including slowing down your breathing. That's not a risk I'm willing to take with you. Second, and this is something I want you to know because it's based on good evidence — opioids are actually not very effective for toothache. The pain in your tooth is being caused by inflammation and pressure inside the tooth itself, and opioids don't address that source. They can mask it temporarily while the problem continues."

"I know that's not what you were hoping to hear, and I'm not dismissing the pain you're in — it is real and it is significant. But the safest and most effective path forward is one I can actually help you with today."

---

Optimise Non-Opioid Analgesia & Offer Emergency Dental Treatment

"Here's what I can do for you right now. The most effective non-opioid pain relief for dental pain — and I mean this, the research shows it matches or exceeds opioids for toothache — is taking paracetamol and ibuprofen together in an alternating pattern. I'd like you to take one gram of paracetamol — that's two standard 500 milligram tablets — and 400 milligrams of ibuprofen at the same time, right now if you haven't eaten already. Then alternate them every three to four hours so you're always getting one or the other working in your system. Do not take more than four grams of paracetamol in twenty-four hours."

"Is there any reason you can't take ibuprofen — stomach problems, blood pressure issues, blood thinners? Good — then this combination is safe for you and it should give you meaningful relief."

"But more importantly, I'd like to examine the tooth today. The most effective thing I can do for your pain is treat the actual problem. If you're willing, I can take a look, take an X-ray if needed, and depending on what I find, I may be able to open the tooth and drain it, or place a temporary dressing that will significantly reduce the pressure and the pain. That is the real treatment here — managing the source."

Candidate indicates they will examine the patient, assess the tooth clinically and radiographically, and offer emergency pulp access or temporary dressing if the clinical picture supports it.

"I also want to try to reach your regular dentist's practice — even if your dentist is away, the practice may have an emergency contact number or a colleague covering. Would you be happy for me to try calling them on your behalf?"

"If I'm not able to provide the emergency care you need here today, I'll personally refer you to a dental emergency clinic that can see you today. I'm not going to send you away without a clear next step."

---

Safety Net, Documentation & Closing

"Before you go — and this is very important — there are some signs that would mean you need to go straight to a hospital emergency department, not wait for a dental appointment. If you notice any swelling spreading into your neck or under your jaw, difficulty opening your mouth fully, any trouble swallowing or breathing, a fever above 38 degrees, or if you start to feel unwell or confused — please go directly to the emergency department and tell them you have a dental infection. Those signs can indicate the infection is spreading, and that requires hospital care urgently."

"Your appointment with your regular dentist is next week — please keep that appointment, and make sure the root canal treatment gets underway. That is the definitive treatment for this condition."

"I'm going to document today's consultation carefully, including what you've told me about your symptoms, your medications, our conversation about the pain relief options, and the treatment we've provided today. You're welcome to a copy of that for your own records."

"Is there anything else you'd like to ask me, or anything that's still worrying you? I want to make sure you leave here feeling heard and with a clear plan."

"Take care of yourself. I hope you get some real relief today — and please don't hesitate to call us if anything changes before your next appointment."

Category:** Communication & ethics · Time:** 11 minutes · Opens with:** Candidate · Difficulty:** Exam-ready

CASE SUMMARY

Female patient with a known diagnosis of irreversible pulpitis (made by her regular dentist) presents demanding opioid analgesics (fentanyl, oxycodone, or tramadol). Claims her regular dentist is away, cannot be contacted, and that standard painkillers are ineffective. Also has a physiotherapist-prescribed pain patch for chronic back pain. Has a dental appointment booked for next week. Candidate must manage the request ethically without prescribing opioids.

CANDIDATE BRIEF

You are a general dentist in a mixed practice. A female patient you have not seen before presents without an appointment requesting an urgent prescription for strong painkillers. She tells you her regular dentist diagnosed her with a tooth problem requiring root canal treatment on her lower right side but he has gone away and she cannot contact him. She says paracetamol and ibuprofen "don't work" and she needs fentanyl, oxycodone, or tramadol. She mentions she uses a pain relief patch prescribed by her physiotherapist for chronic back pain. She has an appointment with her regular dentist next week. You have no previous records for this patient. Your task: take a focused history, manage her request, provide appropriate alternatives, and address her concerns. You have 8 minutes.

EXAMINER CONTEXT

The patient is persistent but not overtly hostile. She presents a plausible story but there are multiple red flags for drug-seeking behaviour: specific opioid requests by name, dentist "unavailable", claims of analgesic failure without trying all options, existing opioid-adjacent medications (pain patch). She will become more insistent if the candidate hedges or seems sympathetic without clear boundaries. She will accept a firm, empathetic, non-judgmental refusal if the candidate offers genuine alternatives and explains the reasoning clearly. She will attempt to escalate ("I'm in real pain, you have a duty of care") if the candidate is vague. Key hidden facts: she has not actually tried high-dose ibuprofen (600 mg with food) or combined paracetamol + ibuprofen; she is not sure what the pain patch contains (it is buprenorphine — a strong opioid — meaning concurrent opioid prescribing would be dangerous).

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

Opening & History (2 min)

Welcome the patient. Take a focused history: HOPC (duration, severity, character of pain, what's been tried), dental history (the diagnosis given, planned treatment), medical history (current medications — specifically ask about the pain patch and what it contains), allergies.

Recognise the Red Flags — INFLECTION 1: Medication history

Ask specifically: "Can you tell me what's in the pain patch?" A strong candidate identifies the buprenorphine/fentanyl patch as a concurrent opioid — making further opioid prescribing dangerous. A weak candidate misses this entirely.

Decline Opioids Clearly and Kindly (2 min) — INFLECTION 2: Firm boundary

"I understand you're in a lot of pain and I want to help you. However, I'm not able to prescribe opioid medications for dental pain in this situation — there are safer options that are actually more effective for toothache, and prescribing strong opioids without knowing your full history could put you at risk." Do not be apologetic or hedge — state it clearly once, then move on to solutions.

Provide Alternatives & Address the Dental Problem (3 min)

  • Optimise non-opioid analgesia: paracetamol 1 g + ibuprofen 400 mg alternating every 3–4 hours (if no contraindications) — evidence shows this combination equals opioid efficacy for dental pain
  • Offer to examine the tooth and provide emergency dental treatment (open access drainage, pulp extirpation, or temporary dressing) — treat the cause, not just the symptom
  • Contact the regular dentist's practice for an emergency referral or after-hours number
  • If unable to treat: refer to a dental emergency clinic today

Documentation & Safety-Net (1 min)

Document the encounter including the request and your reasoning. Advise: if pain becomes unmanageable or there are signs of spreading infection (swelling, difficulty swallowing, fever), present to the emergency department.

KEY POINTS

  • ✅ Takes full medication history including the pain patch — identifies potential opioid-opioid interaction risk
  • ✅ Declines opioid prescription clearly, once, without being accusatory or judgmental
  • ✅ Explains why opioids are not appropriate for dental pain (do not address source, interaction risk, ADA/TGA guidelines)
  • ✅ Offers optimised non-opioid analgesia (paracetamol + ibuprofen combination)
  • ✅ Offers to examine and treat the tooth directly (emergency pulp extirpation or dressing)
  • ✅ Provides onward pathway: emergency referral, regular dentist contact, ED if sepsis signs
  • ✅ Documents encounter and reasoning
  • ❌ Prescribes any opioid — automatic fail on safety grounds
  • ❌ Dismisses or accuses the patient without hearing her story
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • "Paracetamol 1 gram combined with ibuprofen 400 mg alternating every 3–4 hours provides equivalent pain relief to opioids for dental pain — that's the evidence-based approach I'd recommend."
  • "Before we go further — can you tell me what's in the pain patch your physio prescribed? Some patches contain opioids, and combining them could be unsafe."
  • "Opioids don't treat the source of dental pain — they mask it. The most effective thing I can do right now is actually look at the tooth and address what's causing the problem."
Patient Reframes
  • "I hear you — you're in real pain and you need it sorted today. Let me be direct about what I can and can't do, and then let's find you the best solution."
  • "I'm not questioning your pain. I'm telling you that what you're asking for isn't the right tool for this job — and I'd be doing you a disservice if I pretended otherwise."
Curveball Deflectors
  • "But I'm in agony — you have a duty of care!" → "You're absolutely right, and that's exactly why I'm offering to examine and treat the tooth right now — that's the duty of care. I'm also duty-bound not to prescribe medications that could harm you."
  • "My dentist always gives me these." → "I understand that may have been the approach before. I can only make decisions based on my assessment today and current guidelines — I'd encourage you to discuss that with your regular dentist at your appointment next week."
M9-2
MIH in an 11-Year-Old — Second Opinion on GA Extraction
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ▶
STAGE: Opening and History

Candidate greets Liam and his parents warmly, making eye contact with Liam first, then the parents.

"Hi Liam, I'm Dr. [Name] — great to meet you. And you must be Liam's mum and dad — thanks so much for coming in today. Liam, I want to make sure I'm talking to you as much as to your parents, because these are your teeth and your experience matters most. Is that okay?" Pauses for response. "Wonderful. So, Liam, can you tell me in your own words what's been bothering you?"

Listens to Liam describe sensitivity. Then: "You mentioned your back teeth are sensitive — is it more when you drink something cold, eat something sweet, or does it sometimes ache on its own even when you're not eating or drinking?" Listens carefully. "And how long has this been going on — a few weeks, or longer?"

Turning to the parents: "Thank you for that. Now, I understand Liam was seen at the hospital about three months ago and you were given a recommendation you wanted a second opinion on — and I think that's a completely reasonable thing to do. I want to go through everything carefully today. Before I examine him, could I ask a few more questions?"

"Liam, when you were a baby — and Mum and Dad, please help here — did Liam have any serious illnesses in his first three years of life? Anything like a high fever, hospitalisation, breathing problems, or was he premature at birth?" Listens. "Any long-term medications in those early years?" Listens. "And in terms of his teeth now — has he had any fillings before? Any previous treatment on these back teeth?" Listens. "Does anyone else in the family have teeth that are sensitive or have had similar problems?"

---

Examination and Diagnosis

Candidate examines Liam's teeth carefully with a mirror and probe, noting findings aloud.

"Liam, I'm just going to have a careful look — I promise nothing will hurt, I'm just looking." Examines all four first permanent molars and upper central incisors. Notes chalky-white to yellow-brown opaque areas on molar enamel, some surface breakdown on cusp tips, no cavitation extending into dentine. Incisors show demarcated opacities. All primary teeth appear intact and unaffected. Reviews the OPG confirming all permanent teeth developing normally.

"Alright Liam, you can relax your jaw — you've done really well. I can tell you exactly what's going on." Turns to include both Liam and his parents. "Liam has a condition called Molar Incisor Hypomineralisation — we call it MIH for short. What that means is that when Liam's back teeth and front teeth were forming — and that happens in the first few years of life, long before they come through the gum — the enamel didn't mineralise, or harden, as fully as it should. So instead of being smooth, dense and strong like normal enamel, some areas are softer, slightly porous, and more sensitive. That's exactly why cold water or cold food can be quite uncomfortable, Liam."

"Crucially — and I want to be very clear about this — this is not caused by diet, and it's not caused by brushing habits. This is a developmental condition. It happened during the formation of those teeth, most likely linked to an illness or physiological stress in early childhood. There is nothing you or Liam did to cause this."

---

Addressing the Hospital Recommendation Diplomatically

"Now, I want to speak carefully about what the hospital dentist told you, because I want to be respectful to my colleague — they saw Liam three months ago and were working with what they had at that time. What I can tell you is that in my clinical opinion today, based on what I can see, I do not believe extraction under general anaesthesia is the right first step for Liam."

"Liam is eleven years old. His molars, while affected, still have intact dentine — the layer underneath the enamel is not exposed, there are no deep cavities, and there's no sign of nerve involvement. Extraction under GA is generally reserved for MIH-affected teeth where the nerve is irreversibly damaged or where the tooth simply cannot be restored — and we are not at that point. General anaesthesia carries real risks and should only be recommended when there is no viable conservative alternative. Right now, there are several very good alternatives."

Pauses to check for parental understanding. "Does that make sense so far? Do you have questions before I go through the plan?"

---

Conservative Management Plan

"So here is what I'd recommend for Liam, in a logical step-by-step approach." Speaks to both Liam and his parents.

"First, for the sensitivity — we're going to start Liam on a high-fluoride prescription toothpaste, which he'll use at night instead of his regular toothpaste. We can also apply a desensitising agent called Tooth Mousse, which contains a calcium-phosphate complex that helps remineralise and strengthen that softer enamel. Liam, this is something you use at home — it tastes a bit like yoghurt and you just rub it on after brushing."

"Second, today I'd like to apply fissure sealants and protective coatings using a glass ionomer cement over the vulnerable areas on the molars. This seals bacteria out, provides a protective layer, and releases fluoride into the enamel over time — which is exactly what MIH-affected enamel needs."

"Third, for any areas on the molars where the surface has broken down, we can restore those with composite resin or glass ionomer restorations. These are fillings — Liam, a bit like a patch — that reinforce the tooth and prevent further breakdown. Local anaesthetic makes this completely comfortable."

"If a molar were to break down more significantly in the future, one excellent option is a preformed metal crown — sometimes called a Hall crown — which caps the whole tooth, protects it on all sides, and is very durable. That's something we keep in reserve if needed."

"What I'd like to do is see Liam every three to four months so I can monitor all of these teeth closely, catch any changes early, and adjust the plan as needed. MIH-affected teeth can absolutely be maintained into adulthood with the right care."

---

Prognosis and Safety Net

"Liam, the really important message is this — these teeth can be saved with good management. Most children with MIH keep their molars well into adulthood. If your sensitivity improves with the treatments we're starting today, that's a really good sign."

"The only scenario where we would revisit extraction would be if a molar developed irreversible nerve damage despite our best efforts — and if that happened, we'd do it in a very planned way, ideally with an orthodontist involved, to make sure the other teeth shift into the right position afterward."

"I'll write a summary of today's findings and my management plan so you have it in writing, and if you'd like me to correspond with the hospital, I'm very happy to do that professionally."

"Liam — any questions for me? And Mum, Dad — anything at all?" Pauses warmly. "You've done exactly the right thing seeking a second opinion. Let's get started."

Category:** Paediatric dentistry · Time:** 11 minutes · Opens with:** Candidate · Difficulty:** Exam-ready

CASE SUMMARY

11-year-old boy attends with parents for a second opinion. A hospital general dentist recommended extracting his hypomineralised first permanent molars under general anaesthesia. Clinical photograph shows hypomineralised (chalky/opaque) first permanent molars and incisors; primary teeth are unaffected. Candidate must diagnose MIH, present a conservative management plan, and address parental anxiety about the hospital's recommendation.

CANDIDATE BRIEF

You are a general dentist. An 11-year-old boy, Liam Chen, attends with his mother and father. Liam has been complaining of sensitivity to cold in his back teeth for several months. His mother took him to a public hospital dental clinic three months ago, where a general dentist examined him and told the family his back teeth were "defective" and needed to be extracted under general anaesthesia. The parents are unhappy with this recommendation and are seeking a second opinion. Today's examination shows: hypomineralised (chalky-white to yellow-brown) enamel on all four first permanent molars and the upper central incisors; the molars show some surface breakdown on the cusps but no cavitation extending to dentine on all teeth; primary teeth appear clinically normal; OPG confirms all permanent teeth present and developing normally. Your task: diagnose, explain the condition to the family, propose a management plan, and address their concerns about the extraction recommendation. You have 8 minutes.

EXAMINER CONTEXT

The mother is the main spokesperson — anxious, protective, and somewhat sceptical of the hospital recommendation but uncertain what the right path is. The father is quieter but will ask practical questions ("Is this going to cost a lot?"). Liam is cooperative but embarrassed about his teeth and will speak if directly addressed. The parents' main concerns are: (1) why is his enamel like this — did they do something wrong? (2) will the teeth get worse? (3) is GA really necessary? Hidden: the mother did take vitamin D supplements during her third trimester and Liam had a serious febrile illness at age 8 months — this is the likely developmental window for MIH but the candidate doesn't need to pinpoint cause, just reassure it wasn't the parents' fault and it's not hereditary in the typical sense.

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

History (1.5 min)

Confirm symptoms (cold sensitivity, spontaneous pain?), dental history (previous treatment), medical history (illnesses in first 3 years of life, medications, premature birth), family dental history.

Explain the Diagnosis — INFLECTION 1: Naming it clearly

"Liam has a condition called Molar Incisor Hypomineralisation — MIH. It means the enamel on his back teeth and front teeth didn't mineralise fully during early childhood, which makes them softer, more sensitive, and more prone to breaking down. Crucially — this is not caused by diet or brushing habits. It's a developmental issue that happens during tooth formation, usually linked to an illness or medical event in the first few years of life."

Address the GA Recommendation — INFLECTION 2: Conservative first

Explain that extraction under GA is not the first-line approach for MIH in an 11-year-old with teeth that still have intact dentine. Conservative options: (1) desensitising agents and high-fluoride toothpaste for sensitivity; (2) fissure sealants with resin or GIC to protect breakdown-prone areas; (3) composite or GIC restorations for any areas of surface loss; (4) preformed metal crowns (Hall technique) for significantly broken-down molars; (5) regular monitoring every 3–6 months. Extraction is reserved for teeth with irreversible pulpal involvement or where restoration is not viable — not as a first step.

Prognosis & Monitoring (1 min)

With good management, most MIH-affected molars can be maintained into adulthood. If extraction becomes unavoidable later, orthodontic assessment should guide timing (ideally around the calcification of second molars, approximately age 8–10 — already passed, so timing discussion changes).

KEY POINTS

  • ✅ Correctly diagnoses MIH — distinguishes from caries, fluorosis, AI
  • ✅ Explains developmental cause without attributing blame to parents
  • ✅ Presents staged conservative treatment plan before considering extraction
  • ✅ Addresses the GA recommendation diplomatically — does not criticise the hospital dentist
  • ✅ Discusses remineralisation, sealing, and restoration options by severity
  • ✅ Sets appropriate recall interval (3–6 months) and monitoring plan
  • ✅ Involves Liam in the conversation, not just the parents
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • "MIH affects the mineralisation — the hardness — of the enamel, not the structure of the tooth. That means we have real options before we'd ever consider removing a tooth."
  • "The current guidelines recommend protecting and restoring MIH-affected molars first. Extraction under GA is reserved for teeth that are beyond saving — and on today's examination, Liam's teeth aren't there."
  • "High-concentration fluoride varnish applied every 3 months, combined with a prescription-strength fluoride toothpaste at home, is our first line of attack on the sensitivity."
Patient Reframes
  • "This is not anything you did wrong — the enamel was forming when Liam was very young, and things like fevers or illnesses can interfere with that process. It's nobody's fault."
  • "We want Liam to keep these teeth. They're his adult teeth, and with the right treatment, most kids with MIH keep their molars well into adulthood."
Curveball Deflectors
  • "The hospital dentist said they need to come out — are you saying he was wrong?" → "Different clinicians can have different thresholds. What I can tell you is that on my examination today, these teeth have enough structure to treat conservatively. I'd like to give that a proper try before we discuss any more invasive options."
  • "What if it gets worse while we wait?" → "That's exactly why we'll review every 3 months — so if a tooth starts breaking down more quickly, we catch it early and act. We're not waiting and hoping; we're actively monitoring and treating."
M10-1
Incidental White Lesion — Differential Diagnosis & Biopsy Decision
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ▶
STAGE: Opening & Discovery of the Finding

Seats the patient comfortably. Ensures good lighting. Conducts a thorough intraoral examination and notes a white patch on the right buccal mucosa, approximately 10 mm in diameter, irregular in outline, slightly raised, non-removable with gauze, adjacent to the amalgam restoration on tooth 46. Photographs the lesion for baseline documentation.

"Hanna, thank you for coming in today. I've completed your examination and your teeth and gums are looking reasonably well overall — but I have noticed something on the inside of your right cheek that I'd like to talk to you about. I want to reassure you that I'm not alarmed, but I do want to be completely open with you rather than just ignore it.

I've found a small white patch — it's about 10 millimetres across, so roughly the size of a small pea. It has slightly irregular edges, it's sitting just adjacent to one of your back fillings, and it can't be wiped away. You haven't noticed any discomfort from it, and that's consistent with what I'm seeing — it appears to be causing you no symptoms at all. What I'd like to do is ask you a few questions about it, go through what it might be, and then talk about what I think we should do next. Is that alright with you?"

---

Targeted History

"First — how long have you been coming to this practice? You mentioned it's been about two years since your last visit — is that right? So we can't be entirely sure how long this patch has been there. Have you ever noticed any soreness, roughness, or unusual feeling on that side of your cheek — anything at all, even briefly?"

Pauses to allow the patient to respond.

"Do you bite your cheek at all — particularly on that right side? Sometimes people do it habitually, especially under stress, and that can cause changes to the lining of the cheek."

"Now I want to ask you about smoking. You mentioned you smoke occasionally — can you tell me roughly how many cigarettes a day, and for how long you've been smoking?"

Listens. Notes approximately 3 to 5 cigarettes per day for 20 years.

"And alcohol — do you drink regularly? Roughly how many standard drinks in a week?"

"Have you ever had any white or red patches in your mouth before, or had a biopsy of anything in your mouth? Any lumps in your neck you've noticed? Any difficulty swallowing, unexplained weight loss, or persistent earache on that side?"

"Any family history of mouth cancer or throat cancer?"

"Any new medications recently — including over-the-counter tablets, herbal supplements, anything like that?"

Listens carefully and notes responses. The patient has no symptoms, no previous oral lesions, no family history, no neck lumps, no new medications, and no alcohol of concern.

---

Differential Diagnosis — Honest & Structured Communication

"Thank you, Hanna — that's really helpful. Let me now explain what this white patch could be, because there are several possibilities and I think you deserve a clear and honest explanation.

The most likely explanation, given where this patch is sitting — right next to that old amalgam filling — is something called a lichenoid reaction. This is where the tissue reacts to the metal in the filling, a bit like a contact sensitivity. It can produce exactly this kind of white change. That's actually quite common and often resolves if the filling is replaced.

A second possibility is what we call frictional keratosis — basically a thickening of the lining in response to repeated mild trauma, like cheek biting, which you mentioned can happen when you're stressed. The tissue builds up a white, toughened surface in response.

A third possibility is leukoplakia — which simply means a white patch that can't be explained by another cause. Most leukoplakias are benign, but some can show abnormal cell changes over time, so they require monitoring and often a biopsy.

And I do need to mention — and I want to say this calmly, because I am not saying this is the case — but one of the reasons we take white patches seriously is that occasionally they can represent very early changes that, if left undetected, could develop into oral cancer. You smoke, you've been under significant stress, and you're in an age group where we need to be vigilant. I raise this not to alarm you, but because I think it's important you understand why I'm not simply going to tell you it's nothing and send you on your way.

The honest truth is: I cannot tell you with certainty which of these it is just by looking. The only way to know for certain is through a biopsy — a small tissue sample examined under a microscope."

---

Investigations & Management Plan

"So here is what I'd like to do, and why.

First, I've already taken a photograph today so we have a clear baseline — size, shape, colour — all documented.

Second, I'd like to arrange for you to see a specialist — either an oral medicine specialist or an oral and maxillofacial surgeon — who can assess this in more detail and arrange a biopsy if they feel it's indicated. Given that this is a white patch that can't be wiped off, in someone who smokes, and we don't know how long it's been there, I don't want to sit on this for weeks. I'd like that referral to happen within the next two weeks.

Third — and this is something we can do in the meantime — I'd like to discuss replacing that old amalgam filling on the lower right. If this patch is a lichenoid reaction to the metal, removing the source of irritation may cause it to resolve on its own. That would actually be very reassuring diagnostic information. However — and this is important — even if we replace the filling, if the patch is still there in two to three weeks, we proceed with the referral regardless. We don't use 'wait and see' as a reason to delay investigation indefinitely."

"In the meantime, if you notice any change — if it gets bigger, if it becomes sore, if you develop any lumps in your neck, or any difficulty swallowing — I want you to contact us straight away and we will escalate the referral immediately."

---

Lifestyle Advice & Safety Net / Closing

"Hanna, I also want to briefly mention smoking. I understand it can be a difficult habit to address, particularly when you're already under pressure at work. But smoking is one of the most significant risk factors for changes like this in the mouth, and if there's ever a time to think seriously about cutting down or stopping altogether, this is it. I can give you some information, or I can write a referral to your GP who can support you with nicotine replacement or other options — whatever feels manageable for you."

"I know this is probably not what you were expecting today when you came in for a scale and clean. I want to be clear: I am not telling you this is something serious. What I am telling you is that I care enough about your health not to dismiss it, and the right thing to do is investigate it properly. Most of the time, lesions like this turn out to be entirely benign — but the only way to be certain is to find out.

Do you have any questions at all? I'm very happy to go through anything again."

Provides written information. Confirms referral letter will be sent within 24 hours. Books a review appointment in two weeks to assess the lesion and discuss amalgam replacement. Documents full lesion description, photograph, history, differentials, and management plan in the patient record.

Category:** Oral medicine · Time:** 11 minutes · Opens with:** Candidate · Difficulty:** Exam-ready

CASE SUMMARY

Hanna, a 45-year-old new patient, attends for a routine check-up and clean. On intraoral examination you notice a white patch on the right buccal mucosa adjacent to an amalgam restoration. The patient is unaware of the lesion. She is an occasional smoker under significant stress. Candidate must describe the lesion, take a targeted history, provide a differential diagnosis, recommend appropriate investigations, and counsel on next steps including the possibility of biopsy.

CANDIDATE BRIEF

Hanna Papadopoulos, 45-year-old, new patient. She has attended today requesting a scale and clean — her first visit in approximately two years. During your intraoral examination you notice a white patch on the right buccal mucosa. It is approximately 10 mm in diameter, irregular in outline, non-removable with gauze, appears slightly raised, and is positioned adjacent to an old amalgam restoration on tooth 46. The patient has not noticed it and has no oral symptoms. Her medical history is otherwise clear. She is an occasional smoker (3–5 cigarettes/day for 20 years). She has been under significant work stress. No family history of oral cancer. Your task: discuss the finding with the patient, take a targeted history, explain the differential diagnosis, recommend investigations, and outline next steps. You have 8 minutes.

EXAMINER CONTEXT

Hanna is calm but will become visibly anxious the moment the word "cancer" is mentioned — the candidate must balance honesty with appropriate reassurance. She will initially try to minimise ("Is it just from my brace rubbing?" or "Could it just be a bite mark?"). She smokes more than she admits initially — if asked directly, she'll confirm 5–10/day for over 20 years. She has a wedding she's stressed about organising. Hidden: she had a similar white patch previously that "went away on its own" — about 2 years ago on the other side; she didn't mention it. This is an important red flag if the candidate asks about recurrence or previous oral changes. The candidate must not catastrophise, but must not falsely reassure either — the correct position is "most white lesions are benign, but we need to investigate this properly because some can be serious."

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

Describe the Finding (1 min)

Explain calmly that you've noticed something on the inside of her cheek. Use neutral language: "I've found a small white patch — I want to ask you a few questions about it and work out what it might be."

Targeted History — INFLECTION 1: Red flags

Ask: duration (how long has it been there?), symptoms (soreness, bleeding, difficulty eating?), smoking and alcohol history (quantify), previous similar lesions, trauma history (denture, cheek biting, sharp tooth), medications, family history of oral cancer. Key red flag questions: previous oral lesions, previous biopsy, unexplained weight loss or neck lumps.

Differential Diagnosis (2 min) — INFLECTION 2: Honest communication

List differentials in order of likelihood for this patient: (1) Lichenoid reaction — proximity to amalgam restoration (friction or contact allergy); (2) Frictional keratosis — from cheek biting or trauma; (3) Leukoplakia — white patch not explained by any other cause; (4) Oral squamous cell carcinoma — must be excluded; (5) Candidiasis — less likely if non-removable. Explain that most white patches are benign but some require further investigation and that the only way to be certain is a biopsy.

Investigations & Plan (2 min)

Immediate: photograph and measure for baseline. Toluidine blue staining if available. Arrange specialist referral (oral medicine/oral surgery) for biopsy — do not delay more than 2 weeks for a non-removable white lesion in a smoker aged over 45. Interim: consider removing/replacing the adjacent amalgam to see if a contact reaction resolves. Review in 2 weeks — if lesion persists or changes, expedite referral.

KEY POINTS

  • ✅ Describes the lesion systematically (size, colour, texture, borders, removability, site)
  • ✅ Takes targeted history including smoking, alcohol, duration, previous lesions
  • ✅ Provides structured differential — includes OSCC without catastrophising
  • ✅ Recommends biopsy / specialist referral within appropriate timeframe (<2 weeks for suspicious lesion)
  • ✅ Discusses amalgam replacement as a diagnostic manoeuvre for possible lichenoid reaction
  • ✅ Communicates honestly but sensitively — does not dismiss or alarm
  • ❌ Dismisses lesion as "just a bite mark" without investigation
  • ❌ Fails to mention biopsy or specialist referral
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • "Non-removable white patches in a smoker over 40 require a biopsy to rule out a pre-cancerous or cancerous change — that's the standard approach and I'd recommend we don't delay that."
  • "The adjacent amalgam filling is relevant — sometimes metal fillings cause a reaction in the mucosa called a lichenoid reaction. I'd also like to consider replacing that filling as part of the workup."
  • "The fact that you had a similar patch two years ago that resolved is actually important information — it tells us this may be recurring, which changes how urgently I want to get this seen."
Patient Reframes
  • "I want to be straight with you: the vast majority of white patches like this are completely benign. But the only way to know for certain is to have a tiny piece tested. It's a simple procedure and it gives us certainty."
  • "Finding something like this on a check-up is exactly why regular dental visits matter — we've caught it early, when it's most manageable whatever it turns out to be."
Curveball Deflectors
  • "Could it just be from biting my cheek?" → "That's possible — cheek bite marks are common. But this is non-removable, has irregular borders, and you smoke, which puts you in a slightly higher risk category. That's why I don't want to assume — I want us to check it properly."
  • "Do I really need a biopsy — is it going to hurt?" → "It's done under local anaesthetic, takes about 10 minutes, and the discomfort afterwards is minimal. Given your history, the peace of mind is absolutely worth it."
M10-2
Perio Patient — Replacement Options for Missing Teeth (OPG, Bone Loss)
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ▶
STAGE: Opening and Agenda-Setting

"Good morning, David. I'm Dr. Chen — thanks for coming in today. I understand you've been seeing another dentist for quite a few years and you've recently been told you have some bone loss around your teeth, and now you're looking for a second opinion and want to talk about replacing some missing teeth. Is that right? And you've brought along an X-ray today — that's really helpful, thank you. What I'd like to do is ask you some questions first, have a look at the X-ray together, and then talk through your options honestly. Does that sound okay?"

---

History — Identifying Risk Factors

"Let's start from the beginning. Can you tell me roughly when you first noticed problems with your gums, or when your last dentist first mentioned bone loss?" Listens attentively. "And how often were you attending that dentist — were you going regularly, or more when something was bothering you?"

"Do you know if you've ever had any deep cleaning — what dentists sometimes call scaling and root planing, or subgingival debridement? Any gum surgery?" Pauses for response. "And these teeth that are missing — do you have any idea how long ago they were taken out, or whether they were removed because of gum disease, decay, or something else?"

"Alright. Now, I need to ask about your general health because it directly affects what options we have. Are you on any medications, or do you have any medical conditions — things like diabetes, heart conditions, blood pressure problems?" Listens. "Have you had a recent blood test, or do you know if your blood sugar has ever been checked?"

"I have to ask — do you smoke, or have you smoked in the past?" Pauses. "And alcohol — roughly how many standard drinks per week?"

"And at home, how are you finding your oral hygiene routine — brushing, flossing, anything like that? Any bleeding when you brush?" Listens carefully. "And what's your main goal today — what are you most hoping we can sort out for you?" Allows David to express his expectations fully before proceeding.

---

OPG Explanation — Plain Language

"Right, let's look at your X-ray together. This is a panoramic X-ray — it gives us a bird's-eye view of all your teeth and the bone that holds them in place. Now, I want to walk you through what I can see, and I'll use plain language throughout.

Normally, the bone sits quite high up, right up near the necks of the teeth — roughly here. On your X-ray, the bone level has dropped significantly around most of your teeth. We can see it has reduced by roughly forty to fifty per cent of the normal root length across most areas — so essentially, the scaffolding that holds many of your teeth in place has lost about half its height. This is the result of longstanding gum disease — a bacterial infection that, over time, causes the body to break down its own supporting bone.

I can also see at least three posterior teeth are already missing — the gaps are visible here, here, and here. The teeth that remain show what we call widened ligament spaces — that's a sign of stress on the attachment, which is consistent with the bone loss we see. The good news from this particular X-ray is that I don't see any acute abscesses at the root tips, so there's no emergency today.

I want to be honest with you, David — this X-ray tells us that gum disease has been active for a considerable period of time. But I also want to reassure you that this is treatable and manageable. The key is what we do from here."

---

Replacement Options — Honest Sequencing

"Now, I know you came today wanting to talk about replacing those missing teeth — and that's absolutely the right thing to be thinking about. But I need to be upfront with you: we cannot jump straight to replacement right now, because any replacement placed into an unhealthy environment is very likely to fail. The gum disease needs to be addressed first.

Think of it this way — if the foundation of a house is crumbling, you don't build new rooms on top of it. You fix the foundation first.

So let me walk you through the three options for replacing missing teeth, and then explain how bone loss affects each one.

The first option, and generally considered the gold standard, is dental implants. These are titanium posts placed into the jawbone that act like artificial tooth roots, with a crown on top. They look and feel the most like natural teeth, and they're independent — they don't rely on neighbouring teeth. However, implants require adequate healthy bone to anchor into. Given the bone loss we can see on your X-ray, some areas may not have enough bone volume right now without additional bone grafting — where we build up the deficient area before or at the time of implant placement. Beyond that, implants absolutely require the gum disease to be fully controlled first — placing an implant into a mouth with active gum disease dramatically increases the risk of a condition called peri-implantitis, which is essentially gum disease attacking the implant itself, and can cause implant failure. I also need to raise smoking directly — the evidence is very clear that smoking significantly increases implant failure rates. Some studies show up to double the failure rate compared to non-smokers. So if smoking is a factor for you, that's a conversation we really need to have seriously.

The second option is a fixed bridge — where we use the teeth on either side of a gap to support a false tooth in between, all joined together. It's fixed in your mouth — you can't remove it. However, a bridge relies on the neighbouring teeth being structurally sound and periodontally stable. Given the generalised bone loss we see across your X-ray, many of the teeth adjacent to your gaps may not be healthy enough to carry that load. Using a compromised tooth as a bridge support often accelerates its breakdown, so this option has to be assessed very carefully case by case.

The third option is a removable partial denture — a plate that clips in and out. It's the most immediately available option — no surgery required, and it can be made relatively quickly. It's also generally the least expensive. However, most patients find it less comfortable and less stable than the other options, and it requires daily removal and cleaning. It can put some load on remaining teeth, so again the health of those teeth matters.

The sequence for you, David, is clear: first, we treat the active gum disease — through a thorough programme of deep cleaning, scaling and root planing, and improving home care, possibly in conjunction with a specialist periodontist given the extent of what we can see. Then we re-evaluate — typically at around three months — to see how the bone and gums have responded. Once the disease is stable and controlled, we revisit your replacement options with a much clearer picture of what's available to you and what the bone can support."

---

Safety Net and Closing

"I want to check — how are you feeling about everything we've discussed today? I know it's a lot to take in, and it's probably not the quick answer you were hoping for. But I want to be honest with you rather than give you false hope, because the decisions we make now will affect whether any replacement lasts long term.

A couple of things I'd like you to think about before our next visit: your smoking, if that's relevant — I'd strongly encourage you to speak with your GP about smoking cessation support, and I'm happy to give you a referral. There are very effective options available. And if you have any medical conditions or medications you're not sure about, bring a list next time so we can make sure we have the full picture.

My recommendation is that we start with a full periodontal assessment — proper charting of all your pocket depths and gum measurements — and then begin active treatment for the gum disease. I'd also like to refer you to a periodontist for their assessment, given the severity of the bone loss. They specialise in exactly this situation and will be able to give us the most accurate picture of what the remaining teeth can do long-term and what areas might need bone grafting if we do pursue implants later.

Do you have any questions about anything we've covered today? I want to make sure you leave feeling clear on the plan." Pauses and addresses any questions. "Fantastic. Let's get you booked in and start moving in the right direction."

Category:** Periodontics · Time:** 11 minutes · Opens with:** Candidate · Difficulty:** Exam-ready

CASE SUMMARY

45-year-old male with significant generalised bone loss on OPG and multiple missing posterior teeth attends seeking replacement options. He has been with another dentist and is aware of "bone problems." No formal diagnosis required at this visit. Candidate must gather a focused history, explain the OPG findings, discuss how bone loss impacts replacement options, and provide realistic recommendations.

CANDIDATE BRIEF

You are seeing David Kim, 45-year-old male, attending for a second opinion. He has been seeing another dentist for years but that dentist has recently retired. David has been told he has "bone loss around his teeth" and has several missing posterior teeth — he cannot recall which specific teeth were extracted or when. He has brought an OPG taken 8 months ago. The OPG shows: generalised horizontal bone loss averaging 40–50% of root length; multiple missing posterior teeth (at least 3 posterior teeth missing across both arches); remaining teeth show widened PDL spaces; no acute periapical pathology. He wants to know his options for replacing the missing teeth and whether implants are possible. Your task: take a history, explain what the OPG shows, discuss replacement options honestly given the bone loss, and give appropriate recommendations. You have 8 minutes.

EXAMINER CONTEXT

David is pragmatic and direct — he wants facts and numbers, not excessive reassurance. He will ask directly: "Can I get implants or not?" and expects a direct answer. He is worried that bone loss means he has "run out of options" and might end up toothless like his father. He has not been compliant with periodontal maintenance in the past — he'll admit this if asked directly. He smokes 10 cigarettes/day and drinks moderately. Hidden: he stopped flossing about 5 years ago because it made his gums bleed and he assumed that meant he shouldn't do it. He was never told about implant timing or bone grafting. Key examiner note: candidate should explain that implants ARE possible but require: (1) active periodontal disease to be controlled first; (2) bone grafting in areas of significant resorption; (3) smoking cessation strongly advised; (4) strict long-term maintenance.

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

History (2 min) — INFLECTION 1: Risk factor identification

Dental history (when teeth lost, previous perio treatment, compliance), medical history, smoking and alcohol, oral hygiene habits, patient's own goals and concerns.

OPG Explanation (2 min)

"Your X-ray shows bone loss around most of your teeth — the bone that holds teeth in place has reduced by roughly half its normal height in many areas. This is the consequence of longstanding gum disease. It affects what we can and can't do for replacements."

Replacement Options — INFLECTION 2: Honest sequencing

Explain the three options: (1) Dental implants — gold standard, but require treating the gum disease first, possible bone grafting in deficient areas, strong evidence that smoking significantly reduces success rates (up to 2x failure rate); (2) Fixed bridge — requires healthy abutment teeth, not appropriate where adjacent teeth are also periodontally compromised; (3) Removable partial denture — immediately available, no surgical requirements, but least preferred by patients and least stable long-term. Sequence: treat the gum disease → re-evaluate → then plan replacements.

KEY POINTS

  • ✅ Identifies periodontal disease as the active problem that must be addressed before any replacement
  • ✅ Explains OPG findings in plain language — bone loss percentage, missing teeth, overall prognosis
  • ✅ Discusses all three replacement modalities with honest pros/cons
  • ✅ Addresses smoking as a major implant risk factor — smoking cessation discussed
  • ✅ Explains bone grafting as an option where deficiency precludes immediate implant placement
  • ✅ Sets patient expectations: implants possible but not today — treatment sequence explained
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • "Implants are still on the table, but we have to earn them — the gum disease needs to be under control first, or any implant we place will fail for the same reason the teeth around them are struggling."
  • "Smoking doubles the implant failure rate. That's the single most impactful thing you can do to improve your chances — more than any technique or material we choose."
  • "Where the bone level is too low for a standard implant, bone grafting can rebuild what's been lost — but it adds time and cost to the process."
Patient Reframes
  • "You're not out of options — you're at a crossroads. The choices you make in the next 6 months will determine what's possible in the next 20 years."
Curveball Deflectors
  • "Can't we just put implants in now?" → "If we placed implants into bone affected by active gum disease, the bacteria that destroyed your natural tooth bone would do the same to the implant — called peri-implantitis. We'd be setting up a very expensive failure. Treat the disease first."
M10-3
Vague Pain on the Left Side — Interproximal Caries & Open Contact (26/27)
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ▶
STAGE: Opening & History

"Good morning, Maria — I'm Dr. Chen. Welcome, and thank you for coming in today. I understand you're here for a check-up and clean, but I also see in your notes that you've been having some discomfort on your upper left side. I'd really like to hear more about that before we do anything else. Is that okay?"

"Can you tell me in your own words what you've been experiencing?"

Listens attentively. Notes patient describes a vague aching sensation on the upper left side and food catching between her back teeth.

"How long have you been aware of this aching — has it been weeks, months?"

"What tends to bring it on — does cold food or drink trigger it? What about sweet foods, or biting down?"

"And when the ache or sensitivity starts, how long does it last — does it go away quickly once you stop eating, or does it linger for more than a few seconds?"

"Does anything make it better — does it ease off if you take paracetamol or ibuprofen?"

"You mentioned food catching — whereabouts exactly? Between the upper back teeth on the left?"

"I understand you actually mentioned this aching to your previous dentist about eight months ago. Do you recall what was done at that visit — were any X-rays taken at the time?"

"Are you a grinder or a clencher — has anyone ever mentioned that to you, or do you wake up with a sore jaw or headaches? Do you wear a night guard?"

"How would you describe your diet — do you have a lot of sugary or acidic foods or drinks during the day?"

"Any previous treatment on those upper left back teeth — fillings, root canal work, anything like that?"

"Thank you, Maria — that's really helpful. Let me now have a look at the X-ray we've taken today, and then I'll do a couple of simple tests on those teeth, and I'll explain everything I find."

---

Radiograph Interpretation

Systematically examines the bitewing radiograph.

"So I'm looking at your bitewing X-ray — this is a standard X-ray that gives us a very clear view of the back teeth and the bone between them. It's a good-quality image, taken today, and it shows your upper and lower back teeth on the left side."

"Starting with what I can see: both tooth 26 — that's your upper left first molar — and tooth 27 — the second molar behind it — have existing silver amalgam restorations. Now, looking carefully at the contact point between those two teeth — the area where they touch — I can see a darker shadow, a radiolucency, on the distal surface of tooth 26. That shadow extends into the dentine — the deeper layer of the tooth beneath the outer enamel. It's sitting right at the contact between 26 and 27."

"Importantly, I can also see some changes in the bone level right at that contact — the crestal bone between those two teeth shows a slight irregularity, which is consistent with the food trap you've been experiencing."

"The roots of both teeth look structurally sound. The ligament spaces appear within normal limits. There is no obvious periapical pathology — meaning no abscess shadow at the root tips at this stage."

"So in summary: this X-ray shows interproximal decay — decay between the teeth — at the distal surface of tooth 26, which has extended into dentine, combined with an open contact and early marginal bone changes at that site."

---

Clinical Correlation & Diagnosis

"Maria, I want to put all of this together for you — the X-ray findings, the temperature test result, and the symptoms you've described — because they all tell a consistent story."

"The temperature test I did on tooth 26 showed that it responded to the cold stimulus and that the response lasted more than three seconds after I removed the cold. A normal tooth settles very quickly — within a second or two. When the response lingers like that, it tells us the nerve inside the tooth is irritated and inflamed. We call this pulpitis — inflammation of the pulp, which is the nerve-and-blood-vessel tissue in the centre of the tooth."

"Given how long the sensitivity lasted, the clinical picture is consistent with what we call irreversible pulpitis — meaning the pulp is inflamed beyond the point where it's likely to settle on its own, even after we remove the decay. This is important because it guides what treatment we'll need."

"Now, I want to gently address something. You mentioned your previous dentist said everything looked fine eight months ago. I want to be completely clear — I'm not criticising that assessment at all. Interproximal decay — decay between the teeth — is genuinely one of the most difficult things to detect on clinical examination alone. It often can only be seen on a bitewing X-ray, and if a radiograph wasn't taken at that visit, it would have been virtually invisible. This is precisely why bitewing X-rays are such an essential diagnostic tool, and why we take them as part of a thorough new-patient examination. It's very likely this decay was developing at that stage but simply wasn't detectable without the X-ray."

---

Management Plan

"So let me walk you through what I recommend we do, step by step."

"The first priority is to restore tooth 26 — we need to remove the decay between the teeth and place a well-shaped restoration that recreates that contact point between 26 and 27. Restoring a proper contact will eliminate the food trap, which is contributing to the bone changes we can see on the X-ray. I'll use a tooth-coloured composite resin for this, shaped carefully with a matrix band system to rebuild that contact."

"However — and this is the important part — because the temperature test suggests the nerve is irreversibly inflamed, there is a significant likelihood that tooth 26 will need root canal treatment before or instead of a straightforward restoration. Root canal treatment involves removing the inflamed nerve tissue, cleaning and shaping the root canals, and sealing them. The tooth is then restored with a crown to protect it long-term. I want to be honest with you about that so there are no surprises."

"I will also do a full periodontal assessment of the area around teeth 26 and 27 — probing depths, bone levels — to get a clear picture of the health of the supporting structures given those marginal bone changes on the X-ray."

"Regarding your bite and any grinding — if there is evidence of bruxism, I'd recommend a protective night splint once all the treatment is complete, because grinding significantly shortens the lifespan of any restoration."

"I'll also plan a follow-up bitewing X-ray at six months to monitor the adjacent tooth 27 and check healing in that area."

---

Safety Net & Closing

"Maria, I know that's quite a lot of information to take in. Do you have any questions about anything I've explained?"

"To summarise: you have decay between teeth 26 and 27 that has reached the dentine, and the nerve in tooth 26 is inflamed. We need to act on this — the longer we leave it, the higher the risk of the nerve dying completely, which can lead to an abscess, which is much more painful and complex to treat."

"If at any point before your next appointment you develop a spontaneous, throbbing ache that wakes you at night, or a swelling develops, please call us immediately — that would suggest the nerve has moved to an acute state and we'd need to see you urgently."

"I'll book you in for the root canal assessment and restoration of tooth 26 as soon as possible. We'll also schedule your periodontal charting and clean at the same visit. Does that sound okay to you?"

"You've done the right thing coming in today, Maria. We'll get this sorted for you."

Category:** Restorative dentistry · Time:** 11 minutes · Opens with:** Candidate · Difficulty:** Exam-ready

CASE SUMMARY

Female new patient with vague aching pain on the upper left side and food lodgement between 26 and 27. Radiograph shows interproximal caries at the 26/27 contact with marginal bone involvement. Temperature testing shows a prolonged response. Candidate must take a thorough history, interpret the radiograph, formulate a diagnosis, and explain findings and management.

CANDIDATE BRIEF
