You are seeing Maria Stavros, a 45-year-old new patient attending for a check-up and clean. She mentions a vague aching sensation on the upper left side that she mentioned to her previous dentist about 8 months ago but was told "everything looks fine." She also notices food catching between her upper back teeth on the left side. Today's examination: multiple posterior amalgam restorations; tooth 26 and 27 both clinically intact with existing amalgam restorations; food trap noted between 26 and 27 (open contact); temperature test on 26 — prolonged response (35°C, lasts more than 3 seconds after removal of stimulus). Radiograph provided: bitewing showing a radiolucency at the distal surface of 26 involving the interproximal contact with 27, extending into dentine with possible marginal bone involvement at the 26/27 contact point. Your task: take a history, interpret the radiograph, explain your findings, and discuss the diagnosis and management options. You have 8 minutes.

EXAMINER CONTEXT

Maria is frustrated that her previous dentist missed something — she had been mentioning the vague pain for over a year. She is cooperative but wants validation that her concerns were legitimate. She will ask "Why didn't the other dentist find this?" — the candidate should respond diplomatically without criticising the colleague. Key clinical points: the prolonged thermal response suggests the pulp is reversibly or possibly irreversibly inflamed; the marginal bone involvement on the radiograph means this may have a periodontal component as well. Hidden: she grinds her teeth at night (will disclose if asked about sleep or jaw clenching) — relevant to caries risk and restoration longevity.

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

History (1.5 min)

HOPC: duration, character (aching, sharp, spontaneous?), triggers (cold, sweet, biting), duration of response, relieved by anything. Dental history: previous treatment on these teeth, last check-up, any previous symptoms. Social: diet (sugar, acid), grinding, clenching, night guard.

Radiograph Interpretation — INFLECTION 1: Systematic reading

Describe: quality and type of radiograph, patient details, date. Findings: radiolucency at distal 26 / mesial 27 contact, depth (into dentine), involvement of crestal bone at that contact, existing restorations, PDL width, root morphology. Formulate: diagnosis of secondary/interproximal caries distal 26 with open contact and marginal bone involvement. Pulpal status: reversible vs. irreversible pulpitis based on temperature response.

Explain & Manage — INFLECTION 2: Addressing missed diagnosis diplomatically

Explain the findings clearly. Address why it was missed: "Interproximal caries can be very difficult to detect clinically — this is why bitewing radiographs are so important." Avoid direct criticism of the previous dentist. Management: restoration of distal 26 (composite or amalgam), addressing the open contact to eliminate food trap, periodontal assessment of the 26/27 area, pulp vitality monitoring — if irreversible pulpitis, root canal treatment for 26 may be required. Recall X-ray at 6 months.

KEY POINTS

  • ✅ Systematic radiograph interpretation — identifies location, depth, and bone involvement
  • ✅ Correlates radiographic findings with clinical findings (open contact, temperature response)
  • ✅ Distinguishes reversible from irreversible pulpitis based on symptom duration
  • ✅ Addresses the missed diagnosis diplomatically — does not criticise colleague
  • ✅ Proposes complete management: restoration, contact point restoration, perio assessment, RCT if needed
  • ✅ Asks about parafunction (grinding) — relevant to restoration planning and longevity
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • "The X-ray shows decay between these two teeth that's reached well into the dentine — and importantly, it's affecting the bone level at that contact point, which means we need to address both the tooth and the gum around it."
  • "The temperature test is telling me the nerve is irritated — a response that lingers for more than a few seconds after I remove the cold means the pulp is under stress. If we leave this, it could become a root canal situation."
Patient Reframes
  • "Decay between two teeth at their contact point is genuinely difficult to see without an X-ray — it's one of the reasons I take radiographs at every new patient exam. You were right to keep flagging the discomfort."
Curveball Deflectors
  • "Why didn't my old dentist see this?" → "Interproximal decay hides between teeth — it's often invisible to the naked eye until it's quite advanced. Without a recent X-ray at that appointment, it would have been very easy to miss. That's not unusual."
M10-4
MIH vs Amelogenesis Imperfecta — 8-Year-Old, Sensitivity & Appearance
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ▶
STAGE: Opening & Initial History

"Hi Jenny, hi Sophie — lovely to meet you both. I'm Dr [Name]. Sophie, you've been a bit brave coming in today, haven't you? Don't worry, we're just going to have a chat first and then a very gentle look. Jenny, I understand you've got a couple of things you're worried about today — sensitivity in one of the back teeth, and the appearance of the front teeth. Can I ask you some questions first before we have a look?"

"Jenny, I want to make sure I understand both concerns fully, because they may actually be two quite different things. Let me ask about each one separately.

Firstly, the back tooth — how long has Sophie been noticing sensitivity? Is it mainly to cold drinks or food? Does it linger after the cold is gone, or does it settle quickly? Has she had any pain without a trigger — just spontaneous aching?"

"Now, the front teeth — when did you first notice the white chalky patches? Were Sophie's baby teeth affected at all, or did they look normal?"

Pausing to listen. Jenny confirms: sensitivity started about a month ago, cold-triggered, settles within seconds; baby teeth looked completely normal; front teeth have been like this since they came through.

"And Jenny, I want to ask a few background questions that will really help me figure out what's going on. When Sophie was between about six months and three years old — did she have any significant illnesses? Things like ear infections, high fevers, chest infections? Did she take antibiotics during that period?"

"And during your pregnancy with Sophie — did you have any significant illnesses, take any long-term medications, or have any complications?"

"Is there anyone else in the family — yourself, your partner, any siblings — who has teeth that look similar to Sophie's front teeth, with that chalky or different-looking enamel?"

"Finally, what's your water source at home — town tap water or tank water? And are you using fluoride toothpaste?"

Jenny confirms: Sophie had recurrent ear infections and took amoxicillin several times between ages one and two; pregnancy was uncomplicated; Jenny herself has similar-looking front teeth; tap water is used at home.

---

Examination

"Thank you, Jenny — that history is really helpful. Sophie, I'm just going to have a gentle look inside your mouth. I'll use a little mirror and a light — nothing sharp, okay?"

Examines tooth 26: yellowish-brown discolouration on occlusal surface, surface roughness, mild tenderness to percussion, cold test confirms sensitivity with quick resolution. Notes opacity is localised to this single molar.

Examines upper anterior permanent teeth 11, 12, 21, 22: generalised white-creamy opacities affecting the full crown surface bilaterally, rough texture, surface pitting. Notes symmetrical, full-crown involvement across multiple teeth.

Examines primary teeth: clinically normal enamel appearance throughout.

"Thank you, Sophie — you did brilliantly. I'm going to explain everything I found to your mum now."

---

Explaining the Dual Diagnosis

"Jenny, what I've found today is actually two separate conditions affecting different teeth, and I want to explain each one clearly. This is important — these two things are genuinely different problems with different causes, and I want you to understand both."

"The back molar on the upper left — that's called tooth 26 — has a condition called MIH, which stands for Molar-Incisor Hypomineralisation. It's a developmental problem where the enamel on that specific tooth didn't harden properly. The enamel formed, but the minerals didn't deposit into it the way they should have. We know from research that illnesses, high fevers, or antibiotic use — particularly in the first three years of life — can disrupt enamel formation in those specific teeth during that window of development. Sophie's history of ear infections and antibiotic use fits that picture very well. It affects individual teeth in a patchy, localised way — which is exactly what we see with just the one back molar being affected."

"The front teeth are a completely different story. What I see there — the generalised chalky white appearance across the full surface of all four front teeth, with no normal enamel — is consistent with a condition called Amelogenesis Imperfecta. This is a genetic condition where the gene responsible for enamel formation doesn't work properly, so every permanent tooth is affected in a similar way from the very beginning. The fact that your baby teeth looked normal — because primary teeth form earlier — and the fact that you mentioned your own teeth look similar, Jenny, strongly supports this diagnosis. It runs in families."

"I want to be really clear about one thing: neither of these conditions is caused by anything you did wrong. MIH is linked to early childhood illness — Sophie's immune system was working hard fighting infections, and that affected enamel development. Amelogenesis Imperfecta is genetic — Sophie inherited it. You are not to blame for either of these."

---

Management Plan — Tooth 26 (MIH)

"Let me talk about what we do for each condition, because the approaches are quite different.

For the back molar — tooth 26 — our priority is to protect it and manage Sophie's sensitivity. Because Sophie is only eight, this tooth is going to be with her for the rest of her life, so we want to look after it well from the start."

"Today, I'm going to apply a fluoride varnish directly to that tooth. Fluoride varnish is a concentrated fluoride gel that we paint on — it's quick, it doesn't require any needles, and it significantly helps with sensitivity and strengthens the weakened enamel surface. I'd like to do this at every visit."

"Looking at the tooth surface, there is some surface roughness and early breakdown of the enamel. The enamel on MIH-affected teeth is softer than normal and can wear or chip away under biting forces. I'd like to place a protective restoration on that tooth — a filling material called glass ionomer cement, or a composite resin — to seal the surface and prevent further breakdown. This also helps enormously with the sensitivity."

"I'd like to see Sophie every three months for that tooth specifically so we can monitor how it's holding up. If the tooth deteriorates significantly over time, we may eventually discuss a stainless steel crown as a more robust longer-term protection — but let's see how we go with a restoration first."

---

Management Plan — Anterior Teeth (AI) & Safety Net / Closing

"Now, for the front teeth with Amelogenesis Imperfecta — I know the appearance is something you're both concerned about, and I completely understand that. Sophie, when you're a bit older, we will be able to make your front teeth look really beautiful. But right now, at age eight, actually doing cosmetic treatment would cause more harm than good, and I want to explain why."

"Sophie's front teeth are still erupting — they haven't fully come through to their final position yet, and her gums are still settling. If we were to place veneers or crowns on the teeth now, within a year or two those restorations would look wrong because the gum levels will have changed. We'd essentially have to redo them. The right time for definitive cosmetic treatment — composite veneers or, in some cases, porcelain or ceramic crowns — is in the late teenage years, ideally after age seventeen or eighteen when growth is complete and the gum levels are stable."

"What we do right now is protect the teeth so they're in the best possible condition when we do treat them. I'll apply fluoride varnish to the front teeth today as well. I'd ask that Sophie uses a soft toothbrush and a gentle, non-whitening, non-abrasive fluoride toothpaste at home — avoid anything labelled 'whitening' because the abrasives in those can wear the already-fragile enamel surface. Continue brushing twice daily."

"I'd also recommend we take some baseline photographs and X-rays today so we can track how the teeth are developing over time."

"So to summarise our plan: today we apply fluoride varnish to both the back molar and the front teeth; we schedule Sophie's restoration on tooth 26 for as soon as possible; we review Sophie every three months for the molar and every six months overall. Long-term, Sophie's front teeth will have a proper cosmetic treatment plan once she's finished growing — and the results at that stage can be genuinely excellent."

"Do you have any questions, Jenny? Sophie, is there anything you'd like to ask me? You've been absolutely wonderful today."

Category:** Paediatric dentistry · Time:** 11 minutes · Opens with:** Candidate · Difficulty:** Exam-ready

CASE SUMMARY

8-year-old child attends with mother. Two concerns: sensitivity in tooth 26 (first permanent molar) and cosmetic appearance of the front teeth. Clinical images show hypomineralised enamel on tooth 26 (MIH pattern) and generalised white/chalky opacities on the anterior teeth (suggestive of Amelogenesis Imperfecta). Candidate must distinguish between the two conditions, explain to the mother, and formulate management for each.

CANDIDATE BRIEF

You are seeing Sophie Wong, 8-year-old, attending with her mother Jenny. Jenny is concerned about two things: (1) Sophie has been complaining of sensitivity in one of her upper back teeth on the left for the past month, particularly to cold drinks; (2) Jenny has noticed that Sophie's permanent front teeth look different — they have white chalky patches and don't look like normal enamel. The primary teeth appeared normal. Clinical examination today: Tooth 26 — yellowish-brown hypomineralised enamel on the occlusal surface, some surface roughness, TTP mild, cold sensitivity confirmed; Upper anterior permanent teeth (11, 12, 21, 22) — generalised white/creamy opacities affecting the full crown surface, rough texture, some areas of surface pitting; Primary teeth — clinically normal appearance. Your task: explain the findings and diagnosis to Jenny, distinguish between what is affecting the molar vs the front teeth, and outline management for each. You have 8 minutes.

EXAMINER CONTEXT

Jenny is a worried mother — articulate, asks good questions. She wants to understand why this is happening and whether it's her fault (she will ask "Is this because of something I did during pregnancy?"). She also worries about the cosmetic future — "Will her front teeth always look like this?" Sophie is shy but cooperative, will respond if asked directly. Hidden: Jenny took antibiotics during the second trimester of pregnancy (for a urinary tract infection) — she'll mention this if asked about the pregnancy. This is potentially relevant to AI. She also mentions Sophie had numerous ear infections in infancy treated with antibiotics — relevant to the MIH discussion. Key examiner note: the two conditions have different aetiologies, distributions, and management — MIH is localised to first molars and incisors; AI is a generalised genetic condition affecting all enamel.

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

History (2 min) — INFLECTION 1: Separating the two presentations

Ask about: early childhood illness/medications (ear infections, fevers, antibiotics in first 3 years of life — MIH link); pregnancy history (medications, illness — AI link); family history of similar teeth (AI is genetic, may affect siblings or parents); fluoride history (rule out fluorosis); bottle feeding habits (rule out nursing bottle caries pattern).

Explain the Dual Diagnosis — INFLECTION 2: Clarity for the parent

"Sophie appears to have two different enamel conditions. The back molar — tooth 26 — has MIH, which is a developmental issue affecting specific teeth in a specific timeframe during early childhood, often linked to illness or antibiotics in the first 3 years. The front teeth look different — their entire crown surface is affected, which is a different pattern called Amelogenesis Imperfecta, which is a genetic condition where the enamel doesn't form normally across all the permanent teeth." Explain this is NOT the mother's fault, and the two conditions require different approaches.

Management Plan (3 min)

Tooth 26 (MIH): fluoride varnish, GIC or composite restoration if breakdown present, review every 3 months. Front teeth (AI): no urgent treatment at age 8; protect with fluoride varnish; avoid abrasive toothpaste; long-term plan involves composite veneers or crowns after growth is complete (late teens); explain why restoration is deferred — teeth still erupting, gum levels not stable yet.

KEY POINTS

  • ✅ Correctly distinguishes MIH (localised, developmental, acquired) from AI (generalised, genetic)
  • ✅ Takes appropriate history to differentiate — childhood illnesses, family history, pregnancy medications
  • ✅ Explains both conditions in parent-friendly language without blame
  • ✅ Provides separate management plan for each condition
  • ✅ Explains why anterior cosmetic treatment is deferred until growth is complete
  • ✅ Addresses the mother's cosmetic concern with realistic long-term plan
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • "The back tooth and the front teeth are actually two different conditions — same appearance, different cause, different management. I want to explain both separately so you understand what we're dealing with."
  • "Amelogenesis Imperfecta is a genetic condition — it's in Sophie's DNA, not something caused by diet, brushing, or anything during pregnancy. We'll see it in all her permanent teeth."
  • "We don't touch the front teeth cosmetically until she's finished growing — usually 17 or 18. If we do veneers now, the gum line keeps moving and the restoration looks wrong within a year."
Patient Reframes
  • "The sensitivity in the back tooth is the urgent priority — let's fix that first. The front teeth aren't causing pain and there's a clear plan for them when the timing is right."
Curveball Deflectors
  • "Can't you just fix the front teeth now — she's getting bullied at school about them?" → "I completely understand that, and it's heartbreaking. A temporary bonding option to improve appearance is possible as a short-term measure — it won't be perfect but it can make a real difference socially while we wait for the right time for a permanent solution."
M10-5
Geographic Tongue (Benign Migratory Glossitis) — Diagnosis & Reassurance
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ▶
STAGE: Opening & History

"Good morning, Mr Archer, I'm Dr — lovely to meet you. Come on in. So today is a routine check-up, but I understand you've noticed something on your tongue that's been on your mind — is that right? Tell me about it."

Listens as patient describes noticing "strange patches" a few weeks ago.

"Thank you for mentioning that — it's really good that you did. Before I take a look, I'd like to ask you a few questions. How long ago did you first notice these patches — was it a few weeks, or longer? And when you look at them now compared to when you first spotted them, do they seem to be in the same spot, or have they actually moved or changed shape?"

Listens. Patient confirms a few weeks, and the patches do seem to have shifted slightly.

"Right. Are they causing you any discomfort — soreness, burning, or a stinging sensation, particularly with certain foods like spicy dishes, citrus, or anything acidic? What about alcohol?" Listens. "And have you changed your toothpaste recently, or started using any mouthwash?" Listens. "Have you had anything like this on your tongue before, or is this the first time? And does anyone in your family have a skin condition called psoriasis, or has anyone mentioned anything similar on their tongue?" Listens. "And how have things been generally — I understand you've had quite a significant change at work recently?"

Patient confirms the recent promotion, overseas travel, and considerable stress.

"That's really helpful context — I'll explain why in a moment. Any new medications, changes in your diet, or recent illnesses?"

---

Examination

Performs thorough intraoral examination. Inspects the dorsum of the tongue under good light.

Observes: multiple well-defined erythematous areas with a white-yellowish, serpiginous — that is, wavy or map-like — border on the dorsum of the tongue. The borders are slightly raised. No ulceration is present. The pattern is consistent with the patient's description of having shifted position. No other oral mucosal lesions are detected. Palpates the neck — no cervical lymphadenopathy.

"Thank you, Mr Archer. I've had a thorough look and I have a very clear picture of what's going on. I'm going to explain everything to you now."

---

Diagnosis & Reassurance

"So, what you have is a condition called benign migratory glossitis — it also goes by the name geographic tongue, which I think you'll agree is quite a fitting name once I describe it. And the single most important thing I want to tell you right now is this: it is completely benign. It is not cancer, it is not an infection, it is not contagious, and it will cause no long-term harm to your tongue whatsoever. I want you to be completely clear on that before we go further."

Pauses to allow reassurance to land.

"Let me explain what's actually happening. Your tongue's surface is normally covered in tiny projections called filiform papillae — they give it that slightly rough texture. In geographic tongue, small areas of those papillae temporarily disappear, which leaves smooth, red patches. The white or yellowish border you can see is simply the zone where the papillae are in transition — some are shedding, some are regenerating. The whole pattern tends to shift over days to weeks — that's the 'migratory' part — and that's exactly what you've been noticing."

"Now, what causes it? We don't always know the precise trigger in every person, but we do know that stress is one of the most consistently reported factors — and given what you've described with your work situation, that's very likely playing a role for you. Other common triggers include spicy or acidic foods, alcohol, and sodium lauryl sulphate, which is a foaming agent found in most standard toothpastes. There is also an interesting association with a skin condition called psoriasis — even in people who've never had skin symptoms, geographic tongue can be an oral manifestation of the same immune process. It's worth being aware of, particularly given that family history you mentioned."

---

Differential Diagnosis

"I want to be thorough and transparent with you about the other conditions I've considered and why I'm confident this isn't any of them. Oral candidiasis — a fungal infection — can produce white patches, but those can be wiped off easily and the appearance is quite different from what you have. Oral lichen planus produces a lacy, symmetrical pattern on the cheeks and gums rather than this map-like picture on the tongue. I also want to be direct: this does not have any features of concern for oral cancer — there is no induration, no ulceration, no firm base, no lymph node involvement, and the pattern is entirely consistent with geographic tongue. You have none of the red-flag features I would be worried about."

---

Management Plan

"Because this condition is benign and self-limiting, there is no specific treatment required or recommended. What we focus on is managing your comfort and reducing the frequency and severity of flares. Here's my practical advice."

"First, during any flare — or even as a general habit — I'd encourage you to reduce spicy foods, acidic foods such as tomatoes and citrus, and alcohol, as these are the most common dietary aggravators. Second, I'd like you to switch to a sodium lauryl sulphate-free toothpaste — they're widely available at pharmacies and supermarkets. Many patients notice a significant improvement in tongue soreness simply by making that change. Third, and perhaps most importantly for you right now: managing your stress levels will make a real difference. I understand that's easier said than done with a major promotion, but even small strategies — whether that's regular exercise, mindfulness, or speaking with your GP if stress is becoming unmanageable — can reduce flare frequency considerably."

"The condition may come and go throughout your life, and that's completely normal. Many people find it settles during less stressful periods."

---

Safety Net & Closing

"I'd like to review you in six to twelve months at your next routine appointment and take note of how the tongue looks then for comparison. However, I want you to come back sooner — and I mean promptly — if you notice any of the following: any area that becomes persistently painful, any spot that develops a firm or hardened feeling underneath, any bleeding that isn't related to a clear cause, or any patch that simply isn't behaving like the rest and isn't shifting or changing. In that scenario, we would reassess and potentially arrange a biopsy to be absolutely certain. But I want to reiterate — nothing I see today gives me any cause for concern in that regard."

"Do you have any questions about what I've explained? I know it's a lot to take in, but the headline is: this is a harmless, recognised condition, and now that we know what it is, we can keep an eye on it comfortably. You did exactly the right thing by raising it today."

Category:** Oral medicine · Time:** 11 minutes · Opens with:** Candidate · Difficulty:** Exam-ready

CASE SUMMARY

Male patient notices unusual map-like patches on his tongue during a routine check-up. He associates it with recent work stress (promotion involving overseas travel). The clinical appearance is classic benign migratory glossitis. Candidate must explain the diagnosis, reassure appropriately, provide management advice, and cover differential diagnosis.

CANDIDATE BRIEF

You are seeing Mr David Archer, 38-year-old, attending for a routine dental check-up. He mentions he noticed "strange patches" on his tongue a few weeks ago and wants to know what they are. He recently received a significant promotion at work involving extensive overseas travel and has been under considerable stress. On examination: dorsum of tongue shows classic geographic tongue — irregular, well-defined erythematous areas with a white/yellowish serpiginous border; lesions appear to have changed position slightly since he first noticed them; no ulceration; no cervical lymphadenopathy; no other oral lesions. Your task: explain the diagnosis and management, address his concerns, and provide differential diagnosis where appropriate. You have 8 minutes.

EXAMINER CONTEXT

David is a busy professional — he wants a clear, concise answer, not medical waffle. He will ask "Is it cancer?" directly, early in the consultation. He expects an honest, immediate answer. Once reassured it is benign, he will relax and engage well. He is curious about the mechanism and will appreciate a brief explanation. He mentions his wife noticed it and is more worried than he is — he may ask "What should I tell her?" Hidden: he drinks alcohol socially — 3–4 standard drinks several times per week. Alcohol can be a trigger for geographic tongue flare-ups. He does not eat a lot of spicy food but has been eating differently while travelling (richer foods, more spice, different cuisines). Triggers should be identified and discussed.

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

History (1.5 min)

Duration, progression, symptoms (soreness — especially with certain foods), associated factors (stress, diet changes, alcohol, spicy food, certain toothpastes), previous episodes, family history of psoriasis (geographic tongue has an association), medications.

Explain Diagnosis — INFLECTION 1: Immediate reassurance

Name it clearly and reassure immediately: "This is called benign migratory glossitis, also known as geographic tongue. It's completely benign — it is not cancer, it is not contagious, and it won't cause any long-term harm to your tongue." Then explain: the white border represents areas where the tongue's surface cells (filiform papillae) are temporarily absent; the pattern moves ("migrates") over time; triggers include stress, certain foods (spicy, acidic, alcohol), and systemic factors.

Differential Diagnosis (brief)

Mention: psoriasis (strong association — tongue involvement can precede skin involvement); oral lichen planus (lichenoid pattern — different morphology); candidiasis (removable white patches — rule out); in immunocompromised patients, ANUG should be considered but does not fit here.

Management (1.5 min) — INFLECTION 2: Practical advice

No specific treatment required — the condition is self-limiting. Avoid known triggers: reduce spicy/acidic foods and alcohol during flare-ups; manage stress (the most impactful trigger for most patients); use sodium lauryl sulfate-free toothpaste if the tongue is sore. Review in 6–12 months or earlier if worsens or new symptoms develop (pain, bleeding, hardness — would prompt reassessment and biopsy to exclude other pathology).

KEY POINTS

  • ✅ Diagnoses benign migratory glossitis confidently with correct alternative name
  • ✅ Reassures immediately — addresses cancer fear directly
  • ✅ Explains the migratory nature, trigger factors, and benign course
  • ✅ Provides practical avoidance advice: spicy food, acidic food, alcohol, SLS-free toothpaste
  • ✅ Mentions psoriasis association — most candidates miss this
  • ✅ Sets appropriate review (6–12 months) and safety-net criteria for reassessment
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • "This is benign migratory glossitis — it is not cancer, it's not infectious, and it won't harm your tongue. You can tell your wife that with certainty."
  • "There's a well-known association with psoriasis — do you or any family members have psoriasis? It's not a concern, just something I'd note in your file."
  • "SLS — sodium lauryl sulfate — is the foaming agent in most toothpastes. In some people it irritates the tongue surface during a flare. Switching to a SLS-free toothpaste during a bad episode often helps."
Patient Reframes
  • "The stress connection is real — this condition is notorious for flaring up when people are under pressure. Getting the promotion seems to have been the trigger."
Curveball Deflectors
  • "Is it cancer?" → "No. I want to be completely clear about that. Geographic tongue is a benign inflammatory condition — it has a characteristic appearance that I recognise and I have no reason to be concerned about anything more serious today."
  • "Will it go away?" → "For most people it comes and goes throughout their life — it flares with stress or dietary triggers and settles when those factors resolve. It's more about managing triggers than curing it."
M10-6
Oroantral Communication — Disclosure After Upper Molar Extraction
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ▶
STAGE: Opening — Duty of Candour

Checks Mrs Jones is comfortable in the chair, offers a glass of water, and sits at eye level before speaking.

"Mrs Jones, thank you for your patience. The area is still numb so you shouldn't be in any pain right now, and I want to use this time to be completely honest with you about what happened during your extraction today. I need to tell you about two things that occurred during the procedure — neither of them is an emergency, but both are important, and I want to explain everything clearly so you understand exactly where we are and what happens next. Please stop me at any time if you have questions."

Pauses, makes eye contact, and maintains a calm, unhurried tone.

---

Disclosure of Retained Root Fragment

"The first thing I want to explain is that during the extraction, the tooth fractured as I was removing it. This does happen occasionally with upper back teeth, particularly when the roots are long or curved, or the tooth has been heavily restored. I was able to remove the majority of the tooth — approximately two thirds of it — but a very small piece of root, roughly one to two millimetres in size, remains deep in the socket near the floor of your sinus."

Pauses to allow this to register.

"Now, I know that sounds concerning, but I want to reassure you that in this particular situation, leaving that small fragment in place is actually the safer option. The fragment is tiny, there is no sign of infection, and attempting to surgically retrieve it would require opening into the sinus area, which carries a greater risk of harm than the fragment itself. Small root tips in this position are often resorbed naturally by the body, or they simply remain without causing any trouble at all. That said, this decision needs to be made by a specialist, and I am going to refer you to an oral and maxillofacial surgeon for review within the next twenty-four to forty-eight hours so they can assess the fragment with appropriate imaging and advise you on the best course of action."

---

Disclosure of Oroantral Communication

"The second thing I need to tell you about is related to that same area. After I completed the extraction, I performed a routine test to check whether the socket had communicated with your sinus — the air-filled cavity that sits just above that tooth. I asked you to gently hold your nose and breathe out, and what I found was that air bubbled up through the socket. This confirms there is a small opening between the tooth socket and your sinus. We call this an oroantral communication."

Pauses again, speaking slowly and clearly.

"I want to be straightforward with you — this is a recognised complication of extracting upper back teeth, particularly when the roots sit very close to the sinus floor, as yours did. It is not something that resulted from carelessness; it is an anatomical reality we sometimes encounter. The good news is that the majority of these openings close on their own within two to four weeks, provided we take the right steps to protect them while they heal. What I am going to do today is place a small protective plug — called a haemostatic dressing — into the socket to support clot formation and help close that communication. I will also prescribe you an antibiotic and a nasal decongestant to keep the sinus healthy while it heals."

"For antibiotics, I will prescribe amoxicillin five hundred milligrams three times a day for five days. Are you allergic to penicillin at all?"

Waits for response. If no allergy confirmed: "Good. If you were allergic I would prescribe erythromycin instead. I will also give you a saline nasal spray to use twice daily to keep the sinus clear."

---

Post-Operative Instructions and Safety Net

"Now, there are some very important instructions I need you to follow closely, because how you manage the next two weeks will make a significant difference to whether this heals without any further intervention."

"Please do not blow your nose for at least two weeks — this is the most important instruction. Blowing your nose creates pressure that pushes air directly into that socket and can prevent it from closing. If you need to sneeze, please sneeze with your mouth open so the pressure escapes that way instead. Avoid straws, smoking, and anything that creates suction or pressure in the mouth or nose. Eat soft foods on the other side, and avoid very hot food and drinks. Take the antibiotic as prescribed and complete the full course."

Hands written instructions to the patient.

"I also want you to know when to call us immediately — if you notice food or liquid coming out of your nose when you eat or drink, if you develop a fever, increasing facial pain or swelling, or if bleeding from the socket doesn't settle within the next hour or two, please contact us straight away or go to your nearest hospital emergency department."

---

Addressing Concerns and Closing

"Mrs Jones, I can imagine this is a lot to take in. Do you have any questions about anything I've said?"

Pauses and listens actively.

If she asks, "Did you do something wrong?" — responds: "I understand why you are asking that, and it is a fair question. The fracture of the tooth and the communication with the sinus are recognised complications of this type of extraction. Your tooth roots were anatomically close to the sinus floor — that is not something that could have been fully anticipated. I followed safe, careful technique throughout. What is important now is that you have been informed fully and honestly, and that we manage this properly going forward."

"I am going to book your oral surgery referral today — my receptionist will call the oral and maxillofacial surgery clinic as soon as we are finished here to arrange an appointment for tomorrow if at all possible. You will leave today with your written instructions, your prescription, and a follow-up appointment. I will also ensure the specialist receives a full written referral with today's notes and any relevant radiographs."

"Thank you for trusting me with your care, Mrs Jones. Please do not hesitate to call us at any time if you are worried."

Category:** Surgery · Time:** 11 minutes · Opens with:** Candidate · Difficulty:** Exam-ready

CASE SUMMARY

Mrs Elida Jones, a regular patient, has just had an upper left first molar (26) extracted. During the procedure the tooth fractured — 2/3 was removed but approximately 1–2 mm of root tip remains in the socket. Patency testing (Valsalva) confirms an oroantral communication. Candidate must disclose both complications (retained fragment + OAC), explain management, and handle the patient's response.

CANDIDATE BRIEF

Mrs Elida Jones, 52-year-old regular patient. You performed an extraction of tooth 26 today under local anaesthesia. The procedure was more difficult than expected — the tooth fractured during delivery. You were able to remove approximately 2/3 of the tooth but a root fragment of approximately 1–2 mm in length remains in the apical socket, approximately 1–2 mm from the estimated floor of the maxillary sinus. When you tested sinus patency using a Valsalva manoeuvre, air was confirmed bubbling up through the socket — confirming an oroantral communication. The patient is now sitting up, the area is still anaesthetised. You need to: (1) inform Mrs Jones about what has occurred during the extraction; (2) explain the retained fragment and oroantral communication; (3) outline the immediate management; (4) address her concerns. You have 8 minutes.

EXAMINER CONTEXT

Mrs Jones is a regular, trusting patient. Her initial reaction will be confusion ("I thought the tooth was out — what happened?") followed by concern ("Is that serious? What does that mean for me?"). She will not be immediately angry but may become more distressed as she understands the implications. She will ask: "Did you do something wrong?" — the candidate must respond honestly without self-flagellating or being defensive. The duty of candour requires honest, factual disclosure. Hidden: Mrs Jones had sinus problems in the past (chronic sinusitis treated by her GP, resolved) — she should be told this makes her more cautious about sinus involvement; she should be asked about current nasal symptoms. She lives alone and will ask about who she can call if she has problems overnight. This is an opportunity for the candidate to provide a clear safety net.

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

Open with Duty of Candour (1 min) — INFLECTION 1: Honest disclosure

"Mrs Jones, I need to explain what happened during your extraction today, and I want to be completely transparent with you. The procedure was more difficult than expected and two things happened that I need to discuss with you."

Explain the Retained Fragment (2 min)

"When the tooth came out, a very small piece of root — about 1–2 mm — fractured off and remains near the sinus floor. In most cases, a small root fragment in this position can be left in place if it is not infected and not causing symptoms — removing it carries more risk than leaving it, as it would require opening into the sinus area. I will refer you to an oral surgeon for a specialist review within the next 1–2 days."

Explain the Oroantral Communication — INFLECTION 2: Clear, calm explanation

"I also found a small opening between the tooth socket and your sinus — we call this an oroantral communication. It's a recognised complication with upper back teeth, particularly when roots are close to the sinus. Most of these close on their own within a few weeks with the right precautions. I will place a protective plug in the socket today and prescribe antibiotics and a decongestant nasal spray to keep the sinus clear while it heals."

Instructions + Safety Net (2 min)

No nose blowing for at least 2 weeks. No sucking through straws. Sneeze with mouth open. Avoid anything that creates sinus pressure. Take antibiotics (amoxicillin 500 mg TDS 5 days or erythromycin if penicillin allergy) and decongestant. Soft food, no smoking. Return immediately if: bleeding won't stop, pain increases significantly, swelling of face, fever, or fluid/food coming through nose. Provide written instructions. Book oral surgery review for next day.

KEY POINTS

  • ✅ Discloses both complications immediately and honestly — duty of candour
  • ✅ Explains retained fragment rationale for conservative management vs surgical removal
  • ✅ Explains OAC in plain language — what it is, why it happened, prognosis
  • ✅ Prescribes appropriate medications: antibiotic + nasal decongestant
  • ✅ Gives specific post-op instructions for OAC (no nose blowing, sneeze open-mouthed)
  • ✅ Provides urgent oral surgery referral within 24–48 hours
  • ✅ Handles "did you do something wrong?" with honesty, not defensiveness
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • "An oroantral communication is a recognised complication with upper molar extractions — the roots can be very close to or even inside the sinus cavity. It's not due to any error in technique; it's an anatomical risk that I discussed in the consent process."
  • "The most important thing for the next two weeks: do not blow your nose. If you need to sneeze, sneeze with your mouth open. Anything that creates pressure in your sinus could prevent the socket from healing."
  • "A 1–2 mm root fragment in this location, if not infected, is often safer to leave than to remove — disturbing the sinus floor to retrieve it carries a higher risk than monitoring it. The oral surgeon will confirm this at tomorrow's review."
Patient Reframes
  • "I want to be honest with you because you deserve a full explanation and because your healing depends on following the right instructions. The good news is — we've caught both of these today and we have a clear plan."
Curveball Deflectors
  • "Did you do something wrong?" → "This complication occurred during a procedure that was more technically difficult than anticipated. It is a known risk of upper molar extractions when roots are close to the sinus — which I've now confirmed is the case for you. I've managed it appropriately and I'm referring you to a specialist today."
  • "Is there still a hole in my mouth going to my nose?" → "There is a small communication right now, yes. With the protective measures I'm putting in place today and the specialist review tomorrow, the vast majority of these heal completely within 2–4 weeks."
M10-7
Drug-Induced Gingival Enlargement — Cyclosporine + Nifedipine
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ▶
STAGE: Opening & History

"Good morning, Richard — great to see you, though I'm sorry to hear your gums have been giving you trouble. I understand you've got a family wedding coming up next week, so let's work out what's going on and what we can do. I just need to ask you a few questions before we look at the examination findings together. Is that alright?"

"When did you first notice the swelling getting worse? Has it been gradual or fairly sudden?" Listens as patient describes worsening over roughly the past six to eight months. "And have you noticed any bleeding — when you brush, or spontaneously?" Notes generalised bleeding on probing confirmed on examination.

"Can I just check in on your medications — I have cyclosporine and atorvastatin on your file from previous visits. Has anything changed recently?" Waits for patient to confirm that nifedipine was added approximately eight months ago for blood pressure. "And your cyclosporine dose — has that changed at all, or has your transplant team made any adjustments lately?"

"How have you been going with your home care — brushing, flossing? I know last time we spoke things were well under control." Notes patient reports brushing twice daily but flossing has lapsed. "Any other new medications, vitamins, or supplements I should know about?"

---

Examination Summary & Diagnosis

Reviews chart findings with patient. Notes generalised fibrotic gingival overgrowth, more pronounced anteriorly and at interdental papillae, generalised bleeding on probing, probing depths four to five millimetres throughout, and heavy supra- and subgingival calculus. Compares to chart from six months prior showing depths of three to four millimetres and a well-maintained periodontium.

"Richard, thank you for bearing with me. I want to explain exactly what I'm seeing, because this is important and it directly relates to your medications — so I want you to understand the connection."

"What you have is a condition called drug-induced gingival overgrowth. It means that certain medications can cause the gum tissue itself to grow and thicken — it's not an infection you've caught, and it's not a sign that you've been doing the wrong thing. It's a known side effect of specific drugs."

"Now, two of your medications are both individually known to cause this: cyclosporine, which you've been on for fifteen years to protect your transplanted kidney, and nifedipine, the blood pressure tablet that was started eight months ago. Here's what's significant — for fifteen years, your gums were well managed. But over the last eight months, since the nifedipine was added, things have clearly deteriorated. The timing fits exactly. What we think has happened is that nifedipine has tipped the balance. When both medications are present together, the effect on gum tissue is additive — it's greater than either drug alone. The inflammation from plaque accumulation then makes the overgrowth even more pronounced."

---

Management — Dental Treatment

"So, the good news is that this condition is manageable. Let me walk you through the plan, starting with what we do here in the chair."

"First and most importantly, we need to get your oral hygiene back on track — I'd like to go through brushing and interdental cleaning with you today in detail, because we know that excellent plaque control significantly reduces the severity of this overgrowth. That starts today."

"Second, I want to arrange a full course of scaling and root planing — a thorough deep clean of all four quadrants to remove the calculus build-up above and below the gum line. We'll do that over the next few visits."

"We'll then review you at six to eight weeks. In many cases, once we've removed the local irritants and improved your home care, the gum tissue reduces quite substantially on its own — particularly if we're also able to address the medication side, which I'll come to in a moment."

"If after three months of optimal plaque control, combined with any medication changes your doctors make, the overgrowth hasn't resolved, then we'd look at a surgical option — a gingivectomy or a periodontal flap procedure — to remove the excess tissue. That's a straightforward procedure, but we want to exhaust the conservative pathway first."

---

Medical Liaison & Medication Discussion

"Now, here is the part I want to be very clear about, Richard — please do not stop or change either of your medications on your own. Your kidney health depends on cyclosporine, and your blood pressure needs to be managed. What I will do is write a letter to your GP explaining the drug-induced nature of this gum condition and formally requesting that they consider whether nifedipine could be substituted with an alternative antihypertensive. There are other calcium channel blockers and other classes of blood pressure medication that have a much lower association with gum overgrowth — for example, ACE inhibitors have very little association with this condition at all."

"I will also recommend that your GP or cardiologist consider these alternatives in consultation with your transplant physician, because any medication changes need to be coordinated carefully given your immunosuppression."

"Regarding the cyclosporine — I will write to your transplant specialist separately to make them aware of this complication and to ask whether any review of your cyclosporine regimen is appropriate from their end. That decision rests entirely with them — they know your transplant history best — but they should be part of this conversation."

---

Wedding Expectations & Safety Net / Closing

"Now, Richard — the wedding next week. I want to be honest with you, because I know this matters to you. Significant reduction in the swelling in one week is not realistic — the overgrowth we're seeing involves actual tissue change, and that won't reverse in seven days. However, what we can achieve quite quickly is reducing the redness, the puffiness from inflammation, and the bleeding. If we do a professional clean today and you commit to excellent home care every day this week, your gums will look noticeably less inflamed and they won't bleed when you smile or eat. That is achievable, and it will make a real difference to how you present at the wedding."

"Longer term, once we have the medication review underway and your plaque control optimised, I'm genuinely optimistic we can get your gums back to where they were. We've managed your periodontal health well together for twelve years — this is a setback with a clear cause, and now that we know the cause, we can address it properly."

"Do you have any questions about anything I've explained? I want to make sure the medication link makes sense to you, and that you're comfortable with me writing to your doctors." Answers any questions. Books next appointment for scaling within the week. Provides written oral hygiene instructions.

"Take care of yourself, Richard — and enjoy the wedding."

Category:** Periodontics · Time:** 11 minutes · Opens with:** Candidate · Difficulty:** Exam-ready

CASE SUMMARY

Mr Richard Jones, regular patient, presents with swollen bleeding gums before an upcoming wedding. Examination reveals drug-induced gingival overgrowth (DIGO). He is on cyclosporine (kidney transplant, 15 years) and nifedipine (hypertension, 8 months). The recent addition of nifedipine likely explains the worsening. Candidate must diagnose, explain the drug-gingival link, discuss management, and liaise with medical team.

CANDIDATE BRIEF

Richard Jones, 58-year-old, regular patient. He presents today complaining of swollen, bleeding gums. He mentions he has a family wedding to attend in one week and is embarrassed about how his gums look. He has been your patient for 12 years and you have managed his periodontal disease successfully. Recent medical history: kidney transplant 15 years ago, on cyclosporine immunosuppression; hypertension — nifedipine (calcium channel blocker) added 8 months ago; atorvastatin for hyperlipidaemia. Examination: generalised fibrotic gingival overgrowth, more pronounced anteriorly and in interdental areas; BOP++ generalised; probing depths 4–5 mm throughout; heavy supra- and subgingival calculus deposits; plaque accumulation generalised. Previous perio charting (6 months ago): probing depths 3–4 mm, well-maintained. Clearly worse since last visit. Your task: diagnose, explain findings to Mr Jones, address the medication link, discuss management, and outline liaison with his medical team. You have 8 minutes.

EXAMINER CONTEXT

Richard is a pragmatic man who manages his kidney transplant carefully and attends regularly. He will be shocked to learn his blood pressure medication is causing the problem — he started nifedipine 8 months ago and things have clearly deteriorated since. He will ask "Can I stop the nifedipine?" — the candidate should explain that stopping immunosuppressants or antihypertensives without medical supervision could be life-threatening and that this requires a GP/specialist conversation, not a unilateral decision. He will also ask "Will it go back to normal?" — the answer depends on medication change and oral hygiene but generally DIGO improves significantly with scaling + medication substitution. Hidden: his GP prescribed nifedipine without knowing he was on cyclosporine — there is a known pharmacokinetic interaction (cyclosporine increases nifedipine levels). This is not immediately life-threatening but is worth noting in the medical liaison letter.

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

History (1.5 min)

Onset and progression (when did swelling worsen?), oral hygiene habits, medical update (specifically: when was nifedipine started?), any change in cyclosporine dose, other new medications, previous perio treatment response.

Explain Diagnosis — INFLECTION 1: Naming the drug connection

"Mr Jones, this is a condition called drug-induced gingival overgrowth. Two of your medications — cyclosporine and nifedipine — are both individually known to cause gum tissue to enlarge. You've been on cyclosporine for 15 years with relatively stable gums — but nifedipine, which was started 8 months ago, has likely tipped the balance. The timing fits exactly with when your gums worsened."

Management Plan (3 min) — INFLECTION 2: Medical liaison

(1) Dental: intensive OHI, full-mouth scaling and root planing, review at 6–8 weeks — many cases significantly improve with plaque control alone. (2) Medical liaison: write to his GP explaining the drug-induced nature and requesting consideration of substituting nifedipine with an alternative antihypertensive (e.g., amlodipine has a lower incidence of DIGO; ACE inhibitors have even less association). Do NOT tell patient to stop the medication. Transplant physician should also be consulted regarding any potential cyclosporine dose adjustment — do not suggest reducing it without specialist input. (3) If gingival overgrowth persists after 3 months of optimal plaque control + medication change: gingivectomy / periodontal flap surgery to remove excess tissue. (4) Regarding the wedding next week: set realistic expectations — significant improvement in 1 week is unlikely; however, intensive professional cleaning + improved home care will reduce bleeding and inflammation visibly.

KEY POINTS

  • ✅ Correctly diagnoses DIGO — names both cyclosporine and nifedipine as causative agents
  • ✅ Identifies the timing correlation — nifedipine added 8 months ago, worsening since
  • ✅ Does NOT advise patient to stop medications independently
  • ✅ Proposes GP liaison letter requesting nifedipine substitution
  • ✅ Mentions transplant physician involvement for cyclosporine review
  • ✅ Explains the dental treatment ladder: OHI → scaling → review → surgery if needed
  • ✅ Manages the wedding expectation honestly — realistic timeframe for improvement
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • "Cyclosporine and nifedipine are both in the top three medications known to cause gum overgrowth — you're on both. The nifedipine was added 8 months ago, which is exactly when things changed. That's not a coincidence."
  • "I'll write to your GP today explaining the situation and asking them to consider switching the nifedipine — amlodipine is an alternative with a much lower rate of gum overgrowth. But that's a medical decision, not a dental one."
  • "Plaque makes DIGO dramatically worse — the drug creates the tendency, but bacteria drive the severity. Excellent oral hygiene alone often produces a remarkable improvement, even before any medication change."
Patient Reframes
  • "For the wedding — I want to be honest with you. One week isn't enough time to reverse the overgrowth, but a thorough professional clean right now will reduce the bleeding and inflammation significantly. Your gums will look better, even if not perfect."
Curveball Deflectors
  • "Can I just stop taking the nifedipine?" → "Absolutely not without speaking to your GP first. Stopping blood pressure medication suddenly can cause a dangerous rebound in blood pressure. The right path is a managed switch — your GP substitutes one drug for another. I'll support that conversation with a letter today."
  • "Will my gums go back to normal?" → "With a medication change and good plaque control, the majority of patients see substantial improvement — often back to normal. If there's persistent excess tissue after 3 months of treatment, a minor surgical procedure can remove it. The prognosis is good."
M10-8
16-Year-Old with Rampant Caries & Erosion — Dietary + Lifestyle Causes
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ▶
STAGE: Opening and Introduction

Greets both Sam and his father warmly, makes direct eye contact with Sam first, then acknowledges his father.

"Hi Sam, hi Mr Tran, great to see you both today. Sam, I understand you've been getting some sensitivity to cold on a few of your teeth — that's what we're going to focus on today. I want to make sure I understand exactly what's been happening before we talk about what I found on examination. Is that okay?"

Addresses Sam directly throughout. "Sam, I'll be talking mainly to you today because you're my patient — but it's great that your dad is here too. Anything we discuss, we can share with him together."

"So first, how long have you been noticing the cold sensitivity? And is it a sharp, quick sensation that goes away, or does it linger for a while after the cold is gone?"

Listens to Sam's response. Notes that the sensitivity is sharp and short-lived — consistent with dentinal hypersensitivity rather than pulpitis.

---

Dietary and Lifestyle History

"Sam, I want to ask you some specific questions about what you eat and drink, because I think that's going to be really important in understanding what's happening with your teeth. There are no wrong answers here — I just need the full picture."

"I know you started a traineeship about a year ago — congratulations on that, by the way. What's a typical day look like in terms of what you're drinking at the worksite? How many cans of energy drinks or soft drinks would you get through on a workday?"

Listens. Notes two to four cans per day.

"And what about sports drinks — do you have those after training or exercise? How often?"

"What about water — is tap water available at the site, or do you mainly grab cans from a vending machine or servo?"

"Okay. Now, thinking about those drinks — are they usually spread across the day, like sipping one slowly over a few hours, or do you tend to drink them fairly quickly?"

Pauses and notes the answer — frequency and prolonged sipping are the key variables.

"I also want to ask about brushing. I know you mentioned you brush twice a day — that's excellent. Can you tell me when exactly you brush? Like, first thing in the morning, or after breakfast? And do you sometimes brush after having a drink at work?"

This is the critical inflection point. If Sam confirms he brushes shortly after drinking, the candidate responds:

"Right — so that's actually something really important we need to talk about, and it's completely understandable that you'd do that. We tend to think brushing after eating or drinking is always good, but when you've just had something acidic like an energy drink, the acid temporarily softens the enamel surface. If you brush within about thirty to sixty minutes of that, you're actually scrubbing away softened enamel. It's one of those things that seems like good habits but, in this situation, it can make things worse."

"Do you have any issues with reflux or heartburn — like acid coming back up into your throat, especially at night?"

"Any medications at the moment — even vitamins or supplements?"

"And how would you describe your diet otherwise — lots of fruit, flavoured yoghurts, vinegar-based things like pickles or salad dressings?"

---

Explaining the Findings

Turns to face both Sam and his father. Uses the clinical notes and gestures to explain findings clearly. If a mirror is available, shows Sam the white spot lesions directly.

"Sam, I want to explain what I found today, and I want to be really straightforward with you because I think you're old enough to hear this clearly — and it's actually important that you do."

"What I'm seeing is two separate but related problems happening at the same time. The first is called dental erosion. This isn't the same as a normal cavity — it's not caused by bacteria in the same way. It's caused by acid from your drinks dissolving the outer layer of your teeth, the enamel. Energy drinks, soft drinks, sports drinks — they're highly acidic, and every time you have one, there's an acid attack on your enamel that lasts for about twenty to thirty minutes before your saliva can neutralise it. If you're having two to four cans a day, that's potentially two to four hours of acid exposure every day."

"The second problem is rampant cervical caries — which means decay forming at the gum line across multiple teeth simultaneously. This is caused by the sugar in those same drinks feeding the bacteria in your mouth. So unfortunately the drinks are causing both problems at once."

"Here's what concerns me most, Sam. When I saw you twelve months ago, you had no cervical lesions at all. Today I'm seeing white spot lesions — which are the earliest sign of decay — on almost every front tooth, a frank cavity on this tooth here — your upper right lateral incisor — and a cavity on this upper left molar that's reached the dentine. That's a significant amount of change in twelve months."

Turns briefly to Mr Tran. "Mr Tran, I know that's confronting to hear. The good news is that we've caught this at a point where we can stop the progression and reverse some of it. But I do want both of you to understand what's driving it."

Returns focus to Sam. "Sam, if things continue the way they have been for another twelve months, we'd be looking at restorations — fillings — on ten or more teeth. Some of those might need to involve the nerve. So this is genuinely the moment where we can change the trajectory."

---

Management Plan

"So here's what I'd like to do, in two parts — what we do today, and what changes at home."

"Today, I'm going to apply a fluoride varnish to all your teeth. It's a sticky, concentrated fluoride coating that bonds to the enamel surface and helps remineralise those early white spot lesions. It takes about a minute to apply and it's completely painless."

"I'm also going to prescribe you a high-fluoride toothpaste — it's called Duraphat, and it contains five thousand parts per million of fluoride, which is about four times stronger than regular toothpaste. You'd use it exactly like normal toothpaste — a small amount, brush for two minutes, spit but don't rinse. The key is don't rinse after brushing, because you want that fluoride to stay on the teeth."

"I also want to restore those two cavitated lesions — the ones at the gum line on tooth twelve and tooth twenty-six — before the next appointment. They've progressed into dentine, so they need fillings. The white spot lesions on the other teeth we're going to monitor — with the fluoride treatment, many of those can actually reverse without needing fillings."

"Now, the big one — the drinks. I'm not going to tell you to never have a soft drink again, because that's not realistic. But here's what makes the biggest difference: it's not the amount, it's the frequency. Having one can with a meal is far less damaging than sipping on one slowly over two hours at the worksite. The goal is to reduce the number of separate acid attacks per day."

"What I'd suggest: try to swap the between-meal drinks to fluoridated tap water. If you do have an energy drink, have it with a meal, drink it reasonably quickly rather than sipping, and then rinse your mouth with water afterwards. And then wait at least thirty minutes before brushing."

"A fluoride mouthwash is also a great addition — use it at a different time to when you brush. Before bed works well. Swish for thirty seconds, spit, don't eat or drink for thirty minutes after."

"Mr Tran, the most helpful thing you can do is make sure there's tap water and fluoride mouthwash available at home. But ultimately these are Sam's teeth and Sam's choices — and Sam, I think you genuinely get why this matters."

---

Safety Netting and Closing

"Sam, I want to book you back in three months rather than six. Given how quickly things have changed in the last year, I want to be able to see whether the fluoride treatment is working and whether the white spots are stabilising or reversing. Three months is enough time to see a real difference if the habits change."

"In the meantime, if you notice any tooth becoming sensitive to heat as well as cold, or if you get spontaneous pain — a toothache that wakes you up — that's a sign the nerve may be involved and I want to see you sooner. Don't wait for the three-month appointment if that happens."

"Any questions, Sam? Mr Tran, anything from you?"

Listens attentively to both.

Category:** Restorative dentistry · Time:** 11 minutes · Opens with:** Candidate · Difficulty:** Exam-ready

CASE SUMMARY

Sam, 16-year-old male, attends with his father complaining of sensitivity to cold. Examination reveals rampant cervical caries across multiple teeth and early enamel erosion pattern consistent with high-frequency dietary acid exposure. He started a part-time job as an apprentice one year ago and has dramatically increased his soft drink consumption since then. Candidate must complete caries risk assessment, engage both patient and parent, explain findings, and formulate a preventive and restorative plan.

CANDIDATE BRIEF

Sam Tran, 16-year-old, attending with his father. He complains of sensitivity to cold on "a few teeth," particularly the upper and lower front teeth and upper premolars. He was seen at your practice one year ago — at that appointment he had 2 small occlusal lesions (restored) and no cervical lesions noted. Examination today: white spot lesions on the cervical margins of almost all anterior teeth; frank cavitation at the cervical margin of tooth 12; generalised enamel surface loss (dull, rough texture) consistent with acid erosion; tooth 26 shows a cervical lesion extending to dentine; plaque score moderate; BPE 0/1 throughout. His father is present and clearly concerned. Social history: Sam recently started a part-time apprenticeship (construction trade, 3 days/week) and has been drinking 2–4 cans of energy drinks or soft drinks per day at the worksite, plus sports drinks after exercise. Brushes twice daily (morning and after eating at work — this may be worsening erosion). Your task: take a dietary and caries risk history, explain findings to Sam and his father, and formulate a management plan. You have 8 minutes.

EXAMINER CONTEXT

Sam is a typical teenage boy — cooperative but not keen on lectures. He will be defensive if the candidate is preachy about soft drinks ("Everyone at work drinks them"). He responds well to facts and numbers rather than moralistic advice. His father is more alarmed than Sam and may try to take over the conversation — the candidate should engage Sam directly and treat him as the primary patient. Hidden: Sam brushes his teeth immediately after drinking soft drinks or energy drinks because he thinks it helps — this is actually accelerating enamel loss (should wait 30–60 minutes before brushing after acid exposure). He doesn't know this. Also: Sam doesn't drink water at work ("It's boring") — hydration with fluoridated tap water is a free, effective protective factor he's not using. Key challenge: explain acid erosion vs caries clearly (different mechanisms, often coexist), and why the drinking pattern (frequency + type of drink) matters more than total volume.

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

History — INFLECTION 1: Dietary deep-dive

Take a full diet history focused on: frequency of sugary/acidic drinks (how many per day? when? over how long a period?), fluid intake at work, sports drink use, any energy drinks, diet changes in the past year, snacking pattern, medications (some affect saliva), medical history (reflux — an additional acid source). Specifically ask: "When do you brush — do you brush straight after drinks?" This is the hidden inflection point — brushing immediately after acid exposure dramatically worsens erosion.

Explain Findings — INFLECTION 2: Engaging the adolescent

Address Sam directly, use visual aids if possible. "The sensitivity you're feeling is because the outer layer of your teeth — the enamel — has been dissolving. Not from decay in the traditional sense, but from the acid in energy drinks and soft drinks. It's a different mechanism to normal cavities but they can happen at the same time." Use numbers: "Your teeth have changed significantly in 12 months. If we extrapolate that forward 12 more months, you'd be looking at restorations on 10+ teeth."

Management Plan (2 min)

Immediate: fluoride varnish application today; prescribe high-fluoride toothpaste (5000 ppm) for home use. Behavioural: reduce frequency of acidic drinks — not necessarily eliminate, but reduce to mealtimes only; replace with fluoridated tap water between meals; do NOT brush for 30–60 minutes after acidic drink; use fluoride mouthwash at a different time to brushing. Restorative: restore the cavitated lesions (12 cervical, 26 cervical); monitor white spots with fluoride; 3-month recall to assess response. Father's role: supportive, not supervisory — frame this as Sam's choice with real consequences.

KEY POINTS

  • ✅ Distinguishes caries (bacterial) from erosion (chemical/dietary acid) — can coexist
  • ✅ Quantifies dietary acid frequency — identifies frequency as the key variable, not volume
  • ✅ Uncovers the brushing-after-acid habit and corrects it — wait 30–60 minutes
  • ✅ Engages Sam directly — treats him as the primary patient, not the father
  • ✅ Provides fluoride varnish, high-fluoride toothpaste prescription
  • ✅ Restores cavitated lesions; monitors white spots conservatively
  • ✅ Sets 3-month recall given rapid progression
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • "Energy drinks are pH 2.5–3 — that's about as acidic as gastric acid. Each can exposes your teeth to acid for 20–30 minutes while saliva tries to neutralise it. If you're having 3 a day, your teeth are under acid attack for most of your working day."
  • "Brushing after a soft drink actually makes erosion worse — you're scrubbing softened enamel off. Wait 30 to 60 minutes. Rinse with water or chew sugar-free gum instead."
  • "Your teeth changed more in the last 12 months than in the previous 10 years combined. The diet change is the cause — and the good news is it's completely reversible behaviour."
Patient Reframes
  • "I'm not saying never have an energy drink. I'm saying how you drink it matters more than whether you drink it. One can at lunch, finish it quickly, rinse with water — very different from sipping one over two hours."
Curveball Deflectors
  • "Everyone at work drinks them." → "And in 10 years, some of them will have very damaged teeth and some won't — the difference is usually how they drink them, not just that they drink them. You have the advantage of knowing this now, when the damage is still reversible."
  • (Father) "I want you to stop drinking them entirely." → "Sam, what do you think is realistic? The most important thing is what you can actually commit to — one change that sticks is worth more than a perfect plan that doesn't."
PQ-1
Orthodontic Patient Referred for Periodontal Assessment
Station 1  |  Past Questions
■ Cluster 1 — History & Risk Factors

CANDIDATE BRIEF

17-year-old boy came to your practice for consultation. He has seen a dentist 12 months ago. You did CPITN scoring today (Community Periodontal Index of Treatment Needs) which is 444/424 and you have taken bitewing x-ray showing bone loss around molars. Intraoral picture showing crowding and deep bite on anterior. Consult with patient regarding findings.

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

Stage 1 — Acknowledge and Orient (0–1 min)

Acknowledge Jordan's expectation of a quick visit. Explain that the examination has found something important that needs to be discussed before any orthodontic planning can proceed. Use plain language: "Your gum measurements and X-rays have shown something I want to make sure we look into properly." INFLECTION 1 — Candidate must signal that CPITN 4 at age 17 is abnormal, not routine.

Stage 2 — Targeted History (1–4 min)

Systematically elicit: oral hygiene routine (brushing frequency, flossing, toothbrush type); direct question about smoking or vaping; family dental history (early tooth loss in parents); family medical history (diabetes or systemic disease). INFLECTION 2 — Asking about BOTH family dental AND family medical history is the single most differentiating step. Missing either weakens the differential and the management plan.

Stage 3 — Explain Findings (4–6 min)

Explain in age-appropriate terms: the gum pockets are deeper than they should be, the bone holding the teeth is already being lost, and this is happening much earlier than it should. Connect risk factors identified in history to the clinical picture.

Stage 4 — Management Plan (6–9 min)

State four actions clearly: (1) referral to a periodontist — specialist diagnosis and management required; (2) GP referral for fasting glucose and HbA1c given grandmother's type 2 diabetes; (3) specific oral hygiene instruction; (4) brief smoking cessation advice. Explain that orthodontic treatment is deferred until periodontal stability is confirmed — moving teeth through inflamed bone accelerates bone loss.

Stage 5 — Safety Net and Review (9–10 min)

Explain 3-monthly review intervals. Invite questions. Confirm Jordan understands the seriousness without causing panic.

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ CPITN 4 with radiographic bone loss in a 17-year-old is a red flag — not routine adult periodontitis — and must trigger a differential diagnosis workup, not a standard scale and clean
  2. ✅ Direct, non-judgmental question about smoking or vaping is mandatory — Jordan will not volunteer this; nicotine-induced vasoconstriction masks bleeding on probing, making clinical severity worse than it appears
  3. ✅ Both family dental history (father's early tooth loss) AND family medical history (grandmother's type 2 diabetes) must be elicited — together they raise Stage III Grade C periodontitis and systemic manifestation as leading differentials
  4. ✅ Orthodontic treatment must be explicitly deferred with the biological reason stated — orthodontic forces on an actively inflamed periodontium with bone loss accelerate bone destruction and risk pathological tooth migration or tooth loss
  5. ✅ Two specialist/GP referrals are required: periodontist for diagnosis and management of severe early-onset periodontitis, and GP for fasting glucose and HbA1c given the family history of type 2 diabetes
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • CPITN score of 4 means pocketing of 6 mm or greater — finding this in all posterior sextants of a 17-year-old with radiographic bone loss is not within the range of normal variation and cannot be managed as routine adult periodontitis.
  • The differential for generalised severe periodontitis in a teenager includes Stage III Grade C periodontitis — formerly called aggressive periodontitis — which has a strong familial component and a characteristically rapid rate of bone destruction disproportionate to local factors.
  • Nicotine causes vasoconstriction of the gingival microvasculature, which suppresses bleeding on probing — this means the clinical appearance underrepresents the true level of inflammation, and a patient who smokes may look less inflamed than they actually are.
  • Orthodontic forces applied to a periodontium with active inflammation and existing bone loss will accelerate alveolar bone destruction — periodontal stability, confirmed by a periodontist, must be established before any orthodontic treatment is initiated.
  • Given the maternal grandmother's type 2 diabetes, I would refer Jordan to his GP for a fasting glucose and HbA1c — periodontitis can be a manifestation of impaired glucose regulation, and the relationship between diabetes and periodontitis is bidirectional.
  • Review interval for an active high-risk periodontal patient is 3-monthly — not 6-monthly and not annual — because the rate of disease progression in Stage III Grade C periodontitis can be rapid.
Curveball Deflectors
  • Jordan says: 'Can't you just clean my teeth and then I can get my braces? I just want to get this done.' → Validate his frustration directly: 'I completely understand — you came in expecting a straightforward visit and I'm telling you there's more going on. I want to be honest with you because I think you deserve to know what's actually happening. If we put braces on right now without sorting out your gums first, we could make things significantly worse — the forces from braces on already-damaged bone can accelerate bone loss and in the worst case put your teeth at risk. Getting the gum problem properly treated first actually gives your orthodontic treatment the best chance of working well and lasting.'
  • Candidate defaults to 'scale and clean, review in 6 months' without asking why a teenager has generalised CPITN 4 → This is the most common failing in this station. The correct pivot is to recognise that generalised CPITN 4 with radiographic bone loss at age 17 is a clinical red flag that demands a differential diagnosis, not a treatment. A scale and clean without specialist referral, without a systemic screen, and without investigating familial risk factors is inadequate management and would not meet the standard of care. The examiner is specifically watching for whether the candidate asks about family dental history AND family medical history — missing both and proceeding to treatment is the single most penalised error.
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ►
STAGE 1: Acknowledge and Orient

"Hi Jordan, thanks for coming in today. I know you were referred here mainly to talk about your teeth and whether braces might be an option — and we will get to that. But when I did your examination today, I found something in your gums that I think is really important to talk about first, because it actually affects whether orthodontic treatment is safe to start right now. Is that okay if we go through it together?"

Establish rapport and signal that the agenda has shifted without causing alarm. Confirm Jordan is comfortable to proceed. Note his body language — he may appear surprised or slightly defensive.
