STAGE 2: Explain Findings in Plain Language

"So when I measured your gums today, I used a small probe — like a tiny ruler — to check the depth of the space between your gum and your tooth. Healthy gums have a gap of about 1 to 3 millimetres. In your back teeth, those gaps are 6 millimetres or more in every area I checked. That tells me the gum has pulled away from the tooth more than it should. And when I looked at your X-rays, I can see that some of the bone that holds your back teeth in place has already been lost. Now here's the thing — at 17, this level of gum and bone change is not something we'd expect to see. It's not a normal part of growing up, and it's not something a simple clean will fix. It tells me something more significant is going on, and I want to understand why so we can get you the right help."

Use the X-ray to point out bone levels if available. Avoid the word 'disease' initially — introduce it gently once rapport is established. Watch for signs of anxiety or disengagement.

STAGE 3: Targeted History — Elicit Risk Factors

"I'd like to ask you a few questions to help me understand what might be contributing to this — there's no right or wrong answer, I just want to get the full picture. How often do you brush your teeth, and do you floss at all? ... And I have to ask — do you smoke cigarettes or vape at all, even occasionally? Some people smoke socially on weekends and don't think of themselves as smokers, but even that amount can affect your gums quite significantly, so it's really important for me to know. ... Has anyone in your family — mum, dad, grandparents — had problems with their gums, or lost teeth when they were relatively young? ... And on the medical side, does anyone in your family have diabetes or any other health conditions? ... Last one — how are things going generally? Year 12 is a big year. Are you sleeping okay, eating okay? Stress can actually affect your immune system in ways that make gum disease worse, which a lot of people don't realise."

Ask about smoking directly and specifically — Jordan will not volunteer this. Ask about family dental history and family medical history as separate questions. If Jordan discloses grandmother's type 2 diabetes, note this immediately as a trigger for GP referral. If he discloses father's early tooth loss, connect this to possible familial predisposition. Document all findings.

STAGE 4: Management Plan — Explain Next Steps

"Based on everything I've found today, here's what I'd like to do for you. First, I'm going to refer you to a gum specialist — called a periodontist. What you have is beyond what I should be managing on my own in a general practice, and a specialist will be able to do a much more detailed assessment and put together the right treatment plan. Second, because your grandmother has type 2 diabetes, I'd like you to see your GP for a simple blood test — a fasting glucose and something called an HbA1c. There's a well-established link between blood sugar problems and gum disease, and it's worth ruling that out. Third, about your braces — I have to be honest with you. We cannot start orthodontic treatment while your gums are in this state. When we move teeth with braces, we're putting forces on the bone around the teeth. If that bone is already being lost, those forces can make things much worse and could actually put your teeth at risk. Once the periodontist has treated your gums and confirmed things are stable, we can absolutely revisit the orthodontic conversation. Fourth, in the meantime, let's talk about your brushing — I'd like you to brush twice a day, morning and night, and I'll show you how to floss properly today. And regarding the smoking — I'm not here to judge you at all, but even a few cigarettes on weekends is enough to affect your gum healing. Cutting that out completely would make a real difference to how well your gums respond to treatment. I can give you some resources if that would help. I'll also want to see you every three months rather than once a year — your gums need closer monitoring than someone without this level of disease. Do you have any questions about any of that?"

Provide written referral letters for both periodontist and GP. Provide oral hygiene instruction with demonstration. Offer smoking cessation resources appropriate for a 17-year-old. Document all findings, risk factors disclosed, and management plan in the clinical notes. Confirm Jordan's understanding before he leaves.

PQ-2
Caries Risk Assessment: 8-Year-Old — Early Childhood Caries Pattern (Prolonged Bottle Use)
Station 2  |  Past Questions
■ Cluster 1 — History & Risk Factors

CANDIDATE BRIEF

8 years old child came in your practice with mother. Mother is worried about his teeth. On examination you found a lot of carious teeth. Consult with the mother about her concerns. Intraoral picture given for lower jaw, caries on both permanent molars, E/D/C's. Consult with the mother about caries risk assessment and treatment.

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

Stage 1 — Introduction & Rapport (0–1 min)

Greet Mrs Chen and Liam warmly. Acknowledge her concern: "Thank you for coming in — it's really good that you've brought Liam along so we can work this out together." Establish a non-judgemental tone from the outset.

Stage 2 — Structured History (1–4 min)

Take a dietary and feeding history: meals, snacks, drinks, and specifically bottle or sippy cup use. Probe contents, frequency, and timing relative to sleep. INFLECTION 1 — When the nighttime bottle is revealed, ask whether Liam falls asleep with it in his mouth and whether brushing occurs afterwards. Explore duration of the habit.

Stage 3 — Examination & Investigations (4–6 min)

Describe full clinical charting, assessment of pulpal status (pain, swelling, sinus tracts), and request bitewing radiographs. Link the upper-anterior-predominant, lower-anterior-sparing decay pattern to the history. INFLECTION 2 — Recognising this as classic prolonged nocturnal bottle caries pattern, not simply poor brushing, is the key diagnostic pivot.

Stage 4 — Explanation & Counselling (6–9 min)

Explain the cariogenic mechanism in plain language: reduced saliva during sleep allows milk sugars to pool around upper teeth for hours. Frame the habit as common and well-intentioned. Provide a weaning plan — replace bottle contents with water over two to four weeks — and interim harm-reduction: brush before sleep, water only in bottle overnight.

Stage 5 — Treatment Plan & Follow-Up (9–10 min)

Outline restorative needs for affected primary and permanent teeth, prioritised by symptoms and pulpal status. Arrange follow-up. Provide written dietary and hygiene advice. Offer reassurance and praise any positive steps.

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Recognises the upper-anterior-predominant, lower-anterior-sparing decay pattern as classic prolonged nocturnal bottle caries and explicitly links it to the history
  2. ✅ Takes a structured feeding history specifically probing bottle/sippy cup use, contents (milk, chocolate powder), and timing relative to sleep
  3. ✅ Explains the cariogenic mechanism in plain language — reduced salivary clearance during sleep allows prolonged sugar contact with upper teeth
  4. ✅ Provides empathetic, non-judgemental counselling framing the habit as common and well-intentioned, avoiding parental blame
  5. ✅ Gives a clear, practical weaning plan (water substitution over 2–4 weeks) with interim harm-reduction advice, and arranges appropriate restorative treatment and follow-up
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • "The pattern we see — decay on the upper front teeth but the lower front teeth being relatively protected — is a classic sign of what we call prolonged nocturnal bottle caries. The lower lip and tongue physically shield the lower teeth, while the upper front teeth sit right where the bottle teat rests."
  • "During sleep, saliva flow drops to almost nothing. That means milk — which contains lactose, a natural sugar — can sit against the upper teeth for six to eight hours without being washed away, which is exactly the environment bacteria need to produce acid and cause decay."
  • "Adding chocolate powder to the bottle significantly increases the fermentable sugar load, which accelerates the decay process beyond what plain milk alone would cause."
  • "At eight years old, Liam's first permanent molars are already erupted and are also showing decay, so our treatment plan needs to address both the primary teeth and those permanent molars as a priority."
Curveball Deflectors
  • Mother becomes defensive or upset: "I only gave him milk — I thought that was healthy!" → Validate immediately and without hesitation: "You're absolutely right that milk is healthy — it's full of calcium and great for growing teeth and bones. The issue isn't the milk itself; it's purely the timing. When Liam falls asleep with the bottle, the milk sits against his teeth all night with no saliva to wash it away. It's a very common habit and many families are in exactly the same situation — the important thing is that you've brought him in and we can fix this together."
  • Candidate focuses only on brushing technique and diet without identifying or addressing the nighttime bottle habit → Redirect by asking specifically: "Does Liam use a bottle or sippy cup at any point during the day or night?" and "Does he ever fall asleep with a drink in his mouth?" The decay pattern — upper anterior predominance with lower anterior sparing — should prompt the candidate to actively seek the bottle history rather than accepting a generic dietary explanation. Failure to identify the nocturnal bottle as the primary aetiological factor is the most common reason candidates score poorly on this station.
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ►
STAGE 1: Introduction & Rapport

"Hi Mrs Chen, hi Liam — lovely to meet you both. I'm Dr [Name]. Mrs Chen, I can see you're worried about Liam's teeth, and I really want to reassure you that coming in today is exactly the right thing to do. There's no judgement here at all — we're just going to have a good look, ask a few questions, and work out the best plan together. Is that okay?"

Establish a warm, non-judgemental tone. Acknowledge the mother's concern and the likely embarrassment around delayed presentation. Seat Liam comfortably and engage him briefly to reduce anxiety.

STAGE 2: Structured History

"Before I look at Liam's teeth in detail, I'd love to ask you a few questions about what he eats and drinks — it really helps me understand what's going on. Does Liam have any sugary drinks or snacks during the day? What about at night — does he have anything to drink before bed or during the night? Does he use a bottle or a sippy cup at all?"

Listen actively. When the nighttime bottle is disclosed, probe further without alarm: "What's usually in the bottle — milk, juice, something else? Does he sometimes fall asleep with the bottle still in his mouth? And after the bottle, do you usually get a chance to brush his teeth before he's fully asleep?" Also explore: duration of the habit, fluoride toothpaste use, water fluoridation status, and any previous dental visits. Note parental guilt and respond with normalising language throughout.

STAGE 3: Examination, Investigations & Explanation

"Thank you — that's really helpful. Now I'm going to have a proper look at Liam's teeth. Liam, I'm just going to count your teeth and have a little look — you're doing great."

Perform full clinical charting including primary and permanent teeth. Assess for pulpal involvement: spontaneous pain, tenderness to percussion, swelling, sinus tracts. Request bitewing radiographs to assess interproximal caries depth and furcation involvement on primary molars. Note the upper-anterior-predominant, lower-anterior-sparing decay pattern and link explicitly to the history.

"Mrs Chen, I can see quite a lot of decay, particularly on Liam's upper front teeth, and also on some of his back teeth including his new adult molars. The pattern — where the upper front teeth are most affected but the lower front teeth are relatively okay — is actually a very recognisable sign of what we call prolonged bottle caries. Here's why: when Liam falls asleep with the bottle, the milk pools around his upper front teeth all night. During sleep, saliva almost completely stops flowing, so there's nothing to wash the milk away. Milk contains a natural sugar called lactose, and when bacteria in the mouth feed on that sugar for six to eight hours overnight, they produce acid that slowly dissolves the teeth. The lower front teeth are actually protected by the tongue and lower lip, which is why they look better. Adding chocolate powder to the bottle increases the sugar load even further, which speeds the whole process up."

STAGE 4: Counselling, Weaning Plan & Treatment

"I want to be really clear — you gave Liam milk because you wanted to do the right thing for him, and that makes complete sense. This is one of the most common patterns of decay we see in children, and it's entirely fixable. What I'd like to suggest is a gradual plan to wean Liam off the nighttime bottle over the next two to four weeks. We start by diluting the milk a little more each night — half milk, half water — until the bottle contains only water. Water at night is completely safe for teeth. In the meantime, if the bottle is still happening, the single most important thing is to brush Liam's teeth immediately before he falls asleep, after the bottle, using a pea-sized amount of fluoride toothpaste — we'd use a 1000 parts-per-million fluoride toothpaste for his age. Once he's asleep, only water in the bottle. For the teeth themselves, we do need to treat the decay. I'll prioritise the adult molars and any teeth causing him pain first. Some of the baby teeth may need fillings, and depending on how deep the decay is on the X-rays, some may need more involved treatment. I'll go through each tooth with you once we have the X-rays back. I'd like to see Liam again in four weeks to check how the weaning is going and to start treatment — does that work for you?"

Provide written dietary and oral hygiene instructions. Offer a referral to a paediatric dentist if complexity warrants it. Document the caries risk assessment as high. Schedule a follow-up in four weeks. Praise Mrs Chen for attending and for her engagement with the plan.

PQ-3
Management of Denture Stomatitis in a Diabetic Patient
Station 3  |  Past Questions
■ Cluster 2 — Balanced (History informs management)

CANDIDATE BRIEF

65 years old lady, wearing upper denture for 38 years. Current denture is 20 years old. She complained of sore mouth and poor fitting denture. Denture falls during yawning and eating. She has few teeth on the lower jaw but doesn't wear any denture on lower. On examination you found red inflamed palate, upper denture has buccal flange overextension, all the teeth worn out. Consult with the pt about the management.

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

Stage 1 — Focused History (0–3 min)

Introduce and take targeted history: duration of current denture, overnight wear habits, cleaning routine (soaking? denture cleaner?), dry mouth symptoms, sugar intake (boiled lollies). INFLECTION 1 — Ask directly about diabetes: type, medication, and most recent HbA1c. An HbA1c of 8.2% signals poor control and is the systemic key to this case.

Stage 2 — Diagnosis and Explanation (3–5 min)

Diagnose Newton's Type II denture stomatitis (candidal-associated). Explain the multifactorial aetiology to the patient in plain language: fungal reservoir in denture, overnight wear, poor hygiene, xerostomia, and hyperglycaemia all converging. INFLECTION 2 — Failure to link HbA1c 8.2% to immune suppression and candidal susceptibility is a red flag for examiners.

Stage 3 — Immediate Non-Pharmacological Management (5–7 min)

Advise cessation of overnight denture wear immediately. Prescribe a daily soaking regimen using alkaline peroxide or dilute sodium hypochlorite cleaner. Demonstrate/describe correct brushing of the denture. Address the boiled lolly habit — recommend sugar-free alternatives or saliva substitutes for xerostomia.

Stage 4 — Pharmacological Management (7–9 min)

Prescribe miconazole oromucosal gel 2% (Daktarin Oral Gel — TGA approved, available in Australia) applied to the fitting surface of the denture and palatal mucosa QID for 4 weeks. Explain application technique clearly.

Stage 5 — Longer-Term Dental and Medical Plan (9–10 min)

Explain that the current denture requires replacement once infection resolves and diabetes is optimised. Refer to GP for HbA1c review. Discuss that a target HbA1c below 7% improves healing and reduces infection risk. Arrange review in 2–4 weeks to assess treatment response.

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Identifies overnight denture wear and poor hygiene as primary local risk factors for denture stomatitis
  2. ✅ Asks about and correctly interprets HbA1c 8.2% as poorly controlled diabetes contributing to candidal susceptibility
  3. ✅ Diagnoses Newton's Type II denture stomatitis and explains the multifactorial aetiology including xerostomia and hyperglycaemia
  4. ✅ Prescribes miconazole oromucosal gel 2% with correct instructions for application to both denture fitting surface and palatal mucosa
  5. ✅ Recommends GP liaison for diabetes optimisation and explains that a new denture should only be constructed after infection resolution and improved glycaemic control
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • An HbA1c of 8.2% indicates poorly controlled diabetes — this impairs neutrophil function and cell-mediated immunity, significantly increasing susceptibility to oral candidal infection.
  • This is Newton's Type II denture stomatitis — diffuse erythema of the denture-bearing mucosa — most commonly caused by Candida albicans proliferating in the biofilm on the fitting surface of the denture.
  • Miconazole oromucosal gel 2% should be applied to the fitting surface of the denture before insertion and directly to the palatal mucosa four times daily for a minimum of four weeks, continuing for two weeks after symptoms resolve.
  • Wearing a denture overnight prevents the palatal mucosa from recovering and maintains continuous contact with the fungal reservoir — cessation of overnight wear is non-negotiable as part of treatment.
  • A new denture should not be constructed until the infection has fully resolved and glycaemic control has improved — ideally HbA1c below 7% — otherwise the new denture will become reinfected and treatment will fail.
Curveball Deflectors
  • Patient says: 'I have worn my denture to bed for 20 years and never had a problem before — why do I need to take it out now?' → Acknowledge her long habit without dismissing it, then explain: 'I completely understand it feels normal to you after all these years. The difference now is that your blood sugar levels are higher than ideal, which means your body's defences against infection are not as strong as they used to be. The denture is acting like a home for the fungus — if it stays in overnight, the fungus keeps growing and the palate never gets a chance to recover. Taking it out at night is one of the most important things we can do to help this heal.'
  • Candidate prescribes antifungal medication without addressing denture hygiene or overnight wear → This is a red flag. The examiner expects the candidate to recognise that antifungal therapy alone will fail if the denture remains a fungal reservoir. The correct approach is to address denture hygiene and overnight wear first, then layer in pharmacological treatment. A candidate who prescribes nystatin or miconazole without these instructions should be prompted: 'What else would you advise Mrs Walsh to do alongside the medication to make sure the treatment works?'
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ►
STAGE 1: Focused History

'Mrs Walsh, thank you for coming in today. I can see you are having some discomfort and I want to make sure I understand everything that is going on so we can sort this out together. Can I ask you a few questions first? How long have you been wearing this particular denture? And do you take your denture out at night, or do you tend to sleep with it in? How do you clean your denture at the moment — do you soak it in anything overnight, or use a denture cleaning tablet? I also want to ask about your general health — I understand you have diabetes. Are you taking any medication for that, and do you know what your last blood sugar reading or HbA1c result was? Have you noticed your mouth feeling dry at all? I noticed you mentioned using boiled lollies — can you tell me a bit more about that?'

Candidate listens actively and notes: denture worn 24 hours a day, cleaned only occasionally with toothpaste, never soaked. HbA1c 8.2% three months ago — poorly controlled. Dry mouth present. Boiled lollies used as a coping strategy for xerostomia — a significant candidal risk factor due to sucrose exposure. No drug allergies.

STAGE 2: Diagnosis and Explanation

'Mrs Walsh, based on what you have told me and what I can see in your mouth, I believe you have a fungal infection called oral thrush — or more specifically, something called denture stomatitis. It is causing the redness and soreness on the roof of your mouth. This is actually quite common, but in your case several things have come together to cause it. The denture is acting like a home for the fungus — especially because it stays in overnight and is not being soaked regularly. Your blood sugar levels being a little higher than ideal at the moment also means your body is not fighting off infections as easily as it normally would. And the dry mouth you have been experiencing reduces the natural protection your saliva provides. The good news is that this is very treatable, and I am going to go through everything we need to do step by step.'

Candidate clearly names Newton's Type II denture stomatitis and explains the multifactorial aetiology — linking HbA1c 8.2%, xerostomia, overnight denture wear, and poor hygiene — without using jargon. This demonstrates the systemic-oral link the examiner is looking for.

STAGE 3: Non-Pharmacological Management

'The first and most important thing I need you to do is to stop sleeping with your denture in from tonight. I know that might feel strange at first, but it is essential — the palate needs time to breathe and recover. When you take it out at night, please rinse it under water, brush it gently with a soft brush — not toothpaste, as that can scratch the surface — and then soak it overnight in a denture cleaning solution, like Polident or Steradent tablets dissolved in water. This will kill the fungus on the denture itself. I also want to gently suggest that the boiled lollies, while I understand they help with the dry mouth, are feeding the fungus with sugar. I would like to suggest some sugar-free alternatives — there are also saliva substitute sprays and gels available from the pharmacy that can help with the dryness without the sugar.'

Candidate addresses all local risk factors: overnight wear cessation, correct denture cleaning technique, soaking regimen, and dietary modification. Recommends sugar-free saliva substitutes as a TGA-available alternative to boiled lollies.

STAGE 4: Pharmacological and Long-Term Management

'I am also going to prescribe you a gel called Daktarin Oral Gel — it is an antifungal medication. I would like you to apply a small amount to the inside surface of your denture — the part that sits against your palate — before you put it in each morning, and also dab a little directly onto the roof of your mouth. You will do this four times a day for four weeks. It is important to keep going for the full course even if things feel better sooner. Now, regarding your denture itself — I can see it is not fitting well and the edge is a little overextended on the cheek side, which is likely contributing to the soreness. Once the infection has cleared and your blood sugar levels are better controlled, we will look at making you a new denture that fits properly. I would also strongly recommend you make an appointment with your GP to discuss your blood sugar levels — getting your HbA1c closer to the target range, ideally below seven percent, will make a real difference to how well your mouth heals and how well any future dental treatment goes. I would like to see you back in two to four weeks to check how things are improving.'

Candidate prescribes miconazole oromucosal gel 2% (Daktarin — TGA registered in Australia) with correct application instructions for both denture and mucosa, QID for 4 weeks. Defers new denture construction until infection resolution and glycaemic optimisation. Refers to GP for HbA1c review with a clear target. Arranges follow-up. All rubric criteria addressed.

PQ-4
Extraction Planning for a Patient on Denosumab and Warfarin
Station 4  |  Past Questions
■ Cluster 2 — Balanced (History informs management)

CANDIDATE BRIEF

Mr John Smith is a 67 year old patient, attended your surgery today complaining of a swelling and tooth mobility in the lower right side. After examination, you have noticed that the lower right second molar has grade 3 mobility and abscess related to that tooth. The patient has a past medical history of Myocardial infarction, he also has Hypertension for which he is taking atenolol and warfarin. The patient also complains of hypothyroidism for which he is taking thyroxine, and osteoporosis for which he is taking calcium and denosumab iv injection only two days ago. He has also been taking panadeine forte. Manage patients concern regarding the swelling and mobile 45.

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

Stage 1 — Introduction and History (0–3 min)

Greet Mr Smith, acknowledge his pain and anxiety. Take a structured medication history: confirm denosumab dose (60 mg SC), frequency (6-monthly), duration (3 years), and that the last injection was only two days ago. Ask about warfarin — indication, dose, and most recent INR. Ask about all other medications (atenolol, thyroxine, Panadeine Forte). INFLECTION 1 — The two-day interval since denosumab injection is the critical pivot: this dramatically elevates MRONJ risk and changes the management pathway from routine to specialist-liaison required.

Stage 2 — Examination Findings and Diagnosis (3–5 min)

Explain findings in plain language: the lower right back molar has a severe infection and is Grade 3 mobile — it cannot be saved and requires removal. Confirm periapical pathology on radiograph.

Stage 3 — Risk Explanation and Consent (5–9 min)

Explain MRONJ in patient-friendly terms: "Your bone injection helps keep your bones strong, but it can sometimes make it harder for the jawbone to heal after a tooth is removed — this is a rare but serious risk we need to discuss." Explain warfarin management: no need to stop, INR must be checked and confirmed ≤3.5–4.0; local haemostatic measures will be used. INFLECTION 2 — Incorrectly advising the patient to stop warfarin is a common and serious error that examiners will penalise.

Stage 4 — Management Plan and Specialist Liaison (9–12 min)

Given the very recent denosumab injection, discuss temporising: drain abscess acutely, prescribe antibiotics (amoxicillin 500 mg TDS or clindamycin if penicillin-allergic), and defer definitive extraction pending GP/specialist consultation. If extraction proceeds, outline atraumatic technique, primary closure, antimicrobial cover, and close follow-up. Document consent discussion thoroughly.

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Denosumab details must be elicited: 60 mg SC, 6-monthly, 3 years duration, last dose only 2 days ago — this is the highest-risk scenario for MRONJ
  2. ✅ Warfarin does NOT need to be ceased for simple extraction if INR ≤3.5–4.0; local haemostatic measures (sutures, Surgicel, tranexamic acid mouthwash) are sufficient
  3. ✅ MRONJ must be explained in plain language and documented as part of informed consent — patient must understand the risk before any extraction proceeds
  4. ✅ Given the 2-day post-injection window, specialist/GP liaison is mandatory before definitive extraction; temporising with drainage and antibiotics is the safer immediate step
  5. ✅ CTX testing is no longer recommended as a standalone risk-stratification tool in current Australian guidance and should not be used to clear or delay treatment in isolation

  • Denosumab — brand name Prolia — is a RANK-L inhibitor that suppresses osteoclast activity. Unlike bisphosphonates, it does not permanently bind to bone, but the risk of MRONJ is still clinically significant, particularly in the period immediately following an injection. With the last dose given only two days ago, this patient is at elevated risk and specialist liaison is required before we proceed with definitive extraction.

✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ►
STAGE 1: Introduction and Medication History

"Good morning Mr Smith, I'm Dr [Name]. I can see you're in some discomfort today — I want to make sure we look after you properly. Before I explain what's happening with that tooth, I'd like to ask you a few questions about your health and the medications you're taking, if that's okay. Can you tell me all the medications you're currently on?"

Listen as patient volunteers medications. Specifically probe: "You mentioned a bone injection — can you tell me the name of it? How often do you receive it, and when was your last one?" Confirm: denosumab (Prolia) 60 mg subcutaneous, every 6 months, for 3 years, last dose 2 days ago. Then ask: "You're also on warfarin — do you know what dose you take, and have you had a recent blood test to check your INR level?" Confirm INR result and therapeutic range. Document all medications: atenolol, warfarin, thyroxine, calcium, denosumab, Panadeine Forte.

STAGE 2: Explain Findings and Diagnosis

"Mr Smith, I've had a look at your tooth and the X-ray. The lower right back molar has a significant infection around the root — you can see this dark shadow on the X-ray — and the tooth is very loose, what we call Grade 3 mobility. Unfortunately, this tooth is not saveable. The infection is the cause of your swelling and pain, and the tooth will need to come out. I want to be upfront with you about that."

Show radiograph to patient. Confirm periapical radiolucency. Explain that the tooth cannot be root-treated or restored due to the degree of mobility and infection. Transition to risk discussion.

STAGE 3: Informed Consent — MRONJ and Bleeding Risk

"Before we go ahead, I need to explain two important risks specific to you. The first relates to your bone injection — Prolia. This medication works by slowing down the cells that break down bone, which is great for your osteoporosis, but it can sometimes make it harder for the jawbone to heal after a tooth is removed. This is called medication-related osteonecrosis of the jaw — a rare but serious condition where the bone doesn't heal properly. Because your last injection was only two days ago, your risk is higher than usual, and I want to speak with your GP or specialist before we proceed with the extraction, to make sure we're doing this at the safest possible time and in the safest possible way."

"The second risk is related to your warfarin. I want to reassure you — you do not need to stop your warfarin before this procedure. Stopping it could actually put you at risk of a blood clot, which is far more dangerous. Instead, we'll confirm your INR is in a safe range, and we'll use stitches and a special dressing in the socket to control any bleeding. We can also give you a mouthwash called tranexamic acid to help with clotting."

Document consent discussion in notes. Confirm patient understands both risks. Answer any questions. Do not proceed to extraction today without specialist liaison given the 2-day post-denosumab window.

STAGE 4: Immediate Management and Definitive Plan

"Here's what I'd like to do today, Mr Smith. Because of the timing of your bone injection, I don't want to rush into removing the tooth without speaking to your specialist first. What I can do right now is help with the infection — I'll prescribe you a course of antibiotics to bring the swelling under control, and if needed I can drain the area to give you some relief. I'll then contact your GP or specialist today to discuss the best timing for the extraction. Once we have the go-ahead, we'll remove the tooth as gently as possible, stitch the area closed, and keep a very close eye on your healing over the following weeks."

Prescribe amoxicillin 500 mg TDS for 5 days (or clindamycin 300 mg TDS if penicillin-allergic, noting interaction with warfarin — advise GP and consider INR recheck). Arrange GP/specialist liaison letter today. Schedule extraction appointment with MRONJ prevention protocol: atraumatic technique, primary closure, perioperative antimicrobial cover, review at 1 week and 4 weeks. Confirm INR within 24–72 hours pre-extraction. Document all discussions, risks disclosed, and management plan in patient record.

Management of Patient on Denosumab and Warfarin Requiring Extraction

CANDIDATE BRIEF

Mr John Smith is a 67 year old patient, attended your surgery today complaining of a swelling and tooth mobility in the lower right side. After examination, you have noticed that the lower right second molar has grade 3 mobility and abscess related to that tooth. The patient has a past medical history of Myocardial infarction, he also has Hypertension for which he is taking atenolol and warfarin. He has also been taking panadeine forte. Manage patients concern regarding the swelling and mobile 45.

Stage 1 — Focused History and Medication Clarification (0–2 min)

Greet Mr Smith, acknowledge his concern. Confirm denosumab: 60 mg SC, every 6 months, 3 years duration, last dose 2 days ago. Confirm warfarin dose and ask for INR slip — INR 2.4, taken 5 days ago. Note Panadeine Forte use (codeine + paracetamol — relevant to pain management and potential interaction awareness). INFLECTION 1 — Last denosumab dose 2 days ago places the patient at the peak of antiresorptive activity; this is the highest-risk window for MRONJ and must drive the management plan.

Stage 2 — Clinical Assessment and Risk Stratification (2–4 min)

Examine tooth 47 (lower right second molar): grade 3 mobility, periapical abscess confirmed clinically and radiographically. Tooth is unrestorable — extraction is indicated. Identify dual risks: MRONJ from denosumab and bleeding risk from warfarin. Note that CTX testing is no longer recommended as a standalone predictor of MRONJ risk per current Australian guidance.

Stage 3 — Patient Communication and Consent (4–7 min)

Explain MRONJ in lay terms: "A rare condition where the jawbone has difficulty healing after a tooth removal — it does not mean your jaw will definitely rot, but we need to take precautions." INFLECTION 2 — Candidate must not stop warfarin without cardiology input, and must not refuse treatment due to denosumab alone — the infected tooth itself is a greater MRONJ risk than a planned atraumatic extraction.

Stage 4 — Management Plan and Liaison (7–10 min)

Liaise with GP and cardiologist. Prescribe amoxicillin 2 g 1 hour pre-op (or clindamycin 600 mg if allergic). Atraumatic extraction, primary closure, resorbable sutures, haemostatic gauze, pressure pack. Written post-op instructions. Consider specialist referral if any uncertainty. Review at 1 week. Weigh temporising with antibiotics vs. proceeding — given active infection, extraction is appropriate once risks are managed.

  1. ✅ Denosumab last dose 2 days ago — peak antiresorptive activity; highest MRONJ risk window; must be documented and communicated to patient
  2. ✅ Warfarin: continue without cessation for simple extraction if INR ≤3.5 per Australian guidelines; confirm INR on day of procedure (current result 2.4 — within safe range)
  3. ✅ Antibiotic prophylaxis: amoxicillin 2 g orally 1 hour pre-operatively (clindamycin 600 mg if penicillin-allergic) to reduce MRONJ risk
  4. ✅ Atraumatic technique, primary closure where possible, local haemostatic measures (resorbable sutures, haemostatic gauze, pressure pack) and written post-op instructions
  5. ✅ CTX testing is no longer a reliable standalone predictor of MRONJ risk per current Australian guidance — do not delay or clear treatment based on CTX alone

  • Denosumab is an anti-RANKL monoclonal antibody that suppresses osteoclast activity; with the last dose administered only two days ago, the patient is at peak antiresorptive effect, placing them in the highest-risk window for MRONJ following dentoalveolar surgery.
  • Pre-operative antibiotic prophylaxis with amoxicillin 2 g orally one hour before extraction is recommended to reduce MRONJ risk in patients on antiresorptive therapy undergoing dentoalveolar surgery.

STAGE 1: Greeting and Medication History

"Good morning, Mr Smith. I can see you're in some discomfort today — thank you for coming in. I want to make sure I understand everything about your health before we talk about what's happening with that tooth. I'm going to ask you a few questions about your medications if that's okay. [Patient confirms: every 6 months for 3 years, last injection 2 days ago.] "Thank you — that's really important information. And for your warfarin — do you happen to have your most recent INR result with you?" [Patient produces slip: INR 2.4, taken 5 days ago.] "Perfect, that's very helpful. STAGE 2: Explaining the Risks — MRONJ and Bleeding

"Mr Smith, I want to be honest with you about two things we need to think carefully about. The first is your denosumab. This medication works by slowing down the cells that break down bone — which is great for your osteoporosis — but it also means that if we remove a tooth, the jawbone can sometimes have difficulty healing. There's a rare condition called medication-related osteonecrosis of the jaw — sometimes called MRONJ — where the bone doesn't heal properly after a dental procedure. I want to reassure you: this does not mean your jaw will definitely rot. It's a real risk, but with careful planning, antibiotics, and a gentle technique, we can significantly reduce the chance of it happening. And importantly, leaving that infected tooth in place actually increases the risk of this condition — so doing nothing is not the safer choice. The second thing is your warfarin. Because warfarin thins your blood, there is a risk of increased bleeding after the extraction. However, the good news is that current guidelines actually recommend we keep you on your warfarin — stopping it could put you at risk of a clot or a stroke, which is far more dangerous. As long as your INR is within a safe range on the day, we can proceed safely with some extra precautions."

Explain MRONJ in lay terms. Address 'jaw bone rot' fear directly and empathetically. Explain warfarin continuation rationale. Do not suggest stopping warfarin. Do not order CTX as a standalone clearance test.

STAGE 3: The Plan — Liaison, Antibiotics, and Technique

"Here is what I'd like to do. Before we go ahead, I want to speak with your GP and your cardiologist — just to let them know what we're planning and to make sure everyone is on the same page. On the day of the extraction, we'll check your INR again to confirm it's still in a safe range — we're looking for it to be 3.5 or below, and yours is currently 2.4, so that's very reassuring. I'll also prescribe you an antibiotic — amoxicillin — to take one hour before the procedure. This helps protect the jawbone and reduces the risk of that healing problem we discussed. During the extraction itself, I'll be as gentle as possible to minimise trauma to the bone and gum. Afterwards, I'll place some dissolving stitches to help the area close over, use a special gauze to help the blood clot, and give you a pressure pack to bite on. I'll give you written instructions to take home, and I'd like to see you back in one week to check how everything is healing."

Plan: liaise with GP and cardiologist; recheck INR on day of procedure (target ≤3.5); amoxicillin 2 g orally 1 hour pre-op (clindamycin 600 mg if penicillin-allergic); atraumatic extraction; primary closure; resorbable sutures; haemostatic gauze; pressure pack; written post-op instructions; 1-week review. Consider specialist referral if any clinical uncertainty.

STAGE 4: Informed Consent and Closing

"Before we finalise anything, I want to make sure you understand everything we've discussed and that you're comfortable with the plan. The main risks are: a small chance of the jawbone having difficulty healing because of your denosumab — we call this MRONJ — and a slightly increased chance of bleeding because of your warfarin. We're taking every precaution to minimise both of those risks. Do you have any questions? Are you happy for me to contact your GP and cardiologist this week, and then we can schedule the extraction once we've confirmed everything is in order? I'll also give you a written summary of today's discussion to take home."

Obtain verbal informed consent covering MRONJ risk and bleeding risk. Document consent discussion in clinical notes. Provide written post-op instructions. Arrange GP and cardiologist liaison. Schedule extraction with pre-op INR check. Book 1-week post-extraction review. If patient is highly anxious or risks are complex, offer specialist oral surgery referral as an option.

PQ-6
Management of Crown Fracture During Extraction
Station 5  |  Past Questions
■ Cluster 3 — Evaluation & Treatment Planning

CANDIDATE BRIEF

50+ male, came to your surgery on Friday afternoon, he lives in two hours driving distance from the practice, with pain and swelling on upper molar. On examination 16/26 was badly decayed. You attempted extraction, the crown broke. Inform the pt about broken crown and discuss the next step of the treatment. X-ray given showing molar roots are close proximity to sinus, pt taking blood pressure medicine, under control.

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

Stage 1 — Stop, Acknowledge, Reassure (0–1 min)

Candidate stops immediately, places gauze, and says clearly: "Sharon, I need to let you know that the crown of the tooth has broken away — this can happen with heavily decayed teeth and it is a recognised complication. The roots are still there and we need to remove them, but I want to make sure we do this safely." Candidate does NOT minimise or conceal the event. INFLECTION 1 — If the candidate downplays or omits disclosure, Sharon asks directly: "Did something go wrong?" — failure to answer honestly is a critical error.

Stage 2 — Clinical Assessment (1–3 min)

Candidate reviews the radiograph (three divergent, bulbous roots, apices close to sinus floor, no periapical pathology), examines the socket for visible fragments and mobility, and checks for signs of oroantral communication (air passage, fluid, nose bleeding). Documents findings.

Stage 3 — Formulate and Explain the Plan (3–5 min)

Candidate explains that blind forceps extraction of the remaining roots is not appropriate given the anatomy. Offers two options: surgical removal today (flap, sectioning) if within competence, or referral to an oral surgeon. Discusses sinus risk proportionately. INFLECTION 2 — Candidate must not suggest continuing with forceps on fractured roots; this triggers Sharon's safety challenge and is a marking failure point.

Stage 4 — Address Patient Questions and Consent (5–7 min)

Addresses pain management (currently numb; post-op ibuprofen 400 mg + paracetamol 500–1000 mg alternating), cost (private health insurance applicable; estimate provided), timeframe, and referral process. Obtains informed consent for chosen plan.

Stage 5 — Documentation and Safety Net (7–8 min)

Documents complication, clinical findings, plan, and consent in notes. Provides written sinus precaution instructions if proceeding or referral letter with radiograph if referring. Gives after-hours contact details given patient's two-hour travel distance.

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Immediately stops the procedure and honestly discloses the crown fracture complication in plain language without minimising it
  2. ✅ Reviews the radiograph and examines the socket — identifies divergent bulbous roots, sinus proximity, and checks for oroantral communication
  3. ✅ Formulates a safe plan (surgical removal with flap/sectioning or oral surgeon referral) and explicitly avoids blind forceps extraction of fractured roots
  4. ✅ Reasons proportionately about oroantral communication risk: small (≤3 mm) = conservative management + sinus precautions; moderate (3–6 mm) = referral + antibiotics; large (≥7 mm) = specialist flap repair
  5. ✅ Addresses all patient concerns (pain, cost, specialist, timeframe), documents the complication, and provides a safety net given the patient's two-hour travel distance
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • Crown fracture during extraction of a heavily decayed tooth is a recognised intraoperative complication — the roots must be removed but the approach must change: a surgical technique involving a mucoperiosteal flap and root sectioning is indicated, not continued forceps pressure on the remaining root stumps.
  • The radiograph shows three divergent, bulbous roots with apices in close proximity to the maxillary sinus floor — this significantly increases the risk of oroantral communication during surgical removal, and the patient must be counselled about this before we proceed.
  • Oroantral communication management is size-dependent: up to approximately 3 mm can be managed conservatively with a figure-of-eight suture to stabilise the clot and strict sinus precautions; 3–6 mm warrants referral with antibiotic cover such as amoxicillin 500 mg TDS for five days; 7 mm or greater requires specialist surgical flap closure.
  • Sinus precautions include: no nose-blowing, no sneezing with the mouth closed, no drinking through straws, no smoking, and avoiding positive pressure for at least two weeks — I will give you these in writing before you leave today.
  • Given you live two hours from the practice, I want to make sure you have a clear after-hours contact number and written instructions so that if you develop any symptoms — air or fluid coming through the socket, nasal bleeding, or increasing pain — you know exactly what to do and who to call.
Curveball Deflectors
  • Sharon asks: 'Can't you just pull the roots out now with the forceps — I just want it over with?' → Acknowledge her understandable desire to finish today, but explain clearly: 'I completely understand you want this done, Sharon, and so do I. The problem is that the roots that remain have a curved, bulbous shape and they sit very close to your sinus. If I try to grip them with forceps now, there is a real risk of pushing a root into the sinus or causing a communication between your mouth and your sinus — and that would be a much bigger problem to fix. The safest way to remove them is with a small surgical approach, or with the help of an oral surgeon who does this every day. I want to get this right for you, not just get it done quickly.'
  • Sharon becomes distressed and asks: 'Did something go wrong? Are you sure you know what you are doing?' → Do not become defensive. Respond with calm honesty: 'Yes, Sharon, the crown of the tooth broke during the extraction — I want to be completely upfront with you about that. It is a known complication, especially when a tooth is as decayed as this one was, and it does not mean anything was done incorrectly, but it does mean we need to change our approach. I am not going to rush or guess — I am going to make sure the rest of this is handled safely, and I will talk you through every step.' Maintain eye contact, speak slowly, and allow her to respond before continuing.
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ►
STAGE 1: Stop, Disclose, and Reassure

"Sharon, I need to stop for a moment and let you know what has just happened. The crown — the visible part — of the tooth has broken away during the extraction. I want to be completely honest with you about that. This is a recognised complication, particularly when a tooth has been as heavily decayed as this one, and it does not mean you have done anything wrong or that I have. What it does mean is that the roots of the tooth are still sitting in your jaw, and we need to remove them — but we need to use a different, more careful approach to do that safely. You are still fully numb right now, so you should not be feeling any pain. Are you okay? Do you have any questions before I explain what we do next?"

Place fresh gauze over the socket. Maintain calm, unhurried body language. Allow the patient to respond. Do not move on until she signals she has understood and is ready to continue. Document the time and nature of the complication in the clinical notes immediately.

STAGE 2: Clinical Assessment

"Before I explain the plan, I just need to have a careful look at the X-ray again and check the socket — that will help me give you the most accurate information about what we are dealing with."

Review the radiograph: note three divergent, bulbous roots; apices in close proximity to the maxillary sinus floor; no periapical pathology; no hypercementosis. Examine the socket under good light: assess for visible root stumps, mobility of any fragments, and signs of oroantral communication — inspect for visible perforation, ask Sharon whether she has noticed any air or fluid passing through, and ask her not to blow her nose. Note: no communication is visible at this point, but the anatomy makes it a realistic risk during surgical removal. Record all findings.

STAGE 3: Explain the Plan and Sinus Risk

"Sharon, looking at your X-ray, the roots that remain are curved and have a slightly bulbous shape — a bit like the end of a drumstick — which means they cannot simply be lifted straight out. More importantly, the tips of the roots sit very close to your sinus, which is the air space just above your upper back teeth. Because of that, I want to be upfront: there is a small but real risk that during removal, a tiny opening could form between your mouth and your sinus. If that happens, the way we manage it depends on how large it is — a very small one, we can usually manage here with a careful stitch and some simple precautions; a larger one would need a specialist to repair. I am not saying it will happen, but I want you to know about it before we go any further. In terms of the next step, I have two options to discuss with you. The first is that I perform a small surgical procedure here today — I would make a tiny cut in the gum, carefully section the roots, and remove them piece by piece. The second option is that I refer you to an oral surgeon who specialises in exactly this kind of procedure. Given the complexity of your root anatomy and the sinus proximity, I want to be honest with you: referral to an oral surgeon is a very reasonable and safe choice, and I would not hesitate to recommend it. What are your thoughts — do you have any questions about either option?"

Allow the patient to ask questions. If she asks about cost: advise that her private health insurance will likely contribute to the gap; provide a written estimate. If she asks about pain after the anaesthetic wears off: recommend alternating ibuprofen 400 mg and paracetamol 500–1000 mg every four hours as needed, and advise she can take the first dose before the numbness wears off. If she asks about timeframe for referral: advise you will contact the oral surgeon today given it is a Friday afternoon and she lives two hours away, to arrange the earliest available appointment and provide a covering prescription if needed.

STAGE 4: Consent, Documentation, and Safety Net

"Before we go ahead with whichever option you choose, I want to make sure you understand and agree to the plan — that is really important to me. I am also going to give you a printed sheet with instructions to follow at home, including sinus precautions: please do not blow your nose, do not sneeze with your mouth closed, avoid straws, and avoid smoking for at least two weeks — these things help protect the area while it heals. I will write all of that down for you. Because you have a two-hour drive home, I also want to make sure you have our after-hours contact number. If you notice any air or fluid coming through the socket, any bleeding from your nose, or if the pain is not controlled with the tablets I have recommended, please call us or go to your nearest emergency department. You should not be driving if you feel unwell — is there someone who can drive you home today?"

Document in the clinical notes: nature and time of complication, radiographic findings, socket examination findings, management plan discussed, risks explained including oroantral communication, patient's questions and responses, verbal informed consent obtained, and safety net provided. If referring: write a detailed referral letter including the radiograph, the complication, the clinical findings, the patient's medical history (blood pressure medication, controlled), and the urgency. If proceeding surgically: obtain written consent before commencing.

PQ-7
Replacement Options After a Posterior Extraction
Station 6  |  Past Questions
■ Cluster 3 — Evaluation & Treatment Planning

CANDIDATE BRIEF

47 years old lady a new patient in your practice she is a regular dental attendee. You have done some scaling and taken xray; you inform the patient they don't have any new cavities and her gums are healthy. Then she casually asks what replacement options are there for the gap between 34 and 36 (missing 35) present between her teeth. Intraoral picture and Xray of left side given showing gap is small or sometimes normal gap as well. On x-ray 36 has under filled RCT and metallic cap. Management and Replacement options.

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

Stage 1 — Focused History (0–2 min)

Confirm reason for extraction (vertical root fracture of 35), healing status (4 weeks, uneventful), condition of adjacent teeth 34 and 36, medical history (hypertension, Perindopril), and patient priorities: function, aesthetics, longevity, and cost. INFLECTION 1 — Candidate must identify that 34 and 36 are minimally restored before recommending a bridge, as this changes the risk-benefit calculus significantly.

Stage 2 — Explain the 'Do Nothing' Option and Its Consequences (2–4 min)

Clearly explain that leaving the gap untreated is a valid short-term choice but risks over-eruption of the opposing tooth (45), drifting and tilting of 34 and 36, bone loss in the ridge, and progressive difficulty chewing on the left side.

Stage 3 — Present Three Replacement Options (4–8 min)

Implant (best longevity, no adjacent tooth preparation, surgical, costly ~$4,000–$6,000, 6–9 month timeline). Fixed bridge (fixed, predictable, 2–3 appointments, requires preparation of sound adjacent teeth, hygiene demands). Removable partial denture (affordable, non-invasive, but removable and often poorly tolerated). INFLECTION 2 — Candidate must not recommend bridge without acknowledging the irreversible sacrifice of two minimally restored teeth — examiners penalise omission of this ethical point.

Stage 4 — Shared Decision-Making and Next Steps (8–10 min)

Explore patient values (she wants longevity and function, is cost-conscious, dislikes dentures). Recommend radiographic assessment (OPG or CBCT) to confirm bone volume for implant planning. Provide written information and offer a follow-up appointment. Check understanding and invite questions.

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Takes focused history confirming extraction cause, healing, adjacent tooth status, medical history, and patient concerns before presenting options
  2. ✅ Explains consequences of no replacement — over-eruption of opposing tooth, drifting/tilting of adjacent teeth, bone resorption, and functional loss
  3. ✅ Presents all three options (implant, fixed bridge, RPD) with balanced advantages and disadvantages including cost, timeframe, and invasiveness in Australian context
  4. ✅ Highlights that bridge preparation involves irreversible reduction of two minimally restored (sound) teeth — a key ethical and clinical consideration
  5. ✅ Guides shared decision-making by exploring patient values, acknowledges her dislike of dentures, and recommends radiographic assessment as a clear next step for implant planning
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • The implant option is generally considered the gold standard for single tooth replacement because it preserves the adjacent teeth, maintains bone volume, and has a reported survival rate of over 95% at ten years with good oral hygiene.
  • A three-unit fixed bridge would use teeth 34 and 36 as abutments — however, because both of those teeth are minimally restored and otherwise healthy, we would need to permanently reduce them by approximately 1.5 to 2 millimetres circumferentially to accommodate the bridge crowns, which is an irreversible step worth considering carefully.
  • If we leave the space untreated, the opposing lower premolar — tooth 45 — can begin to over-erupt within six to twelve months, and the adjacent teeth 34 and 36 may drift or tilt, which can make future replacement more complex and costly.
  • Before confirming implant suitability, I would want to arrange a CBCT or at minimum a current OPG to assess the available bone height and width at the 35 site, as well as the proximity of the inferior alveolar nerve.
  • Your Perindopril for blood pressure is not a contraindication to implant surgery, but I would liaise with your GP and ensure your blood pressure is well controlled on the day of any surgical procedure.
Curveball Deflectors
  • Patient says: 'Can't you just do the bridge? It sounds simpler and cheaper than an implant.' → Acknowledge her preference and validate that a bridge is a very reasonable option. Then clearly explain the trade-off: 'A bridge is a great fixed solution and I completely understand the appeal. The one thing I want you to be aware of is that to make the bridge, we would need to permanently shave down your teeth on either side of the gap — teeth that are currently in very good shape. Once we do that, those teeth will always need a crown. It's not a decision we can undo, so I want to make sure you have all the information before we decide. That said, if after hearing everything you feel the bridge is right for you, it is absolutely a clinically sound choice.'
  • Candidate jumps straight into listing options without taking any history, or recommends implant without mentioning the need for radiographic bone assessment. → Pause and redirect: always take a brief focused history first to confirm healing, adjacent tooth condition, and patient priorities — this is explicitly on the rubric. For implants, always state that a CBCT or OPG is required to assess bone volume and anatomy before confirming suitability. Skipping either step will cost marks even if the option descriptions are otherwise accurate.
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ►
STAGE 1: Focused History

"That's a great question and I'm really glad you brought it up — it's something we should definitely plan for together. Before I go through the options, do you mind if I ask you a few quick questions so I can give you the most relevant advice? Can you tell me a little about what happened to that tooth — when was it taken out and why?"

Listen for: extraction four weeks ago due to vertical root fracture of tooth 35, uneventful healing, no pain or swelling. Confirm adjacent teeth 34 and 36 are minimally restored. Note medical history — hypertension managed with Perindopril 5 mg, no allergies. Explore patient priorities: she wants something that lasts, restores chewing, and is not a removable plate. Note private health cover with $1,500 annual limit.

STAGE 2: Explain the 'Do Nothing' Option

"The first thing I want to mention is that leaving the gap as it is — at least for now — is an option, but it does come with some risks over time. The tooth directly above the gap in your upper jaw can slowly drift downward to fill the space, which can cause bite problems. The teeth on either side of the gap can also tilt inward. And the bone underneath the gum in that area can gradually shrink away. None of this happens overnight, but it does make replacing the tooth harder and more expensive down the track. So I'd encourage us to make a plan sooner rather than later."

Ensure patient understands the consequences of non-replacement: over-eruption of opposing tooth 45, mesial tipping of 36, distal tipping of 34, alveolar bone resorption, and progressive functional loss on the left side.

STAGE 3: Present the Three Replacement Options

"There are three main ways we can replace that tooth, and I'll walk you through each one so you can decide what feels right for you. The first option is a dental implant. This is where we place a small titanium screw into the jawbone — it acts like an artificial root — and then attach a crown on top. It looks and feels like a natural tooth, it doesn't involve touching the teeth on either side, and it's the option with the best long-term track record — we're talking fifteen or more years with good care. The downside is that it involves a minor surgical procedure, it takes around six to nine months from start to finish, and the cost is typically in the range of four to six thousand dollars, which may not be fully covered by your health fund. I would also need to take a special scan first to check that there's enough bone in that area to support the implant safely. The second option is a fixed bridge. This is a false tooth that's permanently attached to the teeth on either side — so it's fixed in, you can't take it out, and it restores your chewing really well. It's usually completed in two or three appointments and is generally less expensive than an implant. The important thing to know is that to make the bridge, we would need to permanently reshape the teeth on either side of the gap — your teeth 34 and 36 — by trimming them down to fit the bridge over the top. Those teeth are currently in very good shape with only small fillings, so that's an irreversible step, and it's something I want you to weigh up carefully. You'd also need to use a special floss threader to clean underneath the bridge each day. The third option is a removable partial denture — a plate that clips in and out. It's the most affordable option and doesn't involve any preparation of your other teeth. However, I know you mentioned you're not keen on a plate, and that's a very common feeling. They can feel bulky, and some people find them less comfortable for chewing compared to the fixed options."

Tailor language to patient's stated concerns. Acknowledge her dislike of dentures without dismissing the option. Avoid recommending bridge without flagging the irreversible tooth preparation of minimally restored teeth.

STAGE 4: Shared Decision-Making and Next Steps

"You asked which option lasts longest — and honestly, a well-placed implant with good oral hygiene has the best long-term evidence behind it. You also asked whether you'll be able to chew properly again — and yes, absolutely, all three options will restore your chewing function, though the fixed options tend to feel the most natural. Given that you want something that lasts, you're not keen on a plate, and your teeth on either side are in great condition, the implant would be my recommendation to explore first. What I'd suggest as a next step is arranging a scan — either a dental CT or a panoramic X-ray — so we can confirm there's enough bone there to support an implant safely. I can also give you a written cost estimate and a referral to an oral surgeon or implant dentist if you'd like a specialist opinion. Does that sound like a reasonable plan? And please — do you have any questions about anything I've covered?"

Summarise next steps: OPG or CBCT for bone assessment, written treatment plan with cost estimates for all three options, referral if appropriate. Check patient understanding. Document discussion in clinical notes. Confirm follow-up appointment.

PQ-8
Congenital Syphilis Presenting in a Child
Station 7  |  Past Questions
■ Cluster 1 — History & Risk Factors

CANDIDATE BRIEF

Stevie is an 8 year old patient at your clinic, visiting today with her foster carer. Carer is mainly concerned about the appearance of her teeth. You examined her and took the picture and gave the diagnosis of congenital syphilis with motor skill problems, eye sight and hearing issues. Explain the necessary investigation and address concern.

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

Stage 1 — Introduction & Rapport (0–1 min)

Greet both Stevie and the foster carer by name. Acknowledge Stevie at her level ('Hi Stevie, I'm going to talk with your carer for a bit, is that okay?'). Confirm the carer's main concern is the appearance of the teeth. Establish a calm, unhurried tone.

Stage 2 — Focused History (1–4 min)

Ask about pregnancy and antenatal care: number of visits, country of origin, any screening tests. Ask about birth history and early childhood: skin rashes as a baby, eye or hearing concerns, motor development. INFLECTION 1 — Candidate must connect limited antenatal care and refugee background to absent syphilis screening without making assumptions or stigmatising.

Stage 3 — Explain Dental Findings & Diagnosis (4–7 min)

Describe Hutchinson's incisors (notched, screwdriver-shaped central incisors) and mulberry molars as specific patterns seen in congenital syphilis. Explain in plain language: 'These tooth shapes are caused by an infection called syphilis that can pass from a mother to her baby during pregnancy — it is not anything Stevie did, and it is not contagious now.' INFLECTION 2 — Candidate must avoid blaming the biological mother and must not imply current sexual risk.

Stage 4 — Investigations & Referral (7–9 min)

Explain need for blood tests (serology) and urgent referral to a paediatric infectious diseases specialist. Mention eye and hearing review. Raise family screening and public health notification sensitively and confidentially.

Stage 5 — Close & Safety Net (9–10 min)

Summarise next steps clearly. Provide written information if available. Invite questions. Reassure carer that the dental team will support Stevie throughout.

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Correctly identifies and names Hutchinson's incisors (notched, screwdriver-shaped permanent central incisors) and mulberry molars as pathognomonic stigmata of congenital syphilis
  2. ✅ Takes a sensitive antenatal and birth history, identifying absent syphilis screening due to limited antenatal care in a refugee context
  3. ✅ Explains the diagnosis in plain, non-judgmental language — emphasising congenital transmission (mother to baby during pregnancy) and that it is not the child's or carer's fault
  4. ✅ Arranges urgent referral to paediatric infectious diseases for serological confirmation (VDRL, TPHA/FTA-ABS), systemic assessment, and treatment
  5. ✅ Sensitively raises the need for family/contact screening and mandatory public health notification under Australian communicable disease legislation
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • Hutchinson's incisors are pathognomonic of congenital syphilis — they appear as notched, barrel- or screwdriver-shaped permanent central incisors due to Treponema pallidum disrupting ameloblast function during tooth development.
  • Mulberry molars — hypoplastic first permanent molars with multiple poorly formed cusps — together with Hutchinson's incisors form Hutchinson's triad when combined with interstitial keratitis and eighth nerve deafness.
  • Congenital syphilis is a notifiable condition under Australian public health legislation; the treating clinician has a mandatory obligation to notify the relevant state or territory health department.
  • Serological confirmation requires both a non-treponemal test (VDRL or RPR) and a treponemal-specific test (TPHA or FTA-ABS); a reactive result in a child over 18 months is diagnostic of congenital syphilis rather than passive maternal antibody transfer.
  • Penicillin G remains the treatment of choice for congenital syphilis per Australian STI Management Guidelines; dosing and duration are determined by the paediatric infectious diseases team based on clinical staging.
Curveball Deflectors
  • Foster carer becomes distressed and says: 'Are you saying her mother had an STI? That's disgusting — I knew she was neglected.' → Acknowledge the carer's distress calmly: 'I can hear this is upsetting. What I want to make clear is that syphilis during pregnancy can happen to anyone, and many women have no symptoms at all. Without routine antenatal screening — which Stevie's mum may not have had access to — it can go undetected. This is not about neglect; it is about a gap in healthcare. Our focus right now is making sure Stevie gets the right care.' Redirect to the child's wellbeing and avoid reinforcing stigma.
  • Candidate attempts to prescribe antibiotics or arrange treatment themselves rather than referring. → The dentist's role is limited to identifying the dental stigmata, explaining the likely diagnosis, and making an urgent referral to paediatric infectious diseases. Treatment of congenital syphilis — including systemic penicillin G — must be initiated and supervised by a paediatrician or infectious diseases specialist after serological confirmation and full systemic assessment. The candidate should clearly state: 'This is beyond what I can manage in the dental clinic — I am going to arrange an urgent referral today so Stevie can be seen by the right specialist as soon as possible.'
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ►
STAGE 1: Introduction & Rapport

"Hi there, I'm Dr [Name], one of the dentists here. You must be Stevie — it's really nice to meet you. And thank you for bringing her in today. Can I check — you're Stevie's foster carer? Lovely, thank you. Stevie, I'm going to have a little chat with your carer first, and then I'd love to talk to you too, okay? You're not in any trouble at all — we just want to make sure your teeth are being looked after really well."

Establish eye contact with both child and carer. Seat the carer at the same level. Note Stevie's comfort and ensure she feels safe. Confirm the carer's primary concern is the appearance of the teeth.

STAGE 2: Focused History

"Thank you for sharing that with me. I'd like to ask a few background questions — some of them might seem a little unusual for a dental visit, but they'll help me understand what's going on with Stevie's teeth. Is that okay? Do you know anything about Stevie's early life — was she born in Australia? Do you know whether her mum had any check-ups during the pregnancy, or whether any blood tests were done? And when Stevie was a baby, did she have any skin rashes that came and went? Has anyone ever mentioned concerns about her eyesight or hearing? I understand you may not have all of this information, and that's completely fine — anything you can share is helpful."

Listen actively. Note: limited antenatal care, refugee background, no syphilis screening, resolved infantile skin rashes, left eye keratitis scar, right ear hearing difficulty. Do not express alarm. Document responses carefully.

STAGE 3: Explaining the Findings & Diagnosis

"Thank you — that's really helpful. I want to explain what I've found in Stevie's mouth, and I want to be honest with you because I think you deserve to know. Stevie's front teeth have a very specific shape — they're notched at the edge and slightly narrower in the middle, a bit like a screwdriver. Her back teeth also have an unusual bumpy surface. These are very particular patterns that dentists are trained to recognise, and they tell us something important about what happened before Stevie was born. These tooth shapes are caused by an infection called syphilis — it's a bacterial infection that can pass from a mother to her baby during pregnancy, often without the mother even knowing she has it, especially if she didn't have the chance to have routine blood tests during pregnancy. I want to be very clear: this is absolutely not anything Stevie has done, it is not contagious now, and it is not your fault or her mum's fault. It is something that happened before she was born, and the good news is that it is well understood and there is help available."

Pause after delivering the diagnosis. Allow the carer to respond. Maintain calm, warm eye contact. Be prepared for an emotional reaction. Do not rush to the next step.

STAGE 4: Investigations, Referral & Next Steps

"What I'd like to do today is arrange for Stevie to see a specialist — a children's doctor who specialises in infections — as soon as possible, ideally this week. They will do a simple blood test to confirm everything, and they will check that Stevie's whole body is healthy, including her eyes and ears, which you mentioned have had some concerns. If treatment is needed, they will organise that too — it is very effective. I also need to let you know that because this is a notifiable condition in Australia, I have a responsibility to inform the public health team — this is completely confidential and routine, and it is done to make sure anyone who may need support is offered it. It is not about getting anyone into trouble. I will write a referral letter today marked urgent, and I will give you a copy. Do you have any questions for me right now? And Stevie — you've been so patient. You're doing really well."

Write urgent referral to paediatric infectious diseases. Notify state/territory public health unit as per mandatory notification requirements. Arrange dental follow-up for restorative management of Hutchinson's incisors and mulberry molars. Provide written summary for the carer. Document all findings and actions in the patient record.

PQ-9
Patient Mid-RCT Requesting Extraction Instead
Station 8  |  Past Questions
■ Cluster 1 — History & Risk Factors

CANDIDATE BRIEF

Mr Argenti is attending your clinic today and complaining of severe pain coming from one of the tooth on the top left side. You have taken the opg and you can see that some teeth have been Root canal treated few months ago. Patient is very angry and would like to remove these teeth. Give your differentials and explain the necessary investigations and explain extraction option.

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

Stage 1 — Acknowledge and Settle (0–1 min)

Greet Mr Argenti warmly, acknowledge his pain and frustration without judgement. Confirm his identity and which tooth is being discussed. INFLECTION 1 — Candidate must resist the urge to immediately defend RCT; listening first is what separates a pass from a fail.

Stage 2 — Focused History (1–3 min)

Confirm current symptoms: Is the tooth still painful or has it settled? When did pain return or worsen? Explore reason for change of mind — cost, fear, a friend's experience, time off work. Confirm medical history and any contraindications to extraction or RCT.

Stage 3 — Explain Consequences of Extraction (3–5 min)

Explain that extraction is a valid choice but outline the downstream effects: tooth drifting, over-eruption of opposing tooth, bone loss, and the need for a replacement. Present implant, bridge, and denture as options with realistic cost and time comparisons. INFLECTION 2 — Candidate must not omit replacement options; leaving a gap without discussion is a rubric failure point.

Stage 4 — Present RCT Option Fairly (5–7 min)

Explain that the tooth is structurally sound and a good candidate for completion of RCT. Clarify realistic prognosis, number of appointments, and cost. Address the friend's story with evidence-based reassurance — modern RCT has a high success rate when completed properly.

Stage 5 — Shared Decision and Safety Net (7–8 min)

Respect autonomy, confirm his decision, and arrange a clear next step — either book next RCT visit or schedule extraction. Warn that leaving the temporary dressing indefinitely is not safe. Document the discussion.

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Takes focused history to identify current symptoms and the specific reason for change of mind (cost, fear, friend's story, time)
  2. ✅ Explains consequences of extraction: drifting, over-eruption, bone loss, and mandatory need for replacement
  3. ✅ Discusses all three replacement options (implant, bridge, denture) with realistic cost and complexity comparisons
  4. ✅ Warns that leaving the tooth with a temporary dressing long-term is unsafe due to seal breakdown and risk of reinfection or fracture
  5. ✅ Presents a balanced, non-coercive choice between completing RCT and extraction, then confirms a clear interim management plan regardless of the patient's decision
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • A temporary dressing such as Cavit or IRM has a clinical lifespan of approximately four to six weeks — beyond that, microleakage significantly increases the risk of recontamination of the root canal system and potential vertical root fracture.
  • Studies consistently show that root canal treatment has a success rate of approximately 85–95% when completed to a high standard in a tooth with no pre-existing periapical pathology — which is the situation we have here.
  • Following extraction of an upper molar without replacement, the opposing lower molar can begin to over-erupt within six to twelve months, and adjacent teeth will drift, compromising the occlusion and making future replacement more complex and expensive.
  • An implant to replace a single upper molar in Australia typically costs between $4,500 and $6,500 all-inclusive — significantly more than the $2,400 quoted for completing RCT and a crown on the existing tooth.
Curveball Deflectors
  • Patient says: 'My friend had root canal done three times on the same tooth and it still got pulled out — they always fail.' → Acknowledge the friend's experience genuinely: 'That sounds really frustrating for your friend, and I completely understand why that's made you nervous.' Then reframe with evidence: 'What I can tell you is that when root canal treatment is completed properly on a tooth like yours — which has no infection around the root tip and is structurally sound — the success rate is very high, around 85 to 95 percent. Sometimes treatment does need to be retreated, but that's quite different from it always failing. Your situation is actually a good one — we caught it early and the first visit has already settled your pain.'
  • Candidate mistake: Agreeing to extract without discussing consequences or replacement options. → Before proceeding to extraction, always pause and say: 'Before we make that decision, I want to make sure you have the full picture — not to talk you out of it, but so you can make the choice that's right for you.' Then cover drifting, over-eruption, bone loss, and replacement costs. Document that the discussion took place. Extraction without this conversation is an informed consent failure and a rubric fail.
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ►
STAGE 1: Acknowledge and Build Rapport

"Mr Argenti, thank you for coming in today. I can hear that you're in a lot of pain and feeling really frustrated — that's completely understandable, and I want to make sure we sort this out for you properly. Before we talk about what to do next, would it be okay if I asked you a few questions so I can understand exactly what's been happening?"

Sit at eye level, maintain open body language, do not immediately defend the previous treatment plan. Allow the patient to feel heard before any clinical discussion begins.

STAGE 2: Focused History
