"Can you tell me — is the tooth that was treated still hurting you right now, or has the pain actually settled since your last visit? ... And when did you start feeling like you wanted to take it out instead of finishing the treatment? ... Has anything happened — maybe something a friend said, or a concern about cost or time — that's changed how you're feeling about it?"

Listen actively. Identify the specific driver — cost, fear from a friend's story, time off work, or distrust of the procedure. Confirm medical history: no anticoagulants, no medical contraindications to either extraction or continuing RCT. Note that the tooth is currently asymptomatic following the first visit.

STAGE 3: Address Concerns and Explain Consequences of Extraction

"I really appreciate you being honest with me about that. Extraction is absolutely an option — it's your tooth and your choice, and I will support whatever you decide. But I'd be doing you a disservice if I didn't explain what happens after the tooth comes out, so you can make a fully informed decision. When we remove an upper back tooth, the tooth below it — which no longer has anything to bite against — can slowly drift upward out of the gum over the following months. The teeth on either side can also tilt into the gap. Over time, this changes your bite and can make chewing harder. It also means that if you ever want to replace the tooth later, it becomes more complicated and more expensive. The three main options for replacement are a dental implant, a bridge, or a denture. An implant is the closest thing to a natural tooth, but in Australia it typically costs between four and six thousand dollars all up, and it takes several months to complete. A bridge involves crowning the teeth on either side, which means we're cutting into healthy tooth structure. A denture is the most affordable option but it's removable and some people find it less comfortable. So while extraction costs less today, the total cost over time is often higher — and that's something I want you to factor in."

Use the OPG to point out the tooth in question and the adjacent and opposing teeth. Keep language simple. Pause and check understanding before moving on.

STAGE 4: Present RCT Option and Address Friend's Story

"Now, I also want to address what your friend told you — because I think that's really important. Root canal treatment does sometimes get a bad reputation, and I understand why. But what I can tell you is that your situation is actually a very good one. Your tooth has no infection around the root tip, it's structurally sound, and the first visit has already settled your pain — which tells us the treatment is working. When root canal treatment is completed properly on a tooth like this, the success rate is around 85 to 95 percent. That's a very good outcome for keeping your own tooth. I also want to be honest with you about one thing: the temporary filling we placed is designed to last a few weeks, not months. If we leave it too long without either completing the treatment or extracting the tooth, the seal can break down, bacteria can get back in, and we could end up with a more serious infection. So whatever you decide, we do need to make a plan today — we can't leave things as they are indefinitely."

Avoid being defensive or dismissive of the friend's experience. Use evidence-based language. Clearly communicate the risk of inaction — this is a patient safety point and a rubric requirement.

STAGE 5: Shared Decision and Clear Next Step

"So, to summarise your options: we can complete the root canal treatment — probably one or two more appointments — and then place a crown to protect the tooth long-term. Or, if after hearing all of this you still feel that extraction is the right choice for you, we can arrange that and talk about replacement options when you're ready. There's no wrong answer here — I just want to make sure you're choosing with the full picture. What are your thoughts? Do you have any questions about anything I've said?"

Document the conversation in the clinical notes, including that risks and alternatives were discussed and that the patient was given the opportunity to ask questions. Book the next appointment — either for RCT continuation or extraction — before the patient leaves. Do not allow the tooth to remain in limbo with a temporary dressing and no follow-up plan.

PQ-10
Peg Lateral Incisor — Explain and Plan
Station 9  |  Past Questions
■ Cluster 2 — Balanced (History informs management)

CANDIDATE BRIEF

Miss Nguyen is a new patient at your clinic, attending today complaining about the appearance of her front tooth. She works in the pub and her partner thinks she has vampire tooth. MH; patient has anxiety in general and taking diazepam 10mg twice/day. Diagnose and manage patient concern.

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

Stage 1 — Rapport and Concern Elicitation (0–2 min)

Greet Miss Nguyen warmly. Ask open-ended questions: "Can you tell me in your own words what's been bothering you about your smile?" Acknowledge her self-consciousness without minimising it. Note her anxiety and diazepam use — adopt a calm, reassuring tone throughout. INFLECTION 1 — Recognising bilateral involvement (12 and 22) changes the treatment scope and cost conversation significantly.

Stage 2 — Explanation of the Condition (2–4 min)

Explain in plain language: "Your lateral incisors — the teeth just beside your two front teeth — didn't fully develop to their normal size. This is called a peg lateral incisor. It's a developmental variation, not caused by anything you did, and it's quite common. It has nothing to do with your oral hygiene." Confirm no pathology on radiographs.

Stage 3 — Treatment Options (4–8 min)

Present three options in order of invasiveness: (1) Composite resin build-up — conservative, reversible, minimal preparation, ~$200–$400/tooth; (2) Porcelain veneers — superior aesthetics, 10–15 year longevity, minimal irreversible enamel reduction, ~$1,500–$2,500/tooth; (3) Crowns — not indicated here due to excessive tooth reduction required. INFLECTION 2 — Recommending crowns for peg laterals is a common error; examiners will penalise this.

Stage 4 — Shared Decision-Making and Safety Netting (8–10 min)

Address her concern about damaging teeth directly. Recommend composite as a reversible first step. Acknowledge her insurance may assist. Offer a written treatment plan and a follow-up appointment. Given her diazepam use, note that anxiolysis is already managed medically but ensure she has support attending appointments.

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Identifies bilateral peg lateral incisors (12 and 22) as a developmental anomaly — not disease or neglect
  2. ✅ Notes diazepam 10mg BD for anxiety and adapts communication style accordingly — calm, unhurried, non-alarmist
  3. ✅ Presents composite resin build-up as the conservative, reversible, first-line option with approximate Australian cost range
  4. ✅ Explains porcelain veneers accurately — minimal but irreversible enamel reduction, 10–15 year longevity — and correctly excludes full crowns as disproportionate
  5. ✅ Involves patient in shared decision-making, directly addresses fear of damaging natural teeth, and offers a follow-up treatment planning appointment
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • Peg lateral incisors result from a developmental anomaly of the permanent dentition — the tooth bud fails to fully differentiate, producing a conical or peg-shaped crown with normal root morphology.
  • Composite resin build-up for peg laterals is considered additive and reversible — no enamel preparation is required in most cases, preserving the full biological width of the natural tooth.
  • Porcelain veneers require approximately 0.3–0.5 mm of enamel reduction on the labial surface — this is irreversible but minimal, and the preparation is typically confined to enamel.
  • Full coverage crowns are contraindicated as a primary treatment for peg lateral incisors in otherwise healthy dentitions due to the disproportionate sacrifice of sound tooth structure.
  • Diazepam 10mg BD is a Schedule 4 medication in Australia; the candidate should note the patient's existing anxiolytic management and consider its implications for appointment scheduling and informed consent capacity.
Curveball Deflectors
  • Patient asks: 'Will veneers ruin my teeth? I've heard they grind them down to nothing.' → Validate the concern: 'That's a really common worry and it's great you asked. For veneers, we remove a very thin layer — about the thickness of a contact lens — from the front surface only. We keep as much of your natural tooth as possible. Compare that to a crown, which we wouldn't recommend here, where we'd need to remove much more. Composite build-up actually requires no removal at all, which is why I'd suggest starting there.'
  • Candidate recommends full crowns as the treatment of choice for peg lateral incisors. → Redirect immediately — crowns require circumferential preparation removing 60–70% of tooth structure and are disproportionate for a tooth with normal root morphology and no caries. The correct escalation is composite → veneer, not crown. Examiners will specifically penalise crown recommendation as a first-line option here.
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ►
STAGE 1: Rapport and History

"Hi Miss Nguyen, I'm Dr [Name] — lovely to meet you. Please make yourself comfortable. I understand you've come in today because something about your smile has been bothering you. Before we look at anything, I'd love to hear from you — can you tell me in your own words what's been on your mind?"

Listen actively. Allow her to describe the 'vampire tooth' concern without interruption. Acknowledge: "I completely understand why that would affect your confidence — and I want you to know this is something we can absolutely help with." Confirm medical history: note diazepam 10mg twice daily for anxiety. Adopt a calm, unhurried tone. Ask about parafunctional habits (grinding, clenching), previous dental trauma, and smoking. Confirm she is a non-smoker with no allergies.

STAGE 2: Explaining the Condition

"So what I can see — and what the X-rays confirm — is that the two teeth on either side of your front teeth, called your lateral incisors, didn't fully develop to their normal size. This is called a peg lateral incisor. It's a developmental variation — a bit like how some people have different ear shapes — and it has absolutely nothing to do with your oral hygiene or anything you've done. The roots underneath are completely normal and healthy. It's actually quite common, and the good news is it's very treatable."

Use a mirror or diagram to show her which teeth are affected. Confirm bilateral involvement (teeth 12 and 22). Reassure her there is no decay, no infection, and no urgent clinical concern — this is purely a cosmetic issue she has every right to address.

STAGE 3: Treatment Options

"There are a few ways we can improve the appearance of these teeth, and I want to walk you through them so you can decide what feels right for you. The first option — and the one I'd suggest starting with — is a composite build-up. That's where we use a tooth-coloured material, similar to a filling, and carefully shape it around your existing tooth to make it look like a full-sized tooth. The great thing is we don't need to drill or remove any of your natural tooth at all. It's completely reversible, and in Australia it typically costs around $200 to $400 per tooth. The result looks very natural and can last several years with good care. The second option is a porcelain veneer — a very thin ceramic shell that's custom-made and bonded to the front of the tooth. This gives an excellent, long-lasting result — usually 10 to 15 years — but it does require us to remove a very thin layer of enamel from the front surface, about the thickness of a contact lens. That part is permanent, so it's a bigger commitment. Cost-wise, you're looking at around $1,500 to $2,500 per tooth. I'd generally recommend starting with composite to see how you feel about the result before considering veneers. I wouldn't recommend a full crown here — that would involve removing far more of your natural tooth than is necessary, and it's simply not needed in your situation."

Pause and check understanding. Invite questions. Note that her private health insurance may provide a rebate for composite restorations — advise her to check her extras cover. Do not recommend crowns.

STAGE 4: Shared Decision-Making and Close

"I know this is a lot to take in, and there's absolutely no pressure to decide anything today. My recommendation would be to start with the composite build-up — it protects your natural teeth, it's affordable, and if you love the result, that might be all you need. If down the track you want something more permanent, veneers are always an option. I'll put together a written treatment plan for you to take home and look over. Do you have any questions about anything I've mentioned? And is there anything else about the appointment or the process that you'd like me to explain?"

Offer a follow-up treatment planning appointment. Given her anxiety and diazepam use, confirm she has transport home if needed and that appointments can be kept short and comfortable. Document the discussion in the clinical notes including options presented, patient concerns addressed, and that shared decision-making was undertaken. If orthodontic space closure is relevant (diastema present), note a referral to orthodontics could be discussed, but this is not the primary concern today.

PQ-11
Generalised Periodontitis With Replacement Options
Station 10  |  Past Questions
■ Cluster 2 — Balanced (History informs management)

CANDIDATE BRIEF

Miss Luiz is a 55 yr old patient, attending your clinic today complaining of pain, bleeding gums and mobility of left lateral incisor (22). OPG given with boneless around most of the teeth and lateral has boneless up to 90%. Perio chart provided with probing depth of 7-8mm around some of the teeth. MH: she is taking thyroxine for hypothyroidism, bone pain and coeliac disease and taking calcium, vitamin D for bone. Patient wanted to know about replacement option and how we can prevent these long term.

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

Stage 1 — Establish rapport and confirm concerns (0–2 min)

Greet Miss Luiz, confirm her presenting complaints (pain, bleeding, mobile tooth 22), and acknowledge her concerns about keeping her teeth. Confirm medical history: hypothyroidism (thyroxine), coeliac disease, calcium and vitamin D supplementation. INFLECTION 1 — Recognise that coeliac disease and hypothyroidism can impair bone metabolism and healing; this affects prognosis and implant planning.

Stage 2 — Explain diagnosis using OPG and perio chart (2–5 min)

Use the OPG to show generalised bone loss. Explain that tooth 22 has 90% bone loss and Grade 3 mobility — it cannot be saved and must be extracted. Explain that several other teeth have 7–8 mm pockets indicating active, advanced disease. Use plain language: "The bone that holds your teeth like a fence post in the ground has been dissolving away."

Stage 3 — Address smoking and disease control (5–8 min)

Explain smoking is a major risk factor for periodontitis and implant failure. Offer Quitline referral (13 7848). Outline initial periodontal therapy: full-mouth debridement, oral hygiene instruction, and reassessment at 8–12 weeks. INFLECTION 2 — Candidates who skip disease stabilisation before discussing replacements will lose marks; disease must be controlled first.

Stage 4 — Present replacement options with pros/cons (8–12 min)

Present three options: (1) Removable partial denture — affordable (~$1,500–2,500), non-invasive, but less comfortable and aesthetic; (2) Dental implant — most functional, ~$4,000–6,000 per implant, requires bone volume, smoking cessation, and 6–12 month timeline; (3) No replacement for posterior teeth — acceptable short-term but risks drifting, over-eruption, and chewing difficulty.

Stage 5 — Staged treatment plan and follow-up (12–15 min)

Summarise staged plan: initial therapy → extraction of tooth 22 → healing (8–12 weeks) → interim denture if needed → definitive replacement. Arrange next appointment. Provide written information and answer questions.

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Explains generalised periodontitis in plain language using OPG and perio chart — bone loss described as loss of tooth support
  2. ✅ Identifies tooth 22 (and any other hopeless teeth) as non-restorable due to >90% bone loss and Grade 3 mobility, requiring extraction
  3. ✅ Addresses smoking as a critical modifiable risk factor for periodontal disease and implant failure, and offers Quitline referral (13 7848)
  4. ✅ Outlines staged treatment: initial periodontal therapy and disease stabilisation BEFORE any definitive replacement discussion
  5. ✅ Presents all three replacement options (RPD, implant, no replacement) with realistic pros, cons, and Australian cost estimates, involving patient in shared decision-making
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • Tooth 22 has approximately 90% bone loss with Grade 3 mobility — by definition this tooth is hopeless and extraction is indicated; there is no periodontal or restorative treatment that can predictably retain it.
  • Smokers have a two- to three-fold increased risk of periodontal disease progression and implant failure rates are significantly higher — up to 20% higher than non-smokers — which is why smoking cessation is not optional, it is a prerequisite for implant success.
  • We must stabilise the periodontal disease first — placing an implant into an uncontrolled periodontal environment risks peri-implantitis, which is essentially periodontitis around the implant and can cause implant loss.
  • Coeliac disease can impair calcium and vitamin D absorption, which affects bone density and healing — this is relevant to implant osseointegration and we may need to liaise with her physician before proceeding.
  • The reassessment appointment at 8–12 weeks after active periodontal therapy is critical — we need to see pocket depth reduction and resolution of bleeding on probing before we can classify the disease as stable and plan definitive replacements.
Curveball Deflectors
  • Patient says: 'Can't you just pull the wobbly tooth and put an implant in straight away? I don't want to wait months.' → Acknowledge her frustration and desire for a quick solution. Explain that placing an implant immediately into a mouth with active, uncontrolled periodontitis is like building a house on unstable ground — the infection around the remaining teeth can spread to the implant site and cause it to fail. The 8–12 week stabilisation phase protects her investment and dramatically improves the chance of long-term implant success. Offer an interim partial denture to address aesthetics during the healing phase so she is not without a tooth.
  • Candidate jumps straight to implant discussion without addressing periodontal disease control or smoking first. → This is the most common error in this station. The examiner will likely prompt: 'Is there anything you would want to address before planning the implant?' The correct pivot is to return to disease stabilisation: 'Before we can consider any replacement option, we need to get the gum disease under control — otherwise any replacement we place is at high risk of failing. That means a course of deep cleaning, improving your home care routine, and ideally stopping smoking.'
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ►
STAGE 1: Rapport, History Confirmation, and Diagnosis Explanation

"Miss Luiz, thank you for coming in today. I can see you're having quite a bit of discomfort, and I want to make sure we address everything properly. You've mentioned pain, bleeding gums, and that wobbly front tooth — those are all really important concerns and I'm glad you came in. Before I explain what's going on, can I just confirm a couple of things about your health? You're taking thyroxine for your thyroid, and calcium and vitamin D — is that right? And you mentioned coeliac disease as well?"

Confirm medical history. Note that hypothyroidism and coeliac disease can affect bone metabolism and healing — relevant to prognosis and implant planning. Flag for physician liaison if implants are considered. Now transition to diagnosis using the OPG and perio chart.

"So I've had a good look at your X-ray and the measurements we took of your gum pockets today, and I want to explain what we're seeing. You have a condition called periodontitis — that's a serious gum infection where bacteria living under the gumline have been slowly dissolving the bone that holds your teeth in place. Think of your teeth like fence posts — the bone is the ground they sit in. When that ground erodes away, the posts become loose. On your X-ray, I can see that most of your teeth have lost a significant amount of that supporting bone. The wobbly tooth at the front here — your upper left lateral incisor — has lost about 90% of its bone support. I'm really sorry to tell you this, but that tooth cannot be saved. It will need to come out."

Point to tooth 22 on the OPG. Allow the patient to process this. Acknowledge any emotional response before continuing.

STAGE 2: Smoking, Risk Factors, and Disease Control

"Now, one of the most important things I want to talk to you about is smoking. Smoking is one of the biggest risk factors for gum disease — it reduces the blood supply to your gums, which means your body can't fight the infection as well, and it actually masks the bleeding so the disease can progress silently. It also significantly reduces the success rate of dental implants, which I know you're interested in. I'm not here to lecture you, but I do want to be honest with you — if we're going to invest time and money into saving your teeth and replacing the ones we lose, quitting smoking gives us the best possible chance of that working long-term. There's a free service called Quitline — the number is 13 7848 — and I'd really encourage you to give them a call. I can also refer you to your GP for support."

Document smoking status. Offer written Quitline information. Now explain the treatment sequence — disease control must come before replacement planning.

"Before we can even think about replacing any teeth, we need to get this infection under control. What that means is a course of deep cleaning — we call it periodontal debridement — where we carefully clean under the gumline to remove the bacteria and buildup that are driving the disease. I'll also show you how to clean more effectively at home, because your daily routine is just as important as what we do here. After that, we'll review everything in about eight to twelve weeks to see how your gums have responded. Only once the disease is stable can we safely plan for replacements."

STAGE 3: Replacement Options — Pros, Cons, and Costs

"Now, let's talk about your options for replacing the teeth that need to come out. There are three main paths we can take, and I want to go through each one honestly so you can make the best decision for your situation."

"The first option is a removable partial denture — a plate that you take in and out. The advantages are that it's the most affordable option, usually around fifteen hundred to two thousand five hundred dollars, and it doesn't require surgery. The downside is that some people find them less comfortable, they can feel a bit bulky, and they rely on your remaining teeth for support — which means those teeth need to be healthy."

"The second option is dental implants. These are titanium posts that are placed into the jawbone and act like artificial tooth roots — a crown is then attached on top. They look and feel the most natural, and they don't rely on neighbouring teeth. However, they do require adequate bone volume, they take longer — typically six to twelve months from start to finish — and they cost approximately four thousand to six thousand dollars per implant. Importantly, smoking significantly reduces implant success rates, so quitting would be essential before we go down that path."

"The third option, particularly for the back teeth, is to leave the space. This is sometimes acceptable in the short term, but over time the neighbouring teeth can drift and the tooth above or below can over-erupt into the gap, which can cause bite problems and make future replacement more complicated."

Check patient understanding. Invite questions. Tailor discussion to her concerns about appearance and cost.

STAGE 4: Staged Treatment Plan and Next Steps

"So here's what I'd suggest as a plan, and I want you to be part of this decision. First, we start with the deep cleaning and improving your home care — that's our priority. Once we've extracted the wobbly front tooth, we can fit you with a temporary partial denture straight away so you're not without a tooth while everything heals. After eight to twelve weeks, we reassess your gums. If everything is stable and — ideally — you've been able to cut down or stop smoking, we can then have a much more detailed conversation about whether a denture or implants are the right long-term solution for you. We can also look at costs and timing in a way that works with your budget."

"The most important thing I want you to take away today is that this disease is manageable — but it does require us to work together. With the right treatment, good home care, and regular maintenance visits every three to four months, we can protect the teeth you have and give any replacements the best chance of lasting a long time. Do you have any questions about anything I've explained?"

Provide written treatment plan summary. Book next appointment for full-mouth periodontal debridement and oral hygiene instruction. Provide Quitline brochure. Document all discussions in patient notes including informed consent for extraction of tooth 22.

PQ-12
Management of Dental Trauma in a 12-Year-Old
Station 11  |  Past Questions
■ Cluster 3 — Evaluation & Treatment Planning

CANDIDATE BRIEF

12 year old Girl has injuries during hockey. Didn't wear mouth guard. 11 palatally displaced, 21 fracture to enamel dentin area no expose to the pulp. 11 showed no response to vitality test. No X-ray taken. Manage short- and long-term solution. Patient was insisting for antibiotics.

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

Stage 1 — History & Rapport (0–3 min)

Greet Sarah and her mother by name. Acknowledge pain and anxiety. Take focused trauma history: time of injury, mechanism (hockey stick/ball), mouthguard use, fragment location, pain score, cold sensitivity, lip bleeding. Screen for head injury: loss of consciousness, headache, nausea, vomiting — all negative. Confirm tetanus immunisation current. INFLECTION 1 — Candidate must actively screen for head injury before proceeding; failure to do so is a patient safety error.

Stage 2 — Examination & Radiographs (3–7 min)

Systematic extra-oral exam (face, lip laceration — no sutures needed), then intra-oral: soft tissues, occlusion, mobility (none), percussion (tender 11), sensibility testing. Tooth 11: complicated crown fracture, ~2mm pulp exposure, vital. Tooth 21: uncomplicated crown fracture, enamel-dentine, no pulp exposure. Request periapical ± occlusal radiographs immediately for baseline, root development stage, and to exclude root/alveolar fracture.

Stage 3 — Diagnosis & Treatment (7–15 min)

Explain diagnosis in plain language to both Sarah and her mother. INFLECTION 2 — Candidate must identify this as a complicated crown fracture requiring same-day pulp management, not deferral. Perform Cvek partial pulpotomy on 11 (MTA preferred over calcium hydroxide given evidence base): remove 2mm of coronal pulp, achieve haemostasis, place MTA, restore with GIC/composite. Place dentine-bonded composite on 21 to seal exposed dentine and relieve sensitivity.

Stage 4 — Antibiotics Refusal & Post-Op Instructions (15–18 min)

Decline antibiotics respectfully but firmly — no indication in healthy child with no signs of systemic infection; pulp treatment is definitive management. Prescribe paracetamol (15mg/kg) for analgesia. Soft diet 48 hours, gentle oral hygiene, avoid contact sport until reviewed. Provide written emergency contact details.

Stage 5 — Follow-Up & Prevention (18–20 min)

Schedule review at 6–8 weeks (clinical + radiographic), then 6-monthly until root maturation complete. Monitor for pulp necrosis, inflammatory root resorption, periapical pathology. Strongly recommend custom-fitted mouthguard before return to hockey. Document baseline records thoroughly.

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Screen for head injury (LOC, headache, nausea) before any dental assessment — patient safety priority
  2. ✅ Correctly classify tooth 11 as a complicated crown fracture (pulp exposed) requiring same-day Cvek partial pulpotomy, not watchful waiting
  3. ✅ Correctly classify tooth 21 as an uncomplicated crown fracture — dentine seal with composite/GIC is appropriate immediate management
  4. ✅ Decline antibiotics with a clear, evidence-based explanation: no systemic infection signs, pulp treatment is definitive — antibiotics are not indicated per IADT guidelines
  5. ✅ Arrange periapical ± occlusal radiographs immediately for baseline root development, periapical status, and to exclude root or alveolar fracture, then schedule follow-up at 6–8 weeks and 6-monthly until root maturation
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • Tooth 11 has a complicated crown fracture with pulp exposure — because the apex is still open and the root is immature, a Cvek partial pulpotomy using MTA is the treatment of choice to preserve pulp vitality and allow continued apexogenesis.
  • Calcium hydroxide is an acceptable alternative but MTA is preferred due to superior sealing ability and evidence of better long-term pulp survival in immature permanent teeth.
  • Antibiotics are not indicated here — the IADT guidelines do not recommend prophylactic antibiotics for complicated crown fractures in otherwise healthy patients with no signs of systemic infection or immunocompromise.
  • Follow-up radiographs at 6–8 weeks are essential to assess for pulp canal obliteration, internal or external root resorption, and periapical pathology — these are the early signs of pulp necrosis in a traumatised tooth.
  • If pulp necrosis develops in this immature tooth, the management changes to apexification using MTA or calcium hydroxide, or regenerative endodontic procedures — this is why preserving vitality now is critical.
Curveball Deflectors
  • Mother insists: 'She needs antibiotics — the tooth is exposed and could get infected.' → Acknowledge the concern warmly: 'I completely understand why you're worried — it looks very alarming. The good news is that the best protection against infection is the treatment we're doing right now, which seals the nerve and removes any bacteria. Antibiotics work on infections that have already spread through the body, and Sarah doesn't have any signs of that. Giving antibiotics when they're not needed can actually cause resistance, which makes them less effective when she really needs them in the future. So the safest and most effective plan is the pulp treatment today, not antibiotics.'
  • Candidate considers deferring pulp treatment and just placing a temporary dressing to 'wait and see' if the pulp survives. → This is incorrect for a complicated crown fracture with confirmed pulp exposure. Deferral increases the risk of bacterial contamination of the pulp and subsequent necrosis. IADT guidelines recommend partial pulpotomy as soon as possible — ideally within 24 hours of injury. The candidate should proceed with same-day Cvek pulpotomy, not a watch-and-wait approach.
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ►
STAGE 1: Introduction & Trauma History

"Hi Sarah, my name is Dr [Name] — I'm going to look after you today. I can see you've had a rough afternoon. Before I look at your teeth, I just want to ask you and Mum a few quick questions so I can make sure we help you in the best way. Is that okay?" [Pause, make eye contact with Sarah.] "Sarah, can you tell me what happened? When did it happen, and did anything hit your mouth directly?" [Listens.] "Did you black out at all, even for a second? Any headache, feeling sick, or vomiting since it happened?" [Confirms no LOC, no headache, no nausea.] "Good — that's really reassuring. Are you up to date with your needles, Mum — including tetanus?" [Confirms yes.] "And Sarah, on a scale of zero to ten, how bad is the pain right now?"

Documents: injury at hockey 2 hours ago, no mouthguard worn, fragment not retrieved, pain 6/10 worse with cold air, lip bleeding stopped, no head injury symptoms, tetanus immunisation current. Head injury screen negative — safe to proceed with dental assessment.

STAGE 2: Examination & Radiographs

"Sarah, I'm going to have a gentle look at your face and then inside your mouth. I'll tell you everything I'm doing before I do it, and if anything hurts, just raise your hand and I'll stop straight away. Deal?"

Extra-oral: minor lip laceration, no sutures required, no facial swelling or asymmetry, TMJ normal. Intra-oral: tooth 11 — complicated crown fracture, approximately 2mm pulp exposure visible, pink tissue, tender to percussion, not mobile, responds to sensibility testing (vital). Tooth 21 — uncomplicated crown fracture involving enamel and dentine, no pulp exposure, mild sensitivity. Requests periapical radiograph of 11 and 21 immediately: to assess root development stage (open apex confirmed), periapical status, and exclude root or alveolar fracture. Documents baseline radiographic records.

STAGE 3: Diagnosis Explanation & Treatment

"Okay, so here's what I found. Sarah, the front tooth on your right — this one — has a chip that's gone deep enough to reach the nerve inside. I know that sounds scary, but the nerve is still alive, which is actually great news because it means we can treat it today and give the tooth the best chance of healing properly. What I'm going to do is a special procedure where I gently clean the very top of the nerve, place a special medicated material called MTA — think of it like a healing plug — and then seal the tooth up. This gives the nerve the best chance of staying healthy while your tooth root finishes growing. For the other front tooth, the chip hasn't reached the nerve, so I'll just place a tooth-coloured filling to protect it and stop the sensitivity. Both procedures today — does that sound okay to you both?"

Performs Cvek partial pulpotomy on tooth 11 under local anaesthesia: removes approximately 2mm of coronal pulp tissue with a sterile round bur under copious irrigation, achieves haemostasis with saline-moistened cotton pellet, confirms bleeding controlled within 5 minutes (positive prognostic sign), places MTA over pulp stump, seals with glass ionomer base and composite resin restoration. Places dentine-bonded composite resin on tooth 21 to seal exposed dentine.

STAGE 4: Antibiotics Refusal, Post-Op Instructions & Follow-Up

"I do want to address the antibiotics question — it's a really common and understandable concern. The reason I'm not prescribing them is that Sarah doesn't have any signs of an infection that has spread — no swelling, no fever, no pus. The treatment we've just done is actually the most effective way to prevent infection, because we've sealed the nerve away from bacteria. Giving antibiotics when they're not needed can cause resistance, which means they won't work as well if Sarah ever really needs them. So the best medicine today was the procedure itself. For pain, regular paracetamol — fifteen milligrams per kilogram, up to four times a day — will be plenty. I'd also like Sarah to eat soft foods for the next couple of days, brush gently around those teeth, and avoid any contact sport until we've reviewed her. Here's our after-hours number — please call if the pain gets significantly worse, there's any swelling, or the tooth changes colour. We'll see Sarah back in six to eight weeks for a check-up and X-ray, and then every six months until the root has finished growing. And before she goes back to hockey — we really need to get her fitted for a custom mouthguard. That's the single best thing we can do to prevent this happening again."

Documents all findings, treatment performed, radiographs taken, post-operative instructions given verbally and in writing. Schedules 6–8 week review (clinical and radiographic assessment for pulp canal obliteration, root resorption, periapical pathology). Plans 6-monthly monitoring until apexogenesis complete. Refers for custom mouthguard fabrication. No antibiotics prescribed — IADT guidelines confirm no indication in healthy patient with no systemic infection signs.

PQ-13
Management of Post-Surgical Infection Following Extraction
Station 12  |  Past Questions
■ Cluster 3 — Evaluation & Treatment Planning

CANDIDATE BRIEF

Mrs Joshi is a regular patient at your clinic. You removed her upper left first molar (26) which was badly carious on Monday afternoon and today is Friday afternoon and she booked an emergency appointment, complaining about pain, swelling and bad breath which started 2 days after tooth was removed. After examining her mouth, you are suspecting it's a post-surgical infection. Manage patient's condition, explain the reason and further investigation that needs to be done. MH: Allergic to penicillin.

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

Stage 1 — Focused History (0–3 min)

Greet and acknowledge distress. Establish symptom timeline: extraction Monday, symptoms onset Wednesday (48hrs post-op), now Friday. Ask about swelling progression, fever (37.8°C confirmed), trismus, halitosis, analgesia tried (paracetamol + ibuprofen, minimal relief). Ask about difficulty breathing or swallowing — patient denies both. INFLECTION 1 — Elicit penicillin allergy and diabetes: these two facts completely change antibiotic choice and risk stratification.

Stage 2 — Clinical Examination (3–6 min)

Extra-oral: inspect and palpate left mandibular body and submandibular region — indurated, warm, erythematous, tender swelling. Measure mouth opening (~30mm, mild trismus). Critically assess floor of mouth for elevation and check for dysphagia or stridor — absent. Intra-oral: inspect socket 26 for purulent discharge, inflamed margins, retained debris. INFLECTION 2 — Absence of floor-of-mouth elevation and airway compromise means this can be managed in primary care with close review, not immediate hospital referral — but candidate must explicitly check and document this.

Stage 3 — Diagnosis and Explanation (6–9 min)

Explain post-operative odontogenic infection in plain language. Discuss how diabetes impairs immune response and healing. Advise blood glucose monitoring and GP liaison.

Stage 4 — Treatment and Safety-Netting (9–12 min)

Prescribe metronidazole 400mg TDS 5–7 days (penicillin allergy). Consider local irrigation of socket. Arrange OPG. Review in 24–48 hours. Provide explicit red-flag safety-net: hospital immediately if breathing difficulty, swallowing difficulty, floor-of-mouth swelling, or rapidly worsening trismus.

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Elicits penicillin allergy AND Type 2 diabetes early — both are critical modifiers of management
  2. ✅ Checks for airway compromise, floor-of-mouth elevation, and dysphagia — absence of these determines primary care vs. hospital referral
  3. ✅ Prescribes correct penicillin-alternative antibiotic: metronidazole 400mg TDS or clindamycin 300mg TDS for 5–7 days
  4. ✅ Provides explicit safety-net advice with specific red-flag symptoms requiring emergency hospital attendance
  5. ✅ Discusses diabetes impact on infection/healing and advises blood glucose monitoring and GP liaison
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • Given Mrs Joshi's penicillin allergy, I would prescribe metronidazole 400mg three times daily for five to seven days as my first-line antibiotic — if broader gram-positive coverage is needed, clindamycin 300mg TDS is the alternative.
  • I need to specifically check for floor-of-mouth elevation, dysphagia, and any signs of airway compromise — these would indicate a spreading deep space infection requiring immediate hospital transfer.
  • Diabetes impairs neutrophil function and microvascular perfusion, which means Mrs Joshi is at higher risk of infection progression and delayed healing — her HbA1c of around 7 suggests reasonable but not optimal control.
  • Mild trismus at 30mm opening is consistent with local inflammation and muscle spasm — however, if trismus worsens or she develops any difficulty swallowing or breathing, this becomes a surgical emergency.
  • I would arrange an OPG to exclude a retained root fragment or bony pathology contributing to the infection, and review her in 24 to 48 hours to confirm clinical improvement on antibiotics.
Curveball Deflectors
  • Patient asks: 'Can't you just give me stronger painkillers? Do I really need antibiotics?' → Acknowledge her concern and validate that pain relief is important — continue ibuprofen and paracetamol as she has been taking them. However, explain that the infection itself needs to be treated with antibiotics, not just the pain masked. Without antibiotics, the infection could spread to deeper spaces in the neck, which can become life-threatening. The antibiotics are essential, not optional at this stage.
  • Candidate defaults to prescribing amoxicillin 500mg TDS — the most common wrong answer given the documented penicillin allergy → Stop and correct immediately if caught: 'I need to reconsider — Mrs Joshi has a documented penicillin allergy, and amoxicillin is a penicillin-class antibiotic. Cross-reactivity means I cannot prescribe this. The correct choice is metronidazole 400mg TDS, or clindamycin 300mg TDS if broader coverage is required.' Prescribing amoxicillin to a penicillin-allergic patient is a patient safety failure and a likely automatic fail criterion.
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ►
STAGE 1: Introduction and Focused History

'Mrs Joshi, thank you for coming in today — I can see you're quite uncomfortable and I want to help you as quickly as possible. I understand you had your upper left back tooth removed on Monday and you've been having some problems since then. Can you tell me when the pain and swelling first started? And has it been getting worse over time?'

Establish timeline: extraction Monday, symptoms onset Wednesday (48 hours post-op), presenting Friday — 4 days post-extraction. Ask about nature of swelling, fever — she confirms temperature of 37.8°C this morning. Ask about bad breath, trismus, difficulty opening mouth. Critically ask: 'Are you having any difficulty breathing or swallowing at all?' — patient denies both. Ask about analgesia: paracetamol and ibuprofen with minimal relief. Now take medical history: 'Do you have any medical conditions I should know about?' — elicit Type 2 diabetes on metformin, hypertension on perindopril. 'Do you have any allergies to medications, particularly antibiotics?' — elicit penicillin allergy. This is a critical pivot point.

STAGE 2: Clinical Examination

'I'm going to have a look at you now, both outside and inside your mouth. I'll be as gentle as I can. I need to check the swelling carefully and also make sure the infection hasn't spread anywhere it shouldn't have.'

Extra-oral: inspect and palpate left mandibular body and submandibular region — note indurated, warm, erythematous, tender swelling. Assess mouth opening — approximately 30mm, consistent with mild trismus. Critically palpate floor of mouth — no elevation detected. Ask patient to swallow — no difficulty. Check for lymphadenopathy. Intra-oral: inspect socket 26 — inflamed margins, purulent discharge present. Assess adjacent teeth and soft tissues. Document findings clearly. The absence of floor-of-mouth elevation, dysphagia, and airway compromise confirms this infection can be managed in primary care with close monitoring rather than immediate hospital transfer.

STAGE 3: Diagnosis and Explanation

'Mrs Joshi, I can see what's happening here. You've developed an infection in the area where your tooth was removed. This is called a post-operative infection, and it's something we can treat. The good news is that I've checked carefully and the infection hasn't spread to any dangerous areas — your airway is completely clear and you're breathing normally, which is reassuring. However, because you have diabetes, your body's ability to fight infection is a little reduced, which is likely why this has developed. Diabetes can affect how your immune system responds and how quickly wounds heal. I'd like you to keep a close eye on your blood sugar levels over the next few days and let your GP know what's happening — they may want to review your diabetes management while you're fighting this infection.'

Explain diagnosis in plain language. Validate patient's anxiety while being honest about the need for prompt treatment. Document low-grade fever 37.8°C, mild trismus, purulent discharge, submandibular swelling.

STAGE 4: Treatment Plan, Investigations and Safety-Netting

'I'm going to prescribe you an antibiotic called metronidazole — because you're allergic to penicillin, this is the right choice for you. You'll take 400mg three times a day for seven days. Please take it with food to avoid an upset stomach, and avoid alcohol completely while you're on it. Continue your paracetamol and ibuprofen for pain as you have been. I also want to take an X-ray today to make sure there's nothing left behind in the socket that could be causing the infection. I want to see you back here in 24 to 48 hours to make sure you're improving. Most importantly — if at any point you notice swelling under your tongue or the floor of your mouth, difficulty swallowing, difficulty breathing, or your mouth suddenly becomes much harder to open, I need you to go straight to a hospital emergency department and tell them you have a dental infection. Do not wait for a dental appointment. Do you understand those warning signs? Can you repeat them back to me?'

Prescribe metronidazole 400mg TDS for 7 days — correct choice given penicillin allergy. Consider local socket irrigation with chlorhexidine. Request OPG to exclude retained root fragment or bony pathology. Arrange 24–48 hour review. Document safety-net advice given. Advise blood glucose monitoring and GP liaison regarding diabetes management during infection. Provide written post-operative instructions including red-flag symptoms.

PQ-14
Management of a Patient on Prednisone and Alendronate Requiring Extraction
Station 13  |  Past Questions
■ Cluster 1 — History & Risk Factors

CANDIDATE BRIEF

Mrs William is a 55-year-old patient attended your surgery today, complaining of wobbly tooth and she has been getting pain on 37 tooth for last 10 days. The tooth cannot be saved and needs extraction. Medically she is fit and well, she is taking Actonel tablets of 150mg once a month for osteoporosis condition for the last 4 years. She is also taking Prednisolone 10mg for her rheumatoid arthritis for the last 7 years. Please take consent for extraction and address patients concerns.

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

Stage 1 — Introduction and Medication History (0–2 min)

Greet Mrs William, confirm identity, and take a focused medication history: drug name, dose, frequency, duration, and indication for both Actonel (risedronate 150 mg monthly, 4 years, osteoporosis) and Prednisolone (10 mg daily, 7 years, rheumatoid arthritis). Note concurrent use as a compounding risk factor. INFLECTION 1 — Candidate must name both drugs and their durations accurately; missing either fails the medication history criterion.

Stage 2 — MRONJ Risk Assessment and Explanation (2–4 min)

Explain MRONJ in patient-friendly terms: bisphosphonates slow bone turnover, which can impair healing after dental surgery. Risk with oral bisphosphonates is low (<0.1%) but is elevated by corticosteroid use and therapy duration over 3–4 years. Reassure that risk is manageable, not prohibitive. Address her online concerns directly and honestly.

Stage 3 — Adrenal Suppression and Steroid Cover (4–5 min)

INFLECTION 2 — Candidate must identify that 7 years of Prednisolone 10 mg daily causes HPA axis suppression and that perioperative steroid supplementation is required. Plan: liaise with GP/rheumatologist, consider doubling morning dose on day of extraction for minor oral surgery under local anaesthesia.

Stage 4 — Management Plan and Consent (5–7 min)

Explain extraction is indicated and safe with precautions: atraumatic technique, primary closure, chlorhexidine rinse, prophylactic antibiotics, and possible specialist referral given dual risk factors. Obtain verbal consent after confirming understanding of risks, benefits, and alternatives.

Stage 5 — Post-operative Instructions and Safety Net (7–8 min)

Advise on oral hygiene, avoid smoking and alcohol, review at one week, and return urgently if exposed bone, worsening pain, or delayed healing occurs. Document consent and management plan.

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Identifies both medications by name, dose, duration, and indication — risedronate (Actonel) 150 mg monthly for 4 years AND Prednisolone 10 mg daily for 7 years
  2. ✅ Explains MRONJ risk in plain language: oral bisphosphonate risk is low (<0.1%) but is increased by concurrent corticosteroid use and duration >3–4 years
  3. ✅ Identifies adrenal suppression from chronic Prednisolone use and discusses need for perioperative steroid supplementation in liaison with prescribing doctor
  4. ✅ Outlines risk-mitigated extraction plan: atraumatic technique, primary closure, chlorhexidine rinse, prophylactic antibiotics, and low threshold for oral surgery referral
  5. ✅ Provides clear post-operative safety netting: one-week review, return if exposed bone or delayed healing, and documents informed consent
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • The risk of MRONJ with oral bisphosphonates is estimated at less than 0.1%, but concurrent corticosteroid use and duration of therapy beyond three to four years are recognised risk-elevating factors according to the 2022 AAOMS position paper.
  • Seven years of Prednisolone at 10 mg daily is sufficient to suppress the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis; for minor oral surgery under local anaesthesia, current guidelines recommend doubling the usual morning dose on the day of the procedure after liaising with the prescribing physician.
  • Risedronate is a nitrogen-containing bisphosphonate with a long skeletal half-life; unlike IV bisphosphonates used in oncology, the absolute MRONJ risk with oral formulations remains low, but it is not zero, and the patient must be counselled accordingly before consent is valid.
  • Primary wound closure and an atraumatic surgical technique are the two most evidence-supported intraoperative strategies to reduce MRONJ risk in patients on oral bisphosphonates.
Curveball Deflectors
  • Patient says: 'I read online that I should stop my bone tablets before the extraction — should I do that?' → Acknowledge her concern and validate that she has done her research. Explain that for oral bisphosphonates, the evidence does not clearly support a drug holiday improving outcomes, as risedronate has a very long skeletal half-life and stopping it briefly does not meaningfully reduce bone levels. Advise that any decision to pause medication must be made in consultation with her rheumatologist or GP, not unilaterally, as stopping bisphosphonates also carries a risk of fracture. Do not recommend cessation without specialist input.
  • Candidate omits adrenal suppression and proceeds to consent for extraction without mentioning steroid cover → This is the most common critical error. The examiner may prompt: 'Is there anything else about her medications you would like to address before proceeding?' The correct response is to recognise that 7 years of daily Prednisolone at 10 mg suppresses the HPA axis, that extraction is a surgical stressor, and that failure to provide steroid cover risks an adrenal crisis. The candidate should state they would contact her GP or rheumatologist prior to the procedure to confirm a perioperative steroid supplementation plan.
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ►
STAGE 1: Introduction and Medication History

"Good morning, Mrs William. I'm Dr [Name]. I understand you've been having some pain and your tooth has been feeling loose — I'm sorry to hear that. Before we talk about what we're going to do today, I'd like to ask you a few questions about your health and the medications you're taking, so I can make sure we look after you as safely as possible. Is that okay?"

Confirm: (1) Actonel (risedronate) 150 mg once monthly for osteoporosis, taken for 4 years. (2) Prednisolone 10 mg daily for rheumatoid arthritis, taken for 7 years. Note both are current and compliant. Ask about any other medications, supplements, allergies, and previous dental extractions since starting bisphosphonates.

STAGE 2: Explaining MRONJ Risk

"I can see you've done some reading about a condition called osteonecrosis of the jaw — and I want to be honest with you about that. The bone tablet you're taking, Actonel, works by slowing down the natural process your body uses to remodel bone. That's great for your osteoporosis, but it does mean that if we do dental surgery, the bone in your jaw can sometimes be a little slower to heal. In rare cases — and I want to emphasise this is uncommon with the tablet form, we're talking about less than one in a thousand patients — the bone can become exposed and not heal properly. The fact that you've been on it for four years, and that you're also taking Prednisolone, does slightly increase that risk compared to someone who has only just started. But this is a manageable risk, not a reason to avoid treatment you need."

Reassure that MRONJ risk with oral bisphosphonates is low (<0.1%) but is elevated by concurrent corticosteroid use and duration >3–4 years. Do not recommend stopping risedronate without specialist input. Address her online concerns directly and empathetically.

STAGE 3: Adrenal Suppression and Steroid Cover

"There's one more important thing I need to discuss with you about your Prednisolone. When you take a steroid tablet like Prednisolone every day for a long time — and you've been on it for seven years — your body's own stress response system can become a little quieter, because it's been relying on the tablet. Dental surgery, even a straightforward extraction, is a small stress on the body. To make sure your body handles that safely, I'd like to speak with your GP or rheumatologist before we go ahead, to arrange a small increase in your Prednisolone dose on the day of the procedure. This is a routine precaution and nothing to be alarmed about."

Identify HPA axis suppression from 7 years of Prednisolone 10 mg daily. Plan to liaise with prescribing doctor prior to extraction. For minor oral surgery under local anaesthesia, standard approach is to double the morning dose on the day of surgery. Do not proceed without this step confirmed.

STAGE 4: Consent, Management Plan, and Post-operative Instructions

"So here is what I'm proposing. We will go ahead with removing the tooth, because leaving it is not a safe option either — infection in the jaw is also a risk to the bone. I will be as gentle as possible during the procedure to minimise trauma to the surrounding bone and gum, and I'll aim to close the wound with a stitch to help it heal well. I'll also prescribe a chlorhexidine mouthwash and, given your medications, I'll likely recommend a short course of antibiotics as a precaution. Depending on how things look, I may also suggest we refer you to an oral surgeon who specialises in these situations — I want to make the safest choice for you. After the extraction, I'd like to see you back in one week to check healing. If at any point you notice any bone becoming visible in the socket, or the pain gets worse rather than better, or healing seems to be taking longer than expected, I want you to call us straight away. Do you have any questions about anything I've explained?"

Document informed consent including: indication for extraction, MRONJ risk (low but present), adrenal suppression risk and steroid cover plan, management strategy (atraumatic technique, primary closure, chlorhexidine, antibiotics), option of specialist referral, and post-operative safety netting. Confirm patient understanding before proceeding.

PQ-15
Five-Year-Old with a Draining Sinus
Station 14  |  Past Questions
■ Cluster 1 — History & Risk Factors

CANDIDATE BRIEF

Child 5 years old girl has mild discomfort on 64/65 which was filled with composite/GIC by school dentist few months ago (most probably mobile dental clinic). Mum also noticed sinus above the tooth recently. Parent is wondering why she needed all these fillings even though they make sure not to give any sugar in the child's diet. Gather information and Answer parent's concern, no need to give treatment plan or diagnosis.

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

Stage 1 — Introduction & Rapport (0–2 min)

Introduce yourself to Sarah and Lily. Confirm Lily's full name and date of birth; confirm Sarah is Lily's parent/guardian. Use Lily's name, get down to her level, and use simple friendly language to build trust before any clinical discussion begins.

Stage 2 — Focused History (2–6 min)

Ask Sarah about the sinus: onset (~3 months), intermittent discharge of yellow fluid, associated swelling. Elicit the prior toothache 4 months ago that resolved spontaneously — this is the key historical pivot. Ask about fever, facial swelling, difficulty eating, sleep disturbance. Confirm medical history, allergies, medications, immunisation status. INFLECTION 1 — A toothache that 'went away on its own' in a primary molar almost always signals pulp necrosis, not resolution. Candidates who miss this miss the diagnosis.

Stage 3 — Addressing the Diet Concern (6–9 min)

Respond empathetically to Sarah's guilt and confusion about sugar. Explain that caries is multifactorial — frequency of exposure, oral hygiene, saliva buffering, and tooth anatomy all play a role. Identify cordial at kindergarten as a likely risk factor without being accusatory. INFLECTION 2 — Candidates who simply validate the parent's belief that 'no sugar = no decay' miss a critical preventive counselling opportunity and fail to address the root cause of the child's caries risk.

Stage 4 — Explaining the Sinus & Gaining Consent (9–12 min)

Explain the sinus tract in plain language: 'a small tunnel the body made to let the infection drain, like a pressure valve.' Clarify that the absence of pain does not mean the infection is gone. Explain that antibiotics alone will not fix the problem — the source inside the tooth must be treated. Gain consent for examination using positive, child-friendly language with Lily.

Stage 5 — Closing & Next Steps (12–14 min)

Summarise findings, outline that a clinical examination and likely an X-ray will guide the treatment decision. Reassure Sarah that Lily's cooperation history is positive and that the team will keep Lily comfortable throughout.

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Elicit the spontaneously resolving toothache 4 months ago — this is the historical key to diagnosing pulp necrosis in a primary molar
  2. ✅ Explain the sinus tract (parulis) in parent-friendly terms as a 'drainage tunnel' and clarify that absence of pain does not mean absence of infection
  3. ✅ Correctly advise that antibiotics are NOT indicated for a chronic draining abscess without systemic signs — definitive treatment (extraction or pulpectomy) is required
  4. ✅ Address the parent's diet concern non-judgmentally: identify cordial at kindergarten as a caries risk factor and explain the multifactorial nature of early childhood caries
  5. ✅ Gain consent for examination using age-appropriate, positive language with the child; acknowledge Sarah's guilt empathetically without dismissing her concern
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • A toothache that resolves on its own in a child's baby tooth is actually a warning sign — it often means the nerve inside the tooth has died, so the tooth can no longer feel pain, but the infection continues silently at the root tip.
  • The pimple you're seeing is called a sinus tract or parulis — it's a small channel the body has created to drain the infection away from the tooth root. Because it's draining, Lily isn't in acute pain right now, but the infection itself has not gone away.
  • Antibiotics alone won't fix this. The source of the infection is inside the tooth, and until we treat the tooth itself — either by removing the nerve tissue or by taking the tooth out — the infection will keep coming back even if the pimple temporarily disappears.
  • Early childhood caries is caused by how often teeth are exposed to fermentable carbohydrates, not just the total amount of sugar. Cordial — even diluted — contains sugars and acids that can cause decay if sipped frequently throughout the day, especially if teeth aren't brushed twice daily with fluoride toothpaste.
  • Because Lily has no fever, no facial swelling, and no signs of spreading infection, this is classified as a chronic localised abscess. In this situation, Australian and international guidelines do not recommend antibiotics as primary management — definitive dental treatment is the appropriate course of action.
Curveball Deflectors
  • Sarah insists: 'Can't you just give her antibiotics and clear up the infection? I don't want her to have a tooth pulled.' → Acknowledge Sarah's concern warmly: 'I completely understand — no parent wants their child to go through that, and it's a really reasonable question.' Then explain clearly: 'Antibiotics can help if an infection is spreading through the body, but in Lily's case the infection is sitting at the tip of the tooth root. Antibiotics can't get inside a dead tooth to clear the source, so the pimple would come back as soon as the course finished. The only way to truly fix this is to treat the tooth itself — and once we do that, the infection resolves on its own without needing antibiotics at all. We'll make sure Lily is comfortable throughout.'
  • Candidate assumes the tooth in question is 64/65 (upper left) because that is what the brief mentions, and fails to examine or consider 85 (lower right) where the actual pathology is. → Do not anchor on the teeth mentioned in the referral note. The history of a sinus 'above the tooth' requires clarification — ask Sarah to point to exactly where she sees the pimple. During examination, assess all quadrants systematically. The draining sinus on the buccal gingiva in the lower right (tooth 85) is the true pathology. A candidate who treats only the upper left teeth based on the referral, without a full clinical examination, will miss the diagnosis entirely and fail this station.
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ►
STAGE 1: Introduction & Rapport

"Hi there, I'm Dr. [Name], one of the dentists here today. And you must be Lily! I love your [shoes/hair clip] — very cool. And you must be Mum — lovely to meet you. Can I just confirm Lily's full name and date of birth for our records? Perfect, thank you. Lily, is it okay if I have a little chat with Mum first, and then I'd love to have a look at your teeth — I promise we'll just start with a little peek, nothing scary. Does that sound okay?"

Get down to Lily's eye level when speaking to her. Use her name frequently. Seat Sarah where she can maintain eye contact with Lily throughout. Confirm Sarah is Lily's parent or legal guardian before proceeding.

STAGE 2: Focused History

"Sarah, I can see you've noticed a pimple-like spot near Lily's tooth — can you tell me a bit more about that? When did you first notice it? Has it ever burst or released any fluid? Has it come and gone, or has it been there the whole time? And has Lily complained of any pain in that area recently? ... I see — and you mentioned she had a toothache a few months back that seemed to settle on its own. Can you tell me more about that — roughly when was that, and how long did it last before it went away? ... Has Lily had any fever, any swelling of her face or jaw, or has she been off her food or sleep? ... Wonderful. And just so I have the full picture — does Lily have any medical conditions, take any regular medications, or have any allergies that you know of? And is she up to date with her immunisations?"

Document: sinus present ~3 months, intermittent yellow discharge, toothache ~4 months ago that resolved spontaneously (key indicator of pulp necrosis), no current fever or facial swelling, no medical history, no allergies, no medications, immunisations up to date. The spontaneously resolving toothache is the critical historical pivot — flag this internally as strongly suggestive of pulp necrosis.

STAGE 3: Addressing the Diet & Caries Concern

"Sarah, I really appreciate you raising that — and I want you to know, you're clearly doing your best for Lily, and that matters enormously. The relationship between diet and tooth decay is actually a little more complicated than just 'sugar yes or no.' What causes decay is how often teeth are exposed to sugary or acidic things throughout the day, not just the total amount. So for example, if Lily is sipping cordial at kindy — even diluted cordial — over a long period of time, her teeth are being bathed in that liquid repeatedly, which can cause decay even if the overall sugar content seems low. It's the frequency that really matters. Combined with brushing once a day, there may be periods where the teeth aren't getting enough protection. This isn't about blame at all — these are things that are really easy to adjust once we know about them, and I'll give you some practical tips before you leave today."

Deliver this section in a warm, non-judgmental tone. Avoid language that implies parental failure. Identify cordial as a specific risk factor. Mention fluoride toothpaste and twice-daily brushing as key preventive measures. Do not lecture — keep it conversational and solution-focused.

STAGE 4: Explaining the Sinus & Gaining Consent for Examination

"Now, about that pimple you've noticed — what you're describing sounds like what we call a sinus tract. Think of it like a tiny tunnel that the body has created to drain away the infection from the tip of the tooth's root — a bit like a pressure valve. Because it's draining, Lily isn't in a lot of pain right now, which is actually why it can be easy to think it's getting better on its own. But the infection itself hasn't gone away — it's still there at the root, and it will keep coming back until we treat the tooth. I also want to reassure you about antibiotics — I know that might seem like the obvious fix, but antibiotics can't get inside a tooth that's no longer alive, so they can't clear the source of the infection. They might help temporarily if the infection were spreading, but in Lily's situation, treating the tooth itself is what will actually fix the problem. What I'd like to do now, with your permission, is have a gentle look inside Lily's mouth and take a small X-ray so we can see exactly what's happening. Is that okay with you both? ... Lily, I'm just going to use this little mirror — it's like a tiny torch — to have a look at your teeth. You can hold Mum's hand the whole time. Ready? You're doing brilliantly already."

Gain verbal consent from Sarah for examination and radiograph. Use tell-show-do with Lily. Maintain a calm, positive tone. Do not provide a treatment plan at this stage as per the candidate brief — the station ends at consent for examination and addressing parent concerns.

PQ-16
Management of Post-Operative Haematoma Following Dental Treatment
Station 15  |  Past Questions
■ Cluster 2 — Balanced (History informs management)

CANDIDATE BRIEF

Pt comes today complaining of swelling, mild discomfort and limited mouth opening following the IANB that was given a week before because of composite filling/extraction. You did examination today and you noticed patient can open up to 20mm, with swelling. You gave the diagnosis of trismus, hematoma and myospasm. Explain the diagnosis and how will you manage pts concern.

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

Stage 1 — Focused History (0–2 min)

Confirm extraction of LL6 yesterday, difficulty of procedure, onset of swelling within 2 hours, overnight progression, bruising now tracking to neck. Ask specifically about aspirin 100mg daily (antiplatelet), perindopril, and confirm aspirin was correctly continued. Screen for red flags: breathing difficulty, dysphagia, fever, rapidly worsening swelling. INFLECTION 1 — Identifying aspirin as the key contributing factor without suggesting it was an error to continue it is critical. Candidates who say aspirin should have been stopped will lose marks.

Stage 2 — Examination (2–4 min)

Inspect extraoral ecchymosis and swelling distribution. Assess mouth opening (note any trismus component). Examine socket: confirm normal healing, no signs of infection, no dry socket. Palpate for fluctuance or lymphadenopathy. Confirm no stridor or neck rigidity.

Stage 3 — Diagnosis and Explanation (4–6 min)

Explain in lay terms: minor vessel bleeding into soft tissues, spread by gravity and facilitated by aspirin's antiplatelet effect. Reassure that bruising is alarming but benign and self-limiting. INFLECTION 2 — Candidates must not recommend incision and drainage or antibiotics for an uncomplicated haematoma with no signs of infection.

Stage 4 — Management and Safety-Netting (6–8 min)

Warm compresses now (cold compresses past their window), paracetamol for analgesia, soft diet, oral hygiene maintenance. Advise resolution over 1–2 weeks with colour change. Safety-net: return urgently for breathing/swallowing difficulty, fever, rapidly increasing swelling, or signs of infection. Offer review in 5–7 days.

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Identifies aspirin 100mg daily as the key contributing factor and confirms it was correct NOT to stop it pre-operatively
  2. ✅ Screens for and excludes airway compromise, dysphagia, fever, and signs of infection as red flag symptoms
  3. ✅ Explains the haematoma mechanism in plain language — minor vessel bleeding spreading into soft tissues, facilitated by antiplatelet medication
  4. ✅ Provides stage-appropriate management: warm compresses (not cold at this stage), paracetamol, soft diet, reassurance that resolution takes 1–2 weeks
  5. ✅ Safety-nets clearly with specific triggers for urgent return: breathing or swallowing difficulty, fever above 38°C, rapidly increasing swelling, or signs of infection
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • The bruising is tracking down toward the neck because blood follows gravity through the tissue planes — this is expected and does not by itself indicate a dangerous complication, but I will monitor it closely.
  • Aspirin reduces platelet aggregation, which means the blood did not clot as quickly in the small vessels, allowing it to spread more widely into the surrounding tissues — this is why the bruising looks more extensive than you might expect.
  • Cold compresses are most effective in the first 24 hours to limit bleeding; at this stage, warm compresses will help the body reabsorb the blood more quickly.
  • I would be concerned and want you to go to emergency immediately if you develop any difficulty breathing, difficulty swallowing, a fever above 38 degrees, or if the swelling increases rapidly — these would suggest a more serious complication requiring urgent care.
  • There is no indication for antibiotics or surgical drainage at this point — the socket is healing normally and there are no signs of infection.
Curveball Deflectors
  • Patient says: 'Should you have stopped my aspirin before the extraction? Is this your fault?' → Acknowledge the concern empathetically and explain clearly: current Australian and international guidelines recommend continuing low-dose aspirin for cardiovascular patients undergoing routine dental extractions because the risk of stopping it — including heart attack or stent thrombosis — outweighs the risk of increased bleeding. The haematoma is a known, manageable complication, not a result of clinical error. Avoid being defensive; be factual and reassuring.
  • Candidate considers prescribing antibiotics or recommending incision and drainage for the haematoma → Resist this — there are no signs of infection (no fever, no pus, no worsening pain, normal socket healing). Antibiotics are not indicated for an uncomplicated haematoma. Incision and drainage would introduce infection risk and is not appropriate here. Management is conservative: warm compresses, analgesia, reassurance, and monitoring with clear safety-netting.
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ►
STAGE 1: Focused History

"Mrs Hayes, thank you for coming in today. I can see you're worried about the swelling and bruising — that's completely understandable, and I want to make sure we go through everything carefully together. Can you tell me, the tooth was taken out yesterday afternoon — is that right? And when did you first notice the swelling starting?"

Confirm extraction of LL6 yesterday, moderately difficult procedure requiring elevation and sectioning. Establish timeline: swelling within 2 hours, increased overnight, bruising now tracking toward neck. Ask specifically: "Are you on any blood thinners or medications that affect bleeding — for example, aspirin, warfarin, or anything like that?" Identify aspirin 100mg daily (cardiovascular, stent history) and perindopril. Confirm aspirin was correctly continued. Screen for red flags: "Are you having any trouble breathing or swallowing? Any fever or chills? Is the swelling getting worse quickly?" — all absent.

STAGE 2: Examination

"I'd like to have a look at the area now, both outside and inside your mouth, if that's okay. I'll be gentle."

Inspect extraoral ecchymosis and swelling — note distribution and tracking toward neck. Assess mouth opening — within acceptable limits, no significant trismus. Examine socket: confirm normal healing, clot present, no signs of infection, no dry socket, no pus, no erythema beyond expected healing. Palpate for fluctuance and lymphadenopathy. Confirm no stridor, no neck rigidity, no signs of airway compromise.

STAGE 3: Diagnosis and Explanation

"Mrs Hayes, I want to explain what's happened and reassure you. When we removed the tooth, some small blood vessels in the area were disrupted — that's a normal part of any extraction. Usually the blood clots quickly and stays contained. However, because you take aspirin every day for your heart, your platelets — the tiny cells that help blood clot — don't stick together quite as well. This means the blood spread more widely into the surrounding soft tissues rather than clotting in one spot. That's what's causing the bruising you can see on your face and down toward your neck. I know it looks quite alarming, but I want to reassure you — this is called a haematoma, and in your situation, it is not dangerous. The bruising will change colour over the next one to two weeks, going from purple to green to yellow as your body reabsorbs it, and it will fully resolve. The socket itself is healing beautifully — there are no signs of infection."

Deliver diagnosis clearly and in lay terms. Normalise the appearance of the bruising. Avoid suggesting aspirin was an error — it was correct to continue it. Do not recommend antibiotics or drainage.

STAGE 4: Management and Safety-Netting

"Here's what I'd like you to do at home. Because it's been more than 24 hours since the extraction, cold packs won't help much now — instead, I'd like you to apply a warm, moist cloth to the area for about 15 to 20 minutes, three or four times a day. This helps your body reabsorb the blood more quickly. For any discomfort, regular paracetamol — two tablets every six hours as needed — should be enough. Please stick to soft foods for the next few days and keep the area clean with gentle rinsing after meals. I'd like to see you again in about five to seven days to check on your progress. Most importantly, I need you to know when to seek urgent help. Please go straight to the emergency department — or call triple zero — if you develop any difficulty breathing or swallowing, if the swelling increases rapidly, if you develop a fever above 38 degrees, or if you notice pus or worsening pain around the socket. These would be signs of a more serious complication that needs immediate attention. Do you have any questions about anything I've explained?"

Confirm patient understanding. Provide written safety-netting instructions if available. Book review appointment in 5–7 days. Document findings, diagnosis, management plan, and safety-netting discussion in clinical notes.

PQ-17
Chronic Generalised Periodontitis Assessment and Management
Station 16  |  Past Questions
■ Cluster 2 — Balanced (History informs management)

CANDIDATE BRIEF

Mr Boldoski is a 55 yrs old patient, attending your clinic today complaining of bleeding gums and wanted some cleaning. You have examined the patient. OPG taken today and you can see generalized bone loss. You gave diagnosis as generalised periodontitis, stage 4 and grade C. His medical records show that he didn't see GP for 10 yrs. You decided to refer him to specialist. Explain the reason for referral and address pts concern.

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

Stage 1 — Introduction and History Taking (0–2 min)

Greet Mr Boldoski, acknowledge his concern about bleeding gums. Take focused periodontal history: duration of symptoms, previous dental attendance (none for years), oral hygiene habits (brushes once daily, never flosses). INFLECTION 1 — Proactively ask about medical history and smoking. Elicit type 2 diabetes (HbA1c 8.2%) and 30 pack-year smoking history. These are Grade C modifiers that change the entire management pathway.

Stage 2 — Explain Diagnosis in Plain Language (2–4 min)

Explain that this is a serious gum infection — Stage III Grade C periodontitis — with 40–50% generalised bone loss, pockets up to 8mm, and mobility on four back teeth. Clarify that 'cleaning' alone is insufficient. Use the analogy of an infection eating away the foundations of a house.

Stage 3 — Explain Reason for Specialist Referral (4–6 min)

Explain referral to a periodontist is recommended due to: severity of bone loss, deep vertical defects, tooth mobility, and high-risk profile (smoking + uncontrolled diabetes). Periodontist can provide advanced debridement, assess surgical options, and coordinate long-term maintenance. INFLECTION 2 — Address the bidirectional diabetes–periodontitis relationship: poor HbA1c worsens periodontitis; active infection impairs glycaemic control. Strongly recommend GP review.

Stage 4 — Address Patient Concerns and Risk Factors (6–8 min)

Address fear of tooth loss: explain that with specialist care and compliance, teeth can be saved. Address cost: early treatment prevents more expensive tooth replacement later. Offer Quitline referral (13 7848) for smoking cessation. Emphasise that smoking significantly reduces treatment success and healing.

Stage 5 — Summarise, Safety-Net, and Check Understanding (8–9 min)

Summarise the plan: specialist referral letter today, GP referral for HbA1c review, Quitline referral, interim oral hygiene instruction. Ask Mr Boldoski to repeat back key points. Provide written information if available.

KEY POINTS
