  1. ✅ Elicits both smoking (10 cigs/day, 30-year history) and poorly controlled diabetes (HbA1c 8.2%) as Grade C risk modifiers — must ask proactively
  2. ✅ Explains Stage III Grade C periodontitis in plain language including 40–50% bone loss, 8mm pockets, and tooth mobility on 16, 26, 36, 46
  3. ✅ Clearly articulates reasons for specialist referral: disease severity, vertical bony defects, mobility, and compounding systemic risk factors impairing healing
  4. ✅ Discusses bidirectional relationship between diabetes and periodontitis and recommends GP referral for HbA1c optimisation prior to and during treatment
  5. ✅ Addresses smoking cessation with empathy, offers Quitline (13 7848), and explains that smoking reduces treatment success and healing capacity
  6. ✅ Addresses patient concerns about tooth loss and cost with realistic reassurance and explains that early specialist intervention is more cost-effective than tooth replacement
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • Stage III Grade C periodontitis is characterised by generalised bone loss exceeding 33% of root length, probing depths of 5mm or more, clinical attachment loss of 4mm or greater, and in this case tooth mobility — these findings together indicate a complex case beyond routine general practice management.
  • An HbA1c of 8.2% represents suboptimal glycaemic control. The relationship between diabetes and periodontitis is bidirectional — active periodontal infection drives systemic inflammation that impairs insulin sensitivity, and poor blood sugar control creates an environment that accelerates bone destruction and impairs periodontal healing.
  • Smoking is a Grade C risk modifier in the 2017 AAP/EFP classification. A 30 pack-year history significantly reduces the host immune response, impairs neutrophil function, reduces gingival blood flow, and is associated with a two- to sevenfold increased risk of periodontitis progression and reduced response to non-surgical therapy.
  • Referral to a periodontist is indicated here due to: generalised probing depths of 5–8mm, vertical osseous defects at 16, 26, and 36, Grade 2–3 mobility on four teeth, radiographic bone loss of 40–50%, and the presence of two uncontrolled systemic risk factors — smoking and diabetes — that substantially compromise healing and prognosis.
Curveball Deflectors
  • Patient says: 'I just want a clean today — why do I need to see a specialist? Can't you just do it here?' → Acknowledge his preference and validate his concern about cost and convenience. Explain that while a routine clean addresses surface deposits, his condition involves deep infection below the gumline with significant bone loss that requires specialist instruments, expertise, and likely surgical assessment. Doing a superficial clean without addressing the underlying infection would be like painting over a cracked foundation — it would not stop the disease progressing. Reassure him that the referral is in his best interest to save his teeth long-term.
  • Candidate fails to ask about smoking or diabetes and proceeds directly to explaining the referral — common error of omitting history → Before explaining the diagnosis or referral, always take a complete medical and social history. Ask directly: 'Do you have any medical conditions I should know about?' and 'Do you smoke or use any tobacco products?' These are not optional — smoking and diabetes are Grade C modifiers that change the diagnosis classification, prognosis, and entire management plan. Omitting them is a critical error in this station.
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ►
STAGE 1: Introduction and History Taking

"Good morning Mr Boldoski, I'm Dr [Name]. Thank you for coming in today. I understand you've noticed some bleeding from your gums and you'd like a clean — I want to make sure we look after you properly, so I'd like to ask you a few questions first before I explain what I've found. Is that okay?"

Take focused periodontal history: ask about duration of bleeding gums, any pain or sensitivity, whether teeth feel loose, last dental visit, and current oral hygiene routine. Elicit that he brushes once daily and does not floss. Then transition to medical and social history.

"Mr Boldoski, I also need to ask about your general health — do you have any medical conditions or take any medications? And do you smoke or use any tobacco products?"

Elicit type 2 diabetes managed with metformin, HbA1c of 8.2% at last check, and smoking history of 10 cigarettes per day for 30 years. Note that he hasn't seen a GP in 10 years — flag this as a significant concern.

STAGE 2: Explain Diagnosis in Plain Language

"Thank you for sharing that with me — it's really helpful. I want to explain what I've found today. You have a condition called periodontitis — that's a serious infection of the gums and the bone that holds your teeth in place. Think of your teeth like fence posts — the bone is the ground they sit in. In your case, that ground has been eaten away by infection, and in some areas we've lost around 40 to 50 percent of that supporting bone. Some of your back teeth are also starting to feel a little loose because of this."

Use the OPG to point out generalised bone loss and vertical defects at 16, 26, and 36. Explain that this is classified as Stage III Grade C periodontitis — a severe and rapidly progressing form — and that the smoking and diabetes are making it significantly worse and harder to treat.

"I want to be honest with you — this is more than a routine clean can fix. The infection is deep under the gumline, and some areas have pockets up to 8 millimetres deep where bacteria have been building up for a long time."

STAGE 3: Explain Reason for Referral and Address Tooth Loss Concern

"Because of how advanced this is, and because of your diabetes and smoking — both of which affect how your body heals — I'd like to refer you to a specialist called a periodontist. They specialise in exactly this type of condition and have the expertise and equipment to give you the best chance of keeping your teeth. I want to be clear — the goal is absolutely to save your teeth, and with the right treatment and your commitment, that is achievable."

Explain that the periodontist will perform thorough deep cleaning under the gumline (scaling and root planing), reassess healing at 6–8 weeks, and determine whether any surgical treatment is needed for the vertical bony defects. Emphasise that without specialist treatment, tooth loss is a real risk — but with treatment and compliance, it can be minimised.

"I also want to mention something important about your diabetes. There's actually a two-way relationship between gum disease and blood sugar — when your gums are infected, it makes your diabetes harder to control, and when your blood sugar is high, it makes the gum disease worse. Your last HbA1c was 8.2%, which is a little higher than we'd like. I'd strongly recommend seeing your GP to get that reviewed — getting your blood sugar better controlled will genuinely help your gum treatment work better."

STAGE 4: Smoking Cessation, Cost Concerns, and Safety-Netting

"I also want to talk about smoking. I understand it's a personal choice and I'm not here to lecture you — but I do need to be honest with you as your dentist. Smoking is one of the biggest factors making your gum disease worse. It reduces the blood flow to your gums, weakens your immune system's ability to fight infection, and significantly reduces how well the specialist treatment will work. Even cutting down would make a real difference. There's a free service called Quitline — the number is 13 7848 — and your GP can also help with support and medication if you're ever ready to give it a go."

Acknowledge cost concerns empathetically. Explain that while specialist treatment involves an upfront cost, it is far more cost-effective than losing teeth and needing implants or dentures later. Offer to write a referral letter today and a separate letter to his GP regarding HbA1c review and smoking cessation support.

"I know cost is a concern, and I completely understand that. But I want you to think of it this way — treating this now gives us the best chance of keeping your teeth for life. Replacing teeth with implants or dentures is far more expensive and never quite the same as your own teeth. Do you have any questions about anything I've explained today? I want to make sure you feel comfortable with the plan before you leave."

Check understanding by asking Mr Boldoski to summarise the plan back. Provide written information about periodontitis and the referral. Document findings, diagnosis, referral, and patient discussion in clinical notes.

PQ-18
Dietary Advice for an Asthmatic Patient
Station 17  |  Past Questions
■ Cluster 3 — Evaluation & Treatment Planning

CANDIDATE BRIEF

Mr Sam Smith is a 28-year-old gym trainer. You have already done the examination in the last appointment and noticed several interproximal caries. You also noticed that his saliva is thick and stringy. You gave him oral hygiene instructions, advised to get some restorations and to fill the diet chart. He would like to know how to modify his diet. He is very health conscious, following good diet regime. Diet chart given: He is drinking lots of sports drink, coffee and tea with sugar, cereal bars, fizzy drinks fruits, but no vege. He is fit and healthy. Answer patients concern and inform what are the changes he requires to implement. No need to give discuss treatment plan for caries.

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

Stage 1 — Introduction & Diet Chart Review (0–1 min)

Greet Mr Smith warmly. Acknowledge his health-conscious approach positively and non-judgmentally. Confirm you have reviewed his diet chart and will go through it together. INFLECTION 1 — Candidate must recognise that 'healthy' foods (sports drinks, cereal bars, fruit) carry significant cariogenic and erosive risk; failure to challenge these is a common error.

Stage 2 — Identify High-Risk Dietary Items (1–3 min)

Systematically address: (1) sports drinks and fizzy drinks — acidic pH and high sugar, sipping pattern prolongs acid exposure; (2) coffee and tea with sugar — frequency matters; (3) cereal bars — sticky fermentable carbohydrates; (4) fruit without vegetables — acidic, no buffering. Explain the concept of acid attacks and critical pH of 5.5 in simple terms.

Stage 3 — Inhaler Advice (3–4 min)

INFLECTION 2 — Candidate must connect asthma medication to oral health. Salbutamol (Ventolin) reliever is acidic; corticosteroid preventers (if applicable) increase candidiasis and caries risk. Advise: rinse mouth with water and spit after every inhaler use; do not eat or drink (except water) for 30 minutes post-use.

Stage 4 — Practical Alternatives & Fluoride (4–5 min)

Suggest plain water as primary drink; sports drinks only during intense training, followed by water rinse. Replace cereal bars with cheese, unsalted nuts, or fresh fruit. Reduce sugar in hot drinks. Recommend fluoride toothpaste twice daily; consider Tooth Mousse given thick saliva indicating possible reduced salivary flow. Wait 30 minutes after eating before brushing.

Stage 5 — Teach-Back & Follow-Up (5–6 min)

Check understanding using teach-back. Acknowledge motivation. Arrange review in 3–6 months to assess dietary changes and monitor caries/erosion progression.

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Identifies sports drinks, fizzy drinks, and flavoured waters as both acidic (pH below critical 5.5) and high in sugar — sipping pattern is the key risk multiplier
  2. ✅ Connects asthma inhaler use (especially salbutamol reliever) to oral health risk and advises rinsing with water and spitting after every puff
  3. ✅ Recognises that cereal bars and dried fruit are sticky fermentable carbohydrates with high cariogenic potential despite their 'healthy' image
  4. ✅ Notes thick, stringy saliva as a sign of reduced salivary flow (possibly medication-related or dehydration), increasing caries and erosion risk — considers Tooth Mousse or additional fluoride
  5. ✅ Provides practical, gym-trainer-appropriate alternatives (plain water, cheese, nuts, fresh fruit) and uses teach-back to confirm understanding before arranging follow-up
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • Sports drinks typically have a pH between 2.9 and 3.7 — well below the critical pH of 5.5 at which enamel begins to dissolve — and sipping them throughout a workout means the teeth are under continuous acid attack rather than a single brief exposure.
  • Salbutamol (Ventolin) reliever inhalers are themselves acidic, and the propellant can lower the oral pH directly; rinsing with plain water and spitting immediately after each puff is a simple but evidence-based step to reduce this risk.
  • Thick, stringy saliva is a clinical indicator of reduced salivary flow — saliva is our primary natural defence against both acid erosion and caries because it buffers acids, remineralises enamel, and clears fermentable carbohydrates; when flow is reduced, all of these protective mechanisms are compromised.
  • Cereal bars and dried fruit are particularly cariogenic because they combine high fermentable sugar content with a sticky, adhesive texture that prolongs contact time with tooth surfaces — the combination of substrate, frequency, and contact time drives the caries process.
  • The recommended approach after eating is to wait at least 30 minutes before brushing, as the enamel is temporarily softened by acid and brushing during this window causes additional mechanical erosion of the softened surface.
Curveball Deflectors
  • Patient says: 'But sports drinks are marketed as healthy and I need them for energy during training — surely they're fine if I'm exercising?' → Validate his concern and acknowledge that electrolyte replacement has a role during prolonged intense exercise. However, clarify that the marketing of sports drinks as 'healthy' refers to hydration and electrolyte content, not dental safety. Explain that plain water is equally effective for sessions under 60–90 minutes, and that if he does use a sports drink, he should consume it in one sitting rather than sipping, then rinse with plain water immediately afterwards. Avoid being dismissive — frame it as a small, practical adjustment rather than eliminating something he values.
  • Candidate focuses only on sugar and forgets to address the erosive/acidic component, or forgets to ask about inhaler use entirely → This is the most common error in this station. Caries and erosion have different aetiologies — sugar drives caries via bacterial fermentation, while acid (regardless of sugar content) drives erosion directly. A candidate who only says 'cut down on sugar' will miss the erosion diagnosis and the inhaler connection. Always ask: 'Do you use any inhalers or medications?' and always address pH/acid exposure separately from sugar content when discussing sports drinks and fizzy drinks.
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ►
STAGE 1: Introduction & Non-Judgmental Opening

"Hi Mr Smith, great to see you again. Thanks so much for filling in the diet chart — that's really helpful. I can see you put a lot of thought into your diet and you're clearly very health-conscious, which is fantastic. What I'd like to do today is go through the chart together and have a chat about a few small changes that could make a big difference for your teeth. Does that sound okay?"

Review the diet chart openly with the patient. Adopt a collaborative, non-judgmental tone. Acknowledge his gym trainer lifestyle as context for the dietary choices. Note key risk items: sports drinks, fizzy drinks, coffee and tea with sugar, cereal bars, and fruit without vegetables. Also note the clinical finding of thick, stringy saliva from the previous appointment.

STAGE 2: Explaining the Risk — Drinks

"One of the things I noticed on your chart is that you're having quite a few sports drinks and fizzy drinks. Now I know these seem like a healthy choice, especially around training — but here's the thing: these drinks are actually very acidic. The acid in them can soften the outer layer of your teeth, called enamel, and over time that leads to what we call erosion — where the teeth literally wear away. The pH of most sports drinks sits around 3, and our teeth start to dissolve at a pH of 5.5, so they're well below that safe level. The other issue is that sipping on them throughout the day means your teeth are under constant acid attack rather than just a brief one. Plain water is the best option for staying hydrated, and if you do need a sports drink during a really intense session, try to drink it in one go rather than sipping, and then rinse your mouth with plain water straight afterwards. The same goes for the fizzy drinks and the coffee and tea — if you can reduce the sugar in those, or switch to sweetener, that would really help."

Explain the concept of critical pH (5.5) in plain language. Distinguish between erosion (acid-driven) and caries (sugar-driven) without using jargon. Emphasise the sipping pattern as a key risk factor. Recommend plain water as the primary drink.

STAGE 3: Snacks, Inhaler Use & Saliva

"The cereal bars are another one worth looking at. Even though they're marketed as healthy, they're actually quite sticky and high in sugar — they cling to the teeth and the bacteria in your mouth feed on that sugar and produce acid. Fresh fruit, a small piece of cheese, some unsalted nuts, or plain yoghurt are much better options for snacking. Now, I also wanted to ask — you mentioned you use an inhaler for your asthma. Which inhalers are you currently using, and do you do anything after you use them? The reason I ask is that the reliever inhaler — the Ventolin — is actually slightly acidic itself, and it can lower the pH in your mouth. A really simple thing you can do is rinse your mouth with plain water and spit it out after every puff. It takes five seconds and it makes a real difference. Also, I noticed last time that your saliva looked a little thick — that can sometimes happen with certain medications or if you're not quite hydrated enough. Saliva is actually one of your best natural defences against tooth decay and erosion, so keeping well hydrated with plain water throughout the day will help with that too."

Address cereal bars as sticky fermentable carbohydrates. Ask specifically about inhaler type and post-use oral care routine. Advise water rinse and spit after every inhaler use. Connect thick saliva finding to reduced salivary protection. Consider recommending Tooth Mousse (GC) as a remineralising agent given the erosion risk and reduced salivary flow.

STAGE 4: Fluoride, Teach-Back & Follow-Up

"In terms of your brushing routine, make sure you're using a fluoride toothpaste — that's really important for strengthening the enamel. One tip: after eating or drinking anything acidic, wait about 30 minutes before you brush, because the enamel is a little softened straight after and brushing too soon can actually cause more wear. I might also suggest a product called Tooth Mousse — it's a cream you apply to your teeth after brushing that helps remineralise and protect the enamel. We can talk more about that. So just to check I've explained things clearly — can you tell me in your own words what the main changes you're going to try are? ... That's great. I really want to emphasise that you're already doing a lot of things right — it's really just a few targeted swaps. I'd love to see you back in about three months so we can see how things are going and check on those areas we were watching. Does that work for you?"

Recommend fluoride toothpaste twice daily. Advise 30-minute wait before brushing after acidic exposure. Introduce Tooth Mousse as an adjunct remineralising agent appropriate for erosion risk. Use teach-back method to confirm understanding. Arrange 3-month review. Document dietary advice given in clinical notes.

PQ-19
Aboriginal Health Worker on Anticoagulants Presenting with Dental Infection
Station 18  |  Past Questions
■ Cluster 3 — Evaluation & Treatment Planning

CANDIDATE BRIEF

Torre islander nurse comes today complaining of pain from 16. You did the examination and 16 has irreversible pulpitis and pt didn't have money to save the tooth and insisted on pulling it out. Now you have decided to extract the tooth. Xray shows that 16 roots are almost crossing the sinus and there is an infection around 1 root. Patient is interested to know about OAC, Hepatitis B and HIV infection protocol in your clinic.

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

Stage 1 — Introduction & Cultural Safety (0–1 min)

Greet Kylie respectfully, acknowledge her role in the community, and establish rapport. Confirm her preferred name and check she is comfortable. INFLECTION 1 — Failure to acknowledge cultural context or rushing to clinical questions signals poor cultural competency to the examiner.

Stage 2 — Focused History: Medical & Infection Assessment (1–4 min)

Confirm anticoagulant name (apixaban), dose (5mg BD), indication (AF + previous PE), and last dose (this morning). Confirm metformin, no allergies, regular GP at Aboriginal Medical Service. Assess infection severity: fever, swelling progression, trismus, dysphagia, breathing difficulty, floor-of-mouth elevation.

Stage 3 — Diagnosis & Treatment Plan Explanation (4–7 min)

Explain irreversible pulpitis with periapical infection around one root of 16. Roots are close to the maxillary sinus — explain oro-antral communication risk. Confirm extraction is the appropriate treatment and that antibiotics alone will not resolve the infection without source control. INFLECTION 2 — Recommending cessation of apixaban is a critical error; current Australian guidelines support continuing DOACs for simple extractions.

Stage 4 — Anticoagulation Management & Haemostasis (7–9 min)

Explain apixaban does not need to be stopped. Time extraction before morning dose (trough level). Use local haemostatic measures: sutures, haemostatic gauze, pressure pack, post-op instructions. Avoid NSAIDs for analgesia. Prescribe amoxicillin 500mg TDS for 5 days and paracetamol/codeine for pain.

Stage 5 — Infection Control Questions & Closing (9–10 min)

Address OAC, Hepatitis B, and HIV protocol questions: standard precautions apply to all patients universally regardless of known status. Offer GP liaison letter. Provide written post-op instructions. Check understanding using teach-back. Confirm follow-up appointment.

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Confirms apixaban 5mg BD — name, dose, indication (AF + PE), and last dose taken this morning; recognises no INR monitoring needed for DOACs
  2. ✅ Assesses infection severity systematically: fever, swelling progression, trismus, dysphagia, breathing difficulty, floor-of-mouth elevation — and recognises urgent need for source control via extraction
  3. ✅ Correctly states apixaban does NOT need to be ceased for simple dental extraction per current Australian guidelines; advises against stopping given CHA₂DS₂-VASc score of 4 (high stroke risk)
  4. ✅ Times extraction at trough (before morning dose); plans local haemostatic measures (sutures, haemostatic packing, pressure); avoids NSAIDs; prescribes amoxicillin 500mg TDS and paracetamol-based analgesia
  5. ✅ Addresses infection control questions (OAC, Hepatitis B, HIV) using standard precautions framework; communicates in culturally safe manner; offers GP liaison and written post-op instructions with teach-back
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • Apixaban is a direct oral anticoagulant — unlike warfarin, we do not check an INR and we do not need to stop it for a straightforward dental extraction. Current Australian Dental Association and haematology guidelines support continuing DOACs for simple procedures with local haemostatic measures.
  • Given that Kylie has both atrial fibrillation and a previous pulmonary embolism, her CHA₂DS₂-VASc score is 4, which places her at high risk of stroke if anticoagulation is interrupted — stopping apixaban without specialist input would be inappropriate and potentially dangerous.
  • I would time the extraction in the morning before she takes her next dose of apixaban, when the drug level is at its lowest point — this is called the trough level — and I would use sutures, haemostatic gauze, and a pressure pack to control local bleeding.
  • For the infection around the root of 16, antibiotics alone will not resolve this — we need to remove the source, which is the tooth itself. I will prescribe amoxicillin 500mg three times a day for five days to cover the infection before and after extraction.
  • Regarding Hepatitis B and HIV — our clinic uses standard precautions for every single patient, every single time, regardless of whether we know someone's status. This means gloves, masks, eye protection, and sterilised instruments are used universally. This protects both you and our team.
Curveball Deflectors
  • Patient says: 'My last dentist told me I had to stop my blood thinners before any dental work — shouldn't I call my doctor to stop them first?' → Acknowledge her concern respectfully: 'That advice was appropriate for older blood thinners like warfarin, but apixaban works differently. Current guidelines in Australia are clear that for a straightforward extraction like this one, we do not need to stop apixaban. Stopping it actually puts you at risk of a stroke given your heart condition and your history of a blood clot in your lungs. I will use special measures to control any bleeding locally, and if I have any concerns I will contact your GP at the Aboriginal Medical Service before we proceed — but stopping the medication is not the right step here.'
  • Candidate incorrectly recommends stopping apixaban or checking an INR before proceeding → This is a critical error. INR is not relevant to DOAC monitoring — apixaban does not affect INR in a clinically meaningful way. Recommending cessation without specialist input in a patient with AF and previous PE and a CHA₂DS₂-VASc of 4 risks thromboembolic events. The correct answer is to continue apixaban, time the procedure at trough, and use local haemostatic measures. If the candidate is uncertain, the appropriate action is to liaise with the prescribing GP — not to stop the medication unilaterally.
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ►
STAGE 1: Introduction & Cultural Safety

"Hi Kylie, my name is [Candidate Name] and I'm the dentist here today. Thank you so much for coming in — I know you're busy looking after your community clients, so I really appreciate you making the time. Before we get started, I just want to make sure you're comfortable and that I explain everything clearly as we go. Please feel free to stop me and ask questions at any point. Is it okay if I call you Kylie?"

Establish rapport and cultural safety. Acknowledge her role as an Aboriginal health worker. Ensure she feels heard and respected before moving into clinical questioning.

STAGE 2: Focused History — Medical & Infection Assessment

"I'd like to ask you a few questions about your health before we talk about the tooth. You mentioned you're on a blood thinner — can you tell me the name of it and how much you take? And when did you last take it today? ... Thank you — apixaban 5mg twice a day, and you took it this morning. And that's for your irregular heartbeat — your atrial fibrillation — as well as the blood clot you had in your lungs 18 months ago. That's really helpful to know. Are you on any other medications? Any allergies? Do you see a GP regularly? ... Great, and that's through the Aboriginal Medical Service — I'd like to be able to contact them if needed, would that be okay with you? Now, regarding the pain from this tooth — have you noticed any swelling in your face or jaw? Has it been getting worse? Have you had a fever, or felt unwell in yourself? Any difficulty opening your mouth wide, swallowing, or breathing?"

Confirm: apixaban 5mg BD, last dose this morning, indication AF and previous PE. Confirm metformin 1000mg BD, no allergies, regular GP at Aboriginal Medical Service. Assess infection severity — swelling, fever, trismus, dysphagia, breathing difficulty, floor-of-mouth elevation. Document findings systematically.

STAGE 3: Diagnosis & Treatment Plan

"Kylie, I've had a good look at your X-ray and examined the tooth. The nerve inside tooth 16 — that's your upper right back molar — is irreversibly damaged, which means it can't be saved. There's also a small infection around one of the roots. Now, the roots of this tooth sit very close to your sinus — the air space above your upper teeth — so I want to be upfront with you that there's a small chance a tiny opening could form between your mouth and your sinus during the extraction. If that happens, I know exactly how to manage it, and I'll explain that to you if it becomes relevant. The most important thing right now is to remove the tooth, because that's the source of the infection. Antibiotics alone won't fix this — we need to take the tooth out to allow the infection to drain properly. I'll also prescribe you antibiotics to take before and after. Does that make sense so far?"

Explain diagnosis of irreversible pulpitis with periapical infection. Warn about oro-antral communication risk given root proximity to sinus. Emphasise that extraction is source control — antibiotics alone are insufficient. Prescribe amoxicillin 500mg TDS for 5 days. Avoid NSAIDs given anticoagulation; use paracetamol ± codeine for analgesia.

STAGE 4: Anticoagulation Management, Infection Control Questions & Closing

"Now, I know you're worried about your blood thinner — and that's a really important question. The good news is that apixaban is a newer type of blood thinner, and the current guidelines in Australia are clear that we do not need to stop it for a straightforward tooth extraction. Stopping it would actually put you at risk of a stroke or another blood clot, given your heart condition and your history — and that risk is much greater than the risk of a little extra bleeding from a tooth removal. What I will do is schedule your appointment for the morning, before you take your next dose, so the medication is at its lowest level in your body. I'll also place stitches, use a special dressing inside the socket, and give you a gauze pack to bite on. I'll give you clear written instructions to take home. If I have any concerns at all, I'll call your GP at the Aboriginal Medical Service before we go ahead. Regarding your questions about our infection control — for blood-borne viruses like Hepatitis B and HIV, and for patients on blood thinners, we use what's called standard precautions for every single patient, every single time. That means gloves, masks, eye protection, and fully sterilised instruments — regardless of whether we know someone's status. This protects you and our whole team equally. Do you have any other questions? I'd like to check that everything I've explained makes sense — can you tell me in your own words what's going to happen today and what you'll need to do at home?"

Confirm apixaban is NOT ceased. Time extraction at trough — morning before next dose. Local haemostatic measures: sutures, haemostatic gauze, pressure pack. Avoid NSAIDs. Address OAC, Hepatitis B, HIV questions using standard precautions framework — non-stigmatising, universal application. Offer GP liaison letter. Provide written post-op instructions. Use teach-back to confirm understanding. Book follow-up appointment.

PQ-20
Assessment and Management of Lateral Tongue Ulcer
Station 19  |  Past Questions
■ Cluster 1 — History & Risk Factors

CANDIDATE BRIEF

Ulcer on right side of tongue, present for 1 month, complaining of mild discomfort when taking acidic or icy food. She is fit and healthy. Explain the possible reasons, manage patient's concern, discuss further investigations needed.

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

Stage 1 — Introduction and History (0–3 min)

Greet Mr Chen, confirm identity, and establish rapport. Ask open-ended questions about the ulcer: when he first noticed it, whether it has changed in size, and what symptoms it causes. Clarify that it has been present for 5 weeks and is slowly enlarging. INFLECTION 1 — Duration exceeding 3 weeks with progressive enlargement immediately raises the suspicion threshold and should shift the candidate away from a benign or traumatic diagnosis.

Stage 2 — Red Flags and Social History (3–5 min)

Screen systematically for dysphagia, voice change, unexplained weight loss, and night sweats (all absent here). Elicit tobacco history non-judgmentally: "I need to ask about smoking as it can affect healing — how long have you smoked and roughly how many a day?" Calculate pack-year history (~37.5 pack-years). Ask about alcohol in a similar tone. Note family history of lung cancer in brother.

Stage 3 — Clinical Examination (5–8 min)

Examine the ulcer: 2 cm × 1.5 cm, left lateral tongue, middle third, rolled and indurated margins, non-tender, firm, no blanching. Note absence of obvious trauma source. Acknowledge the tight denture complaint as potentially significant. Palpate cervical lymph nodes bilaterally — document firm, non-tender, mobile 1.5 cm left level II node. INFLECTION 2 — Ipsilateral lymphadenopathy in this context elevates suspicion to urgent and mandates same-day referral planning, not observation.

Stage 4 — Explanation and Referral (8–10 min)

Communicate concern empathetically: acknowledge Mr Chen's anxiety, explain that the ulcer has features that need specialist assessment urgently, and be honest that cancer must be ruled out. Arrange urgent referral for incisional biopsy within 2 weeks per Australian Head and Neck Cancer guidelines. Do not offer reassurance or a review appointment as a substitute for referral.

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Duration >3 weeks with progressive enlargement is a hard red flag requiring urgent action, not watchful waiting
  2. ✅ Pack-year history (~37.5) and daily alcohol exceeding Australian guidelines are independent risk multipliers for oral SCC
  3. ✅ Rolled, indurated margins with a non-tender, firm ulcer and no identifiable trauma source are classic features of oral squamous cell carcinoma
  4. ✅ A firm, non-tender, mobile ipsilateral level II lymph node in this context is clinically significant and must be documented and communicated
  5. ✅ Urgent referral for incisional biopsy within 2 weeks aligns with Australian Head and Neck Cancer Society guidelines — 'wait and see' is a failing response
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • "An ulcer that has been present for more than three weeks, is enlarging, has indurated and rolled margins, and is associated with a palpable ipsilateral lymph node must be considered squamous cell carcinoma until proven otherwise."
  • "With approximately 37.5 pack-years of smoking and alcohol intake exceeding Australian guidelines of no more than 10 standard drinks per week, Mr Chen has two of the strongest independent risk factors for oral squamous cell carcinoma acting synergistically."
  • "Under Australian Head and Neck Cancer Society guidelines, this presentation warrants urgent referral for incisional biopsy, ideally within two weeks — a watch-and-wait approach is not appropriate here."
  • "The patient's comment that his denture feels tight is clinically relevant — this may reflect underlying soft tissue change or mass effect rather than a change in denture fit, and should not be dismissed."
Curveball Deflectors
  • Patient says: "Can't we just wait a few more weeks and see if it heals on its own?" → Acknowledge the patient's hope while being honest: "I completely understand you're hoping it will settle, and I wish I could say that was the right approach. But because this ulcer has already been there for five weeks and is getting larger rather than smaller, waiting is not safe. The features I can see and feel mean we need a specialist to look at this urgently — within the next two weeks. Catching something like this early makes a real difference to outcomes."
  • Candidate attributes the ulcer to the tight denture and plans to adjust the denture and review in 2–4 weeks → This is the most common failing response. The tight denture sensation may be a consequence of the lesion, not its cause. There is no sharp or prominent denture flange identified as a trauma source, the ulcer has rolled indurated margins inconsistent with a traumatic aetiology, and it has been enlarging for 5 weeks. Adjusting the denture and reviewing is inappropriate — urgent specialist referral for biopsy must be arranged regardless of any denture adjustment.
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ►
STAGE 1: Introduction and History

"Good morning, Mr Chen. My name is [Candidate Name] and I'm the dentist today. Thank you for coming in. I understand you've noticed something on your tongue — I'd like to ask you a few questions first and then have a careful look, if that's okay with you. Please feel free to tell me as much as you can." "Can you tell me when you first noticed this ulcer?" [Patient: About five weeks ago.] "And has it changed at all since you first saw it — has it gotten bigger, smaller, or stayed the same?" [Patient: It started small but it's slowly getting bigger.] "Has it been painful?" [Patient: Not really, just a bit uncomfortable with acidic or cold food.] "Have you noticed any bleeding from it, or any numbness or tingling in your tongue or lip?" [Patient: No.] "Have you had anything like this before?" [Patient: No, never.]

Candidate notes: 5-week duration, progressive enlargement, minimal pain, no prior history — all features that increase suspicion. Absence of pain does not reduce concern; oral SCC is frequently non-tender.

STAGE 2: Red Flags and Social History

"I need to ask you a few more questions that might seem unrelated but are really important. Have you had any difficulty swallowing food or drinks?" [Patient: No.] "Any changes to your voice, or any ear pain?" [Patient: No.] "Have you lost any weight recently without trying, or had night sweats?" [Patient: No.] "I also need to ask about smoking — I ask everyone this because it can affect healing and overall health. Do you smoke, and if so, how long have you smoked and roughly how many cigarettes a day?" [Patient: About 15 to 20 a day for 45 years.] "Thank you for telling me — I appreciate your honesty. And what about alcohol — do you drink, and roughly how often?" [Patient: Three or four drinks most evenings.] "I appreciate you sharing that. I'm not here to judge — I just need the full picture to help you properly." "Is there any family history of cancer that you know of?" [Patient: My brother died of lung cancer.]

Candidate calculates approximately 37.5 pack-years. Alcohol intake of 3–4 drinks most evenings significantly exceeds Australian guidelines (no more than 10 standard drinks per week). Both are major independent risk factors for oral SCC and act synergistically. Family history of lung cancer noted — does not directly increase oral cancer risk but reflects the patient's personal awareness of cancer.

STAGE 3: Clinical Examination

"Thank you, Mr Chen. I'm now going to have a careful look inside your mouth and also feel the glands in your neck — is that okay? I'll be as gentle as I can and I'll explain what I'm doing as I go." "I can see an ulcer on the left side of your tongue — it's about two centimetres across. I'm going to gently feel around it now." [Palpates ulcer.] "I'm also going to feel the glands in your neck on both sides — this is a routine part of checking the mouth." [Palpates bilateral cervical lymph nodes — finds firm, non-tender, mobile 1.5 cm node at left level II.] "You mentioned your denture has been feeling a bit tight on that side — how long has that been happening?" [Patient: A few weeks, I think.] "That's helpful to know — thank you."

Examination findings documented: 2 cm × 1.5 cm ulcer, left lateral tongue middle third, rolled and indurated margins, non-tender, firm, does not blanch, no identifiable trauma source. Left level II lymph node: firm, non-tender, mobile, 1.5 cm. The tight denture sensation is noted as potentially reflecting soft tissue change rather than a denture fit problem — not to be dismissed or used as an alternative explanation for the ulcer.

STAGE 4: Explanation, Empathy, and Urgent Referral

"Mr Chen, thank you for being so open with me today. I want to be honest with you because I think that's what you deserve. The ulcer I've found has some features that concern me — it's been there for five weeks and it's getting bigger rather than healing, the edges feel firm and raised, and I've found a small gland in your neck on the same side that I'd like a specialist to assess. I can't tell you exactly what this is — only a specialist test can do that — but I do need to refer you urgently to a specialist team who deal with exactly this kind of thing. I'd like to get that referral organised within the next two weeks." "I know this is a lot to take in, and it's okay to feel worried. We're not jumping to conclusions, but we are taking this seriously — and that's the right thing to do. Do you have any questions for me right now?" [Patient: Is it cancer?] "I honestly can't say yes or no to that today — that's exactly why we need the biopsy. What I can say is that we're not waiting, and we're getting you to the right people as quickly as possible. That's the best thing we can do for you right now."

Candidate arranges urgent referral to an oral and maxillofacial surgeon or head and neck oncology team for incisional biopsy, in line with Australian Head and Neck Cancer Society guidelines recommending specialist assessment within 2 weeks for lesions suspicious for malignancy. No watch-and-wait approach. No denture adjustment offered as a substitute for referral. Candidate documents all findings clearly in the patient record and provides Mr Chen with written information about the referral process.

PQ-21
Management of Missing Permanent Lateral Incisor
Station 20  |  Past Questions
■ Cluster 1 — History & Risk Factors

CANDIDATE BRIEF

7-year-old Ella, primary lateral fell off a year before, permanent lateral has not erupted yet, parents are concerned about the gap in middle and the space between central and canine, need to find out more about her situation and answer parents queries. Explain reasons for this and necessary investigations. Picture provided with big diastema in the middle.

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

Stage 1 — Introduction & History (0–3 min)

Greet Ella and Mrs Thompson warmly. Confirm timeline: primary lateral lost ~1 year ago, no adult tooth erupted. Ask about other missing/delayed teeth, general health, syndromes. INFLECTION 1 — Ask specifically about family history of missing teeth; Mrs Thompson reveals her sister had 'small or missing front teeth,' strongly supporting a genetic/hypodontia diagnosis.

Stage 2 — Examination & Radiograph Interpretation (3–6 min)

Assess skeletal relationship (Class I), lip competence, arch spacing, and mobility of retained 62 (Grade II mobile). Interpret radiograph: absent tooth buds for 12 and 22 bilaterally. Confirm no other missing teeth. INFLECTION 2 — Correctly naming the absent teeth as 12 and 22 and using the term 'hypodontia' demonstrates clinical precision the examiner is looking for.

Stage 3 — Explain Diagnosis to Parent (6–9 min)

Use plain language: 'The X-ray shows the adult teeth for those two spots never formed — this is called congenitally missing teeth and it can run in families.' Reassure this is common and manageable. Address Ella's emotional wellbeing if teasing is disclosed.

Stage 4 — Treatment Options & Referral (9–12 min)

Outline three pathways: (1) orthodontic space closure with canine substitution, (2) space opening for future prosthetic replacement, (3) retain primary teeth short-term. Explain implants are contraindicated until growth is complete (~18–21 years for females). Discuss interim options: removable partial denture or resin-retained bridge in adolescence. Refer to orthodontist now for treatment planning.

Stage 5 — Closing & Next Steps (12–14 min)

Summarise clearly, provide written referral, acknowledge cost concerns and private health insurance orthodontic cover. Invite questions. Reassure Ella directly with age-appropriate language.

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Focused history including timing of exfoliation, family history of hypodontia, and exclusion of other missing teeth or syndromes
  2. ✅ Systematic clinical examination: Class I skeletal and dental relationship, arch spacing, Grade II mobility of retained 62, competent lips
  3. ✅ Correct radiographic interpretation: absent tooth buds for 12 and 22 bilaterally — diagnosis of bilateral hypodontia
  4. ✅ Three treatment pathways explained clearly: space closure (canine substitution), space opening (future prosthesis), or retain primary teeth — with orthodontic referral as immediate next step
  5. ✅ Implants contraindicated until skeletal growth complete (~18–21 years in females); interim options include removable partial denture or resin-retained bridge during adolescence
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • The radiograph confirms absence of the permanent tooth buds for teeth 12 and 22 — this is bilateral hypodontia, the congenital absence of two or more permanent teeth, and it is one of the most common developmental dental anomalies, affecting approximately 2–3% of the population.
  • Implants are absolutely contraindicated in a growing child — in females, we typically wait until facial growth is complete, which is around 18 to 21 years of age, confirmed ideally with serial cephalometric records showing no change.
  • The three evidence-based treatment pathways are: orthodontic space closure with reshaping of the canines to mimic lateral incisors, orthodontic space opening followed by a resin-retained bridge or implant at skeletal maturity, or retaining the primary lateral incisor as a natural space maintainer for as long as it remains functional.
  • Hypodontia has a strong genetic basis — the family history of the maternal aunt having small or missing front teeth is clinically significant and consistent with autosomal dominant inheritance with variable expressivity.
  • The retained upper left primary lateral incisor (62) with Grade II mobility will likely exfoliate naturally in the near term; we should monitor it and consider a removable partial denture or space maintainer to preserve aesthetics and space if it is lost before a definitive plan is in place.
Curveball Deflectors
  • Mrs Thompson asks: 'Can Ella just get an implant now? I read online they can do it for children.' → Acknowledge the question respectfully: 'That's a really understandable question and I'm glad you brought it up. Unfortunately, implants are not suitable for Ella at this stage — her jaw is still growing, and if we placed an implant now, it would not grow with her face. It would end up in the wrong position and could cause serious problems. We need to wait until her growth is fully complete, which for girls is usually around 18 to 21 years. In the meantime, there are excellent options to keep her comfortable and confident — including a small removable plate or a fixed bridge that doesn't require surgery — and we'll plan those with the orthodontist.'
  • Candidate incorrectly suggests extracting the retained primary lateral incisor (62) immediately to 'encourage eruption' of the permanent tooth. → This is a critical error — the radiograph confirms there is no permanent tooth bud to erupt. Extracting 62 without a space management plan would worsen the aesthetic gap and allow space loss from drifting of adjacent teeth. The correct approach is to retain 62 for as long as it remains functional, monitor its mobility, and coordinate with an orthodontist before any extraction is considered. Removing it prematurely without a prosthetic or orthodontic plan in place would be clinically inappropriate.
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ►
STAGE 1: Introduction & History

"Hi Ella, hi Mrs Thompson — I'm Dr [Name], lovely to meet you both. Ella, I love your shoes! Mrs Thompson, I understand you're a bit worried about the gap where Ella's tooth came out — I completely understand, and we're going to work through everything together today. Is it okay if I ask you a few questions first before we have a look? So the baby tooth fell out about a year ago — did it fall out on its own, or was it taken out? And has Ella lost any other baby teeth that haven't had an adult tooth come through? Has she had any teeth that seemed to be missing or late coming through anywhere else? And just importantly — does anyone else in the family have missing teeth or very small teeth? Sometimes this runs in families."

Listen carefully for Mrs Thompson's disclosure about her sister. Note Ella's general health — no syndromes, normal development confirmed. Establish that no other teeth are missing. Record that the primary lateral exfoliated naturally approximately 12 months ago.

STAGE 2: Examination & Radiograph Interpretation

"Ella, I'm just going to have a gentle look in your mouth — I'll use this little mirror, nothing sharp, I promise. You're doing brilliantly. Mrs Thompson, while I examine Ella I'll talk you through what I'm seeing. Her jaw relationship looks really well balanced — what we call a Class I, which is great. I can see there's some spacing in the upper front area, and the baby tooth on the left side is a little wobbly — that's normal at this stage. Now, looking at the X-ray you've brought in — this is really helpful. What I can see here is that where we'd expect to find the adult tooth buds forming for both of those lateral incisor positions — that's the teeth either side of the two front teeth — there are no tooth buds present on either side."

Confirm on radiograph: absent tooth buds for 12 and 22 bilaterally. Assess 62 mobility as Grade II. Confirm Class I skeletal and dental relationship, competent lips, good oral hygiene, no other missing teeth. Diagnosis: bilateral hypodontia.

STAGE 3: Explaining the Diagnosis

"So what this means, Mrs Thompson, is that Ella's adult teeth for those two positions simply never formed — they're not hiding up in the gum, they just didn't develop. This is called congenitally missing teeth, or hypodontia, and it's actually one of the most common developmental variations we see — it affects about 2 to 3 in every 100 people. Importantly, it very commonly runs in families, so the fact that your sister also had small or missing front teeth fits perfectly. This is not anything Ella did, not anything you did — it's simply how her teeth developed genetically. I also want to acknowledge — Ella, I hear that some kids at school have said things about the gap. That's really not okay, and I want you to know we have really good ways to help with this, and you're going to have a beautiful smile. We just need to make a good plan."

Use empathetic, unhurried tone. Normalise the diagnosis. Address Ella directly to build trust. Avoid jargon — use 'adult teeth never formed' rather than 'agenesis.'

STAGE 4: Treatment Options, Implant Question & Next Steps

"Now, the really important thing is that there are excellent options for Ella — we just need to plan carefully because she's still growing. There are three main pathways we'd consider with a specialist. The first is using braces to close the spaces and reshape the teeth next to the gap to look like lateral incisors — this works really well and avoids any future surgery. The second is using braces to keep or create the right amount of space, and then when Ella is fully grown, placing a fixed bridge or eventually an implant. The third option for now is to keep the wobbly baby tooth in place for as long as possible as a natural placeholder while we plan. I know you've read about implants, Mrs Thompson, and that's a great question — but unfortunately implants aren't suitable until Ella's jaw has completely finished growing, which for girls is usually around 18 to 21 years. If we placed one now it wouldn't grow with her face. But we absolutely can use a small removable plate or a fixed bridge in her teenage years to keep things looking great in the meantime. The most important next step is a referral to an orthodontist — ideally soon, so we can plan around Ella's growth. I'll write that referral today. Given you have private health insurance with orthodontic cover, it's worth checking your extras cover as that can significantly offset costs. Do you have any questions for me?"

Provide written orthodontic referral. Document findings and diagnosis. Schedule review to monitor 62 mobility. Provide parent-friendly written summary of options if available. Confirm family understands no immediate surgical intervention is appropriate.

PQ-22
Management of Acute Periodontal Abscess
Station 21  |  Past Questions
■ Cluster 2 — Balanced (History informs management)

CANDIDATE BRIEF

Female patient came to your clinic with sore 11 and mobility grade II. A periapical given showing horizontal bone loss around 4,5,6 and bone around 11 was severely lost. The patient is fit and healthy, but she smokes 25 cigarettes/day. Manage the case, give differential diagnosis, and explain treatment options.

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

Stage 1 — Focused History (0–2 min)

Greet patient, confirm identity. Ask about pain onset (2 days), severity (8/10 throbbing), swelling, bad taste (purulent discharge), fever, and dysphagia. INFLECTION 1 Ask specifically about diabetes control — HbA1c 8.2% at last check 6 months ago — metformin dose, and drug allergies. This directly changes antibiotic decision-making and risk stratification.

Stage 2 — Clinical Examination (2–4 min)

Inspect buccal swelling on 46, palpate for fluctuance, test vitality (tooth is vital), assess grade II mobility, and probe disto-buccal pocket (9 mm with purulent discharge). Review radiograph: 60% bone loss, vertical defect distally, no periapical pathology.

Stage 3 — Diagnosis and Differential (4–5 min)

Primary diagnosis: acute periodontal abscess tooth 46. Differential: periapical abscess — excluded by positive vitality and absence of periapical radiolucency. Underlying: generalised chronic periodontitis Stage III Grade B. INFLECTION 2 Failure to confirm vitality is the most common error that leads to incorrect diagnosis and inappropriate endodontic referral.

Stage 4 — Immediate Management (5–7 min)

Drainage via pocket with curette; irrigate with saline and 0.12% chlorhexidine; incise if fluctuant. Prescribe amoxicillin 500 mg TDS for 5 days given suboptimal diabetes control. Paracetamol for analgesia. Warm saline rinses.

Stage 5 — Definitive Treatment and Communication (7–9 min)

Review in 2–3 days. Schedule full-mouth periodontal debridement under local anaesthesia. Counsel on diabetes–periodontitis bidirectional link. Refer to GP for HbA1c review. Reinforce 3-monthly recall and daily interdental cleaning compliance.

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Confirms tooth 46 is vital — the single most important finding that distinguishes periodontal abscess from periapical abscess and drives the correct diagnosis
  2. ✅ Identifies suboptimal diabetes control (HbA1c 8.2%) as a systemic risk factor that mandates antibiotic prescription and GP referral
  3. ✅ Performs pocket probing and identifies 9 mm disto-buccal pocket with purulent discharge as the source of the acute presentation
  4. ✅ Provides immediate drainage (via pocket or incision if fluctuant) and irrigates with saline/chlorhexidine before prescribing amoxicillin 500 mg TDS for 5 days
  5. ✅ Communicates the bidirectional relationship between diabetes and periodontal disease, arranges 2–3 day review, and plans definitive periodontal therapy once acute phase resolves
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • The tooth is vital on pulp sensibility testing, which rules out a periapical abscess — this is a periodontal abscess arising from a pre-existing 9 mm pocket with purulent discharge.
  • Her HbA1c of 8.2% indicates suboptimal glycaemic control, which impairs neutrophil function and increases the risk of systemic spread — this is why I am prescribing antibiotics in addition to local drainage.
  • I am diagnosing this as Stage III Grade B generalised periodontitis based on the 60% bone loss, vertical defect, grade II mobility, and her non-compliance with 3-monthly maintenance over 14 months.
  • Drainage is the primary treatment — antibiotics alone without establishing drainage are insufficient and will not resolve a periodontal abscess.
  • The diabetes–periodontitis relationship is bidirectional: poorly controlled diabetes worsens periodontal destruction, and active periodontal infection further elevates blood glucose — treating one improves the other.
Curveball Deflectors
  • Patient asks: 'Can't you just give me antibiotics and I'll come back when it settles down?' → Acknowledge her concern about time, then explain clearly: 'I understand you're busy, but antibiotics alone won't fix this — the infection is sitting in a pocket and needs to be drained today. Without drainage, the antibiotics can't reach the source of the infection effectively, and there's a real risk it could spread, especially given your diabetes. The procedure itself takes only a few minutes and will give you much faster relief.' Proceed with drainage.
  • Candidate incorrectly diagnoses periapical abscess and suggests root canal treatment → Redirect by confirming vitality: 'Before we consider endodontic treatment, I need to test whether this tooth is alive. I'll use an electric pulp tester and cold test. If the tooth responds normally, the source of infection is periodontal, not pulpal, and root canal treatment would be inappropriate. In this case the tooth is vital, so our management is drainage via the periodontal pocket, not root canal therapy.'
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ►
STAGE 1: History Taking

"Hi Mrs Chen, I'm Dr [Name], one of the dentists here today. I can see you're in quite a bit of discomfort — I want to make sure we sort this out for you as quickly as possible. Can you tell me when the pain started and what it feels like?"

Listen for: onset 2 days ago, worsening yesterday, throbbing 8/10. Then ask specifically: "Have you noticed any swelling? Any bad taste in your mouth? Any fever, chills, or difficulty swallowing?" Confirm bad taste (purulent discharge), swelling appeared yesterday afternoon, no fever, swallowing normal. Then transition to medical history: "I need to ask about your general health — do you have any medical conditions or take any regular medications?" Elicit Type 2 diabetes, metformin 1000 mg BD, HbA1c 8.2% six months ago, no drug allergies. Note: suboptimal glycaemic control is a critical risk modifier for this case.

STAGE 2: Clinical Examination and Diagnosis

"I'm going to have a careful look and feel around that tooth, and I'll do a couple of quick tests to check the nerve is healthy. Let me know if anything is uncomfortable."

Inspect buccal aspect of 46: erythema, localised swelling. Palpate: assess for fluctuance. Vitality testing: electric pulp test and cold test — tooth 46 responds positively, confirming vitality. Assess mobility: grade II. Probe disto-buccal aspect: 9 mm pocket with purulent discharge on probing. Review radiograph: 60% bone loss around 46, vertical defect distally, no periapical radiolucency. Diagnosis: acute periodontal abscess tooth 46, arising from pre-existing deep pocket. Underlying diagnosis: generalised chronic periodontitis Stage III Grade B. Differential excluded: periapical abscess — ruled out by positive vitality and absence of periapical pathology on radiograph.

STAGE 3: Immediate Management

"Mrs Chen, the good news is that the nerve of this tooth is alive and healthy, so we don't need to do a root canal. What's happened is that the infection has built up in a very deep gum pocket around this tooth. I need to drain that infection today — it will give you much faster relief than antibiotics alone. I'll numb the area first so you won't feel anything sharp."

Administer local anaesthesia (inferior alveolar nerve block). Establish drainage via the 9 mm pocket using a curette, gently debriding the pocket and expressing purulent exudate. If fluctuant swelling is present, perform incision and drainage with a No. 15 blade. Irrigate thoroughly with sterile saline followed by 0.12% chlorhexidine gluconate. Prescribe amoxicillin 500 mg orally three times daily for five days — rationale: suboptimal diabetes control (HbA1c 8.2%) impairs immune response and increases risk of systemic spread, making antibiotics clinically indicated alongside local drainage. Advise paracetamol 1 g every six hours as needed for analgesia and warm saline rinses three times daily.

STAGE 4: Definitive Plan and Patient Communication

"I'd like to see you again in two to three days to make sure the infection is settling. Once it has, we'll plan a thorough clean of all your gums under local anaesthetic — that's the proper treatment for the gum disease that caused this in the first place. I also want to mention something important: your diabetes and your gum disease actually affect each other. When your blood sugar is not well controlled, it makes gum disease harder to treat and easier to get worse. And active gum infection can actually push your blood sugar higher. So getting your diabetes checked by your GP is really important — not just for your general health, but for your teeth as well. Would you be okay with making an appointment with your GP soon?"

Book review appointment in 2–3 days to assess resolution of acute infection. Schedule comprehensive periodontal therapy: full-mouth debridement under local anaesthesia in quadrant appointments once acute phase resolves. Reinstate 3-monthly periodontal maintenance recall. Provide oral hygiene instruction including interdental brushing and flossing technique. Issue GP referral letter requesting HbA1c review and optimisation of diabetes management. Document all findings, diagnosis, treatment provided, prescriptions, and follow-up plan in patient records.

PQ-23
Management of Acute Irreversible Pulpitis in a Patient Flying Interstate
Station 22  |  Past Questions
■ Cluster 2 — Balanced (History informs management)

CANDIDATE BRIEF

Mr John Adam is attending your clinic today as an emergency appointment for broken tooth on Lower right back (46). On examination, badly broken tooth, Patient going away for 2 days interstate, no gingival or apical swelling, no lymphadenitis, explain diagnosis, emergency, and definitive management. Pain management.

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

Stage 1 — Focused History (0–3 min)

Greet and establish rapport. Elicit pain onset (3 days), character (throbbing, spontaneous, night pain), progression from cold-triggered to unprovoked, aggravating factors (lying down), and failed relieving factors. Screen for swelling, fever, malaise. Confirm medical history: no allergies, no medications, not pregnant, no contraindications to NSAIDs. INFLECTION 1 — Candidate must identify spontaneous night pain as the hallmark of irreversible (not reversible) pulpitis to correctly diagnose and justify definitive treatment.

Stage 2 — Diagnosis Explanation (3–5 min)

Explain in plain language: "The nerve inside your tooth is severely inflamed and will not settle on its own — we call this irreversible pulpitis." Confirm no swelling or infection spread. Explicitly warn about barodontalgia: pressure changes at altitude can dramatically intensify dental pain, making the flight very difficult to manage. INFLECTION 2 — Failure to mention barodontalgia is a critical omission given the travel context; this is the pivot point of the entire station.

Stage 3 — Emergency Treatment Options (5–8 min)

First-line recommendation: pulpectomy (nerve removal) today before travel — most effective way to eliminate the pain source. If declined or time-limited: arrange emergency dental referral in Brisbane with contact details. Explain both options clearly and without pressure, respecting patient autonomy.

Stage 4 — Analgesia and Safety Netting (8–10 min)

Prescribe ibuprofen 400mg every 6–8 hours with food plus paracetamol 1g every 6 hours, staggered. Advise taking analgesia before boarding. Warn that medication alone is unlikely to fully control irreversible pulpitis. Provide Brisbane emergency dental contact. Advise to seek care immediately if swelling or fever develops.

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Identifies spontaneous night pain and progression from cold-triggered to unprovoked as diagnostic hallmarks of irreversible pulpitis
  2. ✅ Explicitly warns about barodontalgia — pressure changes during flight can cause severe, unmanageable pain in untreated pulpitis
  3. ✅ Recommends pulpectomy today as first-line emergency management before travel, with Brisbane emergency referral as an alternative
  4. ✅ Prescribes staggered ibuprofen 400mg + paracetamol 1g with correct dosing intervals and advises pre-flight dosing
  5. ✅ Demonstrates empathy for travel constraints, acknowledges conference importance, and provides practical safety-netting including Brisbane emergency dental contact
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • "The spontaneous throbbing pain that wakes you at night tells me the nerve is irreversibly inflamed — it will not settle on its own regardless of how much pain relief you take."
  • "When cabin pressure drops during your flight, the gas pressure inside that inflamed tooth can expand and cause severe, sudden pain that no over-the-counter medication will adequately control at altitude — this is called barodontalgia."
  • "The definitive emergency treatment is a pulpectomy — I remove the inflamed nerve tissue today, which eliminates the pain source before you board. This is the most reliable way to protect you during travel."
  • "I would recommend ibuprofen 400mg every six to eight hours with food, staggered with paracetamol one gram every six hours — take your first dose about an hour before you board, but please understand this is a bridge, not a cure."
Curveball Deflectors
  • "Can't I just take strong painkillers and get it treated when I get back?" → Acknowledge the preference empathetically, then explain clearly: irreversible pulpitis does not respond reliably to analgesics alone, and the pressure changes during a 2.5-hour flight carry a genuine risk of severe, uncontrollable pain mid-flight. Offer the pulpectomy today as a straightforward procedure that takes the risk away entirely, and offer Brisbane emergency contact as a fallback — but be honest that neither option is as safe as treating it now.
  • Candidate prescribes antibiotics as the primary management for irreversible pulpitis → Antibiotics have no role in irreversible pulpitis — this is a sterile inflammatory condition, not a bacterial infection, and there is no swelling, fever, or signs of spreading infection. The correct management is pulpal extirpation. Antibiotics would not reduce inflammation, would not prevent barodontalgia, and prescribing them here reflects a fundamental diagnostic error. Redirect to pulpectomy and appropriate analgesia.
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ►
STAGE 1: Focused History

"Hi Mr Adam, I'm Dr [Name] — thanks for coming in today. I can see you're in some discomfort, so let's get to the bottom of this quickly. Can you tell me a bit about the pain? When did it start, and what does it feel like?"

Listen for onset (3 days), character (throbbing, spontaneous), and progression. Then ask directly: "Is the pain waking you at night? Does anything make it better or worse — hot, cold, lying down?" Elicit that cold previously helped but no longer does, and that lying down worsens pain. Screen for systemic spread: "Any swelling in your face or jaw? Any fever or feeling generally unwell?" Confirm medical history: "Any medical conditions, medications, or allergies I should know about? Any chance you could be pregnant?" Document: no allergies, no relevant medications, no contraindications to NSAIDs.

STAGE 2: Diagnosis Explanation

"Thank you for telling me all of that. Based on what you've described — the pain starting spontaneously, waking you at night, and not settling with cold water anymore — and what I can see on examination, the nerve inside your back tooth is severely inflamed. We call this irreversible pulpitis, which means the nerve is too damaged to heal on its own. The good news is there's no sign of infection spreading — no swelling, no fever — so we've caught this at the right stage. Now, I do need to flag something important about your flight. When the cabin pressure changes during take-off and descent, the pressure inside an inflamed tooth can shift dramatically and trigger severe, sudden pain. This is called barodontalgia, and it can be very difficult to manage once you're in the air. I want to make sure we protect you from that."

Observe patient's reaction — if anxious, normalise: "I know this is a lot to take in, especially with your conference coming up. Let me walk you through your options so we can make the best plan together."

STAGE 3: Treatment Options

"The most effective thing we can do today — and my strong recommendation — is to perform what we call a pulpectomy. That means I gently remove the inflamed nerve tissue from inside the tooth under local anaesthetic. It's a straightforward procedure, it takes the pain source away, and it means you can fly and present at your conference without that risk hanging over you. The tooth would then be properly finished when you return. If for any reason you'd prefer not to do that today, the alternative is that I arrange an emergency dental appointment for you in Brisbane as soon as you land — I can give you the contact details for an emergency dental clinic there. I do want to be honest with you though: relying on pain medication alone through the flight is the option I'd be least comfortable recommending, because irreversible pulpitis doesn't respond reliably to analgesics. What are your thoughts?"

Respect patient autonomy. If patient agrees to pulpectomy, proceed. If patient declines, confirm Brisbane referral details and document informed refusal.

STAGE 4: Analgesia and Safety Netting

"Regardless of what we decide today, I'm going to give you a pain management plan. I'd like you to take ibuprofen 400 milligrams every six to eight hours with food — that's an anti-inflammatory — and alternate it with paracetamol one gram every six hours, so you're getting pain relief roughly every three hours around the clock. Make sure you take a dose of both about an hour before you board the plane. If you develop any facial swelling, a fever, or difficulty swallowing at any point, that would mean the infection is spreading and you'd need to go to a hospital emergency department straight away — don't wait on that. Here are the details for an emergency dental clinic in Brisbane in case you need them. And please don't hesitate to call us if anything changes before your flight. I really hope your conference goes well — let's make sure your tooth doesn't get in the way of it."

Provide written instructions for analgesia dosing schedule. Document Brisbane emergency dental contact provided. Record diagnosis, treatment offered, patient decision, and safety-netting advice in clinical notes.

PQ-24
Post-Endodontic Pain Management Following Recent Root Canal Treatment
Station 23  |  Past Questions
■ Cluster 3 — Evaluation & Treatment Planning

CANDIDATE BRIEF

Patient had RCT done on lower right back tooth 3 days ago with another dentist. Previous dentist didn't explain complications of RCT. Patient has an appointment with a dentist in 2 weeks. She came to see you today because she has pain after the treatment. On examination, band (stainless steel) was given to tooth and GIC filled (temporary restoration). Pain on biting, not sensitive to hot or cold. X-ray provided shows slightly inadequate obturation. Patient wants pain management and wants to know why previous dentist did RCT when there was a crack, anything wrong with RCT.

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

Stage 1 — Introduction & Pain History (0–3 min)

Introduce yourself, acknowledge the patient's discomfort, and take a focused pain history: onset, character (throbbing, constant), severity (6–7/10), aggravating factors (biting), relieving factors, and current analgesic use (paracetamol + ibuprofen with minimal relief). Ask about the original indication for RCT — the crack identified after biting hard bread — and the timeline of treatment. INFLECTION 1 Candidates who fail to ask about the crack history miss the cracked tooth syndrome context and cannot form a complete diagnosis.

Stage 2 — Infection Screen & Medical History (3–5 min)

Screen for signs of spreading infection: fever, facial swelling, trismus, pus discharge, lymphadenopathy. Confirm all are absent. Take medical history: well-controlled hypertension on perindopril 5 mg daily, no allergies. Note perindopril relevance — NSAIDs can elevate blood pressure and reduce antihypertensive efficacy, so analgesic choice requires consideration.

Stage 3 — Clinical Examination (5–8 min)

Examine the temporary restoration (intact), perform percussion (TTP ++ on 46), assess mobility (none), palpate buccal mucosa (slightly tender, no sinus), check lymph nodes (clear), inspect crack line, and critically assess occlusion — identifying a high spot on the temporary restoration. INFLECTION 2 Candidates who omit the occlusion check miss the primary treatable cause of pain and cannot justify immediate occlusal adjustment.

Stage 4 — Radiograph Interpretation & Diagnosis (8–10 min)

Request and interpret the PA: obturation to working length, widened PDL space apically, faint crack line. Formulate provisional diagnosis: post-endodontic pain — multifactorial, including occlusal trauma from high temporary restoration, apical periodontitis, and possible crack propagation.

Stage 5 — Management & Patient Communication (10–14 min)

Perform immediate occlusal adjustment. Optimise analgesia with scheduled alternating paracetamol and ibuprofen (with caution given perindopril). Explain why RCT was indicated for a cracked tooth. Stress urgency of definitive crown to splint the crack. Provide safety-netting: return immediately if swelling, fever, or worsening pain develops. Confirm the two-week follow-up appointment with the regular dentist.

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Identifies the high spot on the temporary restoration as the primary immediate cause of post-endodontic pain and performs occlusal adjustment
  2. ✅ Recognises multifactorial aetiology: occlusal trauma + apical periodontitis + possible crack propagation — not simply 'failed RCT'
  3. ✅ Notes perindopril interaction with NSAIDs and counsels accordingly when optimising analgesia
  4. ✅ Interprets the PA correctly — obturation to working length, widened PDL space, faint crack — and does not over-diagnose RCT failure
  5. ✅ Communicates urgency of definitive crown placement to splint the cracked tooth and prevent irreversible fracture, while validating the patient's concerns about the previous dentist
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • The widened PDL space on the X-ray tells me there is some inflammation around the root tip, which is a normal finding in the first one to two weeks after root canal treatment — it does not mean the treatment has failed.
  • The most important finding today is that your bite is slightly high on the temporary filling — this is putting extra pressure on the tooth every time you close, which is very likely the main reason your pain is so severe, and I can adjust that for you right now.
  • Because you are on perindopril for your blood pressure, I want to be careful with anti-inflammatory tablets like ibuprofen — they can reduce how well your blood pressure medication works, so I will recommend you take them only short-term and at the lowest effective dose, and we will monitor this.
  • A cracked tooth that has caused nerve damage or infection is a clear indication for root canal treatment — the previous dentist made the correct decision; the crack is the underlying problem, not the treatment itself.
  • The definitive crown needs to be placed as soon as possible — ideally within the next two weeks as already planned — because the crown acts like a helmet that holds the cracked tooth together and prevents the crack from splitting the tooth completely, which would mean losing it.
Curveball Deflectors
  • Patient says: 'The previous dentist didn't tell me anything about a crack — I think they did something wrong and I want to make a complaint.' → Acknowledge the patient's frustration empathetically without criticising the previous dentist. Say: 'I completely understand why you feel that way — you deserved a full explanation before treatment. From what I can see today, the root canal treatment itself appears to have been performed correctly. The crack in your tooth was the reason the treatment was needed, and it was already present before the procedure. I'd encourage you to raise your concerns directly with that practice, and if you remain unsatisfied, the Dental Board of Australia and AHPRA can provide guidance on the complaints process. My focus today is making sure you are comfortable and that your tooth is protected.'
  • Candidate prescribes antibiotics immediately without clinical evidence of infection. → Resist this. There is no fever, no swelling, no sinus, no lymphadenopathy, and no pus — antibiotics are not indicated at this visit. The correct answer is: 'There are currently no signs of spreading infection, so antibiotics are not needed today. I will adjust the bite, optimise your pain relief, and give you clear instructions to return immediately if you develop swelling, fever, difficulty swallowing, or worsening pain — those would be signs that antibiotics and urgent review are needed.'
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ►
STAGE 1: Introduction & Pain History

"Hi, I'm [name], one of the dentists here. I can see you've come in because you're having pain after your root canal treatment — I'm really glad you came in today rather than waiting. I want to make sure we sort this out for you. Can I ask you a few questions first so I understand exactly what's going on?"

Candidate takes a focused pain history. Establishes: pain is 6–7/10, throbbing, constant, significantly worse on biting, present since the RCT three days ago. Patient is taking paracetamol and ibuprofen together but getting minimal relief. Asks about the original problem — crack identified two weeks ago after biting hard bread, tooth became sensitive to cold and biting, temporary filling placed at that time, then RCT performed three days ago at a different practice while regular dentist was away. Temporary restoration with stainless steel band and GIC placed; told to return in two weeks for a crown.

STAGE 2: Infection Screen & Medical History

"I need to check for any signs that an infection might be developing. Have you had any fever or chills? Any swelling of your face or jaw? Any difficulty opening your mouth wide, or trouble swallowing? Have you noticed any pus or discharge from the gum near that tooth?"

Patient confirms no fever, no facial swelling, no trismus, no pus — gum feels slightly tender. Candidate notes absence of systemic infection signs. Medical history taken: well-controlled hypertension on perindopril 5 mg daily, no known drug allergies. Candidate mentally flags that NSAIDs should be used cautiously and short-term given perindopril interaction.

STAGE 3: Clinical Examination & Radiograph
