"I'm going to have a look and do a gentle examination of the tooth and the surrounding area. I'll also take an X-ray so I can see the root canal treatment and the bone around the root tip. I'll be as gentle as I can — please let me know if anything is uncomfortable."

Examination findings: temporary restoration intact, no obvious defect. TTP ++ on 46. No mobility. Buccal mucosa slightly tender on palpation, no swelling, no sinus tract. No cervical lymphadenopathy. Crack line visible mesiodistally across occlusal surface. Occlusion check reveals a high spot on the temporary restoration when patient taps teeth together — candidate identifies this as a key finding. PA radiograph requested and interpreted: obturation to working length in all three canals, no obvious voids, widened PDL space apically consistent with post-operative inflammation, faint crack line visible from occlusal surface not clearly extending into root on 2D image.

STAGE 4: Diagnosis, Management & Patient Education

"Thank you for your patience. I can now explain what I think is going on and what we're going to do today. There are a few reasons why you're in pain. The most important one I can fix right now is that the temporary filling is sitting slightly too high — so every time you bite, that tooth is taking more pressure than it should. I'm going to gently adjust that today, and that should give you significant relief quite quickly. The X-ray shows the root canal treatment was done to the correct length in all three canals, which is reassuring — the treatment itself looks appropriate. There is some mild inflammation around the root tip, which is completely normal in the first one to two weeks after root canal treatment and should settle on its own. The crack in your tooth was the reason the root canal was needed in the first place — the previous dentist made the right call treating it. To answer your question about why they did the root canal when there was a crack: when a crack damages the nerve inside the tooth, root canal treatment is the only way to save the tooth. The most important next step is getting your crown placed as soon as possible — ideally at your appointment in two weeks. The crown holds the cracked tooth together like a helmet and stops the crack from splitting the tooth further. For pain relief, I'd like you to continue alternating paracetamol and ibuprofen on a regular schedule rather than waiting until the pain is severe — take them every six hours, alternating between the two. Because you're on perindopril for your blood pressure, please only use ibuprofen short-term and at the lowest dose that helps, and let your GP know if your blood pressure readings change. I'm not going to prescribe antibiotics today because there are no signs of infection — but I want you to come back immediately, or go to an emergency dental clinic, if you develop any facial swelling, fever, difficulty swallowing, or if the pain gets significantly worse. Does that all make sense? Do you have any questions?"

Candidate performs occlusal adjustment of temporary restoration intraorally. Documents findings, diagnosis, and management plan. Provides written safety-netting instructions. Confirms two-week follow-up with regular dentist for crown preparation and advises patient to contact that practice to ensure the appointment is prioritised.

PQ-25
Consent for Extraction
Station 24  |  Past Questions
■ Cluster 3 — Evaluation & Treatment Planning

CANDIDATE BRIEF

16 badly broken, unrestorable, needs extraction. Explain procedure, describe complications, and post op instructions. X-ray provided. Smoking history.

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

Stage 1 — Confirm Identity and Tooth (0:00–1:00)

Confirm full name and date of birth. Point to the X-ray and state: 'This is tooth 16, your upper right first molar — that's the tooth we'll be removing today.' Acknowledge anxiety and set a collaborative tone. INFLECTION 1 — Failure to confirm the correct tooth before proceeding is a patient safety failure and likely a critical error on the rubric.

Stage 2 — Explain Procedure and Alternatives (1:00–3:30)

Explain local anaesthetic, loosening of the tooth, and removal in plain language. Confirm the tooth is unrestorable and that root canal treatment is not a viable alternative in this case. Mention approximate time frame (15–30 minutes).

Stage 3 — Risks: Common and Serious (3:30–6:00)

Cover common risks (pain, swelling, bruising, bleeding, trismus, adjacent tooth damage) then serious/specific risks: dry socket, oro-antral communication (upper molar proximity to maxillary sinus), root fracture requiring surgical retrieval, and rare nerve injury. INFLECTION 2 — Oro-antral communication is the high-yield serious risk for UR6 that weaker candidates omit. Examiners specifically look for this.

Stage 4 — Post-Op Instructions and Lifestyle Factors (6:00–8:00)

Gauze pressure for 30 minutes, no rinsing for 24 hours, soft diet, analgesia (paracetamol ± ibuprofen), no smoking for 48–72 hours (dry socket risk), no vigorous exercise. Confirm she can drive (LA only) and is likely fit for work the next day.

Stage 5 — Confirm Consent and Document (8:00–9:00)

Check understanding, invite questions, confirm voluntary consent, and state intention to document in clinical notes including risks discussed and patient agreement.

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Confirms patient identity AND correct tooth (16/UR6) using the X-ray before any discussion proceeds
  2. ✅ Names oro-antral communication as a specific serious risk for upper first molar extraction — the highest-yield examiner checkpoint in this station
  3. ✅ Directly addresses smoking history and links it to increased dry socket risk with a specific timeframe (avoid smoking 48–72 hours)
  4. ✅ Confirms Mrs Collins can drive home after local anaesthetic alone and is likely fit for work the following day — addresses her stated concerns
  5. ✅ Closes the loop: checks understanding, invites questions, confirms voluntary consent, and states documentation intent
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • The roots of your upper back molar sit very close to a sinus cavity just above — there is a small risk of a connection forming between the socket and that sinus, which we would need to manage if it occurred.
  • Dry socket occurs when the blood clot in the socket breaks down before healing is complete — it causes a deep, throbbing pain usually starting around day three, and smoking significantly increases that risk, which is why I strongly recommend avoiding cigarettes for at least 48 to 72 hours.
  • Because this is a local anaesthetic procedure only, it will not affect your ability to drive — you are safe to drive yourself home today.
  • Root canal treatment would normally be an option to save a molar, but given how extensively broken down this tooth is, there is not enough sound tooth structure remaining to restore it, which is why extraction is the recommended treatment.
Curveball Deflectors
  • Patient asks: 'What is dry socket? Is it serious?' → Acknowledge the question warmly: 'That's a really good question.' Explain that dry socket — or alveolar osteitis — happens when the protective blood clot in the socket is lost or breaks down too early, leaving the bone exposed. It causes a dull, throbbing ache that typically starts around day two or three and can radiate toward the ear. It is not dangerous but it is uncomfortable and needs a dressing from us to settle it down. Reassure her it is manageable and that following post-op instructions — especially not smoking and not rinsing forcefully — significantly reduces the risk.
  • Candidate omits oro-antral communication or describes it vaguely as 'a hole' → This is the most common mark-losing error for UR6 consent. The correct approach is to name it specifically and explain the anatomy: the roots of the upper first molar are in close proximity to the floor of the maxillary sinus. An oro-antral communication means a small opening forms between the mouth and the sinus. Signs include air or fluid passing through the socket, or a nasal quality to the voice. If it occurs, it may close spontaneously for small openings or require surgical repair. Do not omit this risk or conflate it with a generic 'hole in the gum.'
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ►
STAGE 1: Confirm Identity and Tooth

"Before we get started, can I just confirm your full name and date of birth for me? Thank you, Mrs Collins. And I can see from your records you've taken some time off work today — I really appreciate that, and I want to make sure we use that time well and get you comfortable with everything before we proceed. I've had a look at your X-ray here, and I want to point out the tooth we're talking about — this one here, tooth 16, your upper right first molar at the back. Does that match your understanding of which tooth we're removing today?"

Point to tooth 16 on the X-ray. Confirm verbal agreement from patient. Note her anxiety and establish rapport. Check medical history confirmation — amlodipine noted, no bleeding disorders, no allergies.

STAGE 2: Procedure Explanation and Alternatives

"I want to explain what the procedure involves so there are no surprises. First, I'll give you some local anaesthetic — a few small injections into the gum around the tooth to numb the area completely. You'll feel some pressure and movement, but you should not feel any sharp pain. If at any point you do, please raise your hand and I'll stop immediately. Once you're numb, I'll use some instruments to gently loosen the tooth from the socket and then ease it out. The whole thing usually takes around 15 to 30 minutes. Now, I do want to mention — in some cases we can save a back molar with root canal treatment, but looking at your X-ray and examining the tooth, it's too badly broken down for that to be a realistic option. There simply isn't enough healthy tooth structure left to restore it, so extraction really is the right treatment here."

Use the X-ray to illustrate. Avoid jargon. Confirm patient understands and accepts that the tooth cannot be saved.

STAGE 3: Risks — Common and Serious

"I do need to go through some of the risks with you — most people sail through this without any problems, but it's important you know what to watch for. Common things after an extraction include some pain and swelling for a few days, possible bruising around the jaw, a small amount of bleeding in the first hour or two, and sometimes some stiffness when opening your mouth. There's also a very small chance of minor damage to the tooth next door during the procedure. Now, for this particular tooth, there are a couple of specific risks I want to mention. One is called dry socket — that's when the blood clot that forms in the socket breaks down too early, leaving the bone exposed. It causes a deep, throbbing ache usually starting around day two or three. It's not dangerous, but it is uncomfortable, and we'd need to see you to place a soothing dressing. The other risk specific to upper back molars is that the roots sit very close to a sinus cavity just above — there's a small chance of a connection forming between the socket and that sinus during the extraction. If that happens, we'd manage it on the day and monitor it closely — small ones often heal on their own. There's also a small chance a root tip might fracture during removal, which may require a minor surgical procedure to retrieve it. Nerve injury is very rare for this tooth but I mention it for completeness."

Pause after dry socket — patient is likely to ask a follow-up question here. Be ready to explain alveolar osteitis in plain language. Oro-antral communication must be named and explained anatomically.

STAGE 4: Post-Op Instructions, Lifestyle, and Consent Confirmation

"After the extraction, I'll ask you to bite down on a gauze pad for about 30 minutes to help the clot form. For the first 24 hours, please don't rinse your mouth, don't use a straw, and avoid anything hot. After that, you can gently rinse with warm salty water. For pain relief, paracetamol — something like Panadol — is a good first choice, and you can alternate with ibuprofen like Nurofen if you need to, as long as that's okay with your stomach. Now, I did notice from your history that you smoke — I'd really encourage you to avoid smoking for at least 48 to 72 hours after the extraction, ideally longer. Smoking is one of the biggest risk factors for dry socket because it reduces blood flow to the area and can dislodge the clot. I know that's not easy, but it makes a real difference. In terms of driving — because we're only using local anaesthetic today, it won't affect your ability to drive, so you're absolutely fine to drive yourself home. And regarding work tomorrow — most people feel well enough to return to a desk job the next day, though everyone's a little different. If you have any concerns, just give us a call. Please do come back or call us if the bleeding doesn't settle within an hour or two, if the pain gets significantly worse after day three, or if you notice any fluid or air coming through the socket. Does all of that make sense? Do you have any questions for me before we go ahead? And just to confirm — are you happy to proceed with the extraction today of your own free will?"

Confirm voluntary consent verbally. Document in clinical notes: tooth confirmed, risks discussed (including dry socket and oro-antral communication), alternatives explained, patient questions addressed, consent given. Note smoking history and advice provided.

PQ-26
Assessment and Management of Palatal Swelling
Station 25  |  Past Questions
■ Cluster 1 — History & Risk Factors

CANDIDATE BRIEF

Mr Michael Jones comes for check-up, he is new to your practice. He is seeing you today and his last check-up was 4 years ago. Large Bluish/dark red swelling on the right side of the palate between 3-7 for 5 years. Complaints about his previous dentist who did RCT filling 4 year ago. How would you gain more information and what special investigation would you do and based on the findings? Give differential diagnosis.

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

Stage 1 — Introduction & Presenting Complaint History (0–3 min)

Introduce yourself, confirm patient identity, and acknowledge anxiety. Ask open-ended questions about the swelling: duration (5 years), onset, growth pattern, pain, bleeding, discharge, and functional impact (swallowing, speech). Clarify the complaint about the previous RCT — which tooth, any symptoms since. INFLECTION 1 — Candidate must distinguish whether the swelling is odontogenic (linked to RCT tooth) or non-odontogenic; adjacent teeth are vital, shifting the differential away from periapical pathology.

Stage 2 — Medical & Social History (3–5 min)

Ask about smoking, alcohol, previous malignancy, medications, allergies. Exclude systemic red flags: fever, weight loss, night sweats, dysphagia, voice change. Patient is a non-smoker, occasional wine drinker, no significant medical history.

Stage 3 — Clinical Examination (5–8 min)

Systematically palpate swelling — size (~2 cm), consistency (firm), surface (smooth), tenderness (non-tender), fluctuance (present). Test vitality of 25, 26, 27 (all vital). Percussion test (non-tender). Inspect for sinus tract (none). Palpate cervical lymph nodes bilaterally (no lymphadenopathy). INFLECTION 2 — Fluctuance in a firm palatal swelling with vital teeth and no lymphadenopathy strongly points to a salivary gland lesion rather than abscess or bony pathology; candidate must articulate this reasoning.

Stage 4 — Differential Diagnosis & Investigations (8–11 min)

Lead differential: minor salivary gland neoplasm (pleomorphic adenoma). Alternatives: malignant salivary gland tumour, palatal abscess, nasopalatine duct cyst. Investigations: CT or MRI of head and neck; urgent referral to oral and maxillofacial surgery within 2 weeks for incisional biopsy.

Stage 5 — Communication, Safety-Netting & Documentation (11–13 min)

Sensitively address cancer concerns without false reassurance. Explain referral rationale. Safety-net: return immediately if rapid growth, pain, bleeding, or dysphagia. Document all findings and referral in patient record.

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Structured history covering duration, growth pattern, pain, bleeding, discharge, and functional symptoms (swallowing, speech, nasal)
  2. ✅ Relevant medical and social history including smoking, alcohol, prior malignancy, medications, and systemic red-flag symptoms
  3. ✅ Systematic palpation of swelling (size, consistency, fluctuance, tenderness) plus vitality testing of adjacent teeth and bilateral cervical lymph node assessment
  4. ✅ Differential diagnosis led by minor salivary gland neoplasm (pleomorphic adenoma), with malignant salivary gland tumour, abscess, and nasopalatine duct cyst as alternatives
  5. ✅ Urgent referral to oral and maxillofacial surgery within 2 weeks for CT/MRI and incisional biopsy, with sensitive communication and clear safety-netting advice
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • The adjacent teeth 25, 26, and 27 are all vital and non-tender to percussion, which effectively rules out an odontogenic or periapical origin for this swelling — this shifts my primary differential to a minor salivary gland neoplasm.
  • The palate posterior to the rugae contains the highest density of minor salivary glands in the oral cavity, making it the most common intraoral site for salivary gland tumours, the majority of which are pleomorphic adenomas.
  • A firm, smooth, non-tender, fluctuant palatal swelling of 2 cm with no lymphadenopathy and no overlying mucosal change in a patient with a five-year history of slow, stable growth is most consistent with a benign salivary gland neoplasm, but malignancy cannot be excluded without histopathology.
  • I would arrange an urgent referral to oral and maxillofacial surgery within two weeks in line with the Australian two-week wait pathway for suspected oral neoplasm, and request CT or MRI of the head and neck prior to or at the time of referral.
  • An incisional biopsy rather than excisional biopsy is the appropriate first-line tissue diagnosis for a palatal salivary gland lesion of this size, as excision without prior diagnosis risks inadequate margins if malignancy is confirmed.
Curveball Deflectors
  • Patient says: 'My last dentist told me it was just an abscess from the root canal — can't you just drain it?' → Acknowledge the patient's concern and validate their previous experience, but explain clearly: 'I understand that was suggested before, and I can see why that would be reassuring. However, the teeth next to this swelling are all healthy and responding normally to our tests, which means it's very unlikely to be coming from a tooth infection. The swelling has also been there for five years without the pain or fever we'd expect with an abscess. Because of that, I need to refer you to a specialist who can take a scan and, if needed, take a small tissue sample to find out exactly what this is. I want to make sure we don't miss anything important.'
  • Candidate incorrectly lists periapical abscess as the leading diagnosis without testing tooth vitality → Vitality testing of teeth 25, 26, and 27 is mandatory before attributing a palatal swelling to odontogenic pathology. All three teeth are vital and non-tender to percussion, and there is no sinus tract — these findings collectively exclude a periapical abscess as the primary diagnosis. Failing to test vitality and defaulting to an odontogenic cause is a critical error that would likely result in a fail on this station.
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ►
STAGE 1: Introduction & History of Presenting Complaint

"Good morning, Mr Jones. My name is Dr [Name] and I'll be looking after you today. Welcome to the practice. I understand you've noticed a swelling on the roof of your mouth — I'd like to ask you a few questions about it before I take a look, if that's okay. How long have you been aware of this lump?"

Patient confirms approximately five years. Candidate continues: ask about onset (gradual or sudden), whether it has grown, any change in size recently, associated pain, bleeding, discharge, or bad taste. Ask about functional symptoms: difficulty swallowing, changes to speech, nasal obstruction, or numbness. Ask what first drew attention to it. Also explore the complaint about the previous dentist — which tooth had the root canal, when, and whether any symptoms followed that treatment. Document all responses.

STAGE 2: Medical, Social & Systemic History

"Thank you. I'd also like to ask a few general health questions. Do you smoke or have you ever smoked? How much alcohol do you drink? Are you on any regular medications, and do you have any allergies? Have you ever been diagnosed with cancer anywhere in your body? And have you noticed any other symptoms recently — things like unexplained weight loss, fevers, or night sweats?"

Patient is a non-smoker, occasional wine drinker, no significant medical history, no medications, no allergies, no prior malignancy, no systemic symptoms. Candidate notes absence of red-flag systemic features. Confirm no difficulty swallowing and no voice changes. Document social history including occupation (primary school teacher) as relevant to general health context.

STAGE 3: Clinical Examination

"I'm going to have a careful look and feel inside your mouth now. I'll be as gentle as possible — please let me know if anything is uncomfortable. I'm also going to feel the glands in your neck, which is a routine part of checking a swelling like this."

Examine the swelling systematically: location (right posterior hard palate, lateral to midline), size (approximately 2 cm diameter), surface (smooth), overlying mucosa (normal, no ulceration), tenderness on palpation (non-tender), consistency (firm), and fluctuance (present). Inspect for sinus tract — none visible. Perform vitality testing (cold test or electric pulp tester) on teeth 25, 26, and 27 — all vital. Percussion test all three teeth — non-tender. Palpate bilateral cervical and submandibular lymph nodes — no lymphadenopathy detected. Document all findings clearly.

STAGE 4: Differential Diagnosis, Investigations & Communication

"Thank you for your patience, Mr Jones. I want to explain what I've found and what I think we should do next. There is a swelling on the roof of your mouth that is about two centimetres across. The good news is that the teeth nearby are all healthy, there's no sign of infection, and the glands in your neck feel normal. However, because this swelling has been there for five years and I can't be certain what it is just by looking and feeling, I need to refer you to a specialist — an oral and maxillofacial surgeon — who can arrange a scan and, if needed, take a very small tissue sample to find out exactly what we're dealing with. I want to be honest with you: most swellings like this in this part of the mouth come from the small saliva glands in the palate and are benign — not cancerous — but we do need to confirm that with proper tests. I'll arrange that referral urgently, within the next two weeks. In the meantime, please come back or call us straight away if the swelling grows quickly, becomes painful, bleeds, or if you have any trouble swallowing."

Differential diagnosis: (1) Minor salivary gland neoplasm — pleomorphic adenoma (most likely given firm, smooth, slow-growing, non-tender, fluctuant swelling with vital adjacent teeth and no lymphadenopathy); (2) Malignant salivary gland tumour — cannot exclude without histopathology; (3) Palatal abscess — less likely given vital teeth, no sinus tract, no tenderness, no fever; (4) Nasopalatine duct cyst — less likely given lateral palatal location. Investigations: CT or MRI head and neck for lesion characterisation and extent; urgent referral to oral and maxillofacial surgery within 2 weeks for incisional biopsy. Document differential, investigations ordered, referral details, and safety-netting advice in patient record.

PQ-27
Assessment and Counselling for Dental Implant Treatment
Station 26  |  Past Questions
■ Cluster 1 — History & Risk Factors

CANDIDATE BRIEF

Patient fit and healthy wants implants in all back teeth, take history and investigate to see if she is suitable for implants. Prosthetic heart valve replacement surgery 2 years ago, takes some medication for blood doesn't know what it is — 2 little pills. Gather information and explain necessary investigations.

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

Stage 1 — Introduction and Chief Complaint (0–1 min)

Greet Mrs Chen, confirm identity, and establish her expectation: she wants implants for all missing back teeth and expects this can happen soon. Set a collaborative tone and explain the consultation will involve some questions before any plan is made.

Stage 2 — Medical History: Cardiac and Anticoagulation INFLECTION 1 (1–3 min)

Explore the prosthetic heart valve: type, date of surgery, current cardiologist. Ask specifically what the two medications are — probe for warfarin or a DOAC. Explain an INR or liaison with cardiologist will be required before surgery. Note antibiotic prophylaxis is NOT routinely recommended for dental implants in prosthetic valve patients per current Australian guidelines, but surgical risk must be assessed.

Stage 3 — Medical History: Diabetes and Bisphosphonates INFLECTION 2 (3–5 min)

Ask about diabetes: HbA1c result and when last checked, metformin dose, GP review frequency. Then specifically ask: 'Do you take any tablets for your bones or osteoporosis?' — eliciting alendronate. Note duration (3 years, oral route). Explain MRONJ risk and need for GP liaison before implant surgery.

Stage 4 — Investigations and Treatment Planning (5–7 min)

Explain OPG is needed first; CBCT may follow. Clarify that immediate implant placement is not possible — bone assessment, medical optimisation, and specialist liaison must occur first. Outline the full implant timeline in lay terms.

Stage 5 — Alternatives, Expectations, and Close (7–8 min)

Present bridge and partial denture as alternatives. Check understanding using teach-back. Summarise next steps: GP letter, blood tests, OPG. Invite questions.

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Identifies anticoagulation therapy (likely warfarin) linked to prosthetic heart valve and requests INR/GP liaison before any implant surgery
  2. ✅ Specifically asks about bone/osteoporosis medications to elicit alendronate use (3 years duration) and counsels on MRONJ risk
  3. ✅ Identifies type 2 diabetes on metformin, asks for HbA1c (last result 7.2%, 8 months ago), and explains need to optimise glycaemic control (target HbA1c ≤7.5–8%) before implant surgery
  4. ✅ Explains that OPG (minimum) and possibly CBCT are required before planning, and that immediate implant placement is not appropriate
  5. ✅ Presents the full implant timeline in lay terms and offers alternatives (bridge, partial denture), checking patient understanding throughout
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • An HbA1c above 7.5 to 8 percent is associated with impaired wound healing and a higher risk of implant failure — we would want to see a current result and ideally optimise your diabetes control before proceeding with surgery.
  • Alendronate is a bisphosphonate medication that affects bone turnover. When taken for more than two years, it carries a risk of a serious complication called medication-related osteonecrosis of the jaw — where the jawbone can fail to heal properly after surgery. We need to discuss this with your GP before we can safely place implants.
  • Because you have a prosthetic heart valve and are on anticoagulation, we will need a current INR result and may need to liaise with your cardiologist before any surgical procedure to ensure it is safe to proceed.
  • A CBCT scan gives us a three-dimensional view of the bone volume, height, and proximity to structures like the sinus and nerve — this is essential for safe implant planning in the upper and lower back regions.
  • Osseointegration — the process where the implant fuses to the bone — typically takes three to six months. After that, we take impressions and place the crown. The full process from first assessment to final crown can take nine to eighteen months depending on whether bone grafting is needed.
Curveball Deflectors
  • Patient says: 'I just want the implants done today — can't you just put them in now?' → Acknowledge her enthusiasm and validate her desire to restore her teeth. Explain clearly but kindly that placing implants without a full assessment would be unsafe — we need to know the bone quantity and quality, check that her medical conditions are optimised, and liaise with her GP about her bone medication and anticoagulation. Rushing the process increases the risk of implant failure and serious complications. Reassure her that you will work as efficiently as possible and outline the realistic timeline.
  • Candidate fails to ask specifically about osteoporosis medications and misses the alendronate → If the candidate only asks 'are you on any medications?' without specifically prompting about bone health or osteoporosis, the patient will not volunteer the alendronate. The correct approach is to ask directly: 'Do you take any tablets for your bones, for osteoporosis, or to prevent fractures?' This targeted question is required to elicit the bisphosphonate history and is a key inflection point in this station.
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ►
STAGE 1: Introduction and Opening

'Hello Mrs Chen, my name is Dr [Name] — lovely to meet you. I understand you're interested in having dental implants to replace your missing back teeth. Before we talk about any treatment, I'd like to ask you some questions about your health and dental history so I can make sure we find the safest and best option for you. Is that okay?'

Establish rapport. Confirm chief complaint. Note patient expects immediate treatment — manage this expectation gently throughout.

STAGE 2: Medical History — Cardiac, Anticoagulation, and Medications

'You mentioned you had a heart valve replacement about two years ago — that's really important for us to know. Are you under the care of a cardiologist at the moment? You also mentioned you take two small tablets for your blood — do you happen to know the name of those? It's quite possible one of them is a blood-thinning medication like warfarin. Before any surgical procedure, we'd need to check your current blood levels and liaise with your cardiologist to make sure it's safe. Now, I'd like to ask about all your other medications — including any tablets you might take for your bones or for osteoporosis. Do you take anything like that?'

Targeted prompt for bisphosphonates is essential here — patient will not volunteer alendronate without this specific question. On eliciting alendronate: note oral route, 3-year duration — elevated MRONJ risk. Document for GP liaison letter.

STAGE 3: Diabetes History and Counselling on Medical Risks

'I can also see from your records that you manage type 2 diabetes with metformin — that's great that it's being managed. Have you had a blood test recently to check your diabetes control? It's called an HbA1c — it gives us an average of your blood sugar over the past three months. When was that last done, and do you remember the result? The reason I ask is that if blood sugar levels aren't well controlled, it can affect how well the bone heals around an implant and increase the risk of infection or implant failure. We'd ideally want your HbA1c to be below about 7.5 to 8 percent before we consider surgery. Regarding your bone tablet — alendronate is a type of medication called a bisphosphonate. It's very effective for protecting your bones, but it does affect how bone heals after surgery. There is a small but serious risk of a condition called osteonecrosis of the jaw, where the bone doesn't heal properly. We would need to write to your GP to discuss this before we could safely go ahead with implants.'

Check patient understanding after each key point. Use teach-back: 'Can I just check — what's your understanding of why we need to speak to your GP before we go ahead?' Avoid alarming language while being honest about risk.

STAGE 4: Investigations, Treatment Options, and Closing

'Before we can plan anything, we'll need to take an X-ray called an OPG — it gives us a full picture of your jaw, the bone levels, and the important structures nearby like the sinus and the nerve. We may also need a more detailed 3D scan called a CBCT to measure the bone precisely. I want to be upfront with you — implants are a wonderful option, but the process does take time. After the assessment, we may need to do some bone grafting if there isn't enough bone. Then the implant is placed and needs three to six months to fuse to the bone before we can attach the crown. The whole process from start to finish can take anywhere from nine to eighteen months. I also want to make sure you know about the alternatives — a fixed bridge, which uses the neighbouring teeth for support, or a removable partial denture. Both are valid options and we can discuss what suits you best. Do you have any questions about what I've explained so far? I'll also write a letter to your GP today to get an updated HbA1c result and to discuss your alendronate before we proceed.'

Summarise next steps clearly: GP referral letter, OPG, blood tests. Provide written information if available. Schedule follow-up once medical clearance is obtained. Document all findings and patient counselling in notes.

PQ-28
Management of Facial Cellulitis in an Uncontrolled Diabetic Patient
Station 27  |  Past Questions
■ Cluster 2 — Balanced (History informs management)

CANDIDATE BRIEF

Mr James Oliver is a new patient in your clinic, complaining of severe pain and facial swelling related to his upper right side for some time. Examination reveals that the upper right first molar is badly carious and beyond restoration, and now it is indicated for removal. He went to see GP before; he gave him antibiotics but it didn't seem to work so GP referred him to see you. Swelling is still there, and he is in a lot of pain. His medical record shows that he has diabetes for the last 8 years and for which he is using metformin. How would you plan his management and gain consent for his treatment plan and discuss possible complications that may happen?

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

Stage 1 — Focused History and Airway Screening (0–3 min)

Greet Mr Oliver and take a targeted history: onset and progression of swelling, fever, malaise, and critically screen for dysphagia, dysphonia, or dyspnoea. INFLECTION 1 — Any airway symptom mandates immediate emergency escalation (call 000 / transfer to ED). Elicit diabetes history: medications (metformin, gliclazide), compliance, last HbA1c, last BSL, and last meal/drink time.

Stage 2 — Systematic Examination (3–6 min)

Record full vital signs (temp 38.4°C, pulse 96, BP 145/88, SpO2 98%). Assess swelling extent, erythema, warmth, fluctuance, and trismus (IIO ~25 mm). Identify the carious upper right first molar as the likely source. Confirm no current airway compromise but note high-risk features.

Stage 3 — Emergency Recognition and Immediate Actions (6–9 min)

Declare this a medical emergency. INFLECTION 2 — Failure to recognise the need for hospital admission in an uncontrolled diabetic with spreading cellulitis and failed oral antibiotics is a critical error. Check point-of-care BSL immediately. Arrange urgent bloods (FBC, CRP, U&Es, blood cultures). Contact medical team.

Stage 4 — Multidisciplinary Management Plan (9–13 min)

Arrange hospital admission. Commence IV amoxicillin-clavulanate (or amoxicillin + metronidazole). Initiate IV fluids. Request OPG ± CT neck. Involve endocrinology/general medicine for glycaemic optimisation. Plan extraction of causative tooth and I&D under controlled conditions in hospital theatre.

Stage 5 — Consent and Complications Discussion (13–15 min)

Explain diagnosis in plain language. Obtain informed consent covering: extraction, possible I&D, IV antibiotics, hospital admission, risks of airway compromise, deep space spread, sepsis, and increased anaesthetic risk due to poorly controlled diabetes.

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Screens for airway compromise (dysphagia, dysphonia, dyspnoea) as the first safety priority — any positive finding requires immediate emergency escalation
  2. ✅ Elicits full diabetes history including HbA1c (9.2%), medications (metformin + gliclazide), compliance, and last meal — all directly affect surgical and anaesthetic risk
  3. ✅ Performs systematic examination including vital signs, swelling assessment, trismus measurement, and intra-oral identification of the causative carious tooth
  4. ✅ Recognises this as a medical emergency requiring hospital admission, IV antibiotics (amoxicillin-clavulanate or amoxicillin + metronidazole), IV fluids, and multidisciplinary care including medical team involvement for glycaemic control
  5. ✅ Plans definitive surgical management (extraction ± I&D) under controlled hospital conditions with appropriate imaging (OPG ± CT neck) and obtains informed consent covering airway risk, sepsis, deep space spread, and anaesthetic risks
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • This patient has a spreading odontogenic cellulitis with systemic signs — temperature 38.4°C, tachycardia, trismus, and failure of oral antibiotics — in the context of poorly controlled type 2 diabetes with an HbA1c of 9.2%. This combination mandates immediate hospital admission; this cannot be managed in a primary care dental setting.
  • I would commence IV amoxicillin-clavulanate 1.2g eight-hourly as first-line, or IV amoxicillin 2g plus metronidazole 500mg eight-hourly as an alternative. If the patient had a penicillin allergy, I would use IV clindamycin 600mg eight-hourly.
  • Before any surgical intervention, I need a point-of-care blood glucose level. Poorly controlled diabetes impairs neutrophil function, wound healing, and immune response, which is why this infection has failed to respond to oral antibiotics and is spreading rapidly.
  • I would request an OPG to confirm the odontogenic source and a CT neck with contrast if I suspect deep space involvement — specifically to rule out parapharyngeal, retropharyngeal, or submandibular space spread, which could compromise the airway.
  • Trismus of 25mm inter-incisal opening in the context of a spreading infection is a red flag for potential airway compromise. I would ensure anaesthetic and airway management teams are involved prior to any surgical procedure, as intubation may be difficult.
Curveball Deflectors
  • Patient says: 'Can't you just give me stronger antibiotics and pull the tooth out here today? I don't want to go to hospital.' → Acknowledge his concern empathetically: 'I completely understand you'd prefer to avoid hospital, Mr Oliver, and I want to make this as straightforward as possible for you. However, I have a duty of care to be honest with you — your infection is spreading and has already not responded to oral antibiotics. Because your diabetes is not well controlled at the moment, your body is finding it much harder to fight this infection. If we try to manage this in the clinic today without IV antibiotics, medical support, and proper monitoring, there is a real risk this infection could spread to your airway and become life-threatening. The safest place for you right now is hospital, where we can give you IV antibiotics, control your blood sugar, and remove the tooth under the right conditions. I would not be doing my job properly if I didn't refer you today.'
  • Candidate attempts to extract the tooth in the dental chair immediately without arranging hospital admission or checking blood glucose → This is a critical error. Extraction in an uncontrolled diabetic with active spreading cellulitis, pyrexia, and failed oral antibiotics risks bacteraemia without adequate antibiotic cover, hypoglycaemic or hyperglycaemic crisis intra-operatively, airway compromise if trismus worsens under local anaesthetic, and inadequate haemostasis due to impaired healing. The correct action is to defer extraction until the patient is admitted, medically stabilised, blood glucose optimised, and IV antibiotics have been commenced — ideally performing the procedure in a hospital operating theatre with anaesthetic support available.
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ►
STAGE 1: Introduction and Focused History

"Good morning, Mr Oliver. I'm Dr [Name], one of the dentists here. I can see you're in a lot of pain and discomfort — I want to help you as quickly as possible, so I'm going to ask you a few important questions first. Is that okay? How long have you had this swelling, and has it been getting bigger over the last day or two? Have you noticed any fever, chills, or feeling generally unwell? This is very important — have you had any difficulty swallowing, any change in your voice, or any trouble breathing at all?"

Screen immediately for airway compromise. If dysphagia, dysphonia, or dyspnoea are present, escalate to emergency services immediately. Continue history: "Can you tell me about your diabetes — what medications are you taking, and have you been taking them regularly? Do you know what your last blood sugar reading was, or your HbA1c? When did you last eat or drink anything today?" Document: metformin 1000mg BD, gliclazide, non-compliant, HbA1c 9.2% three months ago, last ate this morning, last drink two hours ago.

STAGE 2: Systematic Examination

"I'm going to take your temperature, blood pressure, and pulse, and then have a careful look at the swelling and inside your mouth. I'll be as gentle as I can. I also need to check how wide you can open your mouth — just open as wide as you comfortably can for me."

Record vital signs: temperature 38.4°C, BP 145/88, pulse 96 bpm, RR 18, SpO2 98%. Extra-oral: diffuse right facial swelling, erythematous, warm, tense, tender. Trismus: inter-incisal opening approximately 25mm. No stridor, no neck rigidity. Intra-oral: identify grossly carious upper right first molar as likely odontogenic source; assess for vestibular swelling, fluctuance, or pus. Perform point-of-care blood glucose measurement immediately.

STAGE 3: Explanation and Emergency Plan

"Mr Oliver, I want to be very honest with you about what's happening. The infection from your tooth has spread into the tissues of your face, and it's quite serious. The antibiotics your GP gave you haven't been able to control it, and because your diabetes isn't well controlled at the moment, your body is having a harder time fighting this infection than it normally would. This means I can't safely treat you here in the clinic today — I need to arrange for you to go to hospital straight away, where you can receive antibiotics directly into your vein, have your blood sugar managed properly, and have the tooth removed under the right conditions with the right support around you. I know that's not what you were hoping to hear, and I'm sorry — but this is the safest option for you, and I'd be doing you a disservice if I didn't refer you today."

Arrange immediate hospital admission. Contact on-call medical team to co-manage diabetes. Request urgent bloods: FBC, CRP, U&Es, blood cultures, HbA1c. Commence IV amoxicillin-clavulanate 1.2g eight-hourly (or amoxicillin 2g plus metronidazole 500mg eight-hourly). Initiate IV fluid resuscitation. Request OPG; arrange CT neck with contrast if deep space involvement suspected. Ensure nil by mouth status documented for theatre planning.

STAGE 4: Consent and Complications Discussion

"Once you're in hospital and your blood sugar is under better control and the antibiotics are working, the plan will be to remove that tooth — it's too badly damaged to save. If there's a pocket of pus that needs draining, the surgeon may also make a small cut to let that out, which helps the infection clear much faster. I do need to make you aware of some risks. Because the infection is spreading, there's a small but serious risk it could affect your airway — your breathing — which is one of the main reasons we want you in hospital where that can be monitored closely. There's also a risk the infection could spread further into the neck, or enter the bloodstream, which is called sepsis. Your diabetes also means healing may take a little longer than usual, and the anaesthetic team will need to take extra precautions. Do you have any questions about anything I've explained? Is there someone we can call to be with you — your wife perhaps?"

Document informed consent discussion covering: diagnosis (spreading odontogenic cellulitis), proposed treatment (hospital admission, IV antibiotics, extraction ± I&D), and risks (airway compromise, deep space spread, sepsis, impaired healing, increased anaesthetic risk due to poorly controlled diabetes). Arrange transport to hospital. Provide written referral letter to ED with full clinical details, vital signs, medications, allergy status, and last oral intake time.

PQ-29
Uncooperative Four-Year-Old Child: Charting and Diet Counselling
Station 28  |  Past Questions
■ Cluster 2 — Balanced (History informs management)

CANDIDATE BRIEF

4-year-old, multiple caries in primary molars. Child had caries, multiple decays, mostly all molars, came with pain. The child was uncooperative and did not agree to sit on a chair, however you managed to take 2 bitewings. Diet chart provided, left and right bitewings. Now William's mum comes with a diet chart, explain behaviour and dental management and explain why you want this to be done.

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

Stage 1 — Introduction and Behaviour Management (0–3 min)

Introduce yourself to both mother and Mia. Crouch to Mia's eye level; use simple, warm language ('Hi Mia, I'm just going to count your teeth like a game!'). Apply tell-show-do: show the mirror, explain what it does, then gently attempt use. Use praise and distraction. INFLECTION 1 — If the candidate skips child-directed communication and addresses only the mother, Mia remains uncooperative and the examination cannot proceed.

Stage 2 — Charting (3–6 min)

Once cooperation is gained, systematically chart the primary dentition using Palmer or FDI notation. Document white spot lesions on 51/61, visible plaque, and correlate with bitewing findings showing caries in primary molars. Record accurately.

Stage 3 — Diet History (6–10 min)

Review the diet chart with the mother. Ask specifically about frequency, timing, and type of intake: juice boxes (3–4/day), bedtime milk bottle, dried fruit and muesli bar snacking. Identify ECC risk factors clearly. INFLECTION 2 — Candidates who only note 'too much sugar' without addressing frequency and timing (especially the bedtime bottle) miss the core cariogenic mechanism and lose marks.

Stage 4 — Diet and Oral Hygiene Counselling (10–14 min)

Provide specific, practical advice: limit juice to ≤120 mL once daily with meals or replace with tap water; eliminate bedtime bottle or switch to water only; reduce snack frequency. Address fluoride toothpaste concern: recommend low-fluoride toothpaste (400–550 ppm) such as Colgate Minifluoride, pea-sized amount, twice daily, parent-supervised brushing until age 7–8.

Stage 5 — Follow-up and Closure (14–15 min)

Arrange review in 4–6 weeks. Explain importance of regular dental visits for monitoring ECC progression and preventive care. Acknowledge mother's efforts and close with empathy and encouragement.

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Introduces self to both child and parent; communicates at Mia's level using simple language and crouches to eye level
  2. ✅ Applies tell-show-do, positive reinforcement, and distraction to manage Frankl Scale 2 behaviour and gain cooperation for examination
  3. ✅ Systematically charts primary dentition using Palmer or FDI notation; documents white spot lesions on 51/61 and correlates bitewing caries findings
  4. ✅ Identifies all three key ECC risk factors: frequent juice (3–4/day), bedtime milk bottle, and frequent cariogenic snacking — with emphasis on frequency and timing, not just sugar content
  5. ✅ Provides specific dietary and oral hygiene advice including juice reduction, elimination of bedtime bottle, low-fluoride toothpaste (400–550 ppm) twice daily with parental supervision, and arranges 4–6 week review
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • The bedtime bottle is the highest-risk habit here — when Mia falls asleep with milk, saliva flow drops and the lactose sits on her teeth all night, which is exactly how early childhood caries develops so rapidly in the molars.
  • For children under six, we recommend a low-fluoride toothpaste containing 400 to 550 parts per million fluoride — products like Colgate Minifluoride are specifically formulated for this age group and are safe even if a small amount is swallowed.
  • The issue with juice isn't just the sugar content — it's the frequency. Three to four juice boxes spread across the day means her teeth are under acid attack for most of her waking hours, which overwhelms her saliva's ability to remineralise.
  • On the bitewings, I can see interproximal caries in the primary molars, and combined with the white spot lesions on 51 and 61, this is consistent with a diagnosis of early childhood caries — a pattern driven by diet and oral hygiene factors we can address today.
  • Parental brushing or close supervision should continue until Mia is around seven to eight years old — children don't have the fine motor coordination to brush effectively on their own before that age.
Curveball Deflectors
  • Mother says: 'I don't want to use fluoride toothpaste — I've read it's toxic for children and that's why I use the natural one.' → Acknowledge her concern without dismissing it: 'I completely understand why you'd want to be careful — it's great that you're thinking about this. The good news is that the low-fluoride toothpaste I'm recommending, around 400 to 550 parts per million, is specifically designed for young children. At a pea-sized amount twice a day, the amount swallowed is well within safe limits and is actually recommended by the Australian Dental Association. The natural toothpaste without fluoride unfortunately doesn't give Mia's teeth the protection they need, especially given the caries we're already seeing.' Avoid being dismissive or alarmist — validate, then redirect with evidence.
  • Candidate focuses entirely on the mother and neglects to engage Mia, or attempts to chart immediately without behaviour management. → Pause and re-engage Mia directly before proceeding. Crouch to her level, introduce yourself to her specifically ('Hi Mia, my name is Dr [Name] — I love your shoes! Can I show you something cool?'), and use tell-show-do with the mirror before any attempt at examination. Attempting to chart an uncooperative child without behaviour management will fail the station — the examiner context confirms Mia will respond to appropriate techniques if applied correctly.
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ►
STAGE 1: Introduction and Behaviour Management

"Hi there! You must be William's mum — lovely to meet you, I'm Dr [Name]. And this must be Mia! Hi Mia, wow, I love your shoes! My name is Dr [Name] — I'm just going to play a little tooth-counting game with you today, is that okay?"

Crouch to Mia's eye level. Maintain a calm, warm tone. Do not rush toward the chair. Pick up the dental mirror and show it to Mia: "See this little mirror? It's just like the one at home — it just helps me see your teeth. Can I show you how it works on my hand first?" Demonstrate on your own hand, then offer to show Mia's hand. Use praise throughout: "You're doing so well, Mia, you're so brave!" Once Mia is settled, gently guide her to sit in the chair with mum nearby. Attempt a brief visual examination — note white spot lesions on 51 and 61, visible plaque on anterior teeth. Do not force instrumentation if Mia resists.

STAGE 2: Charting

"Mia, you did such an amazing job — you're a superstar! I'm just going to write down what I saw so I can remember to help your teeth."

Chart the primary dentition systematically using Palmer notation (A–E, upper and lower, left and right) or FDI notation (51–85). Document: white spot lesions on 51 and 61 (upper right and left central incisors); visible plaque on anterior teeth; correlate bitewing radiograph findings — interproximal caries in primary molars bilaterally. Record findings accurately in the chart. This pattern is consistent with early childhood caries (ECC).

STAGE 3: Diet History and Counselling

"Thank you so much for bringing in the diet chart — this is really helpful. I can see Mia is having quite a few juice boxes through the day. Can I ask — roughly how many would she have, and does she sip them over time or drink them quickly? And I noticed the bedtime milk bottle — does she tend to fall asleep with it still in her mouth?"

Confirm: 3–4 apple juice boxes daily, bedtime bottle of milk (falls asleep with it), dried fruit and muesli bar snacking. Explain the cariogenic mechanism in plain language.

"So what's happening is that every time Mia has juice or a sweet snack, the bacteria in her mouth produce acid for about 20 to 30 minutes. With 3 or 4 juice boxes spread across the day, her teeth are under acid attack for most of the day — her saliva just can't keep up. The bedtime bottle is actually the biggest concern — when she falls asleep, her saliva flow drops right down, so the milk sits on her teeth all night. That's the main reason we're seeing so much decay in her back teeth. The great news is these are things we can change together."

STAGE 4: Practical Advice and Follow-Up

"Here's what I'd suggest. For the juice, I'd love to get that down to a small glass — about 120 mL — once a day with a meal, and replace the rest with tap water. Sydney tap water has fluoride in it, which actually helps protect her teeth. For the bedtime bottle, the goal is to phase it out — or if that's a big change, we can start by switching it to plain water only. For snacks, dried fruit and muesli bars are quite sticky and sugary — things like cheese, plain crackers, or fresh fruit are much kinder to her teeth. For toothbrushing, I'd recommend switching to a low-fluoride toothpaste — something like Colgate Minifluoride, which has 400 to 550 parts per million fluoride. It's made specifically for children Mia's age and is safe even if a little is swallowed. A pea-sized amount, twice a day — morning and before bed — and I'd encourage you to do the brushing or closely supervise until she's around seven or eight, because little ones don't quite have the coordination to do it thoroughly on their own yet. I know you've been using a natural toothpaste because you were worried about fluoride — that's a really understandable concern, and I'm glad you mentioned it. The low-fluoride option gives her the protection she needs without any risk at this dose. I'd like to see Mia back in about four to six weeks to check how things are going and to plan the treatment for her molars. You're clearly a very caring mum and Mia is lucky to have you looking out for her — these changes will make a real difference."

Book a follow-up appointment in 4–6 weeks. Provide written diet and oral hygiene advice if available. Document all findings, advice given, and planned management in the clinical notes. Ensure Mia leaves with positive reinforcement — sticker or praise — to build a positive dental association for future visits.

PQ-30
Amalgam Filling Complication: Post-Operative Pain Assessment
Station 29  |  Past Questions
■ Cluster 3 — Evaluation & Treatment Planning

CANDIDATE BRIEF

Scarlett Jones is a regular patient in your clinic. She is attending today complaining of severe pain related to one of her lower left first molar tooth. She had an amalgam filling done by one of your colleagues 2 weeks ago while you were away. She is very upset, and she hasn't been able to sleep for the past 2 nights. You took an Xray and found out that there are some caries under amalgam filling and apical radiolucency associated with that tooth and because of which she is experiencing pain. How will you manage her concerns and give her appropriate treatment options?

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

Stage 1 — Empathy and Pain History (0–2 min)

Acknowledge distress and validate concerns. Take structured pain history: onset 2 weeks post-filling, spontaneous throbbing at night, sharp lingering pain to cold (10–20 sec), pain on chewing. Confirm paracetamol use with partial relief. INFLECTION 1 — Spontaneous nocturnal pain plus lingering cold response is the hallmark of irreversible pulpitis; candidates who miss this distinction will misdiagnose.

Stage 2 — Medical History and Clinical Examination (2–4 min)

Confirm no relevant medical conditions, medications, or allergies. Perform percussion (TTP on 36), palpation (no swelling), cold test (lingering >10 sec on 36 vs normal on control), heat test (mild sensitivity). Review radiograph: restoration within 0.5 mm of pulp, no periapical radiolucency present.

Stage 3 — Diagnosis Explanation (4–6 min)

Explain in plain language: the nerve inside the tooth is severely inflamed and cannot heal on its own. This is a known risk when decay is very deep. INFLECTION 2 — Candidates must distinguish irreversible from reversible pulpitis; recommending a wait-and-see approach here is a critical error.

Stage 4 — Treatment Options and Interim Management (6–8 min)

Present root canal treatment (preferred, tooth-preserving) versus extraction (with replacement options). Prescribe alternating ibuprofen 400 mg and paracetamol 1000 mg for interim pain relief. Arrange timely definitive appointment or endodontic referral.

Stage 5 — Addressing Colleague Concerns and Documentation (8–10 min)

Respond professionally without apportioning blame. Explain deep decay is a recognised risk factor. Document all findings, clinical tests, diagnosis, and treatment plan. Inform colleague as professional courtesy and clinical governance obligation.

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Structured pain history identifying spontaneous nocturnal pain and lingering cold response as indicators of irreversible pulpitis
  2. ✅ Appropriate clinical tests performed: percussion, palpation, cold and heat thermal testing on affected and control teeth
  3. ✅ Diagnosis of irreversible pulpitis explained in jargon-free language, distinguishing it from reversible pulpitis
  4. ✅ Both definitive treatment options (root canal treatment and extraction with replacement) discussed with risks and benefits
  5. ✅ Colleague's conduct addressed empathetically and professionally without apportioning blame, with documentation and clinical governance obligations met
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • A lingering cold response lasting more than 10 seconds, combined with spontaneous nocturnal pain, is diagnostic of irreversible pulpitis — the pulp cannot recover and root canal treatment or extraction is the only definitive management.
  • The radiograph shows the restoration base is within 0.5 mm of the pulp with no periapical radiolucency at this stage, meaning we are dealing with pulpal pathology without periapical spread — this is still a restorable tooth with a good prognosis for root canal treatment.
  • Irreversible pulpitis is a recognised complication of deep carious lesions approaching the pulp, even when the restoration is placed correctly — the absence of a documented liner does not automatically constitute negligence but should be noted in the clinical record.
  • Interim analgesia should be alternating ibuprofen 400 mg every 8 hours with paracetamol 500–1000 mg every 6 hours, provided there are no contraindications, as this multimodal approach provides superior pain relief to either agent alone.
Curveball Deflectors
  • Patient asks: 'Did the other dentist do something wrong? Is this their fault?' → Acknowledge her frustration directly: 'I completely understand why you feel that way — you paid for a filling and now you are in more pain. What I can tell you is that when decay is very deep and close to the nerve, there is always a risk that the nerve becomes inflamed, even when the filling is placed correctly. I cannot tell you whether anything was done incorrectly without reviewing all the records, and it would not be fair for me to make that judgement today. What I can do is make sure we get you out of pain and protect your tooth. I will also make sure your treating dentist is informed so we can discuss this together as a team.'
  • Candidate recommends a wait-and-see approach or replaces the filling rather than recommending root canal treatment → This is a critical error. Spontaneous nocturnal pain plus a lingering cold response exceeding 10 seconds confirms irreversible pulpitis — the pulp has no capacity to recover. Replacing the filling or monitoring will not resolve the pathology and will delay definitive treatment, risking progression to acute apical abscess. The correct response is to explain that the nerve is beyond recovery and that root canal treatment or extraction is necessary, then arrange this promptly.
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ►
STAGE 1: Empathy, Rapport, and Pain History

'Scarlett, thank you for coming in today. I can hear how distressing this has been — two nights without sleep is really tough, and I want to make sure we get to the bottom of this and get you some relief. Before I examine you, I would like to ask you a few questions about the pain. Can you tell me when it started? Is it there all the time, or does something set it off? Does anything make it worse — like cold drinks, hot food, or biting down? And does the pain linger after the trigger goes away, or does it settle quickly? Have you had any throbbing pain at night that wakes you up?'

Document: spontaneous nocturnal throbbing pain, sharp lingering pain to cold lasting 10–20 seconds, pain on chewing, partial relief with paracetamol. Confirm medical history — no systemic conditions, no allergies, no current medications beyond over-the-counter analgesia.

STAGE 2: Clinical Examination and Radiograph Review

'I am going to do a few quick tests on the tooth and the ones around it so I can compare them. I will tap gently on the teeth, press on the gum, and use a cold spray briefly — please let me know straight away if anything feels different or uncomfortable.'

Perform percussion testing — tooth 36 is tender to percussion, control teeth normal. Palpation — no swelling, no sinus tract, tissues normal. Cold test with ethyl chloride — tooth 36 produces sharp pain lingering approximately 20 seconds; control teeth respond normally and settle within 2–3 seconds. Heat test — mild sensitivity on 36. Review radiograph: large MOD amalgam, restoration base within 0.5 mm of pulp, no periapical radiolucency identified. Document all findings.

STAGE 3: Diagnosis Explanation and Addressing the Colleague

'Scarlett, based on everything — your symptoms, the tests, and the X-ray — I believe the nerve inside your tooth has become severely inflamed. The technical term is irreversible pulpitis, which means the nerve is beyond the point where it can heal on its own. This has most likely happened because the decay in that tooth was very deep and very close to the nerve before the filling was placed. Even when a filling is done correctly, a nerve that has been under that much pressure from deep decay can sometimes react this way — it is a recognised risk, and unfortunately it can happen even weeks after the filling. I know that is frustrating to hear, especially after what you have already been through and paid for. I want to be honest with you rather than give you false hope that it will settle on its own, because it will not.'

Avoid apportioning blame to the colleague. Acknowledge the patient's frustration empathetically. Note that the absence of a documented liner will be reviewed as part of clinical governance and the colleague will be informed professionally.

STAGE 4: Treatment Options, Interim Analgesia, and Next Steps

'You have two main options. The first is root canal treatment, where we remove the inflamed nerve, clean and seal the inside of the tooth, and then place a crown to protect it. This saves the tooth and is the option I would recommend. It usually takes two or three appointments and I can give you a cost estimate today. The second option is to have the tooth removed. That is simpler and less expensive upfront, but you would then need to think about replacing the tooth — options include an implant or a bridge — otherwise the surrounding teeth can shift over time. In the meantime, I would like you to take ibuprofen 400 mg every eight hours with food, alternating with paracetamol 1000 mg every six hours — this combination works better than either one alone for dental pain. I will arrange an appointment as soon as possible, and if you would prefer to see a specialist endodontist for the root canal, I am very happy to refer you. I will also make sure your treating dentist is informed about what we have found today — that is important so we can all work together to look after you properly.'

Document diagnosis, all clinical test results, radiographic findings, treatment options discussed, patient questions, and agreed plan. Schedule definitive treatment or endodontic referral within the week. Notify colleague via internal clinical governance process. Provide written cost estimate and patient information sheet on root canal treatment.

PQ-31
Management of Cellulitis in an Asthmatic Patient
Station 30  |  Past Questions
■ Cluster 3 — Evaluation & Treatment Planning

CANDIDATE BRIEF

Mr Thomas Edison is attending your surgery today, complaining of pain and swelling associated with one of his teeth on the top left side. Upon examination, you find that he has facial swelling, swollen lymph nodes and has a fever. Xray shows deep caries related to that tooth, with complex root morphology, roots of the root look in close approximation to the maxillary sinus. Patient has an appointment with the oral surgeon tomorrow morning for the removal of this tooth. Medical history given, allergy to penicillin and has Asthma. Manage patients' concerns and give an appropriate treatment plan.

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

Stage 1 — History & Allergy Clarification (0–3 min)

Greet patient, confirm identity. Take focused history of presenting complaint. INFLECTION 1 Confirm penicillin allergy: nature of reaction (rash as a child), classify as hypersensitivity — amoxicillin is therefore contraindicated. Establish that patient stopped amoxicillin after two doses three days ago and sought no alternative. Confirm asthma medications: Seretide BD, Ventolin PRN. Note Ventolin used twice yesterday — flag as suboptimal control.

Stage 2 — Clinical Examination (3–6 min)

Record vital signs: temperature 38.2°C. Assess swelling extent, skin induration, erythema. Check for trismus (absent), test swallowing (uncomfortable but intact), assess for dyspnoea or stridor (absent currently). Palpate lymph nodes — enlarged. Intra-oral: gross caries 36, TTP++, grade II mobility, pus expressible.

Stage 3 — Diagnosis & Risk Recognition (6–8 min)

INFLECTION 2 Recognise spreading odontogenic cellulitis with systemic features (fever, lymphadenopathy, dysphagia, failed outpatient antibiotics) in a medically compromised patient. This is NOT suitable for outpatient management — hospital admission is required for IV antibiotics and surgical source control.

Stage 4 — Treatment Plan & Referral (8–12 min)

Prescribe IV clindamycin as first-line alternative (penicillin allergy, avoid macrolides due to interaction with inhaled corticosteroids). Arrange urgent hospital referral today — do not wait for tomorrow's oral surgery appointment. Coordinate with oral surgeon. Ensure Ventolin inhaler accompanies patient; flag asthma to hospital team.

Stage 5 — Patient Concerns & Safety Netting (12–15 min)

Acknowledge concerns about work and childcare with empathy. Clearly explain clinical urgency. Provide written referral letter. Advise patient to call emergency services if breathing worsens, swallowing deteriorates, or swelling spreads rapidly before reaching hospital.

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Confirms penicillin allergy is a true hypersensitivity (rash) — amoxicillin and all penicillins are contraindicated; do NOT prescribe cephalosporins without careful cross-reactivity assessment
  2. ✅ Identifies failed first-line therapy: patient took only two doses of amoxicillin (which was itself contraindicated) and has now developed spreading cellulitis with systemic features — outpatient oral antibiotics are no longer appropriate
  3. ✅ Selects clindamycin IV as the appropriate antibiotic alternative; recognises macrolides (e.g., erythromycin, clarithromycin) carry QTc prolongation and pharmacokinetic interaction risks with inhaled corticosteroids (fluticasone via CYP3A4)
  4. ✅ Recognises hospital admission is required today — fever 38.2°C, spreading induration, dysphagia, and failed outpatient therapy meet criteria for inpatient IV therapy and surgical source control; do not defer to tomorrow's appointment
  5. ✅ Addresses asthma perioperatively: confirms Ventolin is available and with the patient, notes increased reliever use as a marker of suboptimal control, and communicates asthma status clearly in the hospital referral letter
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • This infection has spread beyond the tooth itself into the surrounding soft tissues and is causing systemic signs — a temperature of 38.2°C, swollen lymph nodes, and difficulty swallowing. That means oral antibiotics at home are no longer safe or sufficient, and you need IV antibiotics in hospital today.
  • Because you had a rash to penicillin as a child, that is a true allergic reaction and I cannot prescribe amoxicillin or any penicillin-based antibiotic. The appropriate alternative for a dental infection of this severity in a penicillin-allergic patient is clindamycin, given intravenously.
  • I also need to be careful with your asthma medications. Some antibiotics — particularly the macrolide group like erythromycin — can interact with the fluticasone in your Seretide inhaler and are best avoided where we have a safer option. Clindamycin does not carry that interaction risk.
  • Your Ventolin use has increased — you used it twice yesterday. Before any procedure, the hospital team will need to know your asthma is as well-controlled as possible. Please make sure your Ventolin inhaler goes with you to hospital.
  • I will be writing a detailed referral letter to the hospital today flagging your penicillin allergy, your asthma medications, and the clinical findings so the team can act immediately on your arrival.
Curveball Deflectors
  • Patient says: 'Can't I just take some antibiotics at home and come back if it gets worse? I really can't go to hospital today — I have no one to pick up my daughter.' → Acknowledge the concern with genuine empathy: 'I completely understand that is incredibly stressful, and I want to help you work through that. But I have to be honest with you — the infection has already spread and is causing a fever and difficulty swallowing. If we send you home with tablets, there is a real risk this could progress to a life-threatening airway emergency within hours. The safest place for you right now is hospital. Let's think together about who might be able to help with your daughter — is there a family member, neighbour, or your daughter's school we could contact while you're here?' Do not compromise on the admission decision.
  • Candidate considers prescribing a cephalosporin (e.g., cefalexin) as the penicillin-allergic alternative → Pause and reconsider: the patient's penicillin allergy is a documented hypersensitivity reaction (rash). Cross-reactivity between penicillins and cephalosporins is estimated at approximately 1–2% for true allergic reactions. In a patient with a confirmed hypersensitivity history, cephalosporins should only be used with caution and ideally after allergy specialist review — they are not a straightforward first-line substitute in this acute setting. Clindamycin is the safer, guideline-supported choice for odontogenic infections in penicillin-allergic patients and avoids this uncertainty entirely.
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ►
STAGE 1: Introduction, History & Allergy Clarification

"Hello Mr Edison, I'm Dr [Name]. I can see you're in quite a bit of discomfort today — thank you for coming in. Before we look at what's happening with your tooth, I need to ask you a few important questions about your health and your medications, because that's going to affect how we treat you safely. Is that okay?"

Confirm presenting complaint: pain and swelling upper left — note the brief states left mandibular findings consistent with tooth 36 (lower left). Clarify with patient. Then address allergy: "I can see in your notes that you're allergic to penicillin. Can you tell me what happened when you took it?" [Patient confirms rash as a child.] "Thank you — that tells me it was a true allergic reaction, so I cannot give you any penicillin-type antibiotic, including amoxicillin. Now, I understand you were prescribed amoxicillin three days ago — were you able to take it?" [Patient confirms she stopped after two doses on day one when she remembered her allergy.] "I'm glad you stopped — that was the right instinct. But it does mean the infection has had three days without effective treatment, which is important context for where we are now." Confirm asthma: "You have asthma — can you tell me what inhalers you use?" [Seretide BD, Ventolin PRN.] "Have you needed your Ventolin recently?" [Used twice yesterday, not today.] Note increased reliever use as marker of suboptimal control.

STAGE 2: Clinical Examination

"I'm going to examine you now — I'll check your temperature, have a look at the swelling, and check inside your mouth. Please let me know if anything is uncomfortable."

Record temperature: 38.2°C — systemic involvement confirmed. Assess facial swelling: indurated, hot, erythematous skin extending to lower border of mandible. Palpate lymph nodes: enlarged. Check mouth opening — no trismus. Ask patient to swallow: "Does swallowing feel normal?" [Reports it is becoming uncomfortable — early dysphagia noted.] Assess for dyspnoea or stridor — absent currently. Intra-oral: gross caries tooth 36, TTP++, grade II mobility, pus expressible from gingival margin. Document all findings clearly.

STAGE 3: Diagnosis & Urgent Management Decision

"Mr Edison, I want to explain what I'm finding and be very straightforward with you, because this is important. The infection from your tooth has spread into the surrounding tissues of your face and neck — we call this cellulitis. You have a fever, your lymph nodes are swollen, and you're starting to find it uncomfortable to swallow. These are signs that the infection is progressing and affecting your body as a whole. Because of this, and because the antibiotic you were given wasn't the right one for you and wasn't taken, the infection has had time to spread. I cannot safely manage this with tablets at home. You need to go to hospital today for antibiotics given directly into a vein, and to have the tooth removed as the source of the infection."

Recognise this as spreading odontogenic cellulitis with systemic features meeting criteria for hospital admission: fever 38.2°C, indurated spreading swelling, early dysphagia, failed outpatient antibiotic therapy, and medical comorbidity (asthma). Do not defer to tomorrow's oral surgery appointment — escalate today. Plan: IV clindamycin (appropriate for penicillin-allergic patients with odontogenic infection; avoids macrolide-corticosteroid interaction risk). Contact oral surgeon to expedite. Write urgent referral letter flagging allergy, asthma medications, and clinical findings.

STAGE 4: Asthma Considerations, Patient Concerns & Safety Netting

"I also want to make sure your asthma is looked after through all of this. You've been using your Ventolin more than usual — that tells me your asthma needs attention too. Please make sure you take both your Seretide and your Ventolin inhaler with you to hospital. I'll make sure the hospital team knows exactly what inhalers you're on so they can keep you safe before and during any procedure. Now — I know this is a lot to take in, and I heard you mention concerns about your daughter and your work. I completely understand how stressful that is. But I have to be honest: if we wait, this infection could spread to your airway and become life-threatening very quickly. Let's use the time we have right now to help you make some calls — is there someone who could help with your daughter while you go to hospital?" [Address practical concerns, offer to assist with contacting school if needed.] "If at any point before you reach the hospital your breathing becomes difficult, your swallowing gets significantly worse, or the swelling spreads rapidly, please call 000 immediately — do not wait. I'm going to call the hospital now to let them know you're coming, and I'll give you a letter to hand to the team when you arrive."

Provide written referral documenting: penicillin allergy (rash, childhood), current asthma medications (Seretide fluticasone/salmeterol BD, Ventolin PRN — increased use noted), clinical findings, temperature, failed prior antibiotic course, and recommendation for IV clindamycin and urgent surgical source control. Confirm patient has both inhalers. Advise patient not to eat or drink in anticipation of possible procedure under sedation or general anaesthesia. Document all discussions and decisions in clinical notes.

PQ-32
Non-Healing Extraction Socket
Station 31  |  Past Questions
■ Cluster 1 — History & Risk Factors

CANDIDATE BRIEF

55 year old female patient had extraction done 4 days ago by another dentist across the road and pain started soon afterwards. Pt complains of bad smell and bad taste. Give possible causes of pain, what investigations will you do and manage patients concern.

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

Stage 1 — Focused History (0:00–2:00 min)

Introduce and establish rapport. Confirm timeline: extraction 4 days ago, difficult procedure (~45 min), pain onset shortly after. Characterise pain: severity 7/10, constant with shooting episodes, not relieved by paracetamol. Confirm bad taste and smell. Ask about prior management attempts (any antibiotics, dressings). INFLECTION 1 — Candidate must ask specifically about diabetes control (HbA1c, recent BGL monitoring) and smoking history (pack-years), not just list conditions. Failure to quantify these misses complicating factor marks.

Stage 2 — Medical & Medication Screen (2:00–3:30 min)

Confirm metformin 1000mg BD, amlodipine. Critically screen for bisphosphonates (MRONJ risk) and anticoagulants (bleeding risk). Confirm no bisphosphonate use here. Note poor diabetic compliance. Quantify smoking: 10 cigarettes/day × 30 years = 15 pack-years.

Stage 3 — Clinical Examination (3:30–5:00 min)

Inspect socket 46: exposed greyish bone, absent clot, minimal granulation tissue, halitosis, tender to gentle probing. Confirm no purulent discharge, no swelling, no lymphadenopathy, no paraesthesia. These findings confirm dry socket and exclude spreading infection or MRONJ.

Stage 4 — Diagnosis & Patient Explanation (5:00–6:30 min)
