Explain dry socket in plain language. INFLECTION 2 — Candidate must link poor glycaemic control and smoking as active barriers to healing, not merely list them. Examiner expects candidate to recommend urgent GP review for HbA1c optimisation, not just note the history.

Stage 5 — Management, Follow-up & Safety-Netting (6:30–8:00 min)

Irrigate with warm saline, place Alvogyl dressing, upgrade analgesia (ibuprofen + paracetamol alternating). Refer to GP for HbA1c review. Offer Quitline referral (13 7848). Review in 48–72 hours. Safety-net: return immediately for swelling, fever, trismus, or difficulty swallowing.

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Provisional diagnosis of dry socket (alveolar osteitis) at site 46 based on exposed grey bone, absent clot, halitosis, and severe pain unrelieved by paracetamol
  2. ✅ Identifies poorly controlled type 2 diabetes (HbA1c 8.2%) and active smoking (15 pack-years) as complicating factors impairing socket healing — not just listed but linked causally
  3. ✅ Screens for bisphosphonates and anticoagulants to exclude MRONJ and bleeding-related complications before proceeding with socket management
  4. ✅ Immediate management: gentle warm saline irrigation, obtundent dressing (Alvogyl), analgesia upgrade to alternating ibuprofen 400mg and paracetamol 1000mg, review in 48–72 hours
  5. ✅ Addresses systemic risk factors: urgent GP referral for HbA1c optimisation, smoking cessation advice with Quitline referral (13 7848), and clear safety-netting for red flags (swelling, fever, trismus, dysphagia)
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • The socket shows exposed bone with a greyish appearance and no residual clot — this is consistent with alveolar osteitis, or dry socket, which typically presents three to five days post-extraction with pain that is disproportionate to the clinical findings and not relieved by simple analgesia.
  • Her HbA1c of 8.2% indicates poorly controlled diabetes, which impairs neutrophil function and angiogenesis — both critical to clot organisation and socket healing — so optimising her glycaemic control is part of the treatment plan, not just background history.
  • Smoking causes vasoconstriction and reduces fibrinolytic activity, which increases the risk of clot dislodgement — at 15 pack-years she is at significantly elevated risk, and this is likely a contributing factor to why the clot failed.
  • Before I place any dressing I want to confirm she has not taken bisphosphonates, as exposed bone in a post-extraction socket in a patient on bisphosphonates would raise concern for medication-related osteonecrosis of the jaw, which has a very different management pathway.
  • I would upgrade her analgesia to alternating ibuprofen 400mg every eight hours with paracetamol 1000mg every six hours — staggered so she is taking something every three hours — and if that is insufficient I would liaise with her GP for a short course of a stronger analgesic.
Curveball Deflectors
  • Patient says: 'Can you just give me antibiotics? The other dentist said I might need them.' → Acknowledge her concern and validate that antibiotics are sometimes discussed, but explain clearly that dry socket is not primarily an infection — it is a healing problem caused by loss of the blood clot. Antibiotics do not treat the underlying cause and are not routinely indicated unless there are signs of spreading infection such as swelling, fever, or purulent discharge, none of which are present today. The most effective treatment is irrigation and an obtundent dressing to settle the exposed nerve endings, combined with better pain relief. If she develops any of those red flag signs, antibiotics would then be reconsidered.
  • Candidate jumps straight to management without asking about bisphosphonate or anticoagulant use. → Pause and return to the medication history before touching the socket. State: 'Before I proceed with any instrumentation of the socket, I need to confirm your full medication list — specifically whether you have ever taken any bone-strengthening medications such as alendronate or zoledronic acid, or any blood thinners such as warfarin or rivaroxaban.' This is a patient safety step. Proceeding without this screen in an OSCE will cost marks on the medical history rubric criterion and may signal unsafe practice to the examiner.
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ►
STAGE 1: Introduction & Focused History

"Hi Mrs Chen, my name is [Candidate Name] and I'm the dentist here today. I can see you've been having a really difficult time since your extraction — I'm sorry to hear that. I'd like to ask you a few questions first so I can understand exactly what's been happening, and then I'll take a look at the area. Is that okay?"

Confirm timeline: extraction of lower right molar four days ago, procedure reportedly difficult and lengthy (~45 minutes). Establish pain onset: began shortly after extraction, now 7/10 severity, constant with occasional shooting episodes, not relieved by regular paracetamol. Confirm presence of bad taste and halitosis. Ask whether any dressings, antibiotics, or other treatment have been provided since the extraction. Ask about swelling, fever, difficulty opening the mouth, or difficulty swallowing — all absent. Confirm no numbness or tingling in the lip or chin (no paraesthesia).

STAGE 2: Medical History & Medication Screen

"I'd also like to go through your medical history with you. I know you have diabetes and high blood pressure — how has your diabetes been going lately? Are you checking your blood sugars regularly? And do you know what your last HbA1c result was? I also want to ask about all the medications you're taking, including any supplements. Specifically, have you ever taken any bone-strengthening tablets — sometimes called alendronate, Fosamax, or similar — or any blood thinners like warfarin or rivaroxaban?"

Document: metformin 1000mg BD, amlodipine for hypertension. HbA1c 8.2% — poorly controlled. No bisphosphonates confirmed — MRONJ excluded as primary diagnosis. No anticoagulants. Quantify smoking: 10 cigarettes per day for 30 years = 15 pack-years. Note poor compliance with BGL monitoring. These findings — poorly controlled diabetes and active heavy smoking — are identified as active complicating factors for impaired socket healing, not merely background history.

STAGE 3: Clinical Examination & Diagnosis Explanation

"I'm going to have a look at the socket now. I'll be very gentle — please let me know if anything is uncomfortable. [After examination] Thank you, Mrs Chen. I can see what's causing your pain. The socket where your tooth was removed has lost the blood clot that normally forms after an extraction. That clot is really important — it protects the bone underneath and helps the area heal. When it's lost, the bone becomes exposed, and that's what's causing this severe, throbbing pain and the unpleasant taste and smell. This is a condition we call a dry socket, and it's actually one of the most painful things that can happen after a tooth extraction. The good news is that it is very treatable."

Clinical findings documented: socket 46 shows exposed bone with greyish discolouration, absent blood clot, minimal granulation tissue, halitosis, tenderness to gentle probing. No purulent discharge, no facial swelling, no lymphadenopathy, no paraesthesia. Provisional diagnosis: dry socket (alveolar osteitis), complicated by poorly controlled type 2 diabetes (HbA1c 8.2%) and active smoking (15 pack-years), both of which impair clot stability, angiogenesis, and tissue healing.

STAGE 4: Immediate Management, Systemic Risk Factors & Safety-Netting

"What I'm going to do right now is gently rinse out the socket with warm salt water to clean it, and then place a special medicated dressing inside it. This dressing contains a soothing agent that will calm down the exposed nerve endings and should give you significant relief — usually within a few hours. For pain relief at home, I'd like you to take ibuprofen 400mg and paracetamol 1000mg in a staggered pattern — so you're taking one or the other roughly every three hours — as long as ibuprofen is safe for you. I'd also like you to see your GP as soon as possible this week, because your diabetes control is making it harder for your body to heal, and getting your blood sugars better managed will really help the socket recover. I'd also like to talk to you about your smoking — I know it's not easy, but smoking reduces the blood supply to healing tissue and was likely a factor in why this happened. There's a free service called Quitline — the number is 13 7848 — and your GP can also help with that. I'd like to see you back here in 48 to 72 hours to check how the dressing is working and change it if needed. And please come back sooner — or go to an emergency department — if you develop any swelling in your face or neck, a fever, difficulty opening your mouth, or any trouble swallowing. Those would be signs of a more serious infection that would need urgent treatment."

Immediate treatment: gentle irrigation of socket 46 with warm saline, placement of Alvogyl obtundent dressing. Analgesia: alternating ibuprofen 400mg (8-hourly) and paracetamol 1000mg (6-hourly), staggered to provide cover approximately every 3 hours; escalate to GP for stronger analgesia if inadequate. Systemic management: urgent GP referral for HbA1c review and glycaemic optimisation. Smoking cessation: brief advice provided, Quitline referral (13 7848) offered. Follow-up: 48–72 hours for dressing review and replacement. Safety-netting: patient instructed to return immediately or attend ED for increasing facial or neck swelling, fever, trismus, or dysphagia.

PQ-33
Assessment and Management of Gingival Ulceration
Station 32  |  Past Questions
■ Cluster 1 — History & Risk Factors

CANDIDATE BRIEF

Mr. Smith is a 65-year-old patient, attending your surgery for the first time today asking for a lower denture to replace his missing teeth. You examined the patient, and you find that the patient is wearing an upper complete denture for the past 8 years with no lower denture. He also complains of angular cheilitis on the right side of his lips. You also notice an ulcer; the patient says that the ulcer has been present there for the last 2 months since he had his lower canine removed. The ulcer is about 2-3mm in size, it's not bleeding, and patient does not experience any pain. He works as a miner and is leaving for work after 3 months. He won't be back until 3 months. How will you manage the patient?

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

Stage 1 — Introduction and History Taking (0–3 min)

Introduce yourself, establish rapport, and acknowledge Mr. Smith's anxiety given his father's history of oral cancer. Take a focused history: duration of ulcer (2 months), precipitating event (extraction of lower canine), pain characteristics, previous similar episodes, and red-flag symptoms including dysphagia, weight loss, and hoarseness. Ask about smoking, alcohol, and occupational exposures. Ask about systemic symptoms to exclude Behçet's, Crohn's, or reactive arthritis. INFLECTION 1 — Candidate must recognise that 2 months duration plus raised rolled borders exceeds the 3-week threshold and cannot be managed conservatively without biopsy.

Stage 2 — Clinical Examination (3–5 min)

Systematically examine the ulcer: site (attached gingiva adjacent to 36), size (1.5 cm), shape (irregular), base (yellowish-white), borders (raised and rolled), surrounding erythema. Palpate for induration. Examine all cervical and submandibular lymph node chains. Note absence of lymphadenopathy.

Stage 3 — Differential Diagnosis and Clinical Reasoning (5–7 min)

State differential: traumatic ulcer (most common), but features — size 1.5 cm, irregular shape, raised rolled borders, 2-month duration — mandate exclusion of squamous cell carcinoma. Aphthous ulcer is less likely. INFLECTION 2 — Candidate must not reassure the patient that this is benign without biopsy confirmation.

Stage 4 — Management and Safety-Netting (7–10 min)

Urgent incisional biopsy referral within 2 weeks. Advise chlorhexidine 0.2% mouthwash, avoid trauma, analgesics if needed. Address angular cheilitis. Explain the plan sensitively, acknowledging his travel timeline. Document all findings. Ensure referral is completed before he departs for work.

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Recognises that 2-month duration with raised rolled borders and irregular shape mandates urgent biopsy — not a watch-and-wait approach
  2. ✅ Asks specifically about red-flag symptoms: dysphagia, weight loss, hoarseness, and previous ulceration episodes
  3. ✅ Performs systematic ulcer examination using SSSBBS framework (site, size, shape, base, borders, surrounding tissues) and palpates for induration and lymphadenopathy
  4. ✅ Formulates a differential diagnosis that includes traumatic ulcer but prioritises exclusion of oral squamous cell carcinoma given clinical features
  5. ✅ Addresses the patient's anxiety sensitively given family history of oral cancer, while providing honest and clear safety-netting advice before his 3-month departure
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • Any oral ulcer persisting beyond 3 weeks without a clear benign cause must be referred urgently for incisional biopsy to exclude oral squamous cell carcinoma.
  • The combination of raised rolled borders, irregular shape, size greater than 1 cm, and 2-month duration are clinical features that cannot be attributed to trauma alone without histological confirmation.
  • Oral squamous cell carcinoma most commonly affects the lateral border of the tongue, floor of mouth, and attached gingiva — this site is consistent with a high-risk location.
  • Absence of lymphadenopathy does not exclude malignancy — up to 30% of early oral SCCs present without palpable nodes.
  • Angular cheilitis in a patient with an upper complete denture and no lower denture is consistent with reduced vertical dimension causing saliva pooling at the commissures, and should be managed with antifungal cream such as miconazole 2% (Daktarin) and denture hygiene advice.
Curveball Deflectors
  • Patient says: 'I'm sure it's just from the tooth being pulled out — can't you just give me something for it and I'll see someone when I get back in 6 months?' → Acknowledge his concern and validate that trauma is the most common cause of ulcers. However, explain clearly but sensitively that because this ulcer has been present for 2 months and has some features that need to be checked more carefully, it would not be safe to leave it for 6 months. Emphasise that early investigation gives the best outcome regardless of what it turns out to be, and that you want to arrange a specialist review before he leaves for work.
  • Candidate prescribes Kenalog in Orabase (triamcinolone) or topical steroids as first-line management without arranging biopsy → This is a critical error. Topical steroids are appropriate for confirmed aphthous ulceration but must never be applied to an undiagnosed ulcer with suspicious features, as they may mask malignant change and delay diagnosis. The correct response is urgent referral for incisional biopsy. Symptomatic relief with chlorhexidine mouthwash is appropriate as an adjunct only.
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ►
STAGE 1: Introduction and History Taking

"Good morning Mr. Smith, my name is Dr. [Name] and I'll be looking after you today. I understand you've come in for a lower denture, but I also want to make sure we take a good look at this ulcer you've mentioned — I want to make sure we give it the attention it deserves. Is that okay with you?"

Establish rapport and acknowledge the patient's concern. Begin focused history: confirm the ulcer has been present for 2 months since the lower canine extraction. Ask whether it has changed in size or appearance since it first appeared. Ask about pain — note the patient reports no pain, but the ulcer is tender on examination. Ask whether he has had similar ulcers before. Ask specifically about red-flag symptoms: any difficulty swallowing, unexplained weight loss, hoarseness, or lumps in the neck. Ask about smoking history and alcohol consumption. Note his occupation as a miner and ask about any chemical or dust exposures. Ask about systemic symptoms: fever, skin or genital ulcers, eye problems, joint pain, or bowel symptoms to exclude Behçet's disease, Crohn's disease, or reactive arthritis.

STAGE 2: Clinical Examination

"I'm going to have a careful look inside your mouth now, and I'll also gently feel around your neck. Please let me know if anything is uncomfortable."

Perform systematic examination of the ulcer using the SSSBBS framework. Document: site — attached gingiva adjacent to tooth 36; size — 1.5 cm; shape — irregular; base — yellowish-white slough; borders — raised and rolled; surrounding tissues — erythema present. Gently palpate the ulcer for induration. Examine all cervical lymph node chains including submandibular, submental, anterior and posterior cervical, and supraclavicular nodes — note no lymphadenopathy is present. Examine the rest of the oral mucosa for additional lesions. Note the upper complete denture and angular cheilitis on the right commissure.

STAGE 3: Differential Diagnosis and Explanation to Patient

"Mr. Smith, I can see why you've been worried about this, especially given what happened with your father. I want to be honest with you. The most common cause of an ulcer like this is irritation or trauma — and the timing after your tooth removal does fit with that. However, because this ulcer has been there for 2 months and has some features I want to look at more carefully, I think it's really important that we don't just leave it and hope it goes away. I'd like to refer you to a specialist who can take a very small sample of the ulcer — it's called a biopsy — so we can find out exactly what it is. This is the safest and most responsible thing to do."

Differential diagnosis: traumatic ulcer is the most common cause given the extraction history, but the 2-month duration, 1.5 cm size, irregular shape, and raised rolled borders are features that mandate urgent exclusion of oral squamous cell carcinoma. Aphthous ulceration is less likely given the single episode, size, and border morphology. Do not reassure the patient that this is benign without histological confirmation. Document the differential clearly in the notes.

STAGE 4: Management Plan and Safety-Netting

"Here is what I'd like to do for you today. I'm going to write an urgent referral to an oral medicine specialist or oral and maxillofacial surgeon so they can see you within the next two weeks and arrange that biopsy. In the meantime, I'd like you to use a chlorhexidine mouthwash — you can get this from any pharmacy — twice a day to keep the area clean. Please avoid anything that might irritate the area, like hard or crusty foods. If the ulcer gets bigger, starts bleeding, or you develop any swelling in your neck, please come back or go to your nearest emergency department straight away — don't wait. I also want to address the soreness at the corner of your mouth — I'll prescribe a miconazole cream for that, which you apply twice a day. And we'll absolutely get started on planning your lower denture as well, but I want to make sure we sort this out first. Given that you're leaving for work in 3 months, it's really important we get this referral done and the results back before you go."

Arrange urgent referral for incisional biopsy within 2 weeks. Prescribe chlorhexidine 0.2% mouthwash (e.g. Savacol) and miconazole 2% cream (Daktarin) for angular cheilitis. Advise dietary modification to avoid trauma. Provide clear safety-netting instructions. Document all findings, differential diagnosis, and management plan. Ensure the referral pathway is completed within the patient's available 3-month window before departure. Do not prescribe topical corticosteroids for an undiagnosed ulcer with suspicious features.

PQ-34
Management of Dental Trauma in a 3-Year-Old Child
Station 33  |  Past Questions
■ Cluster 2 — Balanced (History informs management)

CANDIDATE BRIEF

3-year-old boy comes after 1 week (fell down a week ago) and had a small cut on the lip, mom applied pressure and bleeding stopped. Yesterday she noticed the black discoloration in front tooth (61) and she is here at the dentist. Explain diagnosis, treatment plan and answer questions.

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

Stage 1 — History Taking (0:00–2:00 min)

Greet mother and child warmly. Confirm injury was one week ago, fall from ~1.2m slide platform, witnessed by mother. Ask about immediate symptoms: bleeding (lip laceration, controlled with pressure), and screen for head injury red flags — loss of consciousness, vomiting, altered behaviour, feeding difficulties. Confirm tetanus immunisation is current. INFLECTION 1 — Failure to ask about LOC or tetanus is a significant omission that signals unsafe practice to the examiner.

Stage 2 — Clinical Examination (2:00–5:00 min)

Use tell-show-do with the 3-year-old; involve mother for reassurance. Examine tooth 61 (upper left primary central incisor): note black discolouration, assess degree of intrusion, check occlusion, mobility, and gingival/soft tissue status. Palpate for swelling or sinus tract indicating infection.

Stage 3 — Diagnosis and Explanation (5:00–8:00 min)

Diagnose intrusion injury of primary tooth 61 with subsequent pulp necrosis evidenced by black discolouration at one week. Explain to mother in plain language: tooth pushed up into gum, dark colour indicates nerve damage, monitoring preferred over immediate extraction for primary teeth. INFLECTION 2 — Recommending immediate extraction without clinical indication of infection is incorrect management and will lose marks.

Stage 4 — Treatment Plan and Immediate Advice (8:00–11:00 min)

Advise soft diet, paracetamol or ibuprofen for analgesia (weight-appropriate dosing), gentle tooth brushing. Counsel on sequelae: discolouration, infection, ankylosis, and risk to permanent successor (hypoplasia, dilaceration). Extraction indicated only if infection develops.

Stage 5 — Follow-Up and Safety Netting (11:00–13:00 min)

Schedule review at 1 week, 6–8 weeks, 6 months, then yearly until permanent tooth erupts. Provide clear safety-net advice: return urgently if swelling, sinus tract, pus, fever, or child becomes unwell or stops eating.

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Structured trauma history including time, mechanism, fall height, and immediate symptoms — plus head injury screening (LOC, vomiting, behaviour) and tetanus status
  2. ✅ Age-appropriate behaviour management using tell-show-do, calm demeanour, and active involvement of the mother during examination
  3. ✅ Correct diagnosis: intrusion injury of primary tooth 61 with pulp necrosis (black discolouration at 1 week); checks occlusion, mobility, and soft tissues for signs of infection
  4. ✅ Correct management: allow passive re-eruption for primary intrusion; extraction only if infection develops; soft diet, paracetamol/ibuprofen, gentle oral hygiene
  5. ✅ Counsels on sequelae (discolouration, infection, ankylosis, permanent tooth damage) and arranges follow-up at 1 week, 6–8 weeks, 6 months, then yearly with clear safety-net advice
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • Intrusion of a primary tooth is managed by passive monitoring and allowing spontaneous re-eruption — immediate extraction is not indicated unless there is clinical or radiographic evidence of infection, failure to re-erupt, or risk to the permanent successor.
  • Black discolouration of a primary tooth following trauma indicates pulp necrosis; this alone is not an immediate indication for extraction but requires close monitoring for signs of infection such as a sinus tract, swelling, or periapical pathology on radiograph.
  • The primary concern with intrusion of a primary incisor is damage to the developing permanent successor tooth — specifically enamel hypoplasia or dilaceration of the crown or root of the permanent tooth, which the parent must be counselled about.
  • Follow-up schedule for primary tooth intrusion: review at 1 week post-presentation, 6–8 weeks, 6 months, then annually until the permanent successor erupts — typically around age 6–7 years.
  • Head injury red flags that would require urgent medical referral include: loss of consciousness, persistent vomiting, altered behaviour or drowsiness, unequal pupils, or seizure activity following the traumatic event.
Curveball Deflectors
  • Mother insists: 'Can't you just pull the tooth out now? It looks terrible and I don't want to wait.' → Acknowledge her concern empathetically: 'I completely understand — it looks worrying and I can see why you'd want it sorted today. The reason we prefer to leave it is that baby teeth can actually move back down on their own over the next few months, and removing it now means your son would have a gap for several years until his adult tooth comes through, which can affect his speech and eating. We'll watch it very closely, and if it causes any infection or pain, we will remove it straight away. You're absolutely doing the right thing by bringing him in.' Avoid extraction without clinical indication.
  • Candidate incorrectly states the tooth is 51 (upper right primary central incisor) based on the examiner context, contradicting the candidate brief which states tooth 61. → The candidate brief identifies the tooth as 61 (upper left primary central incisor). Candidates should work from the clinical presentation in the brief. If the examiner probes tooth identification, state clearly: 'On examination I am assessing tooth 61, the upper left primary central incisor, which shows black discolouration consistent with pulp necrosis following the reported intrusion injury.' Do not be distracted by any discrepancy — examine and document what is clinically present and use the FDI notation correctly.
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ►
STAGE 1: History Taking

"Hi there, I'm Dr [Name], lovely to meet you both. And what's your name, mate? That's a great name. Mum, thank you so much for coming in today. I just want to ask you a few questions about what happened before I take a look at his tooth — is that okay?" "So you mentioned he had a fall about a week ago — can you tell me exactly what happened? Where did he fall from, and roughly how high up was he? Was anyone with him when it happened?" "After the fall, did he cry straight away? Did he ever go quiet or seem confused, or did he lose consciousness at all — even for a few seconds? Any vomiting or being sick since then? Has he been eating and drinking normally? Any changes in his behaviour — more sleepy than usual, or not himself?" "The cut on the lip — did that stop bleeding on its own with the pressure you applied? Any other injuries — to his face, his jaw, his neck?" "Is he up to date with all his immunisations, including tetanus? Any medical conditions or medications I should know about?"

Structured trauma history: confirms injury one week ago, fall from ~1.2m slide platform, witnessed by mother. Screens for all head injury red flags — LOC, vomiting, altered behaviour, drowsiness. Confirms tetanus up to date, no medical conditions, lip laceration self-resolved. Documents mechanism and height of fall.

STAGE 2: Clinical Examination

"Okay, that's really helpful, thank you. Now I'm going to have a look at his tooth. [To child] Hey buddy, can I show you something cool? This is my little mirror — look, you can see yourself in it! I'm just going to have a little peek inside your mouth, okay? You're going to be so brave. Mum, would you like to sit him on your lap facing me? That's perfect." "I'm just going to have a gentle look — I'll be really quick and gentle, I promise."

Uses tell-show-do technique. Child seated on mother's lap. Examines tooth 61 (upper left primary central incisor): notes black discolouration of the crown. Assesses degree of intrusion — tooth appears shortened in the arch. Checks occlusion — asks child to bite together gently. Assesses mobility with gentle finger pressure. Examines surrounding gingiva and soft tissues for swelling, sinus tract, or signs of active infection. Notes mild gingival tenderness around 61, no sinus tract, no facial swelling.

STAGE 3: Diagnosis and Explanation

"Thank you for being so good — you were amazing! [To mother] Okay, so I've had a good look and I can explain what's happened. When he fell, his front tooth was pushed up into the gum — we call that an intrusion injury. The dark colour you've noticed is because the nerve inside the tooth has been damaged by the impact, and unfortunately that's caused the tooth to go black. I know it looks alarming, but I want to reassure you that this is actually quite common with this type of injury in young children." "Now, because this is a baby tooth, the best approach is actually to watch and wait rather than remove it straight away. Baby teeth that have been pushed up can often move back down on their own over the next few weeks to months. If we take it out now, he'd have a gap for several years until his adult tooth comes through, which can affect his speech and the way his other teeth sit." "I do need to be honest with you though — there is a risk that the fall may have affected the adult tooth developing underneath. We'll keep a very close eye on that as he grows."

Diagnoses intrusion injury of primary tooth 61 with pulp necrosis. Explains management rationale clearly in lay terms. Counsels on risk to permanent successor — enamel hypoplasia or dilaceration. Confirms no current signs of infection requiring immediate extraction.

STAGE 4: Treatment Plan, Follow-Up and Safety Netting

"For now, here's what I'd like you to do at home. Keep him on soft foods — things like yoghurt, mashed potato, scrambled eggs — for the next few weeks so there's no pressure on that tooth. If he seems uncomfortable, you can give him children's paracetamol or ibuprofen at the right dose for his weight — the packaging will guide you on that. Keep brushing his teeth gently with a soft toothbrush — good oral hygiene will help prevent any infection." "I'd like to see him back here in one week just to check how things are going, then again at around six to eight weeks, then at six months, and then once a year until his adult tooth comes through — usually around age six or seven." "Most importantly, I want you to bring him straight back to us — or go to your nearest emergency department — if you notice any swelling in his face or gum, any pus or a pimple on the gum near that tooth, if he develops a fever, if he stops eating or drinking, or if you're worried about him at any point. You're doing a wonderful job — you absolutely did the right thing bringing him in."

Prescribes soft diet, weight-appropriate paracetamol or ibuprofen (TGA-approved, no aspirin in children). Gentle oral hygiene instruction. Follow-up schedule: 1 week, 6–8 weeks, 6 months, annually until permanent eruption. Clear safety-net advice covering signs of infection, facial swelling, sinus tract, fever, and deterioration. Provides written safety-net information if available.

PQ-35
Amalgam Replacement Discussion
Station 34  |  Past Questions
■ Cluster 2 — Balanced (History informs management)

CANDIDATE BRIEF

Mr Walcott a 55-year-old medically fit patient, attending your clinic today concerned about mercury poisoning due to his amalgam filling that has been present in his mouth for the past 10 years by his previous dentist. He wants to replace all his amalgam fillings with composite. There is no fracture of restoration, pain, or sensitivity. Explain how would you manage this patient and how you plan to address his concerns?

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

Stage 1 — Empathic Opening and Agenda Setting (0–1 min)

Greet Mr Walcott warmly. Acknowledge his concern directly: "It sounds like this has been worrying you, and I'm really glad you've come in to talk about it." Ask open-endedly what he has read or been told, and explore whether he has any symptoms he links to his fillings. INFLECTION 1 — Candidates who skip the source exploration and jump straight to reassurance risk appearing dismissive and lose marks for empathy and information-gathering.

Stage 2 — Evidence-Based Explanation (1–3 min)

Explain the Australian position: amalgam is endorsed as safe by the NHMRC and ADA. Clarify the chemistry — amalgam mercury is inorganic and bound, not the organic methylmercury associated with neurological toxicity. Emphasise that removal itself causes the highest mercury vapour exposure.

Stage 3 — Risk of Unnecessary Replacement (3–4 min)

Outline the harms of elective removal: irreversible tooth structure loss, pulpal risk, cost, and shorter composite longevity in posterior load-bearing areas. INFLECTION 2 — Candidates who agree to replace all fillings without clinical indication fail to demonstrate evidence-based decision-making and risk patient harm.

Stage 4 — Valid Indications and Material Discussion (4–5 min)

State the legitimate reasons for replacement (fracture, secondary caries, poor margins, allergy, aesthetics in visible areas). Discuss composite resin: excellent aesthetics, bonded, but higher wear and technique sensitivity in posterior sites.

Stage 5 — Shared Plan and Follow-Up (5–6 min)

Recommend monitoring with regular review. Provide ADA and NHMRC resources. Document the informed discussion. Invite Mr Walcott to return if concerns persist or symptoms develop.

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Acknowledge Mr Walcott's concerns with genuine empathy and explore the source of his information before providing any clinical explanation
  2. ✅ State the current Australian evidence-based position: amalgam is safe for the vast majority of patients per NHMRC and ADA guidelines, and inorganic amalgam mercury differs fundamentally from toxic organic methylmercury
  3. ✅ Explain that elective removal carries real risks — irreversible tooth structure loss, pulpal damage, new restoration failure, and financial cost — and that mercury vapour exposure is highest during removal, not during function
  4. ✅ Identify the valid clinical indications for replacement (fracture, secondary caries, poor marginal integrity, documented allergy, aesthetic concern in visible areas) and confirm none currently apply to Mr Walcott
  5. ✅ Reach a shared, patient-centred management plan: recommend monitoring and regular review, offer reliable information sources (ADA patient resources, NHMRC guidelines), and document the informed discussion
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • "The mercury in your amalgam fillings is in an inorganic, chemically bound form — it behaves very differently in the body compared to the organic methylmercury found in contaminated fish, which is the type linked to neurological harm."
  • "Interestingly, the highest release of mercury vapour actually occurs at the moment of drilling out an amalgam filling — so removing them unnecessarily would expose you to more mercury, not less."
  • "The NHMRC and the Australian Dental Association both support amalgam as a safe and effective restorative material for the vast majority of patients, and there is no peer-reviewed evidence establishing a causal link between dental amalgam and systemic disease in healthy adults."
  • "Replacing a clinically sound amalgam with composite in a high-load posterior area means we lose healthy tooth structure that we can never get back, and composite restorations in those positions typically have a shorter service life than a well-maintained amalgam."
Curveball Deflectors
  • "But I've read online that amalgam causes Alzheimer's disease and multiple sclerosis — how can you say it's safe?" → Validate his concern first: "I completely understand why that would be alarming to read." Then explain that these claims have been extensively studied and no causal relationship has been established in peer-reviewed research. Distinguish between correlation and causation, and direct him to the NHMRC and ADA as authoritative, evidence-based sources rather than social media. Avoid being dismissive — acknowledge the concern is genuine even if the evidence does not support it.
  • Candidate agrees to replace all amalgams immediately to satisfy the patient → This is the most common critical error. The correct response is to decline elective replacement without clinical indication, explaining clearly that doing so would cause irreversible harm (tooth structure loss, pulpal risk) and increase mercury exposure during removal. A shared decision to monitor is appropriate. Agreeing to unnecessary treatment to avoid conflict fails the evidence-based management criterion and may constitute overtreatment.
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ►
STAGE 1: Empathic Opening and Information Gathering

"Mr Walcott, thank you so much for coming in today and for bringing this up — it's really important that we talk about it properly. I can hear that this has been on your mind, and I want you to know I take your concerns seriously. Before I share anything with you, I'd love to understand a bit more about what you've come across. Can you tell me what you've read or been told about your fillings?"

Listen actively without interrupting. Explore the source — social media, a friend, a website. Then ask: "Have you noticed any symptoms at all that you've been linking to your fillings — things like headaches, fatigue, memory issues, or anything else?" Document that the patient reports no current symptoms and no history of allergy to dental materials.

STAGE 2: Evidence-Based Reassurance

"Thank you for sharing that with me. I can absolutely see why reading something like that would be worrying. What I'd like to do is walk you through what the current evidence actually tells us, and then we can make a decision together that you feel comfortable with. The mercury in your amalgam fillings is in a chemically bound, inorganic form — it's called mercury sulphide, and it behaves very differently in the body compared to the type of mercury that causes harm, which is organic methylmercury — the kind sometimes found in contaminated fish. The Australian National Health and Medical Research Council and the Australian Dental Association have both reviewed the evidence thoroughly, and their position is that dental amalgam is safe and effective for the vast majority of healthy patients. There is no peer-reviewed evidence establishing a causal link between dental amalgam and conditions like Alzheimer's disease or multiple sclerosis."

Speak calmly and avoid jargon. Offer to provide written resources — ADA patient information sheet and NHMRC position statement — so the patient can review them at home.

STAGE 3: Risks of Unnecessary Replacement

"Now, I also want to be really honest with you about what replacing these fillings would actually involve, because I think that's important for your decision. When we drill out an existing amalgam filling, that's actually the moment when the highest amount of mercury vapour is released — so removing them unnecessarily would expose you to more mercury than simply leaving them in place. On top of that, every time we work on a tooth, we have to remove some healthy tooth structure that we can never get back. There's also a small but real risk of irritating the nerve inside the tooth, which in some cases can lead to the need for root canal treatment. And the composite resin fillings we'd place instead, while they look great, do tend to wear faster in the back teeth where you're doing most of your chewing — so they may need replacing sooner, which adds to the cost over time."

Check for understanding. Pause and invite questions. Confirm the patient's fillings are clinically sound — no fracture, no secondary caries, no poor margins — so there is no clinical indication for replacement at this time.

STAGE 4: Shared Plan and Follow-Up

"Based on everything we've discussed, and given that your fillings are in good shape with no signs of any problems, my recommendation would be that we monitor them carefully at your regular check-ups rather than replacing them right now. That said, this is absolutely your decision, and I respect that. If at any point there is a clinical reason to replace one — like a crack, decay forming around it, or if you develop a documented allergy — we would absolutely act on that. I'll print out the ADA patient information on amalgam safety and the NHMRC guidelines for you to take home and read through. If after reviewing those you still have concerns or questions, please don't hesitate to come back and we can talk it through again. I'll make a note in your records of our conversation today and your decision to monitor. Does that sound okay to you?"

Document the full discussion in the patient record, including the information provided, the evidence-based recommendation, and the patient's informed agreement to monitor. Schedule a routine review appointment. No treatment is initiated today without clinical indication.

PQ-36
Antibiotic Prophylaxis in Patient with Joint Replacement
Station 35  |  Past Questions
■ Cluster 3 — Evaluation & Treatment Planning

CANDIDATE BRIEF

Mark Danial is a new patient in your surgery. He is seeing you today, complaining about his upper canine 23 tooth, which is extremely mobile due to bone loss. PA of 23,24,25 was given with 23 severe bone loss (there is bone loss around 24 and 25 as well). 23 roots are close to the anterior wall of the sinus. You decided to extract 23. Patient has joint replacement 6 years ago. He is Allergic to penicillin. He wants antibiotic prophylaxis as his previous dentist was giving him before dental treatment. He is also having asthma and hypertension. Explain the management plan to the pt.

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

Stage 1 — Introduction & Focused Medical History (0–2 min)

Greet Mark, confirm identity, and take a targeted history: type of joint replaced, time since surgery (6 years), any complications, revisions, or infections. Screen for diabetes, immunosuppression, steroid use. Confirm penicillin allergy, asthma, and hypertension medications. INFLECTION 1 — Candidate must identify that 6 years post-op with no complications places Mark in the low-risk category under current guidelines.

Stage 2 — Explain the Planned Procedure (2–3 min)

Outline the extraction of 23, noting severe bone loss, sinus proximity, and the need for careful surgical technique. Confirm Mark understands the procedure before addressing the prophylaxis question.

Stage 3 — Address Antibiotic Prophylaxis with Evidence-Based Reasoning (3–5 min)

Explain that current Australian guidelines (ADA/AAOS) do NOT recommend routine prophylaxis for uncomplicated joint replacements in immunocompetent patients beyond 2 years post-surgery. INFLECTION 2 — Candidate must quantify risk: prosthetic joint infection risk from dental procedure ~0.3% vs adverse drug reaction risk from unnecessary antibiotics in a penicillin-allergic patient ~3%. Prophylaxis is more likely to cause harm than benefit here.

Stage 4 — Acknowledge Exceptions & Offer Liaison (5–6 min)

Clarify when prophylaxis IS considered: within 2 years post-op, immunocompromised patients, history of prosthetic joint infection. Offer to contact orthopaedic surgeon if Mark remains concerned. Validate his previous experience without undermining prior care.

Stage 5 — Confirm Understanding & Close (6–7 min)

Use teach-back to confirm Mark understands the reasoning. Invite questions. Document the discussion and decision in the clinical notes.

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Confirms joint type, time since replacement (6 years), and absence of complications, revisions, or infections before making any prophylaxis decision
  2. ✅ Screens for immunocompromising conditions (diabetes, steroids, immunosuppressants) and correctly identifies Mark as immunocompetent
  3. ✅ Accurately states that current Australian guidelines (ADA/AAOS) do NOT recommend routine antibiotic prophylaxis for uncomplicated joint replacements >2 years post-surgery in immunocompetent patients
  4. ✅ Quantifies the risk-benefit ratio: ~0.3% risk of prosthetic joint infection from dental procedure vs ~3% risk of adverse drug reaction from unnecessary antibiotics in a penicillin-allergic patient — prophylaxis causes more harm than benefit
  5. ✅ Identifies exceptions (within 2 years post-op, immunocompromised, prior prosthetic joint infection), offers orthopaedic surgeon liaison, and confirms patient understanding with empathy and jargon-free language
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • Current Australian guidelines — consistent with the ADA and AAOS — do not recommend routine antibiotic prophylaxis for patients with uncomplicated joint replacements who are immunocompetent, particularly when the replacement is more than two years old with no history of infection or revision.
  • The estimated risk of a prosthetic joint infection arising from a dental procedure is approximately 0.3%, whereas the risk of a significant adverse drug reaction from an unnecessary antibiotic in a penicillin-allergic patient is approximately 3% — meaning prophylaxis is statistically more likely to harm Mark than to protect him.
  • Prophylaxis would be reconsidered if the replacement were within two years of surgery, if Mark were immunocompromised, on immunosuppressive medications, had diabetes, or had a prior history of prosthetic joint infection — none of which apply here.
  • Because Mark has a documented penicillin allergy, the alternative agents — such as clindamycin — carry their own risk profile, including Clostridioides difficile-associated diarrhoea, which further shifts the risk-benefit balance against routine prophylaxis.
Curveball Deflectors
  • Patient insists: 'My previous dentist always gave me antibiotics — why are you refusing to look after me properly?' → Validate his concern empathetically: 'I completely understand why you're worried — your previous dentist was following the guidance available at the time, and they were acting in your best interest. The evidence has been updated since then, and the current guidelines actually show that giving antibiotics routinely can cause more harm than good, especially given your penicillin allergy. I want to make sure I'm giving you the safest care based on the best available evidence. If you'd like, I'm very happy to contact your orthopaedic surgeon so we can make this decision together.' Do NOT prescribe antibiotics simply to appease the patient.
  • Candidate defaults to prescribing clindamycin 'just to be safe' because the patient has a joint replacement and is penicillin-allergic → This is the most common error. Resist the impulse. The correct answer is that no prophylaxis is indicated under current guidelines for this clinical scenario. Prescribing clindamycin unnecessarily exposes Mark to a ~3% adverse drug reaction risk and C. difficile risk, which exceeds the ~0.3% risk of prosthetic joint infection from the dental procedure. If uncertain, the correct action is to defer and liaise with the orthopaedic surgeon — not to prescribe empirically.
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ►
STAGE 1: Introduction & Focused Medical History

"Good morning, Mark. I'm Dr [Name]. Thank you for coming in today. Before we talk about the treatment plan for your tooth, I'd like to ask you a few questions about your medical history so I can make sure everything we do is completely safe for you. Is that okay? You mentioned you've had a joint replacement — could you tell me a bit more about that? Which joint was it, and when did you have the surgery?" [Patient confirms joint replacement 6 years ago.] "Thank you. And since the surgery, has everything gone smoothly? Any infections in the joint, any further operations or revisions, or any ongoing problems?" [Patient confirms no complications.] "That's reassuring. I also want to ask — do you have diabetes, or are you taking any medications that affect your immune system, such as steroids or chemotherapy?" [Patient denies.] "And I can see from your notes that you have a penicillin allergy, as well as asthma and hypertension — are you currently taking any medications for those?"

Candidate takes a targeted history confirming: joint type and timing (6 years ago), no complications or revisions, no immunocompromising conditions, penicillin allergy confirmed, asthma and hypertension noted. Mark is identified as immunocompetent with an uncomplicated joint replacement well beyond the 2-year threshold.

STAGE 2: Explain the Planned Procedure

"Thank you, Mark. Now let me explain what I'm planning to do today. Looking at your X-ray, tooth 23 — your upper canine — has very significant bone loss around it, which is why it's so mobile. Unfortunately, the tooth can't be saved, and the safest option is to remove it. I do want to mention that the roots of this tooth are quite close to your sinus — the air space just above — so I'll be taking extra care during the extraction. I'll let you know what to watch for afterwards in case we need to check that area. Do you have any questions about the procedure itself before we talk about the antibiotic question?"

Candidate explains the extraction of 23, acknowledges sinus proximity as a surgical consideration, and ensures informed consent groundwork is laid before addressing prophylaxis.

STAGE 3: Address Antibiotic Prophylaxis — Evidence-Based Explanation

"Now, I want to address your question about antibiotics before the procedure — it's a really important one, and I want to be completely transparent with you about why I'm recommending we don't use them today. The current Australian guidelines — which are in line with international dental and orthopaedic guidelines — actually advise that routine antibiotics before dental treatment are not recommended for patients who have had a joint replacement, as long as the joint is healthy and the patient's immune system is working normally. Based on everything you've told me, that applies to you. Here's the key reason this matters for you specifically: because you have a penicillin allergy, we'd need to use a different antibiotic — and those alternatives carry their own risks. The chance of your joint being affected by bacteria from this dental procedure is actually very low — around 3 in 1,000. But the chance of having a significant reaction to an antibiotic you don't need is around 3 in 100 — that's ten times higher. So giving you antibiotics today would actually be more likely to cause you harm than to protect you. I know this is different from what you've been told before, and I want to be clear — your previous dentist was following the guidance available at the time, and they were absolutely looking out for you. The evidence has simply been updated since then."

Candidate explicitly states guidelines do not support routine prophylaxis, quantifies the risk-benefit ratio (~0.3% prosthetic joint infection risk vs ~3% adverse drug reaction risk), and validates prior care without undermining trust.

STAGE 4: Exceptions, Liaison Offer & Confirm Understanding

"I do want you to know that there are situations where antibiotics before dental treatment would be appropriate — for example, if your joint replacement had been done within the last two years, if you had a previous infection in the joint, or if your immune system was weakened by a medical condition or medication. None of those apply to you, which is why I'm confident this is the right call. That said, if you'd feel more comfortable, I'm very happy to contact your orthopaedic surgeon before we proceed, so we can confirm this together. Your peace of mind matters to me. Does that make sense? Can I ask you to tell me in your own words what you've understood, just so I know I've explained it clearly? And please — any questions at all, I'm here to answer them." [Document the discussion, the guideline basis for the decision, and the patient's response in the clinical notes.]

Candidate outlines exceptions to the no-prophylaxis rule, offers orthopaedic surgeon liaison as a safety net, uses teach-back to confirm understanding, invites questions, and documents the clinical decision and reasoning. Maintains empathetic, jargon-free communication throughout.

PQ-37
Management of Peri-Implantitis
Station 36  |  Past Questions
■ Cluster 3 — Evaluation & Treatment Planning

CANDIDATE BRIEF

Peri-implantitis of an implant supported bridge extended from 32 to 42. Diagnosis was given with a picture. Pocket depths 6mm and 7mm. Smoker, redness and bleeding gums, main concern was bleeding gums, explain diagnosis, treatment options and management of the patient, answer questions.

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

Stage 1 — History Taking (0–2 min)

Greet Mr Chen, acknowledge his concern about bleeding. Ask about symptom duration (redness 6–8 months, chewing discomfort 2 months). Directly ask about smoking — he smokes 10 cigarettes/day for 30 years (will not volunteer this). Ask about oral hygiene routine and last dental visit (18 months ago). INFLECTION 1 — Failure to ask about smoking misses the primary modifiable risk factor and loses marks on risk-factor discussion.

Stage 2 — Clinical Examination (2–4 min)

Describe probing at six sites per implant: depths 7–8 mm, bleeding on probing, suppuration present, no mobility, visible plaque. Request periapical radiograph — bone loss ~4 mm beyond expected crestal remodelling confirms peri-implantitis. INFLECTION 2 — Candidates must state the diagnostic threshold: bone loss greater than 2 mm beyond expected crestal remodelling plus bleeding on probing = peri-implantitis, not mucositis.

Stage 3 — Diagnosis Explanation (4–6 min)

Explain in plain language: the implant has developed a serious infection in the surrounding bone — like gum disease but around the implant. Distinguish from early-stage mucositis (reversible gum inflammation) versus peri-implantitis (bone loss, less reversible). Validate his anxiety about implant loss honestly.

Stage 4 — Treatment Plan (6–9 min)

Staged approach: (1) Non-surgical debridement with implant-safe instruments + chlorhexidine irrigation; (2) Oral hygiene instruction — interdental brushes, correct technique; (3) Smoking cessation advice and referral; (4) Possible adjunctive antimicrobials (metronidazole or local chlorhexidine gel). If non-surgical fails — surgical options or implant removal discussed honestly.

Stage 5 — Follow-up and Maintenance (9–10 min)

Review at 8–12 weeks to reassess probing depths and bone stability. Emphasise 3-monthly maintenance schedule. Reinforce that smoking cessation and daily interdental cleaning are essential to protect the implant long-term.

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Directly asks about smoking and elicits 10 cigarettes/day — a hidden risk factor that must be actively sought
  2. ✅ States the diagnostic threshold for peri-implantitis: bone loss >2 mm beyond expected crestal remodelling plus bleeding on probing and/or suppuration
  3. ✅ Distinguishes peri-implantitis from peri-implant mucositis clearly in patient-friendly language
  4. ✅ Outlines a staged non-surgical management plan before discussing surgical options, including implant-safe debridement instruments
  5. ✅ Discusses prognosis honestly including risk of implant loss if treatment fails, and arranges 8–12 week review with 3-monthly maintenance thereafter
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • Peri-implantitis is diagnosed when there is bleeding on probing or suppuration, probing depths of 6 mm or greater, and radiographic bone loss exceeding 2 mm beyond the expected crestal remodelling seen after initial implant placement.
  • Non-surgical debridement must use implant-compatible instruments — carbon fibre curettes, titanium scalers, or ultrasonic devices with plastic or titanium tips — to avoid scratching the implant surface and creating a rougher biofilm-retentive surface.
  • Smoking is one of the strongest modifiable risk factors for peri-implantitis — it impairs neutrophil function, reduces vascularity, and significantly compromises the host response to bacterial challenge around the implant.
  • If non-surgical therapy fails to achieve pocket depth reduction and halt radiographic bone loss at the 8–12 week review, surgical access for debridement and possible regenerative or resective procedures should be considered.
  • Peri-implant mucositis is confined to the soft tissue and is reversible with debridement and improved oral hygiene; peri-implantitis involves irreversible bone loss and carries a more guarded prognosis.
Curveball Deflectors
  • Patient says: 'I paid a lot of money for this implant — are you telling me it might just fall out? Can't you just give me antibiotics to fix it?' → Acknowledge his frustration and validate the financial concern. Explain that antibiotics alone cannot treat peri-implantitis — the bacterial biofilm on the implant surface must be physically removed first, otherwise antibiotics have nothing to penetrate. Antibiotics may be used as an adjunct after debridement if indicated, but they are not a standalone cure. Reassure him that with prompt treatment, smoking cessation, and good home care, many implants can be stabilised, but honest prognosis requires reassessment at 8–12 weeks.
  • Candidate diagnoses peri-implant mucositis instead of peri-implantitis, or fails to request a radiograph → The radiograph is essential — clinical probing alone cannot confirm bone loss. With probing depths of 7–8 mm, bleeding on probing, suppuration, and 4 mm of radiographic bone loss beyond expected crestal remodelling, the diagnosis is peri-implantitis, not mucositis. Mucositis is limited to soft tissue with no bone loss. Candidates who do not request imaging or who diagnose mucositis will miss the inflection point and undertreat the condition.
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ►
STAGE 1: History Taking

'Mr Chen, thank you for coming in today. I can see you're concerned about the bleeding around your implant bridge — that's completely understandable, and I want to make sure we get to the bottom of what's going on. Before I examine you, I'd like to ask you a few questions. How long have you noticed the redness and bleeding? Have you had any discomfort when chewing? Do you have any pain at rest, or any swelling of your face or jaw? And I do need to ask — do you smoke or have you smoked in the past? How many cigarettes a day, and for how long? How often do you brush your teeth, and do you use anything between the teeth like floss or interdental brushes? When did you last have a dental check-up?'

Elicit: redness for 6–8 months, mild chewing discomfort for 2 months, no rest pain, no facial swelling. Patient smokes 10 cigarettes per day for 30 years — must be directly asked. Brushes once daily, no flossing, last recall 18 months ago. No diabetes or immunosuppression. Document all findings.

STAGE 2: Clinical Examination and Diagnosis

'I'm going to have a careful look at the gum and bone around your implant now. I'll use a small probe to measure the depth of the pockets around the implant — this tells us how much the supporting tissue has been affected. I'll also take an X-ray so we can see the bone level around the implant precisely.'

Record probing depths at six sites per implant: 7–8 mm, bleeding on probing confirmed, suppuration present, no implant mobility, visible plaque accumulation. Periapical radiograph shows approximately 4 mm bone loss beyond expected crestal remodelling. Diagnosis: peri-implantitis — meets criteria of bone loss greater than 2 mm beyond expected crestal remodelling, plus bleeding on probing and suppuration, with probing depths exceeding 6 mm.

STAGE 3: Explaining the Diagnosis

'Mr Chen, I want to explain what I've found. The implant itself is still firm, which is reassuring. However, the gum and bone around the implant have developed a serious infection — we call this peri-implantitis. Think of it like gum disease, but around the implant rather than a natural tooth. The bacteria have caused some of the supporting bone to break down, which is why you've been getting bleeding and discomfort. This is different from an earlier, milder stage called mucositis, which only affects the gum and is fully reversible. Unfortunately, once bone is lost, it doesn't grow back on its own, so it's really important we treat this now to stop it getting worse. The good news is that the implant is not loose, and with the right treatment and some changes to your routine, we have a good chance of stabilising things.'

Use plain language throughout. Validate anxiety about implant loss. Clearly distinguish peri-implantitis from mucositis. Avoid jargon.

STAGE 4: Treatment Plan, Risk Factors, and Follow-up

'There are a few things working against the implant at the moment that we need to address together. Smoking is one of the biggest — it reduces the body's ability to fight infection and heal, and it significantly increases the risk of losing the implant. I'd strongly encourage you to consider quitting, and I can refer you to a smoking cessation programme or discuss nicotine replacement options. Brushing once a day without cleaning between the implant components also allows bacteria to build up in exactly the places that cause this problem — I'll show you how to use small interdental brushes that are designed for implants. In terms of treatment, the first step is a thorough clean of the implant surface using special instruments that won't damage the implant — this removes the bacterial deposits that are driving the infection. We may also use an antiseptic rinse or gel around the implant. If the infection doesn't respond to this, we may need to consider a small surgical procedure to access and clean the area more thoroughly. In the most difficult cases where the infection cannot be controlled, we may need to discuss removing the implant — but that is not where we are today, and I want to give every opportunity for non-surgical treatment to work first. I'd like to see you again in about eight to twelve weeks to re-measure the pockets and take another X-ray to check whether the bone loss has stabilised. After that, I'd recommend coming in every three months for maintenance — this is really important to keep the implant healthy long-term.'

Staged management: (1) Non-surgical debridement with carbon fibre curettes or plastic-tipped ultrasonic instruments plus chlorhexidine irrigation; (2) Oral hygiene instruction — interdental brushes sized for implant embrasures; (3) Smoking cessation referral — Quitline 13 7848 or NRT via pharmacy; (4) Adjunctive antimicrobials if indicated — local chlorhexidine gel or systemic metronidazole per clinical judgement; (5) Review at 8–12 weeks with repeat probing and radiograph; (6) 3-monthly maintenance schedule. Discuss surgical options and implant removal honestly if non-surgical therapy fails.

PQ-38
Management of a Large Failing Amalgam in an International Student
Station 37  |  Past Questions
■ Cluster 1 — History & Risk Factors

CANDIDATE BRIEF

Mr Sean Hobart, 30-year-old overseas student, came to Australia 2–3 years ago. Chief Complaint: Pain from one of his teeth on the lower right side for the past 2 weeks. Can't locate a particular tooth, but biting on that side makes it worse. Examination Findings: Large MOD amalgam restoration on 46, placed 20 years back. Clinical Image: Intraoral photo showing a large, aged MOD amalgam restoration on lower molar (tooth 46) with visible fracture lines running through the amalgam. Task: Gather information, explain necessary investigations, possible diagnosis and address patient's concern.

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

Stage 1 — Introduction & History (0–3 min)

Greet patient, confirm identity. Take focused history: onset and nature of pain (2 weeks, biting-provoked, non-localised), absence of spontaneous pain, thermal sensitivity, or swelling. Confirm restoration placed ~8 years ago in China. Confirm nil medical history, nil medications, nil allergies. Ask about diet (bubble tea 3–4×/week noted as caries risk) and oral hygiene habits.

Stage 2 — Examination & Investigation Explanation (3–5 min)

Explain clinical findings in plain language: large old filling with visible cracks, risk of decay underneath and tooth fracture. INFLECTION 1 Explain need for periapical and bitewing radiographs plus pulp vitality testing (cold test/EPT) to assess nerve health before any treatment decision is made.

Stage 3 — Diagnosis & Treatment Options (5–8 min)

Explain likely diagnosis: failing large amalgam with possible recurrent caries and cuspal fracture risk. Present options: (1) indirect restoration — ceramic onlay or full crown — preferred for heavily restored molar; (2) large direct composite — possible if sufficient tooth structure remains but higher long-term failure risk. INFLECTION 2 Mention that if decay is close to the nerve, root canal treatment may be required before the crown — this must not be omitted.

Stage 4 — Cost, Timeline & Shared Decision-Making (8–10 min)

Proactively ask about financial concerns. Acknowledge limited Medibank student cover. Provide approximate Australian cost ranges (crown ~$1,500–$2,500; onlay ~$1,000–$1,800; RCT ~$900–$1,500 if needed). Discuss staged treatment and payment plans. Reassure that assessment and temporisation can occur within 1–2 visits before exams. Check understanding using teach-back.

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Focused history confirms biting-provoked pain, no thermal/spontaneous symptoms, no swelling — pointing away from irreversible pulpitis or abscess at this stage
  2. ✅ Periapical and bitewing radiographs plus pulp vitality testing (cold/EPT) are mandatory before any definitive treatment decision
  3. ✅ Indirect restoration (onlay or crown) is the preferred long-term option for a heavily restored lower molar with cuspal fracture risk — direct composite is a compromise option only
  4. ✅ Risk of pulp involvement and possible need for root canal treatment must be explicitly discussed before consent is obtained
  5. ✅ Financial concerns, insurance limitations, staged treatment options, and realistic visit timeline must be proactively explored and addressed
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • A large MOD amalgam on a lower molar leaves the cusps unsupported and at high risk of fracture — this is why we prefer to protect the tooth with a crown or onlay rather than simply replacing the filling like-for-like.
  • Before I can tell you exactly what treatment you need, I need to take two X-rays — a bitewing and a periapical — and do a simple cold test on the tooth to check whether the nerve is still healthy. Without those, I'd just be guessing.
  • If the decay has reached close to the nerve, we may need to do a root canal treatment first before placing the crown. I want to be upfront about that possibility now so there are no surprises.
  • Biting pain without any cold or heat sensitivity is actually a reassuring sign — it suggests the nerve may still be healthy, but we need to confirm that with testing before we proceed.
Curveball Deflectors
  • Patient says: 'Can't you just patch it up cheaply for now? I don't have much money and my exams are in 6 weeks.' → Acknowledge the concern empathetically: 'I completely understand — cost and timing are really important, and I want to work with you on that. What I can do today is take the X-rays and do the nerve test, and if the tooth is stable, we can place a temporary restoration to protect it while you get through your exams. Then we plan the definitive treatment afterwards. I just want to make sure we're not leaving anything that could turn into an emergency during your exam period.' Avoid agreeing to simply 'patch' without investigation — this is a common trap.
  • Patient asks: 'Why can't I just have a white filling instead of a crown? My friend had one and it was much cheaper.' → Validate the question without dismissing it: 'That's a really fair question. A tooth-coloured composite filling is possible, and it's less expensive upfront. The issue with a tooth this size is that the walls of the tooth are quite thin after removing the old filling and any decay — a large filling on a back molar takes a lot of biting force, and there's a real risk it could crack the tooth or the filling fails sooner. A crown or onlay wraps around the tooth and protects those walls. I'll be able to give you a much clearer recommendation once I see the X-rays and how much tooth structure is left.' Do not promise composite is equivalent to a crown for a heavily broken-down molar.
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ►
STAGE 1: Introduction & Focused History

"Hi Wei, I'm Dr [Name], one of the dentists here today. Thanks for coming in. I understand you've been having some pain on the lower right side for about two weeks — is that right? Can you tell me a bit more about it? Is it a constant ache, or does it mainly come on when you bite down?"

Listen for: biting-provoked pain, non-localised, 2-week duration. Then systematically screen: "Does anything make it worse or better? Any pain that wakes you up at night? Any sensitivity to hot or cold drinks — like your bubble tea? Any swelling or bad taste?" Confirm nil spontaneous pain, nil thermal sensitivity, nil swelling. Ask: "Do you know anything about the history of that filling — when it was placed and where?" Confirm placed ~8 years ago in China. Screen medical history: "Are you taking any medications, or do you have any medical conditions or allergies I should know about?" Confirm nil. Note diet risk: "How often would you have sugary drinks or snacks during the day?" — bubble tea 3–4×/week is a caries risk factor to document.

STAGE 2: Explaining Findings & Investigations

"Thanks for telling me all of that, Wei. So looking at the photo of your tooth, I can see there's a large silver filling that takes up most of the biting surface of that back tooth. What concerns me is that I can see some cracks running through the filling, and fillings this large and this old can sometimes hide decay underneath them, or they can cause the walls of the tooth to weaken and crack. The biting pain you're describing fits with that picture. Before I can tell you exactly what's going on, I need to take two X-rays — one that shows the whole tooth including the root and the bone around it, and one that specifically looks for decay between the teeth. I'd also like to do a simple cold test — I just hold a small cold tip near the tooth for a few seconds — to check whether the nerve inside the tooth is still healthy. Is that okay with you?"

Explain rationale for periapical X-ray (root, bone, periapical pathology), bitewing X-ray (recurrent caries, restoration margins), and pulp vitality testing (cold test or EPT). Do not proceed to treatment planning without these. Document findings.

STAGE 3: Diagnosis & Treatment Options

"Based on what I can see so far, my main concern is that this large old filling may have decay underneath it, and the tooth walls around it are at risk of cracking — especially because back teeth take a lot of force when you chew. Once I remove the old filling and any decay, I'll have a much clearer picture. There are two main directions we could go. The first option — and the one I'd generally recommend for a tooth in this situation — is what we call a crown or an onlay. This is a custom-made cap that fits over the tooth and protects those weakened walls. It's the most durable long-term solution. The second option is a large tooth-coloured composite filling. It's less expensive upfront, but on a back molar that takes a lot of biting force, there's a higher chance it could fail or the tooth could crack over time. I want to be upfront about one more thing: if the decay turns out to be very close to the nerve, we may need to do a root canal treatment before placing the crown. I know that sounds daunting, but right now your symptoms are actually reassuring — the fact that you have no cold sensitivity or spontaneous pain suggests the nerve may still be healthy. We'll know more after the X-rays and the cold test."

Address all rubric points: indirect vs direct restoration indications, pulp involvement risk, endodontic possibility. Use plain language. Check understanding: "Does that make sense so far? Do you have any questions about what I've just explained?"

STAGE 4: Cost, Timeline & Shared Decision-Making

"I also want to talk about the practical side of things — cost and timing — because I know those matter. Can I ask, do you have dental insurance at the moment? And is cost something that's on your mind? I want to make sure we come up with a plan that actually works for you. In Australia, a crown typically costs somewhere in the range of $1,500 to $2,500 depending on the material, and if root canal treatment is needed, that's usually an additional $900 to $1,500. A large composite filling would be less — roughly $300 to $500 — but as I mentioned, it carries more risk on this tooth. Your Medibank student cover may contribute a benefit toward some of these costs, and our practice also offers payment plans if that would help. I also heard you mention exams coming up in six weeks — that's really important to factor in. Here's what I'd suggest: we do the X-rays and nerve test today, and if the tooth is stable, I can place a good temporary restoration to protect it while you get through your exams. Then we schedule the definitive treatment — the crown or onlay — once you have more breathing room. I just want to make sure we're not leaving anything that could turn into a dental emergency right in the middle of your exam period. How does that sound to you?"

Proactively raise financial concerns, provide realistic Australian cost ranges, discuss staged treatment and payment plans. Acknowledge study timeline. Use teach-back to confirm understanding. Demonstrate cultural sensitivity throughout — avoid jargon, invite questions, confirm patient feels heard and involved in the decision.

PQ-39
Management of Dental Abscess in a Five-Year-Old Child with Molar Incisor Hypomineralisation
Station 38  |  Past Questions
■ Cluster 1 — History & Risk Factors

CANDIDATE BRIEF

Alice Zang, 5-year-old child, attending with her father for the first time. Chief Complaint: Pain from a tooth on the lower left side. Dad mentions she couldn't sleep last night. Examination Findings: Second primary molar on the left side has large decay with puffy gums around the tooth. She took antibiotics when she was under the age of 2 years due to an ear infection. Clinical Image: Intraoral photo of lower left molar region showing a decayed primary molar with swollen, erythematous gingiva (abscess) and visible tooth breakdown. Task: Gather information, address patient's concern.

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

Stage 1 — Introduction & History (0–3 min)

Greet Alice and her father warmly. Acknowledge the sleepless night and validate the father's concern. Take a focused history: onset, severity (pain scale), systemic symptoms (fever — father reports 37.9°C), eating/drinking, medications taken (paracetamol), allergies, medical history, and previous dental experience. Elicit the history of antibiotics before age 2 — this is a key aetiological clue for MIH. INFLECTION 1 — Connecting early antibiotic/illness history to MIH aetiology separates a strong candidate from an average one.

Stage 2 — Clinical Review & Diagnosis (3–6 min)

Systematically review the clinical findings card and radiograph. Identify: (1) acute dentoalveolar abscess on 46 with buccal fluctuance and periapical radiolucency; (2) MIH pattern on all four first permanent molars and upper central incisors. Note the previous dentist's dismissal of the chalky teeth — this is a missed opportunity for early intervention. Explain diagnosis in parent-friendly language.

Stage 3 — Urgency Assessment & Treatment Options (6–10 min)

Correctly classify as a spreading infection requiring same-day management. Discuss extraction of 46 as the most appropriate definitive treatment given extent of breakdown and child's age. Discuss antibiotic prescription (amoxicillin first-line per Australian guidelines) as adjunct, not replacement, for surgical drainage. INFLECTION 2 — Antibiotics alone without surgical management is a critical error; the candidate must articulate the need for incision and drainage or extraction today.

Stage 4 — Behaviour Management & Long-Term Plan (10–13 min)

Address Alice's dental anxiety sensitively. Discuss options: oral midazolam anxiolysis, nitrous oxide inhalation sedation, or referral for GA if needed. Outline MIH preventive plan: fluoride varnish 6-monthly, fissure sealants on unaffected molars, GC Tooth Mousse or similar CPP-ACP product, and regular 3-monthly review. Close with safety-netting advice for ED presentation.

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Correctly identifies acute dentoalveolar abscess on 46 (not the primary molar) and recognises MIH pattern affecting all four first permanent molars and upper central incisors
  2. ✅ Links early childhood antibiotic use (ear infection before age 2) to MIH aetiology and explains this to the parent in plain language
  3. ✅ Correctly assesses urgency — same-day surgical management (extraction or I&D) is required; antibiotics are adjunctive only and do not replace definitive treatment
  4. ✅ Discusses extraction of 46 as the most appropriate option given extent of caries, MIH-related enamel breakdown, child's age, and difficulty of restoration in an anxious patient
  5. ✅ Provides clear safety-netting advice: return to ED if difficulty breathing/swallowing, rapidly worsening swelling, high fever, or systemic deterioration
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • The infection has spread beyond the tooth into the surrounding bone — this is called a dentoalveolar abscess, and because there is fluctuant swelling today, this needs to be treated surgically today, not just with antibiotics.
  • MIH — Molar Incisor Hypomineralisation — is a developmental condition where the enamel doesn't mineralise properly, most likely related to illness or antibiotic use in the first three years of life. It makes these teeth softer, more sensitive, and much more prone to rapid decay.
  • Antibiotics will help control the spread of infection, but they cannot drain the abscess on their own — we need to remove the source, which in this case means extracting the tooth today or at the very latest tomorrow.
  • Given Alice's age, her level of anxiety, and the extent of treatment she needs across multiple teeth, I would like to discuss the option of treatment under inhalation sedation or, if that is not sufficient, referral for general anaesthetic — I want to make sure we do this safely and as comfortably as possible for her.
  • The periapical radiograph shows a radiolucency at the root tip of 46 indicating bone loss from infection, but importantly there is no involvement of the developing permanent successor, so we have not compromised the adult tooth underneath.
Curveball Deflectors
  • Father says: 'Can't you just give her antibiotics and we'll come back next week when she's feeling better?' → Acknowledge the father's concern and validate that he wants to avoid putting Alice through more stress. Clearly but kindly explain that antibiotics alone are not sufficient — the infection has a physical collection that needs to be drained surgically, and delaying definitive treatment risks the infection spreading to deeper spaces in the neck or face, which can become life-threatening.
