Frame same-day treatment as the safest option for Alice, and reassure him that behaviour management options will be used to make it as comfortable as possible.
  • Candidate focuses management on the lower left primary molar (as described in the candidate brief) rather than correctly identifying 46 (lower right first permanent molar) from the clinical findings card → This is the most common error in this station. The candidate brief mentions lower left pain as the chief complaint, but the clinical findings card clearly identifies the abscess on 46 (lower right first permanent molar). An excellent candidate reconciles this discrepancy — acknowledging the parent's report of left-sided pain while explaining that on examination the acute infection is actually on the lower right side, and that MIH-affected teeth can be sensitive in multiple quadrants simultaneously. Failing to correctly identify 46 as the affected tooth will cost significant marks on the diagnosis and management rubric criteria.
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ►
STAGE 1: Introduction & History

"Hi Alice, hi — and you must be Alice's dad. I'm Dr [Name], lovely to meet you both. I'm so sorry to hear Alice had such a rough night — that must have been really worrying for you. Alice, you're being so brave coming in today. I'm going to have a chat with your dad first and then I'll explain everything to you too, okay? Nothing is going to happen without us talking it through first."

Establish rapport with both child and parent. Direct history questions to father while keeping Alice engaged. Ask: When did the pain start? Has it been getting worse? Has she had a fever — father confirms 37.9°C last night. Is she eating and drinking? Father says soft foods only, paracetamol helping a little. Any swelling of the face? Any difficulty swallowing or breathing? Any allergies or medical conditions? Father confirms nil allergies, nil medical history, immunisations up to date. Ask about previous dental experience — father mentions one filling at age 4 that was difficult. Ask about the chalky teeth — father says previous dentist said just keep them clean. Elicit antibiotic history: father confirms Alice had antibiotics for an ear infection before age 2. Document all findings.

STAGE 2: Clinical Review & Diagnosis Explanation

"Thank you for telling me all of that — it's really helpful. I've had a look at Alice's examination findings and her X-ray, and I want to explain what we're seeing. The tooth that is causing the problem is actually one of Alice's adult teeth on the lower right side — it's called the first permanent molar, and it's one of the most important teeth she'll ever have. Unfortunately, the decay in that tooth has gone very deep and has caused an infection that has spread into the bone and gum around it — we call this a dental abscess. That's why her face is a little swollen and why she's been in so much pain."

Review clinical findings card systematically. Identify acute dentoalveolar abscess on 46: buccal swelling, fluctuance, TTP+++, periapical radiolucency on radiograph, no involvement of permanent successor. Identify MIH pattern: yellow-brown demarcated opacities and post-eruptive breakdown on all four first permanent molars, mild opacities on upper central incisors.

"I also want to talk to you about something called MIH — Molar Incisor Hypomineralisation. This is a condition where the enamel, the hard outer layer of certain teeth, doesn't form properly. It makes those teeth look chalky or discoloured, and it makes them softer, more sensitive, and unfortunately much more prone to getting decay very quickly. Alice has this on all four of her adult back teeth and on her two upper front teeth. The history you mentioned — that she had antibiotics for an ear infection before she was two — is exactly the kind of thing that can affect how enamel develops during those early years. This is not anything you did wrong at all."

STAGE 3: Urgency, Treatment Options & Behaviour Management

"I need to be honest with you about how urgent this is. Because there is a collection of infection with swelling today, we need to treat this today — not next week, and not just with antibiotics. Antibiotics will help stop the infection spreading further, and I will prescribe those, but they cannot drain the abscess on their own. We need to remove the source of the infection. Given how much of the tooth has broken down and Alice's age, I think the best option for that tooth is to take it out. I know that sounds scary, but I want to reassure you that we will do everything we can to make this as comfortable as possible for Alice."

Prescribe amoxicillin 250mg three times daily for five days (weight-appropriate, per Australian Therapeutic Guidelines: Oral and Dental). Confirm no penicillin allergy. Discuss extraction of 46 as definitive management. Acknowledge father's concern about GA. Discuss behaviour management options: oral midazolam anxiolysis as first step, nitrous oxide inhalation sedation, or referral to a paediatric dental specialist or hospital for treatment under general anaesthetic if needed. Explain that the decision will be guided by what Alice can tolerate safely.

"For Alice's other adult teeth that are affected by MIH, I want to put a plan in place to protect them before they end up in the same situation. We'll apply fluoride varnish to strengthen them, place protective sealants on the ones that haven't broken down yet, and use some special creams to help with sensitivity. I'd like to see Alice every three months so we can keep a close eye on things."

STAGE 4: Safety-Netting, Checking Understanding & Close

"Before we finish, I want to make sure you know what to watch out for at home. If Alice develops any difficulty breathing or swallowing, if the swelling spreads rapidly to her neck or eye area, if she develops a high fever above 38.5 degrees, or if she seems very unwell or drowsy, please do not wait — take her straight to the emergency department. These would be signs that the infection is spreading and needs urgent hospital treatment. Do you have any questions for me? I want to make sure you feel comfortable with everything we've discussed."

Check father's understanding using teach-back. Provide written safety-netting information if available. Confirm antibiotic prescription and pain management plan (continue paracetamol, add ibuprofen if tolerated and no contraindications). Book same-day or next-morning appointment for extraction with appropriate behaviour management in place. Document all findings, diagnosis, and management plan. Ensure Alice is praised and reassured throughout.

PQ-40
Assessment and Management of Dental Fluorosis
Station 39  |  Past Questions
■ Cluster 2 — Balanced (History informs management)

CANDIDATE BRIEF

Isla, 15-year-old girl. Chief Complaint: Complaining about white and brown patches on all of her teeth. Examination Findings: White and brown spots throughout the mouth. History: Lived in a rural area until she was 10, then moved to boarding school. Took fluoride tablets until age of 10. Doesn't want any drilling or local anaesthesia. Wants teeth fixed ASAP — has a photoshoot at sister's wedding in a few weeks. Clinical Image: Frontal photo of upper and lower teeth showing generalised white and brown/yellow mottled staining across all visible teeth — classic dental fluorosis presentation. Task: Explain diagnosis, treatment planning and management.

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

Stage 1 — Focused History (0–3 min)

Greet Isla and parent warmly. Take a targeted fluoride exposure history: water source in rural area, fluoride tablet use alongside water supply, toothpaste swallowing in early childhood. Ask about systemic illness, fever, antibiotics, or trauma during tooth development to exclude MIH or amelogenesis imperfecta. INFLECTION 1 — Candidate must identify that fluoride tablets taken in an already-fluoridated rural area represent cumulative excess exposure, not a single cause.

Stage 2 — Diagnosis and Explanation (3–6 min)

Explain in plain language: "The patches are called dental fluorosis — they formed when your teeth were developing as a young child, because the enamel cells were sensitive to higher fluoride levels at that time. Your teeth are completely strong and healthy — this is a cosmetic concern, not a structural one." Reassure parent without assigning blame.

Stage 3 — Management Options (6–9 min)

Outline options in order of invasiveness: (1) monitoring only, (2) microabrasion ± home bleaching, (3) resin infiltration (Icon) — no drilling, no anaesthesia, suitable now. INFLECTION 2 — Candidate must recognise resin infiltration directly addresses Isla's two stated preferences: no drilling and a result before the wedding. Composite or porcelain veneers deferred to adulthood.

Stage 4 — Psychosocial and Shared Decision-Making (9–11 min)

Acknowledge Isla's self-consciousness empathetically. Involve her directly in choosing between options. Set realistic expectations for resin infiltration outcomes. Arrange follow-up and document consent discussion.

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Takes a focused fluoride history covering water fluoride levels, supplement use, and toothpaste swallowing during the critical window of birth to age eight
  2. ✅ Differentiates fluorosis from MIH and amelogenesis imperfecta by asking about systemic illness, fever, antibiotics, and trauma during tooth development
  3. ✅ Explains the diagnosis in plain language — enamel is structurally sound, no increased caries risk, cosmetic issue only — and reassures parent without assigning blame
  4. ✅ Identifies resin infiltration (Icon) as the most appropriate immediate option given Isla's stated preferences of no drilling, no anaesthesia, and an urgent timeline
  5. ✅ Defers irreversible restorative options (composite or porcelain veneers) until adulthood and involves Isla in shared decision-making with empathy for her psychosocial concerns
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • Dental fluorosis occurs during the secretory and maturation phases of amelogenesis — the critical window is birth to approximately age eight for permanent teeth, with the upper incisors most vulnerable between six months and two years of age.
  • The combination of naturally fluoridated rural water, concurrent fluoride tablet supplementation, and toothpaste ingestion represents cumulative fluoride excess — no single source is solely responsible.
  • Resin infiltration with Icon (DMG) is a microinvasive technique that uses a low-viscosity resin to fill subsurface enamel porosities, masking white spot lesions without cavity preparation or local anaesthesia — making it appropriate for a fifteen-year-old who declines drilling.
  • Microabrasion using a slurry of pumice and hydrochloric acid (e.g., Opalustre) removes superficial enamel to a maximum depth of approximately 200 micrometres and is most effective for superficial white or brown spots; it can be combined with home bleaching for enhanced results.
  • Porcelain veneers should be deferred until at least eighteen years of age — ideally until enamel maturation and gingival margin stability are confirmed — to avoid over-preparation of a developing dentition.
Curveball Deflectors
  • Isla says: 'Can't you just bleach them white so they all match? I want it done before the wedding next month.' → Acknowledge her urgency and validate her concern. Explain that bleaching alone tends to lighten the background tooth colour but may initially make white fluorosis spots appear more prominent before they blend in over several weeks. The most suitable option for her timeline and her preference to avoid drilling is resin infiltration — it can often be completed in one to two appointments and works by filling the white spots so they blend with the surrounding enamel. Set realistic expectations: results are significant but may not be perfect, and a review appointment after the procedure would be ideal before the wedding.
  • Parent asks: 'Did I cause this by giving her fluoride tablets? Should I have known better?' → Respond with empathy and reassurance: 'You were doing exactly what you were advised to do at the time — fluoride supplements were recommended to protect children's teeth from decay, and you had no way of knowing the local water already contained higher natural fluoride levels. This is not something you could reasonably have prevented, and it is important to know that Isla's teeth are healthy and strong — this is purely a cosmetic concern. Many families in rural areas with naturally fluoridated water have children with similar findings.' Avoid any language that implies fault or negligence.
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ►
STAGE 1: Greeting and Focused History

"Hi Isla, hi — lovely to meet you both. Isla, I can see you've come in today because you're not happy with the appearance of your teeth, and I completely understand that. Before I explain what I think is going on, I'd like to ask you both a few questions so I can give you the most accurate information. Is that okay?"

Take a focused fluoride exposure history. Ask: Where did Isla live from birth to age ten, and what was the water source — town water, tank water, or bore water? Were fluoride tablets or drops given, and from what age until what age? Did she use fluoride toothpaste as a young child, and did she tend to swallow it? Also ask about any serious childhood illnesses, high fevers, courses of antibiotics (particularly tetracyclines), or any injury to the front teeth — this helps exclude molar-incisor hypomineralisation or amelogenesis imperfecta as alternative diagnoses. Document that Isla lived in a rural area with likely naturally fluoridated water and took fluoride tablets until age ten, representing cumulative fluoride exposure during the critical window of tooth development.

STAGE 2: Explaining the Diagnosis

"Thank you — that's really helpful. I can now tell you what I think is happening. The white and brown patches on your teeth are called dental fluorosis. This is not a disease, and your teeth are not damaged or weak — in fact, they're actually very healthy with no decay at all, which is great news. What happened is that when your teeth were forming under the gum — when you were a very young child — the cells that were building your enamel were exposed to slightly higher levels of fluoride than they needed. This caused a change in the appearance of the enamel as it was forming. It's completely set in now — it won't get worse — and it doesn't affect the strength of your teeth or your risk of getting cavities. It's purely a cosmetic concern."

Reassure the parent directly: "This is something that happened during a very specific window of early childhood development. You were following advice to protect Isla's teeth, and the combination of the local water supply and the supplements together was more than her developing enamel needed at that time. There is no single thing that caused this, and this is absolutely not a reflection of anything you did wrong." Allow time for questions before moving to management.

STAGE 3: Management Options

"Now, the good news is that there are several things we can do, and importantly, Isla, you mentioned you don't want any drilling or needles — so let me start with the options that don't involve any of that. The first option is simply to monitor — your teeth are healthy, and some people choose to leave things as they are, especially knowing the teeth are strong. The second option, and the one I think might suit you best given your sister's wedding coming up, is called resin infiltration. We use a special liquid resin that soaks into the white patches and fills them in so they blend with the rest of your tooth. It takes one or two appointments, there's no drilling, no needle, and results can be quite good. It won't make your teeth look completely uniform, but it can make a real difference. There's also a technique called microabrasion, where we gently polish the surface of the enamel to reduce the appearance of the spots — again, no drilling or anaesthesia needed. Further down the track, when you're a bit older — around eighteen or so — we could also look at options like tooth-coloured coverings called veneers if you wanted a more complete change, but I wouldn't recommend that just yet."

Recommend resin infiltration (Icon, DMG) as the most appropriate immediate option given Isla's age, stated preferences, and timeline. Explain that composite or porcelain veneers are deferred until adulthood to preserve tooth structure and allow gingival margin stability. Document the discussion and options offered.

STAGE 4: Shared Decision-Making and Closing

"Isla, I want to make sure you're part of this decision — these are your teeth and your smile. How are you feeling about what I've described? I know the wedding is coming up soon, so if you'd like to go ahead with the resin infiltration, we can look at getting you in as soon as possible. I also want you to know that it's completely okay to take some time to think about it — there's no urgency from a health point of view. Whatever you decide, I'll be here to support you. Do you have any questions for me?"

Acknowledge Isla's self-consciousness with empathy and validate that her feelings about her appearance are completely understandable. Provide written information about resin infiltration if available. Schedule a follow-up appointment and document the diagnosis, aetiology discussion, management options offered, and Isla's preferences in the clinical notes. Reassure both Isla and her parent that ongoing monitoring will be part of her routine dental care.

PQ-41
Diagnosis and Management of Vertical Root Fracture
Station 40  |  Past Questions
■ Cluster 2 — Balanced (History informs management)

CANDIDATE BRIEF

Mr John Hobbart, new patient. Chief Complaint: Pain on an upper first molar. Examination Findings: Upper first molar on the right side — two segments with a composite restoration in the middle of the tooth (MOD). 8 mm pocket depth noticed on one side of the tooth. Diagnosis: vertical root fracture — tooth needs to be extracted. Medical History: Asthma and arthritis. Taking Ventolin and prednisolone 15mg. Clinical Image: Close-up photo of an upper molar showing heavily restored tooth with visible fracture lines and periodontal breakdown. Task: Explain your diagnosis and manage the patient. No need to explain the extraction procedure.

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

Stage 1 — History Taking (0–2 min)

Introduce, confirm identity, take focused history: onset (~2 months, worsening 2 weeks), character of pain, previous RCT on 36, intermittent gingival 'pimple', avoidance of left-side chewing, no trauma, no fever. Confirm medical history: hypertension on perindopril — no allergies. INFLECTION 1 Candidate must specifically ask about previous endodontic treatment and intermittent sinus tract — failure to do so misses the pathognomonic history.

Stage 2 — Clinical Examination (2–4 min)

Systematic examination: percussion (mild tenderness 36), palpation (buccal erythema/swelling), mobility (none), periodontal probing — isolated 6 mm mesial and 7 mm distal pockets on 36, adjacent teeth 2–3 mm. Request periapical radiograph: J-shaped radiolucency mesial root, adequate root filling, lamina dura loss mesially.

Stage 3 — Diagnosis Explanation (4–6 min)

Explain diagnosis of vertical root fracture clearly and empathetically. INFLECTION 2 Candidate must state the tooth cannot be saved — hedging or offering retreatment is incorrect and loses marks. Confirm patient understanding before proceeding.

Stage 4 — Management and Replacement Options (6–8 min)

Discuss extraction (no procedural detail required). Present three replacement options: dental implant (gold standard, ~$4,000–5,500 AUD), fixed bridge (requires preparation of adjacent teeth, ~$3,000–4,500), removable partial denture (most affordable, ~$1,000–1,500), or no replacement with explanation of consequences. Note perindopril — no significant interaction with local anaesthesia or implant healing.

Stage 5 — Closure and Follow-up (8–9 min)

Summarise plan, provide written information, arrange follow-up, check understanding, invite questions.

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Elicits the pathognomonic triad: root-canal-treated tooth + isolated narrow deep pockets + intermittent sinus tract (history of 'pimple' on gum)
  2. ✅ Requests periapical radiograph and correctly identifies J-shaped radiolucency along mesial root with lamina dura loss as diagnostic of VRF
  3. ✅ Clearly and empathetically communicates that the tooth has an irreversible vertical fracture and extraction is the only option — does not offer retreatment or repair
  4. ✅ Presents all three replacement options (implant, bridge, RPD) plus no-replacement, with balanced pros/cons and approximate Australian cost context
  5. ✅ Acknowledges medical history (hypertension on perindopril) and confirms no contraindications before planning extraction or implant
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • The isolated narrow pocket of 6–7 mm on a single root surface, with normal probing depths on all adjacent teeth, is a hallmark finding of vertical root fracture rather than generalised periodontal disease.
  • The J-shaped radiolucency tracking along the mesial root surface — distinct from a periapical lesion — combined with an intact root filling and no caries, is pathognomonic for vertical root fracture in a root-canal-treated tooth.
  • Vertical root fractures in endodontically treated teeth are irreversible — there is no evidence-based treatment that can predictably save the tooth, and extraction is the definitive management.
  • The intermittent sinus tract that appears and resolves spontaneously is consistent with a fracture-related periodontal-endodontic lesion draining intermittently, not a primary periodontal abscess.
  • Perindopril, an ACE inhibitor, does not contraindicate extraction or implant placement, but the prescribing dentist should be aware of the rare risk of angioedema with ACE inhibitors when planning airway management.
Curveball Deflectors
  • Patient says: 'Can't you just do another root canal or put a crown on it to save the tooth?' → Acknowledge the patient's understandable wish to keep the tooth, then explain clearly: 'I completely understand you'd like to save it — that's always our first preference too. Unfortunately, the fracture runs vertically along the root itself, which means it goes through the foundation of the tooth. Unlike a crack in the crown, this type of fracture cannot be repaired or stabilised with a crown or further root canal treatment. The evidence shows that teeth with this type of fracture cannot be saved predictably, and attempting to keep it risks ongoing infection and bone loss that could affect the options we have for replacement. I know that's not what you were hoping to hear, and I'm sorry.' Do not offer crown or retreatment as a viable option — this is a mark-losing error.
  • Candidate mistakes the isolated deep pocket for localised periodontitis and proposes periodontal treatment rather than extraction → Redirect by emphasising the distinguishing features: the pocket is isolated to a single surface of a single root-canal-treated tooth, adjacent teeth are completely normal, there is no generalised bone loss, and the J-shaped radiolucency tracks along the root rather than around the apex. This pattern is not consistent with localised periodontitis, which would show more generalised or bilateral distribution and would not produce a J-shaped defect. Periodontal treatment would be inappropriate and ineffective for VRF.
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ►
STAGE 1: Introduction and History Taking

"Good morning, Mr Hobbart. My name is Dr [Name] — I'll be looking after you today. Thank you for coming in. I understand you've been having some pain around one of your upper back teeth — is that right? I'd like to ask you a few questions first so I can understand what's been going on, and then I'll have a look for you. Is that okay?"

Take focused history: onset approximately 2 months ago with worsening over the last 2 weeks; dull aching pain, worse on chewing; patient has been avoiding chewing on the left side. Ask specifically about previous dental treatment — root canal treatment completed on this tooth approximately 3 years ago. Ask about any intermittent swelling or 'pimple' on the gum — patient confirms this has appeared and disappeared twice in the past month. No history of trauma. No fever, no facial swelling. Confirm medical history: well-controlled hypertension on perindopril 5 mg daily, no known drug allergies, non-smoker, social drinker.

STAGE 2: Clinical Examination and Radiographic Interpretation

"Thank you for telling me all of that — it's really helpful. I'd like to have a careful look at the tooth and the gum around it now. I'll be gentle, but please let me know if anything is uncomfortable."

Perform systematic examination of tooth 36: percussion — mild tenderness; palpation — slight swelling and erythema of buccal gingiva; mobility — none detected. Periodontal probing of all surfaces of 36 and adjacent teeth: isolated 6 mm narrow pocket on mesial aspect extending toward apex, isolated 7 mm pocket on distal aspect; adjacent teeth 35 and 37 probe at 2–3 mm throughout. Note large MOD amalgam restoration and history of RCT with no post. Request periapical radiograph. Interpret: J-shaped radiolucency tracking along mesial root surface, loss of lamina dura mesially, root filling appears adequate, no periapical radiolucency, no caries. These findings together are pathognomonic for vertical root fracture.

STAGE 3: Explaining the Diagnosis

"Mr Hobbart, thank you for your patience. I've had a thorough look at the tooth and the X-ray, and I want to explain what I've found — I'll try to keep it as clear as possible, and please stop me at any point if you have questions. The tooth had a root canal treatment a few years ago, which means the nerve was removed and the root was sealed. What I'm finding now is that the root itself has developed a crack — a vertical fracture — running along the length of the root. This is different from a crack in the top of the tooth. The deep, narrow pockets in the gum on either side of this tooth, the intermittent swelling you noticed, and the pattern on the X-ray all point to this diagnosis. I want to be honest with you: this type of fracture is unfortunately irreversible. It cannot be repaired with a filling, a crown, or further root canal treatment. The only way to resolve the infection and prevent further bone loss is to remove the tooth. I'm sorry — I know that's difficult to hear, and I wish I had better news."

Check patient understanding. Allow time for questions. Respond empathetically to any distress. Do not offer retreatment or crown as an option — this would be clinically incorrect.

STAGE 4: Management Plan and Replacement Options

"Once the tooth is removed, we have a few options for replacing it — and it's important we discuss them so you can make the decision that's right for you. The first option is a dental implant: this is a titanium fixture placed into the jawbone that acts like an artificial root, with a crown on top. It's generally considered the best long-term option because it doesn't affect the neighbouring teeth and feels very natural. In Australia, this typically costs in the range of four to five and a half thousand dollars, and the process takes several months. The second option is a fixed bridge, where we use the teeth on either side as anchors to support a false tooth in the middle. This is fixed in — you can't take it out — but it does require shaping the adjacent teeth, which are currently healthy. The cost is roughly three to four and a half thousand dollars. The third option is a removable partial denture — a plate you take in and out. It's the most affordable option, usually around one to one and a half thousand dollars, but some people find it less comfortable. Finally, you do have the option of not replacing the tooth at all, though I'd want to explain that over time the neighbouring and opposing teeth can drift or over-erupt into the space, which can cause other problems. There's no pressure to decide today — I'd like you to take some time to think about it, and I can provide you with written information to take home. Do you have any questions about any of those options?"

Note that perindopril does not contraindicate extraction or implant placement. Arrange follow-up appointment. Provide written information on replacement options. Document discussion and patient's response in clinical notes. If implant is chosen, consider referral to an oral surgeon or periodontist for placement. Confirm patient understanding before closing consultation.

PQ-42
Post-Operative Instructions for Patient on Liquid Diet
Station 41  |  Past Questions
■ Cluster 3 — Evaluation & Treatment Planning

CANDIDATE BRIEF

Mr Michael Sian, regular patient. Scenario: You have just extracted a mobile tooth 23. Haemostasis gel applied and suture placed. Medical History: Taking Eliquis to prevent stroke. Medication was NOT stopped prior to extraction (after consulting GP). Previous extraction done 3 years ago when patient was not taking Eliquis. Smokes 25 cigarettes/day. Clinical Image: No intraoral clinical photo — text-only slide on dark background. Task: Give post-extraction instructions to the patient and explain possible complications that may happen.

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

Stage 1 — Confirm Procedure and Check Understanding (0:00–1:00)

Greet the patient by name and confirm what was done: both lower wisdom teeth were surgically removed today, involving gum flaps, some bone removal, and dissolvable stitches placed on both sides. Check the patient understands and address any immediate anxiety. Note that the area is still numb and sensation will return over the next few hours. INFLECTION 1 — Candidate must acknowledge the bilateral surgical nature; failing to do so underestimates recovery expectations and leads to poor advice about return to work and diet timeline.

Stage 2 — Liquid Diet Rationale and Specifics (1:00–2:30)

Explain that the surgical sites need protection while the blood clot forms and healing begins. Recommend a liquid diet for the first 24–48 hours: cool or lukewarm soups, smoothies, protein shakes, milk, yoghurt drinks. Avoid hot, cold, spicy, or crunchy foods. Progress to soft foods (mashed potato, scrambled eggs, soft pasta) from day two or three as tolerated, returning to a normal diet around day seven if comfortable.

Stage 3 — Straw, Rinsing, and Swelling Advice (2:30–3:30)

Explicitly advise no straws — suction dislodges the clot and causes dry socket. No rinsing for the first 24 hours. From day two, gentle warm salt water rinses three times daily. Apply ice packs to the cheeks for 20 minutes on, 20 minutes off, for the first 24 hours to reduce swelling. INFLECTION 2 — Candidate must explain the mechanism of dry socket, not just state the rule; examiners award marks for clinical reasoning.

Stage 4 — Analgesia Plan (3:30–4:30)

Confirm paracetamol 1g every six hours is at home. Recommend adding ibuprofen 400mg every eight hours with food, alternating with paracetamol for better pain control. Advise taking the first dose before the local anaesthetic wears off. Confirm two days off work is appropriate.

Stage 5 — Safety-Net and Emergency Contact (4:30–5:00)

Warn about signs requiring urgent review: uncontrolled bleeding, severe worsening pain after day two or three, fever, increasing swelling, or difficulty swallowing or breathing. Provide the practice emergency number and confirm the patient has safe transport home.

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Confirms bilateral surgical extraction with flaps, bone removal, and sutures — sets accurate recovery expectations
  2. ✅ Liquid diet 24–48 hours with specific examples (cool/lukewarm soups, smoothies, protein shakes, yoghurt drinks), progressing to soft diet over 5–7 days
  3. ✅ No straws — explains suction mechanism causing clot dislodgement and dry socket risk
  4. ✅ Analgesia: paracetamol 1g 6-hourly alternating with ibuprofen 400mg 8-hourly with food; advise taking first dose before numbness wears off
  5. ✅ Safety-net: uncontrolled bleeding, worsening pain after day 2–3, fever, increasing swelling, difficulty swallowing/breathing — provide emergency contact
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • Using a straw creates negative intraoral pressure that can physically dislodge the blood clot from the socket, exposing the underlying bone — this is called dry socket, or alveolar osteitis, and it typically presents as severe, throbbing pain starting around day two to four.
  • Because both sides were done surgically — with bone removal and flaps — swelling will peak around 48 to 72 hours and then gradually improve; this is normal and expected, not a sign of infection.
  • I'd recommend taking paracetamol one gram and ibuprofen 400 milligrams in alternation — so one every three hours staggered — rather than together, as this gives more consistent pain coverage throughout the day. Take the first dose now, before the local wears off.
  • No rinsing at all for the first 24 hours — even gentle rinsing can disturb the clot. From tomorrow, rinse gently with warm salt water — about half a teaspoon of salt in a glass of warm water — three times a day, especially after meals.
  • Two days off work is appropriate given the bilateral surgical nature of what was done today, but everyone heals differently — if you're feeling well and comfortable, you can return when you feel ready.
Curveball Deflectors
  • Patient asks: 'Can I drink coffee?' or 'Can I have a hot drink?' → Acknowledge the question positively, then explain that hot drinks should be avoided for the first 24 hours because heat increases blood flow to the area and can dissolve the clot, increasing bleeding risk. Lukewarm or cool drinks are fine. From day two, warm drinks are generally acceptable as long as they are comfortable.
  • Candidate gives generic single-extraction post-op advice without accounting for the bilateral surgical nature of the procedure → This is the most common error. The examiner context specifies raised flaps, bone removal, and bilateral sutures — this is not a simple extraction. The candidate must explicitly mention that swelling will be more significant, recovery takes longer, the liquid and soft diet timeline is more important, and that bilateral numbness means the patient must be careful not to bite their cheeks or tongue while numb. Failing to address the bilateral surgical context will lose marks on multiple rubric criteria.
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ►
STAGE 1: Confirm Procedure and Acknowledge Anxiety

"Hi Michael — sorry, I should say, hi David. So, we've just finished today and I want to make sure you're comfortable and that you know exactly what to expect over the next few days. Is that okay? Before I go through everything, can I just check — do you have a rough idea of what we did today?"

Allow the patient to respond. Confirm and clarify: "That's right — we removed both of your lower wisdom teeth. Because of the way they were positioned, we had to make a small cut in the gum on each side, remove a little bit of bone, and then place some dissolving stitches to close everything up. It's a bit more involved than a straightforward extraction, so I want to make sure you're well prepared for the next few days. The area is still numb right now from the local anaesthetic — that will wear off over the next one to three hours, so it's a good idea to take some pain relief before it does."

STAGE 2: Diet Instructions — Liquids, Soft Foods, and Timeline

"For the first 24 to 48 hours, I'd like you to stick to a liquid diet. That means things like cool or lukewarm soups — not hot — smoothies, protein shakes, milk, or yoghurt drinks. The reason is that the blood clot forming in each socket right now is really important for healing, and we want to protect it from any pressure or trauma. Hot foods and drinks can dissolve the clot, and anything hard or crunchy can physically disturb it. From around day two or three, you can move on to soft foods — things like mashed potato, scrambled eggs, soft pasta, or well-cooked vegetables. By about day seven, most people are comfortable returning to a more normal diet, but just listen to your body and go at your own pace."

Address the patient's concern about returning to work: "You mentioned you've taken two days off — that's actually exactly right for what we've done today. Given that it was both sides and involved a bit of surgery, two days is appropriate. Most people feel well enough to return to an office job after that, though you might still have some swelling."

STAGE 3: Straw, Rinsing, Ice Packs, and Swelling

"One really important thing — please don't use a straw for at least the first week. When you suck through a straw, it creates a vacuum inside your mouth, and that suction can pull the blood clot right out of the socket. If that happens, the bone underneath is exposed, and that causes a very painful condition called dry socket — it usually starts around day two to four and feels like a deep, throbbing ache that doesn't respond well to normal pain relief. It's one of the most common complications after wisdom tooth removal, so avoiding straws is a simple way to prevent it. Same reason — no smoking, and no alcohol for at least 48 hours."

"For rinsing — don't rinse at all today, even gently. From tomorrow, rinse carefully with warm salt water — about half a teaspoon of salt in a glass of warm water — three times a day, especially after meals. This helps keep the area clean without disturbing the clot. For swelling, apply an ice pack wrapped in a cloth to the outside of your cheeks — 20 minutes on, 20 minutes off — for the first 24 hours. Some swelling and bruising is completely normal and will peak around 48 to 72 hours before it starts to improve."

Respond to coffee question if raised: "Lukewarm coffee is fine from tomorrow — just avoid it very hot for the first 24 hours."

STAGE 4: Analgesia Plan and Safety-Net Advice

"For pain relief — you mentioned you have paracetamol at home. Take one gram — that's two standard 500 milligram tablets — every six hours. I'd also recommend picking up some ibuprofen 400 milligrams from the pharmacy on your way home and taking that every eight hours with food, staggered in between the paracetamol. So rather than taking them both at the same time, you alternate them so you're getting pain relief roughly every three hours. This combination works much better than either one alone. Take the first dose now, before the numbness wears off — it's much easier to stay on top of pain than to catch up once it's already there."

"Now, I want to make sure you know what to watch out for. If you have bleeding that doesn't stop after biting firmly on gauze for 20 minutes, please call us. If you develop severe, worsening pain after day two or three — especially if it feels like it's getting worse rather than better — that could be dry socket and we'd want to see you. If you notice increasing swelling after day three, a fever, or any difficulty swallowing or breathing, please contact us or go to your nearest emergency department straight away. Here is our practice number — please don't hesitate to call, even after hours there is an emergency line. Do you have someone who can drive you home today, or are you okay to get home safely?"

Confirm the patient has the practice contact details. Check for any remaining questions. Summarise key points briefly and wish the patient a smooth recovery.

PQ-43
Management of Recurrent Aphthous Ulceration
Station 43  |  Past Questions
■ Cluster 1 — History & Risk Factors

CANDIDATE BRIEF

Charlotte, 20-year-old student. Chief Complaint: Ulceration for the past 3 days. She is a law student in a lot of stress because of her final exam starting in 2 months. Her sister gets similar ulcers as well. Examination Findings: Ulcer found on the inner side of her lips. Clinical Image: Intraoral photo showing an ulcer on the inner mucosal surface of the lip — consistent with aphthous ulceration. Task: Explain what special test you will do and give your differential diagnosis along with your provisional.

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

Stage 1 — Focused History (0:00–2:00 min)

Greet Charlotte warmly and acknowledge her discomfort. Explore ulcer characteristics: frequency (every 8–12 weeks), duration (7–10 days), current episode 3 days. Ask about triggers: stress, trauma, diet, new toothpaste, menstrual cycle correlation. Note family history (sister affected). INFLECTION 1 — Candidate must ask about systemic symptoms: GI disturbance (coeliac/IBD screen), genital ulcers, eye symptoms, skin rashes to exclude Behçet's syndrome. Failure to ask these questions misses a critical safety net.

Stage 2 — Intraoral Examination (2:00–3:30 min)

Describe ulcer: ~5 mm diameter, round, shallow, yellow-grey fibrinous base, erythematous halo, labial mucosa. Confirm single lesion, no other oral pathology, no lymphadenopathy. Document findings clearly.

Stage 3 — Differential Diagnosis and Provisional (3:30–5:00 min)

Provisional: Recurrent minor aphthous ulceration (RAS). Differentials include: traumatic ulcer, herpetiform ulceration, primary herpetic gingivostomatitis (less likely — no prodrome, no fever), Behçet's syndrome (excluded by absence of genital/ocular/skin involvement), coeliac-associated ulceration. INFLECTION 2 — Candidate must justify provisional over differentials using clinical features: recurrent pattern, characteristic morphology, family history, stress trigger, absence of systemic features.

Stage 4 — Special Tests and Management (5:00–7:00 min)

Blood tests: FBE, iron studies, serum B12, folate, coeliac serology (anti-tTG IgA). Management: triamcinolone acetonide paste (Kenalog in Orabase), chlorhexidine 0.2% or benzydamine mouthwash, analgesic gel (lignocaine). Lifestyle: stress management, avoid trigger foods (acidic, spicy), maintain oral hygiene. Safety net: return if ulcer persists beyond 3 weeks or systemic symptoms emerge — consider specialist referral.

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Asks about systemic symptoms — GI, genital ulcers, ocular symptoms, skin rashes — to exclude Behçet's syndrome and IBD
  2. ✅ Identifies stress and family history as relevant triggers and risk factors for RAS
  3. ✅ Accurately describes ulcer morphology: ~5 mm, round, shallow, fibrinous base, erythematous halo
  4. ✅ Requests appropriate blood tests: FBE, iron studies, B12, folate, and coeliac serology (anti-tTG IgA)
  5. ✅ Provides safety-net advice: return if ulcer persists beyond 3 weeks, increases in size, or systemic symptoms develop
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • Minor aphthous ulcers are typically less than 10 mm in diameter, heal within 7–14 days without scarring, and recur at intervals of weeks to months — Charlotte's presentation is entirely consistent with this pattern.
  • To exclude Behçet's syndrome, I specifically ask about recurrent genital ulcers, uveitis or eye redness, and skin lesions such as erythema nodosum or pseudofolliculitis — the absence of all three makes Behçet's very unlikely here.
  • I would request coeliac serology — specifically anti-tissue transglutaminase IgA with total IgA — because coeliac disease is a recognised systemic association of RAS and can be present without overt gastrointestinal symptoms.
  • Any ulcer persisting beyond three weeks in a young patient must be considered potentially malignant until proven otherwise and warrants urgent specialist referral — this is the critical safety-net threshold.
  • First-line topical treatment in Australia is triamcinolone acetonide 0.1% in Orabase paste applied to the ulcer three to four times daily after meals and at bedtime to reduce inflammation and promote healing.
Curveball Deflectors
  • Charlotte asks: 'Could this be a cold sore? My friend said it looks like one.' → Acknowledge the question respectfully: 'That's a really common question. Cold sores — caused by the herpes simplex virus — typically appear on the outer lip or skin around the mouth, and often start with a tingling or burning sensation before blisters form. Your ulcer is on the inside of the lip, it's a single shallow sore without blisters, and you've had this pattern before — that's much more consistent with an aphthous ulcer, which is not a viral infection and is not contagious. I'm confident these are different conditions.'
  • Candidate jumps straight to management without asking systemic screening questions (Behçet's, IBD, coeliac). → Pause and return to history: 'Before I discuss treatment, I want to make sure I've asked a few important questions. Sometimes recurrent mouth ulcers can be linked to conditions elsewhere in the body. Charlotte, have you ever noticed any ulcers in the genital area, any eye redness or pain, or any skin rashes? And do you have any tummy symptoms like bloating, diarrhoea, or unexplained weight loss?' These questions are non-negotiable for the rubric and distinguish a safe, thorough clinician from one who pattern-matches prematurely.
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ►
STAGE 1: Introduction and Focused History

"Hi Charlotte, I'm Dr. [Name]. I understand you've got a painful ulcer that's been bothering you for the past few days — I'm sorry to hear that, and we'll get to the bottom of it together. I'd like to ask you a few questions first, if that's okay. How long have you been getting these ulcers, and how often do they tend to come back? How long does each one usually last? Have you noticed if anything seems to bring them on — like stress, certain foods, or maybe around your period? Have you had any recent trauma to the area, or changed your toothpaste or mouthwash recently? Does anyone else in your family get similar ulcers?"

Charlotte confirms episodes every 8–12 weeks, lasting 7–10 days, current ulcer 3 days old. Stress is a recognised trigger. Sister is similarly affected — supports genetic predisposition. Document all findings. Now screen for systemic associations.

STAGE 2: Systemic Screening Questions

"I'd like to ask a few more questions that might seem unrelated, but they're really important. Have you ever noticed any ulcers or sores in your genital area? Any redness, pain, or blurred vision in your eyes? Any skin rashes or unusual spots on your body? And what about your tummy — any bloating, diarrhoea, or unexplained weight loss? I ask because sometimes mouth ulcers can be linked to conditions in other parts of the body, and I want to make sure we're not missing anything. Are you on any regular medications, and do you have any known medical conditions?"

Charlotte denies genital ulcers, ocular symptoms, skin rashes, and GI symptoms — this effectively excludes Behçet's syndrome and makes IBD or coeliac disease less clinically prominent, though blood tests are still warranted. She is otherwise well, a non-smoker, and on no medications. Proceed to examination.

STAGE 3: Examination, Differential Diagnosis and Provisional

"I'm going to have a careful look inside your mouth now. I can see a single ulcer on the inner surface of your lip — it's about 5 millimetres across, it's round and shallow, with a yellowish-white coating in the centre and a red border around it. There are no other ulcers or unusual areas in your mouth, and your glands feel normal. This is really reassuring. Based on everything you've told me and what I can see, I believe you have what we call recurrent minor aphthous ulceration — essentially recurrent mouth ulcers. This is a very common, benign condition. It's not contagious, it's not cancer, and it's not a cold sore. The stress of your upcoming exams, combined with a family tendency, is very likely contributing."

Provisional diagnosis: Recurrent minor aphthous ulceration (RAS). Differentials considered and excluded: traumatic ulcer (no history of trauma), primary herpetic stomatitis (no prodrome, no fever, no vesicles, wrong site), Behçet's syndrome (no genital, ocular, or skin involvement), coeliac-associated ulceration (no GI symptoms, but blood tests still indicated). Major aphthous and herpetiform ulceration excluded by size and morphology.

STAGE 4: Special Tests, Management and Safety Net

"I'd like to arrange a simple blood test to check your iron levels, vitamin B12, folate, and also a test for coeliac disease — a condition where gluten affects the gut. These can sometimes be linked to recurrent mouth ulcers even when you feel otherwise well, so it's worth checking. For the ulcer right now, I'd recommend a steroid paste called triamcinolone — you apply a small amount directly to the ulcer three or four times a day after meals and at bedtime. I'd also suggest a chlorhexidine or benzydamine mouthwash to help with pain and keep the area clean. A protective gel from the chemist can also help reduce irritation. In terms of lifestyle, managing your stress as best you can — even with exams coming up — and avoiding very acidic or spicy foods during a flare can make a real difference. Most importantly, these ulcers should heal within 7 to 14 days. If this ulcer is still there after three weeks, gets bigger, or you develop any of those other symptoms we discussed, please come back straight away — we'd want to investigate further and possibly refer you to a specialist. But based on everything today, I'm very reassured this is a benign, manageable condition."

Special tests: FBE, iron studies, serum B12, folate, anti-tTG IgA with total IgA (coeliac serology). Treatment: triamcinolone acetonide 0.1% in Orabase (TGA-approved), chlorhexidine 0.2% mouthwash or benzydamine hydrochloride mouthwash, protective barrier gel. Safety net threshold: ulcer persisting beyond 3 weeks warrants urgent review and possible specialist referral to exclude malignancy. Lifestyle: stress management, dietary trigger avoidance, good oral hygiene.

PQ-44
Assessment and Management of a Missing Maxillary Canine
Station 44  |  Past Questions
■ Cluster 1 — History & Risk Factors

CANDIDATE BRIEF

Julie, 10-year-old girl, attending with her mother. Chief Complaint / Presentation: Bilaterally missing canines in both jaws. Mum is worried about the child's appearance because of splayed front teeth. The front teeth are described as 'too big.' Eye teeth are missing from both jaws. Parent can feel a bulge in the lower jaw assuming teeth are erupting. There is no bulge in the upper jaw. Clinical Image: Intraoral photo of a child's dentition showing marked spacing/splaying of the front teeth, with missing canines, and prominent gingival/bony bulge in the lower jaw. Task: Gather information and explain what to do.

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

Stage 1 — Introduction & History (0–3 min)

Greet Chloe and Sarah. Confirm age (11 years 3 months). Ask: When did the upper left eye tooth come through? Any pain, swelling, or trauma? Any habits (thumb-sucking)? Medical history, medications, allergies? Family history of impacted teeth? INFLECTION 1 — Candidate must elicit that the upper left canine (23) erupted 6 months ago but the right side has not: this asymmetry is the key red flag for impaction.

Stage 2 — Clinical Examination (3–6 min)

Palpate buccal and palatal sulci of upper arch. Assess mobility of retained 53. Check arch space and crowding (~3 mm mild crowding upper arch). Assess occlusion (Class I). Note: no buccal bulge in upper jaw — suggests palatal position of 13.

Stage 3 — Investigations & Interpretation (6–9 min)

Request OPG. Interpret: 13 palatally impacted, lying horizontally, crown pointing mesially at level of apices of 12 and 14. No root resorption. No pathology. INFLECTION 2 — Candidate must correctly identify palatal impaction and absence of resorption, as this directly determines prognosis and treatment urgency.

Stage 4 — Explanation & Treatment Discussion (9–13 min)

Explain in plain language: adult eye tooth is stuck behind the palate and needs help to come through. Remove baby tooth (53). Refer to orthodontist and oral surgeon: surgical exposure, bracket bonded to tooth, orthodontic traction over 18–24 months. Risks if untreated: root resorption of neighbours, cyst, spacing. Early treatment (before 13) improves success.

Stage 5 — Concerns, Referral & Close (13–15 min)

Address cost (private health insurance with ortho cover), Chloe's anxiety about braces, and Sarah's appearance concerns. Arrange urgent orthodontic referral. Provide written information if available.

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Asymmetric canine eruption (23 erupted, 13 not) is the critical red flag — must be elicited in history
  2. ✅ Absence of buccal bulge in upper jaw indicates palatal impaction of 13 — distinguish from lower jaw where buccal bulge suggests normal eruption
  3. ✅ OPG interpretation: 13 horizontally impacted palatally, crown mesially directed at apex level of 12/14, no root resorption — all three components required for full marks
  4. ✅ Prognosis and timing: intervention before age 13 significantly improves success; treatment duration 18–24 months with exposure and orthodontic traction
  5. ✅ Risks of non-treatment must be stated: root resorption of 12 and 14, dentigerous cyst formation, persistent spacing/aesthetic concerns, and occlusal problems
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • The absence of a buccal bulge in the upper jaw, combined with a retained deciduous canine beyond the age of 11, is a strong clinical indicator of palatal impaction of the permanent canine — this requires an OPG to confirm position and assess for root resorption of the lateral incisor and first premolar.
  • On the OPG, tooth 13 is lying horizontally at the level of the apices of 12 and 14 with the crown pointing mesially — this is a high-risk position for root resorption of adjacent teeth, and the absence of resorption at this stage means we have a good window for intervention.
  • The upper left permanent canine erupted six months ago — any asymmetry of more than six months in canine eruption timing is a clinical indication to investigate for impaction on the delayed side.
  • Surgical exposure with orthodontic traction is the preferred treatment when the tooth is in a favourable position with no resorption of adjacent teeth; extraction is reserved for cases where the tooth is non-restorable, severely displaced, or where resorption of adjacent teeth has already occurred.
  • Early intervention before the age of 13 is associated with significantly better outcomes because the alveolar bone is less dense and the periodontal ligament space is more responsive to orthodontic forces.
Curveball Deflectors
  • Sarah says: 'Can't you just take the baby tooth out and wait for it to come through on its own?' → Acknowledge the question empathetically: 'That's a really reasonable thought, and in some cases removing the baby tooth is enough. However, the OPG shows that Chloe's adult eye tooth is lying on its side behind the roof of the mouth — it's pointing in the wrong direction and is too far away from where it needs to be to find its own way through. Without help, it will stay stuck, and over time it can start to damage the roots of the teeth next to it. That's why we need the specialist team involved sooner rather than later.'
  • Candidate incorrectly suggests the upper canine may be buccally impacted because the lower jaw has a buccal bulge → The lower jaw buccal bulge is consistent with normal eruption of the lower permanent canines — this is a separate finding. In the upper jaw, the absence of any buccal bulge with a retained deciduous canine is the key sign pointing to palatal impaction. The OPG confirms the palatal position of 13. Candidates must not conflate the lower jaw clinical finding with the upper jaw diagnosis.
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ►
STAGE 1: Introduction and History

"Hi Chloe, hi Sarah — lovely to meet you both. Chloe, I understand you're here today because some of your adult teeth haven't come through yet, and Mum has noticed your front teeth look a bit spread out. Is that right? I'd like to ask you both a few questions first, and then have a look in Chloe's mouth. Is that okay?"

Confirm age (11 years 3 months). Ask Sarah: "When did the eye tooth on the left side come through?" — establish that 23 erupted approximately 6 months ago but the right side has not. Ask about pain or swelling around the upper jaw. Ask about any history of falls or trauma to the face or teeth. Ask about habits — thumb-sucking (stopped age 7, not clinically relevant now). Confirm medical history: no medical conditions, no medications, no allergies. Note family history — older brother had orthodontic treatment.

STAGE 2: Clinical Examination

"Chloe, I'm going to have a gentle look and feel inside your mouth. Let me know if anything feels uncomfortable. I'm just going to press gently along your gum — I'm checking to feel where that tooth might be hiding."

Palpate the buccal sulcus in the upper right canine region — no buccal bulge palpable. Palpate the palatal mucosa — note any fullness or hard swelling palatally. Assess mobility of retained 53 — Grade I mobility noted. Evaluate arch space: mild crowding approximately 3 mm in upper arch. Assess occlusion — Class I skeletal and dental relationship. Note that the lower jaw shows a visible and palpable buccal bulge consistent with erupting lower permanent canines. Document that 23 is fully erupted and in good position.

STAGE 3: Investigation and Interpretation

"Sarah, I'd like to take a special X-ray called an OPG — it's a panoramic X-ray that shows all of Chloe's teeth and the bones of both jaws in one image. It's a very low dose of radiation and it will tell us exactly where that missing eye tooth is sitting and whether it's causing any damage to the teeth around it."

Request OPG. Interpret findings: tooth 13 is palatally impacted, lying in a horizontal orientation with the crown pointing mesially, positioned at the level of the apices of teeth 12 and 14. No root resorption of adjacent teeth is visible. No associated pathology or cyst formation. Retained 53 is present. All other permanent teeth are erupted appropriately for age. The impacted position and mesial crown angulation confirm this tooth will not erupt spontaneously.

STAGE 4: Explanation, Treatment, and Closing

"Sarah, Chloe — thank you for being so patient. I can now explain what's going on. Chloe's adult eye tooth on the upper right is stuck behind the roof of her mouth. It's lying on its side pointing in the wrong direction, which means it has no way of coming through on its own. The good news is that the X-ray shows it hasn't caused any damage to the teeth next to it yet — which means now is actually a really good time to act.

"What we'd recommend is, first, removing that baby eye tooth — it's already a little wobbly. Then we'd refer Chloe to an orthodontist and an oral surgeon who work together as a team. The surgeon would do a small procedure to uncover the stuck tooth and attach a tiny bracket to it. The orthodontist would then use braces to very gently guide it down into the right position over about 18 to 24 months. Chloe, I know braces sound a bit daunting, but lots of kids your age go through this and it makes a huge difference to your smile.

"If we leave it, there's a real risk it could start damaging the roots of the teeth next to it, or a fluid-filled sac called a cyst could form around it — both of those would make things much more complicated. Treating it now, before Chloe turns 13, gives us the best chance of a great result. In terms of cost, because you have private health insurance with orthodontic cover, a significant portion of the treatment should be covered — the orthodontist's office will be able to give you a detailed breakdown. Do you have any questions? Is there anything I can explain differently?"

Check understanding with both Chloe and Sarah. Address Chloe's concern about braces — normalise the experience. Arrange urgent referral to orthodontist with copy of OPG and clinical notes. Schedule follow-up to confirm referral has been received and acted upon.

PQ-45
Management of Acute Necrotising Ulcerative Gingivitis
Station 45  |  Past Questions
■ Cluster 2 — Balanced (History informs management)

CANDIDATE BRIEF

John Smith, 25-year-old male. Chief Complaint: 'My teeth are bleeding and they hurt. It stings and makes it hard to eat.' Problem has occurred on and off for the past year, gotten worse over the past two months. Went to GP this morning and was given penicillin but hasn't bought it yet. Examination Findings: Ulcers visible around the margins of the gum. Medical/Social History: Medically fit and healthy. Had a viral infection 10 days ago. Smokes 10 cigarettes/day. Takes alcohol once a day. Law student with upcoming exam — stated it was quite stressful. Allergy to penicillin. Clinical Image: Frontal intraoral photo showing classic NUG/ANUG presentation. Task: Explain diagnosis and management for this case.

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

Stage 1 — Introduction and Focused History (0–2 min)

Greet John, confirm identity, establish rapport. Take focused history: onset 4 days ago, worsening pain, bleeding, halitosis, difficulty eating. Ask about stress (exams), smoking (10–15 cigarettes/day recently started), diet, sleep (3–4 hours), oral hygiene lapse. Confirm no fever, no systemic illness, no HIV risk factors. INFLECTION 1 — Identify penicillin allergy before any antibiotic is discussed. This is a patient safety pivot point; failure here risks prescribing a contraindicated drug.

Stage 2 — Examination and Diagnosis (2–4 min)

Systematic oral examination: note fetor oris, punched-out interdental papillae with grey-yellow pseudomembrane (31–41 and upper left), spontaneous bleeding, generalised erythema and oedema, heavy plaque and calculus. Confirm afebrile (36.8°C), no lymphadenopathy — patient is systemically well. Diagnose ANUG confidently.

Stage 3 — Explain Diagnosis to Patient (4–6 min)

Use plain language: "You have a condition called ANUG — a bacterial gum infection made worse by stress, smoking, and reduced sleep. It is not contagious." Address patient anxiety about missing university and about seriousness of condition. Reassure that with treatment, rapid improvement is expected.

Stage 4 — Immediate Management (6–9 min)

Gentle supragingival debridement; warm saline or dilute hydrogen peroxide rinses; soft toothbrush OHI. INFLECTION 2 — Prescribe metronidazole 400 mg TDS for 3–5 days (NOT penicillin/amoxicillin — allergy documented). Advise no alcohol with metronidazole. Analgesia: ibuprofen 400 mg TDS with food or paracetamol 1 g QID. Soft nutritious diet, adequate hydration, improved sleep.

Stage 5 — Review and Long-term Plan (9–10 min)

Review in 24–48 hours. Once acute phase resolves: full periodontal assessment, scaling and root planing, smoking cessation referral to Quitline (13 7848). Emphasise that untreated ANUG can progress to necrotising ulcerative periodontitis.

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Identify penicillin allergy BEFORE prescribing — prescribe metronidazole 400 mg TDS for 3–5 days, not amoxicillin
  2. ✅ Recognise the three cardinal signs of ANUG: punched-out interdental papillae necrosis, grey-yellow pseudomembrane, and severe halitosis (fetor oris)
  3. ✅ Confirm patient is systemically well (afebrile, no lymphadenopathy) to exclude systemic involvement requiring hospital referral
  4. ✅ Reassure patient ANUG is NOT contagious and carries a good prognosis with prompt treatment
  5. ✅ Arrange 24–48 hour review and explain need for definitive periodontal treatment (scaling and root planing) once acute phase resolves
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • The classic triad of ANUG is punched-out interdental papillae necrosis, a grey-yellow pseudomembrane, and severe halitosis — all three are present here.
  • Because John has a documented penicillin allergy, the correct antibiotic is metronidazole 400 milligrams three times daily for three to five days — amoxicillin is contraindicated.
  • He is afebrile at 36.8 degrees and has no lymphadenopathy, which tells me this is localised ANUG without systemic spread — he does not require hospital admission.
  • Metronidazole has a disulfiram-like interaction with alcohol — John must avoid all alcohol for the duration of treatment and 48 hours after the last dose.
  • If this acute episode is not followed by definitive periodontal treatment, ANUG can progress to necrotising ulcerative periodontitis with irreversible bone loss.
Curveball Deflectors
  • Patient says: 'The GP already gave me penicillin — can I just take that?' → Acknowledge the GP's intention, then clearly and calmly explain: 'I can see the GP prescribed penicillin, but your records show you have a penicillin allergy, which means taking it could cause a serious reaction. I'm going to prescribe a different antibiotic called metronidazole, which is actually the first-choice treatment for this type of gum infection. Please do not fill the penicillin prescription.' Document the allergy prominently and notify the GP if appropriate.
  • Candidate attempts to prescribe amoxicillin or augmentin as the antibiotic of choice → Stop and reconsider — the brief explicitly states a penicillin allergy. Amoxicillin and Augmentin are penicillin-class antibiotics and are absolutely contraindicated. The correct first-line antibiotic for ANUG is metronidazole 400 mg TDS for 3–5 days. If metronidazole were genuinely contraindicated (e.g., pregnancy, alcohol dependence), doxycycline 100 mg daily could be considered as an alternative, but this is not the primary answer here.
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ►
STAGE 1: Introduction and History

"Hi John, my name is Dr Smith — I'm the dentist here today. Before we look at what's going on, I'd like to ask you a few questions so I can understand the full picture. Is that okay? First, I can see in your notes that you have an allergy to penicillin — can you tell me what happens when you take it?" [Confirms allergy — documents prominently.] "How long have your gums been painful and bleeding like this? Has anything made it worse recently — stress, changes in sleep, diet, or smoking? Are you feeling feverish or have you noticed any swollen glands in your neck?"

Candidate takes focused history: pain onset 4 days ago, progressively worsening; recent exam stress; smoking 10–15 cigarettes/day (recently started); poor diet, 3–4 hours sleep; oral hygiene lapse due to pain. Confirms afebrile, no lymphadenopathy, no systemic illness, no HIV risk factors. Penicillin allergy confirmed and flagged before any prescribing discussion.

STAGE 2: Examination and Diagnosis

"Thank you, John. I'm going to have a careful look inside your mouth now. I'll be as gentle as I can — please let me know if anything is uncomfortable."

Candidate performs systematic oral examination. Notes: severe halitosis (fetor oris) immediately on approach; punched-out, crater-like necrosis of interdental papillae in the lower anterior region (31–41) and upper left quadrant; grey-yellow pseudomembrane overlying ulcerated tissue; spontaneous gingival bleeding; generalised marginal erythema and oedema; heavy plaque and calculus. Confirms patient is afebrile (36.8°C) and has no cervical lymphadenopathy. Diagnosis: Acute Necrotising Ulcerative Gingivitis (ANUG). No systemic involvement — hospital referral not required.

STAGE 3: Explain Diagnosis and Reassure Patient

"John, based on everything I've found, you have a condition called Acute Necrotising Ulcerative Gingivitis — most people call it ANUG. It's a bacterial infection of the gums that's been triggered by a combination of things: the stress from your exams, the recent smoking, not getting much sleep, and not being able to brush properly because of the pain. The good news is that it's very treatable and you should start feeling significantly better within a few days of starting treatment. I also want to reassure you — this condition is not contagious, so you haven't passed it on to anyone and you can't catch it from someone else. It's not a sign of anything seriously wrong with your overall health either, because your temperature is normal and your glands are clear."

Candidate addresses patient's anxiety about missing university commitments and concerns about contagion. Uses plain, non-alarmist language. Confirms good prognosis with treatment compliance.

STAGE 4: Management Plan

"Here's what we're going to do today and over the next few days. First, I'm going to very gently clean around the gum margins to remove as much of the infected material as I can — I'll use a warm saline rinse to help soothe the area. I'd like you to rinse at home with warm salty water or a diluted hydrogen peroxide mouthwash — I'll show you how to make it — three to four times a day. Use a soft toothbrush and brush as gently as you can around the affected areas — keeping the area clean is really important even though it's uncomfortable. I'm also going to prescribe you an antibiotic called metronidazole — 400 milligrams, three times a day with food, for five days. Because of your penicillin allergy, this is the right antibiotic for you — please do not fill the penicillin prescription from the GP. One very important thing: metronidazole reacts badly with alcohol and can make you feel very unwell, so no alcohol at all while you're taking it and for 48 hours after the last tablet. For pain, take ibuprofen 400 milligrams with food three times a day — that should help more than paracetamol alone. Try to eat soft, nutritious foods, drink plenty of water, and please try to get more sleep now that your exams are finished. And I'd strongly encourage you to stop smoking — even cutting back significantly will help your gums heal much faster. I can refer you to Quitline on 13 7848 if you'd like support with that."

Candidate performs gentle supragingival debridement. Prescribes metronidazole 400 mg TDS for 5 days — NOT penicillin or amoxicillin (allergy). Counsels on alcohol interaction. Recommends ibuprofen 400 mg TDS with food as analgesia. Provides OHI with soft brush. Advises warm saline or dilute hydrogen peroxide rinses. Smoking cessation advice with Quitline referral. Advises soft diet, hydration, and sleep. Arranges review in 24–48 hours. Explains that once the acute phase resolves, a full periodontal assessment and definitive treatment including scaling and root planing will be needed to prevent recurrence and avoid progression to necrotising periodontitis with bone loss.

PQ-46
Chronic Generalised Periodontitis Assessment and Management
Station 46  |  Past Questions
■ Cluster 2 — Balanced (History informs management)

CANDIDATE BRIEF

Mrs Wilson, 45-year-old, new patient. Presentation: Attending today requesting a scale and clean — previous dentist of 20 years has recently retired. Medical history clear. Smokes 10 cigarettes/day. Family history of early tooth loss. Has brought along an OPG taken at her last dental appointment (tooth 48 extracted). Examination Findings: Full periodontal examination performed including periodontal charting. Heavy plaque and calculus deposits, with some bleeding on probing at deeper sites. Generalised probing depths of 5–6 mm. Recession of up to 2 mm on the lower anterior teeth. Clinical Image: OPG showing generalised alveolar bone loss, with extraction site at tooth 48. Task: Explain your diagnosis to Mrs Wilson and work towards gaining informed consent for your management plan.

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

Stage 1 — Welcome and Focused History (0–2 min)

Greet Mrs Wilson warmly; acknowledge the transition from her long-term dentist. Ask directly about bleeding gums, loose teeth, bad taste, and — critically — confirm smoking status and daily oral hygiene habits. INFLECTION 1 Candidate must ask about smoking proactively; failure to identify this as a Grade C modifier is a significant omission.

Stage 2 — Explain Diagnosis in Lay Terms (2–5 min)

Show the OPG and periodontal chart. Explain: "The bone that holds your teeth in place has been damaged around most of your teeth — this is called generalised periodontitis. It is more serious than a standard gum infection and cannot be fixed with a routine scale and clean alone." Quantify: generalised 5–6 mm pockets, up to 2 mm recession, generalised bone loss on OPG.

Stage 3 — Risk Factors and Prognosis (5–8 min)

Link smoking to impaired healing and masked bleeding. Discuss family history as a genetic susceptibility indicator. Be honest: without treatment and smoking cessation, tooth loss is a real risk. With compliance, disease can be stabilised. INFLECTION 2 Candidate must classify this as Stage III periodontitis and recognise smoking as a Grade C modifier — not simply "bad gum disease."

Stage 4 — Staged Treatment Plan and Consent (8–12 min)

Outline: (1) Oral hygiene instruction; (2) Full-mouth scaling and root planing under local anaesthesia across multiple appointments; (3) Reassessment at 6–8 weeks; (4) Possible surgical referral or extraction of non-salvageable teeth; (5) Lifelong 3-monthly supportive periodontal therapy. Obtain verbal consent and address cost and time concerns.

Stage 5 — Smoking Cessation and Close (12–14 min)

Strongly recommend cessation; refer to Quitline 13 7848 or GP for NRT/varenicline. Confirm Mrs Wilson understands her active role. Schedule first active treatment appointment.

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Proactively asks about smoking status and quantifies pack history — identifies it as a Grade C periodontal modifier, not merely a lifestyle factor
  2. ✅ Explains diagnosis as Stage III generalised periodontitis in lay terms using the OPG and chart as visual aids, avoiding jargon
  3. ✅ Outlines a clearly staged treatment plan: OHI → full-mouth SRP under LA → 6–8 week reassessment → surgical/extractive options → lifelong SPT
  4. ✅ Provides specific smoking cessation referral (Quitline 13 7848 or GP for varenicline/NRT) and frames cessation as the highest-impact modifiable risk factor
  5. ✅ Addresses prognosis honestly — tooth loss is possible without compliance — while maintaining therapeutic hope and responding empathetically to cost and time concerns
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • "Mrs Wilson, based on your pocket depths of 5 to 6 millimetres, the bone loss I can see on your X-ray, and the recession on your lower front teeth, this is consistent with Stage III generalised periodontitis — a significant form of gum disease that has already caused lasting damage to the bone supporting your teeth."
  • "Smoking reduces the blood flow to your gums, which means your body is less able to fight the infection and heal after treatment. It also masks bleeding, so the disease can progress silently. This makes smoking the single most important thing we can address alongside your dental treatment."
  • "After the initial scaling and root planing, we will reassess at six to eight weeks. If pockets remain greater than 5 millimetres at that point, we may need to refer you to a periodontist for surgical treatment or discuss whether any teeth are beyond saving."
  • "To keep your teeth long-term, you will need supportive periodontal therapy every three months — not the standard six-monthly check-up — because your disease risk remains elevated while you smoke and while the bone loss is present."
Curveball Deflectors
  • "Can't you just do a scale and clean today and we'll see how it goes?" → Validate the request empathetically: "I completely understand — that's what you came in for today, and I want to help you. The problem is that a standard scale and clean only removes deposits above the gumline, but the infection and calculus in your case extend several millimetres below the gum. Doing only a superficial clean would be like painting over a cracked wall — it would look better temporarily but wouldn't fix the underlying problem. What I'd like to do is start with a thorough clean today and explain exactly what the full treatment involves so we can plan it together."
  • Candidate jumps straight to treatment without explaining the diagnosis or obtaining informed consent → Pause and return to the explanation stage. The examiner expects the candidate to use the OPG and chart as communication tools, explain the diagnosis in lay terms before outlining treatment, and explicitly check patient understanding (e.g., "Does that make sense so far? Do you have any questions before I go on?"). Informed consent requires the patient to understand the diagnosis, the proposed treatment, the alternatives, and the risks of no treatment — all of which must be addressed before proceeding.
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ►
STAGE 1: Welcome and Focused History

"Mrs Wilson, welcome — it's lovely to meet you. I know it can feel a bit strange coming to a new dentist after so many years with the same person, so I want to make sure you feel comfortable today. Before we look at your X-ray and chart together, I'd like to ask you a few questions. Have you noticed any bleeding when you brush, any loose teeth, or a bad taste in your mouth? ... And can I ask — do you smoke at all? ... Thank you for telling me. Ten cigarettes a day is really important information for understanding your gum health. How often are you brushing and flossing at the moment?"

Candidate takes a focused periodontal history: symptom timeline, previous treatment, oral hygiene frequency, and smoking status. Smoking is confirmed and quantified. Family history of early tooth loss is noted as a genetic susceptibility flag. Chart and OPG are retrieved for the next stage.

STAGE 2: Explain Diagnosis Using Visual Aids

"Mrs Wilson, I'd like to show you what we found today and explain what it means. This is your X-ray — you can see the white areas here are your teeth, and the grey area below is the bone that holds them in place. In a healthy mouth, that bone comes right up close to the tooth. In your X-ray, you can see the bone has dropped down significantly around most of your teeth — that's bone that has been lost and unfortunately won't grow back on its own. When I combine that with the measurements I took today — most of your gum pockets are between 5 and 6 millimetres deep, when healthy is around 2 to 3 — and the fact that your gums have pulled back a little on your lower front teeth, this tells me you have a condition called generalised periodontitis. In plain terms, it's a serious form of gum disease that has damaged the bone and support structures around most of your teeth. It's more than a routine gum problem, and it does need more than a standard scale and clean to treat properly. Does that make sense so far?"

Candidate uses OPG and periodontal chart as visual communication tools. Explains Stage III generalised periodontitis in lay terms. Checks patient understanding before proceeding. Avoids jargon.

STAGE 3: Risk Factors, Prognosis, and Smoking Cessation

"There are a couple of things that are making this more challenging for you specifically. Smoking — even 10 cigarettes a day — reduces the blood flow to your gums, which means your immune system struggles to fight the infection, and your gums heal more slowly after treatment. It also tends to mask the bleeding that would normally warn us the disease is active, so it can progress quietly. Your family history of early tooth loss also suggests you may have a natural susceptibility to this type of disease.
