I want to be honest with you, Mrs Wilson — if we don't treat this and the smoking continues, there is a real risk of losing more teeth over time. But I also want you to know that with the right treatment and your commitment to it, we can absolutely stabilise this disease and protect the teeth you have. The single most powerful thing you can do alongside your dental treatment is to stop smoking. I'd love to refer you to Quitline — you can call them on 13 7848 — or we can arrange for your GP to discuss options like nicotine patches or prescription medication. Would you be open to that?"

Candidate identifies smoking as a Grade C modifier and family history as a susceptibility factor. Prognosis is discussed honestly but with therapeutic hope. Smoking cessation referral to Quitline (13 7848) and GP for NRT or varenicline is offered. Patient's emotional response to tooth loss concern is acknowledged empathetically.

STAGE 4: Staged Treatment Plan, Consent, and Maintenance

"So here is what I'd like to do for you, and we can work out a timeline that fits around your life. First, I'll spend time today showing you the most effective way to clean around your gum pockets at home — the technique matters a lot with this condition. Then, over the next few appointments, we'll do a thorough deep clean called scaling and root planing, where we use local anaesthetic so you're completely comfortable, and we clean all the way down to the bottom of those pockets to remove the bacteria and deposits causing the damage. After that, we'll wait about six to eight weeks and reassess — we'll measure the pockets again and see how your gums have responded. If some areas haven't improved enough, we may need to refer you to a gum specialist called a periodontist for further treatment, or in some cases discuss whether a tooth is beyond saving. Once we've got things under control, you'll need to come in every three months for a maintenance clean — not every six months like a standard check-up, because your gums need closer monitoring. I know that's a commitment of time and cost, and I want to be upfront about that. We can absolutely stage the treatment to make it manageable. The investment now is far less than dealing with tooth loss and replacements later. Do you have any questions, and are you happy for us to go ahead with this plan?"

Candidate outlines the full staged treatment plan: OHI, full-mouth SRP under LA, 6–8 week reassessment, possible periodontal surgical referral or extraction of non-salvageable teeth, and lifelong 3-monthly SPT. Addresses cost and time concerns empathetically. Obtains verbal informed consent. Confirms patient understanding and books first active treatment appointment.

PQ-47
Management of Chronic Generalised Periodontitis
Station 46  |  Past Questions
■ Cluster 2 — Balanced (History informs management)

CANDIDATE BRIEF

Mrs Wilson, 45-year-old, new patient. Presentation: Attending today requesting a scale and clean — previous dentist of 20 years has recently retired. Medical history clear. Smokes 10 cigarettes/day. Family history of early tooth loss. Has brought along an OPG taken at her last dental appointment (tooth 48 extracted). Examination Findings: Full periodontal examination performed including periodontal charting. Heavy plaque and calculus deposits, with some bleeding on probing at deeper sites. Generalised probing depths of 5–6 mm. Recession of up to 2 mm on the lower anterior teeth. Clinical Image: OPG showing generalised alveolar bone loss, with extraction site at tooth 48. Task: Explain your diagnosis to Mrs Wilson and work towards gaining informed consent for your management plan.

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

Stage 1 — Introduction and Periodontal History (0–2 min)

Greet Mrs Wilson warmly, acknowledge the transition from her long-term dentist, and take a focused periodontal history: bleeding on brushing, mobility, previous gum treatment, brushing frequency, flossing, and interdental aid use. INFLECTION 1 — Directly ask about smoking pack-years and any medical conditions including diabetes. Patient will only disclose if specifically prompted.

Stage 2 — Explain Diagnosis (2–4 min)

Explain chronic generalised periodontitis in plain language using the OPG as a visual aid. Describe pockets of 5–6 mm, bone loss, and recession as interconnected signs of the same disease process. Avoid jargon — use "infection around the roots" and "bone shrinking away."

Stage 3 — Risk Factor Discussion (4–6 min)

Link smoking and diabetes to disease severity and healing capacity. INFLECTION 2 — Explain the bidirectional relationship between periodontitis and diabetes (each worsens the other). Recommend GP liaison. Use motivational interviewing — explore readiness to quit smoking without being judgmental.

Stage 4 — Management Plan and Informed Consent (6–8 min)

Outline staged plan: oral hygiene instruction, full-mouth scaling and root planing over 2–4 appointments, 6–8 week review, possible periodontist referral. Address cost and time concerns honestly. Explain consequences of non-treatment — progressive bone loss and tooth loss consistent with family history.

Stage 5 — Close and Documentation (8–9 min)

Confirm understanding, gain verbal informed consent, arrange first active treatment appointment, and document plan to write to GP regarding diabetes-periodontal link.

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Directly elicits hidden risk factors — smoking pack-years and diabetes (HbA1c, medication) — which patient only discloses when specifically asked
  2. ✅ Explains chronic generalised periodontitis in patient-centred language using the OPG, linking pockets, bone loss, and recession to the same disease process
  3. ✅ Articulates the bidirectional relationship between periodontitis and diabetes and recommends GP liaison for systemic co-management
  4. ✅ Outlines an evidence-based, staged non-surgical periodontal therapy plan with 6–8 week reassessment and criteria for periodontist referral
  5. ✅ Addresses cost and time concerns empathetically, frames non-treatment consequences (tooth loss) in terms personally relevant to the patient (family history)
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • Probing depths of 5–6 mm with bone loss on the OPG confirm a diagnosis of chronic generalised periodontitis — this is beyond gingivitis and requires active treatment, not just a scale and clean.
  • Smoking reduces blood flow to the gums, which can mask bleeding and suppress the immune response — it is one of the strongest modifiable risk factors for periodontitis and significantly reduces the success of treatment.
  • There is a well-established bidirectional relationship between periodontitis and diabetes — poorly controlled diabetes worsens gum disease, and untreated gum disease can make blood sugar harder to control. Her GP needs to know about this.
  • After scaling and root planing, we reassess at 6–8 weeks. If pockets remain greater than 5–6 mm at that point, referral to a periodontist for surgical assessment would be appropriate.
  • The recession of up to 2 mm on the lower front teeth, combined with the generalised bone loss on the OPG, tells us this disease has been progressing for some time — early intervention now is critical to prevent further tooth loss.
Curveball Deflectors
  • Patient says: 'I just want a scale and clean — can't you just do that today and we're done?' → Acknowledge her request warmly and validate it — explain that a standard scale and clean treats the surface, but her pockets of 5–6 mm mean bacteria are sitting below the gumline where a routine clean cannot reach. Scaling and root planing is a deeper, more thorough treatment that addresses the actual source of the infection. Doing only a superficial clean would be like painting over a damp wall — it would look better temporarily but the damage underneath would continue.
  • Candidate fails to ask about diabetes or smoking and moves straight to treatment planning → This is the most common error in this station. Without identifying smoking and diabetes as active risk factors, the management plan is incomplete and the prognosis discussion is inaccurate. Always take a structured risk-factor history before explaining the diagnosis — ask directly: 'Do you smoke, and if so, how many cigarettes a day and for how long?' and 'Do you have any medical conditions such as diabetes that your doctor manages?' The examiner will be watching for these specific questions.
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ►
STAGE 1: Introduction and History

"Mrs Wilson, welcome — it's lovely to meet you. I can imagine it feels a bit strange coming to a new dentist after 20 years with the same person, so I want to make sure you feel comfortable today. Before I go through what I've found, I'd like to ask you a few questions about your gums and your general health, if that's okay? Have you noticed any bleeding when you brush or floss? Any teeth that feel loose or have shifted? Have you ever had any specific gum treatment in the past — anything beyond a regular clean? How often do you brush, and do you use floss or any interdental brushes between your teeth? I also want to ask — do you smoke at all, and if so, how many cigarettes a day and roughly how long have you been smoking? And do you have any medical conditions that your doctor looks after — things like diabetes, heart conditions, or anything you take regular medication for?"

Listen carefully and document responses. If patient discloses smoking (10/day) and diabetes (metformin, HbA1c 6.8%), note these as critical risk factors. Calculate approximate pack-years: 10 cigarettes/day = 0.5 pack/day × 25 years = 12.5 pack-years. Flag diabetes as bidirectional risk factor requiring GP liaison.

STAGE 2: Explaining the Diagnosis

"Thank you for sharing that with me — it's really helpful. I want to explain what I've found today, and I'll use this X-ray to help show you. What you have is called periodontitis — I know that's a mouthful, so let me explain it in plain terms. It's a serious infection that affects the gum and the bone that holds your teeth in place. When we measured the pockets around your teeth — those little spaces between your gum and your tooth — we found they're between 5 and 6 millimetres deep. Healthy pockets are around 1 to 3 millimetres. The deeper the pocket, the harder it is to clean, and the more bacteria can sit there causing ongoing damage. If you look at this X-ray here, you can see the bone level around your teeth — ideally it should sit up close to the neck of the tooth, but you can see it's dropped down. That's bone that has been lost because of this infection. The gum shrinkage you might have noticed on your lower front teeth is part of the same process. The important thing I want you to hear is: this is treatable. We can stop it from getting worse, and in many cases improve things significantly — but it does need proper treatment, not just a regular scale and clean."

Use OPG as visual aid, point to bone levels. Avoid terms like 'chronic' or 'generalised' without explanation. Confirm patient understanding before moving on.

STAGE 3: Risk Factors and Motivational Discussion

"I want to talk about two things that are having a significant impact on your gum health — your smoking and your diabetes — because understanding these will help us get the best result from treatment. Smoking reduces the blood supply to your gums, which means your body's ability to fight infection and heal is reduced. It's actually one of the biggest factors that makes gum disease worse and harder to treat. I'm not here to lecture you — I know quitting is genuinely difficult — but I do want you to know that even cutting down can make a real difference to how well your gums respond to treatment. There are some great support options available through Quitline on 13 7848, and your GP can also help with nicotine replacement if that's something you'd consider. With your diabetes — this is really important — there's a two-way relationship between gum disease and blood sugar. Uncontrolled gum disease can actually make it harder to manage your diabetes, and higher blood sugar makes gum disease worse. Your GP may not be aware of what's happening with your gums, and I'd like to write to them with your permission so we can work together on your overall health. It's not about getting you in trouble — it's about making sure everyone is on the same page. You also mentioned your mum lost her teeth early — that family history tells us you may have a genetic susceptibility, which makes it even more important that we act now."

Use motivational interviewing — explore readiness to change without pressure. Document smoking history and diabetes details. Obtain consent to write to GP.

STAGE 4: Management Plan, Consent, and Close

"So here's what I'd like to do for you, and I'll explain each step so you know exactly what to expect. First, I'll spend time today going through the best way to clean your teeth at home — the technique, the right brush, and how to use interdental brushes between your teeth. This is the foundation of everything else we do. Then we'll do what's called scaling and root planing — a deeper clean that goes below the gumline to remove the bacteria and buildup from the root surfaces. Because of how many teeth are involved, we'd typically do this over two to four appointments, usually working on one half of the mouth at a time. We can use local anaesthetic so you're comfortable throughout. About six to eight weeks after we finish, we'll bring you back to remeasure all those pockets and see how your gums have responded. In many cases, the pockets reduce significantly. If some areas aren't responding as well as we'd like, I may refer you to a gum specialist — a periodontist — for a further opinion. I know you mentioned cost and time off work are a concern, and I completely understand. I want to be honest with you — this treatment does involve multiple appointments, and there will be fees involved. But I also want you to understand what happens if we leave this untreated: the bone continues to be lost, the pockets get deeper, and eventually teeth become loose and are lost. Given your family history, that's a real risk. Treating this now is genuinely the most cost-effective path. Does that all make sense? Do you have any questions before we get started? I'm happy to go through anything again."

Document verbal informed consent. Schedule first OHI and SRP appointment. Write referral letter to GP outlining periodontal diagnosis, diabetes-periodontal link, and request for HbA1c update. Note smoking cessation advice given and Quitline referral made. Flag for 6–8 week periodontal reassessment in recall system.

PQ-48
Consent for Endodontic Treatment
Station 47  |  Past Questions
■ Cluster 3 — Evaluation & Treatment Planning

CANDIDATE BRIEF

Mr Jonathan, 27-year-old, regular patient. Scenario: You saw him in the last visit and gave the diagnosis of irreversible pulpitis for tooth 16. Patient is back again complaining about pain and does not want extraction. Medical History: Medically fit and healthy. Doesn't drink or smoke. Clinical Image: Periapical radiograph showing tooth 16 (upper first molar) with roots in close proximity to the maxillary sinus. Task: Explain the procedure and gain informed consent for endodontic treatment (roots close to sinus).

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

Stage 1 — Introduction & Identity Check (0–1 min)

Greet the patient, confirm full name and date of birth, and confirm the tooth: "Today we're going to talk about the root canal treatment for your upper right back molar, tooth 16 — is that right?" Establish rapport and acknowledge any anxiety.

Stage 2 — Diagnosis in Plain Language (1–3 min)

Explain irreversible pulpitis: "The nerve inside your tooth has become so inflamed that it can no longer heal itself. That's why a filling won't fix this — the problem is deep inside the tooth." INFLECTION 1 — If the candidate fails to explain why a filling is insufficient, the patient will remain confused and may refuse consent.

Stage 3 — Procedure, Benefits & Risks (3–6 min)

Describe the steps: anaesthetic, removal of nerve tissue, canal cleaning and shaping, obturation, and final crown. State benefits: pain relief, tooth retention. Outline material risks: failure (5–10%), instrument separation, perforation, fracture, need for retreatment or apicectomy. INFLECTION 2 — Candidate must specifically mention the proximity of roots to the maxillary sinus and the risk of oro-antral communication — omitting this is a critical error for this case.

Stage 4 — Alternatives & Pain Management (6–8 min)

Present extraction with replacement options (implant, bridge, denture) or no treatment and its consequences. Reassure about anaesthesia and post-operative analgesia (paracetamol/ibuprofen).

Stage 5 — Confirm Understanding & Consent (8–10 min)

Use teach-back: "Can you tell me in your own words what we've discussed today?" Invite questions, address concerns, and confirm willingness to proceed. Document consent.

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Confirms patient identity and correct tooth (16 — upper right first molar) before any discussion
  2. ✅ Explains irreversible pulpitis in plain language and specifically clarifies why a filling alone is not a viable treatment option
  3. ✅ Describes all procedural steps (anaesthesia, pulp removal, canal cleaning/shaping, obturation, permanent restoration) and realistic appointment number
  4. ✅ Discloses sinus proximity as a specific material risk for this case, alongside standard RCT risks including failure rate (5–10%), instrument separation, perforation, fracture, and need for retreatment or apicectomy
  5. ✅ Addresses pain management explicitly — effective local anaesthesia during treatment, post-operative paracetamol/ibuprofen, and reassurance that modern RCT is generally comfortable
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • "The roots of this particular tooth sit very close to your maxillary sinus — that's the air space just above your upper back teeth. There is a small risk that during treatment we could create a communication between the tooth and the sinus, which we would manage at the time, but it is something I need to make you aware of."
  • "Root canal treatment has a success rate of approximately 85 to 95 percent, meaning there is a 5 to 10 percent chance the treatment may not fully resolve the problem and further intervention such as retreatment or a small surgical procedure called an apicectomy may be needed."
  • "Because the nerve is irreversibly inflamed, it cannot recover — this is different from early inflammation where the nerve can heal. A filling would only address the outer part of the tooth and would not remove the source of your pain."
Curveball Deflectors
  • "My friend told me root canal treatment is extremely painful — I'm terrified." → Acknowledge the concern empathetically: "I completely understand — that's one of the most common worries people have, and it's a very fair question. The good news is that modern root canal treatment is performed under effective local anaesthesia, so the tooth and surrounding area will be thoroughly numb before we begin. Most patients tell us it feels no different to having a filling done. If at any point you feel discomfort during the procedure, please raise your hand and we will stop immediately. Afterwards, some mild soreness is normal for a day or two, which paracetamol or ibuprofen will manage well."
  • Patient asks: "Why can't you just do a filling or put a crown on it instead?" → Do not agree or hedge — this is a critical inflection point. Respond clearly: "That's a really important question. The issue isn't with the outer part of the tooth — it's with the nerve deep inside. The nerve has become so severely inflamed that it cannot heal on its own, no matter what we place on the surface. A filling or crown alone would not remove the source of the infection or inflammation, and your pain would continue or worsen. Root canal treatment is the only way to save this tooth by addressing the problem at its source."
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ►
STAGE 1: Introduction & Identity Confirmation

"Good morning, Mr Jonathan — lovely to see you again. Before we get started, can I just confirm your full name and date of birth for our records? Thank you. So today we're here to talk about the root canal treatment for your upper right back molar — that's tooth 16 — which we discussed at your last visit. Is that right? I know you've been in some pain, and I really want to make sure we go through everything clearly today so you feel completely comfortable before we make any decisions. Does that sound okay?"

Confirm patient identity and correct tooth. Establish rapport. Acknowledge pain and any anxiety before proceeding.

STAGE 2: Diagnosis in Plain Language

"So at your last visit, I diagnosed what we call irreversible pulpitis — let me explain what that means in plain terms. Inside every tooth there is a nerve and blood supply, which we call the pulp. In your case, that nerve has become so severely inflamed — likely from the deep decay in the tooth — that it can no longer heal itself. That's why you've been getting that intense pain with hot and cold, and why it's been waking you up at night. Now, I know you might be wondering — why can't we just do a filling? The reason is that a filling only repairs the outer part of the tooth. The problem here is deep inside, in the nerve itself. No filling or crown placed on the surface will remove that source of pain. The only way to save this tooth is to treat the nerve directly — and that's what root canal treatment does."

Explain irreversible pulpitis clearly. Proactively address the filling question — a common patient misconception and a rubric requirement.

STAGE 3: Procedure, Specific Risks & Benefits

"Let me walk you through what root canal treatment actually involves. First, we'll give you a local anaesthetic injection to completely numb the tooth and the area around it — so you won't feel pain during the procedure. Once you're numb, we make a small opening in the top of the tooth to access the nerve space inside. We then carefully remove the inflamed nerve tissue, clean and shape the canals using very fine instruments, and disinfect everything thoroughly. Once the canals are clean, we seal them with a special filling material. After that, we'll place a permanent restoration — usually a crown — to protect the tooth long-term. This typically takes two to three appointments. Now, I do need to go through some important risks with you. Looking at your X-ray, the roots of this tooth sit very close to your maxillary sinus — that's the air space just above your upper back teeth. There is a small risk that during treatment we could create a small communication between the tooth and the sinus. If that were to happen, we would manage it at the time and monitor it closely. Other risks include: the treatment not fully working — root canal treatment has a success rate of around 85 to 95 percent, so there is a 5 to 10 percent chance we may need to retreat the tooth or perform a small surgical procedure called an apicectomy. There is also a small risk of a fine instrument breaking inside the canal, a perforation of the root, or the tooth cracking over time. The benefits, though, are significant — relief of your pain, and keeping your natural tooth, which is always our preference."

Cover all procedural steps, sinus proximity risk (case-specific), standard material risks with realistic percentages, and benefits. This is the highest-density rubric section.

STAGE 4: Alternatives, Pain Management & Consent Confirmation

"I also want to make sure you know your alternatives. If you decided not to go ahead with root canal treatment, the other option would be to extract the tooth — remove it entirely. If we did that, we could discuss replacing it with a dental implant, a bridge, or a partial denture. The downside is that losing a tooth can affect your bite and the surrounding teeth over time. The third option is to do nothing for now, but I have to be honest with you — without treatment, the infection will spread, the pain will worsen, and there is a risk of a dental abscess, which can become a more serious problem. Regarding pain during the procedure — I want to reassure you. With modern local anaesthesia, root canal treatment is generally very comfortable. Most patients tell us it feels similar to having a filling. If you feel anything at all during treatment, just raise your hand and we'll stop. Afterwards, it's normal to have some mild soreness for a day or two — paracetamol or ibuprofen taken regularly will manage that well. So, I've covered quite a bit today. Can I ask — is there anything you'd like me to go over again, or any questions you have? And how are you feeling about going ahead with the treatment?"

Present all alternatives with consequences. Address pain management with specific reassurance and post-operative analgesia advice. Use teach-back and open invitation for questions. Confirm consent or willingness to proceed. Document discussion in notes.

PQ-49
Management of Apical Root Fragment Retained During Extraction
Station 48  |  Past Questions
■ Cluster 3 — Evaluation & Treatment Planning

CANDIDATE BRIEF

50+ year-old male. Came to the surgery on a Friday afternoon. Lives 2 hours driving distance from the practice. Scenario: Patient presented with pain and swelling on upper right molar side which was badly decayed. Was advised for extraction and agreed. During extraction, palatal root fractured and small apical 1/3 is left behind. Discovered that tooth had a vertical crack after extraction. On radiograph, root was in close proximity to maxillary sinus. Patient is taking blood pressure medication. Currently under control. Clinical Image: Periapical X-ray of the upper molar region showing retained root tip/fragment with a highlighted circle indicating its location close to the maxillary sinus floor. Task: Inform the patient about the broken root and explain further management.

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

Stage 1 — Stop, Stabilise and Disclose (0–2 min)

Pause the procedure. Ensure haemostasis and patient comfort. Calmly and honestly inform the patient: "I need to let you know that a small piece of the root tip has broken off and is still sitting in the bone. I want to explain exactly what that means and what we can do about it." INFLECTION 1 — Failure to disclose promptly or using evasive language here will cause patient anxiety to escalate and risks a duty-of-care failure.

Stage 2 — Explain the Clinical Situation (2–5 min)

Describe the fragment in plain terms: small (3–4 mm), located near the floor of the maxillary sinus, no visible infection, no sinus communication. Reference the X-ray. Explain the vertical crack found in the tooth as context for why the root fractured.

Stage 3 — Present Options with Risks and Benefits (5–8 min)

Option A — Surgical retrieval: risks include excessive bone removal, sinus perforation, nerve proximity, prolonged procedure. Option B — Conservative monitoring: evidence supports leaving small, asymptomatic apical fragments; they often encapsulate or resorb. INFLECTION 2 — Candidates who recommend immediate aggressive retrieval without weighing sinus proximity and fragment size will lose marks for clinical reasoning.

Stage 4 — Shared Decision-Making and Consent (8–10 min)

Recommend monitoring given fragment size, absence of infection, and sinus proximity. Invite patient questions. Gain verbal consent for the agreed plan. Document the discussion.

Stage 5 — Post-Op Instructions and Follow-Up (10–12 min)

Advise: no nose-blowing, watch for pain, swelling, discharge, or bad taste. Prescribe analgesia (e.g. ibuprofen 400 mg if no contraindication, or paracetamol given antihypertensive use). Review in 1–2 weeks; radiographic review at 3–6 months. Provide written instructions and emergency contact details given 2-hour travel distance.

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Honest, timely disclosure of the retained root fragment using plain language — this is a duty-of-care and open disclosure obligation under Australian standards
  2. ✅ Accurate clinical assessment: fragment ~3–4 mm, close to maxillary sinus floor, no infection, no sinus communication — these factors directly drive the management recommendation
  3. ✅ Evidence-based recommendation: small, asymptomatic apical fragments without infection or sinus involvement may be safely monitored — immediate retrieval is NOT always indicated
  4. ✅ Shared decision-making: patient is informed of both options with risks and benefits, her questions are answered, and verbal consent is obtained for the chosen plan
  5. ✅ Safety-netting and follow-up: written post-op instructions, signs of complications clearly explained, review appointment booked, and radiographic monitoring planned at 3–6 months — with written contact details given the 2-hour travel distance
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • Small apical root fragments of 3–4 mm that are asymptomatic, free of infection, and not communicating with the maxillary sinus may be safely left in situ and monitored — this is consistent with current evidence and accepted Australian oral surgery practice.
  • Attempting retrieval of a fragment in close proximity to the maxillary sinus floor carries a real risk of iatrogenic sinus perforation, which would convert a minor complication into a significantly more complex one requiring specialist referral.
  • The presence of a vertical root fracture in the extracted tooth explains the apical fracture and is relevant clinical context — it does not change the management of the retained fragment but should be documented.
  • Post-operative analgesia should be selected with awareness of the patient's antihypertensive medication — NSAIDs such as ibuprofen can interact with antihypertensives and elevate blood pressure; paracetamol 500–1000 mg up to four times daily is a safer first-line choice in this patient.
  • Open disclosure of a procedural complication is a professional and ethical obligation under the Australian Dental Council's professional competencies and the Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care open disclosure framework.
Curveball Deflectors
  • Patient asks: 'Are you going to dig around for it?' — implying she wants it removed immediately → Acknowledge her concern directly: 'That's a completely understandable reaction — your instinct is to want it out, and I want to explain why that might actually cause more harm than good in this situation.' Then walk through the sinus proximity risk clearly. Emphasise that leaving a small, clean fragment is a recognised and safe option, not a shortcut. Avoid being defensive. If she still strongly prefers retrieval after a full explanation, acknowledge her autonomy and discuss referral to an oral and maxillofacial surgeon rather than attempting a risky procedure yourself.
  • Candidate recommends immediate surgical retrieval without discussing conservative monitoring — common wrong answer → This is the most common error. Examiners expect candidates to recognise that evidence supports monitoring of small, asymptomatic apical fragments, especially near the maxillary sinus. Recommending immediate retrieval without weighing the risks of sinus perforation and excessive bone removal demonstrates poor clinical reasoning. The correct approach is to present both options, explain why conservative management is preferred here, and involve the patient in the decision — not to default to 'remove everything' as the safest-seeming option.
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ►
STAGE 1: Stop and Disclose

"Marion, I need to pause and be completely honest with you about something that happened during the extraction. When I removed the tooth, a very small piece of the root tip — about 3 to 4 millimetres, roughly the size of a small grain of rice — broke away and is still sitting in the bone. This is a known complication that can happen, especially with teeth that have curved roots or underlying cracks, and I did find a crack in this tooth after it came out, which explains why it happened. I want to make sure you fully understand the situation and that we decide together on the best way to manage it."

Ensure haemostasis with gauze. Sit the patient upright slightly. Show the periapical radiograph and point to the circled fragment near the sinus floor. Maintain calm, unhurried tone. This is an open disclosure moment — do not minimise or over-reassure prematurely.

STAGE 2: Explain the Clinical Picture

"Looking at your X-ray, the fragment is sitting close to the floor of the sinus — that's the air space above your upper back teeth. The good news is that there's no sign of infection around it, and the socket isn't opening into the sinus. Those are the two things I was most concerned about checking, and both look reassuring right now."

Point to the sinus floor on the radiograph. Confirm no sinus communication by checking for air passage or blood bubbling. Note absence of acute infection clinically and radiographically. Document findings in real time.

STAGE 3: Present Options and Make a Recommendation

"I want to give you two options so you can be part of this decision. The first option is to try to remove the fragment today. The problem is that because it's so close to the sinus, there's a real risk that digging around for it could actually push it into the sinus or create a hole between your mouth and the sinus — and that would be a much bigger problem requiring specialist surgery. The second option — and this is what I'd recommend — is to leave it in place and monitor it carefully. Research shows that small, clean root fragments like this, when there's no infection, very often just get walled off by the body and cause no problems at all. Given how small it is, where it's sitting, and the fact that there's no infection, I think monitoring is the safer and smarter choice for you. But I want to hear what you think."

Pause and allow patient to respond. Answer her questions directly. If she asks about going to hospital, explain that referral to an oral and maxillofacial surgeon is an option if she prefers a specialist opinion, but is not urgently required tonight given the absence of infection or sinus involvement. Document the options discussed and her response.

STAGE 4: Post-Op Instructions, Consent and Follow-Up

"I'm going to give you a written copy of these instructions to take home. For the next few days: avoid blowing your nose, as that can put pressure on the sinus area. Take paracetamol — two 500 mg tablets up to four times a day — for any discomfort. I'm recommending paracetamol rather than anti-inflammatories because of your blood pressure medication, as they can sometimes interact. I want you to call us straight away — even over the weekend, here's our after-hours number — if you notice increasing pain or swelling, a bad taste or smell, any discharge from the socket, or if you feel air or liquid moving between your mouth and nose when you swallow. I'll book you in for a check in one to two weeks, and we'll take another X-ray at around three to six months to confirm the fragment is stable. I'll also write all of this in your notes today so there's a clear record. Do you have any other questions for me before you head off?"

Provide written post-operative instructions including after-hours contact. Prescribe paracetamol 500–1000 mg QID PRN. Book 1–2 week review. Schedule 3–6 month radiographic follow-up. Document in clinical notes: fragment size and location, radiographic findings, sinus proximity, absence of infection and sinus communication, options discussed, patient's questions, agreed management plan, instructions given, and follow-up arranged. Note patient lives 2 hours away — ensure written emergency contact details are provided.

PQ-50
Incidental White Lesion — Differential Diagnosis &amp; Biopsy Decision
Module 10  |  Past Questions
■ Cluster 1 — History & Risk Factors

CANDIDATE BRIEF

Hanna, 45-year-old, new patient. Attending for the first time requesting a routine check-up and clean. Incidental Finding: On intraoral examination, you notice a white patch on the right side of the mouth (buccal mucosa / lateral tongue region adjacent to an amalgam restoration on the right side). Patient is not aware of it. History: Smokes occasionally. Currently under a lot of stress. No other significant medical history mentioned. Clinical Image: Intraoral photo showing a white lesion on the buccal mucosa/lateral border — requires differential diagnosis. Task: Gather information. Determine what special investigations are required. Explain findings and provide a differential diagnosis.

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

Stage 1 — Lesion Description & Initial Disclosure (0–2 min)

Systematically describe the white lesion: site (right buccal mucosa adjacent to amalgam), size, colour, surface texture, border definition, and confirm non-removability with gauze — this single step rules out pseudomembranous candidiasis and anchors the differential. Disclose the finding to Hanna calmly: "I've noticed a small white area on the inside of your right cheek — you may not have been aware of it. I'd like to ask you a few questions about it."

Stage 2 — Targeted History (2–6 min)

Elicit smoking quantity and duration (do not accept 'social smoker' — press for cigarettes per day and years smoked). Ask about alcohol use, oral symptoms (pain, bleeding, dysphagia), trauma or cheek-biting habit, duration of current lesion, and medications. INFLECTION 1 — Ask specifically: "Have you ever noticed anything similar in your mouth before — any white patches or ulcers that came and went?" This unlocks the prior left buccal mucosa episode, elevating the risk profile significantly via field cancerisation.

Stage 3 — Differential Diagnosis (6–9 min)

Present differentials in weighted order: (1) contact lichenoid reaction to amalgam — most anatomically plausible; (2) frictional keratosis from cheek biting; (3) leukoplakia — diagnosis of exclusion; (4) oral squamous cell carcinoma — must be named as a condition to exclude, not a likely diagnosis. Mention candidiasis as less likely given non-removability. INFLECTION 2 — Failure to name OSCC, or naming it without appropriate framing, both lose marks.

Stage 4 — Management & Communication (9–12 min)

Immediate steps: clinical photography and measurement for baseline documentation; toluidine blue staining if available. Referral to oral medicine or OMFS for biopsy within two weeks — non-negotiable given non-removable lesion, 20+ pack-year smoking history, age over 45, and prior lesion at a separate site. Discuss amalgam replacement as a supplementary diagnostic manoeuvre only. Mention importance of cervical lymph node assessment. Reassure Hanna honestly: most white patches are benign, but investigation is the right and responsible step.

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Confirm non-removability with gauze before forming any differential — this is the single most important clinical observation that separates this lesion from candidiasis
  2. ✅ Quantify smoking accurately: 5–10 cigarettes/day for 20+ years — 'social smoker' is not an acceptable endpoint; the true history materially changes the risk profile
  3. ✅ Ask specifically about previous oral white patches or ulcers to uncover the prior left buccal mucosa episode — this is the hidden inflection point and signals field cancerisation
  4. ✅ Name oral squamous cell carcinoma in the differential without catastrophising — frame it as a condition that must be excluded, not a likely diagnosis, and hold the tension between honesty and reassurance
  5. ✅ Refer to oral medicine or OMFS for biopsy within two weeks — advising 'come back in a few months' without a referral plan is a failing response for a non-removable white lesion in a smoker over 45
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • A non-removable white lesion in a patient over 45 with a 20-plus pack-year smoking history must be referred for specialist assessment and biopsy within two weeks — observation alone is not appropriate.
  • The prior white patch on the contralateral buccal mucosa two years ago raises the possibility of field cancerisation — a process where the entire oral mucosa has been exposed to carcinogens and may harbour dysplastic change at multiple sites simultaneously.
  • Non-removability with gauze is the key clinical feature that distinguishes true leukoplakia and its differentials from pseudomembranous candidiasis, which wipes off to leave an erythematous base.
  • Amalgam replacement may be considered as a diagnostic manoeuvre to assess resolution of a possible contact lichenoid reaction, but this is supplementary to specialist referral — it does not replace it.
  • Toluidine blue vital staining can be used as an adjunct to identify areas of increased nuclear activity within a white lesion, helping to guide biopsy site selection, though it is not a substitute for histopathological diagnosis.
Curveball Deflectors
  • Hanna says: 'Oh, it's probably just where I bite my cheek — I do that when I'm stressed. Do we really need to do anything about it?' → Acknowledge her explanation as entirely plausible — cheek biting and frictional trauma are genuine causes of white patches and her stress history supports this. However, explain that because the patch cannot be wiped away and has been present for an unknown duration in someone who smokes, the responsible approach is to have it properly assessed rather than assume a cause. Frame referral as a straightforward precaution, not a cause for alarm: 'Most of these patches turn out to be completely harmless, but the only way to be certain is to have a specialist take a closer look — and that gives us peace of mind either way.'
  • Candidate proposes removing the amalgam and reviewing in three months before any referral → Amalgam replacement is a reasonable supplementary manoeuvre if a contact lichenoid reaction is suspected, but it must never delay specialist referral in a patient with this risk profile. The correct framing is: 'We can certainly plan to replace that filling as part of the investigation, but given your smoking history and the fact that a similar patch appeared on the other side two years ago, I'd want you seen by a specialist within the next two weeks rather than waiting to see if the patch resolves on its own. These two things can happen in parallel.' Proposing amalgam removal as the primary management and deferring referral is a failing response.
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ►
STAGE 1: Lesion Description & Disclosure

"Hanna, thank you for coming in today. While I was having a look around your mouth as part of your check-up, I've noticed something I'd like to tell you about — a small white area on the inside of your right cheek, just near one of your back teeth. You may not have been aware of it at all, and that's completely fine — these things are often picked up incidentally. I'd like to ask you a few questions about it, if that's okay?"

Clinically: the lesion is located on the right buccal mucosa adjacent to the amalgam restoration. It appears as a homogeneous white patch, approximately [estimated size] in diameter, with a slightly raised or flat surface, well-defined borders, and — critically — it does not wipe off when tested with gauze. This non-removability rules out pseudomembranous candidiasis and confirms the lesion warrants further investigation. Document with clinical photography and measure for baseline records immediately.

STAGE 2: Targeted History

"I'd like to ask you a few questions to help me understand this better. Firstly, have you noticed any soreness, bleeding, or difficulty eating or swallowing? ... And do you sometimes bite the inside of your cheek — particularly when you're stressed? ... You mentioned you smoke occasionally — can I ask roughly how many cigarettes a day, and how long you've been smoking? ... And do you drink alcohol at all — even just socially? ... Now, this is an important one: have you ever noticed anything similar in your mouth before — any white patches, ulcers, or areas that looked a bit different and then went away?"

Key findings to elicit: no pain, bleeding, or dysphagia; cheek-biting habit under stress acknowledged; smoking accurately quantified at 5–10 cigarettes per day for over 20 years — do not accept 'social smoker' without pressing for specifics; alcohol approximately 6–8 standard drinks per week. Most critically: direct questioning about previous oral changes reveals a prior white patch on the LEFT buccal mucosa approximately two years ago that resolved spontaneously. This is a significant red flag for field cancerisation and escalates the urgency of specialist referral. No medications, no allergies, no family history of oral cancer.

STAGE 3: Differential Diagnosis

"Let me explain what this patch could be — there are a few possibilities and I want to be straightforward with you. The most likely explanation, given how close it is to that silver filling, is that the lining of your cheek may be reacting to the metal — we call that a lichenoid reaction, and it's quite common. It's also possible it's from the cheek-biting you mentioned, which can cause the skin inside the mouth to thicken and turn white. There's also a condition called leukoplakia — a white patch that doesn't have an obvious cause — which is something we need to rule out. And because I want to be honest with you without alarming you: there is a small possibility that a white patch like this could be an early sign of something more serious, which is exactly why I don't want to just leave it and hope it goes away. Most white patches in the mouth are completely benign — but the only way to know for certain is to have it properly assessed."

Differential diagnosis in weighted order: (1) Contact lichenoid reaction to adjacent amalgam — most anatomically plausible given proximity; (2) Frictional keratosis from cheek biting under stress; (3) Leukoplakia — diagnosis of exclusion once other causes ruled out; (4) Oral squamous cell carcinoma — must be named and must not be omitted, framed as a condition to exclude rather than a likely diagnosis. Candidiasis less likely given non-removability but may be mentioned briefly.

STAGE 4: Management Plan & Reassurance

"Here's what I'd like to do. Today, I'm going to take some photographs and measure the patch carefully so we have a clear record of exactly what it looks like right now. I'm also going to refer you to a specialist — either an oral medicine specialist or an oral and maxillofacial surgeon — and I'd like that appointment to happen within the next two weeks. They'll be able to examine it in detail and, if needed, take a very small tissue sample to look at under a microscope — that's the only way to get a definitive answer. I'd also like to discuss replacing that silver filling at some point, because if the patch is a reaction to the metal, removing the filling may help it resolve — but I want the specialist to see it first before we change anything. I'll also check the lymph nodes in your neck as part of a thorough examination. I know this might feel a bit worrying, Hanna, but I want to reassure you — the vast majority of white patches like this are completely harmless. We're doing this because we want to be thorough and look after you properly, not because I think something is seriously wrong."

Management summary: (1) Clinical photography and measurement — immediate baseline documentation; (2) Toluidine blue staining if available as an adjunct; (3) Urgent referral to oral medicine or OMFS for biopsy within two weeks — non-negotiable given non-removable lesion, 20+ year smoking history, age 45, and prior lesion at a separate site suggesting field cancerisation; (4) Amalgam replacement discussed as supplementary diagnostic manoeuvre, not a substitute for referral; (5) Cervical lymph node assessment noted as important component of full examination; (6) Smoking cessation advice offered sensitively. Advising observation alone without referral is a failing response.

PQ-51
Perio Patient — Replacement Options for Missing Teeth (OPG, Bone Loss)
Module 10  |  Past Questions
■ Cluster 1 — History & Risk Factors

CANDIDATE BRIEF

45-year-old male, new patient. Has been seeing another dentist. Presenting for a second opinion regarding missing teeth and replacement options. Examination Findings: OPG provided showing generalised bone loss and multiple missing posterior teeth. Patient is known to have significant bone loss. Has not been formally diagnosed at this visit. Task: Gather information. Advise on investigations required. Give appropriate replacement options for missing teeth. No need to provide a formal diagnosis. Focus on patient communication, exploring options (implants, bridges, partial dentures), and realistic expectations given bone loss.

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

Stage 1 — Focused History (0–3 min)

Introduce yourself and acknowledge David's reason for attending. Take a structured history: previous dental attendance and any periodontal treatment, recall compliance, oral hygiene habits. INFLECTION 1 Ask directly about flossing — when David reveals he stopped because his gums bled, correct this misconception clearly: bleeding is a sign of inflammation, not a reason to stop. Ask about smoking (pack history), alcohol, and medical history including diabetes screening.

Stage 2 — OPG Explanation (3–5 min)

Explain the OPG in plain language. Use accessible phrasing: "The bone that holds your teeth in place has reduced by roughly half in most areas — this is the result of longstanding gum disease." Note multiple missing posterior teeth and widened ligament spaces. Avoid jargon. INFLECTION 2 Be honest about severity without catastrophising — this is significant but not end-stage.

Stage 3 — Replacement Options (5–8 min)

Address all three modalities. Implants: best long-term outcome but not immediately available — periodontal disease must be controlled first, smoking doubles failure risk, bone grafting may be needed. Fixed bridge: possible in principle but unsuitable here as adjacent teeth are periodontally compromised. Removable partial denture: immediately available, no surgery, but least preferred for comfort and stability.

Stage 4 — Treatment Sequence and Closing (8–10 min)

Lay out the sequence clearly: treat gum disease first, re-evaluate bone and tooth stability, then plan replacements. Strongly advise smoking cessation. Reassure David that options remain — this is not hopeless — but commitment from both sides is required.

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Identify and correct the flossing misconception — bleeding gums indicate inflammation, not a reason to stop interdental cleaning
  2. ✅ Elicit full social history including smoking (10 cigarettes/day × 20 years), alcohol, and ask specifically about diabetes
  3. ✅ Explain OPG findings in plain language — approximately 40–50% generalised horizontal bone loss as a consequence of longstanding periodontal disease
  4. ✅ Discuss all three replacement modalities (implants, fixed bridge, removable partial denture) with honest pros, cons, and patient-specific caveats
  5. ✅ State clearly that active periodontal disease must be stabilised before any replacement option is pursued, and that smoking approximately doubles implant failure risk — smoking cessation is strongly recommended
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • The bone that anchors your teeth has reduced by roughly half in most areas — that is a consequence of longstanding gum disease, and it explains why several teeth have already been lost.
  • Smokers have approximately double the implant failure rate compared to non-smokers — that is not a reason to rule implants out, but it is a reason to take smoking cessation seriously before we go down that path.
  • Bleeding when you floss is not a sign that flossing is causing damage — it is a sign that the gum tissue is inflamed and infected. Stopping flossing actually allows the disease to get worse, not better.
  • Before we can place any implant or bridge, we need to get the gum disease under control first. Placing an implant into an environment with active periodontal disease significantly increases the risk of peri-implantitis and implant failure.
  • In areas where significant bone has already been lost, we may need a bone graft to build up enough volume to support an implant — that is an additional procedure but it is a well-established pathway.
Curveball Deflectors
  • Patient interrupts: 'So can I get implants or not? Just give it to me straight.' → Respond directly without hedging: 'Yes, implants are on the table for you — but not yet, and not without some important steps first. We need to treat the gum disease, get that stable, and I would strongly recommend you stop smoking before we proceed. Once those boxes are ticked, we reassess the bone volume and plan the implant sites. It is a realistic goal, but the sequence matters.' Avoid vague reassurance — David will lose trust if you deflect.
  • Candidate omits the fixed bridge option or dismisses it without explanation. → All three modalities must be discussed. For fixed bridges, acknowledge they are an option in principle, then explain why they are less suitable here: 'A bridge uses the teeth on either side of the gap as anchors. The problem in your case is that those neighbouring teeth already have significant bone loss themselves, which means they may not be strong enough to carry the load of a bridge long-term. It is an option we would need to assess tooth by tooth, but it is not our first choice given the generalised nature of what I am seeing on this X-ray.'
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ►
STAGE 1: Focused History

"David, thanks for coming in. I understand you are here for a second opinion about your missing teeth and what we can do about them — and I want to give you straight answers today. Before I look at the X-ray with you, I need to ask you a few questions so I have the full picture. Is that okay?"

Proceed with focused history. Ask about previous dental attendance: how long with the previous dentist, whether any specific gum treatment was ever done, and whether he kept up with recall appointments. When David admits he did not comply with recall, acknowledge this without judgment and note it as a risk factor. Ask about oral hygiene: "Do you floss or use anything between your teeth?" When David explains he stopped flossing because his gums bled, respond directly: "I am glad you told me that, because this is actually a really common misunderstanding and it is important to correct it. Bleeding when you clean between your teeth is not a sign that the flossing is causing damage — it is a sign that the gum tissue is inflamed and infected. When you stop cleaning there, the bacteria build up and the disease gets worse, not better. We will need to get you back into a routine with interdental cleaning as part of the treatment." Ask about smoking: "Do you smoke?" Note ten cigarettes per day for twenty years. Ask about alcohol — four to five standard drinks on weekends is moderate and noted. Ask about medical history, specifically: "Have you ever been tested for diabetes or told your blood sugar is high?" — David has not been tested; note this and explain that uncontrolled diabetes is a significant risk factor for gum disease and implant healing, and recommend a GP review.

STAGE 2: OPG Explanation

"Alright, let me show you this X-ray and explain what I am seeing in plain terms. This is a panoramic X-ray — it gives us a full view of all your teeth, the bone around them, and the jaw. What I want you to notice is the level of bone here — you can see it has dropped significantly around most of your teeth. In a healthy mouth, the bone comes right up close to the neck of the tooth. In your case, the bone has reduced by roughly half of the root length in most areas. That bone is what anchors your teeth in place, so when it reduces, the teeth become less stable. This is the result of longstanding gum disease — it has been progressing quietly over many years, often without much pain, which is why it can go undetected. I can also see that you have several missing teeth in the back of both jaws, and the remaining teeth show some signs of stress on the ligament that connects them to the bone. There is no acute infection or abscess showing up, which is reassuring — but the overall picture tells me this has been going on for a long time and needs to be addressed properly."

Point to relevant areas on the OPG as you speak. Avoid terms like 'horizontal bone loss' or 'PDL widening' without explanation. Gauge David's response — if he asks how bad it is, be honest: significant but not end-stage, and options remain.

STAGE 3: Replacement Options

"Now, to your main question — what can we do about the missing teeth. There are three main options and I want to walk you through all of them honestly. The first is dental implants. These are titanium posts that go into the jawbone and act like artificial tooth roots — you then get a crown on top. They are the gold standard for replacing missing teeth because they are fixed, they feel natural, and they do not rely on the neighbouring teeth. For you, implants are a realistic goal — but not right now, and there are some important conditions. First, we need to get the gum disease under control before placing any implant. Putting an implant into a mouth with active gum disease significantly increases the risk of the implant failing. Second, in areas where the bone has reduced significantly, we may need a bone graft to build up enough volume to support the implant — that is an additional procedure but it is well-established and routinely done. Third — and I want to be direct with you here — smoking approximately doubles the failure rate of dental implants. That is not a reason to rule them out, but it is a strong reason to seriously consider stopping smoking before we go ahead. The second option is a fixed bridge. This involves crowning the teeth on either side of the gap and suspending a false tooth in between — it is fixed in, you cannot take it out. The issue in your case is that the neighbouring teeth already have significant bone loss themselves, which means they may not be strong enough to serve as reliable anchors. It is something we would assess tooth by tooth, but given the generalised nature of what I am seeing, it is not our first preference. The third option is a removable partial denture — a plate that clips in and out. It is the most immediately available option, requires no surgery, and is the most affordable. The downside is that most patients find it the least comfortable and least stable long-term. It is a valid option, particularly as a short-term measure while we work on the gum disease."

Present all three options without overselling any. Be honest about the RPD being the least preferred. Do not promise implants without the caveats — this is where marks are won or lost.

STAGE 4: Treatment Sequence and Close

"So here is the sequence I would recommend. Step one: we do a thorough assessment of your gum disease — probing depths, full charting — and then we start active treatment, which involves a deep clean to remove the bacteria and deposits from below the gumline. That usually takes a few appointments. Step two: we review how the gums have responded, reassess the bone, and see which teeth are stable and which may be at risk long-term. Step three: once the gum disease is stable, we plan the replacements — and at that point, implants become a much more viable and predictable option. I also want to strongly encourage you to speak to your GP about a diabetes check, and to seriously consider cutting down or stopping smoking before we get to the implant stage. I know that is not easy, but it genuinely makes a significant difference to the outcome. I want to be clear about something, David — this is not a hopeless situation. You have not run out of options. But the sequence matters, and it requires commitment on both sides. If we do this properly, there is every reason to expect a good outcome."

Close with a clear, confident summary. If David raises concern about his father losing all his teeth, acknowledge it directly: 'I understand that fear — and the fact that you are here seeking a second opinion tells me you want to do something about it. That is the right instinct. The difference between your father's situation and yours is that we now have the tools to stop this disease in its tracks, if we act on it.' Arrange next appointment for full periodontal charting and treatment planning.

PQ-52
Vague Pain on the Left Side — Interproximal Caries &amp; Open Contact (26/27)
Module 10  |  Past Questions
■ Cluster 2 — Balanced (History informs management)

CANDIDATE BRIEF

Female, new patient attending for routine check-up and clean. Chief Complaint: Food lodgement between teeth 26 and 27. Vague pain/aching sensation on the upper left side, mentioned at last appointment with previous dentist. Examination Findings: Radiograph provided showing: radiolucency involving the contact point between 26 and 27 (interproximal caries), affecting the marginal bone; Gap/open contact between 26 and 27; Temperature testing: 35°C response noted; Generalised amalgam restorations present. Task: Carry out history taking and examination. Determine investigations. Establish a working diagnosis and explain findings to the patient.

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

Stage 1 — History Taking (0–4 min)

Welcome Maria, confirm chief complaint of food packing and vague upper left aching. Elicit onset (8–18 months), character (dull/aching, not spontaneous), triggers (cold, sweet), and whether pain lingers after stimulus removal. Ask about previous dental visit and what was done. INFLECTION 1 — Ask specifically: "Do you grind or clench your teeth, or wake up with a sore jaw?" Maria discloses nocturnal bruxism only if directly asked.

Stage 2 — Radiograph Interpretation (4–7 min)

Read bitewing systematically: image quality adequate, correct horizontal angulation, patient ID confirmed. Identify radiolucency at distal 26 extending into dentine, open contact 26/27, subtle crestal bone loss at interproximal crest, intact-appearing amalgam restorations on both teeth.

Stage 3 — Clinical Correlation & Pulpal Assessment (7–10 min)

Correlate open contact → food trap → accelerated caries progression and localised bone loss. INFLECTION 2 — Interpret prolonged thermal response at 35°C: lingering response >3 seconds after stimulus removal indicates pulpal inflammation consistent with reversible pulpitis; distinguish from irreversible pulpitis (spontaneous, severe, non-resolving pain). Acknowledge monitoring is required and RCT cannot be excluded.

Stage 4 — Explaining Findings & Handling the Curveball (10–13 min)

Explain findings in plain language. When Maria asks why the previous dentist missed this, validate her concern: interproximal caries beneath a contact point is invisible clinically and requires a bitewing radiograph to detect — without criticising the colleague.

Stage 5 — Management Plan (13–15 min)

Restore distal 26 with contact point re-establishment; periodontal assessment of 26/27; pulp monitoring with review; occlusal splint for bruxism; contingency RCT if symptoms progress; six-month recall bitewing.

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Elicits full pain history including onset, character, triggers, and whether thermal response lingers beyond stimulus removal
  2. ✅ Directly asks about grinding/clenching and integrates bruxism disclosure into material selection and occlusal splint recommendation
  3. ✅ Reads bitewing radiograph systematically — image quality, angulation, then findings — before formulating diagnosis
  4. ✅ Distinguishes reversible from irreversible pulpitis using the duration of thermal response, acknowledging monitoring and RCT as contingency
  5. ✅ Responds to 'Why didn't the other dentist find this?' with empathy and clinical accuracy, validating Maria's concern without disparaging the colleague
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • A prolonged response lasting more than three seconds after the stimulus is removed at 35°C is consistent with pulpal inflammation — this points toward reversible pulpitis, but we need to monitor closely because irreversible pulpitis cannot be ruled out at this stage.
  • Interproximal caries hidden beneath a contact point is not visible on direct clinical examination — a bitewing radiograph is specifically indicated to detect this type of lesion, which is why it can be missed without one.
  • The open contact between 26 and 27 creates a food trap that accelerates caries progression and can contribute to localised bone loss at the interproximal crest, which is exactly what we're seeing on this radiograph.
  • Given that you grind your teeth at night, we need to factor that into our restoration choice and I'd recommend an occlusal splint to protect both the new restoration and your remaining tooth structure.
Curveball Deflectors
  • Maria asks: 'Why didn't the other dentist find this? They told me everything was fine.' → Acknowledge her frustration directly and validate it: 'I completely understand why that's frustrating, and I'm glad you raised it. The type of decay we're seeing here sits between the teeth, hidden beneath the contact point — it's genuinely invisible on clinical examination alone. A bitewing X-ray, like the one we've taken today, is specifically designed to detect this kind of lesion. Without that X-ray, it can be very easy to miss. The important thing now is that we've found it and we can treat it.' Do not suggest the previous dentist was negligent or below standard.
  • Candidate conflates reversible and irreversible pulpitis, or recommends root canal treatment immediately based on the thermal response alone. → Correct approach: a prolonged but eventually resolving response at 35°C is consistent with reversible pulpitis, not irreversible pulpitis. Irreversible pulpitis is characterised by spontaneous pain, severe lingering pain, or pain that does not resolve. Maria's pain is vague and aching rather than spontaneous or severe. The correct management is to restore the tooth, monitor pulp vitality at a review appointment, and advise Maria that RCT may be needed if symptoms worsen or fail to resolve — not to recommend RCT immediately.
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ►
STAGE 1: History Taking

"Hi Maria, welcome — it's lovely to meet you. I understand you're here for a check-up and clean today, and that you've also been having some discomfort on your upper left side. I'd love to hear more about that in your own words — can you tell me what you've been noticing?"

Listen actively. Elicit: onset (~8–18 months), character (dull, aching — not sharp or spontaneous), triggers (cold drinks, sweet foods), and critically whether the ache lingers after the trigger is gone. Ask: "When you have that cold sensitivity, does it go away quickly once the cold is removed, or does it hang around for a while?" Also confirm the food packing complaint between the upper left back teeth. Then ask directly: "Do you ever grind or clench your teeth — or does your partner mention it? Do you wake up with a sore jaw or headaches in the morning?" If Maria discloses bruxism, note this for management planning.

STAGE 2: Radiograph Interpretation

"Maria, I've had a look at the X-ray we took today — it's called a bitewing X-ray, and it's specifically designed to show us what's happening between the back teeth, which is an area we simply can't see just by looking in your mouth. I'd like to walk you through what I can see."

Read systematically: confirm image quality is adequate, horizontal angulation is correct with no overlapping of contacts at 25/26, patient ID confirmed. Then describe findings: "There's a darker area — a radiolucency — at the back surface of your upper left first molar, tooth 26. It's sitting right at the contact point with the tooth behind it, tooth 27, and it's extended through the outer enamel layer into the softer dentine underneath. I can also see that the contact point between these two teeth is open — there's a small gap — which explains why food keeps getting stuck there. And at the very top of the bone between these two teeth, there's a subtle loss of bone height, which tells us the area has been under stress for some time. The silver fillings on both teeth look intact on the X-ray, which is actually why this decay wasn't visible just by looking — it's completely hidden beneath the contact area."

STAGE 3: Pulpal Status & Diagnosis

"The cold test we did today showed that your tooth is sensitive to temperature, and importantly, that sensitivity lingered for a little while after we removed the cold stimulus. That tells me the nerve inside the tooth is irritated — it's reacting more than it should. At this stage, the pattern of your pain — dull and aching rather than sharp or spontaneous — is more consistent with what we call reversible pulpitis, which means the nerve is inflamed but may still be able to recover once we remove the source of the problem. However, I want to be honest with you: we do need to monitor this carefully, because if the nerve has been under pressure for a long time, there's a possibility it may not fully recover, and in that case we'd need to consider root canal treatment down the track. I'll be upfront about that rather than leave you guessing."

Document: prolonged thermal response at 35°C, consistent with reversible pulpitis. Distinguish clearly from irreversible pulpitis. Note that spontaneous pain, severe lingering pain, or failure to resolve post-treatment would indicate irreversible pulpitis requiring RCT. Schedule pulp vitality review.

STAGE 4: Handling the Curveball & Management Plan

"I can completely understand why that's frustrating, Maria, and I'm really glad you brought it up. The decay we've found today sits between the teeth, tucked right under the contact point — and the honest truth is that this type of decay is genuinely invisible on a clinical examination alone. You can't see it by looking, and you can't feel it with a probe. A bitewing X-ray, like the one we've taken today, is specifically designed to find exactly this kind of lesion. Without that X-ray, it can be very easy to miss. What matters now is that we've found it, and we can do something about it. So here's what I'd like to do: firstly, we'll place a filling on the back surface of tooth 26 — I'll make sure we restore the contact point properly so that food trap is eliminated. Given that you grind your teeth at night, I'd also like to discuss making you a custom night splint to protect your teeth and any new restorations. We'll also do a thorough check of the gum and bone around those two teeth. I'll see you back in four to six weeks to check how the tooth is responding, and we'll take another X-ray in six months to make sure everything is tracking well. If at any point the pain becomes spontaneous or more severe before then, I want you to call us straight away."

Management summary: restore distal 26 with appropriate material (consider ceramic or composite given bruxism — discuss with patient); re-establish contact point to eliminate food trap; periodontal assessment of 26/27 region; occlusal splint for bruxism; pulp vitality review at 4–6 weeks; contingency RCT if irreversible pulpitis confirmed; six-month recall bitewing radiograph. Do not criticise previous dentist.

PQ-53
MIH vs Amelogenesis Imperfecta — 8-Year-Old, Sensitivity &amp; Appearance
Module 10  |  Past Questions
■ Cluster 2 — Balanced (History informs management)

CANDIDATE BRIEF

8-year-old child, attending with mother. Chief Complaint: Mother reports sensitivity in tooth 26 (upper left first permanent molar). Also concerned about the appearance of the child's front teeth. Examination Findings / Clinical Images: Image 1: Tooth 26 with yellowish/brown enamel hypomineralisation — MIH presentation on the first permanent molar. Image 2: Anterior teeth showing white/chalky opacities across multiple teeth — suggestive of Amelogenesis Imperfecta affecting enamel formation globally. Dual Diagnosis: MIH (localised — molars and incisors from hypomineralisation during development) vs. Amelogenesis Imperfecta (generalised enamel defect — genetic). Task: Explain differential diagnosis to the mother. Address both concerns: sensitivity in tooth 26 and the appearance of the front teeth. Discuss management options for each.

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

Stage 1 — Establish rapport and acknowledge both patient and parent (0–1 min)

Greet Jenny and Sophie by name. Crouch to Sophie's level: "Hi Sophie, I'm going to have a chat with your mum today, but I want to make sure I talk to you too — these are your teeth after all." Confirm the chief complaints: sensitivity in the back tooth and concern about the front teeth's appearance.

Stage 2 — Targeted history-taking (1–3 min)

Ask systematically: early childhood illnesses and antibiotic use in the first three years of life (MIH aetiology); pregnancy medications and illnesses (AI aetiology); family history of similar enamel appearance in parents or siblings (AI hereditary basis); fluoride exposure history (to exclude fluorosis). INFLECTION 1 — Eliciting Sophie's recurrent ear infections and amoxicillin courses is the pivot that contextualises the MIH diagnosis and directly addresses Jenny's guilt.

Stage 3 — Explain the dual diagnosis in parent-appropriate language (3–5 min)

Name both conditions clearly. Distinguish MIH (localised, acquired, linked to early childhood illness) from Amelogenesis Imperfecta (generalised, present in the genes from birth, may run in families). Exclude fluorosis explicitly: "Fluoride-related changes usually look like faint white lines across the teeth — what we see on Sophie's front teeth is a different pattern, rougher and covering the whole tooth surface." INFLECTION 2 — Addressing Jenny's guilt question with empathy and clinical accuracy is the emotional and mark-earning pivot of the station.

Stage 4 — Condition-specific management plans (5–7 min)

Tooth 26: fluoride varnish today, protective restoration (GIC or composite), three-monthly review. Anterior teeth: defer cosmetic treatment until age 16–18 when growth is complete; interim fluoride varnish, avoid abrasive toothpastes, reassure Sophie that her teeth are stable with good care. Address Sophie directly: "Sophie, we're going to look after your teeth really carefully so they stay strong."

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Elicit recurrent early childhood illness and antibiotic use (birth to age 3) to contextualise MIH aetiology — the ear infection and amoxicillin history is the key hidden detail
  2. ✅ Ask about family history of similar enamel appearance to explore the hereditary basis of Amelogenesis Imperfecta
  3. ✅ Clearly distinguish MIH (localised, acquired, developmental) from AI (generalised, genetic/hereditary) using accessible language — never conflate the two into a single diagnosis
  4. ✅ Address Jenny's guilt directly and empathetically before providing clinical explanation — validate the emotion, then reassure with accuracy
  5. ✅ Defer anterior cosmetic treatment until age 16–18 due to ongoing facial growth and gingival instability — recommending immediate veneers at age 8 is a mark-losing error
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • Tooth 26 shows Molar Incisor Hypomineralisation — the enamel didn't mineralise properly during a specific window between birth and about age three, which is exactly when Sophie was having those ear infections and courses of antibiotics.
  • The front teeth show a different pattern — generalised, rough, full-crown opacities affecting all the permanent incisors with no sharp borders. That distribution, combined with the fact that Sophie's baby teeth looked normal, is characteristic of Amelogenesis Imperfecta, which is a hereditary condition affecting how the enamel-forming genes work.
  • Fluorosis typically produces diffuse, symmetrical white lines or faint mottling — what we see here is rougher, covers the whole tooth surface, and doesn't follow that pattern, so fluorosis is much less likely.
  • For the front teeth, the right time for cosmetic treatment — composite veneers or similar — is around age sixteen to eighteen, once Sophie's face has finished growing and the gum margins have settled. Doing it earlier risks the restorations not fitting properly as she grows.
  • MIH-affected molars have a higher risk of decay because the enamel is structurally weaker, so I'd like to see Sophie every three months rather than the usual six to keep a close eye on tooth 26.
Curveball Deflectors
  • Jenny asks: 'Is this because of something I did during pregnancy — I took antibiotics for a UTI in my second trimester?' → Acknowledge the question warmly before answering: 'Thank you for telling me that — I can hear how much you've been worrying about this, and I want to reassure you straight away that neither of these conditions is caused by anything you did wrong.' Then explain: for MIH, the relevant window is early childhood rather than pregnancy, and Sophie's ear infections are a more likely contributing factor. For AI, it is a hereditary condition — a difference in the genes that guide enamel formation — that is present from conception regardless of what happens during pregnancy. The antibiotic exposure during pregnancy is worth noting in the records but should not be over-attributed as a cause; acknowledge the history honestly without creating false guilt.
  • Candidate conflates both conditions into a single diagnosis of 'enamel hypoplasia' or treats them as the same problem with one management plan → This is the most common mark-losing error. The two conditions have different distributions, different aetiologies, different inheritance patterns, and require different management approaches. A strong candidate explicitly names both conditions separately, explains why the clinical pictures are different, and formulates distinct management plans — one for the symptomatic molar and one for the anterior teeth. Merging them into a single label demonstrates a failure of clinical reasoning that examiners will note.
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ►
STAGE 1: Greeting and rapport — patient and parent

"Hi there — you must be Jenny, and this must be Sophie. I'm Dr [Name]. It's lovely to meet you both." [Crouches to Sophie's level] "Hi Sophie — I love your shoes. I'm going to have a big chat with your mum today, but these are your teeth, so I want to make sure I talk to you too, okay? You just let me know if anything I say doesn't make sense." [To Jenny] "Jenny, I understand you've got two things on your mind today — Sophie's been having some sensitivity in one of her back teeth, and you're also worried about how her front teeth look. Is that right? Let's go through both of those carefully."

Establish that Sophie is the patient, not just the subject of the consultation. Confirm both chief complaints before proceeding to history.

STAGE 2: Targeted history-taking

"Before I explain what I'm seeing, I'd like to ask you a few questions — some might seem a bit unexpected, but they'll really help me understand what's going on. First, when Sophie was a baby and a toddler — up until about age three — did she have any illnesses? Ear infections, chest infections, anything that needed antibiotics?"
