[Elicits ear infection history and amoxicillin courses] "That's really helpful, thank you. And during your pregnancy with Sophie, were you generally well? Any illnesses or medications you needed to take?" [Elicits second-trimester antibiotic course] "Thank you for mentioning that. One more question — does anyone else in the family, yourself, your partner, or any siblings, have teeth that look a bit similar to Sophie's front teeth — chalky, rough, or discoloured?" [Explores family history for AI] "And just to cover all bases — has Sophie ever had fluoride supplements or lived in an area with very high fluoride in the water?"

Systematically elicit MIH-relevant history (early childhood illness, antibiotics birth to age 3), AI-relevant history (pregnancy medications, family history of enamel anomalies), and fluoride history to exclude fluorosis. Document all findings.

STAGE 3: Explaining the dual diagnosis and addressing guilt

"Jenny, I want to answer your question about whether this is something you caused — and I want to be really clear: it isn't. Neither of these conditions is caused by anything you did or didn't do. I know that's probably a relief to hear, but let me explain what I think is actually going on, because there are two separate things happening here and they have different explanations. The back tooth — tooth 26 — shows a condition called Molar Incisor Hypomineralisation, or MIH. What that means is that during a specific window when Sophie was very young — roughly from birth to about age three — the enamel on that tooth didn't harden properly. We think this can happen when a child's body is dealing with repeated illnesses or infections during that time. Given that Sophie had those recurrent ear infections and several courses of antibiotics in her first couple of years, that fits the picture very well. It's not about the antibiotics being harmful — it's about the body's resources being stretched during a critical time for tooth development. Now, the front teeth are a completely different story. What I see there is a generalised pattern — all the permanent front teeth are affected, the texture is rough, and it covers the whole tooth surface rather than appearing as a distinct patch. Importantly, Sophie's baby teeth looked normal, which is a key clue. This pattern is consistent with a condition called Amelogenesis Imperfecta — which is a hereditary condition, meaning it comes from the genes that control how enamel forms. It's something Sophie was born with, and it has nothing to do with anything that happened during pregnancy or childhood. I did want to ask about family history because sometimes we see similar teeth in a parent or sibling. I should also mention — I considered whether this could be related to fluoride, but fluoride-related changes look quite different: they tend to be faint white lines or streaks, very symmetrical. What Sophie has is rougher and more extensive, so fluorosis is not the explanation here."

Name both conditions explicitly. Distinguish aetiology, distribution, and hereditary basis in accessible language. Exclude fluorosis with a brief clinical rationale. Address Jenny's guilt before the clinical explanation — validate emotion first, then reassure with accuracy. Avoid the word 'genetic' without explanation.

STAGE 4: Condition-specific management plans

"So let's talk about what we do from here — and there are two separate plans, one for each condition. For Sophie's back tooth, the priority is protecting it, because teeth affected by MIH have weaker enamel and are more vulnerable to decay. Today I'd like to apply a fluoride varnish to help strengthen the surface and reduce the sensitivity. I'd also like to place a protective filling — we'd use a material that's gentle on the tooth and seals it from the things that are causing the sensitivity. Because MIH teeth need closer monitoring than usual, I'd like to see Sophie every three months rather than every six, just so we can catch any changes early. [To Sophie] "Sophie, that means we'll be seeing a lot of each other — is that okay with you?" [Back to Jenny] "For the front teeth, the honest answer is that the best cosmetic treatment — things like tooth-coloured veneers — works best once Sophie's face has finished growing and her gums have settled into their final position. That's usually around age sixteen to eighteen. Doing it earlier risks the result not fitting properly as she grows. In the meantime, what we can do is apply fluoride varnish to protect the enamel surface, make sure Sophie is using a gentle, non-abrasive toothpaste, and keep a close eye on things. The front teeth are not going to get dramatically worse with good care — they're stable. And when the time is right, there are really good options to improve their appearance. I want Sophie to feel confident about her smile, and we'll get there. Do you have any questions about any of that?"

Deliver separate, condition-specific management plans. For tooth 26: fluoride varnish, GIC or composite protective restoration, three-monthly review. For anterior teeth: defer cosmetic treatment to age 16–18, interim fluoride varnish, avoid abrasive toothpastes, reassurance about stability. Address Sophie directly at least once. Invite questions to close the consultation collaboratively.

PQ-54
Geographic Tongue (Benign Migratory Glossitis) — Diagnosis &amp; Reassurance
Module 10  |  Past Questions
■ Cluster 2 — Balanced (History informs management)

CANDIDATE BRIEF

Male patient, attending for a routine dental exam and check-up. Chief Complaint: Noticed something unusual on his tongue a few weeks ago. Believes it may be related to stress. Recently received a promotion at work involving significant overseas travel — a major life change and stressor. Clinical Image: Classic geographic tongue / benign migratory glossitis — irregular red patches with white/yellow borders on the tongue dorsum, map-like appearance. Task: Explain the diagnosis and management. Address the patient's concerns. Reassure appropriately. Discuss the benign nature, triggers (stress, certain foods), and monitoring.

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

Stage 1 — Immediate Cancer Reassurance (0–1 min)

David asks 'Is it cancer?' within the first minute. INFLECTION 1 The candidate must answer directly and without qualification: 'No — this is not cancer. Nothing I can see here concerns me for malignancy.' Any hedging or deferral here loses David's trust and examiner marks. Introduce the diagnosis by both names immediately after reassurance.

Stage 2 — Focused History (1–3 min)

Systematic questioning covers: duration and migration of patches, soreness, dietary changes with travel (spicy/acidic foods), alcohol intake (do not skip — David will not volunteer this), stress timeline correlating with promotion, toothpaste type (SLS), previous episodes, and family history of psoriasis. INFLECTION 2 Failure to ask about alcohol or psoriasis family history is a common omission that separates pass from merit.

Stage 3 — Diagnosis Explanation (3–5 min)

Explain migratory nature in plain language. Briefly address differentials: oral lichen planus (different morphology, no migration), oral candidiasis (removable plaques, immunocompromised context), and psoriasis association. Link identified triggers — stress, alcohol, dietary change — explicitly to the flare-up.

Stage 4 — Management & Safety-Netting (5–7 min)

No treatment required. Practical advice: reduce spicy, acidic foods and alcohol during flares; consider SLS-free toothpaste; address stress. Review in 6–12 months. Safety-net clearly: return if lesions become painful, bleed, indurate, or stop migrating. Provide wife-friendly summary on request.

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Answer 'Is it cancer?' immediately and unambiguously — 'No, this is not cancer' — before elaborating on anything else
  2. ✅ Name the condition using both terms: geographic tongue AND benign migratory glossitis, and explain the migratory/shifting nature in plain language
  3. ✅ Elicit all three key triggers through direct questioning: psychological stress (promotion), dietary changes with travel (spicy/acidic foods), and alcohol intake (3–4 standard drinks several times per week)
  4. ✅ Mention the psoriasis association — ask about personal or family history of psoriasis, and explain that geographic tongue and psoriasis share a recognised link
  5. ✅ Safety-net clearly: return promptly if lesions become painful, bleed, develop induration, or become fixed and non-migratory — these would warrant reassessment and possible biopsy
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • 'Geographic tongue — formally called benign migratory glossitis — is characterised by loss of filiform papillae in well-demarcated zones with a raised white or yellowish serpiginous border; the patches appear to move because affected areas regenerate while new areas are transiently involved nearby.'
  • 'There is no induration, no ulceration, no fixed lesion, and no lymphadenopathy — none of the features that would prompt me to consider malignancy or arrange a biopsy at this stage.'
  • 'Geographic tongue has a well-established association with psoriasis — the two conditions share similar histological features, and geographic tongue can sometimes precede skin manifestations of psoriasis, so I'd like to ask whether you or anyone in your family has been diagnosed with psoriasis.'
  • 'Oral lichen planus can look superficially similar but typically shows Wickham's striae, bilateral buccal mucosal involvement, and does not migrate — none of which fits what I'm seeing here.'
  • 'Sodium lauryl sulfate, a foaming agent in many standard toothpastes, can exacerbate soreness in geographic tongue — switching to an SLS-free toothpaste is a simple, low-cost step worth trying if the tongue becomes uncomfortable.'
Curveball Deflectors
  • David pushes back: 'But I looked it up online and some sites said it could be oral cancer or a sign of something serious — how can you be so sure?' → Acknowledge his research without dismissing it: 'It's completely reasonable to look it up, and you're right that any unusual mouth change deserves proper assessment — that's exactly why I'm examining it carefully. What distinguishes geographic tongue from anything worrying is a specific combination of features: the patches move over time rather than staying fixed, the borders have a characteristic raised white rim, there's no firmness or ulceration underneath, and the overall pattern is classic. If I saw a fixed, non-healing, indurated lesion, I would refer you immediately. I don't see that here. I'm confident in this diagnosis, and I'll give you clear instructions on exactly what to watch for so you know when to come back.'
  • Candidate mistake — jumping straight into management advice without asking about alcohol intake, assuming stress is the only trigger → Pause and return to history before closing: 'Before I give you the full picture on management, I want to make sure I've asked about a couple of other things that can trigger flare-ups — particularly alcohol intake and any changes to your diet recently. Some people find that alcohol and spicy or acidic foods make the tongue more sensitive during a flare. Has your alcohol intake or diet changed at all, especially with the travel that's come with the new role?' This recovers the missed trigger and demonstrates systematic clinical thinking.
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ►
STAGE 1: Immediate Reassurance & Diagnosis

"David, before we go any further — I can see from the image and your notes that you've been wondering whether this could be something serious. So let me answer that directly: no, this is not cancer. There is nothing here that concerns me for malignancy. What I can see on your tongue is a very well-recognised, completely benign condition called geographic tongue — its formal medical name is benign migratory glossitis. It's more common than most people realise, and it is not dangerous."

Deliver cancer reassurance as the very first clinical statement. Maintain confident, unhurried eye contact. Do not qualify or hedge. Observe that David visibly relaxes — this is the expected response and confirms the approach is working.

STAGE 2: Focused History to Identify Triggers

"Now I'd like to ask you a few quick questions so I can give you the most useful advice. You mentioned the patches started a few weeks ago — have you noticed them shifting position, almost like the pattern changes from week to week? Any soreness or burning, particularly with certain foods? Since the promotion, has your diet changed much — more spicy food, richer meals, different cuisines with the travel? And what about alcohol — roughly how often and how much would you say you're drinking at the moment? I also want to ask about your toothpaste — do you know the brand you're using? And finally, has anyone in your family ever been diagnosed with psoriasis, the skin condition?"

Systematically cover: migration of lesions, soreness, dietary changes, alcohol intake (target: elicit 3–4 standard drinks several times per week), toothpaste brand (SLS), previous episodes, and family history of psoriasis. Do not skip alcohol — David will not volunteer it. The psoriasis question differentiates a strong candidate.

STAGE 3: Explanation, Differentials & Trigger Linkage

"So here's what's happening. Geographic tongue occurs when small projections on the tongue surface — called filiform papillae — temporarily disappear in patches, leaving smooth red areas with a slightly raised whitish border. The reason it looks like it moves is that those areas heal up while new patches form nearby — it's not spreading, it's cycling. It's completely harmless. In terms of what else it could be: a condition called oral lichen planus can look a little similar, but it behaves differently — it doesn't migrate, and it usually affects the cheeks as well. A fungal infection called oral thrush produces white patches that wipe off, which isn't what we're seeing here. Now, putting your history together — the timing lines up very closely with your promotion two months ago, which is a significant stress, and stress is the single biggest trigger for geographic tongue flares. On top of that, the increase in spicy food and alcohol with the travel are both well-known irritants. I'd also mention that geographic tongue has a recognised link with psoriasis — they share some underlying biology — so it was worth asking about your family history there."

Explicitly link stress, dietary change, and alcohol to the flare-up. Address differentials briefly but accurately. Mention psoriasis association clearly.

STAGE 4: Management, Safety-Netting & Wife's Summary

"The good news is that geographic tongue doesn't need any specific treatment — it will settle on its own. What I'd suggest is: during a flare, ease back on spicy, acidic, and very hot foods, and try to moderate the alcohol. If your tongue becomes sore, it's worth switching to a toothpaste without sodium lauryl sulfate — that's a foaming agent in most standard toothpastes that can irritate sensitive tongues; your pharmacist can point you to SLS-free options. Managing stress where you can will also help — I know that's easier said than done with a new role, but even small things make a difference. I'd like to see you again in about six to twelve months for a routine check. But I want you to come back sooner — don't wait — if the patches become painful, if they bleed, if you feel any firmness underneath, or if they stop moving and stay fixed in one spot. Those would be reasons to reassess. As for your wife — here's exactly what to tell her: it's benign, it's not cancer, it's not contagious, it's very common, and it's almost certainly been triggered by the stress and lifestyle changes that came with your promotion. Does that make sense? Any questions?"

Confirm no treatment required. Provide actionable trigger avoidance advice. Recommend SLS-free toothpaste. Address stress sensitively. Set 6–12 month review. Deliver explicit safety-netting criteria. Provide wife-friendly summary verbatim. Check understanding before closing.

PQ-55
Oroantral Communication — Disclosure After Upper Molar Extraction
Module 10  |  Past Questions
■ Cluster 3 — Evaluation & Treatment Planning

CANDIDATE BRIEF

Mrs Elida Jones, regular patient. Scenario: You performed an extraction of tooth 26 (upper left first molar). During the extraction, the tooth fractured. You successfully removed approximately 2/3 of the tooth but 1/3 of the root (~1–2 mm) remains in the socket. On testing sinus patency (Valsalva / nose-blow test), air is bubbling from the socket — confirming oroantral communication (OAC). Task: Explain to the patient what has happened during the extraction. Inform her about: (1) the retained root fragment, (2) the oroantral communication, and (3) immediate and ongoing management. Address her concerns.

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

Stage 1 — Orientation and Disclosure (0:00–1:30)

Candidate signals that there is something important to discuss before Mrs Jones leaves. Discloses both complications — tooth fracture with retained root tip and oroantral communication — clearly and without delay. Uses plain language: "a small piece of root" and "a small opening between your mouth and the sinus above." INFLECTION 1 — Candidate must not minimise or defer disclosure. Duty of candour requires both complications named explicitly.

Stage 2 — Explanation and Empathy (1:30–3:00)

Explains why the tooth fractured (heavily restored, recognised complication). Explains OAC in lay terms — what the sinus is, what the opening means, that it was confirmed by the bubbling test. Acknowledges Mrs Jones's visible distress with genuine empathy, not formulaic phrases. INFLECTION 2 — "Did you do something wrong?" Candidate threads the needle: honest acknowledgement of the complication, clear statement it is a recognised risk, no implication of negligence, genuine apology for the experience.

Stage 3 — Relevant History (3:00–4:00)

Candidate asks about prior sinus problems and current nasal symptoms. Elicits history of resolved chronic sinusitis. Incorporates this into management rationale — sinus mucosa may be more susceptible, reinforcing importance of decongestant and close follow-up.

Stage 4 — Management and Instructions (4:00–5:30)

Checks penicillin allergy before prescribing. Prescribes amoxicillin 500 mg TDS for five days and nasal decongestant spray. Explains socket dressing placed to protect the opening. Gives specific OAC precautions: no nose blowing for two weeks, sneeze with mouth open, no straws, no smoking. Arranges urgent OMFS referral within 24–48 hours for retained fragment and OAC review.

Stage 5 — Safety Net (5:30–6:00)

Addresses Mrs Jones's concern about living alone. Provides written post-operative instructions, practice after-hours contact number, and specific criteria for emergency care: uncontrolled bleeding, worsening facial swelling, fever, or fluid passing through the nose.

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Disclose both complications — retained root fragment AND oroantral communication — explicitly and without delay, fulfilling the duty of candour
  2. ✅ Respond to 'Did you do something wrong?' with honest, measured candour — acknowledge the complication as recognised, do not imply negligence, and do not dismiss the patient's concern
  3. ✅ Elicit prior sinus history (resolved chronic sinusitis) and incorporate it into the management explanation and rationale for close follow-up
  4. ✅ Check penicillin allergy before prescribing; prescribe amoxicillin 500 mg TDS for five days and a nasal decongestant spray; give specific OAC precautions including no nose blowing for two weeks
  5. ✅ Arrange urgent referral to an oral and maxillofacial or specialist oral surgeon within 24–48 hours, and provide a specific, actionable safety net including written instructions, after-hours contact, and clear emergency criteria
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • A root fragment of one to two millimetres, sitting close to the sinus floor, carries a higher risk of being displaced into the sinus during retrieval than of causing harm if left and monitored by a specialist — that is why we are not attempting to remove it today.
  • The oroantral communication was confirmed by the Valsalva test — when you breathed out gently through your nose with it pinched, air bubbled through the socket, which tells us there is a direct opening between your mouth and the sinus above.
  • Before I prescribe the antibiotic, I need to ask — have you ever had a reaction to penicillin or amoxicillin? If not, I will prescribe amoxicillin 500 mg three times a day for five days to protect the sinus from infection.
  • The most important instruction for the next two weeks is: please do not blow your nose. If you need to sneeze, let it out through your mouth. Any pressure you create in the sinus can push air or fluid through that opening and delay healing.
  • Given your history of chronic sinusitis — even though it has resolved — the sinus lining may be a little more sensitive than average, which is exactly why I want the specialist to see you within the next day or two rather than waiting.
Curveball Deflectors
  • Patient asks: 'Did you do something wrong? Should this have happened?' → Acknowledge honestly and calmly: 'The tooth fractured during removal — that is something that can happen with heavily restored upper molar teeth, particularly when the roots are close to the sinus. It is a recognised complication, not something caused by an error in technique. I am genuinely sorry that this has happened to you, and I want to make sure you are fully informed and well looked after from here.' Do not say 'everything was fine' — that is dishonest. Do not over-apologise or imply fault — that is clinically and legally inappropriate.
  • Candidate prescribes antibiotics without asking about penicillin allergy first → Always ask about penicillin allergy before prescribing amoxicillin. If allergy is confirmed, prescribe erythromycin 400 mg four times daily for five days as an alternative. Failing to ask is a mark-losing error and a patient safety issue — the examiner will note it.
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ►
STAGE 1: Orientation and Disclosure

"Mrs Jones, before you go I need to sit down with you and explain what happened during the procedure today. I want to be completely open with you, because you deserve to know exactly what occurred. Is that okay?"

Candidate ensures patient is seated comfortably, maintains calm and warm eye contact, and signals that important information is coming — preparing her emotionally without causing alarm.

"During the extraction, the tooth fractured — it broke apart as I was removing it. This can happen with heavily restored teeth like yours, where the tooth structure has been weakened over time. I was able to remove about two-thirds of the tooth successfully. However, a very small piece of root — roughly one to two millimetres — remains at the bottom of the socket. I also need to tell you that the test I performed after the extraction — where I asked you to breathe out gently through your nose — showed that there is a small opening between your mouth and the sinus cavity that sits just above that area. Air was bubbling through the socket, which confirmed it. Both of these things are important, and I want to explain what they mean and what we are going to do about them."

Candidate discloses both complications — retained root fragment and oroantral communication — clearly and without delay. Plain language used throughout. No jargon introduced without immediate explanation.

STAGE 2: Explanation, Empathy, and the Key Inflection Point

"I can see this is a lot to take in, and I completely understand if you are feeling worried or upset. Please take a moment."

Candidate pauses, acknowledges Mrs Jones's visible distress with genuine warmth. Does not rush past her emotional response.

"The sinus is an air-filled space in your cheekbone, just above the roots of your upper back teeth. In some people — and this is more common than many realise — the roots of the upper molars sit very close to the sinus floor, or even touch it. When a tooth like yours is removed, a small opening can form. It is a recognised complication of upper molar extractions, particularly with teeth that have been heavily restored. The prognosis is generally very good when it is identified and managed promptly, which is exactly what we are doing."

"As for the small root fragment — I know it might seem like we should take it out straight away, but the safest approach is actually to leave it for now. Attempting to retrieve a fragment that small, sitting that close to the sinus, carries a real risk of pushing it up into the sinus itself, which would make things considerably more complicated. A specialist will assess it within the next day or two and make that decision with full information."

INFLECTION POINT — Mrs Jones asks: "Did you do something wrong?"

"That is a completely fair question, and I want to answer it honestly. The tooth fractured during removal — that is what happened. With a tooth that has been as heavily restored as yours, the remaining tooth structure can be quite brittle, and fracture during extraction is a recognised complication. It is not something that happened because of a mistake in technique. I am genuinely sorry that this has happened to you — I know it is not what either of us wanted — and I want to make sure you are fully informed and that we manage this as well as possible from here."

Candidate threads the needle — honest acknowledgement, no implication of negligence, no defensive dismissal, genuine empathy.

STAGE 3: Relevant History

"Before I go through the management plan, I want to ask you a couple of quick questions about your sinuses. Have you ever had any sinus problems in the past — things like chronic sinusitis, frequent sinus infections, or nasal congestion that needed treatment?"

Candidate elicits history of resolved chronic sinusitis managed with nasal corticosteroid spray several years ago.

"Thank you for telling me that. Even though your sinusitis has resolved, the lining of your sinus may be a little more sensitive than average, which means it is even more important that we get you seen by a specialist promptly and that you follow the post-operative instructions carefully. It does not change the overall plan, but it does reinforce why close follow-up matters for you specifically."

Candidate incorporates prior sinus history into management rationale in plain language.

STAGE 4: Management, Medications, and Instructions

"I have placed a small protective dressing in the socket to help cover that opening while it begins to heal. Now, I would like to prescribe you an antibiotic to protect the sinus from infection — before I do, I need to ask: have you ever had a reaction to penicillin or amoxicillin?"

Candidate checks penicillin allergy before prescribing. If no allergy: prescribes amoxicillin 500 mg three times daily for five days. If allergy present: prescribes erythromycin 400 mg four times daily for five days. Also prescribes a nasal decongestant spray to reduce sinus pressure and swelling.

"There are also some very specific instructions I need you to follow for the next two weeks, and these are really important. Please do not blow your nose — not at all, for at least two weeks. If you need to sneeze, let it out through your mouth rather than holding it in or blowing through your nose. Please do not use straws, do not smoke, and avoid anything that creates pressure in your sinuses — so no heavy lifting or straining either. The reason is that any increase in pressure can push air or fluid through that small opening and prevent it from healing. I will give you all of this in writing before you leave."

Candidate provides specific OAC post-operative instructions in plain language. Arranges urgent referral to oral and maxillofacial surgeon within 24–48 hours for review of both the retained fragment and the OAC.

"I am also going to refer you urgently to a specialist — an oral and maxillofacial surgeon — who I would like to see you within the next day or two. They will assess the small root fragment and the opening, and make sure everything is healing as it should. I will make that referral today."

STAGE 5: Safety Net

Mrs Jones asks: "If something goes wrong tonight, who do I call? I live by myself."

"That is such an important question, and I am glad you asked. You will not be on your own with this. I am going to give you a printed copy of all of these instructions to take home. It will also have our practice's after-hours contact number on it, so if you are worried at any point tonight or over the weekend, you can call us directly. If you experience any of the following, I want you to seek emergency care straight away — either call us or go to your nearest emergency department: if the bleeding does not stop or gets worse, if you develop significant swelling in your face or jaw, if you get a fever, or if you notice fluid or food passing up through your nose. Those are the signs that something needs urgent attention. Otherwise, I will be in touch tomorrow to check in on you, and the specialist appointment will be arranged as a priority. Do you have any other questions for me right now?"

Candidate provides specific, actionable safety net: written instructions, after-hours contact number, and clear criteria for emergency care. Offers to follow up proactively. Closes with an open invitation for further questions, maintaining warmth and genuine concern throughout.

PQ-56
Drug-Induced Gingival Enlargement — Cyclosporine + Nifedipine
Module 10  |  Past Questions
■ Cluster 3 — Evaluation & Treatment Planning

CANDIDATE BRIEF

Mr Richard Jones, regular attender. Chief Complaint: Swollen and bleeding gums. Has a wedding to attend next week — wants it resolved quickly. Examination Findings: Generalised gingival enlargement noted on examination. Periodontal charting performed. Medical History: Kidney transplant — taking cyclosporine for 15 years (immunosuppressant); Hypertension — taking nifedipine (calcium channel blocker) for the past 8 months; Taking atorvastatin for cholesterol. Drug-Induced Gingival Overgrowth: Both cyclosporine and nifedipine are well-known causes. The combination significantly increases risk and severity. Task: Diagnose and manage. Address the patient's concerns. Discuss the drug-gingival link, liaison with GP/specialist regarding medication review, and treatment options.

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

Stage 1 — History-Taking and Timeline Elicitation (0–3 min)

Candidate opens with empathy about the wedding, then asks targeted questions to establish onset: "When did you first notice the swelling?" and "When was nifedipine started?" The key pivot is confirming 15 years of stable gums on cyclosporine alone, with deterioration mapping precisely to nifedipine introduction 8 months ago. INFLECTION 1 — candidate must make this temporal correlation explicit, not leave it implied.

Stage 2 — Diagnosis and Explanation (3–6 min)

Candidate names the diagnosis clearly: "Mr Jones, what you have is called drug-induced gingival overgrowth." Both cyclosporine and nifedipine are identified as causative agents. Mechanism explained in lay terms: the medications cause gum cells to overproduce fibrous tissue, and plaque makes it significantly worse. Candidate notes the combination is synergistic — worse together than either alone.

Stage 3 — Medication Safety Counselling (6–8 min)

INFLECTION 2 — Patient asks "Can I just stop the nifedipine?" Candidate must firmly but kindly refuse to endorse this, explaining risks of hypertensive crisis and transplant rejection, and redirecting to the GP and transplant physician as the appropriate decision-makers.

Stage 4 — Dental Management Plan (8–11 min)

Stepwise plan: intensive oral hygiene instruction today, full-mouth scaling and root planing, six-to-eight-week review. If overgrowth persists after three to six months of optimal management, surgical options such as gingivectomy may be required. Medical liaison letters to GP and transplant physician outlined.

Stage 5 — Wedding Expectations and Close (11–13 min)

Honest prognosis: professional cleaning will reduce bleeding and inflammation — some visible improvement is realistic within a week. Structural resolution of the overgrowth itself will take months. Candidate does not promise resolution by the wedding.

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Establish the temporal correlation: stable gums for 15 years on cyclosporine alone; deterioration began 8 months ago coinciding precisely with nifedipine introduction
  2. ✅ Name the diagnosis as drug-induced gingival overgrowth (DIGO) and correctly identify BOTH cyclosporine and nifedipine as causative agents with a synergistic combined effect
  3. ✅ Explicitly advise the patient NOT to stop or alter any medication without GP or transplant physician guidance, citing risks of hypertensive crisis and transplant rejection
  4. ✅ Outline a stepwise dental management plan: intensive OHI + full-mouth SRP now, six-to-eight-week review, and surgical option (gingivectomy/flap) if conservative management fails after three to six months
  5. ✅ Commit to medical liaison: letter to GP requesting nifedipine substitution (e.g., ACE inhibitor, ARB, or amlodipine) and separate contact with transplant physician regarding cyclosporine component and potential CYP3A4 drug interaction
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • Both cyclosporine — your anti-rejection medication — and nifedipine — your blood pressure tablet — are independently known to cause gum overgrowth, and when taken together the effect is significantly worse than either drug alone.
  • The timeline is very telling: your gums were stable for 15 years on cyclosporine, and the swelling began 8 months ago — which maps exactly to when nifedipine was introduced. That is not a coincidence.
  • Plaque and bacteria act as a permissive co-factor — they do not cause this condition, but their presence makes the overgrowth substantially worse, which is why improving your home care is a critical part of treatment.
  • I will write to your GP explaining the diagnosis and requesting consideration of switching nifedipine to an antihypertensive with a lower association with gum overgrowth — options such as an ACE inhibitor, an ARB, or even amlodipine, which is also a calcium channel blocker but has a much lower incidence of this side effect.
  • There is also a potential interaction between cyclosporine and nifedipine that I want to flag to your transplant physician — cyclosporine can affect how nifedipine is broken down in the body, which may mean your nifedipine levels are higher than your GP intended when prescribing the standard dose.
  • If the gum tissue does not respond adequately after three to six months of optimal plaque control, professional cleaning, and medication review, we may need to consider a surgical procedure called a gingivectomy to remove the excess tissue.
Curveball Deflectors
  • Patient asks: 'Can I just stop the nifedipine myself? It's only been 8 months.' → Acknowledge the logic behind the question, then firmly redirect: 'I completely understand why that seems like the obvious solution — and you may well be right that nifedipine is the main driver here. But stopping a blood pressure medication suddenly can cause a dangerous spike in blood pressure, and I am not in a position to advise you to do that. This decision needs to be made by your GP, who can either switch you to a safer alternative or adjust your treatment safely. I will write to them today explaining exactly what I have found and why I believe nifedipine is contributing, so they can act on this promptly. Please do not stop it on your own.'
  • Candidate only identifies nifedipine as the causative drug and overlooks cyclosporine's role → Avoid this by explicitly naming both drugs when delivering the diagnosis. Cyclosporine has been associated with gingival overgrowth for decades and is independently causative — the fact that it did not cause significant overgrowth alone in this patient does not exonerate it. The correct framing is that nifedipine was the precipitating agent that tipped a pre-existing susceptibility into clinically significant disease, and both drugs must be addressed in the management plan and medical liaison.
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ►
STAGE 1: Opening and History-Taking

"Mr Jones, thank you for coming in today. I can see from your notes that you're a regular attender and you've always looked after your teeth well, so I imagine it's been quite distressing watching this happen. I also know you have a wedding coming up next week — I want to make sure we address that directly before you leave today. First, can I ask you a few questions to make sure I have the full picture? When did you first notice the gums starting to swell and bleed? And has it been getting worse gradually, or did it come on quite suddenly?"

Candidate listens for the 8-month onset and correlates it with the nifedipine start date. Follows up: "And when did your GP start you on the blood pressure tablet — the nifedipine?" Confirms the temporal correlation explicitly. Notes that cyclosporine has been on board for 15 years with previously stable gums.

STAGE 2: Diagnosis and Plain-Language Explanation

"Mr Jones, I can tell you what is causing this, and the good news is that we have a clear explanation and a plan. What you have is called drug-induced gingival overgrowth — in plain terms, your gum tissue is swelling and thickening as a side effect of your medications. Both your anti-rejection medication, cyclosporine, and your blood pressure tablet, nifedipine, are known to cause this. When someone is taking both at the same time, the effect is significantly worse than either drug alone — and that fits exactly with what we are seeing. Your gums were stable for 15 years on cyclosporine, and the swelling began 8 months ago, which maps precisely to when nifedipine was introduced. What these medications do is alter the behaviour of cells in your gum tissue, causing them to produce too much fibrous material. Plaque and bacteria around the gum line make this considerably worse — they act like fuel on a fire — which is why your oral hygiene routine, as good as it is, has not been enough to hold it back on its own."

Candidate checks patient understanding and invites questions before proceeding.

STAGE 3: Medication Safety and Medical Liaison

"Now, I can see you are probably thinking — can I just stop the nifedipine? And that is a completely understandable thought. But I have to be very clear with you: please do not stop or change either of those medications without speaking to your doctors first. Stopping a blood pressure medication suddenly can cause a dangerous spike in blood pressure, and stopping your anti-rejection medication even briefly carries a risk of your body rejecting your kidney. Those are not decisions I can make for you, and they are not decisions you should make alone. What I will do is write to your GP today — a detailed letter explaining exactly what I have found, why I believe nifedipine is the likely trigger given the timeline, and requesting that they consider switching you to a blood pressure medication with a much lower risk of this side effect. There are good alternatives — ACE inhibitors, ARBs, or even a different calcium channel blocker called amlodipine, which causes this problem far less often. I will also contact your transplant physician separately, because there is a potential interaction between cyclosporine and nifedipine that is worth flagging — cyclosporine can affect how nifedipine is broken down in the body, which may mean your levels are higher than your GP intended."

Candidate documents plan to write liaison letters to both GP and transplant physician. Does not suggest any dose changes on own authority.

STAGE 4: Dental Treatment Plan and Wedding Expectations

"Here is what we are going to do on the dental side. Today, I want to go through your home care routine with you and make sure we are getting the most out of it — technique, interdental cleaning, the works. I will then do a thorough professional clean, scaling above and below the gum line across your whole mouth. That will remove the plaque and calculus that are driving the inflammation and making the overgrowth worse. I want to see you back in six to eight weeks to assess how the tissue has responded. If the gum overgrowth does not improve adequately after three to six months of optimal home care, professional cleaning, and — hopefully — a medication change, we may need to discuss a minor surgical procedure to remove the excess tissue. It is called a gingivectomy, and it is very effective, but we try conservative treatment first. Regarding the wedding — I want to be honest with you, because I think you deserve a straight answer. The professional clean today will reduce the bleeding and the acute inflammation, and you should see some visible improvement within the week. But the structural overgrowth — the actual thickening of the gum tissue — will not resolve in one week. That takes months. So you will look better, and the bleeding should settle, but I cannot promise your gums will look completely normal by next Saturday. What I can promise is that we are doing everything in our power to get this moving in the right direction as quickly as possible."

Candidate schedules scaling appointment, provides written OHI instructions, and confirms follow-up at six to eight weeks. Sends liaison letters same day. Documents all findings, diagnosis, and management plan in the clinical record.

PQ-57
16-Year-Old with Rampant Caries &amp; Erosion — Dietary + Lifestyle Causes
Module 10  |  Past Questions
■ Cluster 3 — Evaluation & Treatment Planning

CANDIDATE BRIEF

Sam, 16-year-old boy, attending with his father. Chief Complaint: Sensitivity to cold on several teeth. Father is accompanying him. History: Regular patient — seen 1 year ago, teeth were ok at that time; Started a new part-time job as an apprentice approximately 1 year ago; High sugar intake; drinks a lot of soft drink during work; Dietary change coincides with onset of sensitivity. Examination Findings / Clinical Images: Cervical caries on tooth 12 and white spot lesions (early caries) on anterior teeth; White chalky patches (enamel demineralisation) on multiple teeth; Caries at cervical margins of multiple posterior teeth, also affecting the marginal bone in some areas; Erosion pattern consistent with dietary acid exposure. Task: Diagnose and manage. Address both the father's and the patient's concerns. Discuss caries risk assessment, dietary counselling, fluoride therapy, and restorative planning where indicated.

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

Stage 1 — Introduction & Rapport (0–2 min)

Greet Sam first, then Mr Tran. Establish Sam as the primary patient: 'Sam, I'm going to direct most of my questions to you today — you're the expert on your own body.' Acknowledge father's concern and give him a defined role: 'Mr Tran, I'd love to hear your observations too, especially at the end.'

Stage 2 — Dietary & Lifestyle History (2–6 min)

Quantify drink type, frequency, and timing at work, at home, and during exercise. Ask specifically about energy drinks by name. Probe gently when Sam underreports. Rule out GORD, medications, and eating disorders as alternative acid sources. INFLECTION 1 Ask directly: 'Do you ever brush your teeth at work or after having a drink?' — this is the pivotal question that unlocks the most clinically significant modifiable behaviour in the case.

Stage 3 — Explain Findings (6–10 min)

Distinguish caries (bacterial, sugar-driven) from erosion (chemical, direct acid contact) as two separate but coexisting processes. Use the twelve-month timeline concretely: 'One year ago — no lesions. Today — multiple white spots, one cavity, and generalised erosion. That's the rate of damage on your current habits.' Avoid moralising; use numbers and trajectory instead. INFLECTION 2 Correct the brushing habit explicitly: explain that brushing within 30–60 minutes of acid exposure abrades softened enamel and accelerates tooth surface loss.

Stage 4 — Management Plan (10–14 min)

Apply fluoride varnish today. Prescribe Neutrafluor 5000 ppm toothpaste. Advise replacing between-meal acidic drinks with fluoridated tap water. Recommend fluoride mouthrinse at a separate time to brushing. Plan restorations for teeth 12 and 26; monitor white spot lesions with fluoride. Schedule three-month recall. Give Mr Tran a supportive role: 'It would really help Sam if water was easy to grab at home too.'

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Quantify acidic drink frequency, type, and timing at work and during exercise — probe specifically for energy drinks and sports drinks when Sam underreports
  2. ✅ Uncover and explicitly correct the habit of brushing immediately after acid exposure — advise minimum 30–60 minute wait and explain the mechanism of enamel abrasion on softened enamel
  3. ✅ Distinguish dental caries (bacterial, fermentable carbohydrate-driven biofilm acid) from erosion (direct chemical dissolution by dietary acid, bacteria-independent) as coexisting but mechanistically distinct processes
  4. ✅ Engage Sam as the primary patient throughout; acknowledge Mr Tran's concern and assign him a supportive role without allowing him to dominate the consultation
  5. ✅ Deliver a complete, staged management plan: same-day fluoride varnish, prescription Neutrafluor 5000 ppm toothpaste, fluoridated tap water replacement, fluoride mouthrinse, restorations for teeth 12 and 26, conservative monitoring of white spot lesions, and a mandatory three-month recall
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • Brushing within 30 to 60 minutes of acidic drink consumption abrades enamel that has been chemically softened by the acid — this accelerates erosive tooth surface loss and is one of the most damaging habits we can correct today.
  • Caries and erosion are two different diseases happening at the same time. Caries is caused by bacteria in your mouth fermenting sugar and producing acid. Erosion is caused by the acid in the drink itself directly dissolving your enamel — no bacteria involved. Both are being driven by the same drinks, but they need to be understood separately.
  • One year ago your teeth were clinically healthy. In twelve months you have developed white spot lesions on multiple teeth, a cavitated lesion on tooth 12, and generalised erosion. That is a very rapid rate of progression — if we project that forward another twelve months without change, the damage will be significantly worse.
  • I am going to prescribe a high-concentration fluoride toothpaste — 5000 parts per million, which is Colgate Neutrafluor 5000 — rather than standard over-the-counter toothpaste. At your level of caries risk, standard fluoride is not sufficient to remineralise the lesions we are seeing.
  • The two lesions on teeth 12 and 26 have progressed into dentine and require restoration. The white spot lesions on the anterior teeth have not yet cavitated — at this stage, fluoride therapy gives us a genuine opportunity to remineralise them without drilling, but only if we change the diet and brushing habits now.
  • Replacing between-meal soft drinks and energy drinks with fluoridated tap water addresses two problems simultaneously — it removes the acid and sugar source, and it delivers free, evidence-based fluoride remineralisation throughout the day.
  • Given the rate of progression we have documented over the past twelve months, I want to see you back in three months rather than the standard six — we need to check whether the lesions are stabilising or continuing to progress.
Curveball Deflectors
  • Mr Tran interrupts and says: 'I've been telling him this for months — he just won't listen. Can you make him understand how serious this is?' → Acknowledge Mr Tran warmly without allowing him to take over: 'Mr Tran, it's clear you care a lot about Sam's health and you've already noticed these changes — that's really important. I'm going to make sure Sam has all the information he needs to make his own decisions, and I'll explain everything to both of you together at the end. Sam, let me come back to you — can you tell me a bit more about what a typical day at work looks like for you?' This validates the father, redirects to Sam, and avoids the consultation becoming a parent-led lecture.
  • Sam says: 'I already brush my teeth after every drink at work — I thought that was the right thing to do.' → This is the key inflection point — do not dismiss or embarrass Sam. Respond: 'Sam, I'm really glad you told me that, and honestly it makes complete sense that you'd think that — most people would. Here's the problem: when you drink something acidic, the acid temporarily softens the surface of your enamel. If you brush within about 30 to 60 minutes, you're actually scrubbing away that softened layer. Over time, that's one of the fastest ways to lose tooth structure. What I'd recommend instead is rinsing with water straight after the drink, then waiting at least half an hour before you brush. That one change will make a significant difference.' Affirm the instinct, correct the behaviour, explain the mechanism simply.
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ►
STAGE 1: Introduction & Establishing Sam as Primary Patient

"Hi Sam, I'm Dr [Name] — great to meet you. And you must be Sam's dad — thanks for coming in with him today, Mr Tran. Sam, I'm going to direct most of my questions to you today, because you're the one who knows your own body best. Mr Tran, I'd love to hear your perspective too, and I'll make sure we have time for that. Sam, you mentioned some sensitivity to cold — can you tell me a bit about when that started and which teeth it's affecting?"

Seat both patient and father. Position body language toward Sam. Establish rapport with Sam before taking any history. Note father's body language — he appears more anxious than Sam.

STAGE 2: Dietary & Lifestyle History — Uncovering the Key Habits

"Sam, you started a new job about a year ago — congratulations on that, by the way. Can you walk me through what you typically eat and drink on a workday? What do you grab during breaks? ... And specifically — do you drink energy drinks or soft drinks at work? Which ones, and roughly how many a day? ... What about after sport or exercise — do you use sports drinks? ... And at home, what are you usually drinking? ... Do you drink much water during the day? ... Now, one more question that might seem a bit random — do you ever brush your teeth at work, or after having a drink? Like, do you carry a toothbrush with you?"

Probe gently when Sam says 'a couple of drinks' — ask specifically about energy drinks by name (e.g., Monster, Mother, V). Establish the true frequency of two to four cans per day. Ask about sports drinks separately. Rule out GORD: 'Do you ever get heartburn or acid coming up into your throat?' Rule out eating disorders sensitively: 'Have there been any changes to your eating habits or appetite lately?' Document that both are absent. When Sam reveals he brushes immediately after drinks, respond without judgment — this is the clinical pivot of the station.

STAGE 3: Explaining the Findings — Caries vs Erosion, and the Brushing Habit

"Sam, I want to show you what I'm seeing and explain what's causing it — because there are actually two separate things happening at the same time. The first is called dental caries — that's the classic cavity. It happens because bacteria in your mouth feed on sugar, produce acid, and that acid eats into your tooth. The second thing is called erosion — and this one is different. This is the acid in the drink itself directly dissolving your enamel, no bacteria needed. Both are happening in your mouth right now, and both are being driven by the same drinks. Here's the thing that really matters: one year ago, when we last saw you, your teeth were fine. In twelve months, you've developed multiple early lesions, one cavity, and generalised erosion across your teeth. That is a fast rate of change. If we project that forward another year without changing anything, the damage will be significantly worse. Now — about the brushing. I'm really glad you told me you brush after drinks, because I need to correct something important. When you drink something acidic, the acid temporarily softens the surface of your enamel. If you brush within about 30 to 60 minutes, you're scrubbing away that softened layer. It feels like good hygiene, but it's actually one of the fastest ways to lose tooth structure. The fix is simple: rinse with water straight after the drink, then wait at least 30 minutes before you brush."

Use clinical images or a diagram if available. Speak directly to Sam using concrete numbers and the twelve-month timeline. Avoid moralising language. Affirm Sam's instinct to brush before correcting the timing. Check Sam's understanding with a teach-back question: 'Does that make sense — can you tell me back what the difference is between the two things I described?'

STAGE 4: Management Plan & Involving Mr Tran

"Here's what I'd like to do today and going forward. Today, I'm going to apply a fluoride varnish to your teeth — it's a concentrated fluoride coating that helps remineralise the early lesions and protect the enamel. I'm also going to prescribe you a special toothpaste called Neutrafluor 5000 — it has a much higher fluoride concentration than anything you can buy over the counter, and at your level of risk, that's what we need. Use it twice a day instead of your regular toothpaste, and don't rinse after — just spit. I'd also recommend a fluoride mouthrinse, but use it at a different time to brushing — not straight after. In terms of the drinks: I'm not going to tell you to never have a soft drink again, because that's not realistic. What I am asking is that you reduce how often you're having them during the day, and replace the between-meal drinks with fluoridated tap water. Tap water is free, it's available on site, and it actually helps remineralise your teeth throughout the day. Two of your teeth — tooth 12 at the front and tooth 26 at the back — have cavities that have reached the dentine and need to be filled. The white patches on your front teeth haven't turned into cavities yet, and if we act now with fluoride and diet changes, we have a real chance of reversing them without any drilling. I want to see you back in three months rather than six, so we can check whether things are stabilising. Mr Tran, it would genuinely help Sam if water was easy to grab at home — having a water bottle ready to go in the morning makes a real difference. You've clearly been paying close attention to these changes, and that's been important. Sam, do you have any questions about any of this?"

Apply fluoride varnish in-chair. Write prescription for Colgate Neutrafluor 5000 ppm. Schedule restorations for teeth 12 and 26 at next appointment. Document white spot lesions for monitoring. Book three-month recall. Provide written take-home summary of the brushing timing advice and drink replacement strategy. Give Mr Tran a specific, supportive role rather than a supervisory one — frame it as enabling rather than policing.

PQ-58
Drug-Seeking Behaviour — Opioid Request for Dental Pain
Module 9  |  Past Questions
■ Cluster 1 — History & Risk Factors

CANDIDATE BRIEF

Female patient. Tooth known to need RCT — previous dentist diagnosed irreversible pulpitis and recommended root canal treatment. Scenario: Patient presents demanding strong prescription painkillers (specifically fentanyl, oxycodone, or tramadol) for toothache. Claims her regular dentist is away and she cannot contact him. States normal painkillers are not effective. She also has a physiotherapist-prescribed pain relief patch for chronic back pain. Has an appointment with her regular dentist next week. Insisting she needs strong medication urgently. Key Complexity: Drug-seeking behaviour. Task: Manage the patient's request. Address her concerns without prescribing opioids. Provide safe and appropriate alternatives.

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

Stage 1 — Recognition and Empathic Opening

Identify red flags. Acknowledge pain. Set a calm, non-accusatory tone.

Stage 2 — Decline Opioids with Clinical Rationale

Explain why opioids are contraindicated. Reference patch interaction. Maintain boundary firmly but respectfully.

Stage 3 — Offer Alternatives, Safety-Net, Document

Prescribe non-opioid analgesia. Arrange urgent dental referral. Advise on red flag symptoms. Document everything.

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Recognise drug-seeking red flags: requesting opioids by name, regular dentist unavailable, claims standard analgesia ineffective, existing opioid patch
  2. ✅ Empathise with genuine dental pain (irreversible pulpitis is severely painful) without validating the opioid request
  3. ✅ Decline opioids clearly and professionally — cite interaction risk with existing fentanyl patch, dependence risk, and lack of dental indication
  4. ✅ Offer evidence-based non-opioid analgesia: alternating ibuprofen 400 mg + paracetamol 1000 mg every 3–4 hours, and arrange urgent dental referral
  5. ✅ Document refusal with clinical rationale, red flags noted, alternatives offered, and safety-net advice given
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • Ibuprofen 400 mg combined with paracetamol 1000 mg alternating every 3–4 hours provides superior analgesia to opioids for acute dental pain and is the evidence-based first-line regimen per ADA and ANZAAS guidelines.
  • Prescribing opioids alongside an existing fentanyl transdermal patch creates a clinically significant risk of opioid toxicity and respiratory depression — this combination is contraindicated without specialist review.
Curveball Deflectors
  • I have a high tolerance — normal painkillers do nothing for me. → I hear you, and I understand the pain from an inflamed tooth nerve is severe. What I can offer you is a combination of anti-inflammatory and paracetamol at therapeutic doses — this regimen is actually more effective for dental nerve pain than opioids, and it is safe alongside your back pain patch. I am not in a position to add opioids on top of your existing patch today.
  • My regular dentist always gives me something stronger — why won't you? → I can only speak to what is clinically appropriate today. I am not able to verify previous prescriptions, and my responsibility is your safety right now. Given you already have a fentanyl patch, adding another opioid carries a real risk of serious harm. What I can do is arrange an urgent dental appointment and make sure your pain is managed as effectively as possible with the safest options available.
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ►

Stage 1 — Recognition and Empathic Opening

Candidate says:

'Thank you for coming in today. I can see from your notes that you have been diagnosed with irreversible pulpitis — that is genuinely one of the most painful dental conditions there is, and I want to help you manage this as effectively as possible.'

Internal recognition (not spoken aloud): Red flags noted — patient requesting specific opioids by name, regular dentist conveniently unavailable, claims all standard analgesia has failed, existing fentanyl transdermal patch for back pain. Appointment with regular dentist already booked for next week. Pattern consistent with drug-seeking behaviour. Proceed with empathy but firm clinical boundaries.

Stage 2 — Decline Opioids with Clear Clinical Rationale

Candidate says:

'I am not going to be able to prescribe fentanyl, oxycodone, or tramadol today, and I want to be transparent with you about why — not to dismiss your pain, but because it would genuinely not be safe. You are already wearing a fentanyl patch for your back. Adding any further opioid on top of that creates a serious risk of opioid toxicity, including slowed or stopped breathing. That is a risk I cannot expose you to.'
'Beyond the safety issue, opioids are actually not the most effective treatment for dental nerve pain. The evidence shows that a combination of an anti-inflammatory and paracetamol works better for this type of pain than opioids do — and without the risks.'

If patient pushes back — 'normal painkillers do not work for me':

'I understand it may feel that way, and I am not doubting your experience. What I can offer you is a specific combination at the right doses and timing — ibuprofen 400 mg and paracetamol 1000 mg alternating every three to four hours. This is different from taking one or the other occasionally, and it is the regimen that clinical guidelines recommend for exactly this situation.'

Stage 3 — Alternatives, Urgent Referral, Safety-Net, Documentation

Candidate says:

'Here is what I am going to do for you today. I am going to recommend ibuprofen 400 mg and paracetamol 1000 mg alternating every three to four hours — please take them with food. I am also going to contact the emergency dental clinic to arrange an urgent appointment for you today or tomorrow, because the definitive treatment here is addressing the tooth itself, not just managing the pain with medication.'
'I also want to make sure you know when to seek emergency care. If you develop swelling of your face, jaw, or neck, difficulty swallowing or breathing, a high fever, or you feel generally unwell, please go straight to the emergency department — do not wait. Those signs can indicate a spreading dental infection which needs urgent treatment.'

Documentation (candidate to state aloud or write):

  • Patient presented requesting opioid analgesia (fentanyl, oxycodone, tramadol) for known irreversible pulpitis.
  • Red flags for drug-seeking behaviour documented: opioids requested by name, regular dentist unavailable, claims standard analgesia ineffective, existing fentanyl transdermal patch in situ.
  • Opioids declined — clinical rationale: interaction risk with existing fentanyl patch, opioids not first-line for dental pain, appointment with regular dentist already scheduled.
  • Advised alternating ibuprofen 400 mg / paracetamol 1000 mg every 3–4 hours.
  • Urgent dental referral arranged.
  • Safety-net advice given regarding signs of spreading infection.
  • Patient informed of rationale in non-accusatory manner. Consultation conducted respectfully.
PQ-59
MIH in an 11-Year-Old — Second Opinion on GA Extraction
Module 9  |  Past Questions
■ Cluster 2 — Balanced (History informs management)

CANDIDATE BRIEF

11-year-old boy, attending with his parents. Chief Complaint: Sensitivity to cold in his back teeth. History: Mother took him to a public hospital previously. General dentist at the hospital suggested extracting the back teeth under general anaesthesia. Parents seeking a second opinion. Examination Findings / Clinical Image: Photograph showing hypomineralised (chalky/opaque) first permanent molars and incisors. Baby teeth appear normal. Diagnosis: Molar Incisor Hypomineralisation (MIH) — affects permanent molars and incisors, primary dentition unaffected. Task: Diagnose and manage. Address parent's concern about the hospital dentist's recommendation for GA extraction.

MODEL ANSWER STRUCTURE

Stage 1 — Introduction and History (0–3 min)

Greet Liam first, then his parents. Confirm the chief complaint. Ask Liam directly: "Does the pain happen on its own, or only when you have something cold?" Elicit no spontaneous or nocturnal pain — a critical negative finding. Ask Wei about early childhood illnesses; she will disclose bronchiolitis hospitalisation at eight months. INFLECTION 1 — linking the febrile illness to the mineralisation window demonstrates aetiological understanding and opens the reassurance conversation.

Stage 2 — Diagnosis and Explanation (3–6 min)

Name the condition: "Liam has something called Molar Incisor Hypomineralisation — MIH for short." Explain in lay terms that the enamel did not harden properly during early childhood. Distinguish from caries (not caused by bacteria or sugar in the same way), fluorosis (not caused by fluoride), and amelogenesis imperfecta (not hereditary; primary teeth are normal — point to the photograph). Explicitly reassure Wei that this is not caused by diet, brushing, or anything she did during pregnancy. INFLECTION 2 — this reassurance is the emotional pivot of the station; a strong candidate delivers it with eye contact and pauses to let it land.

Stage 3 — Conservative Management Plan (6–9 min)

Present the staged ladder: (1) high-fluoride toothpaste (5000 ppm, e.g. Colgate Neutrafluor 5000) and desensitising agents; (2) fissure sealing with resin composite or GIC; (3) GIC or composite restorations for surface breakdown; (4) Hall-technique preformed metal crowns for significantly broken-down molars. Extraction is the last resort — not indicated today.

Stage 4 — Addressing the GA Recommendation and Recall (9–12 min)

Acknowledge the hospital dentist's recommendation without criticism: "The team there may have been working with a different clinical picture or resource constraints — that recommendation makes sense in some situations." Explain that because Liam has no spontaneous pain and his teeth remain restorable, conservative management should be trialled first. Set recall at three to six months. Address David's cost and prognosis questions honestly.

KEY POINTS

  1. ✅ Elicit absence of spontaneous/nocturnal pain — supports conservative management and argues against irreversible pulpitis
  2. ✅ Name MIH explicitly and distinguish it from caries, fluorosis, and amelogenesis imperfecta using the intact primary dentition as a discriminating feature
  3. ✅ Reassure parents that MIH is developmental — not caused by diet, brushing, or parental actions — and deliver this with genuine empathy directed at Wei
  4. ✅ Present the conservative management ladder in logical order (fluoride/desensitising → fissure seal → GIC/composite → Hall crown) before any mention of extraction
  5. ✅ Address the GA recommendation diplomatically without criticising the hospital dentist, and set a three-to-six-month recall with explanation of post-eruptive breakdown risk
KILLER LINES — SECURE YOUR PASS
Clinical Authority
  • "Because Liam has no spontaneous pain and no pain at night, the pulps of these teeth are most likely still healthy — that means extraction is not indicated at this stage."
  • "MIH affects only the permanent teeth because the mineralisation disturbance occurs in early childhood, after the primary teeth have already formed — that's why his baby teeth look completely normal in the photograph."
  • "The Hall technique — placing a stainless steel crown over the tooth without drilling — is one of the most evidence-supported options for a significantly broken-down MIH molar in a child, and it can be done in the chair without general anaesthesia in most cases."
  • "High-concentration fluoride toothpaste — 5000 parts per million, available on prescription in Australia — can significantly reduce the sensitivity Liam is experiencing and help remineralise the porous enamel surface."
  • "If extraction ever becomes necessary in the future, we would need orthodontic input to manage the space — ideally this decision is made around ages eight to ten when the second molars are forming, so timing becomes more complex now that Liam is eleven."
Curveball Deflectors
  • Wei asks: "So the hospital dentist was wrong? Should we complain?" → Do not agree that the dentist was wrong, and do not encourage a complaint. Say: "I can't speak to exactly what the team saw on that day — there may have been clinical findings or resource factors I'm not aware of. What I can tell you is that based on what I'm seeing today, Liam's teeth are still restorable and I'd like to try a conservative approach first. If that changes, we'll reassess together." This is diplomatic, non-critical, and keeps the focus on Liam's current management.
  • Candidate agrees that extraction under GA is appropriate and begins planning referral without exploring conservative options → This is the most common wrong turn. The absence of spontaneous pain, absence of cavitation, and restorable status of the teeth all contraindicate immediate extraction. A strong candidate explicitly states: "Before we consider extraction, I want to make sure we've tried everything we can to save these teeth — they are Liam's permanent molars and we only get one set." Extraction without trialling conservative management is a mark-losing response.
✦ Complete Model Answer — Verbatim Script ►
STAGE 1: Introduction and History

"Hi Liam — I'm Dr [Name]. Thanks for coming in today. I hear your back teeth have been giving you some trouble. Can I ask you directly — when do they hurt? Is it all the time, or does something set it off?"

Address Liam first to build rapport and signal to the examiner that the child is included. Wait for Liam to confirm cold-triggered sensitivity and deny spontaneous or nocturnal pain. Then turn to Wei: "Mrs Chen, has Liam ever woken up at night with toothache, or complained of pain just sitting quietly?" Confirm the answer is no — this is a critical negative finding. Ask Wei: "Can I ask — did Liam have any significant illnesses in his first year or two of life? Anything that required a hospital stay?" When she mentions the bronchiolitis hospitalisation at eight months, acknowledge it: "Thank you — that's actually a really helpful piece of the puzzle, and I'll explain why in a moment."

STAGE 2: Diagnosis and Reassurance

"So, looking at the photographs and what you've told me, I can give you a clear diagnosis today. Liam has a condition called Molar Incisor Hypomineralisation — most people call it MIH. What that means in plain language is that the enamel — the hard outer layer of his back teeth and his front teeth — didn't harden up properly when it was forming during early childhood. It's a bit like concrete that didn't set quite right. The enamel is more porous, more sensitive, and more fragile than it should be. That's why cold air and cold drinks set it off."

Pause, then address Wei directly with eye contact: "I want to be really clear about something, because I know this kind of news can make parents wonder what they did wrong. MIH is not caused by diet, not caused by too much sugar, and not caused by how you brushed Liam's teeth. It is a developmental condition — it happens during a specific window when the teeth are mineralising, usually in the first three years of life. The bronchiolitis Liam had at eight months — that kind of significant illness during that window is associated with MIH in the research literature. You didn't cause this. This is not your fault." Allow a moment for this to land. Then distinguish from other conditions: "This is different from tooth decay, which is caused by bacteria and acid. It's different from fluorosis, which comes from too much fluoride. And it's different from a hereditary condition called amelogenesis imperfecta — we know it's not that because Liam's baby teeth are completely normal, which you can see in the photograph. MIH only affects the permanent teeth."

STAGE 3: Conservative Management Plan

"Now, here's the good news — there is a lot we can do before we even think about removing these teeth. I want to walk you through the plan step by step. First, we're going to tackle the sensitivity. I'll prescribe a high-strength fluoride toothpaste — it's called Neutrafluor 5000, and it has about ten times the fluoride of regular toothpaste. Used twice a day, it can really calm things down for Liam. We'll also apply a fluoride varnish here in the chair today. Second, for the surfaces of the molars that haven't broken down yet, we can place fissure sealants — a thin protective coating — to stop them from getting worse. Third, if there are any areas where the enamel has already chipped or broken away, we can restore those with a tooth-coloured filling material or a glass ionomer cement. And if a molar is significantly broken down, there's a very effective technique called the Hall technique, where we place a small stainless steel crown over the tooth — no drilling required — which protects it completely. That can be done right here in the chair."

Turn to Liam: "Liam, I also noticed you might be a bit self-conscious about the front teeth — the white-ish patches. We can look at options to improve how those look as you get older, once your teeth have fully come through. You're not stuck with them the way they are." This directly acknowledges Liam's embarrassment and earns marks for child engagement.

STAGE 4: Addressing the GA Recommendation, Prognosis, and Recall

"I want to address what the hospital team suggested, because I understand that's a big part of why you're here. Extraction under general anaesthesia is a legitimate option in some situations — for example, if a tooth has irreversible nerve damage, or if it simply can't be saved. But based on what I'm seeing today — no spontaneous pain, no pain at night, and teeth that are still restorable — I don't think we're at that point with Liam. The team at the hospital may have been working with different information, or different resources, and I'm not here to second-guess them. What I can tell you is that my recommendation today is to try conservative treatment first, because these are Liam's permanent molars and we want to keep them if we possibly can."

Address David directly: "You asked about cost — the treatments I've described range from relatively low-cost options like fluoride varnish and sealants through to restorations and crowns if needed. I'll give you a written treatment plan with estimates so there are no surprises. As for the long-term outlook — MIH teeth can deteriorate over time, which is why I want to see Liam back every three to six months so we can catch any changes early. Many children with MIH keep their molars into adulthood with good management. I won't promise that extraction will never be needed, but it is not where we are today, and we will make that decision together if it ever comes to that." Close by confirming the recall appointment and providing written instructions for the fluoride toothpaste.
